title: Doucette Scores Four, Oliver Nets Hat Trick in Thursday County Soccer
text:
The County Scoreboard: Doucette Scores Four, Hodgdon Boys Roll Thursday
Reece Doucette scored four times to lead Fort Kent past Caribou, while Wyatt Oliver recorded a hat trick as Hodgdon put eight goals on the board Thursday during another busy day of Aroostook County high school soccer.
Fort Fairfield and Central Aroostook split their boys and girls matchups, Ashland earned a nine-goal girls victory, and Foxcroft Academy shut out Presque Isle in boys action.
Here is a look at Thursday's County soccer results.
Girls Soccer
Fort Kent 5, Caribou 1
Reece Doucette turned in a four-goal performance to lead Fort Kent to a 5-1 victory over Caribou.
Laney Caron added Fort Kent's other goal.
Mallory Malmborg recorded two assists for the Lady Warriors, while Ellie Taggett and Lilly Bouchard each added a helper.
Caribou got on the board late in the second half when Quinn Corrigan scored from a Carly Levesque assist.
Ashland 9, Hodgdon 0
Ashland's offense erupted Thursday afternoon as the Hornets rolled to a 9-0 shutout victory over Hodgdon.
Fort Fairfield 3, Central Aroostook 1
Fort Fairfield picked up the girls half of Thursday's County matchup with a 3-1 victory over Central Aroostook.
The Panthers would answer later in the boys contest.
Boys Soccer
Hodgdon 8, MSSM 1
Hodgdon put together one of Thursday's biggest offensive performances in an 8-1 victory over MSSM.
Wyatt Oliver led the Hawks with a hat trick.
Noah Arbab, Finn Gardiner, Mason Polchies and Dawson Stamper also scored for Hodgdon, while Gardiner helped create plenty of offense with four assists.
Aiden Ciarleglio made 18 saves on 28 shots in the Hodgdon net.
Easton Allen scored the lone MSSM goal, while Nemeiah Kibler recorded eight saves on 26 shots.
Central Aroostook 3, Fort Fairfield 1
Central Aroostook answered Fort Fairfield's girls victory by earning a 3-1 win in the boys matchup.
The result gave the Panthers and Tigers a split of Thursday's varsity soccer contests.
Foxcroft Academy 2, Presque Isle 0
Foxcroft Academy kept Presque Isle off the scoreboard and earned a 2-0 Class B North victory over the Wildcats.
Postponements
Thursday's scheduled girls soccer game between Easton and Van Buren was postponed. The matchup has been rescheduled for October 17.
The Houlton-Ashland boys soccer game was also postponed. A makeup date was not immediately available.
Today's County Schedule
Friday, October 9
Girls Soccer
Katahdin vs. East Grand, 3:30 p.m.
Houlton vs. Central, 4 p.m.
Madawaska vs. Southern Aroostook, 4 p.m.
Wisdom vs. Penquis Valley, 4:30 p.m.
Van Buren vs. MSSM, 5 p.m.
Boys Soccer
Wisdom vs. Penquis Valley, 3 p.m.
Katahdin vs. East Grand, 3:30 p.m.
Van Buren vs. Mattanawcook Academy, 5 p.m.
Madawaska vs. Southern Aroostook, 6 p.m.
Football
Stearns/Schenck/Katahdin at Bucksport, 7 p.m.
Fort Kent at Washington Academy, 7 p.m.

title: InvestigateTV+: Wealthy ranchers profit from public lands
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — As family farms struggle to stay afloat, InvestigateTV+ found the benefits of a taxpayer-funded federal land program go to billionaires and big businesses.
Plus, we explore a rise in lithium-ion battery fires, and the unlikely material scientists are using to prevent them.
Then, we share the story of a couple with a cosmic coincidence.
Ranchers profit from public lands
The public lands grazing program, formalized in the 1930s to contain the rampant overgrazing that contributed to the Dust Bowl, has grown to serve operations including billionaire hobby ranchers, mining companies, utilities and large corporate outfits, providing benefits unimagined by its founding law.
President Donald Trump’s administration plans to make the program even more generous — pushing to open even more of the 240 million acres of Bureau of Land Management and Forest Service grazing land to livestock while reducing oversight of the environmental damage.
This, members of the administration contend, will further its goal of using public lands to fuel the economy and eliminate the national debt.
Battery breakthrough
Michigan State University researchers have discovered a way to make lithium-ion batteries safer using an unlikely material: wood waste.
The Butterfly Whisperer
The monarch butterfly, known for its vibrant orange and deep black hues, is dangerously close to disappearing forever.
Born on the same day, now getting married
It’s not out of the ordinary for high school sweethearts to get married. It’s also not too unusual that both of their moms also graduated from the same school.
So, what is so unusual about this love story?
“I was born on July 7th, 2006,” Lorene said.
“[I was born on] July 7th, 2006,” Brayden said.

title: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: Hidden hacker risks
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Your most sensitive information may not be sitting in a computer — it could be inside the printer down the hall. Chris Nakamoto finds why some offices may be leaving that data exposed.
Plus, a family loses their home as firefighters reported trouble getting water pressure.
Then, records raise questions about what city leaders knew.
Network Nightmares
Multifunction printers and copiers inside America’s police stations, hospitals, and schools aren’t just printing documents - they’re storing them. Every warrant, every patient record, every sealed court filing can be saved on an internal hard drive. When the lease ends and the vendor picks up the machine, that data sometimes goes with it. And in most cases, no one has ever asked what happens to it next.
A breach at a company handling government Medicaid data, what the Texas Attorney General called likely the largest data breach in U.S. history, exposed the personal information of more than 25 million Americans, a reminder of what’s at stake when vendors have unchecked access to sensitive records.
A confidential compliance audit obtained by our team documents exactly those gaps at a sheriff’s office, a charter school, and a medical practice. We talk to a public official who discovered the risk at his own agency and a cybersecurity expert who is sounding the alarm.
We investigate who is responsible for protecting your data and whether anyone actually is.
Water pressure problem
Cities across the country are facing pressure to grow—while aging water systems struggle to keep up. In Temple, Georgia, residents say a house fire exposed a dangerous problem: low water pressure as firefighters tried to protect homes.
Our Andy Pierrotti looks at what city leaders knew about the infrastructure concerns—and why they approved major commercial projects anyway.
911 staffing shortage
When someone calls 911, the person on the other end can make a life-changing difference in seconds. But emergency dispatch centers across the country are struggling to fill open positions—putting more pressure on the people who take those calls every day.
Reporter Ann Emmerich takes us inside one Michigan county dispatch center, where new technology is helping train the next generation of dispatchers—while veterans keep answering the call.
Cyber threats impacting food supply
Cyberattacks can do more than compromise personal information or interrupt a business. Experts warn a serious breach can ripple through the services communities rely on—including health care, water, and the food supply.
Reporter Susan Campbell in Arizona shows us how cyber experts are working to get ahead of those threats—and why everyday digital habits can be part of the defense.

title: Military aircraft catches fire during training exercise, officials say
text:
BLADEN COUNTY, N.C. (WECT/Gray News) - A military aircraft caught fire in North Carolina during a training operation on Thursday.
Military officials said an MV-22B Osprey based at Marine Corps Air Station New River was forced to make an emergency landing Thursday morning in the Bladen Lakes State Forest area.
The Osprey was conducting military training operations when it caught fire.
Four Marines were aboard the aircraft, and one was taken to a burn center for injuries, according to White Lake Fire Chief Dale Brennan.
The other three Marines were uninjured and were flown back to base.
Multiple fire crews worked to control the fire.
Brennan said the aircraft had about 6,000 pounds of jet fuel aboard.
The military flew in four officials from Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune to investigate.

title: Maine Hospital Association, others sue the federal government over changes to drug discount program
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Hospital Association, Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor and others filed a lawsuit in federal court in Portland on Friday contesting changes to a discount drug program that saves money for hospitals.
Also listed as plaintiffs are the American Hospital Association and hospitals in New York, Arkansas and North Dakota.
The federal 340B program requires drug companies to sell certain outpatient medications at discounted rates. The savings are reinvested into hospital charity care and other services, such as behavioral health.
The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Portland, contends that changes by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services would expand use of a rebate model that is projected to cost hospitals $1 billion annually. The federal government estimates the cost to hospitals would be $537 million, according to a news release from the plaintiffs on Friday.
“Maine hospitals cannot afford this,” Jeff Austin, president of the Maine Hospital Association, said in a statement in the news release. “They already operate with an average of less than two weeks cash-on-hand, so these significant new costs will jeopardize their ability to care for the most vulnerable patients in their communities and affect the affordability and accessibility of care across Maine.”
HHS officials said in a statement on Thursday, before the lawsuit was filed, that the program needs to change because it has “expanded beyond its original intent to help safety-net providers care for their underserved populations, resulting in large growth in participation and costs associated with the program.”
HHS did not respond to questions from the Portland Press Herald on Friday about the lawsuit.
The federal agency attempted similar revisions to the program in 2025, but federal courts halted the changes because HHS failed to account for the cost to hospitals, according to the plaintiffs’ news release.
“Shortly thereafter, HHS moved forward with a revised version” that was “even more expensive,” according to the news release.
Steve Walsh, president and CEO of the American Hospital Association, said in a statement on Friday that the rebate program would “impose massive new costs and divert resources that support care for millions of patients. We also proposed viable alternatives that would address concerns about transparency and program integrity.”
Molly Jenkins, a spokesperson for the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America trade group, said in a statement on Friday that the HHS changes will stop duplicate discounts and improve accountability. The trade group is not a party in the lawsuit.
“Big, tax-exempt hospitals have long exploited 340B to line their pockets, and now they are fighting commonsense steps to prevent duplicate discounts in the program,” Jenkins said.

title: Isaias could create higher fuel prices. Here’s why
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - Hurricane Isaias is forecast to miss the oil industry’s biggest hubs along the Gulf Coast but could still nudge fuel prices higher if it triggers power outages that shut down refineries for processing crude, according to industry experts.
An extended shutdown of refineries would put a crimp in fuel supplies that already have taken a hit from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Chevron’s facility in Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Vertex Energy’s refinery in Mobile, Alabama, which constitute 2.4% of the nation’s refining capacity, are at risk of flooding and power outages, said Andrew Lipow, a Houston-based oil analyst. Any problems could take the facilities offline at a time when diesel supplies are already low.
Isaias strengthened into a major hurricane Friday as it barreled toward the Gulf Coast, where final preparations were underway for potentially life-threatening storm surges and high winds.
If the storm moves through quickly and its impacts are minimal, refineries would continue to run at reduced capacity and prices for gasoline and diesel could rise just a few cents, said Carl Larry with the energy analysis firm Enverus. But if refineries such as Chevron’s shut down completely, it could take them weeks to recover and that could cause fuel prices to jump more significantly, Larry said.
“Major issues, like a power shutdown, and the prices will spike immediately. It’s possible a dollar,” he said. “Those diesel prices that already are above $6 could start approaching $7.”
Other experts said even if the refineries take a hit, the gas price impacts should be minimal.
“We’re talking about potentially under a million barrels a day, probably somewhere in the ballpark of 500,000 barrels a day, of refining capacity,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “That may have a small impact on gas prices, primarily in the Gulf Coast, but I don’t think it rises to a criteria that would impact gas prices nationally.”
Hurricane Isaias already has caused widespread shutdowns in offshore oil production across the region that provides about 15% of U.S. crude.
Personnel from 121 production platforms — about a third of the facilities in the Gulf — were evacuated, according to the federal Marine Minerals Administration.
Almost two-thirds of oil production was shut down, equal to almost 1.3 million barrels (54 million gallons) a day, the agency said. Chevron, BP and Shell were among companies that reported evacuating personnel and shutting platforms.
The storm’s impact on oil and gas prices so far is dwarfed by the effect of the conflict in the Middle East. And once the storm passes, workers will be able to return to platforms in the Gulf and quickly resume operations, barring significant damage.
“I would expect that the shut-in oil production will probably return pretty quickly within just a couple of days,” De Haan said.
Prices for Brent crude, the international standard, were above $104 a barrel Friday. That price has varied between $96 and nearly $110 over the last month driven by uncertainty over the war with Iran.

title: Friday’s high school football: Kennebunk beats Fryeburg with late TD
text:
Running back Bradley Farrell threw a 5-yard touchdown pass to quarterback Giovanni D’Elia with 7.5 seconds left and Blake Morris made his fifth extra point to give Kennebunk a 35-34 win over Fryeburg Academy in a Class B South football game Friday night in Fryeburg.
The Rams (5-1), who have won four straight, had the ball at the Fryeburg 5 after D’Elia completed a 15-yard pass along the sideline to Peter Landenberger. On first-and-goal, D’Elia went in motion and the snap went to running back Ethan White, who pitched it to Farrell. He found D’Elia open in the corner of the end zone.
Fryeburg (2-4) was in position to win after Marcus Sutton threw a 52-yard touchdown pass to Lars Bruhn with 10:58 left. The Rams had a chance to take the lead later in the fourth but fumbled into the Fryeburg end zone, where it was recovered by Conner Keaten.
Kennebunk force the Raiders to punt, however, and started the winning drive at its own 35 with 1:53 to go.
Fryeburg missed an extra point after Sutton’s 15-yard touchdown pass to Bruhn with 12.4 seconds left in the second quarter.
Kennebunk took a 7-0 lead in the first quarter on a 1-yard run by D’Elia. Fryeburg tied it on a 6-yard run by Buk Awe, before White gave the Rams the lead back on a 6-yard run.
Bruh scored on a 6-yard run to tie it again, but Kennebunk went up 21-14 when Farrell threw a 41-yard pass to Charlie Pentland and Morris made the extra point with 1:01 left in the first half.
Bruh then caught a 90-yard touchdown pass from Sutton to put the Raiders up 27-21 with 2:49 left in the third quarter. White’s 1-yard run on the first play of the fourth quarter put Kennebunk back in front.
PORTLAND 28, BANGOR 21: Alex Martin dove inside the right pylon for a 15-yard touchdown with 13.3 seconds remaining, giving the Bulldogs (5-1) a win over the Rams (2-3) in Portland.
Bangor erased a 21-7 halftime deficit, as Gavin Hughes caught his second and third touchdown passes of the night from Alex Tennett — 19 yards in the third quarter and 37 yards midway through the fourth.
On the ensuing drive, Portland passed up a chance to try a 36-yard field goal after Bangor timeout, and a fourth-down pass fell incomplete. The Rams were quickly forced to punt, however, and a 39-yard pass from Portland QB Reece Wildes to Quinn Derrig moved the ball to the Bangor 15. Martin scored on the next play, racing around right end.
Bangor opened the scoring in the first quarter on a 7-yard reception by Hughes, moments after he caught a short pass from Tennett and raced 70 yards before he was brought down at the 8.
Portland tied early in the second quarter on a 19-yard pass from Wildes to Derrig. Martin then put the Bulldogs ahead with a 1-yard run, and Portland extended its lead to 21-7 when Bailey Jordan picked off a tipped pass in the backfield and rumbled 55 yards for a touchdown.
SOUTH PORTLAND 21, MASSABESIC 18: Chase Lappin caught a 12-yard touchdown pass from Shea Healy with 1:40 left, and Ben Dube sealed it with an interception as the Red Riots (4-2) rallied to beat the Mustangs (4-2) in South Portland.
Massabesic, ranked eighth in the Varsity Maine poll, took the lead with 8:32 remaining in the fourth quarter when Gavin Jipson caught a 23-yard touchdown pass from Cooper Smith.
The Mustangs grabbed a 12-0 lead in the first quarter. Smith fumbled on his way to the end zone, but Nolan Pomerleau recovered it for a touchdown. Gipson then caught a 70-yard TD pass from Smith. Massabesic failed on both 2-point conversion attempts.
South Portland, ranked 10th in the Varsity Maine poll, stormed back with two touchdowns in the final 1:08 of the third quarter. Christopher Salamone scored on a 59-yard run, then the Red Riots recovered a fumble at the Massabesic 25. On the next play, Dube took a shovel pass from Healy into the end zone.
FALMOUTH 35, GORHAM 14: Owen Ross rushed for four consecutive touchdowns as the Navigators (3-3) defeated the Rams (1-5) in Gorham.
The hosts struck first on a 44-yard run by Isaac Vail. Ross answered with a 10-yard touchdown run later in the first quarter, then put Falmouth ahead for good with a 4-yard run in the second.
Ross broke it open with two TDs in the third quarter, from 70 and 14 yards.
After Vail scored on a 5-yard run for Gorham late in the third, Falmouth clinched the victory when Micah Derrig threw a 2-yard touchdown pass to Wes Howard in the fourth.
WINDHAM 34, EDWARD LITTLE 9: Windham quarterback Patrick Davenport finished with three rushing touchdowns and another on the ground, leading the Eagles (3-3) to a win over the Red Eddies (2-3) in Auburn.
Landon Wyman scored two touchdowns — one rushing, one receiving.
Windham led 7-0 after one quarter, thanks to a 12-yard scamper by Davenport.
Edward Little’s Alexander Gagnon kicked a 23-yard field goal at the beginning of the second quarter, but Wyman scored on a 15-yard reverse late in the quarter for a 14-3 halftime lead.
Davenport extended the margin in the third quarter with TD runs of 11 and 71 yards.
Evan Madigan scored EL’s only touchdown from 3 yards early in the fourth quarter. Wyman capped the scoring by catching a 60-yard pass from Davenport.
THORNTON ACADEMY 53, NOBLE 20: Brennan Tabor rushed for four touchdown, Noah Fullerton threw three TD passes, and the Golden Trojans (6-0) charged back from an early 14-0 deficit against the Knights (2-4) in North Berwick.
Tabor scored on runs of 50 and 2 yards in the second as Thornton, the unanimous No. 1 team in the Varsity Maine poll, produced four straight touchdowns for a 26-14 halftime lead. Fullerton started the surge with a 31-yard pass to Logan Leblanc and capped it with a 50-yard to Aiden Morin.
Tabor added TD runs of 7 and 35 yards in the second half. Leblanc caught a 23-yard scoring pass, and Caleb Parenteau scored the final touchdown on an 11-yard run.
Noble jumped in front when Mark LaPointe tossed a 5-yard TD pass to Griffin Ivey, then added to its lead when Caiden Barnes returned an interception 55 yards.
Ivey scored on a 6-yard run in the fourth quarter.
GREELY 35, OCEANSIDE 8: Luke Piper accounted for four touchdowns, including a 52-yard run on the first play from scrimmage, and the Rangers (5-1) downed the Mariners (3-3) in Cumberland.
Piper scored twice and threw touchdown passes to Rocky Axelsen (27 yards) and Jackson Justice (23 yards). He also had a 95-yard punt return negated by a penalty.
Greely led 28-0 at halftime. Noah Allen added a 1-yard TD run in the fourth quarter.
Oceanside averted a shutout when Everett Tolman threw a 19-yard touchdown pass to Carter Elliot midway through the fourth quarter.
OLD TOWN 60, LAKE REGION 20: Ethan Closson passed for four touchdowns, ran 69 yards for a score and returned a kickoff 91 yards as the Coyotes (5-1) beat the Lakers (1-5) in an eight-man game in Naples.
At one point during a 48-point second quarter, the teams scored on three consecutive plays. Closson and Brandon Schanz stared the sequence with a 23-yard touchdown pass — one of three TDs for Schanz. Jayden Cote returned the kickoff 83 yards as Lake Region closed to within 32-20, but Closson followed with his kickoff return.
Closson had two touchdown passes to Schanz, one to Tommy King and one to Alex Bean.
Lake Region quarterback Braydan Wilson scored on a 2-yard run and connected with Cote for a 7-yard touchdown.

title: ‘Battery breakthrough’: Researchers use new material to make lithium-ion batteries safer
text:
EAST LANSING, Mich. (InvestigateTV) - Michigan State University researchers have discovered a way to make lithium-ion batteries safer using an unlikely material: wood waste.
The breakthrough comes as fire officials call rechargeable lithium-ion batteries “ticking time bombs.” These batteries power nearly every device in American homes, from electric vehicles to children’s toys.
“Every home in America has them, whether it’s an electric vehicle, e-bikes, e-scooters, children’s toys, electronic devices, cordless power tools,” said John Newman, East Lansing interim fire chief. “We all have lithium-ion batteries and we charge and use those devices without any consideration.”
Scott Swanson and his family learned about battery dangers the hard way. Last summer, they survived two lithium-ion battery fires in two weeks that destroyed their car and damaged their Meridian Township home.
PREVIOUS COVERAGE:
The culprits were a pair of children’s headphones in the car and a backup battery charger in the home office.
“It just feels like a really random thing that just happens sometimes and I’m not sure there’s a whole lot you can do about it,” Swanson said.
His wife, Rose Tantrophol, said the experience left her shaken.
“After these two fires, I was, it took me a while to feel good using these devices,” Tantrophol said. “But I really don’t have a choice. I mean, all the work that I do is really powered by, you know, devices that have lithium-ion batteries.”
When lithium-ion batteries are damaged, overcharged or exposed to heat, they can start to overheat. That heat feeds on itself in a dangerous chain reaction called “thermal runaway,” which can cause the battery to release flammable gas, catch fire or explode.
Newman said East Lansing has seen at least two lithium-ion battery fires in the past year. One involved an electric scooter. Another destroyed half a house when a cordless power tool battery that was stored on a shelf in a utility room caught fire.
“It can reach temperatures of a thousand degrees in less than a minute and cause an entire room to go into flashover, which is when everything in the room reaches a high enough temperature to burn,” Newman said.
The fires cannot be extinguished with traditional fire extinguishers because the chemical reaction and heat are generated within the battery itself.
A “battery breakthrough”
Dr. Chengcheng Fang, an assistant professor at MSU’s College of Engineering, is leading research to make batteries safer using lignin, a wood product that acts like glue to hold wood together and make it strong.
“We are trying to enable, use different materials, more sustainable materials, from the wood, which is naturally abundant, to make the separator much robust,” Fang said.
Lignin is a waste product in the paper and biofuel industry. It’s cheap and doesn’t need any treatment to function in batteries.
“It has very unique chemical and thermal properties, but it’s underutilized,” Fang said.
Current rechargeable batteries contain plastic films to separate the electrodes, but the material can shrink and melt, causing the battery to short-circuit and explode. The wood waste is more pliable and withstands heat three times better than plastic.
Research shows promising results.
The research, published in the journal Advanced Materials, shows lignin-based batteries last 60% longer than traditional batteries.
“They are enhancing some of the stability of the battery materials to facilitate a lithium-ion transport. So we actually get the demonstration of improvement in the cycle life by 60%,” Fang said.
The technology is patent-pending through the MSU Innovation Center.
Safety recommendations
Fang recommends charging batteries to around 88% rather than 100% to maintain better battery performance longer. She also advises never leaving devices charging overnight, especially on beds or couches.
Lithium-ion batteries should not be thrown in the trash. Stores like Staples and Home Depot have free collection boxes for safe recycling.

title: Every 21 days, she depends on blood donations to survive a rare condition
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - Emily Rodgers is 12. She loves tumbling, the color pink and her best friend.
This seventh grader measures time in 21-day increments.
“I come here every three weeks, and this is my 194th blood transfusion,” Emily said.
Emily has beta thalassemia major, a rare blood disorder that prevents her body from making hemoglobin. Since she was an infant, doctors at Vanderbilt University Medical Center (VUMC) have given her transfusions.
“Her body can’t make blood like healthy people. And so since she was a baby, we’ve actually been giving her transfusions to keep her alive,” said Dr. Jennifer Andrews, Emily’s pediatric hematologist and medical director of the blood bank at VUMC.
Without those transfusions, Emily’s blood cannot carry enough oxygen. As she gets closer to the 21st day, she can feel it.
“Actually, the other day I had to go to the nurse’s office because I was trying to keep myself awake, and my body couldn’t stay awake any longer,” Emily said.
Hospital depends on daily blood donations
Andrews said it is important that the hospital always has blood available for Emily and other patients whose lives depend on immediate access to blood for routine care, emergency situations, surgical procedures, or cancer-related needs.
Most of the blood bags at the hospital come from the nonprofit Blood Assurance, donated by strangers who decided to show up.
“Literally, if you donate blood, it is the difference at Vanderbilt between life and death,” Andrews said.
The process requires constant replenishment, with someone donating every day of the week, 365 days a year.
Four-hour transfusion process
During her recent visit, Emily received two bags of blood, a process that takes about four hours just for the transfusion. She does not complain.
“We all just adore her. Wait till you talk to the nurses, they’re just one. She is one of their favorite patients,” Andrews said.
“This is my home away from home, because we come here so much. But the nurses are basically family, and they treat me so well. They all know me by name, so I just love them so much,” Emily said.
Andrews said there are now possible cures for Emily’s condition, including gene therapy or a stem cell transplant, but for now, transfusions are working best.
For Emily, one bag means three more weeks of life, cheer practice, and that dreaded vocabulary.
“Then when I have my blood, when I go back to school, I can just, like, retain stuff better,” Emily said.
When asked what she would say to someone who donates blood, Emily said, “I would just say thank you, because one bag of blood could save somebody’s life.”
In 21 days, she will be back in the chair, and that depends on who shows up next.
How to donate blood
To keep up with demand, Blood Assurance said the area needs more than 540 blood donors each day. That’s nearly 4,000 donors a week.
Right now, the supply of all blood types is just half of what doctors consider safe, and there is even less of a supply of platelets.
Donating blood is a safe, simple process that takes roughly an hour, with the actual draw lasting around 10 minutes. A single blood donation can save up to three lives, according to the Red Cross.
Blood Assurance operates donation centers throughout Middle Tennessee and accepts walk-ins and appointments.
To schedule an appointment or find a donation center location, visit bloodassurance.org, call 800-962-0628, or text BAGIVE to 999777.

title: Boston Tea Party participant honored with grave marker in Bowdoin
text:
Thomas Brimigion was 19 years old when he helped raid a British ship and toss a bunch of tea into Boston Harbor. This week, a new marker at his gravesite in Bowdoin, Maine, recognizes his role in one of the most consequential events of America’s founding.
The Boston Tea Party Ships and Museum and the organization Revolution 250 are on a mission to find the graves of all the known Boston Tea Party participants and place commemorative markers on them. Brimigion is buried at Woodlawn Cemetery in Bowdoin.
On Thursday, about 20 people gathered at Brimigion’s grave beneath fall foliage to watch the grave-marking ceremony. Many of these witnesses were from Bowdoin, and most said they were here because they were interested in history. Resident Deborah Sprague said she was also there to honor the efforts of a veteran.
The ceremony began with remarks from Evan O’Brien of the Boston Tea Party Ships and Museum, and Jonathan Lane of Revolution 250. Then an actor dressed in period costume — a military uniform and tricorn hat — placed the marker on the grave.
O’Brien said it is challenging to determine who was involved in the Boston Tea Party. He said the event seldom spoken about after the fact, because participants feared retaliation — many even swore an oath that they would not reveal the names of those present. Often, the children of participants were the ones to reveal their identities. In the case of Brimigion, his participation was noted in his obituary, corroborated by Sun Journal articles from 1887 and 1889 written by his children. O’Brien said this evidence is comparable to that of most Tea Party participants.
O’Brien said that Brimigion was a farmer, born in Philadelphia in 1754. Historical records don’t show why he ended up in Boston, but there is substantial evidence that he served in the military during the Revolutionary War. His obituary also stated that he was present at the battles of Bunker Hill, as well as Lexington and Concord, said O’Brien.
It’s also unclear what brought Brimigion north, but in 1785, he married Ruth Jellison. They had at least five children, all born in Bowdoin, said O’Brien.
The Boston Tea Party was a response to the Tea Act of 1773, which gave the British East India Tea Company a monopoly on tea sales in the colonies. Because tea was taxed, the move sparked outrage. When three ships carrying the company’s tea arrived in Boston Harbor, members of the patriot organization the Sons of Liberty snuck aboard and threw over 92,000 pounds of the tea into the harbor. This action was one of many triggers for the American Revolution.
O’Brien said most Boston Tea Party participants were tradesmen — cobblers, coopers and sailors. He said the participants’ lack of elite status, combined with the secrecy surrounding the event, has often meant their efforts have not been recognized.
“Thomas Brimigion is just as important to our region’s history as the names we’re most familiar with — the Paul Reveres, the John Adams, the John Hancocks,” O’Brien said. “And he is worthy of our recognition.”
The project aims to place a marker for every known Boston Tea Party participant. So far, they’ve done over 130 grave-marking ceremonies across 10 states and two European countries.
Town Clerk, Historical Society member and cemetery trustee Melanie Page was at the ceremony. She said she grew up on the road that goes by the cemetery, and still lives there — this is true of six of her nine siblings, four of whom were present at the ceremony.
Page has been mowing the cemetery since she was 15 years old. When she received a call about the grave-marking ceremony for Brimigion, she said she already knew exactly where he was buried.
O’Brien said that the story of the Boston Tea Party has great relevance to the present day, because it illustrates the importance of civic engagement, and the idea that “ordinary people” can make real change.
“We can take inspiration from these people who risked everything for an ideal, and were willing to sacrifice their lives, if need be, for something they deemed worthy of that great sacrifice,” said O’Brien.

title: Throwback Thursday
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Apple cider is easy to find this time of year, but some folks choose to make it old school. It’s the focus of this week’s Throwback Thursday with Brian Bouchard.
These days, making apple cider is usually left to machines, but there was a time when the process took a little more muscle. In this week’s Throwback Thursday, we dial the time machine back to 1985 where WAGM Reporter Laurie Quinlivan captured the Martin family as they tried their hand at making cider the old-fashioned way.
The Martin family was busy making cider today the old-fashioned way. They borrowed the Science Center’s apple press, vintage 1800.
“They bring their own apples and their own containers and they learn how to use a hand cider press, kind of rekindling the lost art of cider making. This is a type of procedure that is all hand done, whereas cider that’s produced today from different commercial industries would be making it by machines and this is kind of the beauty of this program because it’s all done by hand.”
“So what are you doing?”
“Oh, just pressing apples to make some cider right now.”
“Is it hard?”
“Well, sort of. Well, half and half.”
It looked pretty tough to me. These guys are busy grinding the apples, then the mash is pressed and out comes cider. One bushel of apples makes about two to three gallons.
“Isn’t it too cold to be doing this today?”
“Yeah, I think so.”
Grandpa Martin thought so too. He came to supervise, but being older and wiser, he stayed in the truck.
Laurie Quinlivan, Newsline 8.

title: Military aircraft catches fire during training exercise, officials say

BLADEN COUNTY, N.C. (WECT/Gray News) - A military aircraft caught fire in North Carolina during a training operation on Thursday.
Military officials said an MV-22B Osprey based at Marine Corps Air Station New River was forced to make an emergency landing Thursday morning in the Bladen Lakes State Forest area.
The Osprey was conducting military training operations when it caught fire.
Four Marines were aboard the aircraft, and one was taken to a burn center for injuries, according to White Lake Fire Chief Dale Brennan.
The other three Marines were uninjured and were flown back to base.
Multiple fire crews worked to control the fire.
Brennan said the aircraft had about 6,000 pounds of jet fuel aboard.
The military flew in four officials from Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune to investigate.

title: York County Food Hub opens in Biddeford
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
York County Food Hub, a food security nonprofit, leased 7,310 square feet of industrial space at 20 Pomerleau St. in Biddeford with the goal of opening the county’s first regional food security hub.
Greg Boulos and Samantha Marinko of the Boulos Co. represented the tenant. Joseph Atwood of the Dunham Group represented the landlord, Spur Park LLC.
The organization is committed to strengthening the local emergency food system, with a mission to increase food storage capacity and expand local food rescue to better support York County’s network of food pantries and community meal program, which feed nearly 27,000 people.
“Rising food insecurity in York County is a crisis that no single pantry or organization can solve alone,” said Alex Gramling, the hub’s president. “We envision the hub as a community resource providing sorely needed infrastructure for anti-hunger programs, while building a more connected and resilient food security network throughout York County.”
Across York County, there are over 50 food pantries and meal programs operating independently. The capacity of each is limited by storage constraints, staffing and transportation challenges and inconsistent access to food, according to the organization.
At the same time, nutritious food is often wasted — not because it isn’t needed, but because there’s no coordinated way to store it, move it or share it efficiently.
The goal of the centralized food security hub is to expand capacity of local pantries, promote food rescue and encourage regional food sharing.
Site search
Boulos conducted a broad search for the best location that met the hub’s needs: loading docks, commercial kitchen space and equipment, open dry storage and existing cold storage. The Pomerleau Street building checked the boxes plus offered direct access to Interstate 95, an advantage for an operation built around moving food to pantries and meal programs spread across the county.
“Our location and building wish list had four or five must-haves,” said Gramling. “The Biddeford location checked all of the boxes. It was a great find.”
The hub opened Sept. 1. In conjunction with the launch, the organization embarked on a two-year major gift and capacity building campaign called Feed York County, with a goal of raising $3.5 million over two years.
Financial support funds the infrastructure required to source more and healthier foods for pantries, expand food rescue efforts and deliver anti-hunger services.
The concept began in 2024, when leaders of food programs in Kennebunk and Biddeford began discussions around a food hub as a way to expand regional storage capacity and encourage sharing of perishable and surplus food. A steering committee was formed and held monthly meetings to develop the idea and research comparable models.

title: How a Maine Attorney General's Office leak could impact open criminal cases
text:
How a Maine Attorney General's Office leak could impact open criminal cases
A supervisor in the Maine Attorney General’s Office accidentally emailed a document containing confidential information about ongoing criminal cases to dozens of email addresses
How a Maine Attorney General's Office leak could impact open criminal cases
A supervisor in the Maine Attorney General’s Office accidentally emailed a document containing confidential information about ongoing criminal cases to dozens of email addresses
A supervisor in the Maine Attorney General’s Office accidentally emailed a document containing confidential information about ongoing criminal cases to dozens of email addresses, including media organizations such as Maine's Total Coverage.
The 45-page document, addressed to Attorney General Aaron Frey and Criminal Division attorneys and staff, includes summaries and updates about dozens of cases. While much of the information is available in public court records, the document also mentions primary suspects who have not been arrested or publicly named.
Law enforcement expert Noel March told 8 Investigates that releasing such information could jeopardize a police investigation.
"Tipping our hand too early can prompt a prime suspect or even a person of interest to 'cover their tracks' by fleeing the jurisdiction, destroying possible evidence or tampering with potential witnesses," March said.
Other case summaries include graphic details that have not been released publicly and evidence the Attorney General’s office expects to be excluded from its case. A criminal defense attorney said that information could make it difficult to seat an impartial jury.
On Friday, a spokesperson for the Maine Attorney General’s Office wrote that it worked quickly to minimize negative impacts.
"Most immediate was to notify families of victims to prepare them for the possibility that some of the inadvertent recipients might choose to publish this information," the spokesperson said.
8 Investigates also asked whether the office has taken disciplinary action, updated its policies to prevent future leaks, or notified the criminal defense attorneys involved. The office had not responded.

title: What you need to know about South Portland’s public safety referendum
text:
South Portland residents will vote in November on whether to fund a new police and fire station with an $88.6 million bond.
What exactly is on the ballot?
If approved, the proposed bond would provide up to $44.35 million for a new police station to be built on the vacant Walgreens parcel at Cash Corner that the city acquired this year. It would also allocate $44.25 million for a new central fire station to be built on the footprint of the existing central police and fire station.
The city plans to issue the bonds in two phases, starting with the construction of the police station and then the fire station.
Why is the city pursuing new public safety facilities?
Both the city’s police and fire station are aging and falling into disrepair.
The police station, built in 1967, and the fire station, built in 1955, do not meet current codes and have significant mechanical, electrical and plumbing issues. The HVAC systems are past their lifespan, and the evidence room and emergency operation center in the basement regularly flood.
Police Chief Dan Ahern and Fire Chief Phil Selberg have both said the current stations don’t meet modern public safety needs and standards, and their departments are in desperate need of new homes.
There are often technology issues with body cameras docking, and the station doesn’t have the infrastructure to link data from the cruisers, according to Sgt. Shane Stephenson.
And modern law enforcement lockers are twice the size of the ones in the station, Stephenson said, another important thing that a new station could include.
How much would it cost?
A median-priced single-family home valued at $514,000 would expect to pay an additional $255 in property taxes for fiscal year 2028. When the second phase is financed, property taxes for that household would increase an additional $244, making the total estimated tax impact about $500 for fiscal year 2030.
The average annual tax impact for the duration of the bond — from fiscal year 2028 through 2059 — would be about $345, or $28 per month.
Individual households can estimate the projected tax impact using a calculator on the city’s website at southportland.gov.
I’m still making up my mind on which way to vote. What should I do?
The city is hosting a series of events this month to educate the public about this referendum question.
Every Wednesday at 5:30 p.m., residents can take a guided tour of the police and fire stations, which is also an opportunity to chat with staff members about the infrastructure needs.
The city is also hosting a coffee chat on Thursday Oct. 15 at 11 a.m. at Verbena Cafe. It’s a casual opportunity for residents to ask questions of the public safety buildings project team.
On Saturday, Oct. 31, Selberg and Craig Piper, with SMRT Architects and Engineers, will be available at the library from 10 a.m. to noon to answer questions about the proposed new buildings.
If you want more information, consult the city’s public safety buildings resource page.

title: Katie Zacharia selected as next White House press secretary
text:
Katie Zacharia selected as next White House press secretary
President Donald Trump has selected Katie Zacharia, a conservative commentator who worked briefly at the Department of Homeland Security, as his new press secretary, multiple White House officials told CNN.
Related video above: Karoline Leavitt leaving White House
Trump in recent days called a number of his close allies and advisers, including former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to seek their opinion of Zacharia, a person familiar with the discussions said. And the president sought Leavitt’s counsel before making a final decision and offering Zacharia the position, they said.
CNN has reached out to Zacharia, who was in the Oval Office with Trump earlier Friday morning, according to a person familiar.
Zacharia's selection came about quickly. As of last week, she was not being considered for the role, another person familiar said.
Throughout the search to replace Leavitt, the White House struggled with higher-profile names, several of whom had previously criticized Trump. On multiple occasions, senior officials had narrowed down the list, only to find that candidates had said something negative about the president, disqualifying them from the position, according a White House official.
Zacharia's been a frequent guest on Fox, Newsmax and CNN. And according to her LinkedIn profile, she’s served as a senior communications adviser at the Trump Media and Technology Group and Truth Social since June, which followed a two-month stint as a senior official at the Department of Homeland Security.
Zacharia, who has young children and lives in California, commuted back and forth to Washington when she was filling in at DHS. At the time, she told a friend the commute was not sustainable, according to a source familiar with the matter.
Zacharia has also served as a legal adviser for Fix California, a conservative group founded by Trump ally Richard Grenell.
She first came to Washington as an intern for the Republican National Committee during the George W. Bush administration in 2006.

title: Natalie Merchant opens her ‘Cabinet of Wonder’ to local kids with free performance
text:
BAR HARBOR, Maine (WABI) - Natalie Merchant’s schedule of shows in Maine began with a performance for her youngest fans.
Ahead of headlining shows in Bangor and Bar Harbor this weekend, the singer-songwriter spent Friday morning performing as Mother Goose at Bar Harbor’s 1932 Criterion Theatre.
Merchant sang songs from “Cabinet of Wonder,” an early childhood music education resource she created after volunteering in a Head Start classroom.
“Cabinet of Wonder is an enrichment program that I developed with the Chicago Symphony and the Chicago Children’s Theater and the National Head Start Association,” explains Merchant. “It’s all based on traditional nursery rhymes, and it’s about music and movement and poetry and beauty. The show is just an opportunity for children who’ve been learning the program.”
Cabinet of Wonder is a free online program that introduces children to orchestral instruments, genres of music and more through videos and companion teaching guides.
The Criterion Theatre invited area schoolchildren and pre-K-aged children to attend Merchant’s performance free of charge.
“We are presenting this production to kids in the moment when they are the most permeable. And I think Natalie’s message is one of kindness, it’s one of connection, and it’s one of community,” Criterion Theatre’s Executive Director Courtney Sale describes. “So, we want to continue that as they grow and mature in their lives, so it’s important for us to meet them where they are now.”
Merchant says the free screening plays into Cabinet of Wonder’s mission: making the arts accessible at an early age.
“I think that access to the arts is sometimes, well, always limited by economics. So, to provide everything for free was the mission, and something of quality,” Merchant details. “I think that a lot of the educational and entertainment products that are produced for children in this age range, the three to six range, I find they lack a sensitivity to children’s emotional sophistication.”
During Friday’s performance, Merchant taught the children call-and-response rhymes and stepped off the stage to join them in the audience.
After the performance, the children met Mother Goose in person. They left the theater overflowing with photos, hugs and smiles.
“Music is a wonderful community builder. I mean, it’s great for regulating emotion and finding ways to express yourself individually, but also find your place in the group and feel like you belong,” reflects Merchant. “You want to engender that feeling in a child at a very young age so that they crave that for the rest of their lives. They want to be a joiner. They want to be a part of something larger than themselves.”
The Criterion Theatre will host a screening of the one-hour “Cabinet of Wonder” film, which features music videos from the program. Merchant will introduce the film and participate in a Q&A afterward.
Merchant will also perform live at the theater Sunday and Monday nights. She is scheduled to perform Saturday night at the Gracie Theater at Husson University.

title: Affordability crunch takes us back to 1974
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
An unpopular president; surging oil prices causing significant inflation; and an upcoming midterm election.
No, I’m not talking about 2026, but 1974. President Gerald Ford had just pardoned Richard Nixon in September, a decision unpopular with much of the American public who had Watergate still fresh in their minds. Oil prices surged in October 1973 after the OPEC oil embargo, which led to inflation running above 10%. The 1974 midterm elections brought a Democratic landslide victory, with the party winning 49 seats in the House and four in the Senate. Will 2026 be, quoting Yogi Berra, “like déjà vu all over again”?
Current indications suggest it may well be. Many Republican held seats in Congress appear to be up for grabs, even those in some “deep red” districts. Why? An unpopular president, Donald Trump, whose action and inaction is felt to have led to the highest inflation in years.
The question for Democrats, should they prevail Nov. 3, is: How will they govern? The temptation for many Democrats will be to hold endless congressional investigations into President Trump and his appointees for possible corrupt dealings. While I agree that there are valid concerns, is this what voters really want Congress to focus on? From everything I read, I think not.
One word comes up again and again: affordability. Democrats’ failure to address this concern may well lead to problems in the 2028 election. An out-of-touch party is soon an out-of-office party.
Samuel Rosenthal
Portland

title: Maine’s tallest mountain is greening faster than others in New England
text:
You have a registered email address and password on pressherald.com, but we are unable to locate a paid subscription attached to these credentials. Please verify your current subsription or subscribe.
High above the tree line on Katahdin, where biting winds and sub-zero winters hold the rocky landscape in a frozen grip for much of the year, the mountaintop is turning noticeably greener.
Four decades worth of satellite observations reveal that alpine tundra across the Northeast are undergoing widespread vegetation expansion, not just at the advancing tree line but well above it, too. The new growth is transforming rare, high-elevation ecosystems once thought buffered from rapid change.
And Katahdin, Maine’s highest peak at 5,268 feet, is greening faster than any otherNew England summit. Vegetation has increased there by 7.9% from 1984 to 2024, according to a recent study in the journal Ecosphere by scientists at Dartmouth College and the Appalachian Mountain Club.
“Greening isn’t necessarily good or bad, but it’s happening,” said Dartmouth College geographer Jonathan Chipman. “The reason may be a concern. It might mean rare plants are being crowded out by aggressive interlopers that can now live in areas when they couldn’t survive in the past.”
The study used thousands of NASA images to track greening on 35 alpine summits from New York to Quebec. Co-author Jordon Tourville provided field perspective as an alpine ecologist with the Appalachian Mountain Club to explore the potential reasons for the greening.
As a geographer, Chipman said he is often asked to work with other researchers to analyze or map data in their fields of study. As an avid climber, he has long wanted to use his skills to research what is happening at the tops of New England’s summits.
Advertisement
“I grew up in New England,” Chipman said. “I climbed Katahdin when I was a kid. I climbed Mount Washington too many times to count. A lot of people, including me, are very concerned about the future of these precious little sky islands.”
For Mainers who hike Baxter State Park or look up at the Longfellow Mountains, the findings suggest that environmental pressures are actively reshaping the summits of New England that are so isolated that naturalists call them “sky islands.”
These summits support fragile plant communities, such as cushion plants and arctic sedges, that survived the last ice age and thrive in conditions too harsh for trees. Some animals are found only in these areas, such as the Katahdin Arctic butterfly, or breed only here, like the American Pipit.
There are only about 50 square miles of alpine ecosystem in the Northeast, Tourville said.
“That makes it the rarest ecosystem type in the region,” Tourville said. “We suspect that because they’re so small, and because the plants there are already existing really at the edge of what plants can withstand, that any amount of change will destroy this system.”
Across Maine’s six studied alpine summits — Katahdin and North Brother in Baxter State Park and Sugarloaf, Bigelow, Saddleback and Mount Abraham in the Longfellow Range — greenness expanded over the four-decade study period, but not at the same pace.
Advertisement
While Katahdin clocked a 7.9% greening trend, the average greening rate of all the peaks studied was 5.2%. Records show a 5.8% increase at North Brother at Baxter, a 5% increase at Sugarloaf, a 4.8% increase at Saddleback and a 4.7% increase at mounts Bigelow and Abraham.
Ground mapping on Katahdin shows that greening is hitting alpine sedge meadows particularly hard. The windswept lawns of Carex bigelowii appear to be undergoing invasion by the woody dwarf heath shrubs that thrive in warmer temperatures and higher nutrient levels.
Baxter State Park officials acknowledged that the shift is a serious concern. They have been collaborating with other researchers tomap Katahdin’s alpine plant boundaries, monitor trail corridors and track shrub encroachment into sedge meadows, according to park manager Kevin Adam and natural resources director Nava Tabak.
Strict “stay-on-trail” policies, supported by visitor quotas, summit stewards, signage and string fencing are the park’s most vital tools to help the fragile root systems withstand atmospheric stresses, Adam and Tabak said.
But researchers suspect warming temperatures are hardly the only environmental force at play.
The greening trend accelerated through the 1980s and 1990s before flattening around 2005 to 2009, a trajectory that aligns with ecological recovery following federal Clean Air Act regulations that curbed acid rain and sulfur pollution across New England peaks.
Advertisement
“A lot of people focus on temperature, but I think we missed the nitrogen signal,” Tourville said. “The soils in the alpine zone are extremely nitrogen poor. For decades, we essentially dumped nitrogen fertilizer up there. That probably had a pretty profound impact.”
Topography and severe weather also shape the landscape. Sheltered east- and north-facing slopes across the region’s peaks showed rapid greening, but exposed ridges seem to have resisted plant expansion.
For park stewards, the 40-year satellite record provides a crucial baseline to guide future conservation. But it also highlights a fundamental disagreement over how to manage wilderness in an era of global climate change.
Tourville argued that traditional, hands-off wilderness management may no longer be enough.
“My message to them was, it might be time in the near future to rethink that stance in terms of hands-off, no management up in the park, especially in the alpine zone, because climate change does not respect park boundaries,” Tourville said. “And climate change is not hands-off.”
Baxter State Park leadership firmly defended the park’s “Forever Wild” mandate, arguing direct human intervention is not the answer.
“Our response to stressors from climate extremes, as illustrated by this research, is to continue to minimize human impacts so that the natural communities and species have the best chance to adapt,” Adam and Tabak said in an emailed statement. “Though our approach to stewardship of the Park’s alpine areas is unique, these areas may over time serve as an experimental control that can be compared with other northeastern alpine areas that are more directly managed.”
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 9 to include comments from Baxter State Park officials.

title: Mills administration allocates funding to keep PCHC afloat
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Penobscot Community Health Care is set to receive additional funding to avoid bankruptcy and continue serving nearly 50,000 Mainers, with just over two weeks remaining before a funding deadline.
In a letter sent to Lori Dwyer, PCHC’s president and CEO, Mills said the state will make available $2.8 million in Rural Health Transformation Funds to help preserve access to health care for the Maine people served by PCHC.
In late August, PCHC said it needed roughly $3 million within 30 to 60 days to make it through what it called an “immediate crisis.” Oct. 24 would mark 60 days from that announcement.
Over the last few weeks, PCHC has laid off employees, frozen pay, closed offices and cut services amid other cost-saving measures.
Last month, Mills met with PCHC leadership to learn why the federally qualified health center faces a unique crisis compared to others in Maine.
Her office said at the time the administration was exploring potential short-term state funding to keep operations afloat until the Legislature reconvenes.
Mills’ letter to PCHC
Mills full letter to PCHC:
“I am writing with respect to your request on behalf of Penobscot Community Health Care (PCHC) for additional financial support from the State of Maine given the dire fiscal status of the organization. Specifically, you have requested $7 million from the State — $3 million to protect operations through December 2026 and up to $4 million of additional support over the following eight months in order to effectuate a 12-month turnaround plan for PCHC. Your “Turnaround Strategy and Financial Plan” document outlines this $3 million request as $2.71 million of cumulative operating shortfall in September through December 2026 and a 10 percent contingency request.
“I remain deeply concerned about the extent to which the organization finds itself overextended and underfunded due to a lack of appropriate planning and management. This situation is particularly troubling given the significant investments the State has made in federally qualified health care centers (FQHCs), including PCHC, over the last several years. MaineCare’s total spending on FQHC services has increased by nearly 50 percent over the last three years, totaling over $100 million in calendar year 2025. Regarding PCHC in particular, in those same three years, PCHC’s MaineCare encounter rate has reached $283.89 — an increase of 45 percent.
“It is also important to note that in these times of increased costs and a federal regulatory environment that is creating severe financial and operating pressures, there are a number of health care facilities — hospitals, nursing facilities, behavioral health providers, and other FQHCs — also struggling.
“However, with PCHC being the state’s largest FQHC, serving approximately 50,000 patients, I am committed to doing whatever possible to preserve needed services to the people, particularly the most vulnerable, who currently access care at PCHC. To that end, the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) worked intently to identify funding and increase allotments under the Rural Health Transformation Program (RHTP) to PCHC to support expenses related to Electronic Medical Records (EMR) and for the transition to Alternative Payment Models (APM). Specifically, DHHS has identified an additional $2.8 million beyond the original allotments of $316,324 for APM and $543,276 for EMR. This amount will be paid out monthly in accordance with invoices for expenses from PCHC and in amounts of no more than $1.219 million each in October, November, and December. To the extent additional funding is still sought, that request will need to be made in the next legislative session.
“This request came at a time when my options as Governor are limited. With the Legislature not in session, there is simply no way to appropriate funding without their approval. My Administration’s previous statements about limitations on the use of RHTP still stand. Further, it took great effort to identify funding within RHTP that would not negatively impact other providers, many of whom have made difficult decisions to maintain their operations in the current environment. However, under these exceptional circumstances, and in order to preserve access to services on behalf of tens of thousands of Maine people, my Administration worked collaboratively with the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to arrive at this approach. These funds must be used for APM and EMR approved costs, and not for general capital outside of these initiatives.
“Additionally, given this increase in funding to PCHC, and the extremely tentative financial status of the organization, certain reporting will be required as defined in Rider A of the contracts. It is critical to have a full picture of how and why PCHC got into this position and how the management and Board will make changes to restore stability and internal and external trust. The RHTP team will be in touch about next steps toward establishing the contracts with PCHC.
“My top priority has been and remains that the people served by PCHC continue to have access to the health care and other services they need. I appreciate this opportunity to work with PCHC as it pursues long-term sustainability.”
PCHC releases statement
PCHC released this statement Thursday evening:
“We are in receipt of incredible news from Governor Mills and her leadership team. They have identified an additional $2.8 million investment in Penobscot Community Health Care through the Rural Health Transformation Program. These funds will help ensure the future of PCHC and our critical work for the people of Maine. Specifically, they will increase the support for our transition earlier this year to a new electronic medical records system and to alternative payment models. With this investment, PCHC is no longer pursuing an imminent Chapter 11 filing. That is a significant step forward. But the next 12 months will be critical, and we have a great deal of work ahead to put PCHC on solid financial ground.
“On behalf of everyone at Penobscot Community Health Care, I want to thank Governor Mills for her leadership and her commitment to the patients we serve. The Governor, her team, and the Department of Health and Human Services worked tirelessly to find a path forward. They were able to help us efficiently and in a targeted manner while requiring accountability on our part. We know these are public dollars, and we take that very seriously. We look forward to working closely with DHHS, providing regular updates, and being fully accountable for how these funds are used.
“Our work is not finished. In fact, we have asked the following trusted and very experienced Mainers and community health center experts to serve on a Turnaround Advisory Council to help us recover and reinvent how we approach financial strategy so that we can best meet our mission. Among them are Dr. Guy Hudson, CEO, Northern Light Health; Troy Trejo, CEO, Encompass Health Rehabilitation Hospital of Bangor; and Dr. Margaret Flinter, Senior Vice President & Clinical Director, Community Health Center, Inc.
“As we look ahead, I must take a moment to acknowledge PCHC’S incredible staff. Through all of this, their work has not stopped. Every day, they deliver extraordinary care to roughly 50,000 Mainers, many of whom have nowhere else to turn. They should be incredibly proud of themselves for keeping their eye on their mission. I know I am.
“I also want to thank the legislators from across Maine who signed on in support of PCHC and our patients. They stood with us when it mattered. title: Severe turbulence injures at least 8 aboard Avianca flight, forcing emergency landing in Miami
text:
(AP) - At least eight people were injured when an Avianca flight encountered severe turbulence and had to make an emergency landing in Miami early Friday.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said that one person was rushed to a trauma center with severe injuries while seven others were taken to area hospitals in ambulances after the plane landed shortly after 3 a.m. Friday. The airline said nine people — three crew members and six passengers — were affected by the turbulence and needed to be taken to a medical facility.
The Federal Aviation Administration said the Avianca flight was en route from Medellin, Colombia, to John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York when the Airbus A320 had to divert to Miami.
Avianca said the passengers who were not hurt were flown to New York on Friday morning. The airline said “the safety of our customers and employees is, and will remain, the foundation of our operations.”
Serious injuries from in-flight turbulence are rare, but scientists say they may be becoming more common as climate change alters the jet stream. The International Air Transport Association said the number of reports it received about turbulence incidents surged more than 25% last year.
Last summer, 24 people were taken to the hospital after a Delta Air Lines flight encountered turbulence caused by a thunderstorm over Wyoming. The National Transportation Safety Board has said passengers and flight attendants were thrown into the ceiling with enough force to crack some of the interior panels before tossing them back to the floor and then up again. The seat belt sign was off at the time so some passengers were up and drinks were being served when that plane hit the turbulence.
At least 20 passengers have filed lawsuits against Delta over that incident, arguing the airline could have avoided the severe weather.
The FAA recommends that passengers stay buckled whenever possible to protect against unexpected turbulence.

title: ‘Pretty Little Liars’ actor Keegan Allen says he was beaten, robbed at gunpoint in Los Angeles
text:
(Gray News) - “Pretty Little Liars” actor Keegan Allen has shared a video of his bloodied face after allegedly being robbed at gunpoint outside a Los Angeles grocery store.
The actor said he was in a Santa Monica Boulevard parking lot in West Hollywood on Thursday, Oct. 8, when two armed men allegedly stole his watch and threatened to “kill” him, according to an Instagram video.
“I was just robbed of my watch outside of Laurel Supply,” the 37-year-old said in the video.
“These two dudes hit me in the head and pointed a gun at me with a knife and then took off,” he recalled. “They had masks on [and] they took my watch.”
Security footage of the alleged robbery included in the video appeared to show the men with Allen, who seemed to be putting items into his truck in the Laurel Supply parking lot, with one apparently hitting him in the head multiple times with his gun.
The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department confirmed to People that it responded to a call about a robbery in the 8400 block of Santa Monica Boulevard at approximately 9:05 p.m, ABC News reported.
The department did not name Allen in the statement.
Allen continued in the video, saying, “West Hollywood is not safe anymore.”
In further comments, Allen noted he suspected he was “def concussed” and added, “Robbed at gunpoint and knifepoint by two young men that threatened to KILL me over my watch and would have! God said no tonight. My life for a watch.”
