title: Why an Aroostook town’s mural represents more than art
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
An artist’s vision and inspiration from North Carolina turned into a massive community effort that leaders hope will entice people to visit Van Buren.
Leah Cook, a community artist living in Grand Isle, wanted to delve into mural painting. Van Buren Town Manager Luke Dyer was looking for a mural artist. Together, they spearheaded a new 20-panel project to highlight the town’s best features.
Just a few years ago, Van Buren was in the midst of a two-decade decline. Its 1950s boom era had dwindled, along with the population and regional economy, led in part by the 1994 closure of nearby Loring Air Force Base. But a renaissance sparked in 2022, shortly after Dyer came to town. Now, a new mural marks how a determined Maine community can turn sweat into a reboot.
“We are now seeing that work translate into real economic activity. New small businesses have opened in health and wellness, food, retail and vintage collectibles, bringing people downtown and giving them new reasons to visit Van Buren,” Dyer said. “From a management perspective, the most encouraging change is that we are building momentum.”
Each successful project and new business added brings more investment and builds confidence in the town, he said.
Town leaders started looking at successful communities around the country to see what had worked for them, Dyer said. They knew a town in decline couldn’t rebuild quickly, so they planned for slow, sustainable growth.
Within the past four years, Van Buren has netted arts grants, rejoined the state’s Main Street program, signed on with the Maine Department of Transportation’s Village Partnership Initiative for downtown improvement and started a community garden. It’s joined forces with Philadelphia’s Drexel University on an art installation and a business incubator.
It’s seen businesses grow, such as the Northern Maine Kolache Co., which recently expanded and added a drive-thru, and new ventures open, including a taco eatery and charcuterie board crafter.
Cook thought a mural would give residents something to mark how far the town has come, and give visitors a reason to explore. The resulting collage of 20 panels depicts town landmarks, installed on the wall of a building owned by Robert Pelletier and Leland Bonenfant.
“The whole project fits into the larger story of Van Buren’s revitalization, celebrating the positive things that are right here and right now in the community,” Cook said. “There’s a lot of momentum going on internally in Van Buren from folks dedicated and determined to change things for the better. Hopefully this wall-sized display of cheerful art highlighting 20 great features of the town can be a part of that.”
The panels look like giant postage stamps, an idea inspired both by a similar mural in North Carolina and by midcoast Maine artist Peter Walls, who has used shaped panels in his work, Cook said.
She created the first set of 11 panels along with the Van Buren Revitalization Association, Dyer and Maine Creates, a pilot program of the Maine Arts Commission that supports art in rural and underserved communities. The Town Council approved funding to create those 11 pieces, and a grant allowed Cook to expand the project to include nine more panels.
Her goal was to create them in simple designs and colors that were easy to see from a distance. The subjects are on single fields of color with “no painterly brushstrokes,” she said.
Cook and Dyer chose the first 11 locations featured on the panels, but she opened it up to the community for the second set. More than 93 people responded, she said.
More than 330 residents voted to choose the final nine designs. Then work began. The town held community paint days when anyone could help Cook paint. More than 30 from ages 2 to 87 participated, including four generations of the LaJoie family, whose farm is featured on one of the panels.
Nearly 14 community organizations and businesses supported the team through various phases of the project, Cook said.
The town celebrated the unveiling of the completed exterior wall last weekend. Panels include St. Bruno/St. Remi Church, town trails, the library, the sledding hill, the town bandstand, the Acadian Village, historic Gayety Theater and the bridge to Canada.
People have been “positive and excited” about the finished project in person and on social media, Cook said. People have said it’s impressive, colorful and amazing, and many people living away want to see it in person.
Studies have shown public art carries an economic boost, with people spending 1.5 times more in areas near an art walk or trail.
“As soon as you get people out of cars and on foot, there’s a positive benefit to businesses in that area,” Cook said.
But just as important as the art is the message of positivity in a town rebuilding its own story, she added.
Dyer agrees the mural is more than a new art piece.
“We want the mural to do more than beautify a wall. We want it to send a message that Van Buren is proud of who we are, where we come from and where we are going,” he said. “Sometimes revitalization starts with something as simple as giving people a reason to stop instead of driving through.”

title: Cheverus golf repeats as Class A champion
text:
VASSALBORO — With its possession of the Class A state championship at stake, the Cheverus golf team dusted off a familiar gameplan — and even a familiar speech.
Sam Sirois shot even-par 72 for medalist honors, and Keane McGrath and Joe Stratman were among eight players who tied for second with 76s as the Stags successfully defended their state title Friday, shooting 304 to hold off Falmouth (314), Messalonskee (324), Thornton Academy (328), South Portland and Gorham (340 each) at Natanis Golf Course.
Falmouth’s Dante Iannetta, Gorham’s Charlie Sands, Messalonskee’s Greyson Dooley, Bangor’s Jacoby Harvey, Mt. Ararat’s Caleb Greenleaf and Oxford Hills’ Sawyer Poland joined Stratman and McGrath at 4 over.
Lila Dailey of Camden Hills and Jacquelin Sirois of Cheverus shot 97 to share the title in the girls division.
“It feels great, again,” said Sirois, who tied for second individually last year. “Going into this, we didn’t really think we had a shot, so I’m really glad we got it done.”
Such doubt was reasonable after Falmouth rolled to the SMAA championship at the same Tomahawk course on Monday, shooting 304 to beat the Stags by nine shots while getting scores under 80 from five players.
Cheverus coach Billy Goodman told his players there was no way to beat the Navigators if they were that hot, a similar angle he used when addressing the girls basketball team in February before the Stags turned a 19-point deficit into a 63-61 overtime victory against Hampden Academy in the Class A final.
“I told my team going back to Portland, it was kind of like the halftime speech for my basketball team,” he said. “‘If they shoot like that again, they’re going to win.’ But we just had a really good week of practice. A lot of kids focused and did better than Monday.”
The Stags’ roadmap to victory looked like last year’s, when it had the medalist in Mick Madden and a second-place finisher in Sirois. This time, Sirois jumped to the top spot, hitting 11 greens in regulation and carding four birdies, one coming when he rolled in a 20-foot putt on the fourth hole.
“Teamwise, I knew we all had to play well,” Sirois said. “I didn’t want to let my teammates down.”
The rest of the scores fell in line. McGrath, who was third at the SMAAs with a 74, was excellent again, notching 13 pars and an eagle on the par-5 third. Stratman, who had an 81 on Monday, improved by five shots. Ray, who shot 87 on Monday, improved by seven strokes. Garrett Thees went from a 90 to an 84.
“I guess it was Cheverus’ day today. We did really well, everyone kind of came together,” McGrath said. “Everyone was very focused this morning, it was a different mood than the SMAA.”
Stratman didn’t play in the state championship last year. He was front and center this time.
“I fed off the pressure, it’s one of the greatest things to do,” said Stratman, who carded four birdies. “I shot 106 in the qualifiers last year. It really pushed me to work harder.”
Iannetta tied for second for the second straight year. He was joined by Alex Novick (78), Griffin Jacobsen (78) and Anthony Graceffa (82) among the Falmouth scorers.
“I hit the ball pretty solid all day, it’s just putts didn’t fall,” Iannetta said. “Golf’s a game that happens on one day. When a tournament’s only one day long, anything can happen. It’s tough. … I believe we could have gone lower than 304, but it just wasn’t today. It’s unfortunate.”
Messalonskee’s Dooley, the first-place finisher at the KVAC qualifier, notched four birdies, one of which stabilized his round. It came two holes after a triple bogey on the par 3 10th.
“It was basically putting today that saved me,” he said. “It was mostly just a mental game out there, and having to just stay through it the rest of the round.”

title: Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay wins the Nobel Peace Prize for work on international law
text:
Navanethem 'Navi' Pillay wins the Nobel Peace Prize for work on international law
Former U.N. human rights chief Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, a judge on the International Court of Justice, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday in Oslo, Norway.
Related video above: In 2022, Russian journalist auctions Nobel Peace Prize medal for Ukrainian children
The South African-born Pillay, 85 years old, was recognized for her efforts to promote peace and international law, said Jørgen Watne Frydnes, Chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
“At a time when the number of wars and conflicts is rising, and when judges and institutions of international law are under political attack, the Nobel Committee wishes to issue a reminder that the ability to resolve conflicts without force or violence is dependent on the international rule of law,” the committee wrote in a news release.
“An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world.”
Efforts to reach Pillay by phone were not immediately successful.
The award is often considered the most prestigious honor on the planet.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo received nominations for 287 candidates for this year’s prize, and just over a quarter of them are organizations. Experts say the committee typically focuses on the durability of peace, the promotion of international fraternity and the quiet work of institutions that strengthen those goals.
Last year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado won the Nobel Peace Prize for her struggle to achieve a democratic transition in the South American nation, winning recognition as a woman “who keeps the flame of democracy burning amid a growing darkness.”
Machado gave Trump her Nobel medal shortly after the United States ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro. But it was largely a symbolic gesture: the Nobel Committee has said the honor itself cannot be transferred.
Nominations can be made by a select group of people and organizations, including heads of state or politicians serving at a national level, university professors, directors of foreign policy institutes, past Nobel Prize recipients and members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee itself.
Four of this year's Nobels were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.
Canadian poet, essayist and translator Anne Carson won the literature prize Thursday for “bold and inventive” works that fuse the classical and the modern and blur the boundaries of poetry and prose.
The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.
Peace prize hits its 125th anniversary
This year marks the 125th anniversary of the peace prize, which so far has gone to 112 individuals and 28 separate institutions since its inception in 1901. The Red Cross has won three times and the U.N. refugee agency twice.
The prize has gone unawarded on 19 occasions, most of them during the world wars. In 1948, the year Mahatma Gandhi was assassinated, no prize was awarded; he had been nominated 12 times and never won.
In 1939, a Swedish member of parliament nominated Adolf Hitler, then withdrew the nomination, saying it was never meant seriously.

title: Maine to get $38M in heat assistance early from federal government
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The federal government will soon release about $38 million in heating assistance funding to Maine, Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins announced Friday.
The release of Home Energy Assistance Program funds, which usually happens in late October or early November, would be one of the earliest in recent memory. Collins and independent U.S. Sen. Angus King were among 31 senators to sign a letter last month to the Department of Health and Human Services asking for the expedited release of funding.
The HEAP funding, paid through MaineHousing to heating suppliers as a supplement for low-income households’ winter costs, comes as heating oil prices in Maine hover around a record high, set last month at more than $6 per gallon.
Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, stands to gain most from the release of these funds. About 45,000 people received LIHEAP help last year, MaineHousing said.
“I am pleased that these funds are being released to help Mainers afford to heat their homes this winter without having to choose between staying warm and paying for other basic necessities,” Collins said in a news release.
To kickstart the heating oil program, MaineHousing announced this week that it would use about $4 million left over from last winter for about 4,400 vulnerable households across the state.
But that $4 million, combined with the $38 million coming from the federal government this month, will not go as far this winter.
The average HEAP award was set by MaineHousing this summer at about $700, communications director Scott Thistle said Thursday. But after oil costs skyrocketed at the end of the summer and into the fall, the value of that help has fallen significantly, he said.
Last winter, about $23 million in HEAP funding went to heating oil vendors. This year, that number is expected to be about $31 million, Thistle said, including the $4 million in carryover funds.
While about $36.7 million of the federal funding set to be released will go to MaineHousing, about $1.4 million will go to tribal nations: $457,771 will go to the Pleasant Point Passamaquoddy Tribe, $316,098 will go to the Indian Township Passamaquoddy Tribe, $303,530 will go to the Penobscot Nation, and $165,665 each will go to the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians and the Mi’kmaq Nation.
Collins, in the Friday news release, claimed credit for the early release of the funds and touted her work as Senate Appropriations Committee chair to increase HEAP funding nationwide by $20 million. She said she recently spoke with Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, about the importance of releasing the funds.
Last week, though, Gov. Janet Mills wrote to Maine’s congressional delegation demanding that the federal government allocate additional money for heating assistance, saying the war in Iran has made heating oil unaffordable for many and that the assistance won’t go as far as families expect.
Heating oil has become a campaign issue, too, less than a month from Election Day. Collins and her Democratic challenger, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, have blamed each other for high costs. Gubernatorial candidates have also called for more heating assistance.
Applications for heating assistance are open now. Maine residents hoping to apply for HEAP funding or looking for other assistance can contact their local community action program or call 211. The state also releases an annual Winter Heating Guide with cost-saving resources for households of all incomes.

title: Inflatable pumpkin tumbles into traffic, forces driver to swerve
text:
DUBUQUE, Iowa (KCRG/Gray News) — A giant inflatable pumpkin got loose and tumbled through downtown Dubuque on Tuesday afternoon, bumping into parked cars and forcing an SUV to swerve out of the way on Main Street.
“This is not AI-generated. This actually truly happened, and I was the car involved in this,” Pam McCarron said. “I think I was pretty calm, but you don’t see that every day.”
Driver describes the moment
McCarron said she did not expect the inflatable pumpkin to come flying toward her in the wind on her way to a work meeting on Tuesday.
“Is it gonna hit me? Is it gonna hit my car? Is it gonna like go over my car?” McCarron said. “It’s big enough that I couldn’t see around it to know if there was anything on the other side, when [the inflatable] was on the other side of the street. I was like, I don’t know if there’s a car coming.”
Police react to traffic camera video
Dubuque Police Lt. Luke Bock first saw the traffic camera video on Facebook on Thursday morning.
“Immediately I was like, hey, that looks like one of our traffic cameras,” Bock said. “Then I was like, boy, that’s a big pumpkin, so obviously the police officer side of me was like, we don’t really need those things bouncing down the roadway.”
Bock said he can laugh at the video because there was no oncoming traffic at the time.
“It’s entertaining. Like it’s funny to watch it, but you just, I guess, a lot of times you think about what could have happened, what if?” Bock said.
Bock said incidents like this can happen when decorations are not properly grounded.
“We would just ask that you follow the manufacturer’s instructions,” said Bock. “Secure them down to your yard, so that something like this doesn’t happen and we don’t see somebody swerve and potentially get in a crash or obstruct our highways, or hit somebody that’s walking down the roadway.”
A Dubuque homeowner’s experience
Jennifer Edwards said large inflatables can be difficult to stake down.
She is hosting her eighth year of month-long trick-or-treating on Fridays and Saturdays from 5 to 9 p.m. at her home, 3750 Mount Alpine Street, barring bad weather. Her decorations do not include inflatables, despite using them in previous years.
“Safety is a big, big, big concern. Inflatables are really hard to keep staked. They’re really hard to get them to level out and balance them, so we took it out,” Edwards said.
McCarron said the flying pumpkin should serve as a reminder to make sure decorations are stable. She said she now has one question.
“What’s going to pop up today? Like, you know, what’s it going to be, like, you know, Frankenstein or something?” McCarron said.

title: 11-year-old with rare form of muscular dystrophy receives Star Wars-themed wheelchair costume
text:
11-year-old with rare form of muscular dystrophy receives Star Wars-themed wheelchair costume
An 11-year-old boy living with a rare form of muscular dystrophy received a gift from a galaxy far, far away this Halloween season.
Dash Stanton knew something special was hidden beneath a blue sheet Sunday morning at the Minnesota Fire Museum, WCCO reported.
"I feel like this is going to be very, very cool," Dash Stanton said before the reveal.
A self-described Star Wars fan who recently finished watching every movie in the franchise, Dash Stanton eagerly waited to see what had been built for him.
When the cover finally came off, he was greeted by a custom N-1 Starfighter complete with a Grogu, better known as Baby Yoda, figure. The spacecraft attaches to his power wheelchair, turning it into a ride fit for a Jedi.
The creation came from Magic Wheelchair, an Oregon-based nonprofit that designs and builds custom wheelchair costumes at no cost to families.
"It was way cooler than I thought it would be," Dash Stanton said. "Honestly, it's very, very sick."
For his parents, the moment was especially meaningful.
Want more content like this? Subscribe to our News We Love newsletter here.
About a decade ago, they noticed their son was not meeting the physical milestones typical for most children his age.
"After neurologists and physical therapy and all this, we ended up finding out that he had SMA, which is something we had never even heard of before," said his mother, Amanda Stanton.
SMA, or spinal muscular atrophy, is a rare neuromuscular disorder that affects muscle movement.
Despite the diagnosis, Dash Stanton has remained active. He participates in musical theater and excels in power soccer, a sport designed for athletes who use power wheelchairs.
"We've hit a much more stable point. He's doing really well," Amanda Stanton said.
As for Dash Stanton, his immediate goal is a little less ambitious than piloting a starfighter across the galaxy.
He just wants to be the coolest kid out trick-or-treating this Halloween.

title: ‘It sounds so realistic’ — Woman loses $45,000 in jury-duty scam
text:
(Aging Untold) — Missing jury duty can come with real consequences, including fines and jail time.
Scammers have taken advantage of that real fear, often posing as law enforcement to scare victims into handing over personal information, money or both.
In Arizona, one woman hopes that sharing her experience will help warn others after she lost $45,000.
How the scam works
Kristine received a phone call in the early afternoon on July 7 from a man impersonating a police officer. He said that she missed jury duty.
“It sounds so realistic,” said Kristine, who is being identified only by her first name.
“According to them, if I paid the citations which they were trying to give me — failure to appear in court and contempt of court — if I paid those, then the judge would dismiss my case,” she said.
Kristine said she was instructed to go meet with a bond agent and pay up to $16,000 in citations, or she would go to jail.
They told her she also had to pay bond to stay out of jail until she could meet with the judge.
“I said, ‘This is insane, you told me this is what I owe,’ and they said, ‘It’s not a big deal, you’ll get it back. Just go to the bank,’” Kristine said.
Kristine was directed to stop at four different banks to collect $35,000 to pay the so-called bond. At that point, she said she knew something was wrong.
“They followed my car. They tracked all the mileage. I had to keep telling them where I was and how much I’d gone,” she said.
Arizona ranks high for impostor scams
Kristine is not the only person this has happened to.
According to the Federal Trade Commission, Arizona is ranked as the fourth-worst state for so-called impostor scams, losing an estimated $766 million to fraudulent phone calls and payment apps.
Kristine hopes her story can help prevent others from falling victim to these scams and losing thousands of dollars.
“Just follow your gut. Because if I would have done that, it would’ve ended way sooner,” she said.

title: Maine's Jessica Meir Is Back on Earth After Eight Months in Space
text:
Maine’s Jessica Meir Is Back on Earth After Eight Months in Space
After eight months in space, one of Maine’s own is back on Earth with another mission under her belt.
👇 KEEP READING: 23 Famous People You Probably Didn't Know Were Born In Maine 👇
NASA astronaut Jessica Meir and her Crew-12 crewmates returned to Earth on Oct. 8 after nearly eight months aboard the International Space Station.
Meir, Jack Hathaway, Sophie Adenot, and Andrey Fedyaev splashed down aboard SpaceX’s Dragon Freedom spacecraft in the Pacific Ocean off Los Angeles at 11:34 a.m. EDT.
The Crew-12 astronauts spent hundreds of hours conducting scientific research aboard the International Space Station, including studies on stem cells, nutrition, and how spaceflight affects blood flow.
They also tested ways to produce IV fluids in space, supporting research aimed at improving health on Earth and preparing astronauts for future missions to the Moon and Mars.
Meir is a NASA astronaut and marine biologist who was born and raised in Caribou and graduated from Caribou High School.
Selected for astronaut training in 2013, she helped conduct the first all-female spacewalk in 2019 and later commanded NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission to the International Space Station.
And there you have it! Meir has completed another major spaceflight mission, adding nearly eight more months aboard the International Space Station to her career.

During a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, this week, Trump announced that Special Envoy Steve Witkoff is engaged in indirect negotiations with Iranian officials.
"He's working on the Iran deal and doing very well," Trump said. "I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop."
With less than a month until the midterm elections, the Iran war remains a concern for many voters. According to a recent Pew Research survey, 65% of respondents disapprove of how Trump is handling U.S. military action in Iran, while 33% approve.

title: Federal government auditing Maine’s Medicaid program
text:
The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has launched a program integrity audit of Maine’s Medicaid program, federal officials confirmed.
The agency said in a statement Friday that the audit will examine MaineCare’s “oversight operations and processes in high-risk areas.”
“The audit will assess the state’s safeguards against fraud, waste, and abuse, including how it identifies risks, refers suspected fraud, and addresses improper payments,” according to the agency’s statement.
CMS oversees the Medicaid program, which is operated by the states with federal oversight. Medicaid programs, which include insurance and healthcare services for lower-income people, are funded with a blend of federal and state dollars.
The statement offered that no further details, including what specific programs the agency is auditing, will be available while the audit is ongoing.
Maine was in the crosshairs of federal regulators earlier this year, when a U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General audit found the state had made at least $45.6 million in improper payments. The audit, which examined support services for autistic children in 2023, said Maine failed to document services correctly and did not complete “post-payment reviews.”
At the time, Maine officials responded by noting that the Office of Inspector General’s audit did not include accusations of fraud.
In response to CMS announcing that the agency is conducting an audit, Lindsay Hammes, a Maine Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson, said in a statement on Friday that “protecting MaineCare from fraud and abuse is essential to making sure that health care remains available for the people and families who rely on it and that taxpayer dollars are invested responsibly.”
Hammes said the state DHHS has its own program integrity unit to monitor MaineCare programs for fraud. When needed, the Office of the Maine Attorney General will investigate potential crimes, she said.
In late 2025, Maine DHHS suspended payments to Portland-based Gateway Community Services and continues to investigate the provider for accusations of falsifying billing records. Gateway provides Medicaid services for people with disabilities. Gateway officials have denied the allegations.

title: Matt Dunlap understands how we in Maine feel
text:
I recently attended a town hall meeting in Auburn to listen to Matt Dunlap, candidate for Congress. I didn’t know Dunlap. I know Paul LePage, his opponent.
When Dunlap said “government feels more vengeful,” I nodded and noticed others around me doing the same. Government does feel vengeful, right now, especially to hardworking families.
If elected, I believe LePage would reinforce the GOP call to prolong the war and permit the Medicare cuts proposed in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. A LePage victory would result in an echo chamber for MAGA policies. LePage has described himself as “a big fan” of data centers. The values shared by most Americans suggest strong opposition to the war in Iran, tariffs and the development of data centers.
Before becoming Maine’s state auditor, Matt Dunlap served as secretary of state. His values align more closely with working people I know. His experience in both offices demonstrates a balanced approach to public service.
Dunlap’s message to Mainers reflects my priorities, including greater affordability for childcare, lower taxes for working families and reduced tariffs. Mainers also face rising energy costs at the pump and for home heating. As energy demand grows, we will need solutions that reduce our reliance on fossil fuels. I am voting for Matt Dunlap. I hope you will join me in electing new lawmakers who recognize what real Mainers want.
Marianne O’Connor
Lisbon Falls

title: Hockey defenseman Isa Parekh finds early success after transferring to UMaine
text:
ORONO, Maine — Isa Parekh needed a change of scenery.
The University of Maine’s transfer defenseman, after making the Central Collegiate Hockey Association All-Rookie Team in 2024-25 at Bemidji State, suffered a concussion eight games into the campaign last season and wound up underperforming.
“I lost a lot of my confidence. I struggled. I didn’t play too well, especially compared to my freshman year when I had a great year,” said junior Parekh, who decided to enter the NCAA transfer portal.
“It was a hard decision. I loved all my friends there. They’re all great guys,” Parekh said. “But I wasn’t going to get anything done over there, so I wanted to see if anyone else wanted me.”
UMaine head coach Ben Barr called Parekh, who’s making the most of the opportunity. Parekh enters this weekend’s home series against sixth-ranked Quinnipiac tied for the team scoring lead with three points on a goal and two assists, which he tallied in last weekend’s split at Holy Cross.
He is also tied for the team lead in plus-minus at plus-2. Players receive a plus-one if they are on the ice when their team scores an even-strength or shorthanded goal and a minus-one if the opponent scores one.
It only took him 4:54 to register his first point in a Black Bear uniform as he nicely set up a five-on-three power play goal by Robert Morris transfer Tanner Klimpke in last Friday night’s 4-1 victory. Just 2:39 later, he again fed Klimpke, this time for a five-on-four power play goal.
“I came out hot and matched my point total from last year in the first period. It was good to get that monkey off my back,” said Parekh, who had only two assists in 27 games last season after notching three goals and 15 assists in 35 games his freshman year.
In the 3-2 overtime loss Saturday night, he scored UMaine’s first of two goals in a span of 49 seconds with 3:27 remaining as the Black Bears erased a 2-0 deficit.
“On Saturday, it took me about a period to get into the game. I wasn’t really moving my feet,” Parekh said. “But I thought I played really well in the second and third periods. I had an opportunity to go to the net and get a chance and I scored.”
He said the hockey environment has been much different than it was at Bemidji State in Minnesota.
“Here, you get a lot of coaching, a lot of individual video work and a lot of work on individual skills, which I didn’t get there,” Parekh said. “It’s really good here. Everything has been amazing.”
“He’s a good player,” Barr said. “If he stays healthy, he’s going to keep getting better and better every day. He’s very good on the power play. He sees the ice really well and makes the right decisions. It’s nice to have a guy like him who can distribute the puck. He can also shoot it when he gets a chance.”
“He’s a helluva player,” UMaine graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler said. “He is a great puck mover, and he can skate. He can walk the blue line, get the puck to the hole and distribute up top. He had a great weekend on both sides of the puck.”
“I take pride in my skating,” said Parekh, who was a preseason All-CCHA selection in both the coaches and media polls before the 2025-26 season. “I can move east to west pretty well with my edges.”
After last year, Parekh isn’t putting any expectations on himself.
“I just want to go out every game and be myself,” said the 6-foot, 163-pound Parekh. “I want to get back to the hockey I played my freshman year. I want to be more confident. I’ve been working on stuff, and I feel more confident already.”
Klimpke called him a “real good player.”
“He is smooth and skilled. and he is good at finding those passing lanes and moving the puck. We developed a chemistry over the summer, and I hope we can continue to connect on plays like that throughout the year,” Klimpke said.
When he showed up to the optional six-week practice sessions in July in Orono, Parekh was “really nervous but really excited to see what this is. And it is a step above up from where I was. Not player-wise but just in everything we do.”
He said their intense practices prepare them well for games, and he loves the area.
Golf is another of his passions, and he has enjoyed teeing it up across the state, with teammate Charlie Russell being one of his primary playing partners.
He has heard a lot about playing at Alfond Arena, and the energized game night atmosphere. That was one of the reasons he chose UMaine over other schools.
“I’ve heard a lot of stories about playing at Alfond and the fans and how ridiculous it gets,” Parekh said. “I have a buddy at Holy Cross, Owain Johnston, and he said playing there was the most insane thing he has ever done in his life.”

title: Officials release names in fatal Lovell crash Thursday
text:
Authorities Friday released the names of the two people involved in a head-on crash in Lovell Thursday that killed a young Lovell woman and sent an Andover man to the hospital.
Police said Ivy Thomson, 25, died when her 2015 Ford Flex collided head-on with a 2003 Chevrolet Silverado driven by Mark Farrington, 66, in the 600 block of Main Street shortly before noon.
According to authorities, Thomson died at the scene. Farrington was taken to Maine Medical Center in Portland with life-threatening injuries. No information on his condition was offered Friday.
There were no passengers.
The crash was being investigated by the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office, which was assisted by Fryeburg police, Fryeburg rescue, and crews from the Lovell Fire Department.
The investigation is ongoing, authorities said Friday, and may take time to complete. They are asking anyone with information on the crash to contact the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office at (207) 743-9554.

title: Chrysler issues massive recall for 265,000 vehicles over steering risk
text:
Chrysler issues massive recall for 265,000 vehicles over steering risk
Chrysler is recalling more than 265,000 vehicles due to steering issues.
The company announced that 265,512 Ram vehicles have been recalled because water may enter the electric power steering wiring harness and disable steering assist, according to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration notice.
Related video above | How to stay ahead of recalls
The recall covers certain 2022–2026 Ram ProMaster 1500, 2500 and 3500 vehicles, as well as 2024–2026 Ram 3500 Electric vehicles.
A loss of power steering assist can make a vehicle harder to steer, increasing the risk of a crash.
Dealers will inspect the wiring harness and replace it and the electric power steering gear if needed, at no cost to owners, according to the recall notice.
Interim letters warning owners of the safety risk are expected to be mailed starting Nov. 17, 2026.
Chrysler says it will send additional letters when a final remedy is available.
Owners can contact Chrysler at 800-853-1403 and refer to recall number 92D. The affected vehicles’ identification numbers became searchable on NHTSA.gov on October 6, 2026.

title: Maine to get $38M in heat assistance early from federal government
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The federal government will soon release about $38 million in heating assistance funding to Maine, Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins announced Friday.
The release of Home Energy Assistance Program funds, which usually happens in late October or early November, would be one of the earliest in recent memory. Collins and independent U.S. Sen. Angus King were among 31 senators to sign a letter last month to the Department of Health and Human Services asking for the expedited release of funding.
The HEAP funding, paid through MaineHousing to heating suppliers as a supplement for low-income households’ winter costs, comes as heating oil prices in Maine hover around a record high, set last month at more than $6 per gallon.
Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, stands to gain most from the release of these funds. About 45,000 people received LIHEAP help last year, MaineHousing said.
“I am pleased that these funds are being released to help Mainers afford to heat their homes this winter without having to choose between staying warm and paying for other basic necessities,” Collins said in a news release.
To kickstart the heating oil program, MaineHousing announced this week that it would use about $4 million left over from last winter for about 4,400 vulnerable households across the state.
But that $4 million, combined with the $38 million coming from the federal government this month, will not go as far this winter.
The average HEAP award was set by MaineHousing this summer at about $700, communications director Scott Thistle said Thursday. But after oil costs skyrocketed at the end of the summer and into the fall, the value of that help has fallen significantly, he said.
Last winter, about $23 million in HEAP funding went to heating oil vendors. This year, that number is expected to be about $31 million, Thistle said, including the $4 million in carryover funds.
While about $36.7 million of the federal funding set to be released will go to MaineHousing, about $1.4 million will go to tribal nations: $457,771 will go to the Pleasant Point Passamaquoddy Tribe, $316,098 will go to the Indian Township Passamaquoddy Tribe, $303,530 will go to the Penobscot Nation, and $165,665 each will go to the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians and the Mi’kmaq Nation.
Collins, in the Friday news release, claimed credit for the early release of the funds and touted her work as Senate Appropriations Committee chair to increase HEAP funding nationwide by $20 million. She said she recently spoke with Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, about the importance of releasing the funds.
Last week, though, Gov. Janet Mills wrote to Maine’s congressional delegation demanding that the federal government allocate additional money for heating assistance, saying the war in Iran has made heating oil unaffordable for many and that the assistance won’t go as far as families expect.
Heating oil has become a campaign issue, too, less than a month from Election Day. Collins and her Democratic challenger, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, have blamed each other for high costs. Gubernatorial candidates have also called for more heating assistance.
Applications for heating assistance are open now. Maine residents hoping to apply for HEAP funding or looking for other assistance can contact their local community action program or call 211. The state also releases an annual Winter Heating Guide with cost-saving resources for households of all incomes.

title: Beloved pizza brand discontinued after 89-year run
text:
Beloved pizza brand discontinued after 89-year run
Beloved pizza brand discontinued after 89-year run
A decades-old frozen food aisle favorite will disappear from store shelves for good.
Celeste frozen pizza, a staple of home freezers for generations, will be discontinued and phased out of production, Conagra Brands announced in its latest earnings report.
Conagra, which owns brands like Slim Jim, Orville Redenbacher's and Duke’s, announced it has stopped production as it trims its product lineup to focus on brands with stronger growth prospects.
Related video above | The world's largest pizza record attempt
Celeste’s story began in 1937, when Celeste “Mama” Lizio and her husband opened a Chicago restaurant serving generous plates of pasta.
About 25 years later, the couple began selling frozen pizzas and other foods to restaurants.
Quaker Oats bought the business in 1969, but Mama Celeste stayed on as its spokeswoman, bringing her face — and her promise of “abbondanza,” or abundance — to the box.
It became one of the top-selling brands in the '70s and '80s, and a staple of frozen food aisles across the nation for decades to come.
Fans may still find one last personal-size pizza in the freezer, but the clock is ticking on this little slice of Chicago history.

title: Death Notice: Anna Van Der Heide Freeman
Memorial bench displaced during 2024 hurricane washes ashore 1,000 miles away
text:
DUNEDIN, Fla. (Bay News 9) — A memorial bench swept away from a Dunedin, Florida, causeway during Hurricane Helene two years ago has been found more than 1,000 miles away on the coast of Bermuda, according to the family of the man it honors.
The bench was placed along the causeway in 2018 by the aunt of Amanda Sadiku to honor her father, Medhat “Mike” Sadiku, who died in 2012. Amanda Sadiku was in seventh grade at the time of his death.
“My dad always said, ‘It’ll be alright.’ So we thought that would be perfect to put on the bench. It’ll be alright. My dad said that for absolutely everything,” Amanda Sadiku said.
Amanda Sadiku is the oldest of three daughters and remembers her father as a human calculator and the smartest man she has known.
Bench ripped away in 2024
The bench remained on the causeway until 2024, when Hurricane Helene tore it from the concrete slab where it had been fixed.
“There was a few benches that were out here in the water, but every time they pulled out benches, none of them were his. So his bench was marked missing,” Amanda Sadiku said.
The bench stayed missing until Sept. 18 of this year, when a woman in Bermuda contacted the family saying she had found it along the coast there.
“You know, at first we didn’t believe it. We were like, hold on. So we asked her for some pictures and everything else, and it was true, and we all were laughing and crying and everything else, and we were like, ‘So our dad just wanted to go to Bermuda,’” Amanda Sadiku said.
Meteorologist explains possible path
Spectrum Bay News 9 meteorologist Kyle Hanson said the bench’s path likely began with two storms in sequence. He said Hurricane Milton may have come soon enough after Helene to push the bench into the Gulf, where it could have been picked up by the loop current and carried along the Gulf Stream before washing ashore in Bermuda two years later.
“I’d say very lucky, very miraculous. The chance of this happening is lower than 1 in 100, I would say,” Hanson said.
Bench remains in Bermuda
The bench is still in Bermuda.
Amanda Sadiku said her son, Serene, Mike’s first grandson, still enjoys the spot where the bench used to sit.
“They say that babies, they meet their loved ones before they get sent down. So I feel like my son, he knows he has that feeling,” Amanda Sadiku said.
Amanda Sadiku said she is still deciding whether she will travel to see the bench or have it shipped back.

title: A mother’s journey to forgive the man who killed her son
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - Forgiveness is easily said, but often rarely given, just like second chances.
For one Nashville mother, however, forgiveness and a second chance for a career criminal were on a collision course.
Clemmie Greenlee’s lesson in forgiveness came after years of tears, hatred and anger aimed at Kim Birdsong. Then decades later, in a move that’s shocked family and friends, Greenlee found peace after the unthinkable.
On December 9th, 2003, Clemmie’s only child, Rodriguez Greenlee, took his final breath after he was shot. She remembers a late-night phone call. A mad rush to the hospital, only to find her son dead.
“All I did was just climb on top of the bed on him. And I went head to head, nose to nose, lip to lip, body to body. And let him know that you’re getting your rest now. But mama ain’t gonna never, ever, let your name go.” Clemmie said.
The shooter, Kim Birdsong or “Bird,” said he was shot at first and retaliated.
“I stood there and waited,” remembered Birdsong. “I [had] seen one of the guys and it unfolded. I just, I lost my mind at the moment.”
Clemmie was also losing her mind.
“I hate you. I hate you. Whoever you are, I hate you,” Clemmie recounted her grief. “You know, you messed up my whole... I was a happy girl. I don’t care what kind of life I had. I was a happy girl. You took not only my son, you took that away from me.”
When asked how often Clemmie thought about the man who killed her son in the time that followed, she said it was constant.
“Every single second. Every single second,” Clemmie said. “I never let this man out of my mind. I don’t talk about it to my family. I don’t talk about it to no other people, but nobody. Nobody has a clue what I go through. Nobody.”
Birdsong was convicted and sentenced to 8 years for that crime. His rap sheet as a career criminal is extensive.
“My momma never raised me like that. She raised me. She was a loving person, and she raised me to be an honest man. Somewhere along the way, I strayed,” Birdsong admitted.
Meanwhile, Clemmie started a support group for moms who had lost children to violence. In May 2018, however, the grief had taken its toll. She was diagnosed with Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy and needed a heart transplant.
“They told me, actually, ‘Clemmie, your heart is broken’” she said.
Her new heart led to a change of heart.
Her hatred for Birdsong was slipping away.
Yet, how could you forgive someone who killed your only child?
Her family and friends did not understand.
“I used to make a joke every time somebody come at me with something and I don’t want to talk foul about it,” Greenlee said. “I’ll say, let me call 1-800-JESUS and just see what he’d tell me. And I think I played myself into that stupid belief.”
Then years later, in 2019, that fake phone call led to a real call after Clemmie found Birdsong in prison. Surrounded by friends, Clemmie spoke to her son’s killer.
“Probably after 2-3 minutes, I was able to say, ‘Yes, I am here. What is your name?’” Clemmie said as she wiped away tears.
After that conversation, Clemmie went from hating this man to putting money in Birdsong’s prison account. Then, as they wrapped up the call, she had one last inconceivable request.
“I don’t have my child to call me and tell me ‘Happy Mother’s Day’ again. And you took that from me,” Clemmie shared. “And I said, ‘You need to be my son at Mother’s Day and call me and tell me Happy Mother’s Day.’”
We asked Birdsong what that call was like.
“It was good,” he admitted. “I mean, and I’m proud that I was able to do that and give her, you know, some of that.”
Recently, Birdsong was released from prison, and the first person he called was Clemmie. Her heart told her to forgive him, but something was holding her back.
Could she actually do it?
She invited our cameras there as she welcomed her son’s killer into her home.
“He’s in my yard. Not only is he in my yard, but he is on my front porch. I just can’t believe it,” Clemmie said.
Clemmie came face-to-face with the man who killed her son. Years of pain came rushing back. Followed by the undeniable comfort of peace. Tears and hugs followed.
Hurt, heal, let it go.
Words that Clemmie has always lived by, playing out in real time.
As forgiveness is the bridge that connects pain and peace, that bridge is for Birdsong as well.
“I needed you to stand in front of me, looking at him. So, you can say to yourself that I forgive myself,” Clemmie told Birdsong to his face.
In the aftermath of forgiveness comes closure, and that place where Rodriguez Greenlee died - at the corner of Lischey Avenue and Berry Street - is where Clemmie joined her tribe to find her closure.
Hand in hand with Birdsong.
“It’s all I needed,” she said. “I’m good.”
Clemmie said forgiving Birdsong is the hardest thing she has ever had to do, even harder than burying her child.
That forgiveness has brought new beginnings.
Clemmie and “Bird” have spoken every single day since they met in person in 2019. There are also plans for a book. They want to show people that unconditional forgiveness is doable and essential.

title: Senior discounts: Where to find them and why you should ask
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — Senior discounts show up almost everywhere, from museums to hardware stores to prescription drugs, but many older adults hesitate to ask for them.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down where these discounts hide, how to think about accepting them and why asking should become second nature.
Assume a discount exists everywhere you go
“I think the baseline should be the assumption that everybody’s going to give a discount,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “So no matter where you go, I’m going to get a discount. And I’d be brave enough to ask it.”
O’Rourke said the list of places offering senior discounts is long. “Museums, transportation, Amtrak, drug discounts, cell phone plans, property taxes, homeowner’s insurance, the list goes on and on,” she said.
She added one tip for anyone heading out to ask: “Bring your ID.”
Don’t be ashamed to ask
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said some seniors feel uncomfortable requesting a discount, but she compared it to how a veteran might react to being thanked for their service. “You don’t see a veteran at a checkout line when they say, ‘Oh, thank you for your service, here’s your veteran’s discount code’ go, ‘Oh, no, no, no, I don’t want that.’ ... So be accepting of it. You earned it,” she said.
She framed the discounts as a form of respect.
“This is respect and dignity in its best form, to be able to say, hey, you’ve lived enough, you’ve given us enough, we’re going to give you a discount,” Cradduck said. “This isn’t about your income. It’s not about anything else. It’s about you being who you’ve been for us.”
It’s also marketing — and that’s OK
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said seniors shouldn’t assume discounts are only about charity — it could just be about marketing and enticing seniors to spend.
“So remember that this could be marketing. Senior day is maybe a slow Tuesday lunch day, so they want seniors to come in. It is marketing,” Ambrose.
She said many older adults hold tightly to their savings because they worry about outliving their money, and discounts can help ease that hesitation to spend.
“They get a reward for buying at the hardware store,” she said. “Just assume there’s probably one and ask for it.”
For some, the savings are essential
Cradduck said that while some discounts are simply a bonus, for others they make a real financial difference.
“Let’s be honest, there’s a huge percentage that are really living on that fixed income that really do need, really do deserve,” she said.
She pointed to specific examples. “When you think about prescription drugs, utility assistance, property taxes — this could keep me in my home,” Cradduck said. “This could be the difference between whether or not I have to leave my home and move in with my children prematurely, or something else, or whether or not I can stay here.”
Reframe the discount as a raise
O’Rourke described turning 65 and receiving what she called a “pay raise” because of the discounts that became available to her.
“I take pride when I turned 65, I got a pay raise because of all the discounts, and I was very happy,” she said.
She said older adults play an active role in supporting local businesses and organizations.
“I’m proud that our generation supports the culture in the country, that we keep the movie theaters going in the middle of the afternoon,” O’Rourke said. “I think we’re a support structure for a lot of organizations that if we weren’t around, how would they keep their doors open?”
Ambrose also pointed to a shifting population.
“Soon people 65 years of age and older are going to outnumber our people that are 18 and younger,” Ambrose said. “So it’s really important to keep the money changing hands.”
Where to look
Cradduck said there isn’t one master list of every senior discount available, so the best approach is to ask directly.
“There’s not a comprehensive list,” she said. “So assume that everybody is going to offer [a discount], and ask.”
She suggested checking before booking travel or making larger purchases.
“If you want to go see your grandkids ... does the airline offer a senior discount? You want to go on a cruise ship? They may offer it to you,” Cradduck said.
Ambrose said property taxes are a particularly important discount to pursue, since rising taxes can price older residents out of homes they’ve lived in for years.
“Our elders put a lot into these communities,” Ambrose said. “They’ve been paying the taxes, they’ve been building the schools, they’ve been doing all the things so that we have these communities to enjoy.”
Resources
More places where you might be able to get a senior discount:
- Cell phone plans
- Homeowner’s insurance
- Museums
- Transportation
- Prescription drugs
- Property taxes
- Transportation/travel
- Utility assistance
Key takeaways
- Assume a senior discount is available everywhere you go, and ask for it directly.
- Bring identification, since some discounts require proof of age.
- Discounts on prescriptions, utilities and property taxes can make a difference.
- There is no single comprehensive list of senior discounts, so check with individual businesses, airlines, hotels and membership organizations.

title: Man shot after allegedly threatening and attacking DoorDash driver
text:
MARTINEZ, Ga. (WRDW/Gray News) - A man was shot Thursday after allegedly threatening to take a DoorDash driver’s vehicle and firearm before lunging at him, deputies said.
Columbia County deputies went to 3830 Washington Road near Davis Road at around 5:41 p.m. to investigate a reported shooting.
When deputies arrived, a DoorDash driver identified himself as the shooter, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies also found a man who had been shot multiple times in the torso.
A surveillance camera captured the incident on video, deputies said.
Investigators said that moments after the DoorDash driver got out of his vehicle, the man approached the driver and yelled at him, saying, “buy me a 20 piece.”
The man shoved the driver after he refused, witnesses said. The man also appeared to be behaving erratically and was significantly larger than the driver, witnesses said.
Deputies also said that the man approached people entering the Asian Market, yelling aggressively and offering them $20, though it was unclear what he wanted in return.
After the DoorDash driver returned to his vehicle, the man again demanded that the driver buy him a “20 piece,” the sheriff’s office said.
When the DoorDash driver refused, the man allegedly said he was going to take the vehicle and opened the front passenger-side door.
The DoorDash driver, who was in the driver’s seat, took out a firearm and told the man he did not want any more trouble, deputies said.
The man said he would take the firearm, went around the vehicle and lunged through the open driver’s-side door, investigators said.
The DoorDash driver fired three shots, striking the man each time, according to the sheriff’s office.
The man was taken to a hospital, where he underwent surgery, deputies said.
The evidence collected so far indicates the DoorDash driver acted in self-defense, the sheriff’s office said. No charges will be filed against the driver at this time, pending the conclusion of the investigation, authorities said.

title: State representative calls for review after Maine attorney general’s office releases confidential memo
text:
Attorneys and criminal law experts are concerned that the Office of the Maine Attorney General this week accidentally released a confidential document, and one state representative has called for an investigation.
In a statement Friday morning, Rep. Jennifer Poirier, R-Skowhegan, said she wants a thorough review of how the disclosure happened and what will be done to prevent it from happening again. Poirier serves on the state Legislature’s Judiciary Committee.
“The public has a right to expect that state agencies entrusted with sensitive legal information will handle those records responsibly and take every reasonable precaution to prevent unauthorized disclosure,” Poirier said. “When confidential case files are released to the media, the potential consequences for individuals involved and the integrity of legal proceedings must be taken seriously.”
On Thursday, an employee in the office’s criminal division attached the report in an email to more than 70 addresses. The list included more than 20 emails that don’t end with Maine.gov — such as those assigned to employees with the attorney general’s office — including accounts for reporters, news organizations, the judicial branch and what appeared to be a state lawmaker’s private email. A spokesperson for the judicial branch declined to comment on Friday.
The 45-page report listed more than 160 cases, including about 90 homicides, 30 drug matters and more than 20 cases related to alleged crimes dealing with healthcare, taxes, welfare and civil rights.
In a statement Friday, spokesperson Danna Hayes said the office notified families of victims to prepare them for the possibility that “inadvertent recipients” might make the information public.
“We take seriously the integrity of confidential information and the impact of this error,” Hayes said.
A majority of the report’s case summaries match details revealed in public court documents, but several matters detailed in the attachment have not been publicly filed in court, according to the document. That includes four missing persons cases that have been deemed to be homicides, and two investigations of residential care providers accused of theft. In the case summaries for the latter two, the document states that the attorney general’s office is waiting for guidance from federal prosecutors.
The attorney general’s office did not respond to a request to discuss those cases.
What’s been publicly reported about the confidential portions concerned legal experts like Jack Lu, a retired judge in Massachusetts who teaches at the University of Massachusetts-Lowell.
“It is wrong to publicize charges that are not brought,” Lu said.
Speaking generally about unauthorized disclosures in criminal cases — which Lu said is rare, in his experience — he said sometimes cases that aren’t charged can be terminated before they’re filed in court.
“There’s a danger of maligning people without government process,” Lu said.
Brian Wilson, a long-time prosecutor in Massachusetts who directs the Prosecutor Clinic at Boston University School of Law, said prosecutors deal a lot with information in criminal cases that, if disclosed improperly, could put victims or witnesses in danger.
“There may be things that infringe upon witnesses’ privacy rights or can even compromise their safety,” Wilson said. He was not familiar with the specifics of the Maine disclosures.
Wilson also described rules of conduct for prosecutors that bar them from sharing information about a defendant other than for specific purposes. The American Bar Association urges prosecutors to only share “statements that are necessary to inform the public of the nature and extent of the prosecutor’s action and that serve a legitimate law enforcement purpose.”
“You want to avoid a substantial risk of the accused, or the target of the investigation, if they’re not even publicly charged yet, you want to avoid any public condemnation of them,” Wilson said.
One defense attorney, whose case was mentioned in the document, declined to comment, citing an ethical rule for Maine attorneys that requires them not to view what they know to be an inadvertent disclosure, by not reading the content, notifying the sender that it was received and destroying it or returning it to the sender. Another attorney did not respond to a request for comment on what appeared to be non-public details in the document about a client.
Tina Nadeau, director of the Maine Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, said in an email Friday that confidential information involving victims of crimes and people suspected or accused of committing crimes “should be protected fiercely.”
She said she couldn’t speak to how the disclosure happened and that she couldn’t speculate about what might happen as the cases mentioned in the document progress.

title: Borat Warns People Not to See Ali G’s New Film in ‘Who Iz I?’ Trailer

The new Sacha Baron Cohen movie Ali G: Who Iz I? has already garnered complaints that the film and the title character — who Baron Cohen has portrayed for decades on television and one prior film — perpetuates old racist stereotypes.
Now one of the biggest comedy stars of the 2000s have joined calls for the film’s boycott. That’s Borat Sagdiyev, the Kazakh reporter who famously came here to report on our customs for state television, and wound up driving around the United States in an ice cream truck and then chased Pamela Anderson around a Virgin Megastore.
Borat says he has seen Who Iz I? and he’s also heard the complaints that the film is racist.
“Sadly,” Borat added, “it is not.”
Okay, yes, Borat just happens to be Sacha Baron Cohen. And his calls for a boycott of the “dastardly” comedian are just the new trailer for Ali G: Who Iz I? But it’s a pretty clever trailer all the same. Watch it below:

title: 86-year-old volunteer repairs electronics for a good cause
text:
HANOVER, Va. (Aging Untold) — An 86-year-old volunteer in Virginia is helping Habitat for Humanity by taking apart donated electronics and appliances for recycling.
Marshall Johnson helps keep the recycling program running at the Hanover and King William Habitat for Humanity store. The program relies on donations of gently used electronics and appliances.
Johnson has worked as a handyman for most of his life.
“Well, I always enjoy seeing how things are made because all my life I’ve been in our factories and seen all the pieces, parts that go into power tools and appliances,” Johnson said.
From product design to recycling
Johnson previously worked as a product designer for appliance companies, including Black & Decker and Home Depot. His designs are on display at the Hagley Museum and Library in Wilmington, Delaware.
“I’m just innately curious about, how do people make things?” Johnson said.
Johnson, 86, is blind in one eye and uses a cane. He volunteers on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.
“There’s so many wonderful people and products, and that’s the fun I get here is seeing what comes in,” Johnson said.
Johnson sorts through metals and electronics and takes them apart to be sold. The recycling program raises money for Habitat for Humanity and reduces waste at local landfills.
“Don’t take this stuff to the dump, just bring it in here and people like Marshall will be more than happy to spend their time taking it apart,” Mark Adams, a volunteer at the store, said. “Separating a different metals and getting it to the metal recycling places so we can make a few dollars for Habitat.”
Volunteer also delivers food to pantry
Adams said Johnson also delivers food to a church for its food pantry.
“I mean, he gets up in the morning and he’s going, whether he’s volunteering here, delivering or taking food from Feed More to a church in Highland Springs for their food pantry program,” Adams said.

title: Maine Attorney General’s Office accidentally shares confidential case information with media outlets
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - A supervisor within the Criminal Division of the Maine Attorney General’s Office accidentally emailed a document that included confidential case information to a number of media outlets, including WMTW.
The 45-page document, which was sent at 2:50 p.m. Thursday, featured information about dozens of homicide and manslaughter cases in Maine, including the names of suspects who have not yet been charged.
The document also includes details about alleged crimes and evidence gathered that have not been released publicly.
The supervisor who sent the email recalled it at 2:53 p.m., three minutes after it was sent.
At 3:21 p.m., the Attorney General’s Office sent another message asking everyone who received the email to delete it, along with the attached document.
“The inadvertent disclosure of sensitive information by this office was a mistake and we own that,” the Maine Attorney General’s Office said in a statement shared at 6:12 p.m. Thursday. “Unfortunately, a distribution list reserved to push public information out to the media was accidentally used. We will learn from this error and are working hard to ensure this does not negatively impact the significant work we do on behalf of the people of Maine. We respectfully request our partners in the media help us by not compounding our error.”
It appears the intent of the email was to get lawyers and investigators to update their reports for internal use.

A cold front approaches on Tuesday, bringing a chance for more widespread showers. Gusty winds from the southwest on Tuesday shift to northwest Tuesday night, ushering in a colder air mass that will settle in for the remainder of the week.

title: Appeals court dismisses Maine lobster defamation lawsuit
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals overturned a federal judge’s ruling and dismissed the Maine lobster industry’s defamation lawsuit against a California aquarium on Friday.
The Maine Lobstermen’s Association, Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association and three lobster businesses sued the Monterey Bay Aquarium Foundation in 2023 after the organization’s Seafood Watch program put lobster on a “red list,” urging consumers to avoid the seafood. The foundation had claimed measures in the fishery don’t do enough to reduce entanglement or promote recovery of the critically endangered North Atlantic right whale population.
The plaintiffs argued the foundation made “false and defamatory statements” about the Maine lobster industry’s practices and misled consumers and businesses about the fishery’s “integrity.” In the lawsuit, they claimed to lose business, with some consumers specifically citing the red listing.
The foundation moved to dismiss the lawsuit, but a judge allowed the suit to advance in 2025. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals overruled that decision Friday, and ordered the lawsuit to be dismissed.
The court ruled that calls to action, including boycotting products or industries, are protected under the First Amendment, and concluded that the listing did not make any specific reference to the plaintiffs in the case.
“People’s choices have the power to shape the future of the ocean,” the aquarium said in a statement on the court’s decision. “Programs like Seafood Watch guide consumers and businesses toward environmentally sustainable choices that support a healthy, thriving ocean, benefiting food security, fisheries and coastal communities whose livelihoods depend on the ocean.”
Spokespeople for the Maine Lobstermen’s Association and the Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association did not respond to a request for comment Friday evening.
The aquarium assigned Maine lobster a yellow rating on its Seafood Watch in 2014, recommending consumers “be aware there are concerns” with how the seafood is caught and managed. It ultimately gave it a “red” rating, along with other Canadian and U.S. fisheries, in September 2022. It claims one threat to the species is entanglement in fishing gear, including buoy lines used by lobstermen.
In a report on the new red ratings in 2022, the Seafood Watch program advised consumers to avoid “American lobster caught by trap from Georges Bank and the Gulf of Maine stocks due to risks to the critically endangered North Atlantic right whale and insufficient measures for reducing these risks.”
“This decision is a victory for all environmental advocates and freedom of speech,” said Sarah Shahabi, an attorney at the Conservation Law Foundation, which filed a friend-of-the-court brief supporting Monterey Bay Aquarium. “We can’t effectively fight threats to the natural world without naming them. Speaking openly and honestly about environmental challenges is essential to protecting our planet.”

title: Bonny Eagle rolls to 6-0 with impressive win against Oxford Hills
text:
STANDISH — Bonny Eagle’s football team excelled in all facets Friday night and continued to be led by the brilliance of senior quarterback Lucas Klehn.
Klehn ran for 170 yards and four scores and threw a 67-yard touchdown pass as the unbeaten Scots rolled up 497 yards in a convincing 45-6 Class A win against previously unbeaten Oxford Hills.
“There are a lot of good players in the state of Maine, but I find it hard to believe that any of them are playing better than Lucas Klehn. He’s been unbelievable for us,” said Bonny Eagle coach Kevin Cooper.
Oxford Hills (4-1) had allowed only 27 points in its four wins. The Vikings will look to bounce back next Friday at home against Portland — the other top team in Class A North.
“It’s good for these guys to have some adversity,” said Oxford Hills coach Nate Danforth. “The first time this year we’ve had any adversity, really. We just have to get home, figure things out, and get back to work Monday.”
Bonny Eagle, ranked second in the Varsity Maine poll, is 6-0 thanks to Klehn and strong play in all three phases. The Scots play at home next week against Exeter, New Hampshire, then face arch-rival and also unbeaten Thornton Academy in Saco on Oct. 24.
OFFENSE
Klehn set the tone when he tore through the middle of the Oxford Hills defense, making people miss and running through tackles for a 61-yard touchdown. On Bonny Eagle’s next possession, Ben Noe got things rolling with a 30-yard burst, and the Scots unveiled for the first time this season an extremely fast-paced tempo. The seven-play, 81-yard drive took less than two minutes without any clock stoppages. Klehn finished it with a 20-yard run.
“It adds a whole new facet to our offense,” Klehn said. “We looked at their five guys up front and thought our five guys up front were more conditioned. And that turned out to be true and we wore them down real fast.”
Bonny Eagle made it 21-0 in one play, when Klehn threw deep to Drew Gervais. The New England 100-meter track champion in the spring, Gervais saw the ball descending and appeared to give his legs just a bit of extra gas, collecting the ball in stride and easily running to the end zone for a 67-yard score.
The Scots used the supercharged attack once more in the second quarter, going 56 yards in eight plays that took just over two minutes, with Klehn scoring his third TD on a 5-yard run.
Klehn’s fourth touchdown was from 11 yards and capped the scoring.
DEFENSE
Oxford Hills had averaged nearly 35 points in its four wins. The Vikings were without top back Keegan Ridley (nursing an injury), but his brother, Mason, and quarterback Toby Oufiero did combine for 160 rushing yards and the offensive line got a good push quite often. But Oufiero’s 11-yard run in the second quarter that cut the lead to 21-6 was the only touchdown for the Vikings.
“Overall, there’s a lot of good things we can take from our defense today. They have a lot of good offensive players,” Cooper said.
In the second half, Oxford Hills had drives that reached the Scots 9 and 20. Both were stymied by pass breakups from defensive backs Marcus Katane, Noe and Wes Pinkham.
“It’s all about trust. Trust your teammates and then go and get the job done,” Noe said.
SPECIAL TEAMS
Bonny Eagle’s Ben Havu was 6 for 6 on point-after kicks and made the team’s first field goal of the season, a 21-yarder for a 24-6 lead.
His biggest play was as a punter. On fourth-and-17 from his own 15, Havu rolled a bit to his right in the rugby-style approach and then took off. He made a nice move behind blocking to get the first down, ran along his team’s sideline for another 15 or so yards, then avoided a defender and sprinted the rest of the way for an 85-yard score.
STATISTICS
Oxford Hills: Toby Oufiero (7 of 17 passing, 59 yards; 17 carries, 100 yards, 1 TD), Mason Ridley (15 carries, 60 yards), Kamden Record (3 catches, 23 yards)
Bonny Eagle: Lucas Klehn (10 carries, 170 yards, 4 TDs; 4 of 5 passing, 91 yards, 1 TD), Ben Noe (12 carries, 137 yards), Ben Havu (5 carries, 97 yards)

title: Hurricane Isaias could nudge fuel prices higher if Gulf of Mexico refineries lose power
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hurricane Isaias is forecast to miss the oil industry’s biggest hubs along the Gulf Coast but could still nudge fuel prices higher if it triggers power outages that shut down refineries for processing crude, according to industry experts.
An extended shutdown of refineries would put a crimp in fuel supplies that already have taken a hit from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Chevron’s facility in Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Vertex Energy’s refinery in Mobile, Alabama, which constitute 2.4% of the nation’s refining capacity, are at risk of flooding and power outages, said Andrew Lipow, a Houston-based oil analyst. Any problems could take the facilities offline at a time when diesel supplies are already low.
Isaias strengthened into a major hurricane Friday as it barreled toward the Gulf Coast, where final preparations were underway for potentially life-threatening storm surges and high winds.
If the storm moves through quickly and its impacts are minimal, refineries would continue to run at reduced capacity and prices for gasoline and diesel could rise just a few cents, said Carl Larry with the energy analysis firm Enverus. But if refineries such as Chevron’s shut down completely, it could take them weeks to recover and that could cause fuel prices to jump more significantly, Larry said.
“Major issues, like a power shutdown, and the prices will spike immediately. It’s possible a dollar,” he said. “Those diesel prices that already are above $6 could start approaching $7.”
Other experts said even if the refineries that turn oil into fuel for consumers take a hit, the gas price impacts should be minimal.
“We’re talking about potentially under a million barrels a day, probably somewhere in the ballpark of 500,000 barrels a day, of refining capacity,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “That may have a small impact on gas prices, primarily in the Gulf Coast, but I don’t think it rises to a criteria that would impact gas prices nationally.”
As refineries on the coast braced for the storm, it already had caused temporary shutdowns of offshore oil wells that pump about 15% of U.S. crude.
As of Friday, personnel from 129 production platforms — about a third of the facilities in the Gulf of Mexico — were evacuated, according to the federal Marine Minerals Administration.
More than two-thirds of Gulf oil production was shut down as a precaution, equal to almost 1.5 million barrels (61 million gallons) of oil a day, the agency said. Chevron, BP and Shell were among companies that reported evacuating personnel and shutting platforms.
The storm’s impact on oil and gas prices so far is dwarfed by the effect of the conflict in the Middle East. And once the storm passes, workers will be able to return to platforms in the Gulf and quickly resume operations, barring significant damage.
“I would expect that the shut-in oil production will probably return pretty quickly within just a couple of days,” De Haan said.
Prices for Brent crude, the international standard, were above $104 a barrel Friday. That price has varied between $96 and nearly $110 over the last month driven by uncertainty over the war with Iran.

title: Police: Heat was set to 99 degrees in apartment where woman was found dead
text:
Police report: Thermostat was set to 99 degrees in assisted living apartment where woman was found dead
A woman found dead in a Massachusetts assisted living facility last week was found in an apartment where the thermostat was set to 99 degrees, according to a police report obtained by WCVB.
Sheila Szczypinski, 86, was found dead in her apartment at Golden Pond Assisted Living in Hopkinton on Sept. 30.
According to a police report, Szczypinski lived in an "independent care" unit, where she managed her own medication and decided whether to attend meals or events, but staff visited periodically to assist with bathing. An aide who was scheduled to visit Szczypinski found her body in bed.
Szczypinski had last been seen the previous afternoon.
Police described the inside of the apartment as "neat and orderly," but the thermostat was set to 99 degrees.
"I inquired about the high heat in the apartment," an officer wrote in their report. "The staff stated that the heat had only been turned on in the facility the previous day."
Szczypinski's next of kin told investigators that she "got confused easily" and "may have inadvertently turned the heat on too high."
Douglas Noble, the director of operations at the communities at Golden Pond, released a statement, saying in part that the facility is cooperating with its regulatory agencies.
He also mentioned the HVAC systems were working properly at the time of the resident's death.
"Our HVAC system is professionally maintained by a licensed contractor on both a seasonal and as-needed basis and was working properly at the time of this incident," he said in a news release. "Each apartment in our community has an individual thermostat that residents can operate directly, although we encourage our residents to push their call button for staff assistance with it."

title: UMF presents 20th annual Constitution Day U.S. Supreme Court Case Review
text:
FARMINGTON — The University of Maine at Farmington is excited to commemorate Constitution Day 2026 with its 20th annual U.S. Supreme Court Preview and Review. This year’s event will take place on Wednesday, Oct. 14 at 12:30 p.m., in Lincoln Auditorium in the UMF Roberts Learning Center. It is free and open to the public.
Presented by Dr. James Melcher, UMF professor of political science and pre-law advisor, the event will feature an in-depth discussion of cases from the last term of the U.S. Supreme Court and key cases from the upcoming term.

This federal holiday was revised to recognize not only those who have become U.S. citizens, but also the ratification of the U.S. Constitution on Sept. 17, 1787. In addition to renaming the holiday “Constitution Day and Citizenship Day,” the act mandates that all publicly funded educational institutions provide educational programming on the history of the American Constitution on that day.
