title: UMPI unveils sculpture honoring Donald and Linda Zillman
text:
Among the trees and swirling fall leaves at the center of the University of Maine at Presque Isle’s campus on Friday, the university’s president, an artist and others unveiled a large sculpture to honor a late UMPI leader and his wife.
Standing more than eight feet tall, the granite sculpture, titled “Embrace,” sits in the Central Campus Park behind South Hall.
The piece honors the memory of former President Donald Zillman and his wife, Linda Zillman, who became the university’s largest benefactors.
“It’s very, very simple, two forms, one on top of the other,” said Leo-Paul Cyr, UMPI professor emeritus and the artist who created the sculpture. “When I started this process, I thought about the Zillmans, and I knew them very well. And for me they were very simple people and so that’s what I wanted to honor through the work.”
Donald Zillman served as UMPI’s president from 2006 to 2012 after several decades working across the University of Maine System.
He was dean of the University of Maine School of Law from 1991 to 1998, interim provost and academic vice president at the University of Maine from 1999 to 2000 and interim president of the University of Maine at Fort Kent from 2001 to 2002.
His wife, Linda, was an art historian involved with UMPI’s Reed Art Gallery. She helped the gallery acquire 153 original Andy Warhol photographs, one of its most prestigious works, among other items.
Donald Zillman died in July 2023. Linda Zillman died in September 2025.
“I think the most appropriate way to honor the Zillmans is through art,” UMPI President Raymond Rice said. “They were dedicated to education all their lives, but they just loved all performing arts, fine arts, everything.”
Linda Zillman served on the board of the Portland Ballet, several members of which made the trip north to Presque Isle Friday to put on a short performance in their honor.
At UMPI, the Zillmans established a research professorship in 2013 and gave the first money to start the Zillman Family Greenhouse for the agricultural science program. The couple’s estate gave the university $2.1 million last December, its largest-ever donation, along with other gifts over the last 15 years that total more than $3 million.
The Zillmans’ generosity extended to other sects of the UMaine system, including another $2.1 million to the Honors College at the University of Maine and nearly $3 million in separate gifts to the University of Maine Art Gallery in Bangor, which was renamed the Linda G. and Donald N. Zillman Art Museum in 2020 as a result.
Donald Zillman, UMPI’s 10th president, came to the school at a challenging time, as the UMaine system expressed no confidence against two consecutive chancellors and difficult dynamics persisted between faculty and administrators. But his demeanor brought a calm to the chaos, Rice said.
“It is not an overstatement to say, without Don Zillman, I don’t know what direction this institution would have taken,” Rice said. “He had a way of defusing challenging situations, but also getting to the core of things. He took everyone’s concerns seriously and he helped move the institution forward at a time that we weren’t certain what our direction forward was.”
Art from the Zillmans’ estate is on display at the Reed Art Gallery through Oct. 23.

title: Cheverus golf repeats as Class A champion
text:
VASSALBORO — With its possession of the Class A state championship at stake, the Cheverus golf team dusted off a familiar gameplan — and even a familiar speech.
Sam Sirois shot even-par 72 for medalist honors, and Keane McGrath and Joe Stratman were among eight players who tied for second with 76s as the Stags successfully defended their state title Friday, shooting 304 to hold off Falmouth (314), Messalonskee (324), Thornton Academy (328), South Portland and Gorham (340 each) at Natanis Golf Course.
Falmouth’s Dante Iannetta, Gorham’s Charlie Sands, Messalonskee’s Greyson Dooley, Bangor’s Jacoby Harvey, Mt. Ararat’s Caleb Greenleaf and Oxford Hills’ Sawyer Poland joined Stratman and McGrath at 4 over.
Lila Dailey of Camden Hills and Jacquelin Sirois of Cheverus shot 97 to share the title in the girls division.
“It feels great, again,” said Sirois, who tied for second individually last year. “Going into this, we didn’t really think we had a shot, so I’m really glad we got it done.”
Such doubt was reasonable after Falmouth rolled to the SMAA championship at the same Tomahawk course on Monday, shooting 304 to beat the Stags by nine shots while getting scores under 80 from five players.
Cheverus coach Billy Goodman told his players there was no way to beat the Navigators if they were that hot, a similar angle he used when addressing the girls basketball team in February before the Stags turned a 19-point deficit into a 63-61 overtime victory against Hampden Academy in the Class A final.
“I told my team going back to Portland, it was kind of like the halftime speech for my basketball team,” he said. “‘If they shoot like that again, they’re going to win.’ But we just had a really good week of practice. A lot of kids focused and did better than Monday.”
The Stags’ roadmap to victory looked like last year’s, when it had the medalist in Mick Madden and a second-place finisher in Sirois. This time, Sirois jumped to the top spot, hitting 11 greens in regulation and carding four birdies, one coming when he rolled in a 20-foot putt on the fourth hole.
“Teamwise, I knew we all had to play well,” Sirois said. “I didn’t want to let my teammates down.”
The rest of the scores fell in line. McGrath, who was third at the SMAAs with a 74, was excellent again, notching 13 pars and an eagle on the par-5 third. Stratman, who had an 81 on Monday, improved by five shots. Ray, who shot 87 on Monday, improved by seven strokes. Garrett Thees went from a 90 to an 84.
“I guess it was Cheverus’ day today. We did really well, everyone kind of came together,” McGrath said. “Everyone was very focused this morning, it was a different mood than the SMAA.”
Stratman didn’t play in the state championship last year. He was front and center this time.
“I fed off the pressure, it’s one of the greatest things to do,” said Stratman, who carded four birdies. “I shot 106 in the qualifiers last year. It really pushed me to work harder.”
Iannetta tied for second for the second straight year. He was joined by Alex Novick (78), Griffin Jacobsen (78) and Anthony Graceffa (82) among the Falmouth scorers.
“I hit the ball pretty solid all day, it’s just putts didn’t fall,” Iannetta said. “Golf’s a game that happens on one day. When a tournament’s only one day long, anything can happen. It’s tough. … I believe we could have gone lower than 304, but it just wasn’t today. It’s unfortunate.”
Messalonskee’s Dooley, the first-place finisher at the KVAC qualifier, notched four birdies, one of which stabilized his round. It came two holes after a triple bogey on the par 3 10th.
“It was basically putting today that saved me,” he said. “It was mostly just a mental game out there, and having to just stay through it the rest of the round.”

title: Another poll shows Troy Jackson leading a tight Maine Senate race
text:
A new poll released Friday by the Washington Post shows Democrat Troy Jackson maintaining a narrow lead over Republican Susan Collins in Maine’s U.S. Senate race, despite a bombshell report linking Collins’ circle with a convicted fraudster.
Jackson held a four-point lead, 50% to 46%, over the five-term incumbent in the poll — roughly the same as the survey’s margin of error of 3.6 percentage points. Three percent of those polled did not select a choice, while 1% said they’d vote for someone else.
“Another poll shows that Troy is connecting with voters on the issues that matter the most to Mainers,” senior campaign adviser David Farmer said in an emailed statement. “He’s working class and understands the issues that Mainers are facing.”
The survey is further evidence that the closely watched race will likely be a barn burner — one that may hinge on a small pool of undecided voters.
Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and former state Senate president, holds a two-point lead over Collins, according to a polling averages compiled by FiftyPlusOne. But some surveys, including a New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll released two weeks ago, showed Collins with a narrow lead, albeit within the margin of error.
The Post survey, done in partnership with the George Washington University Schar School of Policy and Government, was conducted from Sept. 30 to Oct. 5.
It entered the field a week after ProPublica published a story about how the FBI had years ago begun a sweeping investigation into whether Collins engaged in an illegal pay-to-play scheme by steering government contracts to a donor. (Collins has denied any wrongdoing, saying she was cleared by the Biden administration. ProPublica has reported investigators were looking into Collins’ orbit until President Donald Trump took power in early 2025.)
The Washington Post poll showed the volatile waters that Collins, 73, is trying to navigate to win a sixth term. Fifty-two percent of voters said her 30 years in the Senate was a bad thing. That’s despite respondents giving her a 24 percentage point edge on bringing federal money back to Maine and giving her better marks for bipartisanship.
And President Donald Trump continues to loom large over the race. Sixty-three percent of respondents disapproved of the president’s job performance. And 58% said that Collins sides with Trump too often, compared to 33% who said she’s handled her relationship with the president “about right.”
A majority — 55% — said they wanted Democrats to win the Senate, compared to 42% for Republicans. That metric shows Collins is having at least some success pushing against the national political headwinds.
The top issues for voters were the cost of living (41%), immigration (13%), healthcare (12%) and taxes (6%).
Jackson, meanwhile, had a +1 net approval rating, but 13% of respondents had no opinion or skipped the question. That leaves a small opening for Republicans, who have a significant funding advantage, to introduce the Democrat to voters on their own terms through paid ads.
The 58-year-old Jackson held a 13-point lead among independents, 53% to 40%. His crossover appeal was also higher than Collins, pulling 9% support from Republicans compared to the incumbent’s 6% from Democrats, the poll found.
The survey also asked about Maine’s three-way race for governor. Again, Democrat Hannah Pingree held a double-digit lead over Republican Bobby Charles, 49%-36%. Independent Rick Bennett drew 11% support — his best showing in polling to date.

title: Sexually transmitted diarrhea? What to know about increasingly treatment-resistant infection
text:
Sexually transmitted diarrhea? What to know about the infection that's becoming increasingly treatment resistant
A sexually transmitted infection is on the rise in the United States and the United Kingdom, particularly among the LGBTQ+ population – and it's become increasingly resistant to treatment, according to a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report.
Shigellosis, an infection caused by the Shigella bacterium, can cause severe diarrhea among other symptoms; it can be spread through contaminated water or feces – and can lead to dysentery.
Related video above: Why are infection rates for some STDs at an all-time high?
In recent years, it has increasingly spread through sexual contact, particularly among men who have sex with men, according to reports.
The CDC's report noted that Shigella is becoming increasingly drug-resistant. While the infection can clear up on its own, antibiotics are prescribed in severe cases.
"Most infections resolve without requiring treatment with antimicrobial agents; however, antibiotics are indicated for severe illness or to reduce transmission in high-risk settings," the CDC wrote in the April report.
In 2011, drug resistance was found in 0% of lab samples, which the CDC called isolates; by 2023, drug resistance was found in 8.3% of submitted lab samples, according to the CDC report. The CDC referred to the drug-resistant isolates as XDR cases.
"Earlier U.S. outbreaks involved drug-susceptible strains and primarily affected children; national surveillance data indicate that most XDR cases occurred among adult men," the CDC report wrote.
The Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy spoke with an epidemiologist who was one of the authors of the CDC report.
"Together, it's a very concerning pattern of XDR Shigella strains that are being seen among vulnerable populations," Dr. Naeemah Logan told CIDRAP News.
Meanwhile, another study from the University of Cambridge published in July also shows the infection becoming increasingly drug-resistant in the United Kingdom.
There were more than 2,500 cases in the UK that were potentially acquired during sexual contact last year, the University of Cambridge study noted, citing the UK Health Security Agency.
"The study used techniques deployed during the pandemic to track COVID-19 variants through DNA sequencing, only this time for bacteria instead of a virus," according to the Cambridge study. "It shows sexually transmitted Shigella spreads much faster and is growing drug-resistant much quicker than non-sexually transmitted infection (STI) strains."
In the cases evaluated in that study, about 70% of sexually transmissible Shigella strains were resistant to at least one relevant antibiotic.
What is shigellosis?
Shigellosis, which is an infection with the shigella bacteria, can cause diarrhea and other digestive symptoms, including vomiting, fever and stomach pain, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
It can be spread through contaminated bodies of water, contaminated food or direct contact with feces, which can happen while changing diapers or during sex.
Men who have sex with men are among those who are at higher risk of getting the infection, according to the Cleveland Clinic. Children under the age of 5 in daycare settings and those experiencing homelessness are also more susceptible to being infected.

title: Maine’s tallest mountain is greening faster than others in New England
text:
High above the tree line on Katahdin, where biting winds and sub-zero winters hold the rocky landscape in a frozen grip for much of the year, the mountaintop is turning noticeably greener.
Four decades worth of satellite observations reveal that alpine tundra across the Northeast are undergoing widespread vegetation expansion, not just at the advancing tree line but well above it, too. The new growth is transforming rare, high-elevation ecosystems once thought buffered from rapid change.
And Katahdin, Maine’s highest peak at 5,268 feet, is greening faster than any other New England summit. Vegetation has increased there by 7.9% from 1984 to 2024, according to a recent study in the journal Ecosphere by scientists at Dartmouth College and the Appalachian Mountain Club.
“Greening isn’t necessarily good or bad, but it’s happening,” said Dartmouth College geographer Jonathan Chipman. “The reason may be a concern. It might mean rare plants are being crowded out by aggressive interlopers that can now live in areas when they couldn’t survive in the past.”
The study used thousands of NASA images to track greening on 35 alpine summits from New York to Quebec. Co-author Jordon Tourville provided field perspective as an alpine ecologist with the Appalachian Mountain Club to explore the potential reasons for the greening.
As a geographer, Chipman said he is often asked to work with other researchers to analyze or map data in their fields of study. As an avid climber, he has long wanted to use his skills to research what is happening at the tops of New England’s summits.
“I grew up in New England,” Chipman said. “I climbed Katahdin when I was a kid. I climbed Mount Washington too many times to count. A lot of people, including me, are very concerned about the future of these precious little sky islands.”
For Mainers who hike Baxter State Park or look up at the Longfellow Mountains, the findings suggest that environmental pressures are actively reshaping the summits of New England that are so isolated that naturalists call them “sky islands.”
These summits support fragile plant communities, such as cushion plants and arctic sedges, that survived the last ice age and thrive in conditions too harsh for trees. Some animals are found only in these areas, such as the Katahdin Arctic butterfly, or breed only here, like the American Pipit.
There are only about 50 square miles of alpine ecosystem in the Northeast, Tourville said.
“That makes it the rarest ecosystem type in the region,” Tourville said. “We suspect that because they’re so small, and because the plants there are already existing really at the edge of what plants can withstand, that any amount of change will destroy this system.”
Across Maine’s six studied alpine summits — Katahdin and North Brother in Baxter State Park and Sugarloaf, Bigelow, Saddleback and Mount Abraham in the Longfellow Range — greenness expanded over the four-decade study period, but not at the same pace.
While Katahdin clocked a 7.9% greening trend, the average greening rate of all the peaks studied was 5.2%. Records show a 5.8% increase at North Brother at Baxter, a 5% increase at Sugarloaf, a 4.8% increase at Saddleback and a 4.7% increase at mounts Bigelow and Abraham.
Ground mapping on Katahdin shows that greening is hitting alpine sedge meadows particularly hard. The windswept lawns of Carex bigelowii appear to be undergoing invasion by the woody dwarf heath shrubs that thrive in warmer temperatures and higher nutrient levels.
Baxter State Park officials acknowledged that the shift is a serious concern. They have been collaborating with other researchers to map Katahdin’s alpine plant boundaries, monitor trail corridors and track shrub encroachment into sedge meadows, according to park manager Kevin Adam and natural resources director Nava Tabak.
Strict “stay-on-trail” policies, supported by visitor quotas, summit stewards, signage and string fencing are the park’s most vital tools to help the fragile root systems withstand atmospheric stresses, Adam and Tabak said.
But researchers suspect warming temperatures are hardly the only environmental force at play.
The greening trend accelerated through the 1980s and 1990s before flattening around 2005 to 2009, a trajectory that aligns with ecological recovery following federal Clean Air Act regulations that curbed acid rain and sulfur pollution across New England peaks.
“A lot of people focus on temperature, but I think we missed the nitrogen signal,” Tourville said. “The soils in the alpine zone are extremely nitrogen poor. For decades, we essentially dumped nitrogen fertilizer up there. That probably had a pretty profound impact.”
Topography and severe weather also shape the landscape. Sheltered east- and north-facing slopes across the region’s peaks showed rapid greening, but exposed ridges seem to have resisted plant expansion.
For park stewards, the 40-year satellite record provides a crucial baseline to guide future conservation. But it also highlights a fundamental disagreement over how to manage wilderness in an era of global climate change.
Tourville argued that traditional, hands-off wilderness management may no longer be enough.
“My message to them was, it might be time in the near future to rethink that stance in terms of hands-off, no management up in the park, especially in the alpine zone, because climate change does not respect park boundaries,” Tourville said. “And climate change is not hands-off.”
Baxter State Park leadership firmly defended the park’s “Forever Wild” mandate, arguing direct human intervention is not the answer.
“Our response to stressors from climate extremes, as illustrated by this research, is to continue to minimize human impacts so that the natural communities and species have the best chance to adapt,” Adam and Tabak said in an emailed statement. “Though our approach to stewardship of the Park’s alpine areas is unique, these areas may over time serve as an experimental control that can be compared with other northeastern alpine areas that are more directly managed.”
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 9 to include comments from Baxter State Park officials.

title: Nobleboro Approves $10.4 Million Bond for School Repairs
text:
The Nobleboro Central School gymnasium had a full house on Monday, Oct. 5 as residents approved the issuance of a $10,400,000 bond for repairs to the older wing of the school.
Residents voted 181-94 to authorize the Nobleboro Select Board to issue general obligation bonds or notes in the name of the town not to exceed $10,400,000.
The bond proposal comes after elevated levels of mold were found in the older wing of the school in March. Even with mold remediated, the wing remains closed until necessary repairs, including drainage updates, siding and roof replacements, and more, are completed.
With approval, the town’s debt totals $11,200,000. Of that amount, $800,000 is for bonds outstanding and unpaid.
According to the warrant, the estimated cost of the bond for a 20-year term with annual payments at an interest rate of 4.2% is $15,577,280.
The vote came after an hour and a half of questions ahead of the meeting as well as discussion when the article was brought to the floor. Many residents asked variations of how the situation got to be as bad as it was and who was responsible for the issues.
“Every last one of us is to blame on this problem,” Nobleboro School Committee Chair Matt Benner said.
Benner later clarified that he was not blaming anyone specific for the problem, but the fault was in the yearly decisions to put off maintenance. To reduce the tax burden every budget season, maintenance was usually hit with the most reductions, he said.
“Nobody likes to get rid of people, so the easy lines to reduce have always been maintenance lines,” Benner said.
Tensions were high in the room as some residents voiced concerns about the cost of the bond. Rebecca Hart said she used to clean the school when she was in sixth grade and that she takes offense of Benner “blaming all of us for this.”
“Shame on your for not doing a better job with your money,” Hart said.
In response, Benner said he wasn’t stating that it was the whole town’s fault but other school committee leaders from the past who let it slide.
Other residents had concerns about the tax impact of the bond. Benner said the mil rate will increase $1.20, or $120 per $100,000, with the first increase not hitting tax bills until 2028.
“The $10.4 (million) is to bring the building up to par,” Benner said. “The rest of the building, it’s going to be about a two-year project.”
During voting, resident Bill Soares made a motion to amend the total bond amount to $5,400,000. He said he is “100%” in favor of repairing the school, but wants to amend the total to lessen the cost burden.
“The amendment protects our kids’ health tonight, allows for the balance of the work to be structurally structured for maximum cost effectiveness through transparent local bids later,” Soares said.
In response, former select board member Richard Powell said he believes the school is in its present situation because of how conservative the town has been toward building maintenance.
It is also not guaranteed the full $10.4 million will be needed and there are possibilities of future state funding, he said.
“This is for our kids,” Powell said. “This is our school. Are we going to let these people come in town and tell us what to do? I say no.”
School committee member Jake Maxmin said Soare’s idea was not “fiscally responsible.” He used the example of someone going to the bank and taking out a mortgage for half the amount it will take to build a house and then going back for the rest.
“This school has served us as a community,” Maxmin said. “It served our children and I think this vote is more so about what kind of community we want to be going forward.”
A flyer passed out at the meeting presented the budgeted scope of work to be completed by Energy Efficient Investments. Kerri Warms, vice president of the New Hampshire-based company, sat with the school committee at the special town meeting.
Warms said when the company evaluated the situation, it decided that it would save the town money to do the project all at once instead of breaking it into parts, mostly because of inflation.
Soares’ amendment failed.
The work on the exterior and building envelop, including siding and windows, gutter installation, and foundation work, is estimated to cost a total of $1,240,175.
The cost for abatement and mold and asbestos remediation totals $604,002. The mold remediation was completed in late August, days before the school year started.
Site and civil work, including the installation of a perimeter drain around the older wing of the building, will cost a total of $1,010,000. The work will include a moisture barrier to the foundation to prevent future water intrusion.
Heating, air conditioning, and ventilation systems throughout the school will receive $4,912,443 worth of work, including the replacement of the boiler system, installation of new underground liquid propane tanks, new ductwork for ventilation, the installation dehumidification equipment and comfort cooling, and other new equipment.
Electrical work is expected to cost $345,000 and will include the installation of equipment to serve the new HVAC system and other updates to wiring around the school.
The new fire alarm system will cost $365,000 and a new access control and security system will cost around $38,000.
The cost of administration area reconfiguration totals $402,500 for work to be done in the office spaces housing the principal and other administrative staff members, including the relocation of the nurse’s office and the creation of more space for front office staff.
Architectural upgrades will cost $587,000 for projects throughout the school, including the installation of quartz tile throughout, new casework, and modifications to door swings.
Replacement of existing shingled roods with new roofing systems will cost $895,259.
The projected work is expected to happen within a two-and-a-half-year time period, according to school officials.
Some residents questioned what will happen if the costs exceed the bond amount. Warms said the wording of the article is that the cost cannot exceed that number and the plan is to start planning as soon as funding is approved so the town can have a “stronger chance” of staying under budget.
Benner said there are also plans to create a strategic plan for all of the work.
All other warrant articles passed with limited discussion.
Residents authorized town staff, boards, and committee to conduct fundraising on behalf of the town.
Nobleboro Select Board Chair Jon Chadwick said on Sept. 23 the select board didn’t realize that in order to fundraise, it needed voter approval so the question now will be in the warrant. With the article’s approval, town officials can now solicit and accept voluntary donations, gifts, grants, sponsorships, and fundraising process on behalf of Nobleboro.
Article 3, which asked if residents would allow the select board to establish and modify the format, layout, design, and method of publication of the town’s annual report, was also approved.
Chadwick said the question came after he spent some time observing other towns’ annual reports and found that he liked some of the formatting he has seen.
After a nomination from the floor, resident Cole Pendleton was elected to fill a vacant seat on the budget committee.
For more information, call 563-8816 or go to nobleboro.maine.gov.

title: Community rallies after donation box for 4-year-old’s medical treatments is stolen
text:
WAUSAU, Wis. (WSAW/Gray News) — The Wausau, Wisconsin, community is showing support after a donation box for a 4-year-old with cerebral palsy was stolen.
The former owner of Townline Market has raised money for his grandson for years.
“Someone saw the opportunity to go take a little extra cash for themselves, not caring that it’s for a sick little guy,” said David Jagler, the former owner of Townline Market.
A temporary jar is now at the counter, where donations have been coming in quickly. Jagler also raises money for Cashton Krause with golf ball and chocolate bar sales.
Cashton often travels out of state and out of the country for cerebral palsy treatments. They’re expensive and usually aren’t covered by insurance.
“We keep striving to give him every opportunity that we possibly can,” said Jennifer Imhoff, Cashton’s mother.
The family is also living in a rental home that isn’t accessible to people with disabilities. They lost their home in the Ringle tornado.
“It’s a lot. We already had our plates very full with Cashton and things that come along with having a child with a brain injury, and it just kind of added another level of stress that we didn’t really need on our plates,” Imhoff said.
Donations continue
“This has kind of been like a blessing in disguise because we’ve taken in so much more than that little box would have otherwise, and it’s going to all go to a good cause,” Jagler said.
The theft has prompted calls and donations from people looking to help. Some have dropped off $100 bills or mailed money.

title: Maine hockey takes step toward ‘big boy hockey’ in loss to Quinnipiac
text:
ORONO — The video, played approximately five minutes before the start of the University of Maine men’s hockey home opener Friday night, gave the Alfond Arena crowd a new cheer.
The video showed Quinnipiac coach Rand Pecknold, at a press conference earlier this week, describing what it’s like to play at Alfond. This is big boy hockey, he said.
It was the highest compliment Pecknold, whose Bobcats have numerous NCAA tournaments and a national title to their credit, could pay the Black Bears and their fans. Seconds after the puck dropped to start the game, the students filling the balcony above Quinnipiac goalie Christian Kirsch adopted the saying as their own.
“Big boy hockey!” they cheered. “Big boy hockey!”
Quinnipiac took a 2-1 win. There are no moral victories, but the Black Bears and their fans can take from the game that playing hard, gritty hockey will keep them in more games than not.
The Black Bears definitely played big boy hockey Friday. Getting that to translate into wins, with a little more offense, is the next step.
“That’s going to be the challenge for our guys this year,” Maine coach Ben Barr said. “Can we stay at it and stay at it, keep staying at it, and eventually find a little break as far as putting the puck in the net.”
Take the first period, for example. Maine controlled play for much of those first 20 minutes. The Black Bears outshot the Bobcats by a wide margin, 18-5.
Maine still went into the first intermission down 2-1.
A power-play goal by Lee Parks just 2:39 into the game staked the Black Bears to a 1-0 lead, but it lasted barely two minutes. The Bobcats took the lead for good midway through the first period when Ethan Wyttenbach scored on a breakaway.
One of the top scorers in the nation last season, Wyttenbach loitered in the neutral zone like he was waiting for an Uber, and the Black Bears lost track of him. When he got the outlet pass from defenseman Jan Golicic, Wyttenbach was able to charge at Maine goalie Albin Boija without resistance and gave his team the lead.
It’s a spooky thing, when 5,000 people go quiet. Not silent, that’s different. Silent serves a purpose. Quiet is more disconcerting than silence. Quiet comes when there’s something to say but nobody wants to say it. Nothing but nervous coughs, mumbles and murmurs instead of cheers.
That’s what happened in Alfond Arena in the aftermath of Wyttenbach’s goal. That’s the big boy hockey to which Pecknold referred.
Maine captain Owen Fowler was right when he said that’s the kind of hockey the Black Bears played for most of the game. He was right when he said they just missed that finishing touch. Quinnipiac is ranked No. 6 in the latest USCHO.com poll and scored 16 goals in a pair of wins last weekend, including 10 against New Hampshire. Holding the Bobcats to two is an accomplishment, but really only if you score three.
“Around the net, we have to bear down. I think that’s the biggest focus right now,” Fowler said.
The Black Bears were physical, and Fowler thought they wore down the Bobcats.
“If you watched that game, I think they didn’t want to go back on pucks a lot of the time,” he said. “I think we just need to bring that again (Saturday).”
A second-period breakaway by Maine’s Judah Makway ended with a shot over the crossbar. A 5-on-3 power play in the third ended without the equalizing goal. These are the things Maine needs to fix as the season progresses. The effort is there, Barr said, and so is the talent. Now comes the mental piece.
“We’ll do it all over again tomorrow night. That’s the awesome part,” Barr said.
When the Black Bears start seeing the hard work translate to goals, that’s when you’ll know they’re really playing the kind of hockey Pecknold warned his team about.

title: Quinnipiac hockey edges UMaine
text:
ORONO, Maine — The University of Maine’s hard-working hockey team did what it needed to do against the sixth-ranked Quinnipiac University Bobcats, swarming the puck and limiting the high-scoring visitors to few Grade-A scoring chances.
Quinnipiac, which has reached the NCAA Tournament the last seven seasons, scored 16 goals in its first two games.
But the Bobcats proved that they can also win a low-scoring affair even when they are getting significantly outshot.
Sophomore right wing Ethan Wyttenbach, the 2025-26 Tim Taylor National Rookie of the Year, scored one goal and assisted on Mason Marcellus’ goal as the Bobcats triumphed 2-1 in UMaine’s home opener Friday night.
Quinnipiac, now 3-0, received 33 saves from freshman Christian Kirsch while 1-2 UMaine got 20 stops from Albin Boija.
UMaine outshot Quinnipiac 35-23 and had a decided edge in offensive zone time.
The teams will play again Saturday night at 7.
Despite carrying the play in the first period and outshooting Quinnipiac 18-5, the opportunistic Bobcats took a 2-1 lead into the intermission.
UMaine’s Lee Parks’ power play goal opened the scoring just 2:39 into the game but the Bobcats’ Marcellus equalized just 2:11 later and Wyttenbach broke the tie at the 10:22 mark.
UMass Lowell transfer Parks scored his second goal in as many games as he found himself at the far post to the right of Kirsch and Will Gerrior made a perfect cross-ice feed and he one-timed a short wrist shot into the short side corner.
Senior left wing Marellus tied it when he worked a nifty give-and-go with Wyttenbach, who was positioned behind the net.
His low wrister from the middle of the slot off Wyttenbach’s pass beat Boija to the goalie’s right side. It was his third of the season.
UMaine’s Max Scott had broken his stick and gone to the bench for another one.
Midway through the period, freshman defenseman Jan Golicic found Wyttenbach alone behind the Black Bear defense and he broke in on Boija before making a few clever moves and roofing a backhander.
Wyttenbach’s goal was his third.
“Our defense fell asleep,” said UMaine head coach Ben Barr. “Against a team like Quinnipiac, if you make a mistake, they make you pay.”
The scoreless second period was more evenly played and the Black Bears had the best chance of the period when left wing and Alaska-Anchorage transfer Judah Makway was able to free himself from a Bobcat and break in alone.
He pulled the puck to his backhand but missed the net.
Quinnipiac outshot UMaine 9-6.
UMaine had a golden opportunity to tie the game in the third period when they had a five-on-three for 54 seconds.
But the Black Bears never generated a high-quality chance in the five-on-three or the ensuing five-on-four.
They did generate an even-strengh three-shot flurry during a scramble but Kirsch made saves off Lukas Peterson, Tanner Klimpke and Sam Alfano and one of the shots squeezed through his pads but rolled just wide of the far post.
Just after the Bobcats failed to sew up the win after UMaine pulled Boija in favor of the extra attacker by missing a pair of wide-open nets, they were assessed a penalty with 22 seconds left.
But UMaine failed to take advantage on the six-on-four after pulling Boija again.
“The guys played hard. They scored one more than we did,” said Barr. “You can’t fault the effort. It was similar to last Saturday night (in a 3-2 overtime loss to Holy Cross). We obviously had chances. We had the five-on-three in the third but we just couldn’t capitalize.
”That’s going to be the challenge for our guys this year. Can we keep staying on it and eventually find a little bit of a break as far as putting the puck into the net,” added Barr.
One of the major issues was faceoffs as the Black Bears won only 36.9 percent of the faceoffs and that prevented them from gaining offensive zone possession, especially with the man-advantage.
“They were the best face-off team in the nation last year and I think they probably are again this year,” said Barr. “When you start chasing the puck a lot, that makes it hard. We’ve got to be better there.”
Scott won 10 of his 17 faceoffs but the rest of the team won just 14 of 48.
UMaine graduate student left wing and captain Owen Fowler said the team played a good 55-minute game.
“Those five minutes, we had a mental lapse,” said Fowler. “And that’s a team that’s really good over there and they execute on their chances.”
Fowler said when it comes to producing goals, “we definitely have to bear down around the net. That’s the biggest focus right now. Overall, we can take a lot of good from this game. That’s one of the best teams in the country right now and for most of that game, we had them in the cave. It’s that little bit (more) we need from each guy and when we connect on that, it definitely will help us.”

title: Ella Langley concert canceled due to 'serious security threat'
text:
Ella Langley show canceled in Oklahoma due to bomb threat
An Ella Langley concert scheduled to take place in Tulsa, Oklahoma, on Friday night was canceled due to a bomb threat.
Venue officials with the BOK Center announced the cancellation on Friday.
"Due to a serious security threat involving the safety of fans, venue personnel, and the artist, Ella Langley’s scheduled performance tonight at the BOK Center in Tulsa has been canceled," officials said in a social media post, but information about the alleged threat was not released.
The "Choosin' Texas" singer also posted about the last-minute cancellation on her Facebook page, saying that the threat involved "the safety of my fans, the venue staff, and my team."
"This decision was made under the advisement of local authorities, the venue, and my security team. I know how much time, travel, money, and planning goes into coming to a show, and I can’t tell you how sorry I am," Langley wrote on her Facebook page on Friday night. "This is not a decision that was made lightly. I was so looking forward to spending tonight with you, but your safety will always mean more to me than anything else. I refuse to put anyone in harm’s way."
Venue officials said they would soon provide more information about ticket refunds. Additional details about the security threats were not immediately disclosed.
Video below: Bomb threat forces cancellation of Ella Langley’s sold-out Tulsa concert
Tulsa police explained that they conducted a sweep of the building with their K-9 and bomb teams, along with BOK Center security, and found no evidence of danger. After a second call was made threatening the lives of attendees, they performed another sweep and again found no credible threat.
“We advised the group that was supposed to perform tonight that we did not find a credible threat, and we would never tell anybody if we couldn’t find a credible threat to cancel their event, so they made the decision to cancel their event tonight,” said Capt. R.G. Meulenberg of the Tulsa Police Department.
Fans who traveled to Tulsa for the concert expressed their disappointment. Addie Hobson and Reese Maley shared their frustration.
“I really wanted to go to the Zoo Amphitheater when she came a few months ago, and I missed that, so I was like, she’s coming again; this is my second chance, we’re going to go, so I splurged, I splurged! And bought them two months ago,” Hobson said.
It is not yet clear whether the concert will be rescheduled or if refunds will be issued.

title: The sorority I never wanted to join
text:
Expert Care. Close to Home.
As New England’s largest independent oncology practice North of Boston, we have worked hard to make it easier for our patients to access our world class cancer care close to home. As we continue to grow, we look forward making groundbreaking cancer expertise accessible to more patients in Maine and New Hampshire.
Last fall, my youngest left for college. For the first time in more than two decades, both of my kids were out of the house. I loved raising them, but was excited about what came next and about having a little more room for me. I had even given this new chapter a name:
“Sophie 2.0.”
I had plans: travel more, continue a national leadership program, spend more time with friends and say yes to things I hadn’t always had time for.
Then, on Oct. 10, 2025, I was diagnosed with invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC) — three words I had never heard before and a type of breast cancer I knew absolutely nothing about. Sophie 2.0 was still going to happen. It just wasn’t going to look anything like I had imagined.
Once the initial shock wore off, I realized I had no idea what to do next. I’m originally from California, and navigating the medical system in Maine was still largely unknown territory.
Through the kindness and connections of friends, I was quickly referred to New England Cancer Specialists and an amazing medical team.
I walked into my first appointment with my surgeon, Dr. Paige Teller, petrified. She looked at me and said, “You’re going to be OK.”
I will never forget those words. Dr. Teller’s compassion and confidence cut through the fear and uncertainty. I walked out knowing I could face whatever came next.
Having an oncologist you trust completely matters enormously when you’re living with cancer, and I found that in Dr. Chiara Battelli. She brings an incredible depth of knowledge to my care, but just as importantly, she listens and makes me an active participant in every decision.
That feeling extends throughout NECS. I have always felt cared for as a person first and a cancer patient second, with kindness, warmth and genuine respect. Going through cancer has made me realize what an extraordinary resource NECS is for our state. Mainers shouldn’t have to leave Maine to receive outstanding cancer care. I feel incredibly fortunate that we have it right here.
I quickly learned how many specialties can be part of breast cancer care: surgeons, oncologists, radiologists, genetic testing, and plastic and reconstructive surgery. Having so much of that care on one campus has made an enormous difference. With Plastic + Hand Surgical Associates alongside NECS, the many moving pieces of my care have been incredibly well connected and coordinated.
My plastic surgeon, Dr. Katharine Connolly, has been an important part of that care. Reconstruction is deeply personal, and Dr. Connolly understood that from the beginning. Her remarkable surgical skill and the way she has cared for me helped me through a part of cancer that changes not only your body, but how you see yourself.
Dr. Connolly didn’t just help reconstruct my body. She helped me feel whole again.
I’m used to being the one who takes care of things, so cancer taught me something about letting others take care of me. It brought women into my life who understood without much explanation. I’ve often said breast cancer is the sorority you never wanted to join. I never would have chosen what brought us together, but I am incredibly grateful that we found one another.
An important note: before my diagnosis, I had gotten behind on my mammograms. I was busy, and my own health kept getting pushed further down the list.
Thankfully, my cancer was caught early. I firmly believe early detection saved my life. If there is one thing I hope another woman takes from my experience, it’s this: check your breasts monthly. If you feel something, have it checked. Make the appointment and keep it. Don’t let being busy keep you from taking care of yourself.
Now a year later, cancer is part of Sophie 2.0, but it isn’t all of it. There have been extraordinary friendships, incredible medical care and a much clearer understanding of what matters to me and of how precious this life really is. This fall, I’m participating in the Penobscot Bay YMCA’s LIVESTRONG program to get stronger. And in July 2027, I’m taking on the TRI for a Cure.
For much of the past year, my calendar was filled with appointments, surgeries and things I didn’t choose. Now I get to start filling it with things I do. Cancer is part of my life now, and in some ways, always will be. But it doesn’t get to decide what comes next.
I do.
Sophie 3.0 is next, and she has plans.

title: Isaias is expected to strengthen into a major hurricane as it nears the US Gulf Coast
text:
BAYOU LA BATRE, Ala. (AP) — Isaias was expected to strengthen into a major hurricane Friday as it headed toward the U.S. Gulf Coast, where final preparations were being made for potentially life-threatening storm surges and high winds.
The hurricane is forecast to make landfall late Friday somewhere along the Alabama-Florida line and create dangerous conditions in the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, the National Hurricane Center said.
The Category 2 storm was packing 110 mph (177 kph) winds early Friday, just shy of Category 3 status, and was expected to continue strengthening. Category 3 storms, considered major hurricanes, are capable of causing devastating damage, the center said.
Isaias was expected to weaken quickly as it hits shore and be downgraded to a tropical storm by Saturday afternoon as it moves north and inland along the Alabama-Mississippi line, the center said.
“Preparations should be rushed to completion as the weather will go downhill quickly today,” the hurricane center said in an early morning forecast. “While the storm is not expected to make landfall at peak intensity, it is likely that Isaias will still be a significant hurricane when it reaches the coast.”
Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, was centered about 200 miles (322 kilometers) south-southeast of the mouth of the Mississippi River and moving to the north at about 15 mph (24 kph), the center said.
It was expected to make landfall between Mobile Bay on the Alabama coast and Choctawhatchee Bay in the Florida Panhandle in the evening.
Besides wind and storm surges, the hurricane will likely bring flash flooding and spawn tornadoes, the hurricane center said.
A hurricane warning was in place from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the western Florida Panhandle. Tropical storm warnings were issued from southeastern Louisiana to Aucilla River along Florida’s Big Bend.
Preparations have been going on for days. On Thursday, residents boarded up windows and stacked sandbags while thousands of National Guard soldiers were deployed.
Isaias is expected to bring a storm surge as high as 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2 meters), with the deepest water hitting immediate coastal areas, along with large and dangerous waves, the hurricane center said.
Coastal communities moved quickly to prepare Thursday, as Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey ordered non-residents to immediately evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island. Videos on social media showed traffic at a standstill on a highway leading out of Gulf Shores, where double-red beach flags signaled water access was closed.
Several counties announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency for dozens of counties, with Florida’s Ron DeSantis saying about 5,000 National Guard troops were expected to mobilize by Friday.
On Dauphin Island, a 15-mile (24-kilometer) barrier island off the Alabama coast, officials encouraged voluntary evacuations, particularly on its popular western section, which is vulnerable to storm surge.
Mayor Jeff Collier said he did not anticipate substantial damage, “but at the same time, these things are very fickle and a little jog here or there, or some last-minute increase in strength — we just have to be prepared for the worst.”
Meanwhile in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Simon, which formed as a tropical storm on Wednesday off of Mexico and became a hurricane late Thursday, was forecast to strengthen into a Category 4 hurricane.
___
Rico reported from Atlanta and Collins reported from Hartford, Connecticut. Also contributing were Associated Press reporters Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama; Hallie Golden in Seattle; Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; John Raby in Charleston, West Virginia; Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas; and Julie Walker in New York.

title: Maine hockey takes step toward ‘big boy hockey’ in loss to Quinnipiac
text:
ORONO — The video, played approximately five minutes before the start of the University of Maine men’s hockey home opener Friday night, gave the Alfond Arena crowd a new cheer.
The video showed Quinnipiac coach Rand Pecknold, at a press conference earlier this week, describing what it’s like to play at Alfond. This is big boy hockey, he said.
It was the highest compliment Pecknold, whose Bobcats have numerous NCAA tournaments and a national title to their credit, could pay the Black Bears and their fans. Seconds after the puck dropped to start the game, the students filling the balcony above Quinnipiac goalie Christian Kirsch adopted the saying as their own.
“Big boy hockey!” they cheered. “Big boy hockey!”
Quinnipiac took a 2-1 win. There are no moral victories, but the Black Bears and their fans can take from the game that playing hard, gritty hockey will keep them in more games than not.
The Black Bears definitely played big boy hockey Friday. Getting that to translate into wins, with a little more offense, is the next step.
“That’s going to be the challenge for our guys this year,” Maine coach Ben Barr said. “Can we stay at it and stay at it, keep staying at it, and eventually find a little break as far as putting the puck in the net.”
Take the first period, for example. Maine controlled play for much of those first 20 minutes. The Black Bears outshot the Bobcats by a wide margin, 18-5.
Maine still went into the first intermission down 2-1.
A power-play goal by Lee Parks just 2:39 into the game staked the Black Bears to a 1-0 lead, but it lasted barely two minutes. The Bobcats took the lead for good midway through the first period when Ethan Wyttenbach scored on a breakaway.
One of the top scorers in the nation last season, Wyttenbach loitered in the neutral zone like he was waiting for an Uber, and the Black Bears lost track of him. When he got the outlet pass from defenseman Jan Golicic, Wyttenbach was able to charge at Maine goalie Albin Boija without resistance and gave his team the lead.
It’s a spooky thing, when 5,000 people go quiet. Not silent, that’s different. Silent serves a purpose. Quiet is more disconcerting than silence. Quiet comes when there’s something to say but nobody wants to say it. Nothing but nervous coughs, mumbles and murmurs instead of cheers.
That’s what happened in Alfond Arena in the aftermath of Wyttenbach’s goal. That’s the big boy hockey to which Pecknold referred.
Maine captain Owen Fowler was right when he said that’s the kind of hockey the Black Bears played for most of the game. He was right when he said they just missed that finishing touch. Quinnipiac is ranked No. 6 in the latest USCHO.com poll and scored 16 goals in a pair of wins last weekend, including 10 against New Hampshire. Holding the Bobcats to two is an accomplishment, but really only if you score three.
“Around the net, we have to bear down. I think that’s the biggest focus right now,” Fowler said.
The Black Bears were physical, and Fowler thought they wore down the Bobcats.
“If you watched that game, I think they didn’t want to go back on pucks a lot of the time,” he said. “I think we just need to bring that again (Saturday).”
A second-period breakaway by Maine’s Judah Makway ended with a shot over the crossbar. A 5-on-3 power play in the third ended without the equalizing goal. These are the things Maine needs to fix as the season progresses. The effort is there, Barr said, and so is the talent. Now comes the mental piece.
“We’ll do it all over again tomorrow night. That’s the awesome part,” Barr said.
When the Black Bears start seeing the hard work translate to goals, that’s when you’ll know they’re really playing the kind of hockey Pecknold warned his team about.

title: Maine GOP holds press conference to criticize gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Maine House Republican Assistant Leader Katrina Smith criticized Pingree’s record in the Mills administration, citing low childhood literacy rates in 2024. Smith also cited what she described as a lack of child-welfare oversight on the Children’s Cabinet while four children died in 2021 under Department of Health and Human Services supervision.
Maine mother Jennifer Navarro joined Smith and said there is a lack of services and providers for children with autism and other disabilities.
Smith and Navarro questioned Pingree’s role in the issues they raised.
“When a child qualifies for services, but no provider is available, the burden does not disappear. It falls on the family,” Navarro said.
“So now, when Hannah Pingree asks the Maine people to make her governor, I believe it is entirely fair to ask about the results of the government that she helped to lead. Where was Hannah,” Smith said.
Smith said Pingree should answer for the outcomes during her time in the Mills administration. Smith said Maine needs accountability and change.
Campaign responds
A spokesperson for Pingree’s campaign responded to a request for comment:
“This is a new low for the Maine GOP, which will say anything to attack Hannah Pingree, whether it’s true or not. Hannah’s role in the Mills Administration had nothing to do with child protective services, autism waitlists, or test scores. As a mom, she takes these issues personally and is focused on solutions for Maine families. The attacks change week to week, but this one is bad even for them.”

title: ‘Waves are really big’: Beachgoers make last trip to Florida’s Gulf Coast before Hurricane Isaias
text:
PENSACOLA BEACH, Fla. (WALA/Gray News) - Hurricane Isaias will soon impact the Gulf Coast, and many people in Florida wanted to make one last trip to see Pensacola Beach up close before the weather takes a turn.
Stephanie Dzugan, a visitor, said she was explaining the situation to her son.
“I was explaining to my son that this is kind of the calm before the storm, sun shining. It’s beautiful, enjoy it, then follow directions and take heed and let mother nature do what she does,” Stephanie Dzugan said.
Paul Dzugan, a visitor, described the conditions at the beach.
“It’s really cool. It’s pretty beautiful and the waves are really big. I wouldn’t recommend going boogie boarding or scuba diving, and it’s really good for sea shelling,” Paul Dzugan said.
Lifeguards warn of rip current danger
While many found the waves exciting, they’re also dangerous. Lifeguards have already moved their stands off the beach and made the switch to double red flags Thursday morning to urge people to stay out of the water as the storm moves closer.
Dave Greenwood, chief of water safety, said rip currents pose the greatest risk.
“Rip currents are deadly. That’s the biggest weather phenomenon related death is by rip currents so we keep them out of the water. We’re doing preventative actions and even after the storm passes, there’s still going to be wave energy moving on shore, so be aware of that,” Greenwood said.
Visitors weigh travel plans
Several beachgoers were in town on vacation. Trey Hermann said he plans to leave for Atlanta before Pensacola International Airport closes at 10 a.m. Friday.
“Since it’s tonight, I feel like I should be alright. If I was flying out tomorrow, I’d be more concerned for sure. I think I’ve had enough time and I’d rather be going out tonight than being stuck without a ride,” Hermann said.
Others said they plan to move farther away from the coast and ride the storm out.
“We just got down here a day or two ago, and in Knoxville, we didn’t know there was a hurricane coming. We’re going to pray, we’re going to be smart and we’re going to ride it out,” Stephanie Dzugan said.
Larry Toomey, a resident, said he isn’t concerned.
“I have no fear. I don’t board up. I don’t do anything. I’ve lived here all my life basically,” Toomey said.
Beachgoers urge taking storm seriously
While there isn’t much fear over the storm, beachgoers say it’s important to have a plan and take it seriously.
“There was someone last night at a restaurant and he was asking me, ‘Should I change my flight?’ And I said, ‘If the locals are taking it serious, then I would take it serious.’ So that’s my advice. If you see the locals getting gas, taking the boats up, putting them in dry storage, I would probably get out of dodge,” Hermann said.

title: Letter: Susan Collins must continue to protect Maine’s ports
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mainers understand what it means to live and work along the water. With a coastal economy supporting more than 90,000 jobs and generating nearly $7 billion a year, our state thrives on bustling ports. Our success isn’t possible without Maine’s hard-working longshoremen and women who deserve the safest working conditions. That’s why an effort in Congress to rollback the use of a clean emissions technology is concerning.
This issue is about whether or not Maine gets to decide its own port protection policies. Every state should be entitled to protect their air quality from pollutant-emitting vessels, many of which are foreign-flagged ships. If Congress strips these regulations now, the decision would undermine the tools that every coastal state needs to ensure the livelihoods of the countless fishermen, dock workers, and families who breathe that air every day.
Sen. Susan Collins has demonstrated her record of prioritizing Maine’s port and maritime infrastructure. Opposing the rollback of this technology is a chance to keep that streak going. Preserving the use of this emissions technology protects port communities, while rejecting it sends a message to foreign countries that our ports are fair game to release their ships’ toxins.
Let’s draw the line now while we still can. A vote against these attempts to dismantle such essential technology is a vote for the hard-working Mainer who depends on that clean air and port. Maine’s beautiful coastline is one of our state’s greatest assets, and I hope Collins continues to see it that way.
Daniel Allen
Buxton

title: Trump strikes deal with Putin to get diesel in sharp reversal of US policy weeks before midterms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
Trump’s shocking announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it “a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners,” according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.
Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Zelenskyy said.
Trump’s move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing new sanctions on Russia, given that the law that passed overwhelmingly by Congress directs the administration to target countries that purchase Russian oil and gas. Lawmakers this week had urged the Trump administration to act quickly to use the tools available to help Ukraine.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, along with Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, called Trump’s announcement a betrayal of Ukraine, the European allies and U.S. national security.
“Enough is enough,” the senators wrote. “The President must end his war with Iran instead of funding Russia’s war machine.”
Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel future prices dipped on the news on Friday, the national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. remained high at $6.28, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.
Trump did not address the sanctions or Russia’s war but said, “Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority.”
Trump said later as he left the White House for a campaign rally, that he was thankful for the deal. “I want to thank President Putin. To be honest with you, we have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it’s diesel, which is what we want. So, thank you,” Trump said. He did not answer shouted questions about the criticism from Zelenskyy.
Washington and Moscow offer few details on deal
The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the Russian diesel or when it would become available.
A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said during their call he and Trump dedicated “significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis” and also discussed “the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations.”
Russia “confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets,” Putin said. “I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy.”
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov, speaking later to reporters, wouldn’t say whether the U.S. made any concessions in exchange for the supplies, or what, if anything, was promised to Russia in exchange.
Trump and Putin’s deal draws immediate backlash
Zelenskyy, in a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it “with further terror and perfidy.” He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.
“It plays into Russia’s hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-sponsored the Russia sanctions law, said Trump’s decision “makes us complicit in Putin’s war against Ukraine.” In his scathing statement, Blumenthal invoked the memory of Sen. Lindsey Graham, a Trump ally and Russia hawk, for whom the law is named.
“This agreement with a murdering dictator is a stain on our nation’s character, an insult to Lindsey Graham’s memory, and directly contrary to Congress’s intent in our bipartisan sanctions bill,” he said.
Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump’s announcement “infuriating.”
“This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn’t the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia,” Beyer said in a statement on X.
The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.
It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned the imports because of Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Treasury Department moves to ease diesel sanctions for six months
Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.
This is the latest license the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war early this year. But it is the first to ease sanctions on diesel for longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war in February 2022.
The license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday.
The extensions underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow’s ability to profit from its energy exports.
It’s unclear how the move will impact oil prices
“What does this do to prices? I think probably not much,” said Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist and expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
But, Seigle said the new deal is a “great benefit to Russia and to Putin,” who are currently trying to offload their summer-grade diesel for the heavier winter and arctic grades that they will need in the coming months.
“It’s kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic,” said Michael Lynch of the Energy Policy Research Foundation, a non-partisan research institution focused on energy and economics.
“If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they’ll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now,” Lynch said.
Russia, once a major exporter of diesel, has banned exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand inside the country because of Ukraine’s repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries. The International Energy Agency says Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30%.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told state news agency Tass that Russia is “immediately starting to lift restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule.” He said Moscow could start supplies to the U.S. this month and Russia’s domestic market will be “fully supplied” with diesel, as well.
___
Associated Press writers Will Weissert, Konstantin Toropin and Lisa Mascaro in Washington, Alex Veiga in Los Angeles and Farnoush Amiri in New York contributed to this report.

title: Jonathan Bush is pumping thousands of dollars into the Bangor City Council election
text:
Jonathan Bush, the wealthy tech entrepreneur and cousin of former President George W. Bush who made an unsuccessful bid for the Republican gubernatorial nomination in Maine this year, is now setting his sights on local elections — including in Bangor.
Bush plans to invest $100,000 in the Bangor, Lewiston and Waterville council elections this year with his nonprofit, Maine for Keeps, and has already dedicated $50,000 to the effort himself, he said. He’s not sure how the money will be split between the three cities.
The Cape Elizabeth politician raised more than $2.5 million for his earlier gubernatorial campaign, much of it coming from his own personal funds.
“I love Maine. I want to be useful, and obviously my fellow Republicans didn’t think I’d be perfectly useful as a candidate. So what else can I do to be helpful?” Bush said. “And it seems like the area that’s getting the least attention but has the most, in my view, sort of troubling direction, are the city councils.”
The influx of cash could greatly influence city council elections, which don’t see much serious fundraising or outside attention. It’s likely unprecedented for Bangor, where council candidates typically raise between a few hundred and a couple thousand dollars for lawn signs and campaign literature but where big outside money rarely comes into play.
Bush said he chose the three cities because although he lives in the Portland area, “I don’t see a path for any of the reasonable councilors to win in Portland,” whereas in Bangor, Lewiston and Waterville, “it’s close enough that maybe a little bit of extra awareness and campaigning might tip towards more reasonable, independent-minded, kind of what I would call ‘Chamber of Commerce’ candidates.”
Bush pointed to issues like stalled development, business flight, property tax crises and debates over harm reduction programs as reasons why the cities needed new leadership.
“These are races that have a vastly more immediate and pressing impact on Mainers’ quality of life,” he said, adding that the investments will focus on “getting awareness up about the importance of a city council election [and] the specifics of the situation in those cities.”
When asked if he sees any downsides to putting so much money into a smaller local election, Bush said, “Obviously, I’m practiced in the art of putting a lot of money in and losing. … But it doesn’t mean you don’t keep trying harder.”
He’s holding an event in downtown Bangor’s West Market Square at 9 a.m. on Monday alongside Jim Deyermond, chair of the Maine Republican Party, and Philip Henry, a Bangor real estate investor who is often vocal at Bangor City Council meetings and is involved with a new political action committee in the city.
Henry, for his part, said he thinks Bush’s effort will make the biggest difference in terms of awareness around the race.
“I think that you need to have some sort of professional marketing firm that has that ability to understand where people see information, how they get information, and I think that that’s probably how it will best be used,” he said of the money.
He referenced light turnout in local elections and what he sees as “less than qualified people” on the council, saying he hopes to see larger turnout and more informed voters this year.
“I think most people that have spent their lives in Bangor realize that something has to happen,” Henry said, acknowledging that some residents may be skeptical of influence from someone who doesn’t live in Bangor.
“It’s time for change, and I’m glad that some people are bringing more visibility to this,” he added.
Henry is one of many residents feeling a growing frustration with the Bangor City Council over its inability to address persistent challenges like the city’s homelessness crisis. Meetings have been packed in recent months, and a record 12 candidates are running for three open seats.
Henry’s political action committee, Concerned Citizens of Bangor, endorsed candidates Anthony Cote, Terry Dinkins and Joseph Pratt on social media Thursday evening. In less than two weeks since registering, the PAC already raised more than $20,000, according to reports obtained from the city clerk’s office.
Lewiston voters will elect a mayor and councilors in three of the city’s seven wards this year. Waterville is electing a mayor.
Maine for Keeps can’t endorse candidates, per the organization’s bylaws, Bush said. He plans to personally endorse candidates in the three cities in the coming weeks.
The entrepreneur and multimillionaire is known for co-founding Athenahealth in the 1990s and has had a growing presence in Maine politics since moving to Cape Elizabeth in 2021.
Bush has been critical of President Donald Trump and billed himself as a “disruptor” in the governor’s race, running on promises to cut taxes and make the state more business-friendly. He was in attendance at a fundraiser for Republican Sen. Susan Collins at Moody’s in Gorham in late September.
Beyond the financial investment, Bush is bringing some high-powered friends into the fray.
He’s recruited Vincent Harris to organize the local election efforts, he said. Harris, an internet-savvy conservative strategist, boasts a resume including work for Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party and a pro-Trump SuperPAC in 2024.
Harris is also a senior strategist for Bobby Charles, the Republican nominee for governor who beat out Bush and several other candidates in the primary.

title: Spruce Mountain football bests Cape Elizabeth in 8-man battle
text:
LIVERMORE FALLS — It doesn’t matter if it’s through the air or on the ground, Spruce Mountain quarterback Dylan Jewett always seems to find the end zone.
Jewett was responsible for four touchdowns Friday night (one passing, three rushing) as he led the Phoenix to a 40-28 win over Cape Elizabeth in an eight-man football Large School South clash.
“That kid, he can change the game in the blink of an eye, and sometimes we have to talk to him a little bit to realize that,” said Spruce Mountain coach Devin Roberts. “And once he knows it in the game, he does it.”
In Spruce Mountain’s 36-34 loss to Orono on Oct. 2, Jewett was also responsible for four touchdowns, rushing for one, throwing for two and returning a kick for a score.
“I think a lot of it goes to the line and coach just making the right play call, and my guys just block for me, so (I) just take advantage of that,” Jewett said.
HOW IT HAPPENED
Spruce Mountain (4-2) took the lead on its first offensive play, a 56-yard run by Jewett. Cape Elizabeth (4-2) answered with a 13-yard touchdown run by quarterback Rosco Hampton.
The Phoenix and Capers went back-to-back again on their ensuing drives, which resulted in a 14-yard touchdown pass from Jewett to Levi Richards, and a 2-yard touchdown pass from Hampton to Liam Brown.
Jewett’s 72-yard touchdown run with just under two minutes to go in the second quarter gave Spruce Mountain a 20-14 lead. Cape Elizabeth answered again in the third quarter, scoring two touchdowns (a 6-yard run from Hampton and a 9-yard pass from Hampton to Sam Hews) to take a 28-20 lead with just under 17 and a half minutes left in the game.
The Phoenix scored the next three touchdowns to take control. After Spruce Mountain tied the game, the Capers had a chance to regain the lead, but their drive stalled at the Spruce Mountain 9 when Levi Richards recovered a fumble by Hews. Jewett and Owen Kelvey scored for Spruce Mountain to put the game away.
UNSUNG HERO
Not only did Spruce Mountain’s Levi Richards catch a touchdown pass and a 2-point conversion, but the wide receiver/cornerback also recovered the fumble that shifted the game in the second half. His defensive effort led to the touchdown that gave the Phoenix a 34-28 lead in the fourth quarter.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “We came into the game knowing we had to win if we wanted to seal a spot, (a top-four spot) for playoffs, so it was a big game for us.” — Dylan Jewett
• “We feel like we’ve beaten the teams we’re supposed to beat, and the two teams (Yarmouth, Spruce Mountain) that we really had circled on our schedule, we just have to play a full four quarters. In both of those games, we’ve had some turnovers in areas of the field where we were going to take the lead or increase the lead, and it just didn’t work out that way.” — Cape Elizabeth coach Issiah Bachelder
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Spruce Mountain: Dylan Jewett (three rushing touchdowns; one passing touchdown), Owen Kelvey (two rushing touchdowns)
• Cape Elizabeth: Rosco Hampton (two rushing touchdowns, two passing touchdowns)

title: Partners for Peace holds walk and vigil in Lincoln for Domestic Violence Awareness Month
text:
LINCOLN, Maine (WABI) -October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month.
For over 50 years, local nonprofit Partners for Peace has been dedicated to serving and supporting survivors in Penobscot and Piscataquis counties.
Thursday night, the organization held a walk and vigil at the Lincoln gazebo.
Their theme to mark the month is “Every Story Matters.”
Their goal is to create a space to allow those affected by domestic abuse and violence to share their stories.
“It’s so wonderful to be here in Lincoln. We love being here every year to have this close-knit community come together and hear the stories of survivors and walk together, remember together, and just be here in community. This was an annual event that we held for many, many years before the pandemic. Last year was the first year that we brought it back. And then this being the second year, we have such a great turnout and we anticipate that that will happen every single year,” said Casey Faulkingham-Bixby, Partners for Peace director of development and engagement.
There are plenty of ways you can get involved, too.
You can host a fundraiser or donation drive, make a donation to Partners for Peace, or simply share their social posts and promote events.
To see a full list of events, visit PartnersForPeaceME.org.
And, if you or someone you know has been impacted by domestic abuse, help is just one call away.
The Partners for Peace helpline is 1-800-863-9909.
