title: Maine Sunday Telegram, Portland Press Herald and reporters receive top New England newspaper awards
text:
The Maine Sunday Telegram, Portland Press Herald and two reporters have been honored with top awards at the New England Newspaper & Press Association’s annual fall conference.
The 2026 New England Newspaper Awards were announced Friday at a summit in Sturbridge, Massachusetts, hosted by the New England Newspaper & Press Association. The organization is the professional trade organization for newspapers in Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont.
The Portland Press Herald won first place for New England Newspaper of the Year for large circulation weekday publications, and the Maine Sunday Telegram won first place for New England Newspaper of the Year for large circulation Sunday publications.
“The newspaper of the year awards are a testament to the hard work of our entire newsroom staff,” said Scott Monroe, managing editor of the Maine Trust for Local News, which owns the papers. “We’ve invested in quality community and state coverage, and these awards help demonstrate that commitment is paying off for our audience.”
The runners-up in the weekday category were The Providence Journal of Rhode Island and the Bangor Daily News. The runners-up in the Sunday category were The Sunday Republican of Springfield, Massachusetts, and The Berkshire Eagle of Pittsfield, Massachusetts.
The Telegram also won the Sunday Newspaper of the Year category last year.
In other awards announced at Friday’s summit, Press Herald education reporter Riley Board’s coverage of an abuse lawsuit against Bath’s Hyde School won a Publick Occurrences award that recognizes the best work that New England newspapers produce each year. Board’s coverage examined allegations of forced labor and emotional abuse at the nearly 60-year-old private boarding school in Bath.
Emily Duggan, an education reporter for the Sun Journal and Kennebec Journal/Morning Sentinel, was also selected to receive one of the association’s A-Mark Prizes for her parents’ rights groups reporting, which investigated how Maine school boards have been confronted with organized — and sometimes disruptive — efforts to remake local education policies. The A-Mark prizes honor outstanding investigative journalism that reveals hidden truths, holds power to account, or drives public awareness or reform.
“We’re thrilled that the enterprising coverage from Riley and Emily won such distinguished recognition among the best journalism in New England,” Monroe said.
Runners-up in Maine also receiving A-Mark prizes were Sawyer Loftus from the Bangor Daily News/ProPublica, for coverage of U.S. Department of Agriculture foreclosures, and Callie Ferguson and Josh Keefe from the Bangor Daily News/The Maine Monitor for coverage of a Limerick man’s violent arrest at the hands of Maine State Police.
Ferguson, deputy investigations editor for the Bangor Daily News, was also recognized with the New England Journalist of the Year award for her reporting on the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surge in Maine in January.

title: Turn down the heat on Maine’s annual furnace debate
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
It’s strange when a war halfway across the globe could have you fumbling to operate a TV remote in winter gloves, but that’s where we are — or are about to be.
With temperatures in Maine dipping into the 30s overnight and heating oil prices hovering around a record-high $6 a gallon, the annual debate about when to turn on the heat is already underway.
For many Mainers, this is not a First-World problem but an unbearable expense on top of already strained finances. (If you’re in that position, see our guide for where to find heating and other assistance.) Here, however, I’m focusing on households where this is primarily a source of relationship strife — a battle between the budget watchers and those who want to be cozy.
Even for these relatively fortunate people, though, it’s not always as simple as it seems.
“This is exactly the kind of disagreement that can sound trivial from the outside but actually taps into a lot of the things couples argue about,” said Andrea Medaris, director of Psychology Specialists of Maine’s Center for Relationships in Brunswick.
To help sort it out, we turned to Maine experts for their advice about staying warm this winter without going broke (or breaking up).
If it’s about cost
The chillier half of the household has an uphill battle this year. Former TV meteorologist Keith Carson has a solution: math.
Many frugal Mainers live by the rule “no heat until trick or treat,” if not “turkey meat.” In a video for Maine Conservation Voters, the spokesman (and occasional Press Herald weather writer) shows how crunching some numbers can help your case for cranking up the heat when the temperature drops, rather than holding out for a certain date.
Turning the thermostat down by one degree for three hours on a 20-degree day in February will cover the cost of heating up the average Maine house on a 40-degree fall morning, he explains.
In theory, by agreeing to do that later, you should get your way now. But you’ll have to brush up on your algebra.
If it’s about comfort
Now, for a science lesson.
A lot of these arguments stem from biological differences that determine how well we can tolerate the cold. We know smaller people, with a higher ratio of skin surface area to body mass, lose heat more easily, while more muscular people retain it better.
For advice on how to keep your core temperature up, we turned to Tim Smith, founder of the Jack Mountain Bushcraft School in Masardis, who provided the list of tips he gives guests of his guided snowshoe trips in Aroostook County.
Some were practical: wear a hat, then another one, then a hoodie over that. Others were on the silly side, like keeping a picture of Timothee Chalamet in your chest pocket. (He had Patrick Swayze on there, until some younger associates informed him they didn’t know who that was.)
Another — to drink warm liquids, “especially ones that are bad for you” — is only half true. Although alcohol will make you feel flushed, Smith said, it actually lowers your body temperature.
But there was one unconventional method for keeping warm that seemed like it could work for warring couples: Putting cayenne pepper in your socks will irritate the skin and drive circulation, he said. If your shivering partner happens to like a foot rub, you can keep the argument at bay by offering one, extra spicy.
If it’s about something else
Medaris, the psychologist, said the meanings that get attached to conflicts like these — that one person is constantly critical or the other always gets their way — is what couples need to step away from when the heat debate starts escalating.
“One person is cold, the other is thinking about the heating bill, and pretty quickly it can turn into ‘you’re unreasonable’ or ‘you don’t care that I’m uncomfortable,’” she said.
Her advice is to “get on the same side against the problem,” recognizing each person’s needs and working together on a solution, whether that’s agreeing on a thermostat range or putting a space heater in a certain room.
Efficiency Maine has all sorts of tips for keeping in the heat — with caulk, window treatments, reflectors and weather stripping — perfect for a joint DIY project that could help with both comfort and cost.
If that doesn’t go well, research the rates for seeing a couples therapist. That might prompt the stingy spouse to give up a few degrees on the thermostat.

title: Public executions in the US were once a community spectacle and then they stopped
text:
Public executions in the US were once a community spectacle and then they stopped
For about nine decades, executions in the U.S. have been private affairs, often shrouded in secrecy. The stunning Pentagon announcement Thursday that the first military execution in more than 65 years will be livestreamed could change that.
Allowing the world to watch Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan face the firing squad in December would make it the first public execution since two hangings in the 1930s in Kentucky and Missouri drew crowds.
In 1936, a man who reportedly confessed to the rape and murder of a woman was hanged in front of thousands in Owensboro, Kentucky, while the following year, hundreds watched a man in Missouri be hanged.
Proposal harkens back to a bygone era
A livestreamed execution is reminiscent of a bygone period in America's history in which public executions were seen as deterrents to crime as well as popular ceremonies, said Michael L. Radelet, professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder, who has done extensive research on executions.
Parents and teachers would often bring children along to teach them a lesson. The events would sometimes feature a choir, a preacher giving an “execution sermon” and the condemned, who was typically a man being hanged, giving a long speech to the crowd.
In an execution in Leadville, Colorado, in the late 1800s, Radelet said Cyrus Minich, who was being put to death, told the crowd, “Therefore, I apologize and I’m ready to go. Goodbye, goodbye.”
The crowd reportedly responded: “Goodbye Cy, goodbye Cy.”
“This is in the days before TV, so not much going on often in big cities, certainly in rural areas, too, so they were there just for the spectacle,” Radelet said, adding that sometimes it would draw a crowd because the person was so hated.
Video below: Women are rarely executed in the U.S. Here's the data.
Thousands watched country's last public execution
The 1936 hanging in Kentucky of Rainey Bethea is often considered the last public execution in the country, said Radelet.
Bethea was a Black man who reportedly confessed to the rape and killing of a 70-year-old white woman, but was never charged with murder, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Thousands of people attended the event, which was held in a parking lot so the courthouse lawn wouldn’t be damaged by the crowd, according to the center.
But there was also one the following year in which Roscoe “Red” Jackson in Missouri was hanged. The Los Angeles Times reported that some people were given passes to watch, while others climbed trees or cut peepholes to catch a glimpse of the morning execution.
States started to change the policy as an increasing number of people witnessed botched hangings and as broader concerns grew over the events, Radelet said.
“Instead of promoting the sanctity of life and how solemn the circumstance was, with people applauding and having a carnival-like atmosphere, that really turned people off," he said.
Oklahoma City bomber's execution was on CCTV
Robin Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said they have no record of any execution being livestreamed.
The closest came in 2001, when Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh was executed at a federal prison in Terre Haute, Indiana. Then-U.S. Attorney General John Ashcroft announced that victims could attend in person or view it through a closed-circuit television
But will the Army's announcement about livestreaming the execution of Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding many others in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, change the situation?
Maher said she sees Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's comments as “simply aspirational.”
“There is currently no regulation or precedent for an execution to be livestreamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public,” she said in a statement.
Hasan could choose to resist execution and file a habeas petition — a legal request to review the legality of a detention — in civilian court, which could significantly delay the execution, experts said.
Execution would raise both legal and social questions
Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said the announcement raises many legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.
“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” Semel said, adding that she was skeptical that the administration had given a second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.
Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process “much more transparent” and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails. Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when a botched execution in Tennessee has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes.
“I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it’s happening,” she said.

title: Michael Kearns, one of Hollywood’s first openly gay actors, dies at 76
text:
Michael Kearns, one of Hollywood’s first openly gay actors, dies at 76
Michael Kearns, one of Hollywood’s first openly gay actors, has died. He was 76.
The actor, playwright and HIV/AIDS activist died Oct. 5. His cause of death has not been released.
Kearns publicly disclosed that he was HIV-positive in 1991, when few actors had done so.
Related video above | Remembering those we lost in 2026
He used his work in theater and activism to address AIDS and challenge the stigma.
Kearns’ screen career included roles in the films “Body Double” and “And the Band Played On,” as well as appearances on television series including “Cheers,” “Beverly Hills, 90210” and “Life Goes On.”
In “Life Goes On,” he played a character with HIV, bringing the disease into a mainstream television drama during a period when AIDS was heavily stigmatized.
His stage work included directing Robert Chesley’s “Jerker,” a play about gay men during the AIDS crisis.
Kearns’ death was confirmed by filmmaker, professor and Kearns’ longtime friend Roland Palencia, who wrote in part, “Michael's legacy in theaters, in performances, in wherever he went and touched, including our hearts, is unparalleled. All I know is that where his soul travels, it will be a much more interesting place, by far, ever!”

title: ‘Felt like God told me’: 18-year-old goes viral for giving older stranger the shoes off his feet
text:
MARICOPA, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A young man in Arizona is being recognized for his kindness and caring good deed that was caught on camera, unbeknownst to him.
Jordan Hope, 18, didn’t know anyone was watching when he pulled over to help a stranger outside a Maricopa storefront. But by the next day, a lot of people were.
Yareli Madrid captured the moment on video over the weekend that showed Hope stopping to help an older man he spotted walking in a Walgreens parking lot with his shoes barely hanging onto his feet.
“Watching this young man take the shoes off his own feet and give them to an older man who needed them truly touched my heart,” Madrid said in the post. “What makes it even more special is that he did it without anyone watching, without cameras, without expecting recognition or praise. He simply saw someone in need and helped from the goodness of his heart.”
Madrid added a message to Hope’s parents: “If this is your son, you did something right. Please know he is amazing.”
The post quickly drew hundreds of comments, including from someone who said they recognized Hope as a former student, leading the post back to the young man.
“I had no idea,” Hope said of the moment he learned he’d been filmed. “I saw a truck facing me, and I did not know what they were doing. And then the next day, after I found out that it was on Facebook, I was like, whoa.”
‘I just felt like God told me to go over’
Hope said he was on his way to the bank to deposit some money when he passed the Walgreens and noticed the man’s worn-out shoes.
“I looked at his feet, and his shoes were like maybe a fourth on his foot,” Hope said. “I just felt like God told me to go over there, turn around, and just give him some new slides. So I took off my own shoes. I gave them to him, and I just felt like I brought maybe a peace in his life.”
After driving away, something told him to turn back.
Hope found the man inside the Walgreens trying to buy candy and bought it for him. That’s when he learned the man’s wife had died just two weeks earlier.
“That honestly broke my heart,” Hope said. “I just think he needed a friend. It’s hard asking for help sometimes. And I’m just glad that God brought me there in that moment to just show my light on other people.”
Hope offered to take the man to lunch at Culver’s, but a medical condition that causes severe leg swelling made it hard for him to get into Hope’s car. So Hope called him a rideshare, met him at the restaurant, picked up the food, followed him home — and stayed a while just to talk.
“So he didn’t feel that loneliness, you know?” Hope said.
‘We’re hungrier, and we just want to help’
Hope has stayed in touch, checking in on the man by phone every day.
A GoFundMe started on the man’s behalf has already raised more than $2,000 within a couple of days, money Hope said will go toward groceries and other expenses.
Asked why he stopped when so many others might have just walked by, Hope credited his parents, his youth pastor and his faith.
“It wasn’t something out of my comfort zone,” he said. “I knew a tug pulled on my heart, and it was definitely from God... He interrupted my plans for that day to carry on his plans.”
The recent high school graduate, who runs his own computer-building business in Maricopa and Casa Grande, pushed back on the idea that young people don’t care about others.
“People say that this newer generation is just like they don’t care, you know? But I don’t believe that,” Hope said. “I believe that we’re hungrier and we just want to help as much as we can, and we need to be that light.”
As for what’s next, Hope said he hopes to keep building his business while staying active as a leader at his church.
“I’m just a man trying to spread positivity in the Lord’s work,” he said.

title: InvestigateTV+ Weekend: Hidden hacker risks
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Your most sensitive information may not be sitting in a computer — it could be inside the printer down the hall. Chris Nakamoto finds why some offices may be leaving that data exposed.
Plus, a family loses their home as firefighters reported trouble getting water pressure.
Then, records raise questions about what city leaders knew.
Network Nightmares
Multifunction printers and copiers inside America’s police stations, hospitals, and schools aren’t just printing documents - they’re storing them. Every warrant, every patient record, every sealed court filing can be saved on an internal hard drive. When the lease ends and the vendor picks up the machine, that data sometimes goes with it. And in most cases, no one has ever asked what happens to it next.
A breach at a company handling government Medicaid data, what the Texas Attorney General called likely the largest data breach in U.S. history, exposed the personal information of more than 25 million Americans, a reminder of what’s at stake when vendors have unchecked access to sensitive records.
A confidential compliance audit obtained by our team documents exactly those gaps at a sheriff’s office, a charter school, and a medical practice. We talk to a public official who discovered the risk at his own agency and a cybersecurity expert who is sounding the alarm.
We investigate who is responsible for protecting your data and whether anyone actually is.
Water pressure problem
Cities across the country are facing pressure to grow—while aging water systems struggle to keep up. In Temple, Georgia, residents say a house fire exposed a dangerous problem: low water pressure as firefighters tried to protect homes.
Our Andy Pierrotti looks at what city leaders knew about the infrastructure concerns—and why they approved major commercial projects anyway.
911 staffing shortage
When someone calls 911, the person on the other end can make a life-changing difference in seconds. But emergency dispatch centers across the country are struggling to fill open positions—putting more pressure on the people who take those calls every day.
Reporter Ann Emmerich takes us inside one Michigan county dispatch center, where new technology is helping train the next generation of dispatchers—while veterans keep answering the call.
Cyber threats impacting food supply
Cyberattacks can do more than compromise personal information or interrupt a business. Experts warn a serious breach can ripple through the services communities rely on—including health care, water, and the food supply.
Reporter Susan Campbell in Arizona shows us how cyber experts are working to get ahead of those threats—and why everyday digital habits can be part of the defense.

title: 5 months late, Paul LePage’s financial disclosure is in. Here’s what it says.
text:
Almost five months after the deadline, former Gov. Paul LePage’s campaign has submitted the required paperwork to Congress disclosing his personal finances.
The report was due May 15 for all candidates for Congress; the 78-year-old former Maine governor was at that point running unopposed for the Republican nomination for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District. He’s now in a tight general election race against Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap, who submitted his disclosure on the day of the deadline.
As The Washington Sun first reported Tuesday, LePage’s failure to tell the clerk of the House of Representatives about his finances violated federal ethics law. Late reporters are subject to a $200 fine, per the disclosure form, and the U.S. attorney general can bring additional civil proceedings against candidates who knowingly and willingly fail to file a financial disclosure, with penalties up to $75,540.
LePage campaign strategist Brent Littlefield did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but members of the campaign told The Sun this week that the “completely unintentional” delay in filing was a “simple oversight” that “slipped through the cracks.”
The disclosure, now publicly available, was received by the House clerk Tuesday, processed Thursday and posted online shortly thereafter.
LePage reported receiving $39,671 in Social Security so far this year and $22,764 from his state pension. His wife, Ann LePage, also received Social Security and wages from her job at Cook’s Landing Pizzeria & Pub in Edgecomb.
That’s not too different from last year’s report, which LePage filed on time: The LePages received about $70,000 in Social Security in 2025, and LePage’s state pension paid him about $30,000.
Listed the same as last year’s filing, too, is the rental property LePage leases in Augusta from Shawn Moody — a LePage ally who ran in the 2018 gubernatorial race. He reported liability of up to $15,000 for the lease.
According to voter registration records, LePage lives in the Augusta apartment above a barber shop near the Augusta Memorial Circle rotary, next door to one of Moody’s collision repair shops.
The financial disclosure notes that the rental agreement began in May 2025, the same month LePage announced his candidacy for Congress.
LePage did not report owning any individual stocks and said he agreed with Dunlap, his competitor, on banning congressional stock trading, in a recent debate.
The only new item in LePage’s assets in this report is an account with an “SCCU,” valued between $1,000 and $15,000. There are four locations of Space Coast Credit Union, commonly abbreviated as SCCU, within a half-hour drive of LePage’s former home in Ormond Beach, Florida.

title: Vance expresses doubts about Pentagon plan to livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution
text:
HEBRON, Ky. (AP) — Vice President JD Vance cast doubt Friday on whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December but told reporters that if it is livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.”
The Republican vice president said, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” when asked about the plans that the Pentagon confirmed Thursday. But Vance then tried to set aside the controversy over the plans for a public execution and said Hasan’s crimes should not be forgotten.
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting spree at the military base in 2009.
“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said.
“Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it,” he added.
Vance is a convert to the Catholic Church, which has long opposed capital punishment.
President Donald Trump had endorsed Hasan’s execution by firing squad during a Wednesday political event in Texas, suggesting “he deserves it.”
However, Trump was noncommittal when asked Friday whether he wanted the execution livestreamed. “Well, they’re making a determination about that,” Trump told reporters before traveling to a political event in Syracuse, New York.
But he again endorsed the firing squad as the method.
“He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad,” Trump told reporters. “I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him.”
Trump did not answer when asked if he would watch a livestreamed execution.
Earlier Friday morning, the head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the U.S. government’s decision to livestream Hasan’s execution.
“It is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War’s decision to publicly livestream the execution,” Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the conference, said in a statement. He added that the decision was “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.”
Trump approved the execution by firing squad days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection late last month pushed Tennessee’s governor to halt further executions in that state this year.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
From Congress, lawmakers from both parties, Republicans and Democrats, widely condemned what they called the “gruesome” and “disgusting” decision to livestream the execution and implored the Pentagon to reverse course.
“Beyond disgusting,” said Sen. Thom Tillis, the Republican from North Carolina. “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”
The lawmakers said the authoritarian-style spectacle would send a message that runs deeply counter to American values and its system of justice, and risks putting U.S. service personnel and others overseas at risk of blowback.
Virginia Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Intelligence Committee, condemned Hegseth’s plan, saying there’s a reason why “almost no countries in the world engage in this barbaric practice.”
Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said how the U.S. carries out its system of justice matters, and urged the Pentagon “to reverse this gruesome decision.”
Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah pointed to Rome’s bloody spectacles of the past said Hegseth’s plan to livestream the execution risks “feeding that appetite” for corrosive entertainment.
“I urge him to reconsider,” Curtis said.
___
This story has been corrected to show the military base’s name is Fort Hood, not Ford Hood.
___
Associated Press writers Will Weissert and Lisa Mascaro in Washington and Holly Meyer in Nashville, Tennessee, contributed to this report.

title: Letter: Troy Jackson offers a welcome contrast to Susan Collins
text:
While I never have voted — nor will I — for Sen. Susan Collins, I admit her success, in what is still a predominantly male body (women make up only 27% of the U.S. Senate), is commendable. She works hard; her staff are responsive to constituent needs; and she secures earmark funding for the state.
But, quite honestly, none of those qualities is particularly remarkable; each of Maine’s members of Congress do those things.
What is remarkable to me is that she has consistently voted for (95% of the time) the policies of President Donald Trump that have had such a devastating impact on our state, our nation, and the world. For example, since the start of Trump’s second term, Maine has lost $944 million of funding across multiple domains: healthcare, nutrition, transportation, environmental protection, etc. This is more than twice the amount of money Collins’ website says she has brought into the state in FY26 ($425 million). People who can no longer feed their families or access healthcare reap no benefits from many of the earmarks Collins has secured, even while non-Mainers, who have made enormous contributions to her campaign, have.
Her opponent, Troy Jackson, offers a stark and welcomed contrast. He will stand up to the devastating, often heartless, actions of Trump and his team. Jackson has a strong record of supporting reproductive rights, universal free school meals, expanded childcare affordability, paid family medical leave, among other policies that make life more affordable and equitable for all Mainers. Jackson will fight for all Mainers.
Sandy Butler
Orono

title: 5 months late, Paul LePage’s financial disclosure is in. Here’s what it says.
text:
Almost five months after the deadline, former Gov. Paul LePage’s campaign has submitted the required paperwork to Congress disclosing his personal finances.
The report was due May 15 for all candidates for Congress; the 78-year-old former Maine governor was at that point running unopposed for the Republican nomination for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District. He’s now in a tight general election race against Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap, who submitted his disclosure on the day of the deadline.
As The Washington Sun first reported Tuesday, LePage’s failure to tell the clerk of the House of Representatives about his finances violated federal ethics law. Late reporters are subject to a $200 fine, per the disclosure form, and the U.S. attorney general can bring additional civil proceedings against candidates who knowingly and willingly fail to file a financial disclosure, with penalties up to $75,540.
LePage campaign strategist Brent Littlefield did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but members of the campaign told The Sun this week that the “completely unintentional” delay in filing was a “simple oversight” that “slipped through the cracks.”
The disclosure, now publicly available, was received by the House clerk Tuesday, processed Thursday and posted online shortly thereafter.
LePage reported receiving $39,671 in Social Security so far this year and $22,764 from his state pension. His wife, Ann LePage, also received Social Security and wages from her job at Cook’s Landing Pizzeria & Pub in Edgecomb.
That’s not too different from last year’s report, which LePage filed on time: The LePages received about $70,000 in Social Security in 2025, and LePage’s state pension paid him about $30,000.
Listed the same as last year’s filing, too, is the rental property LePage leases in Augusta from Shawn Moody — a LePage ally who ran in the 2018 gubernatorial race. He reported liability of up to $15,000 for the lease.
According to voter registration records, LePage lives in the Augusta apartment above a barber shop near the Augusta Memorial Circle rotary, next door to one of Moody’s collision repair shops.
The financial disclosure notes that the rental agreement began in May 2025, the same month LePage announced his candidacy for Congress.
LePage did not report owning any individual stocks and said he agreed with Dunlap, his competitor, on banning congressional stock trading, in a recent debate.
The only new item in LePage’s assets in this report is an account with an “SCCU,” valued between $1,000 and $15,000. There are four locations of Space Coast Credit Union, commonly abbreviated as SCCU, within a half-hour drive of LePage’s former home in Ormond Beach, Florida.

title: Maine to get $38M in heat assistance early from federal government
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The federal government will soon release about $38 million in heating assistance funding to Maine, Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins announced Friday.
The release of Home Energy Assistance Program funds, which usually happens in late October or early November, would be one of the earliest in recent memory. Collins and independent U.S. Sen. Angus King were among 31 senators to sign a letter last month to the Department of Health and Human Services asking for the expedited release of funding.
The HEAP funding, paid through MaineHousing to heating suppliers as a supplement for low-income households’ winter costs, comes as heating oil prices in Maine hover around a record high, set last month at more than $6 per gallon.
Maine, as the state most reliant on heating oil, stands to gain most from the release of these funds. About 45,000 people received LIHEAP help last year, MaineHousing said.
“I am pleased that these funds are being released to help Mainers afford to heat their homes this winter without having to choose between staying warm and paying for other basic necessities,” Collins said in a news release.
To kickstart the heating oil program, MaineHousing announced this week that it would use about $4 million left over from last winter for about 4,400 vulnerable households across the state.
But that $4 million, combined with the $38 million coming from the federal government this month, will not go as far this winter.
The average HEAP award was set by MaineHousing this summer at about $700, communications director Scott Thistle said Thursday. But after oil costs skyrocketed at the end of the summer and into the fall, the value of that help has fallen significantly, he said.
Last winter, about $23 million in HEAP funding went to heating oil vendors. This year, that number is expected to be about $31 million, Thistle said, including the $4 million in carryover funds.
While about $36.7 million of the federal funding set to be released will go to MaineHousing, about $1.4 million will go to tribal nations: $457,771 will go to the Pleasant Point Passamaquoddy Tribe, $316,098 will go to the Indian Township Passamaquoddy Tribe, $303,530 will go to the Penobscot Nation, and $165,665 each will go to the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians and the Mi’kmaq Nation.
Collins, in the Friday news release, claimed credit for the early release of the funds and touted her work as Senate Appropriations Committee chair to increase HEAP funding nationwide by $20 million. She said she recently spoke with Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, about the importance of releasing the funds.
Last week, though, Gov. Janet Mills wrote to Maine’s congressional delegation demanding that the federal government allocate additional money for heating assistance, saying the war in Iran has made heating oil unaffordable for many and that the assistance won’t go as far as families expect.
Heating oil has become a campaign issue, too, less than a month from Election Day. Collins and her Democratic challenger, former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, have blamed each other for high costs. Gubernatorial candidates have also called for more heating assistance.
Applications for heating assistance are open now. Maine residents hoping to apply for HEAP funding or looking for other assistance can contact their local community action program or call 211. The state also releases an annual Winter Heating Guide with cost-saving resources for households of all incomes.

title: Hermon race track to end season with its biggest payout ever
text:
A pro stock driver could leave with $35,000 in their wallet on Sunday at the inaugural Bar Harbor Bank and Trust 200 in Hermon.
It’s the highlight of a three-day weekend of racing at the Speedway Presented by Bar Harbor Bank and Trust and will conclude the first season under the track’s new owner, former NASCAR Cup Series race winner Ricky Craven of Newburgh.
There will be a 12-lap pro stock heat race, a 15-lap pro stock consolation race, heat races and a feature race in each of the Vintage, Road Runner and Sport 4 classes.
The BHBT 200 will be the last race of the day and will pay $15,000 to the winner and will also pay a driver $100 for each lap led.
It represents the most lucrative payout to a race winner in the 60-year history of the track, which used to be called Speedway 95.
Racing begins at 6 p.m. Friday, with three 33-lap segment races that comprise the Ikey Dorr Memorial Crown Vic 100-lapper, along with a 25-lap Dash 4 Cash Super Street/Street Stock shootout race and 10-lap Crown Vic heat race.
The Ikey Dorr Memorial, named after the Addison driver who died of an apparent heart attack while racing at the Hermon track, will pay $5,000 to the winner.
Saturday’s racing begins at 2 p.m. and will involve 10-lap Super Street/Street Stock and eight-lap Northeast Pro Sprint Series Series and Crown Vic heat races followed by a 12-lap Super Street/Street consolation race and then the 20-lap NEPS, 30-lap Crown Vic and 100-lap Super Street/Street Stock feature events.
The 100-lap Super Street/Street Stock winner will pocket $5,000.
There will be no shortage of contenders at the BHBT 200 with Austin Teras from Gray and D.J. Shaw from Center Conway, New Hampshire, headlining the list.
Teras and Shaw have each won a Granite State Pro Stock Series race at Speedway this season.
Teras was the U.S. Army 100 winner in June, and Shaw finished second. Rounding out the top five were Mike Hopkins of Hermon, Josh St. Clair from Liberty and Mathew Bourgoine from Stetson.
Hopkins, St. Clair and Bourgoine are also among the entrants.
Shaw captured the Stan Meserve Classic 128 at Speedway last weekend. Teras finished ninth.
Warren’s Sylas Ripley was second behind Shaw followed by Windham’s Cole Robie, Scarborough’s Garrett Hall and Gilmanton, New Hampshire, driver Casey Call.
Hall was the only one who hadn’t entered the race as of the Sept. 30 entry list.
Five Oxford 250 winners are included in the field including this past August’s victor, Brandon Barker from Windham.
Teras won the 2025 Oxford 250, Joey Polewarczyk from Hudson, New Hampshire, won it in 2012, and veteran Mike Rowe from Turner is one of the four three-time Oxford 250 winners as he took the checkered flag in 1984, 1997 and 2005.
Hopkins, Berwick’s Joey Doiron and current Granite State Series points leader Jeremy Sorel of Westfield, Massachusetts, will also be among the drivers to watch.
Sorel is followed in the Granite State Series points race by Polewarczyk, Shaw, Durham’s Evan Beaulieu and Woolwich’s Jamie Wright.
Shaw has won three of the six races he has been involved in. Beaulieu and Wright will also be in the field.

title: Visit 1778 at Pownalborough Court House
text:
On Saturday, Sept. 19, visitors to Pownalborough Court House in Dresden will have the opportunity to interact with life in 1778, when the American Revolution was still being fought and the new nation was taking shape.
Historical theater reenactors portraying real people who lived and worked in the region will be incorporated into the Court House's regular museum tours throughout the day. Meet Samuel and Elizabeth Goodwin, who lived at the Court House and operated its tavern; Doctor Colman, a local physician; Martha McGill, a local resident; and militia members Corporal Jacob Lowel and Christopher Erskin. Their stories offer perspectives on community life, medicine, family, and military service in this region during the Revolutionary War.
At 1 p.m., Anette Ruppel Rodrigues, portraying the mother of a Hessian soldier, will present The British King's German Allies in the American War of Independence: A Mother's Perspective, exploring the experiences of German soldiers who served with the British Crown and the families who accompanied them.
Regular tours begin on the hour from 10 a.m. through 3 p.m., with the historical interpreters incorporated into the tour experience. The special presentation will take place separately from tours at 1 p.m. in the courtroom.
All are welcome. Admission is $15 for adults, and free for children, active-duty military personnel, and LCHA members.
Lincoln County Historical Association is a non-profit organization that provides stewardship for the 1754 Chapman-Hall House in Damariscotta, the 1761 Pownalborough Court House in Dresden, and the 1811 Old Jail and Museum in Wiscasset. For more information, please visit www.lincolncountyhistory.org or Facebook at Lincoln County Historical Association (Maine).

title: Demolition of collapsed Old Town bridge to begin Tuesday
text:
Demolition of collapsed Old Town bridge to begin Tuesday
MaineDOT says the work will require intermittent closures of the temporary bridge over the Stillwater River.
Demolition of collapsed Old Town bridge to begin Tuesday
MaineDOT says the work will require intermittent closures of the temporary bridge over the Stillwater River.
The Maine Department of Transportation will begin demolishing the damaged spans of the new Llewellyn Estes Bridge in Old Town next week, with intermittent closures expected on a nearby temporary bridge.
According to MaineDOT, demolition work will begin Tuesday, Oct. 13, on the bridge over the Stillwater River.
The demolition comes after a portion of the new bridge collapsed during construction earlier this year.
The temporary bridge will periodically close between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. beginning Tuesday. Officials say the closures could continue into the week of Oct. 19, depending on construction progress, weather and other conditions.
Crews will carefully separate the damaged spans from the bridge's pier and abutment before breaking them into smaller pieces and lifting them out of the river.
MaineDOT says the temporary closures are necessary because of the damaged spans' proximity to the temporary bridge and the heavy equipment required for demolition.
Drivers traveling along Stillwater Avenue will be directed to a detour using Bennoch Road, North Main Street and College Avenue during closures.
The department says that message boards will provide advance warning of closures. Motorists should expect delays and allow for extra travel time.
Officials say the need for closures will decrease as demolition work progresses farther away from the temporary bridge.

Knife-wielding woman allegedly threatened to 'eat' Bangor man
text:
An Augusta woman allegedly threatened to “eat” a Bangor man and then showed up with a knife outside his home.
Sarea Duane, 22, has been charged with criminal threatening with a dangerous weapon, according to Katy England, a spokesperson for the Bangor Police Department.
Duane allegedly called the man and threatened to “eat” him. Then she allegedly showed up about 1:50 a.m. Thursday outside his Center Street home, where she brandished a knife and again threatened to “eat” him.
She was arrested and taken to the Penobscot County Jail, where she remained early Friday afternoon.

title: Patriots’ banged-up secondary will be tested by Raiders QB Kirk Cousins
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Kirk Cousins’ torrid start has been one of the NFL’s biggest surprises.
The 38-year-old Las Vegas Raiders quarterback is looking to keep it going this week at New England against a Patriots defense that is suddenly having trouble keeping its secondary healthy.
Despite his first loss of the season last week against Kansas City, Cousins is up to 11 touchdown passes — the fastest he has reached that total through four games in his 15-year career. His previous best was 10 TDs through four games in 2018. It has helped quiet the chatter about him being simply a bridge quarterback to Fernando Mendoza, who Las Vegas took No. 1 overall in April.
Cousins said he’s just enjoying seeing the resilience of the entire team in Klint Kubiak’s first season, a group Cousins said is confirming what he observed from them going back to spring workouts.
“These guys, they want to do it the right way. Football means something to them,” Cousins said. “They’re hardworking, listen well, and it makes it a joy to be the quarterback for a group of guys like that. But you’ve got to go prove it again every week.”
That next challenge is a Patriots team that avoided a 1-3 start with a win over Buffalo last week. Not only did quarterback Drake Maye break out of an early season funk with three touchdown passes, but the defense, which played without star cornerback Christian Gonzalez (shoulder), was able to slow Bills quarterback Josh Allen.
Gonzalez was ruled out for the second straight game on Friday, along with fellow starting cornerback Carlton Davis (neck) and rookie Channing Canada (hamstring). Another cornerback, Charles Woods (shoulder) was listed as questionable.
Wide receiver Mack Hollins (calf) was also ruled out. Defensive tackle Christian Barmore (shoulder) and running back Rhamondre Stevenson (knee) were among those listed as questionable.
Whoever is available Sunday, Maye said carrying as much of the momentum they can from last week is the goal.
“You would like to say everybody — especially on offense — you’d like to say that the first three weeks weren’t what we wanted to put out there,” Maye said. “You have to try to build off last week, knowing that it’s not just going to do it for you. You have to put the work in and the focus, and hopefully continue to catch a trend and catch a stride.
Need to know
Las Vegas (3-1) at New England (2-2)
When/where to watch: 1 p.m. Sunday, CBS.
Latest odds: Patriots by 3 1/2.
Against the spread: Raiders 4-0; Patriots 2-1-1.
Last week: Raiders lost to Chiefs 30-27; Patriots beat Bills 29-26.
Last meeting: Raiders beat Patriots 20-13 on Sept. 5, 2025, in Foxborough, Mass.
Series record: Patriots lead 20-18-1.
Matchup to watch
The Raiders’ red-zone defense vs. the Patriots’ red-zone offense. Las Vegas has been susceptible to giving up big plays this season. Once inside the 20, opponents have feasted, scoring touchdowns on 10 of 13 (76.9%) of their trips. But the Patriots have struggled in the red zone through four games, scoring on just four of nine (44.4%) of their opportunities.
Stats and stuff
• Las Vegas and Detroit are the only teams that have scored 25 or more points in each game this season. It’s the second time in franchise history the Raiders have accomplished that in their first four games of a season. The 2002 team was the other one to do it.
• The Raiders lead the NFL with nine takeaways, one more than four other teams. That total is tied for sixth in franchise history with the 1972 team for the most through four games in a season.
• Las Vegas has 12 sacks and allowed five, and the Raiders’ seven-sack differential is tied with the Lions for the league’s best.
• The Raiders’ Dylan Laube leads the NFL with a 33.4-yard kickoff return average.
• The Patriots, including the playoffs, have won nine of their past 10 home games, including a 20-3 win over Pittsburgh in Week 2.
• New England is looking to snap a three-game losing streak to Las Vegas.
• Maye’s seven interceptions are one shy of the eight he threw in the regular season last year.
AP Sports Writer Mark Anderson in Las Vegas contributed.

title: El Niño's storm-killer winds and climate's warming waters in fight over future of Hurricane Isaias
text:
A supersized El Niño’s decapitating winds and the Gulf of Mexico’s toasty, storm-fueling waters are battling over the future strength of Hurricane Isaias. And the storm’s tilt and eye show who’s winning.
For now, it’s the waters charged by climate change.
All Atlantic hurricane season there has been “this battle between shear and just the overall conducive conditions,” said Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach.
El Niño — the natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps weather worldwide — dominated. Its wind patterns smothered almost any wisp of a storm from strengthening in the Atlantic, while boosting what will soon be record high levels in the Pacific, Klotzbach said.
Wind shear versus warm waters
It’s called wind shear and it pushes the tops and middle of storms around, making them lopsided and keeping them from making a complete circular eyewall, which is when storms can really power up, Klotzbach and University at Albany’s Kristen Corbosiero said.
The other ingredients for a storm to turbocharge a storm are pushing back. There is plenty of fuel in warm water and moisture. The Gulf of Mexico is about 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5 degrees Celsius) warmer than normal. The 86 degree waters (30 degrees Celsius) are 100 to 500 times more likely to be that extra hot because of climate change from the burning of coal, oil and gas, said climate scientist Kristina Dahl, vice president of the nonprofit Climate Central, which calculates the boost global warming causes to extreme weather.
“But there’s a certain point where it’s like, I don’t care how hot the waters are and how much moisture you have, if shear gets to a certain point, the shear is gonna win,” Klotzbach said.
The thunderstorm seeds of something bigger earlier in the week grew from circular winds over Central America but often were lopsided and couldn’t quite form a crucial eyewall, all because of El Niño’s high-level strong winds that pushed a would-be storm’s top sideways, experts said.
Then a window of moderation opened for just a couple of days, but it was enough, Corbosiero said. It makes sense it was in the Gulf of Mexico and in October, because El Niño has less of an effect in the Gulf than it does in the main Atlantic, she said. And storms often pop up in that region in October because of more northerly storm systems that help foster the right conditions.
Wind shear wasn’t exactly low, but it was a moderate level, when other factors like unusually warm waters and heavy moisture can kick in. Isaias rapidly intensified from 40 mph to 80 mph (64 kph to 129 kph) in a day and by late Wednesday, Isaias became the latest-in-the-season first Atlantic hurricane to form since 1914, Klotzbach said.
“The warm waters and high moisture won,” Klotzbach said. Isaias Friday was not tilting and had a strong eye, the hurricane center said.
By Friday morning, Isaias blew past the threshold for becoming a major hurricane with winds of 111 mph (178 kph), strengthening to 120 mph winds (195 kph). The National Hurricane Center forecasts it to weaken to a strong Category 2 storm before landfall.
What to expect before landfall
Before Isaias comes ashore — forecast for probably somewhere from the Mississippi and Alabama coast to the Florida Panhandle late Friday night or early Saturday — the wind shear will strengthen from moderate levels of around 20 mph (32 kph) to 52 mph (84 kph) and then Isaias will start to struggle, which is good news for coastal residents, Klotzbach said.
But as of Friday morning, hurricane center forecasters said the coast is in “a tenuous spot” because it would only take a six-hour delay in the onset of that more intense wind shear for Isaias to bring a stronger-than-expected landfall. Regardless of what will happen with wind shear, it will still be a dangerous hurricane when it hits land, forecasters said.
“Once it gets to the coast, we know that the storm surge is going to be deeper and farther reaching because of sea level rise caused by climate change,” Dahl said. “So in this part of the world, there’s been about six and a half inches of sea level rise over the past 100 years or so that’s attributable directly to climate change.”
The National Hurricane Center is calling the surge “life-threatening.”
A warmer atmosphere means storms hold and then dump more rain, worsening flooding, Dahl said. The hurricane center is warning about urban, river and flash flooding in the Southeast this weekend.
“There’s a little bit of a battle here going on, but I think the really important thing to remember is that climate change is like this long-term big kahuna warming everywhere, and El Niño’s like a little icing on the cake,” Dahl said.

title: Portland Public Schools launches new Black History curriculum, first of its kind in Maine
text:
Portland Public Schools launches new Black History curriculum, first of its kind in Maine
The district says its new curriculum will connect students with African American history through classroom lessons and visits to historic Portland landmarks.
Portland Public Schools launches new Black History curriculum, first of its kind in Maine
The district says its new curriculum will connect students with African American history through classroom lessons and visits to historic Portland landmarks.
Portland Public Schools is rolling out a new Black History curriculum this fall, becoming the first school district in Maine to develop a full K-12 curriculum focused on the subject, according to district officials.
The district announced Thursday that students in grades 6 to 11 will be learning through the new curriculum, which includes exploring African American history in Portland.
As a part of the rollout, all seventh graders will participate in fieldwork along the Portland Freedom Trail, which highlights historically significant sites connected to the city's African American community.
Students will visit the Portland Museum of Art to view works by contemporary African American artists and participate in workshops led by Black educators and artists.
The fieldwork is part of a seven-week unit called "Freedom Trails," which connects 19th-century African American history with Portland's local history, including the role of Black Mainers in the abolitionist movement.
The district said more than 25 contributors helped to develop the program for the past 6 years.
Students are scheduled to participate in fieldwork at the Portland Museum of Art on Oct. 15 and along the Portland Freedom Trail on Oct. 19.

title: Maine attorney files ethics complaint against Sen. Susan Collins
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - A Maine attorney has filed a complaint with the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Ethics against Sen. Susan Collins, hoping the committee will investigate allegations reported by ProPublica that Collins accepted campaign donations in exchange for government contracts.
The bipartisan committee, which is composed of three Democrats and three Republicans, provides ethical guidance and investigates complaints against senators and Senate staff members.
“I believe that it’s important to demand the best of our elected officials,” said Valerie Adams, who filed the complaint. “I believe that these are issues that we as voters should pay attention to, and I hope that the committee will act on it and open an investigation.”
Anyone can file a complaint. The committee receives dozens of allegations each year, but according to annual reports reviewed by 8 Investigates, most are dismissed, either because of a lack of evidence or because the alleged conduct does not violate Senate rules.
Over the last five years, 91% of complaints were dismissed without an investigation.
“I believe the issue needs media attention in order to put pressure on the committee to open an investigation,” Adams said.
Complaints that are not dismissed proceed to an initial inquiry. Over the past five years, 63% of complaints that reached this stage were ultimately dismissed.
For minor violations, the committee can issue a public or private letter telling a senator they violated Senate ethics rules. It issued three letters over the past five years.
If the committee finds serious ethical concerns, it may open a formal review, which could result in disciplinary action. The committee opened one review over the past five years. The review was closed after its subject, New Jersey Sen. Robert Menendez (D), resigned.
The committee has not issued any formal sanctions in recent history.
“I don’t think we should ever lose hope that what we’re doing will matter, and whether or not an investigation is opened, I think it’s important that the issue is getting attention, and I think it’s important to request that an investigation be opened,” Adams said.
In response to the complaint, a Collins campaign spokesperson wrote: “This is getting to be pathetic. For the third consecutive week, a recently failed Democratic candidate has parroted false charges that they know nothing about, against Susan Collins.”
Adams previously worked as an assistant district attorney for Cumberland County. This spring, she lost her primary race against incumbent District Attorney Jacqueline Sartoris.
Because of confidentiality requirements, much of the committee’s work takes place behind closed doors.

title: Maine Attorney General’s Office accidentally shares confidential case information with media outlets
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - A supervisor within the Criminal Division of the Maine Attorney General’s Office accidentally emailed a document that included confidential case information to a number of media outlets, including WMTW.
The 45-page document, which was sent at 2:50 p.m. Thursday, featured information about dozens of homicide and manslaughter cases in Maine, including the names of suspects who have not yet been charged.
The document also includes details about alleged crimes and evidence gathered that have not been released publicly.
The supervisor who sent the email recalled it at 2:53 p.m., three minutes after it was sent.
At 3:21 p.m., the Attorney General’s Office sent another message asking everyone who received the email to delete it, along with the attached document.
“The inadvertent disclosure of sensitive information by this office was a mistake and we own that,” the Maine Attorney General’s Office said in a statement shared at 6:12 p.m. Thursday. “Unfortunately, a distribution list reserved to push public information out to the media was accidentally used. We will learn from this error and are working hard to ensure this does not negatively impact the significant work we do on behalf of the people of Maine. We respectfully request our partners in the media help us by not compounding our error.”
It appears the intent of the email was to get lawyers and investigators to update their reports for internal use.

title: Glenburn Elementary's Halloween Trail Opens Nightly Through October 31st, Free Admission And Family-friendly Scares
text:
Glenburn’s Getting Spooky With A Haunted Trail And A ‘Boos & Bumpers’ Event This Month
Six years ago, as folks were looking for fun ways to celebrate the Halloween season amidst a pandemic, the Glenburn Parks and Rec Department created a spooky, family-friendly trail behind the Glenburn Elementary School at 991 Hudson Road that gave small groups an excuse to get outside and enjoy a little holiday fun.
Since then, it's grown to become a much-loved tradition in this small Penobscot County town.
Read More: Is Bangor Opera House Haunted? Take a Halloween Tour & Find Out
The trail is decorated with a different theme each year. There's never anything too jumpy or gory, so it's ok for kids of all ages.
The roots and stumps are well marked in white paint, so you don't trip and there are cameras monitoring the trail as well, for safety.
Some tips for you, if you've never been: wear comfy shoes, bring a flashlight and stay on the path.
There's a bit of a walk from the end of the trail to the parking lot, but they do sometimes have hayrides that you can hop onto to hitch a ride back.
Read More: Must Visit Haunted Attractions in New England
This year's Haunted Halloween Trail will run nightly from 4-9 PM from Friday October 24th through Saturday, October 31st.
The trail is free to visit.
The night it opens (10/24), is also the night of the Glenburn Parks and Rec's 'Boos and Bumpers' Bash at the elementary school.This is a free Trunk-or-treat event, for all ages.
That will take place from 4 PM to 6:30 PM.
"Trunks decorated & full of treats for the all the little goblins, 3 food trucks to take care of your supper, Brick & Embers Pizza, McPhees along with Nate & Ollies rolled ice cream will have some special fall flavors to try."

title: The pro-life movement is the selfish movement
text:
Dan Pryor of Gorham makes the argument in an Oct. 1 letter (“Remember: Abortion kills human life”) that abortion is both selfish and destroys a unique human life. As he puts it, “abortion is the self-centered murder of the innocent.”
There are two sides to this argument. On the other side:
To quote the headline of an Oct. 1 report in this newspaper, “Every day, thousands of residents face the hardest financial choices, as households struggle to afford basic expenses.” Being able to afford basic expenses becomes that much more difficult as the number of children in a family grows.
The amount of carbon dioxide dumped into the atmosphere increases with each increase in the number of people on the planet. The same goes for how long it takes to commute to work, and for how much a house costs. More people exacerbate problems that we could otherwise live with.
Educational expenses are driving up property taxes, and those expenses increase with an increase in the number of students. The pro-life movement would make life miserable for all of us, by increasing global warming, hunger, property taxes and time on the road, in order to save a fetus that would never know it is alive.
The letter read, “There is nothing more selfish in America than the ‘pro-choice’ abortion movement.” In reality, there is nothing more selfish or short-sighted than the “pro-life” movement.
William Vaughan Jr.
Chebeague Island

title: Falmouth residents rally against proposed CMP transmission line upgrade
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
When Roger Brothers moved to Falmouth with his young family three years ago, he didn’t think twice about the transmission lines running through an easement on his property. With towering trees running on both sides of the power corridor between his home and the suburban road, he said it felt like he lived in the woods, despite being just a five minute drive from Portland.
Now, some trees along the corridor will have to be cleared as the transmission line gets an upgrade, a project that has Brothers worried about the future of the land where he planned to raise his children. At a meeting with a dozen neighbors in August, he learned he was not alone in his concern.
“It’s really getting to the point where it could be too late. We really need our representatives to advocate for us and protect us. Please help us,” said Brothers at the Falmouth Town Council meeting on Sept. 28.
As Maine utility regulators will soon deliberate whether to allow a transmission upgrade project running throughout the greater Portland area, some abutters are sprinting to oppose the project in time.
Falmouth residents — primarily organized under the Alliance for Responsible Infrastructure, which includes concerned abutters of the project from neighboring communities — claim Central Maine Power’s proposed Greater Portland Transmission Upgrades Project would negatively impact the health, property value and woodlands of their communities.
“The impact on Falmouth will be sprawling and permanently scar its landscape,” said Jaime Batista, a leader of the Alliance for Responsible Infrastructure, which filed to become a nonprofit.
The proposed infrastructure project runs from Yarmouth down around Falmouth into Portland, with a separate leg going up through Westbrook. It would upgrade two substations in Cumberland and Portland, build a new Portland substation, rebuild a transmission line between Cumberland and Falmouth and in Westbrook, and install a new transmission line between Portland and Cumberland.
The new poles for the transmission lines would range from 80-110 feet in height. Residents say this would tower above all the area’s foliage, while a CMP spokesperson says it would mostly be shorter than the tallest trees. Abutters say the upgrade would require clearcutting trees along 135-foot-wide corridor, though CMP says on the the majority of the route, the project would use compact spacer-cable design and not need the whole 135 feet. On some areas of the line, the 135 right-of-way already exists, said CMP.
According to CMP, the upgrade is necessary to strengthen the energy grid in Greater Portland, which has over 200,000 CMP customers and critical facilities such as hospitals, schools and residences that would be better protected from widescale power outages by the project.
“In Falmouth, the primary driver is reliability: three substations rely on a single transmission line, creating the risk that one outage could interrupt service across the entire community, as occurred in 2023,” wrote a CMP spokesperson in an email.
The transmission upgrades will also allow for more growth in the region and enable more climate-friendly electrification of existing infrastructure, said the CMP spokesperson.
Abutters and other residents in Falmouth are concerned about the proximity of the line to hundreds of homes and the possible future site of the future public middle school, the loss of trees that would be cut down to expand the existing corridor, the decrease of the value of properties that are in sight of the update and the environmental impacts of maintaining the broadened route.
At the Town Council meeting, several residents said that if the line were built next to their homes as proposed, they likely would move out of town.
“When you first hear about it, your heart sort of sinks,” said Joseph Smith, a neighbor of Brothers who arranged the meeting of concerned neighbors with his wife Anya Petersen.
That gathering prompted the neighbors to rapidly organize, sending out 2,500 flyers to abutters in other towns to make them aware of their concerns, creating an elaborate website with project updates and petitions, speaking during public comment about their concerns at Falmouth and Portland council meetings and entering the review process with state regulators.
“We realized we have some autonomy here,” said Smith.
As is typical for projects of this voltage, CMP asked the Maine Public Utilities Commission for a certificate of public convenience and necessity, which uses sworn testimony and evidence to determine the project serves a public need, said a PUC spokesperson. The process, which started after the PUC determined that CMP’s application was complete in July, typically takes around a year.
If the project is approved by the PUC, the project would take between three and four years to complete, according to the CMP website.
While anyone can submit comments about a project being reviewed by the PUC, the facts within them cannot be treated as evidence. However, if an individual or municipality files to be an intervenor in a case they can submit official testimony, make legal arguments and question witnesses as part of the review process. All written testimony from intervenors, including from the Alliance for Responsible Infrastructure and the support they hope to receive from municipalities, must be submitted by Oct. 23 to be included in the public record.
On Sept. 2, on the behalf of the Alliance for Responsible Infrastructure Batista filed a late petition to be an intervenor, which was granted. On Sept.14, he then filed a motion asking the Public Utilities Commission to create a threshold merit phase in its review of the project, meaning an independent party would review what CMP has calculated as the need for the project.
“We just want CMP to be held accountable for the need for this expansion,” said Portland resident Rita Clare, who rents a condominium near the transmission corridor, where she loves to bird. “We just want to buy some time to see if this is actually necessary.”
In a response filed with the PUC on Sept. 28, CMP asked that the motion be denied, saying that the PUC’s existing examination the project’s need that is already part of the review process makes the requested step duplicative and unnecessary delays the approval of the project.
“The requested threshold phase would not make the record fairer or clearer,” said the CMP filing.
In an unrelated ruling this week, the PUC denied CMP’s requested rate increase of almost $70 million. The rejection caused CMP to halt 19 transformer improvements and other infrastructure plans. The Greater Portland Transmission Upgrades Project is not one of the plans impacted.
At the Falmouth Town Council meeting on Sept. 28, residents spoke for hours both against the proposed Greater Portland Transmission Upgrades Project and how CMP has failed to properly inform them about the plan, with many saying they heard about it within the past month or several days.
“I’m incredibly troubled by multiple reports that many property owners and key stakeholders heard little or absolutely nothing directly from CMP about a proposal with such significant implications,” said Councilor Alisa Morton at the meeting.
“This is a half a billion dollar project that has flown under the radar of many, many people,” said Councilor Sean Mahoney, who also disclosed that he works for Conservation Law Foundation, which is also an intervenor in this project.
A spokesperson for CMP said that in December 2025, the company held open houses in each of the five communities where the upgrades are planned, which were noted on the project website and on the Town of Falmouth’s Facebook page and municipal website.
On Sept. 18, CMP sent abutters notices about an impending open house, with postcards going out on Oct. 1 detailing open houses in each of the towns between Oct. 28 and Nov. 12, said the spokesperson. The open house in Falmouth will be held at Falmouth Elementary School the evening of Nov. 5 — almost two weeks after the intervenor deadline, noted Morton.
At the behest of the public, Falmouth Town Councilors approved a motion authorizing council leadership and town staff to send a letter to CMP conveying the disappointment and anger heard from residents and asking for more information about the project.
The letter said that while the town’s initial role was to facilitate sharing of information about the project, the unanswered questions about its impact changed the council’s approach as the inventor testimony deadline nears.
“That, coupled with residents’ concerns, has prompted the Council to consider stronger action and seek your direct engagement in obtaining clear answers from CMP” said the letter.
The council additionally made an order directing town staff to file with the PUC support of the Alliance for Responsible Infrastructure’s motion to establish a threshold merits phase.
At the next Town Council meeting on Oct. 14, the council will consider a resolution regarding the proposed project, a current draft of which asks for clearer answers from CMP and supporting the request that the PUC to review the necessity of the upgrades.
“The town must advocate for residents and protect Falmouth’s interests in both public and private property,” said Morton. “In my view, that means publicly opposing the proposal as submitted and pressing CMP to justify the need and scale of the project.”
The resolution, if passed, would likely also be filed as-written to the PUC case, said town staff.
Following the submission of testimony by Oct. 23, on Dec. 2 all parties will cross-examine the testimony at an intervenor technical conference in Hallowell on Dec. 2. Following deliberation from PUC commissioners, the commission will file a final order, said a PUC spokesperson.

title: Federal government auditing Maine’s Medicaid program
text:
The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has launched a program integrity audit of Maine’s Medicaid program, federal officials confirmed.
The agency said in a statement Friday that the audit will examine MaineCare’s “oversight operations and processes in high-risk areas.”
“The audit will assess the state’s safeguards against fraud, waste, and abuse, including how it identifies risks, refers suspected fraud, and addresses improper payments,” according to the agency’s statement.
CMS oversees the Medicaid program, which is operated by the states with federal oversight. Medicaid programs, which include insurance and healthcare services for lower-income people, are funded with a blend of federal and state dollars.
The statement offered that no further details, including what specific programs the agency is auditing, will be available while the audit is ongoing.
Maine was in the crosshairs of federal regulators earlier this year, when a U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General audit found the state had made at least $45.6 million in improper payments. The audit, which examined support services for autistic children in 2023, said Maine failed to document services correctly and did not complete “post-payment reviews.”
At the time, Maine officials responded by noting that the Office of Inspector General’s audit did not include accusations of fraud.
In response to CMS announcing that the agency is conducting an audit, Lindsay Hammes, a Maine Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson, said in a statement on Friday that “protecting MaineCare from fraud and abuse is essential to making sure that health care remains available for the people and families who rely on it and that taxpayer dollars are invested responsibly.”
Hammes said the state DHHS has its own program integrity unit to monitor MaineCare programs for fraud. When needed, the Office of the Maine Attorney General will investigate potential crimes, she said.
In late 2025, Maine DHHS suspended payments to Portland-based Gateway Community Services and continues to investigate the provider for accusations of falsifying billing records. Gateway provides Medicaid services for people with disabilities. Gateway officials have denied the allegations.

title: The reason Maine must retire Susan Collins from the U.S. Senate
text:
Peter L. Murray is an attorney who lives in Portland.
As the fall campaigns heat up, the Troy Jackson-Susan Collins contest has rightfully commanded the most attention of Maine voters. Susan Collins has represented our state in the Senate for nearly 30 years. She is a veteran among her colleagues and chairs the Appropriations Committee, an important committee for her constituents back home.
Collins has claimed, with some justification, to be a voice for moderation among the baying of her MAGA fellow senators. In her campaign, she stresses her experience, her political savvy and what she has done for the state of Maine in terms of business for the Bath Iron Works, other federal projects and earmarks.
Her opponent, Troy Jackson, has no such federal track record. His experience so far has been entirely within the state of Maine, where he has worked for conventional Democratic priorities and on improving the lot of working people. He is earnest, dedicated and politically straightforward.
All this having been said, there is one overarching and compelling reason why we Mainers must retire Susan Collins and elect Troy Jackson to the U. S. Senate. Our country is under the domination of a dangerous chief executive. So far, the Republican majorities in Congress have failed to restrain any of his erratic and destructive excesses, both in foreign policy and domestic administration.
The president has felt free to levy war, impose irrational tariffs, antagonize our international allies, oppress and terrify immigrants on American soil, kill civilians abroad without trial and even undertake bizarre construction projects in Washington, all in violation of the law and the Constitution, with a supine and quiescent Congress totally failing to raise effective objection or control. Unless countered and restrained, he will continue this kind of behavior for another two years with who-knows-what consequences.
Only by electing Democratic majorities in both the House and Senate is there any hope of activating our constitutional checks and balances to prevent our country from going further off the rails at the hands of of this modern Caligula.
In the Senate, it is very close. The change of a single Senate seat can spell the difference between a Senate that will bow to the will of the president and one that will stand up against his worst impulses. Even if Susan Collins imagines that she would not follow the president’s line on every vote, she would be counted as a Republican in determining the leadership of the Senate and in generating its majorities on most legislation.
It has been repeatedly pointed out that regardless of her protestations of independence, she has voted with the president so far over 90% of the time. Those who argue that Susan Collins’ seniority will enable her to do more for the state of Maine need to keep in mind that her seniority will only count if the Republicans maintain control of the Senate, which will mean further chaos and destruction at the hand of an errant president.
We must vote for Jackson, because a vote for Collins is a vote for Trump. We cannot afford to weigh the relative expertise and experience of the two candidates. For this one time, we have to vote based solely on party affiliation.
Persons who wish the status quo to continue, and perhaps worsen, as the president becomes ever more erratic and irrational, can vote for Susan Collins. The rest of us, Democrats, independents and, yes, Republicans who are concerned and horrified by the current presidency, must support her Senate challenger and make sure that he takes her place.
Our experience with or under our current chief executive shows us the urgent need for reform of our constitutional structure to prevent such a political leader from asserting and misusing such power ever again. But in the meantime, in the current crisis, we here in Maine owe it to our country to do everything we can to help restore the effectiveness of our existing checks and balances by retiring Susan Collins and electing Troy Jackson to the United States Senate.
