title: A mother’s journey to forgive the man who killed her son
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - Forgiveness is easily said, but often rarely given, just like second chances.
For one Nashville mother, however, forgiveness and a second chance for a career criminal were on a collision course.
Clemmie Greenlee’s lesson in forgiveness came after years of tears, hatred and anger aimed at Kim Birdsong. Then decades later, in a move that’s shocked family and friends, Greenlee found peace after the unthinkable.
On December 9th, 2003, Clemmie’s only child, Rodriguez Greenlee, took his final breath after he was shot. She remembers a late-night phone call. A mad rush to the hospital, only to find her son dead.
“All I did was just climb on top of the bed on him. And I went head to head, nose to nose, lip to lip, body to body. And let him know that you’re getting your rest now. But mama ain’t gonna never, ever, let your name go.” Clemmie said.
The shooter, Kim Birdsong or “Bird,” said he was shot at first and retaliated.
“I stood there and waited,” remembered Birdsong. “I [had] seen one of the guys and it unfolded. I just, I lost my mind at the moment.”
Clemmie was also losing her mind.
“I hate you. I hate you. Whoever you are, I hate you,” Clemmie recounted her grief. “You know, you messed up my whole... I was a happy girl. I don’t care what kind of life I had. I was a happy girl. You took not only my son, you took that away from me.”
When asked how often Clemmie thought about the man who killed her son in the time that followed, she said it was constant.
“Every single second. Every single second,” Clemmie said. “I never let this man out of my mind. I don’t talk about it to my family. I don’t talk about it to no other people, but nobody. Nobody has a clue what I go through. Nobody.”
Birdsong was convicted and sentenced to 8 years for that crime. His rap sheet as a career criminal is extensive.
“My momma never raised me like that. She raised me. She was a loving person, and she raised me to be an honest man. Somewhere along the way, I strayed,” Birdsong admitted.
Meanwhile, Clemmie started a support group for moms who had lost children to violence. In May 2018, however, the grief had taken its toll. She was diagnosed with Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy and needed a heart transplant.
“They told me, actually, ‘Clemmie, your heart is broken’” she said.
Her new heart led to a change of heart.
Her hatred for Birdsong was slipping away.
Yet, how could you forgive someone who killed your only child?
Her family and friends did not understand.
“I used to make a joke every time somebody come at me with something and I don’t want to talk foul about it,” Greenlee said. “I’ll say, let me call 1-800-JESUS and just see what he’d tell me. And I think I played myself into that stupid belief.”
Then years later, in 2019, that fake phone call led to a real call after Clemmie found Birdsong in prison. Surrounded by friends, Clemmie spoke to her son’s killer.
“Probably after 2-3 minutes, I was able to say, ‘Yes, I am here. What is your name?’” Clemmie said as she wiped away tears.
After that conversation, Clemmie went from hating this man to putting money in Birdsong’s prison account. Then, as they wrapped up the call, she had one last inconceivable request.
“I don’t have my child to call me and tell me ‘Happy Mother’s Day’ again. And you took that from me,” Clemmie shared. “And I said, ‘You need to be my son at Mother’s Day and call me and tell me Happy Mother’s Day.’”
We asked Birdsong what that call was like.
“It was good,” he admitted. “I mean, and I’m proud that I was able to do that and give her, you know, some of that.”
Recently, Birdsong was released from prison, and the first person he called was Clemmie. Her heart told her to forgive him, but something was holding her back.
Could she actually do it?
She invited our cameras there as she welcomed her son’s killer into her home.
“He’s in my yard. Not only is he in my yard, but he is on my front porch. I just can’t believe it,” Clemmie said.
Clemmie came face-to-face with the man who killed her son. Years of pain came rushing back. Followed by the undeniable comfort of peace. Tears and hugs followed.
Hurt, heal, let it go.
Words that Clemmie has always lived by, playing out in real time.
As forgiveness is the bridge that connects pain and peace, that bridge is for Birdsong as well.
“I needed you to stand in front of me, looking at him. So, you can say to yourself that I forgive myself,” Clemmie told Birdsong to his face.
In the aftermath of forgiveness comes closure, and that place where Rodriguez Greenlee died - at the corner of Lischey Avenue and Berry Street - is where Clemmie joined her tribe to find her closure.
Hand in hand with Birdsong.
“It’s all I needed,” she said. “I’m good.”
Clemmie said forgiving Birdsong is the hardest thing she has ever had to do, even harder than burying her child.
That forgiveness has brought new beginnings.
Clemmie and “Bird” have spoken every single day since they met in person in 2019. There are also plans for a book. They want to show people that unconditional forgiveness is doable and essential.

title: Hurricane Simon strengthens to a Category 2 storm, the National Hurricane Center says
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Hurricane Simon has strengthened to a Category 2 storm and was forecast to approach Mexico’s coast as a major hurricane this weekend, the National Hurricane Center said Friday.
The center said maximum sustained winds have increased to nearly 100 mph (155 kph), and that Simon is expected to continue strengthening rapidly during the next day or so. Simon is forecast to become a major hurricane by late Friday and strengthen further on Saturday.
U.S. forecasters earlier issued a hurricane warning for parts of the central and southwest coast, where hurricane-force winds were expected within 36 hours.
Simon is expected to bring heavy rainfall over parts of southwestern Mexico, with rain possibly concentrated across the coast of Jalisco and parts of Michoacan, Colima and Nayarit. Forecasters warned of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Simon was centered about 335 kilometers (210 miles) south of Manzanillo and 500 kilometers (310 miles) south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes.
The state of Jalisco suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas. It also asked the tourism sector in Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for U.S. tourists, to ensure that both workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones by Friday afternoon.
“If we let our guard down and try to come up with a last-minute action plan, it is highly likely that lives will be lost,” said the state director of civil protection, Sergio Ramírez.
Governor Pablo Lemus urged the public to stay informed at all times given the hurricane’s “highly erratic behavior,” which has caused it to change direction between Manzanillo and Puerto Vallarta.
“What is certain is that it will hit the coast of Jalisco with very heavy rains starting this Friday, throughout the weekend, and on Monday,” he said.
The state of Guerrero has also suspended classes and non-essential activities in areas along the coast and in the central part of the state due to heavy rains brought by Simon since Thursday.
The flooding hit the port of Acapulco the hardest, where some streets were turned into rivers, with vehicles swept away by the current and homes and businesses flooded. There have been no reported casualties, said Governor Evelyn Salgado.
The U.S. Embassy also issued alerts advising against entering the water or walking on the beach and urging travelers to heed the warnings of local authorities.
Farther north, Tropical Storm Rachel was expected to reach Baja California, northwestern Mexico and Southern California this weekend. It had maximum winds of 85 kph (50 mph) and was forecast to weaken, though it may bring heavy rain to the area.
Tropical storm activity has been above average this season in the Pacific, due to the effects of a strong El Niño.
The climate phenomenon typically depresses storm activity in the Atlantic. Hurricane Isaias, which was expected to hit the U.S. Gulf Coast late Friday or Saturday, developed more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season.

title: 4 Maine food products win Golden Fork Awards
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Four Maine-based products won Golden Fork Awards Thursday as part of the biennial Maine Food Producer Showcase.
Haymay Creamery of Farmington won Best in Show, Savory, for Pudge, a washed-rind cheese made with milk from local farms. Portland’s Molässa won Best in Show, Sweet, for their Hot Molasses, a light, sweet molasses with caramel notes.
Mark Foods/Bristol Seafood of Portland won Best in Show, Seafood, for Wilder Miso Sablefish; and Portland’s Three of Strong Spirits won Best in Show, Beverage, for Valley Cove Rum, a blend of three of the distillery’s oldest barrels.
The event, held at Portland’s Holiday Inn by the Bay, featured more than 70 of the state’s food, beverage and seafood producers. The gathering attracted hundreds of buyers, distributors, retailers, chefs, foodservice professionals and industry partners, and was presented by University of Maine System Graduate & Professional Center (Maine Center).
“The Maine Food Producer Showcase creates meaningful connections between producers and the buyers, distributors and industry partners who can help them grow,” said Naomi Neville, program director of the Maine Center’s Food Accelerators, in a media statement. “Each year we see new relationships formed, new products discovered and new opportunities created for Maine businesses and our broader food economy.”

title: Embattled Madawaska town manager resigns and forfeits public hearing
text:
David Daigle, the embattled town manager of Madawaska, resigned Thursday night, ending his monthlong suspension over the financial mismanagement of a music festival that overran its budget.
Daigle’s resignation came during an evening Select Board meeting. The meeting’s sole agenda item was an executive session for personnel matters, which was anticipated to be used to schedule a public hearing that would allow testimony regarding Daigle’s suspension as the board moved to fire him with cause.
Daigle had requested the hearing last week — as is his right under Maine municipal law, which requires a strict process for a manager to be fired. That hearing will no longer be held.
“Dave tendered his resignation last night and the Board has accepted it,” Select Board Chair Renee Deschaine said. “The town is looking forward to the future.”
Dechaine said the board and Daigle had reached an agreement, the terms of which she declined to discuss. The Bangor Daily News has filed a Freedom of Access Act request to obtain the agreement.
Daigle had been on paid leave since Sept. 3. The Select Board has cited his handling of a music festival in late August as the reason for his removal.
The former town manager was one of two lead organizers for Northern Maine Summerfest, a single-day festival that brought a handful of relatively unknown artists to perform on the shores of Long Lake.
The festival ran $15,000 over budget and generated significantly less revenue than expected, leaving the town short more than $41,000 that the Select Board opted to cover using funding from an economic development reserve account.
The move avoided taking money from the town’s undesignated fund, which would have required calling a special town meeting for the public to vote.
“There was a number, and it was exceeded, and that’s a problem,” Deschaine said during a Sept. 15 meeting.
Daigle also faced a separate controversy from allegations that he used his Facebook account to send unwanted sexually explicit messages and video clips to people, though Deschaine has said the board’s decision was not related to that.
The Select Board hired retired former town manager Dan Foster to serve as the town’s manager as the board searches for a permanent replacement. Foster spent 15 years at the helm of Fort Fairfield and worked as Madawaska’s interim manager for several months before the town hired Daigle in 2024.

title: Severe turbulence injures at least 8 aboard Avianca flight, forcing emergency landing in Miami
text:
(AP) - At least eight people were injured when an Avianca flight encountered severe turbulence and had to make an emergency landing in Miami early Friday.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said that one person was rushed to a trauma center with severe injuries while seven others were taken to area hospitals in ambulances after the plane landed shortly after 3 a.m. Friday. The airline said nine people — three crew members and six passengers — were affected by the turbulence and needed to be taken to a medical facility.
The Federal Aviation Administration said the Avianca flight was en route from Medellin, Colombia, to John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York when the Airbus A320 had to divert to Miami.
Avianca said the passengers who were not hurt were flown to New York on Friday morning. The airline said “the safety of our customers and employees is, and will remain, the foundation of our operations.”
Serious injuries from in-flight turbulence are rare, but scientists say they may be becoming more common as climate change alters the jet stream. The International Air Transport Association said the number of reports it received about turbulence incidents surged more than 25% last year.
Last summer, 24 people were taken to the hospital after a Delta Air Lines flight encountered turbulence caused by a thunderstorm over Wyoming. The National Transportation Safety Board has said passengers and flight attendants were thrown into the ceiling with enough force to crack some of the interior panels before tossing them back to the floor and then up again. The seat belt sign was off at the time so some passengers were up and drinks were being served when that plane hit the turbulence.
At least 20 passengers have filed lawsuits against Delta over that incident, arguing the airline could have avoided the severe weather.
The FAA recommends that passengers stay buckled whenever possible to protect against unexpected turbulence.

title: Legendary coach, Hall-of-Famer Mike Ditka dies at age 86
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Mike Ditka, who personified the toughness and grit of Chicago in a Hall of Fame career as a player and coach of the Bears and the leader of arguably the most dominant team in NFL history, has died. He was 86.
Ditka’s family announced the death on Friday in a statement.
“It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka,” the family said. “While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears’ Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever.”
Nicknamed “Iron Mike” as a player, Ditka helped revolutionize the tight end position, then moved to the sidelines and took over as Chicago’s coach. His 1985 team featured one of the game’s most dominant defenses ever. It also had enough outsized personalities to record a rap video, “The Super Bowl Shuffle,” and back up their boasting in the championship game three months later.
He was arguably the NFL’s most recognizable — and imitated — personality during his time as Chicago’s coach with his thick but neatly groomed mustache and sweater vest with “BEARS” emblazoned across the chest. The iconic look is still mimicked by fans at Bears games decades later. That along with his fiery, red-faced sideline tantrums inspired the popular “Da Bears” skit on “Saturday Night Live” during the 1980s.
After retiring as a coach, Ditka became a restaurateur, pitchman and TV personality, as well as a forceful advocate for improved medical and retirement benefits for former players.
Ditka was tough and gruff, the quintessential Chicago Bear. He did everything from order off the menu to knock defensive backs on their butts with a growl. His adopted hometown reveled in every minute.
Still revered as “Da Coach” and ringmaster of the 1985 Bears, one of the most dominant and perhaps the zaniest Super Bowl-winning team in league history. Ditka was enshrined in the College and Pro Football Halls of Fame and the Bears said during a ceremony in 2013 that his “No. 89” jersey will be the last one retired by the team.
“Player. Coach. Legend,” the Bears wrote in a tribute on social media. “Mike Ditka embodied the spirit of Chicago and will be deeply missed.”
He was born in Carnegie, Pennsylvania, the son of a welder who changed the family name from Dyczko. He grew up in nearby Aliquippa, close to the coal-mining and steel-manufacturing plants that dotted the western part of the state, a big, talented, three-sport athlete and All-American at Pitt whose bruising style made his first nickname, “Iron Mike,” a good fit.
Selected fifth overall by flinty Chicago owner George Halas in the 1961 draft, Ditka went on to Rookie of the Year honors, multiple Pro Bowl trips and the 1963 NFL Championship. In the bargain, he and Baltimore’s John Mackey changed the tight end position and offensive schemes forever. He was a battering ram of a blocker, but Ditka was just as likely to catch a short pass and pinball through an entire secondary or outrace a lone safety on a deep touchdown throw.
He left Chicago in 1966, playing briefly for Philadelphia and Dallas. He moved to the sideline in 1973 as an assistant to the revered Tom Landry and stayed with the Cowboys for eight seasons, before returning to a hero’s welcome in Chicago as head coach in 1982.
Ditka’s return to the Bears lasted 10 tumultuous years, including five straight NFC Central titles, the Super Bowl win, a DUI conviction, a heart attack, a long-running feud with defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan and, finally, a new nickname — “Da Coach.”
To Hall of Fame linebacker Mike Singletary, the seeds of what was to come were planted in Ditka’s first meeting with the team. He laid out his vision, saying Chicago would be in the Super Bowl in three years — and many of the players in the room would not be around for it.
“When I first heard him when he walked in the room, to me Coach Ditka had the opportunity to be the greatest coach of all time because he had the fire,” Singletary said at the Bears’ 100th anniversary celebration in June 2019. “I don’t know George Halas coached. But I can imagine that the fire and intensity and passion that Coach Ditka exuded that first day set the tone for exactly what he said: ‘Three years from now, we’re going to be in the Super Bowl.’ And that was 1982. In ’85, we were there and it was because of that vision.”
The public beefs with Ryan mirrored the behind-the-scenes battles that Ditka waged trying to contain a team bristling with outsized personalities.
“It was more than a team,” Ditka once said. “It was a team of characters that had character that played for a crazy man, who let him be crazy and had fun doing it and don’t apologize for it ever. I wouldn’t want to be one of these suits walking around on the sideline today.
“I have no desire to be that. I was what I was and they were what they were and, damn, it was fun.”
It wasn’t until two dozen players recorded “The Super Bowl Shuffle” — an audacious rap-styled video released three months ahead of the 1986 title game — that the rest of the football world wondered whether Ditka was losing his grip.
His players never did.
“We call him ‘Sybil’ after that girl in the movie,” quarterback Jim McMahon once explained. “You know, the one that had all those personalities. Mike will be calm one minute, then throw a clipboard the next. People don’t understand that, but we do.”
The Bears demolished the New England Patriots 46-10 in the Super Bowl, but Ditka often said he regretted having McMahon and defensive tackle William “The Refrigerator” Perry run for touchdowns instead of Walter Payton, Chicago’s loyal and long-suffering running back.
Ryan departed for a head coaching job in Philadelphia soon after. While the Bears continued to be a contender for most of the next five years, a 5-11 season prompted Ditka’s departure in 1992.
After a five-year absence, he returned to coaching with the New Orleans Saints, but failed to revive the franchise. His tenure with the team might be best remembered for the trade before the 1999 NFL draft when he dealt a package of eight draft picks — including each one the Saints had that year and two of its first three selections in 2000 — to Washington to move up from 12th overall to No. 5 so New Orleans could select running back Ricky Williams.
After a miserable 1999 season ended with a 3-13 record — Ditka’s worst as either a player or coach — he left the sidelines for good.
His face and demeanor were so familiar by then that a second act became an easy segue. Ditka began building a stable of restaurants and appeared as himself in TV sitcoms from “Cheers” to “Third Rock from the Sun,” as well as shows such as “L.A. Law.”
He also stayed close to the game as an NFL analyst and game-day show personality at ESPN. Ditka’s high-profile status also made him an effective advocate to secure improved health and retirement benefits for former players.
His name also circulated for years in Illinois political circles. Though he never ran for office, Ditka described himself as a staunch conservative and was mentioned several times as a possible Republican candidate, including a congressional race against then state Rep. Barack Obama for the U.S. Senate.

title: CMMC in Lewiston is pushing back against nurses union election
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston has filed objections to the union election nurses won overwhelmingly last month, raising concerns that employees could not freely choose whether to vote.
Objections go through the National Labor Relations Board, the federal agency that oversees labor practices and certifies elections.
The nurses have also filed complaints with the board against the hospital, claiming that CMMC retaliated against protected union activities when it fired or suspended 20 nurses in the week before the vote to join the Maine State Nurses Association and National Nurses United.
Amid the claims of union retaliation, CMMC asked the board to block the election. The NLRB denied the request Sept. 22. The election took place two days later, with the nurses approving the union by a vote of 204-21.
Now, in a request for review of that denial, the hospital is claiming the NLRB should have blocked the union election like it did at Saint Francis Hospital in Illinois, which is also owned by Prime Healthcare Foundation.
Union officials in Illinois asked the NLRB to block Saint Francis’ Sept. 17 union election on the grounds that a free and fair vote was not possible because Prime Healthcare Foundation was breaking the law. The board granted the request on Sept. 14.
According to union officials, Prime Healthcare Foundation illegally fired between 13 and 45 per diem nurses during a public campaign to join National Nurses United in Illinois.
CMMC says that precedent warrants review of “the unexplained denial” of CMMC’s request to block the election in Lewiston, which hospital officials say “permitted the election to proceed without addressing whether materially overlapping allegations at Central Maine and (Saint Francis) presented materially different risks to employee free choice.”
Union officials countered that the cases are legally distinct.
In the meantime, the union says it is still fighting for the 20 suspended and terminated nurses to be reinstated.
“Nurses are continuing to work with community members and elected officials to get all the nurses reinstated,” union officials said Tuesday.

title: Another poll shows Troy Jackson leading a tight Maine Senate race
text:
A new poll released Friday by the Washington Post shows Democrat Troy Jackson maintaining a narrow lead over Republican Susan Collins in Maine’s U.S. Senate race, despite a bombshell report linking Collins’ circle with a convicted fraudster.
Jackson held a four-point lead, 50% to 46%, over the five-term incumbent in the poll — roughly the same as the survey’s margin of error of 3.6 percentage points. Three percent of those polled did not select a choice, while 1% said they’d vote for someone else.
“Another poll shows that Troy is connecting with voters on the issues that matter the most to Mainers,” senior campaign adviser David Farmer said in an emailed statement. “He’s working class and understands the issues that Mainers are facing.”
The survey is further evidence that the closely watched race will likely be a barn burner — one that may hinge on a small pool of undecided voters.
Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and former state Senate president, holds a two-point lead over Collins, according to a polling averages compiled by FiftyPlusOne. But some surveys, including a New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll released two weeks ago, showed Collins with a narrow lead, albeit within the margin of error.
The Post survey, done in partnership with the George Washington University Schar School of Policy and Government, was conducted from Sept. 30 to Oct. 5.
It entered the field a week after ProPublica published a story about how the FBI had years ago begun a sweeping investigation into whether Collins engaged in an illegal pay-to-play scheme by steering government contracts to a donor. (Collins has denied any wrongdoing, saying she was cleared by the Biden administration. ProPublica has reported investigators were looking into Collins’ orbit until President Donald Trump took power in early 2025.)
The Washington Post poll showed the volatile waters that Collins, 73, is trying to navigate to win a sixth term. Fifty-two percent of voters said her 30 years in the Senate was a bad thing. That’s despite respondents giving her a 24 percentage point edge on bringing federal money back to Maine and giving her better marks for bipartisanship.
And President Donald Trump continues to loom large over the race. Sixty-three percent of respondents disapproved of the president’s job performance. And 58% said that Collins sides with Trump too often, compared to 33% who said she’s handled her relationship with the president “about right.”
A majority — 55% — said they wanted Democrats to win the Senate, compared to 42% for Republicans. That metric shows Collins is having at least some success pushing against the national political headwinds.
The top issues for voters were the cost of living (41%), immigration (13%), healthcare (12%) and taxes (6%).
Jackson, meanwhile, had a +1 net approval rating, but 13% of respondents had no opinion or skipped the question. That leaves a small opening for Republicans, who have a significant funding advantage, to introduce the Democrat to voters on their own terms through paid ads.
The 58-year-old Jackson held a 13-point lead among independents, 53% to 40%. His crossover appeal was also higher than Collins, pulling 9% support from Republicans compared to the incumbent’s 6% from Democrats, the poll found.
The survey also asked about Maine’s three-way race for governor. Again, Democrat Hannah Pingree held a double-digit lead over Republican Bobby Charles, 49%-36%. Independent Rick Bennett drew 11% support — his best showing in polling to date.

title: Subtle Change Coming to Target Stores in Maine This November
text:
Subtle Change Coming to Target Stores in Maine This November
Earlier this year, Target announced that some sweeping changes were coming to their stores across the United States.
Some of those changes would be more obvious than others. That included Target ending their partnership with Ulta and launching their own beauty studio within stores.
Another promised change from Target was expanding their grocery department at all Target stores that offer them. But shoppers across Maine will notice another subtle change on top of new items.
Target Will Have Dedicated Grocery Employees at Stores Across Maine
As Target works towards expanding their popular Good & Gather brand, some feedback from regular Target shoppers has inspired another change.
According to Supermarket News, one of the top complaints of Target shoppers who consistently shop for groceries at their stores was the lack of dedicated employees in the grocery section.
That will change at stores in Maine and across the country in November as Target will roll out dedicated grocery employees. You'll be able to spot those employees as they will adorn hats and aprons versus the typical Target employee outfit.
Target Has Been Quietly Changing Other Sections of Their Stores Across Maine
Beyond the introduction of the Target Beauty Studio, there have been some other subtle changes happening inside Target stores.
Target has been merging some of their departments including electronics, books and toys. Target will trim some of their electronics offerings where sales have slowed and increase stock of plushies, Legos and more unique toys and games that customers are more likely to be after.
Shoppers will also changes in the home goods and clothing sections.
From bedding to decorative items and more, Target plans to redo about 75% of their home goods department by the end of the year.
Target also plans to collaborate with more designers and feature unique items that customers can only find through Target. There will also be an advanced partnership with Levi's Jeans, which will be more widely available at Target stores nationwide.

title: Canceled: ArtsFarmington presents Stories through music
Service dog nonprofit hosting Barktoberfest event Saturday in Alfred
text:
ALFRED — In the back of an SUV at Alfred Park, two puppies sit eagerly, barking at the nearby dogs whose ranks they will soon join.
The two puppies — later named Harley and Tanner — watch as Cashew, a 2-year-old Great Dane, continues his training to be a mobility service dog. Trainer Doug Wiggin affects a limp as he walks alongside Cashew, helping the dog get used to supporting people with mobility issues.
Nearby, Onyx, another Great Dane in training, gets used to waiting patiently with other dogs.
Cashew and Onyx will be among several dogs representing Mobility Danes of New England on Saturday at the organization’s second annual Barktoberfest. The event, hosted at Spacious Skies Walnut Grove Campground in Alfred, is both a fundraising opportunity and a chance for the organization to connect with Mainers who might want to volunteer or be matched with a mobility dog.
Barktoberfest will take place from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. and will feature a dog costume parade, raffles, a food truck and more. Tickets will cost $15 or $10 if purchased online in advance.
Karen Boomhower, secretary of the board for Mobility Danes, said Barktoberfest was one of the organization’s favorite events last year.
“It’s just going to be a fun day,” she said. “Bring a costume for your dog, walk in the parade; it’s not just about raising money, but also about awareness and getting the word out.”
Since 2003, Mobility Danes has matched more than 200 dogs to owners in need.
The application process is designed to ensure the right dog will be matched with the right recipient. The organization will schedule Zoom calls with possible recipients to understand more about the person’s needs, ability and the structure of their gait to make sure the dog they are matched with will be the perfect fit.
Lynn George, president of the organization’s board, said many recipients are veterans, but the organization has also matched dogs with people with multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s disease and other mobility issues.
The dogs’ training periods vary but are usually 1 to 2 years. They work on balance, temperament, using steps and even helping their handler to keep moving or getting up after falling.
Wiggin, who volunteers as a trainer, said his favorite part of Barktoberfest is seeing past recipients from the program attend with their dogs.
“Seeing all the dogs that have since graduated from the program and doing what they are trained to do is just the best,” Wiggin said. “Nothing beats that.”

title: Hurricane Simon strengthens to a Category 2 storm, the National Hurricane Center says
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Hurricane Simon has strengthened to a Category 2 storm and was forecast to approach Mexico’s coast as a major hurricane this weekend, the National Hurricane Center said Friday.
The center said maximum sustained winds have increased to nearly 100 mph (155 kph), and that Simon is expected to continue strengthening rapidly during the next day or so. Simon is forecast to become a major hurricane by late Friday and strengthen further on Saturday.
U.S. forecasters earlier issued a hurricane warning for parts of the central and southwest coast, where hurricane-force winds were expected within 36 hours.
Simon is expected to bring heavy rainfall over parts of southwestern Mexico, with rain possibly concentrated across the coast of Jalisco and parts of Michoacan, Colima and Nayarit. Forecasters warned of life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Simon was centered about 335 kilometers (210 miles) south of Manzanillo and 500 kilometers (310 miles) south-southeast of Cabo Corrientes.
The state of Jalisco suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating dozens of people from at-risk areas. It also asked the tourism sector in Puerto Vallarta, a popular destination for U.S. tourists, to ensure that both workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones by Friday afternoon.
“If we let our guard down and try to come up with a last-minute action plan, it is highly likely that lives will be lost,” said the state director of civil protection, Sergio Ramírez.
Governor Pablo Lemus urged the public to stay informed at all times given the hurricane’s “highly erratic behavior,” which has caused it to change direction between Manzanillo and Puerto Vallarta.
“What is certain is that it will hit the coast of Jalisco with very heavy rains starting this Friday, throughout the weekend, and on Monday,” he said.
The state of Guerrero has also suspended classes and non-essential activities in areas along the coast and in the central part of the state due to heavy rains brought by Simon since Thursday.
The flooding hit the port of Acapulco the hardest, where some streets were turned into rivers, with vehicles swept away by the current and homes and businesses flooded. There have been no reported casualties, said Governor Evelyn Salgado.
The U.S. Embassy also issued alerts advising against entering the water or walking on the beach and urging travelers to heed the warnings of local authorities.
Farther north, Tropical Storm Rachel was expected to reach Baja California, northwestern Mexico and Southern California this weekend. It had maximum winds of 85 kph (50 mph) and was forecast to weaken, though it may bring heavy rain to the area.
Tropical storm activity has been above average this season in the Pacific, due to the effects of a strong El Niño.
The climate phenomenon typically depresses storm activity in the Atlantic. Hurricane Isaias, which was expected to hit the U.S. Gulf Coast late Friday or Saturday, developed more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season.

title: Congregants celebrate the reconstruction of one of America's oldest Black churches
text:
WILLIAMSBURG, Va. (AP) — The reconstruction of one of the nation’s oldest Black churches, where congregants gathered in secret before building a meeting house in Virginia, was celebrated Friday.
Hundreds of residents gathered for a community-wide re-dedication of the original First Baptist Church of Williamsburg, which was established in 1776 by enslaved and free African Americans in defiance of laws that prevented them from congregating.
In 1805, its original parishioners built the church house, known as the African Baptist Meeting House, with recycled bricks and materials they scrounged. A tornado in 1834 destroyed the church, which was rebuilt in 1856 before it was turned into a parking lot a century later by the Colonial Williamsburg Foundation, a living history museum, because it didn’t match the 18th century aesthetic of the town at the time.
Since then, the 16-foot by 32-foot church has been reconstructed, after archaeologists in 2021 uncovered the church’s original foundation, as well as 62 graves linked to the congregation.
“What this day means and shows is that Black history is American history, and we’re an example for the rest of the nation,” Reginald F. Davis, pastor of First Baptist, told The Associated Press on Friday.
“A church that has a history that was during the signing of the Declaration of Independence, you cannot erase us out of American history because we have been at the outset and formulation of the nation,” said Davis, who leads the current 215-member congregation in a 20th century church on Scotland Street, less than a mile from the original site.
For decades, Colonial Williamsburg didn’t tell the story of the church’s history as a pioneer of Black American faith traditions. More than half of the 2,000 people who lived in Williamsburg in the 18th century were Black, with few of them free. But in recent years, the museum has resuscitated the church’s traditions, starting with Friday’s celebration of the building’s 250th anniversary.
“I wanted them to know that we were always here, where when the doors of the Colonial Williamsburg Foundation first opened, the restoration, and even before then, we were sometimes present, but not able to speak,” said Janice Canaday, community engagement manager at the Colonial Williamsburg Foundation.
“This is a reclamation, a reclaiming of the narrative,” she said.
From past to present
On Friday, the event began with a procession symbolizing the ways the historic congregation has continued a multigenerational fight for education, faith, and freedom.
The mood was set with a performance by the Nassau Street Remembrance Choir, before an invocation from Davis and speeches from Virginia state Senator Mamie Locke and James Ingram, a museum interpreter who has for 26 years portrayed Gowan Pamphlet, First Baptists’ pastor when the original church structure was built.
In a 2025 AP interview, Ingram said Pamphlet was “a precursor to someone like Frederick Douglass, who would be the precursor to someone like Martin Luther King Jr.”
Pamphlet, an enslaved tavern worker, preached about equality in the face of laws that prohibited large gatherings of African Americans out of fear of slave uprisings. Ingram handed the mantle off to the new Pamphlet interpreter, Brandon Lee, who debuted at the dedication.
‘We were just so elated’
In addition to discovering the original church’s foundation, archaeologists uncovered the graves of 62 community members. DNA tests and bone analyses for three sets of remains linked them back to the African Baptist Meeting House congregation.
But it was oral tradition that served as the first hint in the discovery, where stories of ancestors buried in the area led to a search.
“We knew the building was here, and we knew that there were maybe burials behind it,” said Jennifer Wilkoski, director of architectural preservation and research at Colonial Williamsburg.
When the church’s original structure was discovered in 2021, Davis called it “a rediscovery of the humanity of a people.”
“We were just so elated that those people who had been buried and forgotten, have now been unearthed and given the recognition as human beings, as they should have been,” he said. “It’s a wonderful time to shed light on our history in light of the erasure of so many things within our history.”
Construction is nearly finished
The meeting house reconstruction, built at its original site, honors its original character. Archaeologists and Colonial Williamsburg’s construction team modeled the new church out of pine and white oak woods, and recreated details like the original half-round brick steps.
Wilkoski said the materials for the original church demonstrated the resourcefulness of the congregants, who likely included carpenters with the skills necessary to build the church.
Modern renovations include an HVAC system for Virginia’s hot summers, a refreshed altar table for sermons, shutters, and handblown glass windows. Last year, Colonial Williamsburg considered glassless windows but has since had to reconsider to build the cooling HVAC system.
“It’s not church stained glass, but we call it restoration glass, handmade like they would’ve had in the 18th and early 19th century,” Wilkoski said.
Finishing touches on the church will wrap in the next few months and will include an ADA- accessible ramp.
Davis, the First Baptist pastor, said the meeting house structure is overdue recognition for “those of us who are still working to make America a more perfect union.”
____
Nancy Jiang reported from New York.

title: ‘We couldn’t believe it’: Couple reeling after losing life savings in $14 million Ponzi scheme
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
TOMAHAWK, Wis. (WSAW/Gray News) - A Wisconsin couple says they are having to adjust their life after losing hundreds of thousands of dollars to someone they considered a close friend.
Brian and Jeanine Tesch said they have been left with barely any money in their accounts thanks to Stanley Pophal, who, federal prosecutors say, defrauded 190 investors of $14.25 million over six years in a multimillion-dollar Ponzi scheme.
The couple said the investment began with a $165,000 check before Pophal came for their life savings.
“We wanted to have a beautiful future when we retired, help our kids out and our grandchildren. But that was taken away from us,” Jeanine Tesch said. “He talked us into selling our home and our land and everything.”
Pophal promised their investments would double in five years and that he would have their backs if they didn’t. He sent them several checks, including some for $6,000 and one for $35,000.
Jeanine said he was dangling a carrot in front of them, taking advantage of their decadeslong friendship.
“He was like a brother to me,” Brian Tesch said. “Right up until the end, actually. Right up until the last week.”
Pophal was trying to get their 401(k). But before he got access to it, the Teschs said they saw his mug shot.
“Our hearts just sank. We started bawling and just trembling. And we couldn’t believe it,” said Jeanine Tesch.
They later learned he had spent investors’ money on snowmobiles, bikes, cars and other items.
The Teschs said the paperwork they signed appeared legitimate, and they did not expect Pophal to be unable to repay them.
IRS Criminal Investigation Acting Special Agent in Charge Robert Kuszynski said Pophal was very good at convincing people.
“The victims of the Pophal investigation were charmed by an individual. Uh, and he made promises and provided information that was false that any investor could have, uh, seen and believed to be true,” Kuszynski said.
Pophal was ordered to pay $14.25 million in restitution. However, the Teschs have not received anything yet.
They had planned to retire in Florida. Instead, they now split their time between a trailer in Tomahawk and a rental in Mexico, where Jeanine Tesch said the lower cost of living helps them make ends meet.
“The life savings that we had, the hopes and the dreams for a bright future. And now we just struggle to find joy in living. And not the future that we hoped for or we dreamt of that he took away from us. And from so many other families. It’s devastating right in your own hometown,” Jeanine Tesch said.
They also can’t afford to be in Wisconsin for the birth of their newest grandchild.
“The devastation that Stan has done to us and our families and our friends and all the other victims won’t define us,” said Jeanine Tesch. “There will be judgment day for Stan Pophal. He didn’t get justice here, but I believe someday he will.”
The Teschs said Pophal would often capitalize on people’s faith, saying he was working in God’s name. The couple said it’s their faith that is keeping them going after everything.

title: Cormier Wins Week Five; Watt and Good Share Girls Honor
text:
Van Buren’s Cormier, SA’s Watt, Ashland’s Good Named Week Five Athletes of the Week
The votes are in for Fall Week Five Athlete of the Week, and this week produced three winners.
Gavin Cormier of Van Buren earned the boys honor, while the girls voting finished in a tie between Aolie Watt of Southern Aroostook and Arihanna Good of Ashland.
All three were selected from another strong group of nominees representing soccer, golf and cross country programs from across Aroostook County.
Boys Athlete of the Week: Gavin Cormier, Van Buren
Cormier earned the Week Five boys honor following his performance for the Van Buren boys soccer team against Houlton.
Cormier scored the Crusaders’ lone goal in the game, creating the opportunity and finishing the play before leaving the contest prior to halftime.
County voters ultimately gave Cormier the most support on the Week Five boys ballot.
Girls Athletes of the Week: Aolie Watt and Arihanna Good
For the first time this fall, the girls Athlete of the Week voting ended in a tie.
Aolie Watt of Southern Aroostook earned her share of the honor after providing all of the offense in the Warriors’ 2-1 victory over Hodgdon, scoring both Southern Aroostook goals.
Arihanna Good of Ashland also finished atop the voting after being recognized for her work on the defensive end. Good has been a strong presence for Ashland, winning possession, helping move the ball forward and creating opportunities for teammates from the back line.
With the final vote totals even, Watt and Good are both Fall Week Five Girls Athletes of the Week.

Collins won the PVC Boys Golf Championship after shooting a 74, finishing two strokes ahead of the field.

Cormier scored Van Buren’s goal against Houlton before leaving the game prior to halftime.

Witmer finished 46th overall in 17:00.21 at the Festival of Champions, leading the eligible Aroostook County boys in the statewide field.

Watt scored both goals in Southern Aroostook’s 2-1 victory over Hodgdon.

title: Turn down the heat on Maine’s annual furnace debate
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
It’s strange when a war halfway across the globe could have you fumbling to operate a TV remote in winter gloves, but that’s where we are — or are about to be.
With temperatures in Maine dipping into the 30s overnight and heating oil prices hovering around a record-high $6 a gallon, the annual debate about when to turn on the heat is already underway.
For many Mainers, this is not a First-World problem but an unbearable expense on top of already strained finances. (If you’re in that position, see our guide for where to find heating and other assistance.) Here, however, I’m focusing on households where this is primarily a source of relationship strife — a battle between the budget watchers and those who want to be cozy.
Even for these relatively fortunate people, though, it’s not always as simple as it seems.
“This is exactly the kind of disagreement that can sound trivial from the outside but actually taps into a lot of the things couples argue about,” said Andrea Medaris, director of Psychology Specialists of Maine’s Center for Relationships in Brunswick.
To help sort it out, we turned to Maine experts for their advice about staying warm this winter without going broke (or breaking up).
If it’s about cost
The chillier half of the household has an uphill battle this year. Former TV meteorologist Keith Carson has a solution: math.
Many frugal Mainers live by the rule “no heat until trick or treat,” if not “turkey meat.” In a video for Maine Conservation Voters, the spokesman (and occasional Press Herald weather writer) shows how crunching some numbers can help your case for cranking up the heat when the temperature drops, rather than holding out for a certain date.
Turning the thermostat down by one degree for three hours on a 20-degree day in February will cover the cost of heating up the average Maine house on a 40-degree fall morning, he explains.
In theory, by agreeing to do that later, you should get your way now. But you’ll have to brush up on your algebra.
If it’s about comfort
Now, for a science lesson.
A lot of these arguments stem from biological differences that determine how well we can tolerate the cold. We know smaller people, with a higher ratio of skin surface area to body mass, lose heat more easily, while more muscular people retain it better.
For advice on how to keep your core temperature up, we turned to Tim Smith, founder of the Jack Mountain Bushcraft School in Masardis, who provided the list of tips he gives guests of his guided snowshoe trips in Aroostook County.
Some were practical: wear a hat, then another one, then a hoodie over that. Others were on the silly side, like keeping a picture of Timothee Chalamet in your chest pocket. (He had Patrick Swayze on there, until some younger associates informed him they didn’t know who that was.)
Another — to drink warm liquids, “especially ones that are bad for you” — is only half true. Although alcohol will make you feel flushed, Smith said, it actually lowers your body temperature.
But there was one unconventional method for keeping warm that seemed like it could work for warring couples: Putting cayenne pepper in your socks will irritate the skin and drive circulation, he said. If your shivering partner happens to like a foot rub, you can keep the argument at bay by offering one, extra spicy.
If it’s about something else
Medaris, the psychologist, said the meanings that get attached to conflicts like these — that one person is constantly critical or the other always gets their way — is what couples need to step away from when the heat debate starts escalating.
“One person is cold, the other is thinking about the heating bill, and pretty quickly it can turn into ‘you’re unreasonable’ or ‘you don’t care that I’m uncomfortable,’” she said.
Her advice is to “get on the same side against the problem,” recognizing each person’s needs and working together on a solution, whether that’s agreeing on a thermostat range or putting a space heater in a certain room.
Efficiency Maine has all sorts of tips for keeping in the heat — with caulk, window treatments, reflectors and weather stripping — perfect for a joint DIY project that could help with both comfort and cost.
If that doesn’t go well, research the rates for seeing a couples therapist. That might prompt the stingy spouse to give up a few degrees on the thermostat.

title: Christa Pike is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt, her attorneys say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike has begun walking and eating again at a hospital a week after surviving Tennessee’s attempt to execute her with lethal drugs, her attorneys said Thursday.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state sought to give her a lethal injection eight days ago for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The drug didn’t kill her, and her arms were left burned and blistered, according to her lawyers. For the first few days of her hospitalization, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator.
Her first steps on Wednesday were “limited,” and she required some assistance as she walked on Thursday, her lawyers said in a statement. She is also regaining mobility in her arms, and she was able to eat for the first time.
But the lawyers warned uncertainty remains about her physical recovery and her legal standing after the attempt to carry out her death sentence.
Questions remain about Pike’s recovery and legal case
The failed execution on Sept. 30 has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty. Texas on Wednesday carried out the first execution in the U.S. since the Tennessee attempt.
“While her physical recovery has been remarkable, significant questions remain about the long-term effects of what she endured,” her attorneys said in Thursday’s statement. “Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die.”
Pike regained consciousness Tuesday and was able to speak after awakening, they said.
They initially described her as “confused” soon after regaining consciousness, and said Thursday that she continued to struggle with concentration and memory. Doctors say it is too early to assess the long-term impacts, the attorneys added.
It also remains unclear whether Tennessee will try to execute her again. Her attorneys have said that they will urge Republican Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison without parole.
“She should never be subjected to another execution attempt,” they said in the statement.
What went wrong with the execution remains unclear
Lee has since postponed the state’s only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of why the execution failed. The state’s prison chief resigned after the execution attempt.
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream.
Pike’s attorneys wrote in a court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed.”
State officials have offered no explanation of what occurred.
As the process got underway, Pike was asked if she had a final statement and she spoke of being at peace. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm hurt. Later, she appeared to lose consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily until media witnesses were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took her to a hospital.

title: Marvel Announces ‘Zodiac’ TV Series
text:
Marvel Announces ‘Zodiac’ TV Series for Disney+
Marvel’s TV output has certainly slowed significantly in the last few years, especially on the live-action side. The early 2020s were filled with new Disney+ for new characters: Moon Knight, Ironheart, Ms. Marvel, She-Hulk. Echo.
Marvel had announced a new show like that in a while; the only upcoming series on their docket after VisionQuest were animated; more episodes of things like Marvel Zombies, X-Men ’97, and Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man.
Or, at least, that was the case until New York Comic-Con this year, where Marvel surprisingly announced an upcoming Disney+ show that I feel confident saying no one would have predicted: Zodiac.
At the studio’s TV panel at Comic-Con, the company’s Head of Television Brad Winderbaum said that the show is “a spy thriller. And for anyone who knows the comics, if you look closely at this title design, you’ll see a few clues about where we’re going.”
Obviously the logo above features a S.H.I.E.L.D. emblem inside the “A.”
READ MORE: See Famous Marvel Actors’ Yearbook Photos
The “Zodiac” name has been used by a bunch of different characters in Marvel comics, most super-villains who use the various astrological signs as their alter egos. Every few years a new Zodiac group would pop up to threaten the Avengers or the Defenders or whoever.
If Marvel tells me they are making a Zodiac show and it will involve S.H.I.E.L.D. I would assume it somehow involves Nick Fury and Scorpio — the alias of one of the members of Zodiac that has also been used by multiple people, some of whom have direct connections to Fury. The very first Scorpio was Jake Fury, Nick’s brother. Later comics introduced a Mikel Fury, who was Nick Fury’s son. With no inside knowledge, I would just guess you’d see one of those two characters on this show. Either that or Jake Gyllenhaal is gonna show up and draw some cartoons and crack some ciphers. One or the other.
Marvel says Zodiac will premiere on Disney+ in 2028. The next Marvel TV series, VisionQuest, debuts next week on DIsney+.

title: Dr. Oz defends rural health care spending amid Medicaid cut questions
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Cost of health care is a major issue for voters ahead of the midterms, and the Trump administration is trying to get ahead of the messaging. Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, sat down with Gray Media Washington News Bureau reporter Molly Martinez, and the conversation grew heated.
Dr. Oz’s authority over spending is limited by Congress. The Trump administration is touting a record $50 billion in spending for rural health care approved in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The actual numbers tell a different story.
“The Big Beautiful Bill cut $137 billion in rural health care spending. That’s there was money there. So this seems to be a solution to a problem that the administration may have created,” Martinez asked Oz.
“You’re repeating talking points that are not only wrong but deliberately duplicitous. What is wrong? That number is incorrect,” Oz responded.
The $137 billion cut figure is a direct analysis from the non-partisan KFF group. The non-partisan Congressional Budget Office estimates 10 billion Americans will lose health care as a result of the Big Beautiful Bill in the next decade.
Oz was pressed on why reform was necessary.
“Some states like New York and California take advantage of the system and those states take money from the federal coffers of other states, because why should Kentucky and Mississippi and New Mexico be paying higher federal taxes so that California and New York can put more money into programs?” Oz said.
Leslie Dach, an Obama alumnus and chair of Protect Our Care, responded.
“It is not true that the big blue states are the ones who benefit because there’s equal access in 49 states. So you know, he’s just using kind of a stereotype to make believe that certain people probably in red states or rural states are getting ripped off,” Dach said.
The administration maintains that pulling nearly a trillion dollars in health care spending is in the name of fraud prevention and financial solvency. Dach said there is a human cost.
“He acts as if all these actions they’ve taken were making health care better. That is the biggest boldfaced lie everywhere. Go ask people who are shutting down their hospitals has to last, can’t find a maternity ward, have a heart attack and has to drive the people who can’t afford their health insurance anymore,” Dach said.
The Trump administration has vowed to expand spending, including $17 million for new mental health clinics in North Carolina.

title: 4 Wabanaki chiefs back Hannah Pingree in Maine governor’s race
text:
Tribal leaders from four Wabanaki communities in Maine endorsed Democrat Hannah Pingree in the race for governor, she announced at a news conference Friday on the Penobscot reservation, Indian Island.
Chiefs Clarissa Sabattis, of the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians; Kirk Francis, of the Penobscot Nation; and Sheila McCormack, of the Mi’kmaq Nation were all present to make the announcement, alongside Maulian Bryant, Penobscot Nation Tribal Councilor, and Donna Loring, a Penobscot elder, former tribal representative and adviser to two governors.
“Sovereignty is not a favor from the state. It is overdue,” Pingree said. “Restoring it means Tribal Nations will have the same rights and autonomy as every other federally recognized Tribe. It is an issue of fairness.”
Chief William “Billy” Nicholas Sr. of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Motahkomikuk was not present but also endorsed Pingree. His counterpart on the other Passamaquoddy reservation at Sipayik, Amkuwiposohehs “Pos” Bassett, did not make an endorsement in the race.
Pingree, a Democrat, has pledged to sign in the first 100 days legislation that would recognize full tribal sovereignty.
Such legislation would alter the terms of the 1980 settlement act to recognize the unrestrained authority of tribes over tribal lands, and could make federal Indian law applicable in Maine.
“In my many years of working on Tribal sovereignty, I cannot recall a gubernatorial candidate making such a specific public commitment,” Loring said, according to a copy of her remarks.
Pingree has made a point in her campaign to highlight that this is one of the issues where she does not align with Gov. Janet Mills, who has long opposed the sweeping reforms to Maine’s approach to tribal relations.
On stage in the second gubernatorial debate Thursday night, Pingree distanced herself from Mills on the issue.
Independent Rick Bennett, a state senator from Oxford County and former Republican, highlighted his own bona fides on the topic Thursday, noting that he has sponsored the kind of legislation sought by tribal leaders in the past and was named a tribal champion by the Wabanaki Alliance.
The endorsement can be read as a tactical choice by tribal leaders, who are banking on the hope that the next governor will be more friendly to their cause. Although both Bennett and Pingree are aligned with tribal interests, Bennett has lagged in polls and fundraising to both Pingree, the clear front-runner, and Republican Bobby Charles.
And more importantly, Pingree has made a point to visit tribal communities, including Motahkomikuk. Bennett would likely have been a contender for an endorsement from leaders at that reservation, Chief Nicholas said in an interview, if he had made an effort at outreach.
“He hasn’t paid a visit here, and Hannah has, and she’s been in contact with our community, and she’s came and visited,” Nicholas said.
Charles, a Leeds lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state, has not said that he supports tribal sovereignty.
“My attitude on this is, ‘Come to me as governor. Sit down and put it before me,'” he said during the debate. “We’ve talked details with them, and as a lawyer, I understand the complexity.”
Nicholas said neither he nor anybody in his office had been contacted by Charles.
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.

title: Troy Jackson reacts to Barack Obama endorsement for Maine Senate seat
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson addressed former President Barack Obama’s endorsement of his campaign after a tour of the Augusta Food Pantry Thursday morning.
“President Obama was someone that I really respected. I disagree with him on some things. I disagree with him on trade issues. But, I’m happy to have his endorsement because, overall, I think what he tried to do for the country was positive,” Jackson said.
Obama cites Jackson’s record
Obama shared his support for Jackson in a video released Wednesday morning. Obama pointed to Jackson’s working-class roots and record of lowering prescription drug costs, delivering universal school meals, raising wages and protecting abortion rights in Maine.
Collins campaign reacts
Sen. Susan Collins’ campaign responded to the endorsement in a statement, saying in part: “The fact that Troy Jackson is endorsed by Obama, funded by Chuck Schumer, and campaigning with Bernie Sanders this weekend tells you how much the national Democratic machine wants to control Maine’s Senate seat.”

title: Maine hospitals sue over planned changes to 340B program
text:
MAINE (WABI) - The Maine Hospital Association, Eastern Maine Medical Center, and several other hospitals are suing the federal government over planned changes to a prescription-drug discount program.
The lawsuit challenges a proposed rebate system for the 340-B program, which helps hospitals serving low-income and rural communities afford care and medications.
The American Hospital Association and Maine Hospital Association say the changes could shift costs onto hospitals and create major administrative burdens.
They estimate those costs could top one billion dollars a year. That’s more than the federal government’s estimate of 537 million dollars.
The new system is set to take effect in January.

title: Two powerful earthquakes and multiple aftershocks rock Panama
text:
PANAMA CITY (AP) — Two powerful 7.7 and 6.6 magnitude earthquakes and a series of aftershocks struck Panama Friday afternoon, collapsing buildings near the epicenter and prompting evacuations across the country, the U.S. Geological Survey said.
The earlier quake, felt as far away as neighboring Colombia, was centered about 10 kilometers (6 miles) southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, the USGS said. It struck at a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles).
The USGS initially reported the first quake as magnitude 8, then revised it to 7.6 and later to 7.7.
Visibly shaken residents of Panama City gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact on Friday.
“We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re okay, though we’re very scared,” Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared.”
Multiple aftershocks continued to rattle Panama, including several measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2. Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, though many were too weak to be felt.
Calls for calm and reports of collapsed buildings
Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino called for calm on Friday, writing on X: “What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder.”
Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said on the Telemetro Reporta news channel that damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos. He said there were no reports of damage in the capital, which is known for its hundreds of skyscrapers.
Smith said several injuries have been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonomé, around 93 miles (150 km) from the capital. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage in the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel. No casualties were immediately reported.
Local news outlets also reported that the Church of San Atanasio, a colonial-style Catholic church in Panama’s Los Santos province, had collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938. Elsewhere, including in Veraguas province, large fissures ran along roadways.
Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region’s busiest airports with more than 20 million travelers in 2025, said it would temporarily suspend operations and activated evacuation plans. It said operations would resume once security conditions have been checked.
The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the key global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialized technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage.
Tsunami warnings as far as Chile’s Easter Island
The last major earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991. A magnitude 7.4 quake, centered in nearby Costa Rica killed 23 people, injured 559, and left thousands of people homeless in the border Bocas de Toro region.
Earthquakes are common, especially along Panama’s border with Costa Rica and its Pacific coast, because of the interaction of several tectonic plates, including Cocos, Nazca, and Caribbean plates.
Panama lies along the “Ring of Fire,” a 40,000-kilometer (25,000-mile) arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world’s earthquakes occur.
The National Weather Service issued a tsunami warning Friday for the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua and Guatemala. It warned that waves ranging from 3 to 9 feet (1 to 3 meters) above tide may occur in some coastal areas of Panama.
Alerts were also issued in El Salvador and as far as Chile’s Easter Island, about 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles) off Chile’s mainland coast. Chile’s government placed the island under a precautionary advisory.
Nearby countries sent messages of support Friday afternoon. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, whose country was recently hit by earthquakes, expressed his solidarity with the Panamanian people and their government during what he called “difficult times.”
“Panama is not alone! You can count on Colombia’s support and our full willingness to provide whatever assistance is needed,” he wrote on X.
The U.S. Embassy in Panama said it was “closely monitoring” the aftermath of the quake and accounting for the welfare of its citizens in Panama, a well-known retirement destination for Americans.
___
Janetsky reported from Mexico City, and Solís reported from Panama City. Gabriela Molina in Quito, Ecuador, Clara Preve in Buenos Aires, Argentina, Eléonore Hughes in Rio de Janeiro, María Verza in Mexico City and Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, contributed.

title: Increased immigration enforcement could cost Maine economy billions, report says
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Increased immigration enforcement could cost Maine billions in annual economic activity, report finds
The director of the Maine Office of New Americans (ONA) is providing new insight into a recent report that analyzed the impact of immigration enforcement on the state's economy.
The report commissioned by the ONA, which was released last month, states that an estimated 33,079 foreign-born workers in Maine generated approximately $2.25 billion in personal income and an estimated $177 million in state income tax revenue from 2020 to 2024. According to the report, modeling estimates that immigrant employment helps support approximately 73,780 total jobs statewide, $3.7 billion in wages and salaries, nearly $8.4 billion in state GDP and nearly $15 billion in total economic output.
In addition, the report modeled the potential economic effects of federal immigration enforcement activity in Maine by using three illustrative low/mid/high scenarios that combine direct workforce removals with broader deterrence-related labor force withdrawal. Depending on the assumed scale of enforcement, these scenarios produce an initial labor force loss of 840 to 7,050 workers, which is concentrated in healthcare, manufacturing, construction, accommodations and food services, and agriculture. The report goes on to state that once broader economic links are incorporated, the effects range from approximately 1,800 to 15,100 jobs statewide and $395 million to $3.3 billion in lost annual economic output.
ONA Director Julia Trujillo Luengo, who assumed the office in July, recently sat down for an interview with Maine's Total Coverage to discuss the report. She said that the report tried to factor in how foreign-born workers may respond to increased immigration enforcement in the state.
"I may have fear of showing up on the job site because somebody else disappeared yesterday or was taken away, so then I may not show up," Trujillo Luengo said. "That's something that we also try to bring into the report, that hard-to-measure chilling effect."
The full interview with Trujillo Luengo will air at 10 a.m. Sunday on "Total Maine."

title: Hurricane Isaias lashes the US Gulf Coast with wind and rain hours before it comes ashore
text:
GULF BREEZE, Fla. (AP) — Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast on Friday as a dangerous Category 2 hurricane, hammering communities in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle with damaging winds, heavy rain, flooding and life-threatening storm surges.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season made landfall near Destin, Florida, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said. It had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (169 kph). The storm weakened to just below major hurricane status before it came ashore and by early Saturday was no longer considered a hurricane as its wind speeds continued to decrease.
“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard “throughout the region.”
Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars, and seafood shacks. Forecasters warned the conditions could also stir up tornadoes across the Florida Panhandle and into southern Georgia.
“We’re watching it very closely, the hurricane,” President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House late Friday night as he returned from a rally in upstate New York, adding that it was “under control.”
Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.
More than 664,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.
Many are braving Isaias at home
Tim Mowry, who rode out the storm from his home in Pensacola, said the wind was so intense it sounded like a train whistle as it whipped through a crack in his patio door. He lost power around 4:30 p.m. but was able to rely on a generator. Standing water also covered his backyard, and parts of his fence were ripped down, but overall he said the storm wasn’t as bad as he expected.
“As far as Pensacola-wise, we really got fortunate,” Mowry said.
One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could reach 3 to 5 feet (0.91 to 1.52 meters) from Dauphin Island, Alabama, to Florida’s Aucilla River, according to the hurricane center.
Dangerous conditions are expected throughout the western panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, the National Hurricane Center said. Several counties announced mandatory evacuations while Mobile, Alabama, imposed a curfew through Saturday morning.
In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle closed, according to the company’s website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often serves as a measure of a storm’s severity.
Kelsei Frazier, a Florida native living in Pace and no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.
“We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it’s not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed,” said Frazier.
DeSantis warned residents to expect gasoline shortages and bridge and highway closures.
The state’s National Guard deployed about 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, and search-and-rescue teams were ready to respond, while some prisons evacuated inmates.
The whole region could get soaked
Isaias was already slowing after landfall, and it was expected to weaken further and be downgraded to a tropical storm by Saturday afternoon, the center said.
Still, heavy rain is forecast as it moves inland, with 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama to southwestern Georgia.
Isaias grounds flights but likely to miss oil hubs
The storm grounded most Friday flights at several panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt emergency response efforts.
Isaias was expected to miss the oil industry’s biggest hubs along the Gulf Coast, but fuel prices could rise if power outages shut down refineries for processing crude, industry experts said.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Hurricane Simon became a Category 4 storm early Saturday, ahead of a projected landfall in Mexico this weekend.
___
Megnien reported from Panama City, Florida, Golden reported from Seattle, and Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio. Seth Borenstein and Collin Binkley in Washington; Rio Yamat in Las Vegas; Gerald Herbert in Pensacola, Florida; Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut; Sarah Raza in Sioux Falls, South Dakota; Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama; and Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas contributed to this report.
