title: CMMC in Lewiston is pushing back against nurses union election
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston has filed objections to the union election nurses won overwhelmingly last month, raising concerns that employees could not freely choose whether to vote.
Objections go through the National Labor Relations Board, the federal agency that oversees labor practices and certifies elections.
The nurses have also filed complaints with the board against the hospital, claiming that CMMC retaliated against protected union activities when it fired or suspended 20 nurses in the week before the vote to join the Maine State Nurses Association and National Nurses United.
Amid the claims of union retaliation, CMMC asked the board to block the election. The NLRB denied the request Sept. 22. The election took place two days later, with the nurses approving the union by a vote of 204-21.
Now, in a request for review of that denial, the hospital is claiming the NLRB should have blocked the union election like it did at Saint Francis Hospital in Illinois, which is also owned by Prime Healthcare Foundation.
Union officials in Illinois asked the NLRB to block Saint Francis’ Sept. 17 union election on the grounds that a free and fair vote was not possible because Prime Healthcare Foundation was breaking the law. The board granted the request on Sept. 14.
According to union officials, Prime Healthcare Foundation illegally fired between 13 and 45 per diem nurses during a public campaign to join National Nurses United in Illinois.
CMMC says that precedent warrants review of “the unexplained denial” of CMMC’s request to block the election in Lewiston, which hospital officials say “permitted the election to proceed without addressing whether materially overlapping allegations at Central Maine and (Saint Francis) presented materially different risks to employee free choice.”
Union officials countered that the cases are legally distinct.
In the meantime, the union says it is still fighting for the 20 suspended and terminated nurses to be reinstated.
“Nurses are continuing to work with community members and elected officials to get all the nurses reinstated,” union officials said Tuesday.

title: Obituary: Normand R. Lamie
text:
Normand R. Lamie
LEWISTON – Normand R. Lamie, of Lewiston, passed away on September 30, 2026, following a challenging battle with pancreatic cancer.
Norm was born in Lewiston on March 21, 1952, the son of Armand and Rose (Morin) Lamie.
Norm married the love of his life, Susan D. Flagg, on October 11, 1975 in Nobleboro, Maine.
Norm’s devotion to his family was at the heart of everything he did. He instilled the importance of hard work and good education in his children. His loving nature and generous spirit will be deeply missed by family and many friends. Norm especially enjoyed spending time with his seven grandchildren, Madelyn and Aidan Adams of Otisfield, Maine, Avah and Ethan Lamie of White River Junction, Vermont, Austin McGregor of Litchfield, Maine, Emma McGregor of Sabattus, Maine, and Kody McGregor of Lewiston, Maine. He also enjoyed great-grandson Kingston McGregor of Litchfield, Maine.
He is survived by his wife, Susan Lamie, his daughter Kathryn Adams of Otisfield, and her husband Ryan, son Nathan Lamie of White River Junction, Vermont and his wife Sara, his daughter Kimberly McGregor of Lewiston, and his sister Denise Powell and her husband Bill of South China, Maine. He is also survived by many nieces and nephews for whom he cared very much.
He was predeceased by his parents, his brother Larry Lamie, and his sister Lorraine Roberge.
Norm’s career included working for the City of Lewiston Public Works Department, Auburn Water & Sewer District, and as Chief Engineer with the State of Maine Drinking Water Program. He was President of the Maine Water Utilities Association in 1994 and President of the New England Water Works in 2005. He closed out his nearly 50-year career in the drinking water profession working as an independent contractor helping small water utilities in Maine with financial and operational issues with the Maine Rural Water Association.
Norm enjoyed nearly 40 years of professional networking and fellowship with Rotary. He became a charter member of the Auburn Lewiston Rotary Breakfast Club in 1991. He served as Club President in 1994 and as Club Treasurer since 2016.
Norm’s interest in genealogy came about in later years. His genealogy research uncovered many interesting facts about ancestors and historical connections that he freely shared with extended family. Norm was able to trace his ancestry back many generations to France. He served on the Board of Directors and Treasurer of the Maine Franco-American Genealogical Society since 2022. In the years to come, future generations will recognize the impact of having Norm in their family tree and feel a sense of pride.
The family extends a heartfelt thanks to the compassionate and talented medical team who cared for Norm during his illness, especially Dr. Daniel Rausch of Cancer Care Center at Central Maine Medical Center, the talented and caring team of staff and doctors at Infusion Care, and the caring professionals from Hospice & Palliative Care Service provided by Andwell Health Partners.
Relatives and friends are invited to attend a Celebration of Life for Normand on Monday, October 12, 2026 from 4PM to 7PM at The Fortin & Pinette Group, 217 Turner Street Auburn, ME 04210.

title: Matt Dunlap understands how we in Maine feel
text:
I recently attended a town hall meeting in Auburn to listen to Matt Dunlap, candidate for Congress. I didn’t know Dunlap. I know Paul LePage, his opponent.
When Dunlap said “government feels more vengeful,” I nodded and noticed others around me doing the same. Government does feel vengeful, right now, especially to hardworking families.
If elected, I believe LePage would reinforce the GOP call to prolong the war and permit the Medicare cuts proposed in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. A LePage victory would result in an echo chamber for MAGA policies. LePage has described himself as “a big fan” of data centers. The values shared by most Americans suggest strong opposition to the war in Iran, tariffs and the development of data centers.
Before becoming Maine’s state auditor, Matt Dunlap served as secretary of state. His values align more closely with working people I know. His experience in both offices demonstrates a balanced approach to public service.
Dunlap’s message to Mainers reflects my priorities, including greater affordability for childcare, lower taxes for working families and reduced tariffs. Mainers also face rising energy costs at the pump and for home heating. As energy demand grows, we will need solutions that reduce our reliance on fossil fuels. I am voting for Matt Dunlap. I hope you will join me in electing new lawmakers who recognize what real Mainers want.
Marianne O’Connor
Lisbon Falls

title: Here's What You Need to Know About the Min Wage Increase in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
We have some good news for people working minimum wage hourly jobs and jobs where a significant portion of your pay is based on tips and gratuities.
The Increase to Maine's Minimum Wage
According to an article on the WABI website, Maine law requires the Maine Department of Labor to review and adjust the state’s minimum wage each year based on changes in the cost of living in the Northeast. This requirement was approved by Maine voters in 2016.
Because of this, the state's minimum wage will increase from $15.10 to $15.70 on January 1st, 2027
Maine's Tip Wage Is Increasing
If you work a job where a significant amount of your pay comes from tips, we've got some good news.
Maine’s minimum cash wage for tipped workers will increase from $7.55 to $7.85 per hour, and their combined wages and tips must equal at least $15.70 per hour. Workers must also earn at least $199 per month in tips to qualify as service employees.
The Overtime Exemption Level Is Increasing
If you work a salaried position, there is a good chance that you are "exempt". Basically, that means that you are required to perform your duties no matter how many hours it takes. This means you may end up working 35 hours or 55 hours. The benefit is that you will always make the same amount of money. The downside is that you may work way more than 40 hours in a week and get stuck with the same pay.
For years, there has been an exemption level. Basically, a certain minimum salary to make it lawful for you to be exempt from overtime. If you were paid over that, you could not get overtime. If you were paid less, you could claim overtime if you worked more than 40 hours a week.
That amount is now increasing.
As of January 1st, it will go from $45,300 to about $47,100.
A Brief History of Minimum Wage Laws in the United States
According to the Economic Policy Institute, the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) was created during the Great Depression in the 1930s, when millions of Americans struggled to find work and support their families.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the law on June 25, 1938. It established a federal minimum wage, limited the number of hours employees could work before earning overtime pay, and placed restrictions on child labor. The first minimum wage was $0.25 per hour.
Supporters believed the law would protect workers from unfair treatment and improve working conditions. Although some businesses argued that higher wages would cost jobs, the FLSA became an important step toward protecting American workers.

title: 2026 midterm election: Which states allow mail-in voting?
text:
Midterm election: How have states' mail-in voting policies changed since 2000?
President Donald Trump on Saturday encouraged voters to "vote early, vote by mail or vote in person on Election Day" in a video posted on Truth Social.
Trump also promoted the Republican Party website, Swamp the Vote USA, which offers guidance on voters' options in the post.
The message is a change in tone from Trump's criticisms of mail-in voting. In late March, Trump signed an executive order calling for three major changes to federal elections:
- Compiling a state citizenship list
- Requiring unique intelligent mail barcodes on all mail-in and absentee ballots
- Limiting the U.S. Postal Service to mailing ballots only to voters who had indicated they intended to vote by mail.
In mid-September, the Supreme Court blocked the Postal Service from enacting the new mail-in voting restrictions for the midterm election. The high court did not rule on the legality of the executive order.
Eight states and the District of Columbia have universal mail-in voting for their elections. The Get the Facts Data Team looked at how voting options, like mail-in ballots and early voting, have changed since 2000.
Which states allow voting by mail?
Every state allows some form of mail-in voting or absentee ballots, but some require voters to provide a reason.
Since 2000, the availability of mail-in and early voting in states has increased. In 2000, only 21 states allowed voters to vote early in person or by mail without an excuse.
The COVID-19 pandemic helped increase the use of mail-in voting after 11 states temporarily expanded access in 2020. For that election, a majority of states allowed voters to cast a mail ballot without an excuse. Mississippi was the only state that required voters to provide a reason to vote by mail and did not offer early in-person voting.
For this midterm election, 37 states and the District of Columbia will allow voters to request and cast a mail ballot without providing a reason. These states and Washington, D.C., also allow voters to cast ballots early in person before Election Day.
Mail-in ballots and voter turnout
Nearly one in three voters cast their ballots by mail in the 2024 general election, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission. That was slightly lower than in the 2022 midterm election, when about 32% of voters cast a mail ballot.
Voting by mail spiked during the 2020 election, with 43% of voters casting their ballots that way. In-person voting was limited due to the COVID-19 pandemic and several states temporarily expanded access to mail-in voting.
With more states allowing voters to cast ballots by mail in 2020, voter turnout reached its highest level at 161.3 million.
Turnout fell to 112.1 million during the 2022 midterm election, reflecting the common trend of presidential elections drawing higher turnout than midterm elections.

title: Feds release nearly $37M in heating aid for Maine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Trump administration is releasing nearly $37 million in heating aid for Maine.
That comes after U.S. Sen. Susan Collins met this week with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and White House budget director Russell Vought, her office announced Friday morning.
This season Maine is getting about $36.7 million in Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program funds, while the state’s four federally recognized tribes will receive $1.4 million to help their members stay warm.
Collins’ office called this one of the earliest releases in the program’s history.
“With home heating oil costs soaring, many Maine families and seniors on limited incomes are facing the prospect of extraordinarily high heating bills this winter. That is why I urged the Administration to expedite the release of this critical assistance, and why I fought so hard to protect and increase funding for LIHEAP. I am pleased that these funds are being released to help Mainers afford to heat their homes this winter without having to choose between staying warm and paying for other basic necessities,” Collins said in a statement.
The unlocked heating assistance comes as Mainers face higher costs to stay warm this winter. This week the average price for a gallon of heating oil was $5.97, up 79% from the same time last year, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources.
That means it will cost Mainers about $725 more to fill a standard 275-gallon tank.
In eastern and Down East Maine, prices range from a low of $5.50 to a high of $6.30.
Collins, U.S. Sen. Angus King and more than two dozen other senators last month pressed the Trump administration for a swift release of heating aid. Gov. Janet Mills has called on Congress to increase funding for heating assistance, pointing to the economic impact of President Donald Trump’s war in Iran.
That ongoing war has been the primary factor driving up heating oil and gasoline prices. The war effectively halted shipments in the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas flows.
Additionally, Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure and Houthi strikes on Saudi energy production sites have further constricted global supplies in recent weeks, according to Reuters.
Mainers can apply for the heating aid through their local community action agency. Eligibility is determined by income, household size and availability of resources.

title: New Balance unveils Cooper Flagg logo
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
New Balance has unveiled a new Cooper Flagg logo.
The New England athletic apparel company released the logo Thursday. It features a stylized “CF,” with a pine tree design on the “C,” an homage to the Newport phenom’s Maine roots.
“The logo design represents me. It connects to my name, but also to my roots, which is something that was really important to me,” Flagg said in a statement. “Where I’m from, there are a lot of trees, so you’ll see the pine tree cutouts on the side as a reminder of staying true to who I am and where I grew up. I wanted to include hints of Maine while keeping the design clean and something that feels like me.”
In 2024, Flagg signed an endorsement deal with New Balance while still a player at Duke University. New Balance released its first Flagg exclusive shoe last year.
After inking the deal, Flagg signed with the NBA’s Dallas Mavericks.
With the Mavericks, Flagg averaged 21 points per game, the most for any rookie; became the youngest player to score 50 points in a single NBA game; and is the second-youngest to score 1,000 points.
The top draft pick ahead of last season, Flagg went on to become the second-youngest Rookie of the Year, behind only Lebron James.
Last month, a Flagg trading card sold for more than $8 million at an auction, making it the fifth most expensive sports card sale ever, just edging out a Honus Wagner card that sold four years ago for $7.25 million.

title: Every 21 days, she depends on blood donations to survive a rare condition
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (InvestigateTV) - Emily Rodgers is 12. She loves tumbling, the color pink and her best friend.
This seventh grader measures time in 21-day increments.
“I come here every three weeks, and this is my 194th blood transfusion,” Emily said.
Emily has beta thalassemia major, a rare blood disorder that prevents her body from making hemoglobin. Since she was an infant, doctors at Vanderbilt University Medical Center (VUMC) have given her transfusions.
“Her body can’t make blood like healthy people. And so since she was a baby, we’ve actually been giving her transfusions to keep her alive,” said Dr. Jennifer Andrews, Emily’s pediatric hematologist and medical director of the blood bank at VUMC.
Without those transfusions, Emily’s blood cannot carry enough oxygen. As she gets closer to the 21st day, she can feel it.
“Actually, the other day I had to go to the nurse’s office because I was trying to keep myself awake, and my body couldn’t stay awake any longer,” Emily said.
Hospital depends on daily blood donations
Andrews said it is important that the hospital always has blood available for Emily and other patients whose lives depend on immediate access to blood for routine care, emergency situations, surgical procedures, or cancer-related needs.
Most of the blood bags at the hospital come from the nonprofit Blood Assurance, donated by strangers who decided to show up.
“Literally, if you donate blood, it is the difference at Vanderbilt between life and death,” Andrews said.
The process requires constant replenishment, with someone donating every day of the week, 365 days a year.
Four-hour transfusion process
During her recent visit, Emily received two bags of blood, a process that takes about four hours just for the transfusion. She does not complain.
“We all just adore her. Wait till you talk to the nurses, they’re just one. She is one of their favorite patients,” Andrews said.
“This is my home away from home, because we come here so much. But the nurses are basically family, and they treat me so well. They all know me by name, so I just love them so much,” Emily said.
Andrews said there are now possible cures for Emily’s condition, including gene therapy or a stem cell transplant, but for now, transfusions are working best.
For Emily, one bag means three more weeks of life, cheer practice, and that dreaded vocabulary.
“Then when I have my blood, when I go back to school, I can just, like, retain stuff better,” Emily said.
When asked what she would say to someone who donates blood, Emily said, “I would just say thank you, because one bag of blood could save somebody’s life.”
In 21 days, she will be back in the chair, and that depends on who shows up next.
How to donate blood
To keep up with demand, Blood Assurance said the area needs more than 540 blood donors each day. That’s nearly 4,000 donors a week.
Right now, the supply of all blood types is just half of what doctors consider safe, and there is even less of a supply of platelets.
Donating blood is a safe, simple process that takes roughly an hour, with the actual draw lasting around 10 minutes. A single blood donation can save up to three lives, according to the Red Cross.
Blood Assurance operates donation centers throughout Middle Tennessee and accepts walk-ins and appointments.
To schedule an appointment or find a donation center location, visit bloodassurance.org, call 800-962-0628, or text BAGIVE to 999777.

title: Digging dangers: Why underground utility damage is on the rise
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - We rely on natural gas and electricity every day to heat and light our homes. But one mistake underground can turn an energy source into an instant threat.
In 2024, the country saw more than 83,000 reports of damage to gas and electrical lines. One in four of those damage reports were because people failed to call 811.
That number connects you to a free, national service designed to prevent damage to utility lines by marking where they are located. Calling 811 is required by law.
In January, Molly Krummenacher came home to find her hot water heater and dryer on fire, water spewing like a fountain after an excavator hit her electric line.
“It’s just sheer panic and disbelief,” she said.
AT&T was in the area to install fiber optic internet, but hired subcontractor USIC to mark the electric lines. Molly said there was no flag or marking for the electrical line.
The incident caused a surge that turned neutral wires into live wires, resulting in $20,000 in damage.
“It’s just a really frustrating and sad situation that innocent, you know, civilians get put in by big corporations,” Molly said.
An increase in damage
The incident is part of a growing trend. Common Ground Alliance data shows more than half a million reports of damage to underground utilities at dig sites in recent years.
In Missouri, more than 10,000 reports have been filed in recent years, with close to 6,500 in Illinois. The numbers are ticking up each year.
“Unfortunately, the data shows that the incident rate is increasing with the amount of construction that we’re seeing across the country,” said Sarah Magruder Lyle with the Common Ground Alliance.
The region has seen multiple home explosions in recent years linked to digging incidents, including blasts in O’Fallon, Jefferson County and Glendale. Some have been deadly.
A 5-year-old was killed outside Kansas City last year when his home exploded. His sister and father were badly hurt.
Magruder Lyle said infrastructure is constantly changing, with massive upgrades to the internet driving much of the digging activity.
“The amount of fiber that is being put in the ground right now, you know, all the other infrastructure pales in comparison,” she said.
Understanding what’s happening at dig sites requires looking underground. Burying utilities dates back to ancient times, but over time, more pipes and wires have been placed underground for water, sewage, electricity, internet and gas.
Knowing exactly where those utilities are underground is now a complex problem.
“It is changing constantly, and it’s changing quickly,” Magruder Lyle said.
Common Ground Alliance data shows many locate requests are late, missing or inaccurate, with blame shared by those locating the lines, those digging and people who try to find utilities in the first place.
“Not contacting 811 is a quarter of the incidents we see,” Magruder Lyle said.
Digging damage to underground utilities is preventable, she said.
Missouri strengthened its dig laws last year. New utility lines must now be buried with a detectable location device like tracer wire or locator tape. Magruder Lyle said electronic geo-location mapping technology is needed, too.
“All roads lead back to mapping,” she said.
When asked if more still needs to be done, she said: “Absolutely. We can always do better.”
To protect yourself, Magruder Lyle said, pay attention to dig notices, paint markings and flags.
“If you don’t see something, then say something. This is actually the opposite of what we hear. If you don’t see paint on the ground, it’s okay to ask,” she said.
Back in Ballwin, crews returned to digging one day after the fire.
“It feels like I have a second job,” Molly said.
She said she got the runaround on who was responsible until she mentioned she’d called the news station. Two hours later, she received a call from USIC.
The company has paid her insurance deductible. Still, Molly said she worries about future consequences.
“We could be dropped by our insurance for something we had absolutely no control of,” she said.
“It’s a really scary thought,” she said.
Molly said a neighbor’s home was also damaged by the electrical surge.
AT&T provided a statement:
“As we bring high-speed fiber internet to more communities, we strive to minimize disruption for residents. If any property damage occurs, please know that we take the concerns of those affected very seriously. In this case, our contractor has reached out to the homeowner and is working to resolve her concerns.”
USIC did not respond to a request for comment. The company is currently being sued by the Glendale homeowner whose home exploded in August 2025.
What the colored markings mean
If you’ve ever wonder what the colored markings in your yard or along the street mean, we reached out to an expert to explain.
Erik Phillips is vice president of operations for UtiliQuest, which helps to prevent damages to utility lines.
Phillips said red covers electrical lines, orange covers phone lines and yellow covers gas.
Blue markings are for water while green represents sewer and storm drains.
And experts are Common Ground Alliance say even if a contractor is doing the work, it’s your responsibility to call 811 before the digging starts.
Whether it’s a big construction project or planting shrubs, residents must call 811 before digging.

title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Federal Reserve’s Lisa Cook in latest effort to fire her
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump opened another chapter in his effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday by establishing a “committee of inquiry” to investigate allegations that she made false statements in mortgage applications.
The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House Nov. 5, Trump said in a written memo, that Cook “shall” attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing wouldn’t be public but a transcript would be published, the memo said.
Trump’s extraordinary demand that Cook testify before the committee will likely renew concerns about threats to the Federal Reserve’s independence as the president demands the central bank cut its key interest rate. Just last month, the Fed raised its key rate instead, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed earlier this year.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in the memorandum.
Trump and some of his economic advisers have blamed the Fed’s broader rate-setting committee, which includes 12 voting members and 19 officials in total, for the rate hike. Cook is one of the 12 participants on the committee that votes on interest-rate decisions. The vote to lift rates Sept. 16 was unanimous.
The move follows a Supreme Court ruling in June that Cook could keep her job after Trump sought to fire her last year. That ruling included a footnote that said nothing prevented Trump from “trying again” as long as she was given proper notice and an opportunity to respond to the charges.
Cook has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.

title: Spruce Mountain football bests Cape Elizabeth in 8-man battle
text:
LIVERMORE FALLS — It doesn’t matter if it’s through the air or on the ground, Spruce Mountain quarterback Dylan Jewett always seems to find the end zone.
Jewett was responsible for four touchdowns Friday night (one passing, three rushing) as he led the Phoenix to a 40-28 win over Cape Elizabeth in an eight-man football Large School South clash.
“That kid, he can change the game in the blink of an eye, and sometimes we have to talk to him a little bit to realize that,” said Spruce Mountain coach Devin Roberts. “And once he knows it in the game, he does it.”
In Spruce Mountain’s 36-34 loss to Orono on Oct. 2, Jewett was also responsible for four touchdowns, rushing for one, throwing for two and returning a kick for a score.
“I think a lot of it goes to the line and coach just making the right play call, and my guys just block for me, so (I) just take advantage of that,” Jewett said.
HOW IT HAPPENED
Spruce Mountain (4-2) took the lead on its first offensive play, a 56-yard run by Jewett. Cape Elizabeth (4-2) answered with a 13-yard touchdown run by quarterback Rosco Hampton.
The Phoenix and Capers went back-to-back again on their ensuing drives, which resulted in a 14-yard touchdown pass from Jewett to Levi Richards, and a 2-yard touchdown pass from Hampton to Liam Brown.
Jewett’s 72-yard touchdown run with just under two minutes to go in the second quarter gave Spruce Mountain a 20-14 lead. Cape Elizabeth answered again in the third quarter, scoring two touchdowns (a 6-yard run from Hampton and a 9-yard pass from Hampton to Sam Hews) to take a 28-20 lead with just under 17 and a half minutes left in the game.
The Phoenix scored the next three touchdowns to take control. After Spruce Mountain tied the game, the Capers had a chance to regain the lead, but their drive stalled at the Spruce Mountain 9 when Levi Richards recovered a fumble by Hews. Jewett and Owen Kelvey scored for Spruce Mountain to put the game away.
UNSUNG HERO
Not only did Spruce Mountain’s Levi Richards catch a touchdown pass and a 2-point conversion, but the wide receiver/cornerback also recovered the fumble that shifted the game in the second half. His defensive effort led to the touchdown that gave the Phoenix a 34-28 lead in the fourth quarter.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “We came into the game knowing we had to win if we wanted to seal a spot, (a top-four spot) for playoffs, so it was a big game for us.” — Dylan Jewett
• “We feel like we’ve beaten the teams we’re supposed to beat, and the two teams (Yarmouth, Spruce Mountain) that we really had circled on our schedule, we just have to play a full four quarters. In both of those games, we’ve had some turnovers in areas of the field where we were going to take the lead or increase the lead, and it just didn’t work out that way.” — Cape Elizabeth coach Issiah Bachelder
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Spruce Mountain: Dylan Jewett (three rushing touchdowns; one passing touchdown), Owen Kelvey (two rushing touchdowns)
• Cape Elizabeth: Rosco Hampton (two rushing touchdowns, two passing touchdowns)

title: Concierge medicine vs. direct primary care: what to know before you pay out of pocket
text:
(Aging Untold) — Health care can get complicated fast, and not all doctors take the same approach. Some are moving away from traditional insurance models to spend more time with patients and focus on root causes and long-term wellness. That shift can mean paying out of pocket, and it isn’t the right fit for everyone.
What are the options?
Two of the options are concierge medicine and direct primary care.
“With concierge medicine, you have your own doctor and you pay privately for that,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said.
She said direct primary care is concierge. It’s a membership organization, but the doctor also takes insurance.
“The cost for concierge-type medicine is more expensive. Direct primary care is less expensive, but you’re a member and you have access to the doctor — 24/7 appointments, and your care is more on the preventive side,” O’Rourke said.
Why Dr. Rhea Rogers made the switch
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said her own path moved from traditional obstetrics and gynecology into an integrative approach before she transitioned fully into functional medicine.
“What made that decision for me is I always felt like patients need to have the options that are available to them, and I would give those to them,” Rogers said.
She said she would let them know which route insurance would cover and which it would not.
“It came to a point of do no wrong and do no harm,” Rogers said.
“When you start to understand what’s really happening at a cellular level with a person, I couldn’t help them with that model,” Rogers said. “So I had to go all the way where I could tell them, “This is what’s going on, and this is what I can do to help you.’”
Rogers said many patients come to her after they’ve exhausted the traditional system.
“When they’ve exhausted the traditional system and they’re sick, and they don’t feel well, and they’re like, ‘I don’t care what it costs, I need me back,’” she said.
Weighing cost and coverage
Rogers said the traditional model also includes some preventive care, such as screenings.
Concierge medicine and direct primary care are two types of out-of-pocket care, but O’Rourke said that there are other types as well.
“A lot of cosmetic (care) is out-of-pocket, even cosmetic dentistry,” Cradduck added. “Unfortunately, there are a lot of people who just can’t afford this, though they would love to be healthier and love to be able to come see you.”
Cradduck said affordability can become “the stepping stone” to accessing functional medicine and cellular-level care.
O’Rourke agreed affordability is tied to liquid income but said establishing a relationship with a physician can help even without a membership model.
“If you can’t afford concierge or direct primary care, establish that partnership with a physician as best as you can so that you can get some preventive care,” she said. “Just ask those types of questions.”
“I do think there’s an affordability issue for many people, but I also think many people could afford it, and it’s a mindset issue,” Ambrose said.
“What I tell people — I’m going to invest in myself. It’s an investment, just like you’d invest in anything else,” Rogers said.
Rogers compared traditional insurance to driving a major highway. “In functional medicine, I’m going to take the personalized scenic route,” she said.
“If I take the personalized scenic route, then I might have five or 10 more years of work and income versus having to medically retire,” Cradduck said.
She said that, over time, this approach could help people stay productive and earn more.
She added that some employers are beginning to take notice. “That’s why you’re seeing companies now start to employ that functional medicine model, because they see the difference in their workers,” she said.
Key takeaways
- Concierge medicine means a private doctor you pay for directly. Direct primary care is a membership model where the doctor may still accept insurance.
- Costs vary by model. Direct primary care memberships can start at around $50 a month and go up, while concierge memberships start around $200 a month and up.
- Pros include 24/7 access. Members may get more time with their doctor, less waiting, same-day appointments and direct phone access.
- Cons include added expense. Out-of-pocket costs apply, and with some memberships, separate insurance coverage is still needed.

title: Biddeford looks to mitigate rising complaints of needle waste, public encampments
text:
BIDDEFORD — Williams Court Park was busy on a sunny October afternoon as nearly a dozen people, dressed in layers of mismatched clothing and toting carts full of their belongings, found refuge in the grass. It was clear that they were waiting to spend the night at Seeds of Hope, a nearby overnight shelter.
Across the street, a woman in a bright green shirt leaned against a stone wall, fiddling with what looked like a syringe. In the morning, volunteers at the nearby Biddeford Community Garden would find syringes just like it.
Managing needle waste and public camping has been one of the biggest problem areas in the city, General Assistance Administrator Jake Hammer said at a City Council meeting Tuesday.
“We’re trying to figure out how we use the resources we have already to pinpoint this area,” he said.
Residents say they’re seeing an increase in encampments, trash and needle waste, and some are taking to social media and city meetings to complain.
Since July, the police department has responded to 45 calls to the park for issues like drug complaints, disturbances, suspicious activity and trespassing. Over the same time period, the city’s code enforcement compliance officer has responded to encampments over 50 times.
Williams Court Park isn’t the only problem area in the city — officers often respond to similar calls about the area near Lincoln and Pearl streets, Horrigan Court near the railroad tracks and the Eastern Trail, Hammer said.
Holly Culloton, director of Biddeford Community Gardens, said her team often finds used syringes and other debris in the raised garden beds at Williams Court Park.
“This summer has been really tough,” Culloton said. “It’s been really problematic.”
Gardeners also witness frequent drug use, Culloton said, and one was assaulted by a homeless person in the park. At times, she said, she’s considered simply “turning the garden over to them.”
“What do we do when we have a sharps container that isn’t being used regularly? What do we do when there are needles on the ground and in garden beds for little kids to find?” Culloton asked the City Council on Tuesday. “What do we do when freaky drug users are shooting up, taking who knows what, and having crazy and violent behaviors?”
A POSSIBLE SOLUTION
Because Biddeford is a service center city — meaning people have access to resources like Seeds of Hope, soup kitchens, food pantries, grocery stores and healthcare — Hammer said he doesn’t believe people experiencing homelessness will leave. Instead, the goal is to connect them with resources and limit dangerous waste.
While General Assistance is working with Seeds of Hope to get people housed and off the streets, Hammer said there needs to be a solution for those who refuse to go inside.
“We can offer beds, if we have beds to offer,” Councilor Lisa Vadnais said Tuesday. “But they can still say ‘no.’ I think the reason they say ‘no’ is because they don’t really like the restricted rules that they have to follow being in a shelter.”
To help mitigate the impacts of encampments, Hammer proposed a pilot program that would pair a compliance officer and a housing navigator to monitor encampments and work together to get people off the streets.
“The goal, from the municipal side, is to get people not living outside,” Hammer said.
The city is also working with Maine Access Points, a nonprofit that provides overdose prevention and harm reduction services. Maine Access Points staff members and volunteers routinely answer calls for cleanups in Biddeford, primarily after an encampment has been moved by the city.
Anna McConnell, executive director of Maine Access Points, said the organization has also been working to place sharps containers in areas frequented by drug users.
“When we hear complaints and we go into the community to find trash and waste, it’s often in situations where people have been camping and were quickly and forcibly displaced,” McConnell said.
By working with city staff and the City Council, McConnell hopes to improve responsiveness to encampments — but also to better help the people living in those encampments.
“We’re really in the process right now of trying to improve the systems,” McConnell said. “I’m so impressed with how many people are coming together around this issue to make an impact.”

title: “The system said he’d fail. He built this instead.”
text:

title: How Texas landowners are fighting back against Trump's border wall
text:
RUIDOSA, Texas (AP) — The message from the Trump administration has been clear: It is moving ahead with a $46 billion border wall project stretching from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.
But in Texas’ Big Bend region, the administration has run up against intense opposition from landowners, many of whom are unwilling to cede parts of their property for what they see as a waste of taxpayer dollars.
That resistance is complicating President Donald Trump’s signature infrastructure project in a fight that has become a test of just how far the administration will go to fulfill its vision of a fortified southern border.
The administration has committed billions of dollars and waived environmental and other protections to plow ahead with the project despite the region’s historically low illegal crossings, its formidable natural barriers and a surge of bipartisan opposition that has scrambled traditional border politics.
The federal government has sweeping authority to force the project through. But a judge has now paused construction across the region, giving a major boost to landowners who have sought to impede the wall by refusing to cooperate with government surveyors, protesting at county meetings and gearing up for court battles.
“Landowner resistance has slowed this project to a crawl,” said David Keller, a landowner suing to stop the Big Bend border plans. The administration, he added, was “woefully unprepared for the hornet’s nest they stirred up.”
Trump has long pledged to build the border wall
Building a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border has long been a key campaign promise for Trump. And the administration pushed ahead with it after Republicans last year approved $46 billion for the border wall as part of a sweeping immigration enforcement package.
Although illegal crossings have plummeted under Trump, the administration says walls, vehicle barriers, surveillance technology and patrol roads are needed to keep them low.
Customs and Border Protection says it’s building an average of about 12 miles or 20 kilometers of barrier a week and had recently hit a milestone of more than 200 miles (320 km) of new walls built under the second Trump administration.
In Big Bend, where construction began in September, the administration plans to spend $7.5 billion to fortify the border along a region stretching more than 500 miles (800 km).
In August, the Border Patrol arrested 8,870 people along the southern border. In Big Bend, which makes up roughly one quarter of the entire U.S.-Mexico border, it arrested 161.
“The American people have already seen the consequences of an unprotected border,” said CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott after a lawsuit filed by landowners against the Big Bend project. “We cannot allow any region — including Big Bend — to be exploited again.”
Landowners gird for court battles
Unlike in other border areas, much of the land in Texas is privately or state owned.
The government must acquire authorization from owners to survey and build and if they refuse, can take them to court. The process by which the government takes someone’s property for public use in exchange for compensation is known as eminent domain and courts generally defer to the government in these cases.
That hasn’t stopped Dianna and Dan Burbach.
The Burbachs began receiving paperwork in July seeking permission to survey their property, along with a map showing where the project would run behind their house. An August letter said the government had an “immediate need” to enter and warned that it could go to court within 90 days.
Dianna, 63, and her husband, 79, arrived 25 years ago and raised four children in their orange adobe house on property stretching to the Rio Grande. Now retired, they worry construction could worsen flooding and leave 15 acres (6 hectares) of their land behind the wall.
“We’re going to let them take us to court, do eminent domain,” Dianna said. “We’ll fight it that way.”
A Justice Department official said CBP has reached agreements with dozens of Big Bend landowners but that the administration has hired eminent domain attorneys in Texas in anticipation of the disputes. Across the southern border, about 70 such cases have been referred to the department during Trump’s second term, and 50 have already been resolved — none required going to trial, said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the government.
The No Big Bend Wall Coalition, which says its network includes more than 200 landowners, recently sued to block construction. The plaintiffs argue that Homeland Security is misusing its authority in a region with little illegal cross-border activity.
Lawsuits aiming to stop or slow the border wall projects have largely been unsuccessful. But in a major win for opponents, a federal judge temporarily barred wall construction in the Big Bend area. Plaintiffs argued the administration had overstepped its congressional authority by issuing sweeping waivers to bypass environmental and other regulations.
Keller said the judge’s ruling was “unqualified good news” but uncertainty over its future meant the landowners would continue their fight.
It’s not immediately clear how long the judge’s order will slow the government, which late Thursday asked the judge to put aside her order while they appeal.
The administration also argued in the court filing that leaving segments along the border without adequate border security infrastructure could lead to a funnel effect where illegal immigration or smuggling would flow to the area that was least fortified — specifically the Big Bend region.
Protesting contractors and lobbying local officials
Other opponents are pressing local governments not to assist contractors. Charlie Angell, a tourism operator notified that the government wanted access to his land for the border project, and his partner, Bibiana Gutierrez, attend county meetings throughout the region.
They and other land and business owners have staged protests, patrolled areas where contractors are working to look for possible violations, and hung signs telling contractors they’re not welcome at local hotels or restaurants.
In Terrell County, residents unsuccessfully urged officials not to lease airport land to a barrier contractor. In Jeff Davis County, a proposed agreement allowing another contractor to use a county road has so far not been approved.
The financial incentives for some of these cash-starved counties are clear and some local officials have argued they have little leverage on a federal plan.
“We’re not in control of the border wall. We’re not,” Terrell County Judge Dale Lynn Carruthers told a room crowded with people who had come to speak out against the airport lease. She said if they didn’t lease the land, the contractor would just buy it elsewhere. “We’re just a little old Terrell County.”
But Angell and Gutierrez argue that the local opposition has more strength than some might realize.
“If we had rolled over, the wall would be up,” Gutierrez said.
CBP said it continues seeking voluntary access agreements while completing the project’s design but will refer disputes to the Justice Department when necessary. Landowners will be compensated regardless of how access is obtained, the agency said.
The opposition has bipartisan support
After a yearslong surge in crossings at the southern frontier, border security and immigration were key reasons Republicans voted for Trump and his approval ratings on those issues are among his strongest.
But with illegal crossings plummeting, even some Republicans who voted for Trump on the issue of border security have questioned the need for the multi-billion dollar infrastructure through Big Bend.
Local sheriffs opposed the project early, and bulldozing in Big Bend National Park prompted Republican Sen. John Cornyn to press Homeland Security about Texans’ concerns.
Laura Allen, a Republican rancher who voted for Trump twice, is now receiving notices that a vehicle barrier will cross the property where her family raises sheep and goats. She credits Trump with shutting down the border but says spending billions on barriers in Big Bend is unnecessary.
“I didn’t vote for a wall,” she said. “I wanted our border secured. He accomplished that.”
Terrell County’s Republican sheriff, Thad Cleveland, who spent 26 years in the Border Patrol, is among those speaking out against the project in Big Bend. He said that in the rugged county he polices, drones and surveillance towers make more sense than a wall to find and stop illegal border crossers.
“We have the advantage of time and distance out here,” he said.
The land itself is a natural deterrent, critics say
In some areas, the river is flanked on both sides by steep limestone cliffs, and up and down the region, people have to trek through inhospitable desert terrain to get to the nearest paved road or pass through Border Patrol checkpoints.
Reaching Gary Grabowske’s land requires grinding along rocky mountain trails and through gullies carved by flash floods. From the top of a 450-foot cliff (137 meters), the Rio Grande is visible far below. There is no electricity, running water or internet and, Grabowske argues, no plausible route for a vehicle entering from Mexico.
“You can’t take a dirt bike to the bottom,” said Grabowske, gesturing to the canyon below. “You can’t take a mule to the bottom. You’re scrambling down there, hand over fist.” He added: “There’s no vehicle in the world that could cross any of this.”
Opponents say the fight reaches beyond whether a wall makes sense in Big Bend. They see it as a test of how far the federal government can go when landowners stand in the way of one of its priorities.
“We’re a pretty tough bunch,” said Allen. “But if we’re going to be run over and have our land taken by our own government, what makes anybody else in this United States think that they’re exempt?”
Ranchers try to resist
The Zuberbueler ranch in Val Verde County was founded in 1898. Brothers Bill and Patrick own and lease thousands of acres of the craggy land stretching to the river. Their Angora goats and Rambouillet sheep roam over the land, stopping at a network of water troughs.
Bill remembers when, back in February, he first got the letter giving him five days to respond to a request to access his property for construction and raising the possibility of the government using eminent domain. He worries about how the construction will affect his livestock, especially their water supply. And while his animals could pass through the vehicle barriers, the cowboys herding them could not.
“There’s not a lot of grass out here, but every square foot is important to my bottom line,” said Bill.
They have so far refused to allow anyone onto their land to survey or build. They feel the weight of their family’s legacy and the sacrifices previous generations made to build the ranch up.
“Regardless of what happens, we have to say we tried,” said Patrick.
__
Associated Press writer Alanna Durkin Richer contributed from Washington.

title: AT&T data breach settlement gets final approval. See how much customers could receive
text:
(Gray News) - A federal judge has granted final approval to AT&T’s $177 million settlement involving breaches that exposed customers’ personal information.
Last year, AT&T reached a combined $177 million settlement over two data breaches that were disclosed in 2024 and established a claim form for affected customers to submit.
The reported data involved in the breaches belonged to millions of current and former AT&T customers and dated as far back as 2019.
Now, with the judge’s final approval, those who submitted a claim could receive their payments soon.
According to the settlement, consumers impacted by the first breach may be eligible for up to $5,000, and those affected by the second breach may be eligible for up to $2,500.
Final payment amounts were expected to vary depending on the losses documented by each claimant and the total number of settlement claims received.
Those with knowledge of the settlement said most eligible customers were expected to qualify for payments ranging from $6.50 to $40.
Payments are said to be going out after the appeals period has expired, with the settlement calling for payments to be distributed within 60 days of the effective date.

title: State warns of contractor scams as Hurricane Isaias approaches
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MONTGOMERY, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - The Alabama Home Builders Licensure Board is warning homeowners about the potential for scams, fraud and price gouging during storm cleanup, repair and rebuilding as Hurricane Isaias threatens the Gulf Coast and central Alabama.
The board is urging residents to be cautious when hiring anyone to repair storm damage or purchase needed items.
Emergency proclamation triggers felony law
Gov. Kay Ivey issued an emergency proclamation Wednesday covering dozens of counties ahead of the potential hurricane landfall, including Autauga, Baldwin, Barbour, Bibb, Bullock, Butler, Chambers, Chilton, Clarke, Choctaw, Coffee, Conecuh, Coosa, Covington, Crenshaw, Dale, Dallas, Elmore, Escambia, Geneva, Greene, Hale, Henry, Houston, Lee, Lowndes, Macon, Marengo, Mobile, Monroe, Montgomery, Perry, Pickens, Pike, Russell, Sumter, Tallapoosa, Tuscaloosa, Washington and Wilcox counties.
The proclamation triggers consumer protection laws, including the Aggravated Home Repair Fraud law, which makes unlicensed homebuilding a class C felony when services are offered after an emergency declaration.
License requirements
A state homebuilders license is required when the cost of a job exceeds $10,000. The Home Builders Licensure Board encourages consumers to seek licensed professionals even when the cost of work does not exceed that amount.
A roofer’s license is required for replacing a storm-damaged roof when the cost of the job exceeds $2,500. Performing or offering unlicensed services is normally a class A misdemeanor, but becomes a felony when someone takes advantage of homeowners after an emergency weather event.
“With the Governor’s emergency proclamation, anyone unlicensed who takes advantage of Alabamians with storm damage to their homes, the Home Builders Licensure Board will work with law enforcement and district attorneys to charge and prosecute you for the felony crime of aggravated home repair fraud,” said Seth Gowan, executive director of the Alabama Home Builders Licensure Board. “Taking advantage of fellow Alabamians who suffer damage or loss of property will not be tolerated,” Gowan said.
Steps before hiring a contractor
The Alabama Home Builders Licensure Board outlined steps consumers should take before hiring anyone to perform repairs:
- Ask if the contractor is licensed with the Alabama Home Builders Licensure Board and ask to see the license card. Consumers can also verify licensure status by calling 1-800-304-0853 or visiting www.hblb.alabama.gov.
- Ask for and check references, especially if the builder makes unsolicited contact or is from out of town.
- Make sure quotes and contracts are in writing and include the Home Builders Licensure Board license number. Licensed homebuilders must use a written contract that includes the contractor’s full name, address, telephone number, a description of the work to be performed, starting and estimated completion dates, and the total cost of the job.
Gowan encouraged residents “to be cautious and patient. Work with your insurance company, check to make sure contractors are licensed, ask a lot of questions, and if you believe a contractor is not in the area for the right reasons, call law enforcement.”
Reporting fraud
Consumers may report alleged fraud or price gouging to the Attorney General’s Office for investigation. Complaints can be filed online at www.alabamaag.gov under the “consumer complaint” link, or by calling the Consumer Interest Division toll-free at 1-800-392-5658.
For information about home repair licensing and potential fraud, contact the Home Builders Licensure Board at 445 Herron St., Montgomery, Alabama 36104, 334-242-2230 or 1-800-304-0853, or visit www.hblb.alabama.gov.

title: Runners in their 70s celebrate 50 years of running half marathon
text:
Two runners celebrate 50 years of running half marathon
The OUC Orlando Half Marathon is celebrating its 50th anniversary this year, and two runners are celebrating 50 years of running every race.
Alan Musanti, 76, and Gary Kane, 78, are preparing to continue a streak that began when the race was first held five decades ago.
"I'm very proud of being able to hang in all that time," Musanti said.
Reflecting on last year's race, Kane said, "When I crossed the finish line last year, I just wanted to sit down someplace and die."
The two runners didn't know each other when their journey began, but over the years, marriages, kids and jobs brought them together — along with their shared commitment to running the OUC and maintaining their streak.
"I remember one year when we started out of Church Street Station; it poured rain the whole time," Musanti said. "And that was kind of fun, because once you're wet, it's fun to run in the rain."
Kane recalled his first race vividly.
"I remember turning the corner at the first, you know, at the Chamber of Commerce building, seeing my finish line, and I broke into tears. I was just so happy to, and I thought, 'I'll never do this again,'" Kane said.
Over time, the streak became a significant part of their lives.
"It was maybe at 15 or so it started to feel like a big number," Musanti said. "And at one point I started to question, 'Am I happy about the streak or am I not happy about the streak?'"
As experts on the course, Musanti and Kane shared advice for runners tackling the downtown route.
"Keep looking down if you're running on brick," Musanti said. "Be careful for the occasional loose brick and be careful for the slippery wet bricks."
"The course is nice, the shade is great, but the crowds are the best," Kane said.
When asked if they plan to continue the streak beyond this year, Kane said, "I am told by my wife the answer to that question is no. But we'll wait and see. I mean, God knows, you know, she might be out of town. Well, I won't tell her."
Musanti expressed hope to keep going but acknowledged the uncertainty of age.
"I hope to keep going, but one never knows at this age," Musanti said.
For now, Musanti and Kane are focused on celebrating their 50-year commitment, with family cheering them on as they cross the finish line for the 50th time.

title: BDN’s Callie Ferguson takes home top New England journalism award
text:
A Bangor Daily News investigations reporter has been honored with a top New England prize recognizing outstanding journalism.
Callie Ferguson, the deputy investigations editor for the BDN’s Maine Focus team, was awarded the AP Sevellon Brown NE Journalist of the Year, a prize named in honor of the late journalist Sevellon Brown, during a Friday ceremony for the New England Society of News Editors.
That was in recognition of Ferguson’s coverage of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s raids and arrests in Maine. Her work highlighted the lives of working immigrants caught up in President Donald Trump’s push to ramp up deportations after his second inauguration, particularly during ICE’s so-called Operation Catch of the Day.
Ferguson’s examination of court records found, contrary to ICE’s claims otherwise, that just 11 of the immigrants caught in the January surge had a criminal record, undercutting the Trump administration’s claim of targeting “the worst of the worst.”
Michael Shepherd, the BDN’s politics and investigations editor, called it “one of the most complete public accountings” of ICE’s activity in New England.
This is just the latest accolade for Ferguson in recent years.
“Few New England journalists under 35 carry a resume like Callie’s,” Shepherd wrote in his letter nominating Ferguson for the award.
Ferguson was a 2022 Livingston Award finalist, a 2023 New York Times local investigations fellow and won the New England First Amendment Coalition’s Michael Donoghue Freedom of Information Award and a Sidney Award for her contribution to the BDN’s “Lawmen Off Limits” series investigating the lack of accountability among Maine’s sheriffs.
Ferguson and Josh Keefe of the Maine Monitor were selected to receive an A-Mark Prize for their reporting on the use of force by Maine State Police after a 2024 incident in which a state trooper pinned a handcuffed man to the ground and repeatedly punched him in the face while arresting him in rural York County.
Sawyer Loftus, an investigative reporter with the BDN’s Maine Focus team, has also been selected to receive an A-Mark Prize for his reporting on USDA foreclosures of homes purchased through its rural development mortgage program.
A-Mark Prizes recognize “outstanding investigative journalism that uncovers hidden truths, holds power to account, and drives meaningful public awareness or reform.”
The BDN also was honored as a distinguished newspaper in the 2026 weekday edition, large circulation.

title: State representative calls for review after Maine attorney general’s office releases confidential memo
text:
Attorneys and criminal law experts are concerned that the Office of the Maine Attorney General this week accidentally released a confidential document, and one state representative has called for an investigation.
In a statement Friday morning, Rep. Jennifer Poirier, R-Skowhegan, said she wants a thorough review of how the disclosure happened and what will be done to prevent it from happening again. Poirier serves on the state Legislature’s Judiciary Committee.
“The public has a right to expect that state agencies entrusted with sensitive legal information will handle those records responsibly and take every reasonable precaution to prevent unauthorized disclosure,” Poirier said. “When confidential case files are released to the media, the potential consequences for individuals involved and the integrity of legal proceedings must be taken seriously.”
On Thursday, an employee in the office’s criminal division attached the report in an email to more than 70 addresses. The list included more than 20 emails that don’t end with Maine.gov — such as those assigned to employees with the attorney general’s office — including accounts for reporters, news organizations, the judicial branch and what appeared to be a state lawmaker’s private email. A spokesperson for the judicial branch declined to comment on Friday.
The 45-page report listed more than 160 cases, including about 90 homicides, 30 drug matters and more than 20 cases related to alleged crimes dealing with healthcare, taxes, welfare and civil rights.
In a statement Friday, spokesperson Danna Hayes said the office notified families of victims to prepare them for the possibility that “inadvertent recipients” might make the information public.
“We take seriously the integrity of confidential information and the impact of this error,” Hayes said.
A majority of the report’s case summaries match details revealed in public court documents, but several matters detailed in the attachment have not been publicly filed in court, according to the document. That includes four missing persons cases that have been deemed to be homicides, and two investigations of residential care providers accused of theft. In the case summaries for the latter two, the document states that the attorney general’s office is waiting for guidance from federal prosecutors.
The attorney general’s office did not respond to a request to discuss those cases.
What’s been publicly reported about the confidential portions concerned legal experts like Jack Lu, a retired judge in Massachusetts who teaches at the University of Massachusetts-Lowell.
“It is wrong to publicize charges that are not brought,” Lu said.
Speaking generally about unauthorized disclosures in criminal cases — which Lu said is rare, in his experience — he said sometimes cases that aren’t charged can be terminated before they’re filed in court.
“There’s a danger of maligning people without government process,” Lu said.
Brian Wilson, a long-time prosecutor in Massachusetts who directs the Prosecutor Clinic at Boston University School of Law, said prosecutors deal a lot with information in criminal cases that, if disclosed improperly, could put victims or witnesses in danger.
“There may be things that infringe upon witnesses’ privacy rights or can even compromise their safety,” Wilson said. He was not familiar with the specifics of the Maine disclosures.
Wilson also described rules of conduct for prosecutors that bar them from sharing information about a defendant other than for specific purposes. The American Bar Association urges prosecutors to only share “statements that are necessary to inform the public of the nature and extent of the prosecutor’s action and that serve a legitimate law enforcement purpose.”
“You want to avoid a substantial risk of the accused, or the target of the investigation, if they’re not even publicly charged yet, you want to avoid any public condemnation of them,” Wilson said.
One defense attorney, whose case was mentioned in the document, declined to comment, citing an ethical rule for Maine attorneys that requires them not to view what they know to be an inadvertent disclosure, by not reading the content, notifying the sender that it was received and destroying it or returning it to the sender. Another attorney did not respond to a request for comment on what appeared to be non-public details in the document about a client.
Tina Nadeau, director of the Maine Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, said in an email Friday that confidential information involving victims of crimes and people suspected or accused of committing crimes “should be protected fiercely.”
She said she couldn’t speak to how the disclosure happened and that she couldn’t speculate about what might happen as the cases mentioned in the document progress.

title: Winslow football tops MCI in clash of D North leaders
text:
PITTSFIELD — Against a pass-heavy foe, a Winslow football team that’s been a brick wall defensively this season knew it was in for something different Friday night.
The Black Raiders came prepared — and in a battle of Class D North’s No. 1 and No. 2 teams, that Winslow defense backed up another stellar performance from its running game in a 38-6 victory over Maine Central Institute on Friday at Alumni Field.
The top-ranked Black Raiders recorded five interceptions and five sacks. They also rushed for 351 yards as they moved closer toward clinching the top playoff seed in the region.
“The biggest thing I’ve noticed with these kids is how they play together as a unit,” said Winslow coach Wes Littlefield. “Everybody has a job to do, and they’re very focused on their jobs and want to improve every week. At practice, they’re always asking, ‘Coach, what can I do to get better?’”
HOW THEY DID IT
• Winslow (5-1) shut down MCI’s passing game. When MCI quarterback Caleb Rush left the game early in the second quarter, the Huskies didn’t stop going to the air. The Black Raiders, though, intercepted second-string QB Landen Gosselin once and third-stringer Alex Sevigny four times.
“(The key was) staying on our man, making sure that we weren’t giving up any unnecessary slants and keeping inside shade,” said Alyx Hardy, who had two interceptions. “It was just following all the rules coach gives us — read steps, watch our keys, watch the quarterback, keep your eyes on the ball, and break on it when we have the chance.”
• The Black Raiders’ running game excelled yet again. Isaac Bulger and Michael Loubier combined for 288 yards. Bulger broke off several big runs outside the tackles as Winslow built a 16-0 less than five minutes into the first quarter.
WHAT IT MEANS
• Winslow is almost certain to have the No. 1 seed in Class D North. The Black Raiders already had a lead of nearly 30 points in the Crabtree rankings entering Friday, and a win over the second-place Huskies will put even more distance between the two.
UNSUNG HERO
It’s not easy for a freshman to make a huge impact on the defensive line, but that’s exactly what Chase Rancourt did. He was key to a Winslow front that put pressure on MCI’s quarterbacks all night, recording a sack in the first quarter and causing havoc on seemingly every down.
NOTABLE QUOTABLES
• “It’s a group of kids that’s just working hard and busting their butts every week. That young line we have, it’s that time of year where they’re going to get better and better, and they keep doing that. Collectively, I thought tonight was a nice showing of some good football.” — Wes Littlefield
• “Our key was just blocking up front. We stayed on our blocks, and that allowed (Michael Loubier and I) to get through. At times, we were getting a little mad at each other, but after halftime, we all cooled each other off. It worked well.” — Isaac Bulger
STAT LEADERS
• Winslow: Isaac Bulger (13 carries, 190 yards, touchdown; 17-yard receiving touchdown; sack), Michael Loubier (14 carries, 98 yards, two touchdowns; interception), Ben Thomas (two sacks), Layne Ferran (two interceptions), Alyx Hardy (two interceptions)
• MCI: Brayden Badger (two catches, 82 yards), Landen Gosselin (two catches, 22 yards, touchdown)
UP NEXT
• Winslow: vs. Morse (4-2), 1 p.m. next Saturday
• MCI: at Belfast (2-4), 7 p.m. next Friday

title: Patriots’ banged-up secondary will be tested by Raiders QB Kirk Cousins
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Kirk Cousins’ torrid start has been one of the NFL’s biggest surprises.
The 38-year-old Las Vegas Raiders quarterback is looking to keep it going this week at New England against a Patriots defense that is suddenly having trouble keeping its secondary healthy.
Despite his first loss of the season last week against Kansas City, Cousins is up to 11 touchdown passes — the fastest he has reached that total through four games in his 15-year career. His previous best was 10 TDs through four games in 2018. It has helped quiet the chatter about him being simply a bridge quarterback to Fernando Mendoza, who Las Vegas took No. 1 overall in April.
Cousins said he’s just enjoying seeing the resilience of the entire team in Klint Kubiak’s first season, a group Cousins said is confirming what he observed from them going back to spring workouts.
“These guys, they want to do it the right way. Football means something to them,” Cousins said. “They’re hardworking, listen well, and it makes it a joy to be the quarterback for a group of guys like that. But you’ve got to go prove it again every week.”
That next challenge is a Patriots team that avoided a 1-3 start with a win over Buffalo last week. Not only did quarterback Drake Maye break out of an early season funk with three touchdown passes, but the defense, which played without star cornerback Christian Gonzalez (shoulder), was able to slow Bills quarterback Josh Allen.
Gonzalez was ruled out for the second straight game on Friday, along with fellow starting cornerback Carlton Davis (neck) and rookie Channing Canada (hamstring). Another cornerback, Charles Woods (shoulder) was listed as questionable.
Wide receiver Mack Hollins (calf) was also ruled out. Defensive tackle Christian Barmore (shoulder) and running back Rhamondre Stevenson (knee) were among those listed as questionable.
Whoever is available Sunday, Maye said carrying as much of the momentum they can from last week is the goal.
“You would like to say everybody — especially on offense — you’d like to say that the first three weeks weren’t what we wanted to put out there,” Maye said. “You have to try to build off last week, knowing that it’s not just going to do it for you. You have to put the work in and the focus, and hopefully continue to catch a trend and catch a stride.
Need to know
Las Vegas (3-1) at New England (2-2)
When/where to watch: 1 p.m. Sunday, CBS.
Latest odds: Patriots by 3 1/2.
Against the spread: Raiders 4-0; Patriots 2-1-1.
Last week: Raiders lost to Chiefs 30-27; Patriots beat Bills 29-26.
Last meeting: Raiders beat Patriots 20-13 on Sept. 5, 2025, in Foxborough, Mass.
Series record: Patriots lead 20-18-1.
Matchup to watch
The Raiders’ red-zone defense vs. the Patriots’ red-zone offense. Las Vegas has been susceptible to giving up big plays this season. Once inside the 20, opponents have feasted, scoring touchdowns on 10 of 13 (76.9%) of their trips. But the Patriots have struggled in the red zone through four games, scoring on just four of nine (44.4%) of their opportunities.
Stats and stuff
• Las Vegas and Detroit are the only teams that have scored 25 or more points in each game this season. It’s the second time in franchise history the Raiders have accomplished that in their first four games of a season. The 2002 team was the other one to do it.
• The Raiders lead the NFL with nine takeaways, one more than four other teams. That total is tied for sixth in franchise history with the 1972 team for the most through four games in a season.
• Las Vegas has 12 sacks and allowed five, and the Raiders’ seven-sack differential is tied with the Lions for the league’s best.
• The Raiders’ Dylan Laube leads the NFL with a 33.4-yard kickoff return average.
• The Patriots, including the playoffs, have won nine of their past 10 home games, including a 20-3 win over Pittsburgh in Week 2.
• New England is looking to snap a three-game losing streak to Las Vegas.
• Maye’s seven interceptions are one shy of the eight he threw in the regular season last year.
AP Sports Writer Mark Anderson in Las Vegas contributed.

title: Trump establishes committee to investigate Federal Reserve’s Lisa Cook in latest effort to fire her
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump opened another chapter in his effort to fire Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook Friday by establishing a “committee of inquiry” to investigate allegations that she made false statements in mortgage applications.
The inquiry will include a hearing at the White House Nov. 5, Trump said in a written memo, that Cook “shall” attend to answer questions from the committee. The hearing wouldn’t be public but a transcript would be published, the memo said.
Trump’s extraordinary demand that Cook testify before the committee will likely renew concerns about threats to the Federal Reserve’s independence as the president demands the central bank cut its key interest rate. Just last month, the Fed raised its key rate instead, led by Chairman Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed earlier this year.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump wrote in the memorandum.
Trump and some of his economic advisers have blamed the Fed’s broader rate-setting committee, which includes 12 voting members and 19 officials in total, for the rate hike. Cook is one of the 12 participants on the committee that votes on interest-rate decisions. The vote to lift rates Sept. 16 was unanimous.
The move follows a Supreme Court ruling in June that Cook could keep her job after Trump sought to fire her last year. That ruling included a footnote that said nothing prevented Trump from “trying again” as long as she was given proper notice and an opportunity to respond to the charges.
Cook has denied any wrongdoing and has not been charged with a crime.
