title: Decoding Medicare Advantage, from cost to coverage options
text:
(Aging Untold) — Choosing between Medicare Advantage, also known as Medicare Part C, and traditional Medicare can feel overwhelming, especially when health needs and budgets don’t always point to the same answer.
The Aging Untold experts are walking you through what families should weigh first — from monthly costs to doctor networks to a one-time enrollment rule many people don’t know about.
Start with your budget and your health history
“I think the first thing I would look at is your budget. What can you afford?” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “Typically, the Medicare Advantage plans are less expensive. Traditional Medicare, you have a supplemental plan that’s got a higher cost.”
O’Rourke said family health history matters just as much as the monthly premium.
“The other thing I look at is your family history of chronic diseases. Like do you have Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, then it’s going to be very expensive to manage,” O’Rourke said.
Check your doctors and your state’s network first
O’Rourke said patients should confirm whether their own doctors accept the plan — and that those doctors have stayed in the plan’s network.
“Do your doctors take a Medicare Advantage plan that you’re looking at? And have they switched in and out of the plans, because you don’t want to have them in one plan and then have to switch to another, and then you’ve lost your doctor,” O’Rourke said.
She said network size can vary significantly by state.
“In some of the states, the Advantage plan has such a big network that it is almost as if you have traditional Medicare, because everybody participates in that Advantage plan,” O’Rourke said. “So I think it’s important to look at your state and how big that network is to know that might be the best option for you and be affordable.”
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck added that some Advantage plans include day programs with meals, occupational therapy visits and support that allows family caregivers to keep working.
“There are some that offer day programs with meals, and it helps the family members out so they can go to work and their loved ones are here being cared for and watched. They’re getting PT (physical therapy) and OT (occupational therapy) and visits right there,” Cradduck said.
Still, she cautioned the plans aren’t one-size-fits-all.
“If you’re chronically ill, probably the Advantage plan may not be the best choice,” Cradduck said.
O’Rourke agreed, noting the decision circles back to affordability.
“It might not. And then you have to go all the way back to your money. And can you afford the supplemental plan?” O’Rourke said.
The one-time enrollment window to know about
O’Rourke said there is a single opportunity to enroll in Medicare without being screened for preexisting conditions.
“What I want also people to remember is that you get one time signing up with no medical preexisting conditions. Once you sign up for Medicare, whether it’s the private through Medicare Advantage plan or traditional Medicare, that’s the one time you get to go in with preexisting conditions,” O’Rourke said.
She said that window closes after 12 months.
“After that, 12 months after that, you are subjected to medical underwriting, which means if you have a preexisting condition, they can deny you. So if you go back to traditional Medicare, you’ll get traditional Medicare, but you might not get the supplemental insurance,” O’Rourke said.
Comparing the perks of each plan type
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, asked whether traditional Medicare offers more perks for people managing chronic conditions.
“Would you say that they get more perks with the traditional Medicare if you have a lot of chronic diseases,” Rogers asked.
O’Rourke said the value of “perks” looks different depending on the plan.
“When you say perks, I think dental, transportation — that’s what I think of in terms of perks, that traditional Medicare with a supplemental plan, although it’s more expensive, you don’t have the complication of doctors not taking the insurance,” O’Rourke said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose mentioned that some plans might offer gym memberships or devices like a watch.
“And when I think of perks, I think about on Medicare Advantage, they might be offered a gym program like Silver Sneakers. They might be offering a watch. They might be offered some things, and so it can look very attractive because you can look more affordable, and you get some free stuff with it,” Ambrose said.
Cradduck said quality varies plan to plan.
“What I know is there are programs that are absolutely wonderful. It doesn’t mean that all of them are. So it’s not a one-size fits all,” she said.
Build a team — and ask who they’d choose for their own family
Ambrose recommended building relationships with professionals ahead of time, rather than deciding alone.
“I think it’s really good to start building kind of your aging team — have professionals in different fields that you already know, have relationships with, and ask professionals who they would recommend. Like, who would you go to for your mama?” Ambrose said.
She said working with a licensed specialist who revisits the plan annually matters, since plans change even when a person’s medications don’t.
“I think it’s really helpful to be with a licensed professional that this is their specialty, and they’re helping guide you each year to make sure that, as plans change — you might not change, your meds might not change, but your plan might change,” Ambrose said. “And so you got to figure out which is the right plan. And the right plan isn’t what everybody thinks is the best plan.”
Ambrose added that the right plan is personal — even within the same household.
“It’s what is the best plan for you,” she said. “And so even a husband and wife usually don’t have the same plans.”
O’Rourke pointed to two main resources for help: a licensed Medicare insurance broker or a volunteer counseling network.
“You can use a licensed Medicare insurance broker. There’s also fabulous volunteer networks,” O’Rourke said.
In California, Cradduck said that volunteer network is called HICAP.
“We have a program called HICAP, and it is a volunteer organization, but it usually takes somebody that’s been in the field that has worked in either medical offices and they’re oftentimes retirees. They’re not just grabbing somebody that’s totally uninformed off the street,” Cradduck said. “And those folks are amazing at guiding them through this process.”
Ambrose said the key follow-up question is whether that help continues beyond initial enrollment.
“What I would want to know is they might help a lot in getting the initial plan for the year, but will they be there to help you throughout the year when you have questions or challenges? So you want to ask those questions,” Ambrose said.
Learn more
Key takeaways
- Start with budget. Medicare Advantage plans typically cost less upfront than traditional Medicare with a supplement.
- Consider family health history. Chronic conditions are costly to manage.
- Confirm your doctors are in-network — and staying there. O’Rourke said patients should check whether their doctors accept the plan and haven’t recently switched networks.
- Network size varies by state. In some states, Medicare Advantage plan networks are broad enough to function much like traditional Medicare, O’Rourke said.
- You get one shot at guaranteed enrollment. O’Rourke said there’s a single window to enroll without medical underwriting; after 12 months, preexisting conditions can affect eligibility for supplemental coverage.

title: Trump says US to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.
Trump’s shocking announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it “a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners,” according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.
Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Zelenskyy said.
Trump’s move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing new sanctions on Russia, given that the law that passed overwhelmingly by Congress directs the administration to target countries that purchase Russian oil and gas. Lawmakers this week had urged the Trump administration to act quickly to use the tools available to help Ukraine.
Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, along with Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, called Trump’s announcement a betrayal of Ukraine, the European allies and U.S. national security.
“Enough is enough,” the senators wrote. “The President must end his war with Iran instead of funding Russia’s war machine.”
Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel future prices dipped on the news on Friday, the national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. remained high at $6.28, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.
Trump did not address the sanctions or Russia’s war but said, “Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority.”
Trump said later as he left the White House for a campaign rally, that he was thankful for the deal. “I want to thank President Putin. To be honest with you, we have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it’s diesel, which is what we want. So, thank you,” Trump said. He did not answer shouted questions about the criticism from Zelenskyy.
Washington and Moscow offer few details on deal
The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the Russian diesel or when it would become available.
A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said during their call he and Trump dedicated “significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis” and also discussed “the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations.”
Russia “confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets,” Putin said. “I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy.”
Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov, speaking later to reporters, wouldn’t say whether the U.S. made any concessions in exchange for the supplies, or what, if anything, was promised to Russia in exchange.
Trump and Putin’s deal draws immediate backlash
Zelenskyy, in a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it “with further terror and perfidy.” He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged.
“It plays into Russia’s hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.
Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-sponsored the Russia sanctions law, said Trump’s decision “makes us complicit in Putin’s war against Ukraine.” In his scathing statement, Blumenthal invoked the memory of Sen. Lindsey Graham, a Trump ally and Russia hawk, for whom the law is named.
“This agreement with a murdering dictator is a stain on our nation’s character, an insult to Lindsey Graham’s memory, and directly contrary to Congress’s intent in our bipartisan sanctions bill,” he said.
Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump’s announcement “infuriating.”
“This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn’t the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia,” Beyer said in a statement on X.
The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.
It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned the imports because of Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Treasury Department moves to ease diesel sanctions for six months
Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.
This is the latest license the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war early this year. But it is the first to ease sanctions on diesel for longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war in February 2022.
The license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday.
The extensions underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow’s ability to profit from its energy exports.
It’s unclear how the move will impact oil prices
“What does this do to prices? I think probably not much,” said Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist and expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
But, Seigle said the new deal is a “great benefit to Russia and to Putin,” who are currently trying to offload their summer-grade diesel for the heavier winter and arctic grades that they will need in the coming months.
“It’s kind of shuffling deck chairs on the Titanic,” said Michael Lynch of the Energy Policy Research Foundation, a non-partisan research institution focused on energy and economics.
“If we get diesel from Russia, basically it means that their existing customers are not going to get it and they’ll have to go somewhere else, and that will keep the price basically where it is now,” Lynch said.
Russia, once a major exporter of diesel, has banned exports since July as it has struggled to meet demand inside the country because of Ukraine’s repeated attacks on Russian oil refineries. The International Energy Agency says Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30%.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told state news agency Tass that Russia is “immediately starting to lift restrictions on diesel exports ahead of schedule.” He said Moscow could start supplies to the U.S. this month and Russia’s domestic market will be “fully supplied” with diesel, as well.
___
Associated Press writers Will Weissert, Konstantin Toropin and Lisa Mascaro in Washington, Alex Veiga in Los Angeles and Farnoush Amiri in New York contributed to this report.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Cooler Friday, Sunshine Returns for the Weekend
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Thursday. Showers will continue to taper off across northern Maine tonight as the system responsible for today’s unsettled weather gradually pulls away. A few isolated showers could linger across the north through around midnight, but skies will trend clearer overnight. Friday brings a cooler and somewhat breezy day, with a few additional showers possible later in the afternoon. The better weather arrives for the weekend, with plenty of sunshine expected Saturday before temperatures warm noticeably on Sunday.
Temperatures tonight look to fall into the mid to upper 30s across much of Aroostook County, including around 37 degrees in Presque Isle, 39 degrees in Caribou and near 35 degrees in Houlton. Some of our colder locations across western and northern Aroostook County could fall closer to the lower 30s.
Winds remain out of the west to southwest around 5 to 10 mph overnight, with skies becoming partly cloudy to mostly clear. Patchy frost will be possible in some of the colder locations by Friday morning, especially across northwestern portions of the region.
Friday will have a noticeably cooler feel across northern Maine. High temperatures look to reach only the lower to mid 50s across much of Aroostook County, including around 55 degrees in Caribou and Presque Isle, with Houlton closer to 57 degrees.
We should see a decent amount of sunshine during the morning hours before some additional clouds begin to build during the afternoon. A few scattered showers will also be possible later in the day, especially across northern and western portions of the region. West winds will become more noticeable as well, generally around 10 to 15 mph with gusts reaching 20 to 25 mph at times.
Saturday is shaping up to be the nicest day of the upcoming stretch, with high pressure building into the region and plenty of sunshine expected. Temperatures remain on the cool side, with highs generally in the lower 50s across northern Maine, but the dry weather should make for a nice fall day.
Sunday brings a noticeable warm-up as winds turn more southwesterly. High temperatures could climb into the mid to upper 60s across much of the region, running around 10 to 15 degrees above average for this time of year. Sunshine should remain fairly plentiful through much of the day, although clouds may begin to increase later as our next system approaches.
Rain chances begin to return heading into Monday and Tuesday, but there remains some uncertainty regarding the exact timing and how much precipitation reaches the region. A separate area of low pressure developing over the Great Lakes early next week will likely bring a better chance for rain by Tuesday.
The latest Drought Monitor shows a significant worsening of drought conditions across Aroostook County compared to last week. While the entire county was classified in moderate drought last week, around three-quarters of the county is now classified in severe drought, with only about 24 percent remaining in the moderate drought category.
Unfortunately, the rainfall we’ve received recently has not been enough to provide meaningful relief. The next potential opportunity for more widespread rain arrives early next week, but confidence remains too low at this point to say whether it will be enough to make much of a difference.
For more details on Friday’s cooler weather, the sunny weekend ahead and our next chance for rain early next week, make sure to check out this evening’s First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: The pro-life movement is the selfish movement
text:
Dan Pryor of Gorham makes the argument in an Oct. 1 letter (“Remember: Abortion kills human life”) that abortion is both selfish and destroys a unique human life. As he puts it, “abortion is the self-centered murder of the innocent.”
There are two sides to this argument. On the other side:
To quote the headline of an Oct. 1 report in this newspaper, “Every day, thousands of residents face the hardest financial choices, as households struggle to afford basic expenses.” Being able to afford basic expenses becomes that much more difficult as the number of children in a family grows.
The amount of carbon dioxide dumped into the atmosphere increases with each increase in the number of people on the planet. The same goes for how long it takes to commute to work, and for how much a house costs. More people exacerbate problems that we could otherwise live with.
Educational expenses are driving up property taxes, and those expenses increase with an increase in the number of students. The pro-life movement would make life miserable for all of us, by increasing global warming, hunger, property taxes and time on the road, in order to save a fetus that would never know it is alive.
The letter read, “There is nothing more selfish in America than the ‘pro-choice’ abortion movement.” In reality, there is nothing more selfish or short-sighted than the “pro-life” movement.
William Vaughan Jr.
Chebeague Island

title: Cormier Wins Week Five; Watt and Good Share Girls Honor
text:
Van Buren’s Cormier, SA’s Watt, Ashland’s Good Named Week Five Athletes of the Week
The votes are in for Fall Week Five Athlete of the Week, and this week produced three winners.
Gavin Cormier of Van Buren earned the boys honor, while the girls voting finished in a tie between Aolie Watt of Southern Aroostook and Arihanna Good of Ashland.
All three were selected from another strong group of nominees representing soccer, golf and cross country programs from across Aroostook County.
Boys Athlete of the Week: Gavin Cormier, Van Buren
Cormier earned the Week Five boys honor following his performance for the Van Buren boys soccer team against Houlton.
Cormier scored the Crusaders’ lone goal in the game, creating the opportunity and finishing the play before leaving the contest prior to halftime.
County voters ultimately gave Cormier the most support on the Week Five boys ballot.
Girls Athletes of the Week: Aolie Watt and Arihanna Good
For the first time this fall, the girls Athlete of the Week voting ended in a tie.
Aolie Watt of Southern Aroostook earned her share of the honor after providing all of the offense in the Warriors’ 2-1 victory over Hodgdon, scoring both Southern Aroostook goals.
Arihanna Good of Ashland also finished atop the voting after being recognized for her work on the defensive end. Good has been a strong presence for Ashland, winning possession, helping move the ball forward and creating opportunities for teammates from the back line.
With the final vote totals even, Watt and Good are both Fall Week Five Girls Athletes of the Week.

Patrick Collins, Presque Isle, Golf
Collins won the PVC Boys Golf Championship after shooting a 74, finishing two strokes ahead of the field.
Gavin Cormier, Van Buren, Soccer
Cormier scored Van Buren’s goal against Houlton before leaving the game prior to halftime.
Conor Schmidt, Katahdin, Soccer
Schmidt recorded 3 goals and an assist in Katahdin’s 7-0 victory over East Grand.
Jacob Tuttle, Hodgdon, Soccer
Tuttle put together a big offensive performance with 2 goals and 2 assists for Hodgdon.

Witmer finished 46th overall in 17:00.21 at the Festival of Champions, leading the eligible Aroostook County boys in the statewide field.

Aolie Watt, Southern Aroostook, Soccer
Watt scored both goals in Southern Aroostook’s 2-1 victory over Hodgdon.
Joey Richardson, Katahdin, Soccer
Richardson was nominated as one of Katahdin’s top offensive threats and leading shooters.

Korzekwa captured the PVC Girls Golf Championship after shooting an 86.

Ezell scored 4 goals and added an assist against Van Buren, then followed that performance with 2 more goals against Old Town.

title: Greater Augusta Utility District completes $2M PFAS filtration project
text:
AUGUSTA — When the staff at the Greater Augusta Utility District learned PFAS levels in drinking water on the east side of the Kennebec River had exceeded the allowable limit in 2024, it shut the well off and got to work on a solution.
After a year and a half of designing, funding and installing a new filtration system, staff turned the water back on this summer, PFAS-free.
Brian Tarbuck, general manager of the utility district, said it’s not exactly clear what contributed to the increase of PFAS in the river and drinking water.
“(There’s) no particular smoking gun,” Tarbuck said. “I think probably the level of the PFAS in the river fluctuates quite a lot. Nobody tests it all the time enough to see if there’s any trends, so it’s hard for us to know.”
The well on the east side of Augusta is close to the river, which has been found to contain PFAS — or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances — a group of man-made chemicals sometimes called forever chemicals that break down very slowly. As a result, the chemicals stay in the environment for a long time, posing health and environmental risks.
The Greater Augusta Utility District installed the well near the river in 2015, before it knew the river contained PFAS, Tarbuck said. Over time, the standards for the allowable limits of PFAS in drinking water continued shrinking. At the end of November 2024, the water tested at 23.3 parts per trillion, more than the 20 parts per trillion limit.
When they shut off the well, they were able to instead supply east side residents with water from three wells located near Bond Brook.
Luckily, the utility district had also been conducting pilot testing for PFAS filtration systems leading up to having to shut off the well, so they were in a good position when it came time to act. The staff spent about a month designing a new system to filter the chemicals, and then had to go through the process of permitting and securing funding.
“The timing was crazy good,” Tarbuck said. “And then, because of emerging contaminants, there was a lot of money available, so we were able to bring in a lot of grant money. So as we saw, something like this costs a couple of million bucks, but it didn’t really hurt the ratepayers all that much.”
The project, which cost around $2 million, was funded through a grant from the Maine Drinking Water Program, the state entity that regulates public water systems. It offers money to deal with emerging contaminants like PFAS. The utility district was able to adapt an existing building near the well to fit the new equipment, which saved them from having to develop a new facility.
The team at the utility district was able to complete much of the project internally without hiring a lot of outside help, also allowing them to save time and money.
The new system does not filter PFAS particles out of the water; it absorbs them, explained Andy Begin, assistant general manager and chief engineer. The chemicals that are absorbed are then sent to a landfill for disposal.
The project was localized to the east side of the river because the wells on the water supply on the west side are farther from the river. The utility district is planning to install an additional well on the west side in the next two years, so if anything goes wrong with one of the existing three west side wells, another will be available.
“We’re in a good tactical position, so that anything that happens, like an ice storm or something, that might take out one of those wells, it means we’ve got other wells to rely on,” Tarbuck said. “The idea that we have water from different physical locations is important, and the fact that there’s no PFAS in that water is, of course, hugely important, as we go forward.”

title: 2 charged in theft by deception at Wiscasset business
text:
Wiscasset Police Department posted the following press release on its Facebook page Sept. 10:
On Aug. 10, Officer Jonathan Barnes responded to Ingram Fine Arts, located at 85 Main St., for a report of a theft. During the investigation, it was learned that on Aug. 9, a male and female entered the business and inquired about gold pieces. The couple selected a piece of gold artwork valued at $8,000. A lower price was negotiated and the pair counted out the cash that consisted of $100 bills. When the store owner's attention was diverted, the two suspects substituted the currency with a stack consisting primarily of $1 bills concealed under a $100 bill.
Surveillance footage was obtained, and photographs of the suspects were distributed to law enforcement agencies across the country. With assistance from Lincoln County Sheriff's Office, Kennebunk Police Department, Fairfax County (Virginia) Police Department, and Melbourne (Florida) Police Department, the suspects were identified as Mircea Lucaci and Maria Rostas. Both individuals were found to have outstanding arrest warrants in multiple states for similar theft-related offenses. The investigation indicated that the two may allegedly be associated with a Romanian theft ring targeting gold.
As a result of the investigation, arrest warrants were prepared and issued.
Mircea Lucaci, 35, of Woodside, New York was charged with Theft by Deception, Class C.
Maria Rostas, 49, of Flushing, New York is charged with Theft by Deception, Class C.

title: State representative calls for review after Maine attorney general’s office releases confidential memo
text:
Attorneys and criminal law experts are concerned that the Office of the Maine Attorney General this week accidentally released a confidential document, and one state representative has called for an investigation.
In a statement Friday morning, Rep. Jennifer Poirier, R-Skowhegan, said she wants a thorough review of how the disclosure happened and what will be done to prevent it from happening again. Poirier serves on the state Legislature’s Judiciary Committee.
“The public has a right to expect that state agencies entrusted with sensitive legal information will handle those records responsibly and take every reasonable precaution to prevent unauthorized disclosure,” Poirier said. “When confidential case files are released to the media, the potential consequences for individuals involved and the integrity of legal proceedings must be taken seriously.”
On Thursday, an employee in the office’s criminal division attached the report in an email to more than 70 addresses. The list included more than 20 emails that don’t end with Maine.gov — such as those assigned to employees with the attorney general’s office — including accounts for reporters, news organizations, the judicial branch and what appeared to be a state lawmaker’s private email. A spokesperson for the judicial branch declined to comment on Friday.
The 45-page report listed more than 160 cases, including about 90 homicides, 30 drug matters and more than 20 cases related to alleged crimes dealing with healthcare, taxes, welfare and civil rights.
In a statement Friday, spokesperson Danna Hayes said the office notified families of victims to prepare them for the possibility that “inadvertent recipients” might make the information public.
“We take seriously the integrity of confidential information and the impact of this error,” Hayes said.
A majority of the report’s case summaries match details revealed in public court documents, but several matters detailed in the attachment have not been publicly filed in court, according to the document. That includes four missing persons cases that have been deemed to be homicides, and two investigations of residential care providers accused of theft. In the case summaries for the latter two, the document states that the attorney general’s office is waiting for guidance from federal prosecutors.
The attorney general’s office did not respond to a request to discuss those cases.
What’s been publicly reported about the confidential portions concerned legal experts like Jack Lu, a retired judge in Massachusetts who teaches at the University of Massachusetts-Lowell.
“It is wrong to publicize charges that are not brought,” Lu said.
Speaking generally about unauthorized disclosures in criminal cases — which Lu said is rare, in his experience — he said sometimes cases that aren’t charged can be terminated before they’re filed in court.
“There’s a danger of maligning people without government process,” Lu said.
Brian Wilson, a long-time prosecutor in Massachusetts who directs the Prosecutor Clinic at Boston University School of Law, said prosecutors deal a lot with information in criminal cases that, if disclosed improperly, could put victims or witnesses in danger.
“There may be things that infringe upon witnesses’ privacy rights or can even compromise their safety,” Wilson said. He was not familiar with the specifics of the Maine disclosures.
Wilson also described rules of conduct for prosecutors that bar them from sharing information about a defendant other than for specific purposes. The American Bar Association urges prosecutors to only share “statements that are necessary to inform the public of the nature and extent of the prosecutor’s action and that serve a legitimate law enforcement purpose.”
“You want to avoid a substantial risk of the accused, or the target of the investigation, if they’re not even publicly charged yet, you want to avoid any public condemnation of them,” Wilson said.
One defense attorney, whose case was mentioned in the document, declined to comment, citing an ethical rule for Maine attorneys that requires them not to view what they know to be an inadvertent disclosure, by not reading the content, notifying the sender that it was received and destroying it or returning it to the sender. Another attorney did not respond to a request for comment on what appeared to be non-public details in the document about a client.
Tina Nadeau, director of the Maine Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, said in an email Friday that confidential information involving victims of crimes and people suspected or accused of committing crimes “should be protected fiercely.”
She said she couldn’t speak to how the disclosure happened and that she couldn’t speculate about what might happen as the cases mentioned in the document progress.

title: ICE officers shot New York man whose 5-year-old was in his car, official says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal immigration officers opened fire on a Dominican man whom they were trying to arrest in New York because they believed their lives were in danger, a senior Immigration and Customs Enforcement official said Friday.
Marcos Charles made the comments alongside U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and other immigration officials during a news conference in Washington meant to “highlight the dangerous consequences of sanctuary city policies.”
The 28-year-old man, whom New York City police identified as Oscar Belgal, was shot in the neck Thursday as he drove his car with a 5-year-old boy inside, officials said.
ICE agents didn’t know the child was in the car, but Belgal “was aware” and chose to evade officers, Mullin said.
Belgal was shot “superficially” in the neck as ICE officers attempted to arrest him, Charles said.
ICE had issued a detainer on Belgal and that he runs with a gang known for thefts using weapons and mopeds, he said. Officers used vehicles to block him in as he attempted to drive off. Instead, Charles said, he accelerated his vehicle toward officers, smashing some of their vehicles.
Protesters and local officials decried the shooting as an example of the dangers of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
Much of Mullin’s remarks were reserved for excoriating New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his immigration policy.
“Sanctuary politicians, they create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for the American citizens to be safe,” he said.
Mullin said ICE has requested more than 14,000 detainers in the state of New York for individuals in local custody that they’re seeking to deport.
“Silence. Absolute silence is what we have gotten back,” he said. “Why would they release these individuals back onto the streets?”
“We’re enforcing our nation’s laws. We’re not picking and choosing,” Mullin continued. “Why is that controversial? We should all want law and order on our streets.”

title: Maine hospitals are suing the federal government over drug pricing
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The American Hospital Association, joined by the Maine Hospital Association and several hospitals, including Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center, sued Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the federal Department of Health and Human Services Friday over changes to a drug pricing program that the organizations say could cost struggling hospitals more than $1 billion.
The 340B drug pricing program was established by Congress in 1992 to help safety-net healthcare providers buy outpatient drugs at a discount, protecting low-income patients from rising drug prices.
But this summer, the Trump administration announced changes to a pilot effort that will allow some pharmaceutical companies to offer rebates instead of upfront discounts, a controversial move. The changes are set to go into effect Jan. 1.
Maine hospitals warn that the Trump administration’s changes to the program could upend an already-fragile financial ecosystem for the state’s medical providers. Much of the state is designated as a health professional shortage area, and Northern Light, the largest hospital system serving northern and eastern Maine, is working to recover from significant losses in recent years.
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
“This revised pilot helps modernize program oversight by improving visibility into 340B transactions while helping preserve the program’s long-term sustainability for the patients and communities it was created to serve,” Tom Engels, administrator for the federal Health Resources and Services Administration, said in a statement earlier this year.
The American Hospital Association and the other parties in the lawsuit say those changes would impose significant costs and divert resources away from caring for patients. The hospitals estimate the changes could add $1 billion annually in administrative costs, far higher than the $537 million federal government estimate.
The federal government previously tried to advance a similar rebate program in 2025 but was blocked by the U.S. District Court in Maine and the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. The government has said the changes will improve transparency as the pharmaceutical industry has argued that hospitals abuse the discount program.
Lance Walker, the Maine district court judge who issued the injunction last year, wrote in his decision that the pilot “likely fails to consider and reasonably explain the impact of a rebate model on 340B hospitals, who rely on upfront price concessions to stretch few resources as far as possible to serve rural and poor communities.”
Jeff Austin, president of the Maine Hospital Association, said in an affidavit that the state has been losing hospital capacity for a decade, pointing to four hospital closures and 10 birthing units that have shuttered. Twenty-seven Maine hospitals participated in the drug pricing program in fiscal year 2024, he added.
“Maine hospitals cannot afford this rebate program,” Austin said in a statement. “They already operate with an average of less than two weeks cash-on-hand, so these significant new costs will jeopardize their ability to care for the most vulnerable patients in their communities and affect the affordability and accessibility of care across Maine.”
Dr. Guy Hudson, Northern Light Health president and CEO, said that “for rural health systems in Maine, these changes will divert resources away from direct patient care and create new financial challenges at a time when healthcare providers are already under strain.”
Aside from EMMC, the two hospital associations are joined in the lawsuit by 340B safety-net hospitals in North Dakota, Arkansas and New York.

title: Hidden Valley Farm Owners Win Statewide Conservation Award
text:
For almost 50 years, the founders of Hidden Valley Nature Center and owners of Hidden Valley Farm have been leaders in conservation efforts in Lincoln County.
On Sept. 17, Bambi Jones and Tracy Moskovitz were awarded the Natural Resources Council of Maine’s People’s Choice Award, one of organization’s many Conservation Leadership Awards. The People’s Choice Award is nominated by peers and chosen by popular vote, the honor going to volunteers who have dedicated their lives to conservation.
“It means a lot because it’s the People’s Choice Award,” Moskovitz said.
The Natural Resources Council, the largest environmental advocacy organization in Maine, is dedicated to protecting, restoring, and conserving the state’s environment. Executive Director Justin Strasburger said the Conservation Leadership Awards are a way for the organization to recognize work and leadership efforts across the state.
Strasburger said because the People’s Choice Award is nominated by members of the organization, it highlights community members who might otherwise go unknown.
“While I mentioned that sometimes this could be a way for folks not on our radar screen, Bambi and Tracy are very much on our radar screen,” Strasburger said. “They’ve been longtime supporters of (Natural Resources Council of Maine) and very deserving of this work.”
In their time maintaining their vast acreage, the two have dedicated their lives to sustainable forestry and using public lands for recreation, according to Strasburger. He said the creation of Hidden Valley Nature Center and Hidden Valley Farm is a great example of being stewards of the land, especially with how Jones and Moskovitz let their neighbors and community use it.
“In Maine, the vast majority of land is privately owned and if we’re getting serious about conservation and making sure that we are protecting the land, it’s incumbent upon a lot of individuals to care enough to take care of the land, their own land, and steward it for generations to come, and that’s the kind of thing that Bambi and Tracy have been sort of shining examples of,” Strasburger said.
Moskovitz and Jones moved to Maine in 1978 and bought 100 acres on Hollywood Boulevard in Whitefield to establish Hidden Valley Farm.
Over the years, the property started to grow and evolve, eventually amassing 2,000 acres of forest, hiking trails, and more by 2007. In a joint effort with their neighbors, Moskovitz and Jones put permanent easements on 1,000 of their combined acres through Maine Farmland Trust.
The same year, the two opened Hidden Valley Nature Center on 1,000 acres of the property. It is currently the largest private land holding open to the public in Lincoln County, according to the Maine Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association.
In 2016, Hidden Valley Nature Center was sold to Midcoast Conservancy while Moskovitz and Jones retained their 1,200 acres of property. The decision came after joining forces with numerous land trusts to expand their approach to conservation so it includes forestry and recreation.
Moskovitz said most land trusts were passive holders of property. With this in mind, Moskovitz and Jones thought it was important to be more engaged with the community because the higher involvement meant the more funds could be raised to protect the land.
When talking about the award, Moskovitz said the recognition is good to bring more attention to conservation efforts, not only the ones in their backyard. Jones said the relationship the two have built with their neighbors also plays into the maintenance of their land.
“We’re trying to do our share, and maybe a little bit more than our share, of developing a really good, healthy, and fun community of people, and the land conservation, and trails, and activities on the land are all things that tend to bring people together, tend to get them out of their houses, off their couches, take a walk, take a ski, take a bike ride, and have accessible, beautiful places with lots of trails is a real positive asset,” Moskovitz said.
The People’s Choice Award is not the first recognition the two have received. In 2024, they were awarded the New England Leopold Conservation Award, making them the first recipients in Maine to earn the honor.
The two were nominated for the award by Alna resident Cathy Johnson, who has known them for 40 years. She said Moskovitz and Jones are deserving of the recognition because of their dedication to conservation and education in Lincoln County.
Johnson gave kudos to all of the educational activities they have held for all ages, but especially for children who were given the opportunity to learn outdoors at Hidden Valley.
Others can look to Moskovitz and Jones as examples of leaders in ensuring land is open to the public for recreational needs, as well as protected, Johnson said.
“They really spent their adult lives preserving land in Lincoln County,” Johnson said.
Beyond their work for the environment, Johnson said Moskovitz and Jones are just overall good people. She recalled that whenever she would be out in public with the two, they seem to “know everyone.” She said she believes this because of how easy it is to connect with them.
“Bambi and Tracy are two of the most amazing people,” Johnson said.
Earlier this year, Moskovitz and Jones said they are looking to either gift or sell Hidden Valley Farm to an appropriate nonprofit organization. In the months since, the two said they have spoken with multiple organizations and should come to a decision by the end of the year.
It is important to both Moskovitz and Jones that whoever takes over is compatible and supportive of the community that makes up the 3-mile stretch of Hollywood Boulevard. Some of the residents have been friends for a long time, Moskovitz said in a February interview, and they all help each other when it is needed.
Moskovitz and Jones are in no rush to leave their 2,550-square-foot home, built out of wood harvested on their property. They said once they decide the course of action, they expect a two- to five-year transition period in the event the sale or transfer of the property needs to happen in phases. Once that is done, the two will be moving into their second home in Damariscotta.
“Part of the requirement is that whatever happens with the land is that it has to still remain accessible to the public in general, and more specifically to our neighbors who know the trails and have used them for years and help maintain them, help create them,” Jones said.

title: Failed executions troubled other states before Christa Pike. Here’s what happened
text:
(AP) - Tennessee’s bungled attempt to execute Christa Pike was not the first time a state has failed to carry out a lethal injection over problems in the death chamber.
Pike, 50, has regained consciousness and is speaking a week after Tennessee gave her two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Outgoing Republican Gov. Bill Lee has ordered a review into what went wrong and the state has not said whether they will again try executing her, which experts say could wade into uncharted legal waters.
Pike, who was sentenced to die for torturing and killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995, is one of at least eight condemned inmates in the U.S. who left their state’s execution chamber still alive because of problems carrying out the punishment, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Pike is the only one who was actually administered lethal drugs before the process was halted, according to the organization.
Not all have faced execution a second time. Three of the inmates would die years later in prison, two remain alive and two were executed after another attempt.
Lethal injection failures in Ohio
Ohio unsuccessfully tried to put Romell Broom to death by lethal injection in September 2009. The execution was called off after two hours when technicians could not find a suitable vein, and Broom cried in pain while receiving 18 needle sticks.
Broom died in December 2020 of possible complications of COVID-19 while on Ohio’s death row.
Ohio also failed to execute another inmate, Alva Campbell, in November 2017 by lethal injection. The execution was halted after executioners couldn’t find a usable vein.
Campbell was found unresponsive in his death row cell in March 2018. It was determined that he died from natural causes.
Alabama executed inmates a second time after failed attempts
Alabama called off the execution of Doyle Lee Hamm in February 2018 because of problems getting the intravenous line connected. A doctor hired by Hamm’s legal team later wrote in a report, filed in court, that Hamm had to be carried back to his cell by correctional officers after the execution was called off because he was in so much pain.
Hamm died of natural causes on death row in November 2021.
In September 2022, Alabama unsuccessfully executed Alan Eugene Miller by lethal injection when executioners spent more than an hour trying and failing to properly insert the catheter, repeatedly puncturing Miller with needles trying to find a vein. At one point, they left him hanging vertically on a gurney before state officials made the decision to call off the execution, according to news coverage at the time.
Miller had originally asked for nitrogen gas, but the Alabama Department of Corrections told a federal district court that they could not complete the execution that way.
The state successfully executed him two years later in September 2024 with nitrogen gas.
Almost two months after failing to execute Miller, Alabama had a second failed execution, when executioners did not have enough time to get a second IV line in before the death warrant expired at midnight for Kenneth Eugene Smith.
Smith was the first person to die by nitrogen gas as an execution method in January 2024.
Idaho prisoner remains alive
Idaho halted the execution of Thomas Eugene Creech in February 2024 after medical team members repeatedly failed to find a vein to carry out the lethal injection. In some cases, they couldn’t access the vein, and in others they could but had concerns about vein quality. They attempted sites in his arms, legs, hands and feet. At one point, a medical team member left to gather more supplies.
After eight attempts, the prison warden told them to give up. Creech remains alive and on death row.
Pike was the 2nd failed execution in Tennessee this year
Four months before Pike’s execution went awry, Tennessee officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers in May after his executioners tried and failed for over an hour to establish an intravenous line.
Lee announced soon afterward that the state would not try to execute Carruthers again for at least a year. Tennessee prison officials have said medical personnel had quickly established a primary IV line but were unable to find a suitable vein for a backup line as required by the state’s execution protocol. Efforts to insert a central line also failed.
Carruthers remains alive and on death row.

title: Troy Jackson reacts to Barack Obama endorsement for Maine Senate seat
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson addressed former President Barack Obama’s endorsement of his campaign after a tour of the Augusta Food Pantry Thursday morning.
“President Obama was someone that I really respected. I disagree with him on some things. I disagree with him on trade issues. But, I’m happy to have his endorsement because, overall, I think what he tried to do for the country was positive,” Jackson said.
Obama cites Jackson’s record
Obama shared his support for Jackson in a video released Wednesday morning. Obama pointed to Jackson’s working-class roots and record of lowering prescription drug costs, delivering universal school meals, raising wages and protecting abortion rights in Maine.
Collins campaign reacts
Sen. title: Fire district eyes ownership of Howland station after bond payoff
text:
HOWLAND, Maine (WABI) -The Central Maine Highlands Fire and EMS District No. 1 Board of Directors discussed the future of the district’s fire station during its monthly meeting Thursday night.
The board weighed whether to remain in the newly constructed facility in Howland or pursue building a new station at another location.
Following discussion, the board decided to send a question to the Howland Select Board asking whether the town would consider selling the building to the fire district at the end of its 27-year lease period, when the existing bond is expected to be paid off.
If the Howland Select Board agrees to move forward with the proposal, the question could then be placed on the ballot for a referendum vote during Howland’s 2027 municipal elections.
The fire district currently operates out of the Howland Municipal Building, which was constructed in 2021 and opened in 2022. The facility was originally built specifically to house the Howland Fire Department.
Howland voters approved borrowing $3.4 million through the Maine Municipal Bond Bank to finance the project.
The town has nearly 27 years remaining on the bond, with annual payments of approximately $217,000.
Since the building opened, the Howland Fire Department has transitioned into a regional fire district, governed by a board of directors appointed by the select boards of its eight member communities and by commissions representing two counties.
The board serves Burlington, Edinburg, Enfield, Howland, Lowell, Maxfield, Passadumkeag and Seboeis Plantation, as well as unorganized territories in Hancock and Penobscot counties.
“The big thing is, is that we want to get to the end of the bond at like 27 years from now, whatever the number is that the bond ends and not have to pay anymore because we just paid for it. So we want to, we want to take, it would take over a quarter million dollars of cost out of our balance sheet. We don’t have to pay it because we own it,” said District No. 1 Board President Bob Genest.
Under the current arrangement, the district leases the fire station portion of the building from the town of Howland for $288,000 annually.
The town is responsible for utilities and building maintenance costs under the lease.

title: The best way to see Maine’s foliage, lakes and landmarks isn’t what you might think
text:
This past summer, I found myself thinking about how cool it would be to see Katahdin from the air.
I’ve hiked the mountain. Now why not fly around it, too?
Then I thought, well, wait — why not go in the fall and get the bonus of seeing Maine’s foliage from the air?
So that’s what I did.
Last week, I took a 30-minute scenic flight with Katahdin Air, departing from Spencer Cove on Ambajejus Lake. It was over way too quickly, but it offered a completely different perspective on a part of Maine I’ve spent plenty of time exploring from the ground.
We flew over Abol Bridge and followed the West Branch of the Penobscot River toward Ripogenus Dam, spotting the familiar Telos Road and Cribworks. I quizzed myself, trying to identify the peaks and lakes we passed.
The morning fog had cleared by the time I was in the air, but white clouds covered the north side of Katahdin.
At one point, I spotted Wassataquoik Lake and learned that it’s home to Arctic char and is the largest and deepest lake entirely within Baxter State Park.
But you can’t land a plane there. If you want to fish it, you’ll have to hike more than 20 miles round-trip, depending on the route. Planes are only permitted to land on Matagamon, Nesowadnehunk and Webster lakes within Baxter.
Scenic flights are worth the money. But they’re even more appealing when the flight itself is a way to get somewhere you couldn’t easily reach by vehicle.
There are several companies around Maine that offer sightseeing flights and other ways to explore the state from the air.
Katahdin Air, for example, flies passengers to remote lakes and sporting camps for lodging or dinner. The company also offers flights to see historical sites, including the abandoned 1930s-era Eagle Lake and West Branch steam locomotives, often called the ghost trains, within the Allagash Wilderness Waterway.
Currier’s Flying Service, based in Greenville, is another option. I haven’t flown with them yet, but I plan to. The company offers flights around Katahdin and tours featuring Mount Kineo, Moose Mountain, Lobster Lake and North Bay. They also offer flights specifically for spotting moose.
Other scenic flights around Maine offer views of places such as the Belgrade Lakes and Acadia National Park.
And a small plane can be useful for more than sightseeing.
Fall foliage is seen from the air near Katahdin (left), the Telos Road (top right) and the West Branch of the Penobscot River (bottom right). Credit: Susan Bard / BDN
I know a Maine guide who flew every fall for seven or eight years to help locate moose before hunting season. From the air, he could cover a huge area and get a sense of where bulls were concentrated before heading into the woods.
That got me thinking about my next trip.
My flight around Katahdin was mostly about seeing the scenery. But ideally, my next flight will take me somewhere that isn’t easy — or even possible — to reach by vehicle.
I need to figure out where, but it will include a fishing rod.

title: Legislative Republicans call for investigation into AG email leak
text:
Maine Republicans call for investigation into AG email leak
At least two Republicans on the Legislature's Judiciary Committee have called for an investigation into how the Attorney General's Office accidentally emailed confidential information to its media list.
Maine Republicans call for investigation into AG email leak
At least two Republicans on the Legislature's Judiciary Committee have called for an investigation into how the Attorney General's Office accidentally emailed confidential information to its media list.
Maine is the only state in the country where the legislature elects the state Attorney General. Now, Republicans say they're concerned about the AG's office sending confidential information to its media list.
"I think it's incredibly concerning," Rep. Rachel Henderson, R-Rumford, said.
Henderson sits on the legislature's Judiciary Committee, which works closely with the Attorney General's office. She and other Republicans on the committee are calling for an investigation by the Government Oversight Committee.
"The legislature, we hire our constitutional officers. We elected the attorney general. Although I did not vote for Attorney General Frey, he is the one that's in the office now, and the legislature has oversight of that office, and we need to exercise that power," Henderson added.
She said she wants the committee chairs, Democrats, Sen. Anne Carney and Rep. Amy Kuhn, to call the committee back for a hearing or to hold a public hearing in January when the legislature is back in session.
Democratic leadership and Democrats on the committee have not responded to our request for comment.
In a statement from the Attorney General's Office, a spokesperson wrote, "This was a serious, but entirely human error. Immediately upon discovery of the mistake, the office began working to limit any impacts of potential dissemination."
Frey terms out at the end of the year, then the legislature will be tasked with electing a new AG in January.

title: 3D-Printed Meat Now Arriving in Maine Grocery Stores
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
3D-Printed Meat Now Arriving in Maine Grocery Stores
There is little debate that people in America love to eat meat. Over the last couple of years, meat consumption in the U.S. has increased despite prices going up.
Because of that rising demand as well as the spike in prices, both customers and suppliers have been looking at ways to satisfy demand while keeping prices stable.
And the best way to reach that goal seems to be in the form of 3D-printed meat.
Perfecta Plant-Based Meat Begins to Roll Out in Stores Across Maine
Across a handful of grocery stores in Maine, you'll begin to see a new option showing up in the meat department.
The brand is called Perfecta. It is a plant-based meat that offers a different style than other plant-based meat offerings. Perfecta uses 3D-printing technology to better mimic traditional cuts of beef, poultry and fish.
Currently, Perfecta is slowly phasing in some of their products at independent grocery stores and co-ops throughout Maine.
While you won't find Perfecta at larger stores like Hannaford, Market Basket or Shaw's yet, Perfecta hopes that will change by the end of this year.
Perfecta is Bringing Three Different Meat Options to Stores Currently
While Perfecta plans to offer additional items like salmon, tuna and filet mignon in the future, their current focus is rolling out three specific 3d-printed meat options this year.
Those three initial options are plant-based marbled steak, plant-based chicken breast and plant-based whitefish patties.
The question remains on whether consumers in the northeast will actually buy-in. According to ScienceDirect, there still remains a rather large stigma about plant-based meats and specifically plant-based meats that are 3D-printed for effect.

title: Aging Untold: Why more LGBTQ+ older adults are living openly
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore the courage, newfound freedom and unique challenges of coming out later in life.
Plus, find out how opting for out-of-pocket medical care works and why paying cash on purpose makes sense for some patients.
We also introduce an 86-year-old volunteer using his product-design background to repair and recycle electronics for a local charity.
Some older adults in the LGBTQ+ community find that age brings the courage and confidence to come out later in life.
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said some factors that lead people to come out later in life could include the death of those who would not have accepted the relationship or a loved one who initially wasn’t able to accept it changing their mind.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said there is a physical toll that comes with hiding one’s identity for years.
Some doctors are moving away from traditional insurance models. The shift can mean paying out of pocket, and it isn’t the right fit for everyone.
Two of the options are concierge medicine and direct primary care.
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said with concierge medicine, you have your own doctor and you pay privately for that. Direct primary care is concierge with a membership organization, but the doctor also takes insurance.
Dr. Rogers said her own path moved from traditional obstetrics and gynecology into an integrative approach before she transitioned fully into functional medicine.
Cradduck brought up affordability and said a lot of people who would love to be healthier cannot afford out-of-pocket care.
Scammers have posed as law enforcement to scare victims into handing over personal information, money or both.
An Arizona woman is sharing her story of losing thousands in a jury-duty scam when it happened to her.
“It sounds so realistic,” said Kristine, who is being identified only by her first name.
She is explaining how it happened in hopes it will prevent others from becoming victims.
Marshall Johnson is 86 years old and helps Habitat for Humanity by taking apart donated electronics and appliances for recycling.
He worked as a product designer for appliance companies, including Black & Decker and Home Depot. His designs are on display at the Hagley Museum and Library in Wilmington, Delaware.
Learn more about Marshall and the recycling program, which raises money for Habitat for Humanity and reduces waste at local landfills.

title: Patriots’ banged-up secondary will be tested by Raiders QB Kirk Cousins
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Kirk Cousins’ torrid start has been one of the NFL’s biggest surprises.
The 38-year-old Las Vegas Raiders quarterback is looking to keep it going this week at New England against a Patriots defense that is suddenly having trouble keeping its secondary healthy.
Despite his first loss of the season last week against Kansas City, Cousins is up to 11 touchdown passes — the fastest he has reached that total through four games in his 15-year career. His previous best was 10 TDs through four games in 2018. It has helped quiet the chatter about him being simply a bridge quarterback to Fernando Mendoza, who Las Vegas took No. 1 overall in April.
Cousins said he’s just enjoying seeing the resilience of the entire team in Klint Kubiak’s first season, a group Cousins said is confirming what he observed from them going back to spring workouts.
“These guys, they want to do it the right way. Football means something to them,” Cousins said. “They’re hardworking, listen well, and it makes it a joy to be the quarterback for a group of guys like that. But you’ve got to go prove it again every week.”
That next challenge is a Patriots team that avoided a 1-3 start with a win over Buffalo last week. Not only did quarterback Drake Maye break out of an early season funk with three touchdown passes, but the defense, which played without star cornerback Christian Gonzalez (shoulder), was able to slow Bills quarterback Josh Allen.
Gonzalez was ruled out for the second straight game on Friday, along with fellow starting cornerback Carlton Davis (neck) and rookie Channing Canada (hamstring). Another cornerback, Charles Woods (shoulder) was listed as questionable.
Wide receiver Mack Hollins (calf) was also ruled out. Defensive tackle Christian Barmore (shoulder) and running back Rhamondre Stevenson (knee) were among those listed as questionable.
Whoever is available Sunday, Maye said carrying as much of the momentum they can from last week is the goal.
“You would like to say everybody — especially on offense — you’d like to say that the first three weeks weren’t what we wanted to put out there,” Maye said. “You have to try to build off last week, knowing that it’s not just going to do it for you. You have to put the work in and the focus, and hopefully continue to catch a trend and catch a stride.
Need to know
Las Vegas (3-1) at New England (2-2)
When/where to watch: 1 p.m. Sunday, CBS.
Latest odds: Patriots by 3 1/2.
Against the spread: Raiders 4-0; Patriots 2-1-1.
Last week: Raiders lost to Chiefs 30-27; Patriots beat Bills 29-26.
Last meeting: Raiders beat Patriots 20-13 on Sept. 5, 2025, in Foxborough, Mass.
Series record: Patriots lead 20-18-1.
Matchup to watch
The Raiders’ red-zone defense vs. the Patriots’ red-zone offense. Las Vegas has been susceptible to giving up big plays this season. Once inside the 20, opponents have feasted, scoring touchdowns on 10 of 13 (76.9%) of their trips. But the Patriots have struggled in the red zone through four games, scoring on just four of nine (44.4%) of their opportunities.
Stats and stuff
• Las Vegas and Detroit are the only teams that have scored 25 or more points in each game this season. It’s the second time in franchise history the Raiders have accomplished that in their first four games of a season. The 2002 team was the other one to do it.
• The Raiders lead the NFL with nine takeaways, one more than four other teams. That total is tied for sixth in franchise history with the 1972 team for the most through four games in a season.
• Las Vegas has 12 sacks and allowed five, and the Raiders’ seven-sack differential is tied with the Lions for the league’s best.
• The Raiders’ Dylan Laube leads the NFL with a 33.4-yard kickoff return average.
• The Patriots, including the playoffs, have won nine of their past 10 home games, including a 20-3 win over Pittsburgh in Week 2.
• New England is looking to snap a three-game losing streak to Las Vegas.
• Maye’s seven interceptions are one shy of the eight he threw in the regular season last year.
AP Sports Writer Mark Anderson in Las Vegas contributed.

title: MSSM Named Maine’s Top Public High School by Niche
text:
LIMESTONE, Maine (WAGM) - A Limestone school is proving big achievements can come from a small community. The Maine School of Science and Mathematics in Limestone was named Maine’s number one public high school by Niche for 2027. NewsSource8’s Karri Triplett spoke with students and staff about what the recognition means to them.
Karri: The Maine School of Science and Mathematics was named Maine’s number one public high school in Niche’s 2027 rankings. Niche is an online platform that uses public data and user reviews to help families compare schools. Students and staff at MSSM say they are proud of the recognition.
MSSM student Ahliya Roy says she wasn’t surprised the school ranked number one. “That doesn’t surprise me but it’s good to see that we’re getting the recognition even though we’re like a small school in the middle of nowhere. It’s nice to see.”
Roy says MSSM’s advanced curriculum and the dedication of its faculty and students helped set the school apart. “People truly love learning and being here and exploring new classes. Even though we’re a public school our curriculum looks really different compared to a lot of other schools and we don’t just have your AP dual enrollment. We just do a lot more advanced topics and stuff like that. And the teachers, they have really high degrees and they’re very educated and super passionate about their jobs and not just teaching but the subject that they’re teaching. So, I think it’s just both the students’ love for learning and the teachers’ passions.”
Music instructor Brett Vanderlaan says the ranking reflects the strong community among MSSM faculty members. “It doesn’t surprise me when I think about the faulty. I think that’s one of the things. It’s my second year here and one of the most impressive things beyond the students is the dynamic quality of the faculty and the interactions that we are able to have. We are supported by one another, and we are supportive of one another. So, we’re not isolated teachers in a classroom bound by four walls. We’re really integrated into the community.”
Vanderlaan says the recognition affirms the work students and teachers put in every day. “It helps to hopefully affirm everyone that what we’re doing is worthwhile and on the right track and I think even for students to some degree. To know that they’re in an environment that is actually giving them that very wonderful privilege to be learning here with the faculty and with their fellow classmates probably gives them a little boost as well. Just acknowledgement and recognition of what they’re a part of.”
School leaders say they are already looking toward the future through a strategic-planning process focused on MSSM’s long-term goals and they hope to hold onto the number one spot again next year.

title: CMMC in Lewiston is pushing back against nurses union election
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Central Maine Medical Center in Lewiston has filed objections to the union election nurses won overwhelmingly last month, raising concerns that employees could not freely choose whether to vote.
Objections go through the National Labor Relations Board, the federal agency that oversees labor practices and certifies elections.
The nurses have also filed complaints with the board against the hospital, claiming that CMMC retaliated against protected union activities when it fired or suspended 20 nurses in the week before the vote to join the Maine State Nurses Association and National Nurses United.
Amid the claims of union retaliation, CMMC asked the board to block the election. The NLRB denied the request Sept. 22. The election took place two days later, with the nurses approving the union by a vote of 204-21.
Now, in a request for review of that denial, the hospital is claiming the NLRB should have blocked the union election like it did at Saint Francis Hospital in Illinois, which is also owned by Prime Healthcare Foundation.
Union officials in Illinois asked the NLRB to block Saint Francis’ Sept. 17 union election on the grounds that a free and fair vote was not possible because Prime Healthcare Foundation was breaking the law. The board granted the request on Sept. 14.
According to union officials, Prime Healthcare Foundation illegally fired between 13 and 45 per diem nurses during a public campaign to join National Nurses United in Illinois.
CMMC says that precedent warrants review of “the unexplained denial” of CMMC’s request to block the election in Lewiston, which hospital officials say “permitted the election to proceed without addressing whether materially overlapping allegations at Central Maine and (Saint Francis) presented materially different risks to employee free choice.”
Union officials countered that the cases are legally distinct.
In the meantime, the union says it is still fighting for the 20 suspended and terminated nurses to be reinstated.
“Nurses are continuing to work with community members and elected officials to get all the nurses reinstated,” union officials said Tuesday.

title: More than 100 service members meet newborns for first time as USS Abraham Lincoln docks
text:
SAN DIEGO (CNN) — The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in Southern California Thursday, marking the end of the second-longest Navy aircraft carrier deployment since the Vietnam War.
About 5,000 sailors and Marines returned home Thursday.
Among them were 122 new fathers, including one who was greeted with, “Hello, daddy’s home.”
“I can’t explain it. This is incredible,” one returning service member said.
Record time at sea
The Lincoln left San Diego in late November 2025. The deployment lasted 322 days, with most of that time spent aboard the vessel. The ship set a record for the most consecutive days at sea without a port call.
“Two-hundred-sixty-five continuous days,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said.
During a speech Wednesday, Hegseth announced that sailors aboard the Lincoln and other ships in its strike group would receive the Presidential Unit Citation, the U.S. military’s highest honor for a unit in battle.
The carrier played a leading role in support of Operation Epic Fury, the joint U.S. and Israeli military campaign against Iran.
Morale concerns during deployment
Reports of worsening morale and mental health among crew members brought the unit into the spotlight during the deployment.
“It’s been trying, but one thing, sailors and marines are a lot tougher than many people think, but we’re ready to get home,” said Lt. James Holliday, chaplain.
In September, a letter from the Navy’s acting secretary revealed “a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group.”
In August, a sailor went overboard but was rescued.
The Lincoln was relieved in the Middle East by the USS George Washington.

title: Isaias may weaken before landfall, but storm surge and flooding remain threats
text:
(AP) - A supersized El Niño’s decapitating winds and the Gulf of Mexico’s toasty, storm-fueling waters are battling over the future strength of Hurricane Isaias. And the storm’s tilt and eye show who’s winning.
For now, it’s the waters charged by climate change.
All Atlantic hurricane season there has been “this battle between shear and just the overall conducive conditions,” said Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach.
El Niño — the natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps weather worldwide — dominated. Its wind patterns smothered almost any wisp of a storm from strengthening in the Atlantic, while boosting what will soon be record high levels in the Pacific, Klotzbach said.
Wind shear versus warm waters
It’s called wind shear and it pushes the tops and middle of storms around, making them lopsided and keeping them from making a complete circular eyewall, which is when storms can really power up, Klotzbach and University at Albany’s Kristen Corbosiero said.
The other ingredients for a storm to turbocharge a storm are pushing back. There is plenty of fuel in warm water and moisture. The Gulf of Mexico is about 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5 degrees Celsius) warmer than normal. The 86 degree waters (30 degrees Celsius) are 100 to 500 times more likely to be that extra hot because of climate change from the burning of coal, oil and gas, said climate scientist Kristina Dahl, vice president of the nonprofit Climate Central, which calculates the boost global warming causes to extreme weather.
“But there’s a certain point where it’s like, I don’t care how hot the waters are and how much moisture you have, if shear gets to a certain point, the shear is gonna win,” Klotzbach said.
The thunderstorm seeds of something bigger earlier in the week grew from circular winds over Central America but often were lopsided and couldn’t quite form a crucial eyewall, all because of El Niño’s high-level strong winds that pushed a would-be storm’s top sideways, experts said.
Then a window of moderation opened for just a couple of days, but it was enough, Corbosiero said. It makes sense it was in the Gulf of Mexico and in October, because El Niño has less of an effect in the Gulf than it does in the main Atlantic, she said. And storms often pop up in that region in October because of more northerly storm systems that help foster the right conditions.
Wind shear wasn’t exactly low, but it was a moderate level, when other factors like unusually warm waters and heavy moisture can kick in. Isaias rapidly intensified from 40 mph to 80 mph (64 kph to 129 kph) in a day and by late Wednesday, Isaias became the latest-in-the-season first Atlantic hurricane to form since 1914, Klotzbach said.
“The warm waters and high moisture won,” Klotzbach said. Isaias Friday was not tilting and had a strong eye, the hurricane center said.
By Friday morning, Isaias blew past the threshold for becoming a major hurricane with winds of 111 mph (178 kph), strengthening to 120 mph winds (195 kph). The National Hurricane Center forecasts it to weaken to a strong Category 2 storm before landfall.
What to expect before landfall
Before Isaias comes ashore — forecast for probably somewhere from the Mississippi and Alabama coast to the Florida Panhandle late Friday night or early Saturday — the wind shear will strengthen from moderate levels of around 20 mph (32 kph) to 52 mph (84 kph) and then Isaias will start to struggle, which is good news for coastal residents, Klotzbach said.
But as of Friday morning, hurricane center forecasters said the coast is in “a tenuous spot” because it would only take a six-hour delay in the onset of that more intense wind shear for Isaias to bring a stronger-than-expected landfall. Regardless of what will happen with wind shear, it will still be a dangerous hurricane when it hits land, forecasters said.
“Once it gets to the coast, we know that the storm surge is going to be deeper and farther reaching because of sea level rise caused by climate change,” Dahl said. “So in this part of the world, there’s been about six and a half inches of sea level rise over the past 100 years or so that’s attributable directly to climate change.”
The National Hurricane Center is calling the surge “life-threatening.”
A warmer atmosphere means storms hold and then dump more rain, worsening flooding, Dahl said. The hurricane center is warning about urban, river and flash flooding in the Southeast this weekend.
“There’s a little bit of a battle here going on, but I think the really important thing to remember is that climate change is like this long-term big kahuna warming everywhere, and El Niño’s like a little icing on the cake,” Dahl said.
