title: Breast cancer care is evolving in Maine
text:
Providing high-quality affordable care, educating tomorrow's caregivers and researching better ways to provide care.
For many people, breast cancer treatment is about more than removing a tumor or stopping a disease. Increasingly, patients and doctors are also focused on what life looks like after treatment, including long-term recovery and physical comfort.
Across Maine, patients are benefiting from leading-edge advances in breast cancer care previously not available locally. MaineHealth physicians are bringing some of these specialized surgical options closer to home, giving patients access to innovative treatments without needing to be away from their communities and support systems.
These advances reflect a growing focus on treating the whole patient. In addition to targeting cancer, newer surgical techniques aim to reduce complications, support recovery and improve quality of life long after treatment is finished.
One recent example is a procedure known as S-LYMPHA, which was first performed in Maine earlier this year by MaineHealth breast surgeon Dr. Ekaterini Tsiapali. The procedure is designed for patients who require an axillary lymph node dissection, a surgery that removes lymph nodes from the underarm when breast cancer has spread to those areas.
While often an important part of treatment, lymph node removal can increase the risk of lymphedema, a condition that causes swelling in the arm and can become a lifelong concern for some people. This condition can affect daily activities and often requires ongoing management.
The S-LYMPHA procedure is designed to help reduce that risk. During surgery, tiny lymphatic vessels are connected to a nearby vein, creating a new pathway for lymphatic fluid to drain from the arm. By performing the procedure at the same time as cancer surgery, surgeons may be able to lower the likelihood of lymphedema developing later. For patients who may face barriers with out-of-state travel, having this specialized treatment available locally through MaineHealth can make a meaningful difference during an already challenging time.
Another recent advancement reflects a growing focus on survivorship and life after breast cancer treatment.
In 2026, MaineHealth became the first health system in Maine to offer nerve- and nipple-sparing mastectomies for eligible breast cancer patients. The first surgery was performed by Dr. Tsiapali, in collaboration with Dr. Katharine Connolly of Plastic & Hand Surgical Associates, with the surgical team having achieved specialized training for this procedure.
Loss of sensation in the breast has been a common outcome following a mastectomy. With this newer approach, surgeons work to preserve the sensory nerve to the nipple and reconnect it using a nerve graft during reconstruction. For some patients, this creates the potential to regain sensation following surgery.
The goal extends beyond reconstruction itself. Preserving sensation may help patients feel more connected to their bodies and can play an important role in physical and emotional recovery after treatment. While the procedure is not appropriate for every patient, it represents an important advancement in how breast cancer care is delivered.
Increasingly, specialists are focused not only on treating cancer but also on reducing complications and supporting recovery. Advances once focused largely on survival are now being paired with efforts to help patients maintain function, comfort and confidence throughout survivorship.
That broader perspective reflects how breast cancer care has changed over time. Today, MaineHealth patients benefit from a coordinated approach that extends well beyond the operating room. Care may begin with screening and early detection, followed by diagnostic imaging, surgery, medical oncology, radiation therapy, rehabilitation services and long-term follow-up. Specialists from multiple disciplines work together to help guide patients through each phase of their journey, which can be an otherwise overwhelming and difficult experience.
Breast Cancer Awareness Month serves as an opportunity to highlight not only the importance of screening and early detection, but also the progress being made in treatment and survivorship. From reducing the risk of complications such as lymphedema to preserving sensation after a mastectomy, advances in breast cancer care at MaineHealth are improving results for some patients beyond just removing their cancer.
The approach to care at MaineHealth is focused on supporting the whole person – from screening and diagnosis to treatment and survivorship. For patients and families, that means having trusted experts by their side through every stage of the breast cancer journey.
For more information, visit mainehealth.org/breastcancer.

title: Maine military moms celebrate new chapter of Blue Star Mothers of America
text:
When Maine mothers of military personnel saw in March that war in Iran was escalating, they bonded together to organize a statewide support network for active duty service members, military mothers, families and veterans.
Rosie Vanadestine of Skowhegan and Jane Thorndike of Avon, who both have sons who are gunnery sergeants in the U.S. Marines, along with 10 other military mothers, worked to establish a Maine chapter of the Blue Star Mothers of America.
“It has been a long road getting over the finish line that is for sure,” Vanadestine, president of the chapter, wrote in an email Wednesday. “This group of women are amazing. We have become so important to each other and have become the first outreach when any of us are struggling. The more I learn and the more organizations we are connecting to, the more excited I am about what (Blue Star Mothers of America) ME3 will accomplish in service of our active military, our veterans and all the military families here in Maine.”
The formation of the Maine chapter was inspired by Vanadestine when her child entered military service. After discovering there was no active chapter in the state, she started outreach, which quickly gained momentum.
With the official installation ceremony completed at the national level, a local celebratory event is planned for Oct. 25 in Augusta.
Thorndike is happy the chapter is finally established. “Blue Star Mothers is a way for us ‘moms’/stepmoms/grandmothers or even other family members to support one another and to give back to our veterans and service members. ‘Once a mom, always a mom,’” Thorndike wrote in a message.
Her son, Gunnery Sgt. Barry Thorndike II, who was deployed on the USS Abraham Lincoln for over seven months in the Middle East, got off the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier when it arrived in San Diego on Thursday. He will be stationed there for the next two years.
“Both my boys will stand on USA soil again. I thank God and that hardworking USS Abraham Lincoln crew for getting him back to us,” Thorndike wrote Thursday.
Thorndike’s husband and sister-in-law were on the way to see him Wednesday. Thorndike stayed behind because of work and other obligations.
“Military families should never have to walk this journey alone. Our mission is to support troops, veterans, military families, and the families of fallen heroes while supporting one another through every stage of military life,” Vanadestine wrote.
Blue Star Mothers of America is a national nonprofit organization founded in 1942 and chartered by Congress in 1960. With more than 6,000 members across 200 chapters nationwide, the organization provides support, service, and advocacy for military communities across the country.
Leaders of the Maine chapter plan to provide peer support for military families, send care packages to deployed service members, assist veterans, support Gold Star families, participate in community service projects, and partner with organizations serving Maine’s military and veteran communities.
Full membership is open to mothers, stepmothers, grandmothers, foster mothers, and female legal guardians of active-duty service members, National Guard members, Reservists, veterans, and fallen service members. Associate membership is available for all other family members and individuals seeking opportunities to support the organization’s mission through volunteer service and community involvement.
Anyone wanting more information can contact Vanadestine by email at [email protected] or by phone at 207-576-2960.
The celebratory event for the new Maine chapter is planned for 2 p.m. Oct. 25 at VFW Post 886 at 509 Leighton Road in Augusta. It is intended to bring together military families, veteran organizations, elected officials, community leaders and members of the public to celebrate the milestone and formally launch the new Maine chapter.
The distinguished guest speaker is Maj. Gen. Diane L. Dunn, who serves as the 41st adjutant general of the Maine National Guard and commissioner of the Department of Defense, Veterans and Emergency Management. Light refreshments will follow.
Anyone interested in learning more about the Blue Star Mothers organization is invited to attend.

title: Longtime Acadia visitors vent about speed and disruptive impact of e-bikes in park
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mount Desert Island residents have grown weary of the staggering rise of e-bikes on Acadia National Park’s sprawling carriage road system.
It’s been roughly seven years since the National Park Service announced a blanket policy allowing Class 1 e-bikes — which cannot travel faster than 20 mph— in parks across the country.
Since then, many MDI residents have grown tired of the persistent congestion, speed and generally disruptive impact that some say has accompanied the electric bicycles’ introduction to park life. But while e-bikes have annoyed many longtime park visitors, they’ve also provided others, some of whom have various physical limitations, with a new way to enjoy Acadia’s beauty.
The rise of e-bikes comes at a turbulent time for Acadia and the entire park service, which has seen significant funding cuts and staff layoffs under the Trump administration. Staffing cuts have resulted in fewer rangers to enforce the speed limit or verify that Class 2 and 3 e-bikes — which have a throttle, can travel up to 28 mph and are only allowed on paved roads — stay off the gravel carriage roads.
It is also another example of how some local residents have begun to bristle at the ever-increasing growth of tourism on MDI, where Acadia had an all-time record high in annual visits last year. Twice in recent years, voters in Bar Harbor have cast ballots in support of enacting strict limits on cruise ship visits, and the town currently has an ongoing temporary ban on hotel development.
On Acadia’s carriage roads, some residents who have walked them for decades — on their own or with their dogs, or horseback riding along the 45-mile network of paths — have stopped using them altogether, particularly in the park’s busy summer season, as e-bikes overtake the once-peaceful trail system.
“A lot of people on foot that used to be harmonious with the cycling crew have pretty much abandoned being out there because we don’t stand a chance,” local resident Meredith Gabbard said. “[The park] has chosen the rights of e-bike people over the rest of the park users.”
E-bikes, which are estimated to make up roughly half of all bicycle traffic on the gravel paths, are different from traditional bikes, Gabbard said, adding that she and her husband Michael Woodworth, a lifelong island resident, have been visiting the carriage roads for decades.
Many e-bikers travel in large groups, often with tour guides who offer lessons on how to ride the machines on the carriage road system. But that guidance seems insufficient for locals who say the large groups — some of which exceed a dozen riders — take over the trail network, flying by walkers and traditional bikers alike, according to the couple and others interviewed for this article.
Residents have complained about e-bikes swerving dangerously close to other cyclists, walkers and horseriders, exceeding the 20-miles per hour speed limit and riding on the wrong side of the road.
“I hike and I take my dog, and [e-bikers] don’t announce if they’re coming up on your left,” Gabbard said. “We’ve been driven off of the road. My dog won’t even go on the carriage roads anymore — the bikes terrify him.”
The problem has grown so severe that a number of Bar Harbor residents have formed an “underground task force” to discuss the rise of e-bike related safety concerns, Gabbard said.
“Everybody just feels like we can’t use the park anymore,” she said. “The park can’t police it. The rental places should take some ownership on what they’re renting and where the bikes are going.”
A recent Faceboost post with a photo of a local company unloading e-bikes at Eagle Lake boat landing drew 145 comments, many from locals complaining of the surge in e-bikes and congestion they cause.
The park service has listened to these concerns. Yet after a study with the Worcester Polytechnic Institute, the park found that e-bikers were riding on average 12 mph, while traditional cyclists were averaging 11 mph, Acadia Superintendent Kevin Schneider told the Acadia Advisory Commission in mid-September.
In other words, the findings didn’t indicate that e-bikers are speeding.
The park service did not respond to an inquiry from the Bangor Daily News about e-bike related accidents in Acadia.
Stephanie Clement, vice president of conservation for the nonprofit group Friends of Acadia, said that many of Acadia’s visitors each year have never been there before, and likely are unfamiliar with the conditions they encounter while riding through the park.
“Roughly half of Acadia’s visitors are first-time visitors, which makes education about how to recreate responsibly and safely on the carriage roads really important,” Clement said. “Many visitors have never ridden a bike on a road shared with horses, for example, so helping them understand how to safely navigate those interactions benefits everyone. This education is important for people on both e-bikes and traditional bikes.”
Park officials are considering requiring a concessions contract for e-bikes within park boundaries, with hopes that the park would have more of a say in educating bikers on carriage road etiquette, Schneider said.
The contract would only apply to businesses that deliver e-bikes and customers to locations inside Acadia, not to companies with storefronts outside park borders and whose customers travel into the park on their own.
Woodworth, who once cycled competitively, agreed that visitors’ unfamiliarity with how to handle a bicycle, let alone an e-bike, is part of the problem.
“What I see is people that aren’t experienced in operating a bicycle and all of a sudden they can go 20 miles per hour uphill,” Woodworth said. “There’s nothing good that’s going to come from that. It’s dangerous.”
Another island resident who asked not to be identified said she hadn’t been on the carriage roads in more than a year because of the e-bikers and her concern for her safety, adding “it’s very depressing.”
“Someone’s going to get killed,” said the woman, who has lived on the island for nearly three decades. She said didn’t want to be identified because of the vitriol she’s experienced on social media after expressing safety concerns around e-bikes.
Curt Bonney, who has been horseback riding on the carriage roads since the 1970s, said traditional cyclists were “annoying, but you could work with them.” The e-bikes, however, often spook his horses, Bonney said, adding that he’s been on riding trips before during which a friend nearly lost control of their horse because an e-biker came too close to the 1,000 pound-animal.
“Then e-bikes came on the scene: at first they were a novelty, but now they go 20, 25, 30 miles an hour, they make no noise and it spooks the horse,” Bonney said. “All of a sudden, there’s a flock of 20 bikes coming right at you. They take up the whole road. They’re not being rude, they’re not being mean — they are unaware.”
But for many park visitors, e-bikes are the only way they can enjoy Acadia’s trademark picturesque carriage roads. E-bikes allow people who may be unable to use a traditional bike — because of their age or various physical limitations — to ride miles of the trail network.
“I think they’re an asset — we’ve gone 20 miles [today],” said Karin Saltonovitz, a visitor from the Chicago area, who was riding an e-bike Tuesday afternoon along the Eagle Lake carriage roads. “I don’t think I would have done it without it. There’s no way we could do that.”
Saltonovitz was riding between 11 and 17 mph, she said, adding that her experience had been peaceful and everybody was “playing by the rules and biking responsibly.”
Early Tuesday afternoon, roughly every 10 minutes, a swarm of e-bikers, many of whom were part of a tour group, stopped by the Eagle Lake boat landing, a popular carriage road access point. After a brief photo session, they would mount their e-bikes and continue on their tour or leisure ride.
John Frank, a 71-year-old first time e-bike rider visiting from Texas, was one of roughly a dozen members of a guided carriage road tour.
“I can understand the concern because sometimes it feels like I’m going faster than the suggested 20 mile per hour speed limit,” Frank said, adding that he wasn’t sure how fast he was going because his bike didn’t have a speedometer.
Another e-bike rider, Jeanette Viruet, of New Jersey, who declined to provide her full name, suggested the park should have some sort of speed radar that tickets — or somehow holds riders accountable — if they’re exceeding the speed limit. She said she noticed many of the faster riders are children or young people.
Mark and Danielle Nespeca, an elderly couple from California, rented e-bikes because they anticipated their ride around Eagle Lake would involve more hills. The couple was instructed by their rental company on how to ride safely and politely, they said.
The Nespecas were told to ride single-file, though they noticed that not all bikers were following those directions, they said.
Glenn Tucker, owner of Acadia Bike on Cottage Street in downtown Bar Harbor, said Tuesday that, like all local bike rental businesses, the only e-bikes his store rents out are in the Class 1 e-category. Tucker coordinated with the park service and the Worcester Polytechnic Institute for the e-bikes study. Researchers placed trackers on his fleet of e-bikes to assess how fast they were averaging.
“The statistics speak for themselves, but there are people out there who bring their own [higher class] bikes that have throttles on them,” Tucker said. “They’re not supposed to be on the carriage roads. I think there are some instances of speeding.”
Tucker’s shop provides renters with an extensive lesson on how to ride e-bikes safely on the carriage roads, he said, estimating that about half his customers rent e-bikes and the other half go for traditional bicycles. The informational session is more in-depth for e-bikes than it is for regular bicycles, he said.
The rental shop does not allow children under 14 to ride an e-bike. Tucker, who has run his rental shop for three decades, said he tries to encourage parents to rent regular bicycles for kids.
Tucker’s website reminds customers that his shop can cancel a reservation at an employee’s discretion if they are “not convinced that you are able to safely ride an e-bike.”
Some rental shops deliver e-bikes to various destinations around the park, including the Hulls Cove Visitor Center and Eagle Lake boat ramp.
“We’re not doing that, because it leads to congestion,” Tucker said. “It takes up and parking places and we don’t think the park needs that. We see the congestion, especially at the visitor center, but it’s also happening at Eagle Lake. We don’t play any part in that.”
Tucker only rents bicycles from his downtown storefront and does not deliver them to any areas of the park.
Tucker added he has not seen an uptick in bicycle-related accidents since the introduction of e-bikes.
“They do open accessibility to people who otherwise wouldn’t go out there, so that has been a positive,” Tucker said. “But it has led to some congestion on the carriage roads, and I think that’s especially a concern to walkers out there.”
Independent of the congestion, locals worry it may take a tragedy before the park addresses the safety concerns that come from the surge of e-bikes in Acadia.
“My biggest thing is that someone is going to get seriously hurt,” Gabbard said. “I would hate for it to take [that] for somebody to make some sort of change with what’s going on in the park.

title: Skowhegan pastor says shelter completed court-mandated move
text:
SKOWHEGAN, Maine (WABI) -A Skowhegan pastor says his shelter has already completed a court-mandated move of 42 residents after the town said the facility failed to meet code requirements.
In September, Trinity Evangelical Free Church in Skowhegan was given until Oct. 17 to relocate residents of Shelters by Jesus after the facility failed to meet fire suppression system and monitored alarm system requirements.
Pastor Richard Berry said residents of Shelters by Jesus have been moved to what was originally the men’s shelter as renovations to the church and shelter occur, with women housed upstairs and men downstairs.
Skowhegan Town Manager Aaron Miller said the town plans to follow up with the church to confirm the move by the Oct. 17 deadline.

title: Legendary coach, Hall-of-Famer Mike Ditka dies at age 86
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Mike Ditka, who personified the toughness and grit of Chicago in a Hall of Fame career as a player and coach of the Bears and the leader of arguably the most dominant team in NFL history, has died. He was 86.
Ditka’s family announced the death on Friday in a statement.
“It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka,” the family said. “While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears’ Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever.”
Nicknamed “Iron Mike” as a player, Ditka helped revolutionize the tight end position, then moved to the sidelines and took over as Chicago’s coach. His 1985 team featured one of the game’s most dominant defenses ever. It also had enough outsized personalities to record a rap video, “The Super Bowl Shuffle,” and back up their boasting in the championship game three months later.
He was arguably the NFL’s most recognizable — and imitated — personality during his time as Chicago’s coach with his thick but neatly groomed mustache and sweater vest with “BEARS” emblazoned across the chest. The iconic look is still mimicked by fans at Bears games decades later. That along with his fiery, red-faced sideline tantrums inspired the popular “Da Bears” skit on “Saturday Night Live” during the 1980s.
After retiring as a coach, Ditka became a restaurateur, pitchman and TV personality, as well as a forceful advocate for improved medical and retirement benefits for former players.
Ditka was tough and gruff, the quintessential Chicago Bear. He did everything from order off the menu to knock defensive backs on their butts with a growl. His adopted hometown reveled in every minute.
Still revered as “Da Coach” and ringmaster of the 1985 Bears, one of the most dominant and perhaps the zaniest Super Bowl-winning team in league history. Ditka was enshrined in the College and Pro Football Halls of Fame and the Bears said during a ceremony in 2013 that his “No. 89” jersey will be the last one retired by the team.
“Player. Coach. Legend,” the Bears wrote in a tribute on social media. “Mike Ditka embodied the spirit of Chicago and will be deeply missed.”
He was born in Carnegie, Pennsylvania, the son of a welder who changed the family name from Dyczko. He grew up in nearby Aliquippa, close to the coal-mining and steel-manufacturing plants that dotted the western part of the state, a big, talented, three-sport athlete and All-American at Pitt whose bruising style made his first nickname, “Iron Mike,” a good fit.
Selected fifth overall by flinty Chicago owner George Halas in the 1961 draft, Ditka went on to Rookie of the Year honors, multiple Pro Bowl trips and the 1963 NFL Championship. In the bargain, he and Baltimore’s John Mackey changed the tight end position and offensive schemes forever. He was a battering ram of a blocker, but Ditka was just as likely to catch a short pass and pinball through an entire secondary or outrace a lone safety on a deep touchdown throw.
He left Chicago in 1966, playing briefly for Philadelphia and Dallas. He moved to the sideline in 1973 as an assistant to the revered Tom Landry and stayed with the Cowboys for eight seasons, before returning to a hero’s welcome in Chicago as head coach in 1982.
Ditka’s return to the Bears lasted 10 tumultuous years, including five straight NFC Central titles, the Super Bowl win, a DUI conviction, a heart attack, a long-running feud with defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan and, finally, a new nickname — “Da Coach.”
To Hall of Fame linebacker Mike Singletary, the seeds of what was to come were planted in Ditka’s first meeting with the team. He laid out his vision, saying Chicago would be in the Super Bowl in three years — and many of the players in the room would not be around for it.
“When I first heard him when he walked in the room, to me Coach Ditka had the opportunity to be the greatest coach of all time because he had the fire,” Singletary said at the Bears’ 100th anniversary celebration in June 2019. “I don’t know George Halas coached. But I can imagine that the fire and intensity and passion that Coach Ditka exuded that first day set the tone for exactly what he said: ‘Three years from now, we’re going to be in the Super Bowl.’ And that was 1982. In ’85, we were there and it was because of that vision.”
The public beefs with Ryan mirrored the behind-the-scenes battles that Ditka waged trying to contain a team bristling with outsized personalities.
“It was more than a team,” Ditka once said. “It was a team of characters that had character that played for a crazy man, who let him be crazy and had fun doing it and don’t apologize for it ever. I wouldn’t want to be one of these suits walking around on the sideline today.
“I have no desire to be that. I was what I was and they were what they were and, damn, it was fun.”
It wasn’t until two dozen players recorded “The Super Bowl Shuffle” — an audacious rap-styled video released three months ahead of the 1986 title game — that the rest of the football world wondered whether Ditka was losing his grip.
His players never did.
“We call him ‘Sybil’ after that girl in the movie,” quarterback Jim McMahon once explained. “You know, the one that had all those personalities. Mike will be calm one minute, then throw a clipboard the next. People don’t understand that, but we do.”
The Bears demolished the New England Patriots 46-10 in the Super Bowl, but Ditka often said he regretted having McMahon and defensive tackle William “The Refrigerator” Perry run for touchdowns instead of Walter Payton, Chicago’s loyal and long-suffering running back.
Ryan departed for a head coaching job in Philadelphia soon after. While the Bears continued to be a contender for most of the next five years, a 5-11 season prompted Ditka’s departure in 1992.
After a five-year absence, he returned to coaching with the New Orleans Saints, but failed to revive the franchise. His tenure with the team might be best remembered for the trade before the 1999 NFL draft when he dealt a package of eight draft picks — including each one the Saints had that year and two of its first three selections in 2000 — to Washington to move up from 12th overall to No. 5 so New Orleans could select running back Ricky Williams.
After a miserable 1999 season ended with a 3-13 record — Ditka’s worst as either a player or coach — he left the sidelines for good.
His face and demeanor were so familiar by then that a second act became an easy segue. Ditka began building a stable of restaurants and appeared as himself in TV sitcoms from “Cheers” to “Third Rock from the Sun,” as well as shows such as “L.A. Law.”
He also stayed close to the game as an NFL analyst and game-day show personality at ESPN. Ditka’s high-profile status also made him an effective advocate to secure improved health and retirement benefits for former players.
His name also circulated for years in Illinois political circles. Though he never ran for office, Ditka described himself as a staunch conservative and was mentioned several times as a possible Republican candidate, including a congressional race against then state Rep. Barack Obama for the U.S. Senate.

title: “It looks like a car. Then it drives into the lake.”
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Classic Amphicars — vehicles that drive on land and “swim” in water — gathered at Put-in-Bay, Ohio for a club meetup.
Built in Germany between 1961 and 1968, the rare cars require both their land and water drive systems working in sync, making a fully functional model a genuine feat.
Owners say the amphibious cars steal the show at any car event, drawing bigger crowds than Lamborghinis or Mustangs.

title: 48th Annual New England Auto Auction brings record-setting Kissel to Owls Head Transportation Museum
text:
OWLS HEAD — The 48th Annual New England Auto Auction brought four days of collector activity to the Owls Head Transportation Museum this August, with two historic vehicles now making an even more lasting impact on the Museum and its visitors.
The centerpiece of this year’s auction was the rare 1922 Kissel 6-45 Speedster, known as the “Gold Bug” which sold for $244,750, believed to be the highest sale price recorded for this vehicle in history. One of an estimated 35 surviving Gold Bugs, the Kissel drew significant interest from bidders participating in person, by phone and online.
Following the auction, the buyer made the decision to loan the Kissel to the Owls Head Transportation Museum, allowing visitors to experience this exceptional piece of automotive history as part of the Museum’s collection. The vehicle will provide an opportunity for visitors to see one of the most distinctive American automobiles of the Jazz Age in person while supporting the Museum’s mission to preserve and share transportation history.
Another significant addition came from a 1924 Dodge Brothers Series 116 Touring Car, which was sold to benefit individuals and families affected by the May 2026 Robbins Lumber fire in Searsmont. The vehicle sold for $6,600, with proceeds directed to the Robbins Lumber Relief Fund through the Town of Searsmont. Following the sale, the new owner chose to donate the Dodge back to the Owls Head Transportation Museum, making this historic vehicle one of the museum’s ride automobiles.
The four-day auction event welcomed nearly 2,000 visitors and included 2 Preview Days, the community-focused Rev It Up Party, and two days of auction activity. In total, 214 vehicles crossed the block, with 189 finding new owners, representing an approximately 88% sell-through rate.
As one of OHTM’s largest fundraisers, the New England Auto Auction helps support the Museum’s year-round work preserving and operating its collection while providing educational programs, hands-on experiences and community events.
The Museum thanks the consignors, bidders, volunteers, sponsors and visitors who made the 48th Annual New England Auto Auction possible and helped create a lasting legacy for these historic vehicles.
Owls Head Transportation Museum is a nonprofit educational organization dedicated to preserving, operating and sharing the history of transportation through its collection, educational programming, demonstrations and hands-on experiences.

title: Obituary: James R. Hoare
text:
WEST BATH – James Hoare, of Meetinghouse Lane, died peacefully at home Sept. 17, 2026.
Born in Boston, Mass. in 1948 to James and Mary (Walsh) Hoare formerly of Galway, Ireland, he graduated from St. Sebastian’s, attended Harvard College, and traveled extensively in Brazil and southern Africa before starting a family with Sarah Bean in Gloucester, Mass.
After moving to Maine in 1974 and completing architectural studies, James began his career designing homes and commercial buildings across the Midcoast region. A thoughtful communicator, he encouraged collaborative relationships with clients and builders based on mutual understanding. He formed lasting bonds of friendship with so many across the construction community which he valued greatly.
Divorced in 1982, he raised daughter, Molly, jointly. In 1991, James married Jane McGuire, becoming a devoted stepfather to Maura. Happiest at home with his family about him, he loved them all.
A voracious reader who treasured music and art, writing and
drawing, he was also expert at keeping his dogs happy, boon companions walking together in all weather.
James is survived by his wife Jane; daughters Molly Hoare (Andy Estes) and Maura McGuire-Bruce; grandchild, Rowan (Noah) Roth, grandchildren François and Augustine Letendre, their father Tyler Warnke.
He was predeceased by brothers Paul and John.
A service honoring James will be held Saturday 1 p.m., Oct. 24, at Popham Chapel, 969 Popham Rd., Phippsburg, followed by a gathering at the Chapel House.
Condolences may be made online at http://www.directcremationofmaine.com.
Donations may be made to
American Diabetes Association or West Bath Fire Department

title: Fact-checking the 2nd debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson
text:
For the second time in three days and with two more debates to go next week, Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson faced off Thursday over abortion, the Iran war, tariffs, energy and their track records in Washington and Augusta.
The five-term incumbent again touted her experience and legislative wins while critiquing Jackson’s record and blasting several of his statements as false. The former Maine Senate president continued to press Collins on illegal donations her PAC received during her 2020 bid that led to an FBI investigation, while seeking to tie her to President Donald Trump.
Here are a few fact-checks as the candidates prepare for debates Tuesday hosted by WABI and WAGM, and Thursday by News Center Maine, Portland Press Herald and Maine Public. The last debate will be held with a live audience at Gracie Theater in Bangor.
‘Making money’ off Iran war
Jackson accused Collins and her husband, former lobbyist Tom Daffron, of profiting from the war in Iran. He suggested the senator and others weren’t doing more to stop the unpopular conflict because they were making money off it.
Collins immediately called the claim “absolutely outrageous,” demanding an apology.
A liberal outlet promoted by the Maine Democrats in September highlighted her husband’s stock holdings, including in Boeing and RTX stock. Both companies make weapons used in the war, but the report did not show the couple making money because of her votes.
RTX is down 10% since the war began, and Boeing has been sluggish. The war helps bring Boeing federal contracts, but it disrupts supply chains.
Collins initially voted against nine war powers resolutions, but since the conflict hit the 60-day deadline for congressional approval under the War Powers Act, she joined Democrats five times in voting to end the war.
The couple’s assets total between $4 million and $10 million, mostly in mutual funds and stocks. Collins’ team has said a third-party adviser manages her husband’s investments and no individual stocks had been bought or sold from his account in more than three years.
‘Big Tobacco’ and a Jackson deflection
Seeking to contrast with Jackson and a PAC he previously led while in the State Legislature, Collins said she has “never accepted any donations from Big Tobacco. Troy has.” But her 2020 campaign took almost $12,000 from tobacco industry PACs and employees, according to OpenSecrets. That put her at 18th among senators during the cycle.
Like many Democrats, Jackson has rejected corporate PAC money during his campaign. Looking to push back on Jackson’s pledges of transparency and critique on her wealthy donors, Collins has put the spotlight on a recent Washington Post analysis finding that the Maine Senate’s Democratic campaign arm under Jackson’s leadership took money from tobacco, gambling and pharmaceutical companies.
Jackson’s explanation on the matter Thursday changed from what he told reporters in August, when he said he was one of “a number of people that made those decisions, what we took and what we didn’t.”
Jackson said during the debate that he was not the final decider on which donors the committee took money from. However, he was listed as the group’s principal officer from 2017 to 2024.
Jackson also said in August that the group “didn’t take pharma money.” But state campaign finance reports show the PAC received thousands of dollars from drug companies, including Merck and Johnson & Johnson. The group also received $12,000 from tobacco giant Altria, $3,000 from DraftKings and more than $4,000 from FanDuel.
Collins ignores part of ProPublica report
Collins said again Thursday that allegations of a pay-to-play scheme reported by ProPublica involving her or her staff were false and had been settled under former President Joe Biden.
“These allegations are absolutely false, and they’ve been proven false,” Collins said. “But Troy and [Senate Minority Leader] Chuck Schumer keep running false ads to try to convince you otherwise.”
That doesn’t address the central point of ProPublica’s piece. By late 2024, agents had asked supervisors to OK a broader bribery investigation that could have involved Collins and other lawmakers, the outlet reported.
Collins and campaign manager Steve Abbott note Kao’s corruption claims came after he pleaded guilty in 2022 to the illegal donations and fraud tied to a pandemic loan program. Abbott said investigators never came back to Collins’ team after that.
“We did not hear a word in 2024 or 2025,” Abbott said.

title: NFL Week 5 schedule, prediction and more
text:
NFL Week 5 schedule, prediction and more
NFL Week 5 schedule, prediction and more
A bye week comes for some teams for the first time in the 2026 NFL season. There are still plenty of action-packed matchups ahead in Week 5. The Carolina Panthers and Kansas City Chiefs both get an early rest, while 30 other teams are in play this week.
Video above: Eagles offensive lineman Lane Johnson retires after 14 seasons
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the Miami Dolphins, Los Angeles Chargers, Houston Texans and Tennessee Titans are all still searching for their first win. The Texans and Titans face off this week, so at least one team is guaranteed to be off the skid.
The Minnesota Vikings and San Francisco 49ers are the only two unbeaten teams left.
Here's a look at what's ahead this week, with predictions by Matthew Peaslee of the Hearst National Team. Peaslee went 8-8 in his Week 4 predictions and sits at 37-27 on the year.
All game times are in Eastern Standard Time.
Thursday, Oct. 8
Tampa Bay Buccaneers (0-4) vs. Dallas Cowboys (2-2), 8:15 p.m.
The Cowboys almost blew the game last week against Dallas and they can't let that affect them this week. CeeDee Lamb should have a big game if Dak Prescott can effectively get him the ball and he will extend his league-leading receiving yards total to well over 500 yards after a big win.
Prediction: Cowboys 28, Buccaneers 13
Sunday, Oct. 11
Philadelphia Eagles (2-2) vs. Jacksonville Jaguars (3-1), 9:30 a.m.
The Jaguars may not be America's team, but they could be considered Europe's team. This is the 15th time Jacksonville will play an overseas contest and it enters this contest with the Eagles at 7-7 in international games. The Jaguars can record a winning record overall when Trevor Lawrence rolls and the defense stiffles the Eagles, who haven't been as dominant on the ground this season. If the Jacksonville defense can force at least two turnovers, this one won't even be close.
Prediction: Jaguars 38, Eagles 24
Cincinnati Bengals (2-2) vs. Miami Dolphins (0-4), 1 p.m.
The Bengals didn't think they'd be in this position, faltering in their last two games, so a meeting with the winless Dolphins couldn't have come at a better time for Joe Burrow's crew. Could it be a trap game, though? Not with the way Burrow played last week, throwing for 428 yards with a throwing and running touchdown. The Miami defense can't stop him as Burrow is climbing up the passing leaderboard this year, currently ranking fifth in the NFL with 1,171 yards.
Prediction: Bengals 28, Dolphins 21
Las Vegas Raiders (3-1) vs. New England Patriots (2-2), 1 p.m.
The Raiders lived up to the hype last week, but just couldn't hang on in the end against the Chiefs. Another test comes this week to prove if they're for real. The Patriots, meanwhile, came on strong in the final quarter to earn an exciting win against the Bills. The Las Vegas offense, led by Kirk Cousins, is stronger than the New England offense, led by Drake Maye. While this won't be a high-scoring affair, the home crowd lifts the Patriots above .500.
Prediction: Patriots 24, Raiders 23
Minnesota Vikings (4-0) vs. New Orleans Saints (1-3), 1 p.m.
The reason why the Vikings are 4-0 is because of an upstart defense that leads the league with 16 sacks. The unit only allows 289.3 yards and just over 12 points per game and the Saints don't have the offensive firepower to match up well against them. However, the Minnesota offense has been dealing with injuries. The Vikings won't go undefeated this season, but they can still put together a few more wins before that first loss comes down.
Prediction: Vikings 17, Saints 10
Cleveland Browns (3-1) vs. New York Jets (1-3), 1 p.m.
There may not be two more tortured fanbases in the NFL. In 2026, the Browns feel like they're on top of the world while the Jets are still the Jets. New York is actually favored in this one, but the Cleveland momentum should override the home crowd in MetLife Stadium. The Browns defense has been strong even without Myles Garrett because Mason Graham has stepped up and has totaled four sacks through the first four weeks.
Prediction: Browns 38, Jets 33
Indianapolis Colts (2-2) vs. Pittsburgh Steelers (2-2), 1 p.m.
The Colts' offense is steady and efficient while the Steelers' offense is, at times, chaotic. Jonathan Taylor anchors a consistent rushing attack and Daniel Jones does a good jobs spreading things around to his talented receivers. Aaron Rodgers, meanwhile, has been inconsistent and not always on the same page as his coaching staff. He's been sacked 13 times and has thrown four interceptions. If Jaylen Warren can match the output of his counterpart in Taylor, it will be a close game. Pittsburgh, though, lost a close one last week and will need to shake that off at home.
Prediction: Steelers 23, Colts 21
Houston Texans (0-4) vs. Tennessee Titans (0-4), 1 p.m.
Something has to give, and one team will have to win this game. If the Texans can play as well as they did against the Cowboys last week and lose, they can play that well against the Titans and win. Will Anderson Jr. leads a decent Houston defense, which is third in the NFL in sacks with 14 as a team. C.J. Stroud is definitely the heart and soul of this team and can set the tone against a Titans defense, which isn't as bad as the winless record may suggest.
Prediction: Texans 33, Titans 27
New York Giants (3-1) vs. Washington Commanders (1-3), 1 p.m.
Star quarterback Jayden Daniels is likely to return for the Commanders after sustaining an elbow injury in Week 2. title: Crystal Hefner Wants Jessica Biel to Know the Truth About 'Playmates'
text:
Hugh Hefner’s Widow Crystal Urges Jessica Biel to Rethink Her Role in ‘Playmates’
Crystal Hefner has a message for Jessica Biel about her upcoming movie Playmates — and she's asking the actress to reconsider her role.
The 40-year-old widow of Playboy founder Hugh Hefner took to Instagram on Thursday (Oct. 8) to address Biel, 44, after the actress was cast in the film as a fictionalized version of Hugh's wife.
Crystal's warning comes as Hollywood revisits the Playboy world, which she says was far different from the glamorous image often portrayed onscreen.
Crystal Hefner Calls Out Jessica Biel
Please reconsider playing Hugh Hefner's 'wife' if this film intends to romanticize him or the Playboy world. was actually his wife, and I experienced sexual, emotional, financial and physical abuse in this relationship.
READ MORE: Hugh Hefner Widow Crystal Says Playboy Mogul Was Bad at Sex, Was ‘Relieved’ When It Was Over
She also pointed to allegations from other women involving rape, coercion, drugging and exploitation, along with what she described as "deeply troubling concerns" allegedly involving minors.
"I hope everyone involved in this film takes the time to listen to the women who lived it before helping Hollywood turn it back into nostalgia," Crystal concluded.
What Is 'Playmates' About?
Written and directed by Lorraine Nicholson, Playmates also stars Lily-Rose Depp, Bill Pullman and Indiana Elle. Pullman will portray Hugh, who died in 2017 at age 91.

title: Maine hockey takes step toward ‘big boy hockey’ in loss to Quinnipiac
text:
ORONO — The video, played approximately five minutes before the start of the University of Maine men’s hockey home opener Friday night, gave the Alfond Arena crowd a new cheer.
The video showed Quinnipiac coach Rand Pecknold, at a press conference earlier this week, describing what it’s like to play at Alfond. This is big boy hockey, he said.
It was the highest compliment Pecknold, whose Bobcats have numerous NCAA tournaments and a national title to their credit, could pay the Black Bears and their fans. Seconds after the puck dropped to start the game, the students filling the balcony above Quinnipiac goalie Christian Kirsch adopted the saying as their own.
“Big boy hockey!” they cheered. “Big boy hockey!”
Quinnipiac took a 2-1 win. There are no moral victories, but the Black Bears and their fans can take from the game that playing hard, gritty hockey will keep them in more games than not.
The Black Bears definitely played big boy hockey Friday. Getting that to translate into wins, with a little more offense, is the next step.
“That’s going to be the challenge for our guys this year,” Maine coach Ben Barr said. “Can we stay at it and stay at it, keep staying at it, and eventually find a little break as far as putting the puck in the net.”
Take the first period, for example. Maine controlled play for much of those first 20 minutes. The Black Bears outshot the Bobcats by a wide margin, 18-5.
Maine still went into the first intermission down 2-1.
A power-play goal by Lee Parks just 2:39 into the game staked the Black Bears to a 1-0 lead, but it lasted barely two minutes. The Bobcats took the lead for good midway through the first period when Ethan Wyttenbach scored on a breakaway.
One of the top scorers in the nation last season, Wyttenbach loitered in the neutral zone like he was waiting for an Uber, and the Black Bears lost track of him. When he got the outlet pass from defenseman Jan Golicic, Wyttenbach was able to charge at Maine goalie Albin Boija without resistance and gave his team the lead.
It’s a spooky thing, when 5,000 people go quiet. Not silent, that’s different. Silent serves a purpose. Quiet is more disconcerting than silence. Quiet comes when there’s something to say but nobody wants to say it. Nothing but nervous coughs, mumbles and murmurs instead of cheers.
That’s what happened in Alfond Arena in the aftermath of Wyttenbach’s goal. That’s the big boy hockey to which Pecknold referred.
Maine captain Owen Fowler was right when he said that’s the kind of hockey the Black Bears played for most of the game. He was right when he said they just missed that finishing touch. Quinnipiac is ranked No. 6 in the latest USCHO.com poll and scored 16 goals in a pair of wins last weekend, including 10 against New Hampshire. Holding the Bobcats to two is an accomplishment, but really only if you score three.
“Around the net, we have to bear down. I think that’s the biggest focus right now,” Fowler said.
The Black Bears were physical, and Fowler thought they wore down the Bobcats.
“If you watched that game, I think they didn’t want to go back on pucks a lot of the time,” he said. “I think we just need to bring that again (Saturday).”
A second-period breakaway by Maine’s Judah Makway ended with a shot over the crossbar. A 5-on-3 power play in the third ended without the equalizing goal. These are the things Maine needs to fix as the season progresses. The effort is there, Barr said, and so is the talent. Now comes the mental piece.
“We’ll do it all over again tomorrow night. That’s the awesome part,” Barr said.
When the Black Bears start seeing the hard work translate to goals, that’s when you’ll know they’re really playing the kind of hockey Pecknold warned his team about.

title: Aging Untold: Why more LGBTQ+ older adults are living openly
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we explore the courage, newfound freedom and unique challenges of coming out later in life.
Plus, find out how opting for out-of-pocket medical care works and why paying cash on purpose makes sense for some patients.
We also introduce an 86-year-old volunteer using his product-design background to repair and recycle electronics for a local charity.
Some older adults in the LGBTQ+ community find that age brings the courage and confidence to come out later in life.
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said some factors that lead people to come out later in life could include the death of those who would not have accepted the relationship or a loved one who initially wasn’t able to accept it changing their mind.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said there is a physical toll that comes with hiding one’s identity for years.
Some doctors are moving away from traditional insurance models. The shift can mean paying out of pocket, and it isn’t the right fit for everyone.
Two of the options are concierge medicine and direct primary care.
Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said with concierge medicine, you have your own doctor and you pay privately for that. Direct primary care is concierge with a membership organization, but the doctor also takes insurance.
Dr. Rogers said her own path moved from traditional obstetrics and gynecology into an integrative approach before she transitioned fully into functional medicine.
Cradduck brought up affordability and said a lot of people who would love to be healthier cannot afford out-of-pocket care.
Scammers have posed as law enforcement to scare victims into handing over personal information, money or both.
An Arizona woman is sharing her story of losing thousands in a jury-duty scam when it happened to her.
“It sounds so realistic,” said Kristine, who is being identified only by her first name.
She is explaining how it happened in hopes it will prevent others from becoming victims.
Marshall Johnson is 86 years old and helps Habitat for Humanity by taking apart donated electronics and appliances for recycling.
He worked as a product designer for appliance companies, including Black & Decker and Home Depot. His designs are on display at the Hagley Museum and Library in Wilmington, Delaware.
“There’s so many wonderful people and products, and that’s the fun I get here is seeing what comes in,” Johnson said.
Learn more about Marshall and the recycling program, which raises money for Habitat for Humanity and reduces waste at local landfills.

title: Key money lessons parents should teach teens before college
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — For a young adult stepping into college or a first job, financial decisions can feel overwhelming. Teresa Murray, a consumer watchdog with US PIRG, said that makes financial planning for teens and young adults especially important.
“We’re kind of assuming here that once somebody’s in high school or going off to college, that their parents have already taught them a little bit about needs versus wants and being able to budget your spending, not blowing your allowance every week,” Murray said. “But it’s always important for young adults, high schoolers going off to college, to be able to figure out needs versus wants and avoid the impulse spending.”
One key lesson, Murray said, is helping young adults understand how credit works and how long it follows them.
“You need to explain to them, like, hey, your credit history lives with you for a while,” Murray said. “If you have a lousy credit score, once you graduate from college, you’re going to have difficulty renting an apartment no matter how good of a job you have, without having a co-signer.”
Murray said another overlooked lesson is the connection between sharing too much personal information online and financial risk.
“They have open accounts, open profiles with Facebook or Instagram or whatever, and they’re spraying it all over the place,” Murray said. “It’s about protecting your personal information, which could end up hurting you financially, but it’s also about protecting your safety and the safety of those around you.”
Murray said simply keeping track of spending, even informally, helps young adults understand how quickly costs add up.
“Even if they’re using cash, they should just jot it down,” Murray said. “Just have a note on your phone that you keep track of your expenses. Round them off — you don’t have to have it exactly to the penny. And then you look back and you’re like, ‘Oh, dang, I had this and I had this.’ It adds up quickly.”
Budgeting, credit, privacy and tracking spending are small habits that can pay off for years to come, according to Murray.
The FDIC also offers tips for parents on its website, including information on youth banking programs — partnerships between schools and banks that allow students to open a real savings account and begin building good money habits while still in the classroom.

title: Maine military moms celebrate new chapter of Blue Star Mothers of America
text:
When Maine mothers of military personnel saw in March that war in Iran was escalating, they bonded together to organize a statewide support network for active duty service members, military mothers, families and veterans.
Rosie Vanadestine of Skowhegan and Jane Thorndike of Avon, who both have sons who are gunnery sergeants in the U.S. Marines, along with 10 other military mothers, worked to establish a Maine chapter of the Blue Star Mothers of America.
“It has been a long road getting over the finish line that is for sure,” Vanadestine, president of the chapter, wrote in an email Wednesday. “This group of women are amazing. We have become so important to each other and have become the first outreach when any of us are struggling. The more I learn and the more organizations we are connecting to, the more excited I am about what (Blue Star Mothers of America) ME3 will accomplish in service of our active military, our veterans and all the military families here in Maine.”
The formation of the Maine chapter was inspired by Vanadestine when her child entered military service. After discovering there was no active chapter in the state, she started outreach, which quickly gained momentum.
With the official installation ceremony completed at the national level, a local celebratory event is planned for Oct. 25 in Augusta.
Thorndike is happy the chapter is finally established. “Blue Star Mothers is a way for us ‘moms’/stepmoms/grandmothers or even other family members to support one another and to give back to our veterans and service members. ‘Once a mom, always a mom,’” Thorndike wrote in a message.
Her son, Gunnery Sgt. Barry Thorndike II, who was deployed on the USS Abraham Lincoln for over seven months in the Middle East, got off the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier when it arrived in San Diego on Thursday. He will be stationed there for the next two years.
“Both my boys will stand on USA soil again. I thank God and that hardworking USS Abraham Lincoln crew for getting him back to us,” Thorndike wrote Thursday.
Thorndike’s husband and sister-in-law were on the way to see him Wednesday. Thorndike stayed behind because of work and other obligations.
“Military families should never have to walk this journey alone. Our mission is to support troops, veterans, military families, and the families of fallen heroes while supporting one another through every stage of military life,” Vanadestine wrote.
Blue Star Mothers of America is a national nonprofit organization founded in 1942 and chartered by Congress in 1960. With more than 6,000 members across 200 chapters nationwide, the organization provides support, service, and advocacy for military communities across the country.
Leaders of the Maine chapter plan to provide peer support for military families, send care packages to deployed service members, assist veterans, support Gold Star families, participate in community service projects, and partner with organizations serving Maine’s military and veteran communities.
Full membership is open to mothers, stepmothers, grandmothers, foster mothers, and female legal guardians of active-duty service members, National Guard members, Reservists, veterans, and fallen service members. Associate membership is available for all other family members and individuals seeking opportunities to support the organization’s mission through volunteer service and community involvement.
Anyone wanting more information can contact Vanadestine by email at [email protected] or by phone at 207-576-2960.
The celebratory event for the new Maine chapter is planned for 2 p.m. Oct. 25 at VFW Post 886 at 509 Leighton Road in Augusta. It is intended to bring together military families, veteran organizations, elected officials, community leaders and members of the public to celebrate the milestone and formally launch the new Maine chapter.
The distinguished guest speaker is Maj. Gen. Diane L. Dunn, who serves as the 41st adjutant general of the Maine National Guard and commissioner of the Department of Defense, Veterans and Emergency Management. Light refreshments will follow.
Anyone interested in learning more about the Blue Star Mothers organization is invited to attend.

title: SUV crashes into Bonny Eagle school bus on Route 22 in Westbrook, police say

WESTBROOK, Maine (WABI) - Part of Route 22 in Westbrook was closed after an SUV crashed into a Bonny Eagle school bus Friday morning, according to police.
The Westbrook Police Department said that at about 9:30 a.m., an SUV crossed the center line of County Road (Route 22) and collided with the school bus.
A Maine’s Total Coverage photographer captured video of the crash scene, which shows the crash happened near Haven’s Candies.
Video from the scene shows the school bus sustained serious damage as a result of the collision, which sent the SUV off the road and into a ditch.
Police said there were about 12 children and some adult chaperones on the school bus at the time of the crash.
No one was seriously injured, according to police.
The area of County Road where the crash happened remained closed while both vehicles were removed from the scene. The Maine’s Total Coverage photographer who went to the scene captured video of the SUV being pulled out of the ditch by a tow truck.
The crash is being investigated by the Westbrook Police Department’s reconstruction team, which will be assisted by the Maine State Police, according to authorities.

title: Digging dangers: Why underground utility damage is on the rise
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - We rely on natural gas and electricity every day to heat and light our homes. But one mistake underground can turn an energy source into an instant threat.
In 2024, the country saw more than 83,000 reports of damage to gas and electrical lines. One in four of those damage reports were because people failed to call 811.
That number connects you to a free, national service designed to prevent damage to utility lines by marking where they are located. Calling 811 is required by law.
In January, Molly Krummenacher came home to find her hot water heater and dryer on fire, water spewing like a fountain after an excavator hit her electric line.
“It’s just sheer panic and disbelief,” she said.
AT&T was in the area to install fiber optic internet, but hired subcontractor USIC to mark the electric lines. Molly said there was no flag or marking for the electrical line.
The incident caused a surge that turned neutral wires into live wires, resulting in $20,000 in damage.
“It’s just a really frustrating and sad situation that innocent, you know, civilians get put in by big corporations,” Molly said.
An increase in damage
The incident is part of a growing trend. Common Ground Alliance data shows more than half a million reports of damage to underground utilities at dig sites in recent years.
In Missouri, more than 10,000 reports have been filed in recent years, with close to 6,500 in Illinois. The numbers are ticking up each year.
“Unfortunately, the data shows that the incident rate is increasing with the amount of construction that we’re seeing across the country,” said Sarah Magruder Lyle with the Common Ground Alliance.
The region has seen multiple home explosions in recent years linked to digging incidents, including blasts in O’Fallon, Jefferson County and Glendale. Some have been deadly.
A 5-year-old was killed outside Kansas City last year when his home exploded. His sister and father were badly hurt.
Magruder Lyle said infrastructure is constantly changing, with massive upgrades to the internet driving much of the digging activity.
“The amount of fiber that is being put in the ground right now, you know, all the other infrastructure pales in comparison,” she said.
Understanding what’s happening at dig sites requires looking underground. Burying utilities dates back to ancient times, but over time, more pipes and wires have been placed underground for water, sewage, electricity, internet and gas.
Knowing exactly where those utilities are underground is now a complex problem.
“It is changing constantly, and it’s changing quickly,” Magruder Lyle said.
Common Ground Alliance data shows many locate requests are late, missing or inaccurate, with blame shared by those locating the lines, those digging and people who try to find utilities in the first place.
“Not contacting 811 is a quarter of the incidents we see,” Magruder Lyle said.
Digging damage to underground utilities is preventable, she said.
Missouri strengthened its dig laws last year. New utility lines must now be buried with a detectable location device like tracer wire or locator tape. Magruder Lyle said electronic geo-location mapping technology is needed, too.
“All roads lead back to mapping,” she said.
When asked if more still needs to be done, she said: “Absolutely. We can always do better.”
To protect yourself, Magruder Lyle said, pay attention to dig notices, paint markings and flags.
“If you don’t see something, then say something. This is actually the opposite of what we hear. If you don’t see paint on the ground, it’s okay to ask,” she said.
Back in Ballwin, crews returned to digging one day after the fire.
“It feels like I have a second job,” Molly said.
She said she got the runaround on who was responsible until she mentioned she’d called the news station. Two hours later, she received a call from USIC.
The company has paid her insurance deductible. Still, Molly said she worries about future consequences.
“We could be dropped by our insurance for something we had absolutely no control of,” she said.
“It’s a really scary thought,” she said.
Molly said a neighbor’s home was also damaged by the electrical surge.
AT&T provided a statement:
“As we bring high-speed fiber internet to more communities, we strive to minimize disruption for residents. If any property damage occurs, please know that we take the concerns of those affected very seriously. In this case, our contractor has reached out to the homeowner and is working to resolve her concerns.”
USIC did not respond to a request for comment. The company is currently being sued by the Glendale homeowner whose home exploded in August 2025.
What the colored markings mean
If you’ve ever wonder what the colored markings in your yard or along the street mean, we reached out to an expert to explain.
Erik Phillips is vice president of operations for UtiliQuest, which helps to prevent damages to utility lines.
Phillips said red covers electrical lines, orange covers phone lines and yellow covers gas.
Blue markings are for water while green represents sewer and storm drains.
And experts are Common Ground Alliance say even if a contractor is doing the work, it’s your responsibility to call 811 before the digging starts.
Whether it’s a big construction project or planting shrubs, residents must call 811 before digging.

title: Obituary: Richard “Dick” Gray
text:
BRUNSWICK – Retired U.S. Navy Master Chief Richard “Dick” Gray passed away at home on Oct. 6, 2026, surrounded by his family.
Dick was born in Deblois, Maine Oct. 25, 1936, the eldest of Jennie and Clyde Gray’s five sons. He attended Calais High School and married Delia “Dee” right after returning from Navy Boot Camp. They were married 70 years.
Dick was predeceased by his parents; and brother, Ronald Gray.
He is survived by his wife, Delia; and his children, daughter, Cindy and husband Leon Dudley of Vassalboro, his son, Michael and wife Beverly Gray of Topsham, daughter, Jo Anne and husband Bruce Dempsey of Wayland, Mich., and daughter, Dianne Gray of Brunswick. He is survived by 10 grandchildren; and 11 great-grandchildren. He is also survived by three of his brothers, Robert, Royce “Jack” and Randy Gray.
Dick went into the Navy directly from high school, he spent 32 years in service to his country with tours around the world. Dick served in the U.S. Navy as a P-2 aircrewman and a P-3 Flight Engineer in VP squadrons 21, 45, 30, and 10, amassing over 20,000 flight hours. He then served as the maintenance master chief at VP-26. He retired in 1976 and spent five years as the service manager at Dow Motors in Ellsworth. He was then voluntarily recalled to active duty and spent 12 years as a command master chief at VP-23, NAS Sigonella, VP-11, NAS Brunswick, and VQ-2 in Rota Spain before retiring again from the Navy in 1992.
After retiring Dick served on the Ellsworth School Board for 20 years, was president of the Maine State School Board, worked as service manager at Darlings in Ellsworth and Northeast Ambulance.
Dick was the patriarch of the family, always with a helping hand, a quick wit and ready smile. He started his mechanical career taking apart everything he could reach as a child, including the kitchen appliances. He was an incredible husband, son, big brother, uncle, cousin, Father and Pop-Pop.
The family would like to thank CHANS Hospice staff for their exceptional care at the end of Dick’s life.
There will be no service. Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.
“Fair winds and following seas, shipmate, we have the watch, you stand relieved.”
In lieu of flowers, the family asks that donations be made to the Brunswick Naval Aviation Museum in Richard’s name.

title: Maine Sunday Telegram, Portland Press Herald and reporters receive top New England newspaper awards
text:
The Maine Sunday Telegram, Portland Press Herald and two reporters have been honored with top awards at the New England Newspaper & Press Association’s annual fall conference.
The 2026 New England Newspaper Awards were announced Friday at a summit in Sturbridge, Massachusetts, hosted by the New England Newspaper & Press Association. The organization is the professional trade organization for newspapers in Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont.
The Portland Press Herald won first place for New England Newspaper of the Year for large circulation weekday publications, and the Maine Sunday Telegram won first place for New England Newspaper of the Year for large circulation Sunday publications.
“The newspaper of the year awards are a testament to the hard work of our entire newsroom staff,” said Scott Monroe, managing editor of the Maine Trust for Local News, which owns the papers. “We’ve invested in quality community and state coverage, and these awards help demonstrate that commitment is paying off for our audience.”
The runners-up in the weekday category were The Providence Journal of Rhode Island and the Bangor Daily News. The runners-up in the Sunday category were The Sunday Republican of Springfield, Massachusetts, and The Berkshire Eagle of Pittsfield, Massachusetts.
The Telegram also won the Sunday Newspaper of the Year category last year.
In other awards announced at Friday’s summit, Press Herald education reporter Riley Board’s coverage of an abuse lawsuit against Bath’s Hyde School won a Publick Occurrences award that recognizes the best work that New England newspapers produce each year. Board’s coverage examined allegations of forced labor and emotional abuse at the nearly 60-year-old private boarding school in Bath.
Emily Duggan, an education reporter for the Sun Journal and Kennebec Journal/Morning Sentinel, was also selected to receive one of the association’s A-Mark Prizes for her parents’ rights groups reporting, which investigated how Maine school boards have been confronted with organized — and sometimes disruptive — efforts to remake local education policies. The A-Mark prizes honor outstanding investigative journalism that reveals hidden truths, holds power to account, or drives public awareness or reform.
“We’re thrilled that the enterprising coverage from Riley and Emily won such distinguished recognition among the best journalism in New England,” Monroe said.
Runners-up in Maine also receiving A-Mark prizes were Sawyer Loftus from the Bangor Daily News/ProPublica, for coverage of U.S. Department of Agriculture foreclosures, and Callie Ferguson and Josh Keefe from the Bangor Daily News/The Maine Monitor for coverage of a Limerick man’s violent arrest at the hands of Maine State Police.
Ferguson, deputy investigations editor for the Bangor Daily News, was also recognized with the New England Journalist of the Year award for her reporting on the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surge in Maine in January.

title: Why kidney stones hurt so much — and how to prevent them
text:
(Aging Untold) — A kidney stone may be tiny, but anyone who’s had one knows the pain can feel anything but small. Hydration, diet and certain medical conditions can all affect your risk.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, breaks down what causes kidney stones, why they hurt so much and what you can do to lower your risk.
What exactly is a kidney stone?
“They’re hard, mineral and salt deposits that form from the kidneys,” Rogers said. “They’re really small, but just think of anything that’s blocking something. So you’re actually providing a blockage in a small tube in your body. And that’s very, very painful, excruciating pain.”
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said she has had four kidney stones and nothing she has experienced has been as painful.
“This is like putting a jagged stone through a straw,” Cradduck said. “This took me to my knees.”
What causes them
Several factors contribute to kidney stone formation, Rogers said.
“What forms these kidney stones are a lot of times our genetics, family history, dehydration — diet plays a huge role too. And certain medications,” she said.
She explained that a natural compound in urine called citrate normally helps protect against stones. A reduction in it also reduces the protective factor.
“There actually is a natural compound in your urine that’s actually protective. It’s called citrate,” Rogers said. “And so anything that reduces that citrate reduces the ability of your urine to be able to form around those calcium stones and diminish those.”
She said high sodium intake can reduce citrate levels, while foods high in oxalate — such as spinach and beets — can raise uric acid levels and contribute to stone formation for some people.
“So you can eat a low oxalate diet if you’ve been having consistent stones,” Rogers said.
Infections can also contribute to forming stones.
“There’s some infections that will cause you to get a stone also with the bacteria,” Rogers added.
How to lower your risk
Rogers said boosting citrate levels naturally can help protect against stones.
“Anything that increases that citrate in your urine will be protective, like lime and lemon in your water. That helps,” she said. “Decrease the sodium. Animal fat, protein diets — those tend to be higher in uric acid. So you can try to minimize that.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke mentioned resources for people managing recurring stones.
“I was reading about the National Kidney Foundation being of help — the stonecollab.org can be of help,” she said. “So get some resources.”
(Find more resources below.)
O’Rourke added that climate matters too.
“Warmer climates — you’re dehydrated more, so drink more,” she said.
Doctors can also analyze a passed stone to determine its cause.
“What’s really important for people is when you do pass a stone, a lot of times we’ll take that stone to see what it really is made out of,” Rogers said. “That will help you to see why you got it in the first place.”
Resources/Links to learn more
Key takeaways
- Dehydration is a leading risk factor. Warmer climates and low fluid intake directly contribute to painful mineral deposits forming in the kidneys.
- Kidney stones are mineral and salt deposits that block small tubes in the body, causing severe pain.
- Genetics, family history, diet and certain medications all play a role in whether stones form.
- Citrate naturally protects against stones, and drinking water with lime or lemon can help boost it.
- High sodium, animal protein and high-oxalate foods like spinach and beets can increase risk for some people.
- Stress has also been linked to kidney stone development, alongside genetic factors.

title: ‘Get the heck out’: Officials make desperate plea to residents as Hurricane Isaias approaches
text:
(Gray News) - Officials issued a desperate plea as Hurricane Isaias approaches the Gulf Coast with possible “devastating” winds.
Florida Sen. Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible and warned in a social media post: “This is your LAST CHANCE to get prepared. Listen to local officials. If they say evacuate, then GET THE HECK OUT.”
Isaias has grown into a Category 3 storm, the first of an unusually quiet Atlantic season. The storm is expected to make landfall Friday night.
Forecasters warned of a significant storm surge, damaging winds, flooding and possibly even tornadoes before the storm loses steam as it moves inland and delivers strong winds and rain well north into Atlanta.
Isaias is expected to come ashore between Mobile Bay on the Alabama coast and the city of Destin in the Florida Panhandle — a low-lying coastal stretch known for powdery white sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks.
One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could be as high as 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters), according to the National Hurricane Center. Places most at risk include Florida’s Pensacola Beach and the Gulf Islands National Seashore.
Scott said he had spoken to President Donald Trump the day before and the president told him the Federal Emergency Management Agency would be there to respond following the storm.
