title: Wilton prepares for November election with new voting equipment
text:
WILTON — The Wilton Select Board unanimously approved closing the town office Nov. 3 to accommodate Election Day staffing needs as officials prepare to use new voting equipment and process absentee ballots.
The decision, made Oct. 6, will allow municipal employees to assist with election operations amid staffing shortages and vacancies. The closure applies only to this year’s election, rather than establishing a permanent policy.
“Due to our current staffing levels and vacancies, we have fewer personnel available,” Town Manager Maria Greeley said.
Greeley said closing the office would allow the town to make better use of available employees. Election staffing plans call for two ballot clerks during the day and four in the evening, in addition to town office employees assisting with polling operations.
Board members discussed closing the office for all future elections but ultimately approved the closure for this Nov. 3 only.
“I think we see how it goes and then make that decision in 2027,” Select Board member Nancy Allen said.
Officials also announced the arrival of new DS300 ballot tabulators and an ExpressVote machine ahead of the November election. Testing of the equipment is expected to be completed by Oct. 16.
Wilton plans to begin processing absentee ballots Oct. 29 at 9 a.m., using a second tabulator provided by the state.
Regular absentee voting closes Oct. 29, with special-circumstances applications beginning Oct. 30. Beginning Oct. 14, residents must register to vote in person through Election Day.
Property taxes are due Nov. 2, so the Election Day closure will not affect the payment deadline. Regular town office services will be unavailable Nov. 3, although code enforcement operations will continue.
The Select Board’s Nov. 3 meeting also was canceled, with its next regular meeting scheduled for Nov. 17.

title: Obituary: Ronald “Ron-Ronnie” E. Pelletier
text:
ORR’S ISLAND – Ronald “Ron-Ronnie” E. Pelletier, 88, passed away peacefully at his home Sept. 20, 2026. He had lived on Orr’s Island with his beloved wife, Irene, his high school sweetheart, for the past six years.
Ron was born in Topsham on April 16, 1938, to Emile and Leona Burbee Pelletier. He graduated from Edward Little High School in Auburn in 1957.
Ron served in the U.S. Army at Fort Belvoir, Virginia, from 1959 to 1965. His love of cars and trucks began at an early age and remained a lifelong passion, leading him to a career owning and operating transmission shops in Virginia, Florida, and Arkansas.
Ron was a deeply religious man of faith. His belief in the Lord was evident in the way he lived, and his generosity and willingness to help others touched the lives of many who knew him. Ron enjoyed buying peanuts from Virginia and making his famous peanut brittle, which he loved sharing with family, friends, and anyone who crossed his path.
Ron’s love for his family was unwavering and unconditional. He devoted his time, knowledge, and heart to those he held most dear.
He was predeceased by his parents; and siblings, Barbara, Gene, and Sherman Pelletier.
Ron is survived by his wife M. Irene David Thibault Pelletier; his children, Anne-Marie Pelletier, Jeffrey Pelletier, Lisa Brasch, and Mary Ann Moser; stepchildren, Lisa and husband Roger Aube, Paula Malin, D. Jayson and wife Hollie Crowell Thibault; brother, Maurice Pelletier of Kentucky; many grandchildren; and great-grandchildren. He also shared a special bond with his loving niece, Anna Pelletier Sliger, and his loving nephew, Maurice Pelletier Jr.
Visiting hours will be held Sunday, Oct. 18, from 12 p.m. to 2 p.m. at Daigle Funeral Home, 819 High St., Bath. Burial with military honors will follow at Orr’s Island Cemetery, followed by a gathering at the Bailey Island Library Hall, Bailey Island.
Condolences may be shared at http://www.DaigleFuneralHome.com.

title: Vance expresses doubts about Pentagon plan to livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution
text:
HEBRON, Ky. (AP) — Vice President JD Vance cast doubt Friday on whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December but told reporters that if it is livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.”
The Republican vice president said, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” when asked about the plans that the Pentagon confirmed Thursday. But Vance then tried to set aside the controversy over the plans for a public execution and said Hasan’s crimes should not be forgotten.
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting spree at the military base in 2009.
“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said.
“Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it,” he added.
Vance is a convert to the Catholic Church, which has long opposed capital punishment.
President Donald Trump had endorsed Hasan’s execution by firing squad during a Wednesday political event in Texas, suggesting “he deserves it.”
However, Trump was noncommittal when asked Friday whether he wanted the execution livestreamed. “Well, they’re making a determination about that,” Trump told reporters before traveling to a political event in Syracuse, New York.
But he again endorsed the firing squad as the method.
“He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad,” Trump told reporters. “I really don’t care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him.”
Trump did not answer when asked if he would watch a livestreamed execution.
Earlier Friday morning, the head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the U.S. government’s decision to livestream Hasan’s execution.
“It is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War’s decision to publicly livestream the execution,” Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the conference, said in a statement. He added that the decision was “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.”
Trump approved the execution by firing squad days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection late last month pushed Tennessee’s governor to halt further executions in that state this year.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
From Congress, lawmakers from both parties, Republicans and Democrats, widely condemned what they called the “gruesome” and “disgusting” decision to livestream the execution and implored the Pentagon to reverse course.
“Beyond disgusting,” said Sen. Thom Tillis, the Republican from North Carolina. “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”
The lawmakers said the authoritarian-style spectacle would send a message that runs deeply counter to American values and its system of justice, and risks putting U.S. service personnel and others overseas at risk of blowback.
Virginia Sen. Mark Warner, the top Democrat on the Intelligence Committee, condemned Hegseth’s plan, saying there’s a reason why “almost no countries in the world engage in this barbaric practice.”
Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska said how the U.S. carries out its system of justice matters, and urged the Pentagon “to reverse this gruesome decision.”
Republican Sen. John Curtis of Utah pointed to Rome’s bloody spectacles of the past said Hegseth’s plan to livestream the execution risks “feeding that appetite” for corrosive entertainment.
“I urge him to reconsider,” Curtis said.
___
This story has been corrected to show the military base’s name is Fort Hood, not Ford Hood.
___
Associated Press writers Will Weissert and Lisa Mascaro in Washington and Holly Meyer in Nashville, Tennessee, contributed to this report.

title: FBI arrests suspect in ShinyHunters hack of the bureau's jobs portal
text:
The FBI has arrested an accused co-conspirator of a criminal hacking group that said last month that it had breached the bureau’s jobs portal and obtained sensitive and personal data on nearly all employees of the law enforcement agency, Director Kash Patel said Friday.
The arrest was the latest targeting ShinyHunters, the group that claimed responsibility for the hack, as the FBI continues a global investigation into the breach of its network, which Patel said “occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor.”
“We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate,” Patel said in a statement.
The identity of the person arrested was not immediately clear, nor what charges they might face.
In a message taking responsibility for the hack and announcing the collection of sensitive information, ShinyHunters said it had taken action over false allegations contained in an FBI public advisory from May that described the organization as a “cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion.”
That advisory characterized ShinyHunters as “threat actors” who often “use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims,” commonly harass or threaten people and “may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”
Experts said that although the data that appeared to be compromised was the type of personal information that is routinely accessed during a breach, the hack nonetheless had alarming national security implications given that it could expose agents and their families to extortion, swatting and other harassment and because the identities of spouses were also said to have been obtained.

title: Jury finds man guilty of Calais teen's 1984 slaying
text:
If you or someone you know needs resources or support related to sexual violence, contact the Maine Coalition Against Sexual Assault’s 24/7 hotline at 800-871-7741.
The Bangor man accused of killing a Calais teen more than 40 years ago has been found guilty.
It took the jury only an hour to return a guilty verdict against 67-year-old Raymond Brown on Thursday, according to CBS affiliate WABI.
The trial began Monday.
On Aug. 25, 1984, Brown killed 18-year-old Linda Maxwell, whose naked body was found near a boat landing on the St. Croix River in Robbinston. Brown confessed to a cellmate earlier this year that he had suffocated Maxwell in a bog after she threatened to tell people that he raped her, prosecutors said this week.
He was among a group of people drinking with Maxwell the night of her death, and Brown, who was married at the time, had been seen flirting with her and had told others he wanted to have sex with her, according to prosecutors.
Brown offered to give Maxwell a ride home and later claimed to have dropped her off at a variety store.
Brown, who was living in Pembroke at the time of Maxwell’s death, had five criminal convictions prior to the slaying, including felony burglary and simple assault. In the mid-1980s, he twice was charged with gross sexual misconduct and also was accused once of rape, according to Bangor Daily News archives.
A gross sexual misconduct charge was dismissed in September 1984 after a grand jury declined to indict Brown. He was found not guilty in July of the same year on the rape allegation. A second gross sexual misconduct case against Brown was dismissed in September 1985.
Maxwell’s death was originally classified as a drowning, but police exhumed her embalmed body in 2024 for a limited autopsy.
Brown was arrested on a murder charge in May 2025 during a traffic stop in Bangor.
He will be sentenced at a later date, WABI reported.
Brown faces 25 years to life in prison.
BDN writer Sabrina Martin contributed to this report.

title: Concierge medicine vs. direct primary care: what to know before you pay out of pocket
text:
(Aging Untold) — Health care can get complicated fast, and not all doctors take the same approach. Some are moving away from traditional insurance models to spend more time with patients and focus on root causes and long-term wellness. That shift can mean paying out of pocket, and it isn’t the right fit for everyone.
What are the options?
Two of the options are concierge medicine and direct primary care.
“With concierge medicine, you have your own doctor and you pay privately for that,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said.
She said direct primary care is concierge. It’s a membership organization, but the doctor also takes insurance.
“The cost for concierge-type medicine is more expensive. Direct primary care is less expensive, but you’re a member and you have access to the doctor — 24/7 appointments, and your care is more on the preventive side,” O’Rourke said.
Why Dr. Rhea Rogers made the switch
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said her own path moved from traditional obstetrics and gynecology into an integrative approach before she transitioned fully into functional medicine.
“What made that decision for me is I always felt like patients need to have the options that are available to them, and I would give those to them,” Rogers said.
She said she would let them know which route insurance would cover and which it would not.
“It came to a point of do no wrong and do no harm,” Rogers said.
“When you start to understand what’s really happening at a cellular level with a person, I couldn’t help them with that model,” Rogers said. “So I had to go all the way where I could tell them, “This is what’s going on, and this is what I can do to help you.’”
Rogers said many patients come to her after they’ve exhausted the traditional system.
“When they’ve exhausted the traditional system and they’re sick, and they don’t feel well, and they’re like, ‘I don’t care what it costs, I need me back,’” she said.
Weighing cost and coverage
Rogers said the traditional model also includes some preventive care, such as screenings.
Concierge medicine and direct primary care are two types of out-of-pocket care, but O’Rourke said that there are other types as well.
“A lot of cosmetic (care) is out-of-pocket, even cosmetic dentistry,” Cradduck added. “Unfortunately, there are a lot of people who just can’t afford this, though they would love to be healthier and love to be able to come see you.”
Cradduck said affordability can become “the stepping stone” to accessing functional medicine and cellular-level care.
O’Rourke agreed affordability is tied to liquid income but said establishing a relationship with a physician can help even without a membership model.
“If you can’t afford concierge or direct primary care, establish that partnership with a physician as best as you can so that you can get some preventive care,” she said. “Just ask those types of questions.”
“I do think there’s an affordability issue for many people, but I also think many people could afford it, and it’s a mindset issue,” Ambrose said.
“What I tell people — I’m going to invest in myself. It’s an investment, just like you’d invest in anything else,” Rogers said.
Rogers compared traditional insurance to driving a major highway. “In functional medicine, I’m going to take the personalized scenic route,” she said.
“If I take the personalized scenic route, then I might have five or 10 more years of work and income versus having to medically retire,” Cradduck said.
She said that, over time, this approach could help people stay productive and earn more.
She added that some employers are beginning to take notice. “That’s why you’re seeing companies now start to employ that functional medicine model, because they see the difference in their workers,” she said.
Key takeaways
- Concierge medicine means a private doctor you pay for directly. Direct primary care is a membership model where the doctor may still accept insurance.
- Costs vary by model. Direct primary care memberships can start at around $50 a month and go up, while concierge memberships start around $200 a month and up.
- Pros include 24/7 access. Members may get more time with their doctor, less waiting, same-day appointments and direct phone access.
- Cons include added expense. Out-of-pocket costs apply, and with some memberships, separate insurance coverage is still needed.

title: Bonny Eagle school bus involved in Westbrook crash
text:
SUV crashes into Bonny Eagle school bus on Route 22 in Westbrook, police say
Part of Route 22 in Westbrook was closed after an SUV crashed into a Bonny Eagle school bus Friday morning, according to police.
The Westbrook Police Department said that at about 9:30 a.m., an SUV crossed the center line of County Road (Route 22) and collided with the school bus.
A Maine's Total Coverage photographer captured video of the crash scene, which shows the crash happened near Haven's Candies.
Video from the scene shows the school bus sustained serious damage as a result of the collision, which sent the SUV off the road and into a ditch.
Police said there were about 12 children and some adult chaperones on the school bus at the time of the crash.
No one was seriously injured, according to police.
The area of County Road where the crash happened remained closed while both vehicles were removed from the scene. The Maine's Total Coverage photographer who went to the scene captured video of the SUV being pulled out of the ditch by a tow truck.
The crash is being investigated by the Westbrook Police Department's reconstruction team, which will be assisted by the Maine State Police, according to authorities.

title: ‘Pretty Little Liars’ actor Keegan Allen says he was beaten, robbed at gunpoint in Los Angeles
text:
(Gray News) - “Pretty Little Liars” actor Keegan Allen has shared a video of his bloodied face after allegedly being robbed at gunpoint outside a Los Angeles grocery store.
The actor said he was in a Santa Monica Boulevard parking lot in West Hollywood on Thursday, Oct. 8, when two armed men allegedly stole his watch and threatened to “kill” him, according to an Instagram video.
“I was just robbed of my watch outside of Laurel Supply,” the 37-year-old said in the video.
“These two dudes hit me in the head and pointed a gun at me with a knife and then took off,” he recalled. “They had masks on [and] they took my watch.”
Security footage of the alleged robbery included in the video appeared to show the men with Allen, who seemed to be putting items into his truck in the Laurel Supply parking lot, with one apparently hitting him in the head multiple times with his gun.
The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department confirmed to People that it responded to a call about a robbery in the 8400 block of Santa Monica Boulevard at approximately 9:05 p.m, ABC News reported.
The department did not name Allen in the statement.
Allen continued in the video, saying, “West Hollywood is not safe anymore.”
In further comments, Allen noted he suspected he was “def concussed” and added, “Robbed at gunpoint and knifepoint by two young men that threatened to KILL me over my watch and would have! God said no tonight. My life for a watch.”

title: ICE officer shoots a man while making an arrest in New York, officials say
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A federal immigration officer shot a Dominican man in the neck as he drove in a car with a 5-year-old boy Thursday afternoon, officials said. The Department of Homeland Security said it was seeking to arrest the man in a “targeted enforcement operation,” but protesters and local officials decried it as an example of the dangers of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
The 28-year-old man, whom city police identified as Oscar Belgal, survived and was treated at a hospital.
DHS did not describe exactly what led to the shooting, saying only that “during the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon” and that the man was injured.
But city Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Belgal was pulling into a parking space when a federal officer in plainclothes approached with gun drawn, followed by another federal officer who also wasn’t in uniform. Belgal started to pull the car forward, and then at least one of the officers fired seven rounds, hitting the man below his left ear, Tisch said at a news conference near the shooting site late Thursday.
The child was unharmed and with a relative, said Tisch, who noted that city police weren’t involved in the operation but heard the shots and responded.
DHS said in a statement that it was seeking to arrest a “criminal illegal alien” with a grand larceny conviction and a history of other arrests. But an irate Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the shooting an outrage.
“There is no justification for what we have seen today,” Mamdani said. He said the federal officers who surrounded the vehicle wore construction vests and masks, making it difficult to identify them as immigration officers.
The mayor, a Democrat, said he had spent two hours Thursday night pressing Republican President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to release the wounded man, to no avail, and urging them to stop immigration enforcement operations in the city. He said that late Thursday night, federal authorities removed the man from the hospital and took him away.
Gov. Kathy Hochul, also a Democrat, said in a statement that she had delivered a similar message to Trump and Mullin by phone.
Videos show aftermath of the shooting
The gunfire erupted around 4 p.m. in Marble Hill, a small part of Manhattan that is attached to the Bronx.
Tisch said that an NYPD security camera had recorded some of the events leading up to the gunfire, but not the shooting itself.
Pedro Almaraz, an employee at a nearby restaurant, said he heard several gunshots and saw a man on the ground surrounded by several officers wearing face masks and vests with Department of Homeland Security branding. Witnesses, he said, were screaming.
Bystander videos and photos posted by on social media showed a man sitting on the ground with his hands behind his back, in the immediate aftermath of the shooting. Another video shows New York City police officers picking up Belgal and carrying him into a police vehicle.
Nearby, a damaged car sat blocking the roadway with small holes in two of its windows. Tisch said the shooting left the car with a bullet entry point on its front windshield and an exit point in one of its rear windows.
Heated protest and press conference
At a heated press conference at the shooting scene Thursday night, several local politicians condemned the shooting.
“We are heartbroken and enraged,” City Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, a Democrat who emigrated from the Dominican Republic and now represents areas including Marble Hill. Some other elected officials cursed ICE and Trump, a Republican.
Demonstrators at the scene chanted, “ICE off our streets now!” and then marched to the hospital where the injured man was being treated. A sizable crowd blocked an intersection at the hospital entry, and as police began to set barricades so that ambulances and other vehicles could pass, some protesters shoved at the barriers and hurled water bottles at officers.
More clashes at the barricades followed, and police made some arrests.
Homeland Security blames “sanctuary policies”
DHS complained that its officers “are forced to make arrests at large in the community in unpredictable and dangerous environments” when “dangerous illegal aliens” get released. The agency blamed “reckless sanctuary policies” in Democrat-led areas. There is no clear definition of sanctuary jurisdictions, but the term is generally applied to state and local governments that limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
Belgal had been arrested on a robbery charge in 2023, later pleaded guilty to grand larceny and was sentenced to probation, Tisch said, adding that he later was arrested on a drug-sale charge that hasn’t yet been resolved. Electronic court records show that Belgal has pleaded not guilty in the drug case.
ICE agents have fired their guns during more than a dozen vehicle stops since last year, killing at least four people and wounding others. In late September, ICE ordered its officers not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training.
Marble Hill resident Alfred Silva, 38, called for federal officers to more clearly identify themselves, saying one was wearing a construction safety vest.
“We need to have better transparency to understand who we’re dealing with, because anybody in the street can just put on a vest and pull out a gun and claim to be ICE,” he said.
“I feel like regardless if you’re left or right, we should understand that this shouldn’t be happening.”
___
Associated Press writer Michael R. Sisak contributed.

title: 5 months late, Paul LePage’s financial disclosure is in. Here’s what it says.
text:
Almost five months after the deadline, former Gov. Paul LePage’s campaign has submitted the required paperwork to Congress disclosing his personal finances.
The report was due May 15 for all candidates for Congress; the 78-year-old former Maine governor was at that point running unopposed for the Republican nomination for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District. He’s now in a tight general election race against Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap, who submitted his disclosure on the day of the deadline.
As The Washington Sun first reported Tuesday, LePage’s failure to tell the clerk of the House of Representatives about his finances violated federal ethics law. Late reporters are subject to a $200 fine, per the disclosure form, and the U.S. attorney general can bring additional civil proceedings against candidates who knowingly and willingly fail to file a financial disclosure, with penalties up to $75,540.
LePage campaign strategist Brent Littlefield did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but members of the campaign told The Sun this week that the “completely unintentional” delay in filing was a “simple oversight” that “slipped through the cracks.”
The disclosure, now publicly available, was received by the House clerk Tuesday, processed Thursday and posted online shortly thereafter.
LePage reported receiving $39,671 in Social Security so far this year and $22,764 from his state pension. His wife, Ann LePage, also received Social Security and wages from her job at Cook’s Landing Pizzeria & Pub in Edgecomb.
That’s not too different from last year’s report, which LePage filed on time: The LePages received about $70,000 in Social Security in 2025, and LePage’s state pension paid him about $30,000.
Listed the same as last year’s filing, too, is the rental property LePage leases in Augusta from Shawn Moody — a LePage ally who ran in the 2018 gubernatorial race. He reported liability of up to $15,000 for the lease.
According to voter registration records, LePage lives in the Augusta apartment above a barber shop near the Augusta Memorial Circle rotary, next door to one of Moody’s collision repair shops.
The financial disclosure notes that the rental agreement began in May 2025, the same month LePage announced his candidacy for Congress.
LePage did not report owning any individual stocks and said he agreed with Dunlap, his competitor, on banning congressional stock trading, in a recent debate.
The only new item in LePage’s assets in this report is an account with an “SCCU,” valued between $1,000 and $15,000. There are four locations of Space Coast Credit Union, commonly abbreviated as SCCU, within a half-hour drive of LePage’s former home in Ormond Beach, Florida.

title: MaineCare expands coverage for people leaving incarceration and Wabanaki healing practices
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - MaineCare is expanding coverage for people leaving jail or prison and for Wabanaki tribal members.
Last month, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services approved a waiver allowing MaineCare to cover services for eligible people up to 60 days before they’re released from jail or prison.
“Throughout this process, we have worked very closely with the Sheriff’s Association, the Department of Corrections, as well as advocates from the Maine Prisoner Advocacy Coalition and the Maine Reentry Network. And all of them said the same thing. This is needed in Maine and this is going to be so important,” said Courtney Pladsen, MaineCare medical director.
MaineCare will now be required to cover case management and reentry planning, substance use treatment, clinical consultation and medications at release for eligible people up to 60 days before release.
“So helping every person who has MaineCare, who moves through a jail or prison, leave those facilities with a plan and really come out with the goal of decreasing recidivism so that way folks have what they need to not end up back in the jail or prison,” Pladsen said.
Coverage for traditional Wabanaki healing
The waiver also requires MaineCare to provide reimbursement for traditional Wabanaki healing practices.
“This allows us to not have so many barriers to deliver these services. So we’re excited about the partnership. It allows us to partner with state government and assure that these services are well offered to our communities for as long as they need them,” said Lisa Sockabasin, co-CEO of Wabanaki Public Health & Wellness.
Sockabasin said having state support for traditional healing provides an opportunity for connection.
“Why would you not lean into that? It offers you an opportunity to connect, connect to culture, connect to ceremony, connect to each other, connect to your own healing, and always connecting to Mother Earth,” Sockabasin said.
Communication seen as key to implementation
Both organizations said communication has been and will continue to be crucial to implementation of the traditional healing practices coverage.
“Oh that’s vital. Without ongoing collaboration, these initiatives will fall flat. It’s on the state to continue to build these trusted partnerships for us to continue to engage those trusted partners every step of the way, and I’ve been dedicated to that. ” Pladsen said.
Sockabasin said implementation will take at least a year.
More information about the waiver can be found on Maine.gov.

title: New York prosecutors seek to sustain their case against Luigi Mangione, despite his federal plea
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — New York prosecutors sought Friday to keep their murder case going against Luigi Mangione, arguing that his federal guilty plea shouldn’t end a separate, state-court case over the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.
The state and federal prosecutions center on “different harms, different evils, different purposes, different crimes,” Manhattan Assistant District Attorney Joel Seidemann and colleagues wrote in a court filing.
Mangione’s defense lawyers are trying to get the state murder and weapons charges thrown out, citing double jeopardy. It’s the legal precept that broadly prevents a person from being repeatedly prosecuted for the same crime, though the particulars can be complicated and disputed when different courts are involved.
In response to prosecutors’ filing Friday, Mangione’s attorneys pointed to their own previous court papers arguing that the state and federal governments are “prosecuting the same man twice for the same event.”
A ruling is expected in late autumn.
At stake is whether Mangione will continue to face a trial in a New York state court in Manhattan and, potentially, how much prison time he will serve if he’s convicted. He’s already looking at the likelihood of a lengthy federal sentence. A state conviction, if there is one, could add more time.
The Manhattan prosecutors argue that double jeopardy doesn’t apply to Mangione’s situation. Though their case and the federal prosecution both concern Thompson’s December 2024 killing, the Manhattan prosecutors contend that the specific charges involve different legal elements and criminal conduct.
Mangione pleaded guilty in August to federal stalking and cyberstalking charges, admitting in court that he traveled across state lines to New York to kill Thompson and then shot him from behind on a Manhattan street. The 28-year-old said he gunned for the CEO after experiencing years of severe back pain and “navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system.”
In the state case, meanwhile, Mangione pleaded not guilty in 2024 to murder, weapons and fake-ID charges. If he goes to trial, his admission in federal court might be used against him.
Thompson, 50, led one of the United States’ largest health insurers. His killing — with ammunition that authorities said was marked “delay,” “deny” and “depose” — alarmed the healthcare industry while baring the anger that many Americans feel about it. Some people cast Mangione as a valiant figure, even as others, including public officials, said the killing was anything but heroic.
Mangione, a scion of a prominent Maryland real estate family, has undergraduate and master’s degrees in computer science. He worked for a car-buying website for a time. He never had UnitedHealthcare’s insurance, police said.

title: Severe turbulence injures at least 8 aboard Avianca flight, forcing emergency landing in Miami
text:
At least eight people were injured when an Avianca flight encountered severe turbulence and had to make an emergency landing in Miami early Friday.
Miami-Dade Fire Rescue said that one person was rushed to a trauma center with severe injuries while seven others were taken to area hospitals in ambulances after the plane landed shortly after 3 a.m. Friday. The airline said nine people — three crew members and six passengers — were affected by the turbulence and needed to be taken to a medical facility.
The Federal Aviation Administration said the Avianca flight was en route from Medellin, Colombia, to John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York when the Airbus A320 had to divert to Miami.
Avianca said the passengers who were not hurt were flown to New York on Friday morning. The airline said “the safety of our customers and employees is, and will remain, the foundation of our operations.”
Serious injuries from in-flight turbulence are rare, but scientists say they may be becoming more common as climate change alters the jet stream. The International Air Transport Association said the number of reports it received about turbulence incidents surged more than 25% last year.
Last summer, 24 people were taken to the hospital after a Delta Air Lines flight encountered turbulence caused by a thunderstorm over Wyoming. The National Transportation Safety Board has said passengers and flight attendants were thrown into the ceiling with enough force to crack some of the interior panels before tossing them back to the floor and then up again. The seat belt sign was off at the time so some passengers were up and drinks were being served when that plane hit the turbulence.
At least 20 passengers have filed lawsuits against Delta over that incident, arguing the airline could have avoided the severe weather.
The FAA recommends that passengers stay buckled whenever possible to protect against unexpected turbulence.

title: The pro-life movement is the selfish movement
text:
Dan Pryor of Gorham makes the argument in an Oct. 1 letter (“Remember: Abortion kills human life”) that abortion is both selfish and destroys a unique human life. As he puts it, “abortion is the self-centered murder of the innocent.”
There are two sides to this argument. On the other side:
To quote the headline of an Oct. 1 report in this newspaper, “Every day, thousands of residents face the hardest financial choices, as households struggle to afford basic expenses.” Being able to afford basic expenses becomes that much more difficult as the number of children in a family grows.
The amount of carbon dioxide dumped into the atmosphere increases with each increase in the number of people on the planet. The same goes for how long it takes to commute to work, and for how much a house costs. More people exacerbate problems that we could otherwise live with.
Educational expenses are driving up property taxes, and those expenses increase with an increase in the number of students. The pro-life movement would make life miserable for all of us, by increasing global warming, hunger, property taxes and time on the road, in order to save a fetus that would never know it is alive.
The letter read, “There is nothing more selfish in America than the ‘pro-choice’ abortion movement.” In reality, there is nothing more selfish or short-sighted than the “pro-life” movement.
William Vaughan Jr.
Chebeague Island

title: Few countries still hold public executions. Here's where
text:
Few countries still hold public executions. Here's where
The United States could join just a handful of countries that are carrying out judicial public executions in the modern era.
While public records are limited, there were at least 17 public executions carried out in 2025, according to data from Amnesty International.
Iran publicly executed at least 11 people, and Taliban-led Afghanistan publicly executed at least six people in 2025, per Amnesty International's report.
Saudi Arabia has also held frequent public executions in the 21st century, although the Get the Facts Data Team was unable to obtain the exact number in recent years at the time of publication.
Last historic public executions
The United States has not held a public execution in almost a century.
The most recent public execution, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, was in 1937 when a man was publicly hanged in Missouri for murder.
France held its final public execution two years after the United States.
The United Kingdom ended public executions in 1868, about 70 years before the last public execution in the U.S.
Livestreamed execution
The Pentagon announced on Thursday that the execution of the 2009 Fort Hood shooter — who killed 13 people and injured 32 others — will be livestreamed to the public.
The execution is scheduled to take place by firing squad on Dec. 3, and it will be the first military execution in 65 years.
The Death Penalty Information Center told the Get the Facts Data Team that it has no record of any execution being livestreamed to the public in the U.S.
In 2001, live video of the execution of the Oklahoma City bomber was shared through a closed-circuit television to survivors and the families of victims. It was not made public.
In 2006, videos of former Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein's execution were widely circulated online. While Hussein was executed on a joint Iraqi-U.S. base, the execution was carried out solely by Iraq.
On Friday, Vice President JD Vance said he was uncertain whether the execution would be livestreamed.
"I don't know that that's actually going to happen," he told reporters when asked about the Pentagon's plans.

title: Alleged Flydubai hijacker planned ‘suicide attack’ on Tel Aviv’s airport, early investigation finds
text:
Alleged Flydubai hijacker planned ‘suicide attack’ on Tel Aviv’s airport, early investigation finds
The alleged Flydubai hijacker had planned to crash the plane into Ben Gurion Airport near Tel Aviv and was inspired by the 9/11 attacks, a preliminary investigation has found.
Hamam al-Hammami, the suspect in the hijacking attempt and co-pilot on board last week’s flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv, wanted to carry out a similar attack to Sept. 11, 2001, which led him to pursue an aviation career, according to a statement from the United Arab Emirates’ attorney general.
“The idea of carrying out a similar operation using an aircraft became firmly established in his mind, which, according to his confessions, was connected to his decision to pursue a career in aviation,” the statement said.
The pilot also aimed to carry out “a premeditated plot with a terrorist objective, aimed at taking control of the aircraft and using it to carry out a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport,” with the aim of causing “the greatest possible number of casualties,” it added.
An Israeli official and an Israeli source familiar with the matter told CNN earlier that the alleged hijacker likely wanted to target the airport, the country’s main international gateway.
Al-Hammami, 29, was stopped by the actions of the captain and several passengers who restrained him and took back control of the airplane.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Isaias strengthens into Category 3 hurricane on path toward the US Gulf Coast
text:
GULF BREEZE, Fla. (AP) — Isaias crashed into the U.S. Gulf Coast on Friday as a dangerous Category 2 hurricane, hammering communities in Alabama and the Florida Panhandle with damaging winds, heavy rain, flooding and life-threatening storm surges.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season made landfall near Destin, Florida, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said. It had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (169 kph). The storm weakened to just below major hurricane status before it came ashore and by early Saturday was no longer considered a hurricane as its wind speeds continued to decrease.
“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard “throughout the region.”
Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white-sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars, and seafood shacks. Forecasters warned the conditions could also stir up tornadoes across the Florida Panhandle and into southern Georgia.
“We’re watching it very closely, the hurricane,” President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House late Friday night as he returned from a rally in upstate New York, adding that it was “under control.”
Roads in Destin were flooded, while in nearby Pensacola, police warned residents to stay off the streets because of debris across roadways. While the extent of the damage was not immediately known, many area residents posted pictures online of downed trees and power lines, and one social media video showed a roof being ripped off an inn in Pensacola.
More than 664,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power early Saturday, according to poweroutage.com.
Many are braving Isaias at home
Tim Mowry, who rode out the storm from his home in Pensacola, said the wind was so intense it sounded like a train whistle as it whipped through a crack in his patio door. He lost power around 4:30 p.m. but was able to rely on a generator. Standing water also covered his backyard, and parts of his fence were ripped down, but overall he said the storm wasn’t as bad as he expected.
“As far as Pensacola-wise, we really got fortunate,” Mowry said.
One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could reach 3 to 5 feet (0.91 to 1.52 meters) from Dauphin Island, Alabama, to Florida’s Aucilla River, according to the hurricane center.
Dangerous conditions are expected throughout the western panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, the National Hurricane Center said. Several counties announced mandatory evacuations while Mobile, Alabama, imposed a curfew through Saturday morning.
In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle closed, according to the company’s website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often serves as a measure of a storm’s severity.
Kelsei Frazier, a Florida native living in Pace and no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.
“We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it’s not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed,” said Frazier.
DeSantis warned residents to expect gasoline shortages and bridge and highway closures.
The state’s National Guard deployed about 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, and search-and-rescue teams were ready to respond, while some prisons evacuated inmates.
The whole region could get soaked
Isaias was already slowing after landfall, and it was expected to weaken further and be downgraded to a tropical storm by Saturday afternoon, the center said.
Still, heavy rain is forecast as it moves inland, with 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama to southwestern Georgia.
Isaias grounds flights but likely to miss oil hubs
The storm grounded most Friday flights at several panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt emergency response efforts.
Isaias was expected to miss the oil industry’s biggest hubs along the Gulf Coast, but fuel prices could rise if power outages shut down refineries for processing crude, industry experts said.
Meanwhile, in the Pacific, Hurricane Simon became a Category 4 storm early Saturday, ahead of a projected landfall in Mexico this weekend.
___
Megnien reported from Panama City, Florida, Golden reported from Seattle, and Seewer reported from Toledo, Ohio. Seth Borenstein and Collin Binkley in Washington; Rio Yamat in Las Vegas; Gerald Herbert in Pensacola, Florida; Dave Collins in Hartford, Connecticut; Sarah Raza in Sioux Falls, South Dakota; Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama; and Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas contributed to this report.

title: Obituary: Anna Van Der Heide Freeman
text:
ATHENS – On Oct. 5, 2026, Anna Margaretha Van Der Heide Freeman passed peacefully at the age of 89, in the farmhouse in West Athens, where she had lived off and on for the past 55 years.
Born in 1937 in Amsterdam to Seintje Hamme, a Jewish vaudeville actress and Carel Van Der Heide, a Freudian psychoanalyst, her family emigrated to the United States in 1939 to escape the Nazis and World War II. Her family moved around the country during her early years, and ultimately settled in Los Angeles, Calif. where she grew up in Beverly Hills and attended Westlake School for Girls, graduating in 1953.
Although she started college at Wellesley as a dutiful daughter with strict expectations, her life changed forever when, traveling through Europe, she was introduced to beatnik poets and bohemian lifestyles. After returning to California, where she graduated from UC Berkeley in 1963, she had many adventures as a young woman acting in plays and films, and traveling the world with figures such as Gregory Corso, Judd Hirsch, and John Huston.
Living in New York’s Greenwich Village in the ’60s she met and had a daughter with Crescenzo Giasullo, and studied acting with Uta Hagen. Later, she was introduced to her future partner Bob Freeman, who was part of a group of artists and homesteaders moving from cities to rural areas such as Central Maine in the early 1970s. By 1972 Anna and her growing family had moved to the backwoods of West Athens to live “the good life.” Anna was part of the creative explosion of visual and performing arts in the region. She was a founding thespian with the In Spite Of Life Players and Cornville Players, and was a mainstay of the unique Fourth of July performances that took place in West Athens for many decades.
Later in life, she lived in Gainesville, Fla. and San Francisco, Calif., but always kept returning to her West Athens farmhouse and her cherished community of artists, hippies, homesteaders, and Mainers. Anna loved connecting with people, and connecting people with one another. For many years, she wrote a weekly social column, the “View from Athens” in the 1970s, and her “West Athens Clarion” in the digital age. She thrived on knowing–and being known by–nearly everyone in central Maine; befriending strangers at diners and in supermarket checkout lines was standard practice. She thrived on drama and emotion, and wasn’t shy about stirring some up when she felt that more was needed.
Anna was a great reader of books, and a staunch advocate of public libraries. She wrote hundreds of poems over a span of decades, and authored years of columns for the Morning Sentinel expressing her progressive political views, and the challenges and joys of being a single mother in rural Maine. She was a prolific playwright, and directed many of her plays in theaters throughout the state. She was a talented pianist and violinist, who won the East Benton Fiddle Contest multiple times during its early years. And she had a unique eye for beauty, nurtured by lifelong friendships with artists.
Above all, her greatest artistic love was the theater. She spent much of her adult life directing and acting in plays, sometimes both simultaneously! In addition to her work with the In Spite Of Life Players, she was a founding member of the Acrosstown Repertory Theater in Gainesville, Fla. In Maine, she directed and performed in countless theatrical productions in theaters from Lakewood to the East Madison Square Garden to the West Athens Gravel Pit, sharing her love of theater writing and performing original plays with students in Athens and Madison. Of the many roles she played, none suited Anna more than Mama Rose from the musical “Gypsy.”
Anna was predeceased by her partners Crescenzo and Bob; and her brother, Charles.
She is survived by her siblings Thomas and Douglas; her children Gia Giasullo (Erez), Ezra Freeman (Mala), and Peter Freeman (Joannie); her grandchildren Zoe, Ada, Zadek, Samir, Lennox, and Cosmo; and her beloved Morkie, Herbie.
Anna’s family wishes to thank Maine Hospice, Mike and Amber Lambke, Sally Barrows, Liz Heard, and Robin LeBrun for their exceptional support and care.
Visitors will be welcome at our West Athens home, 24 North Road, through Sunday, Oct. 11.

title: ICE officers shot New York man whose 5-year-old was in his car, official says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal immigration officers opened fire on a Dominican man whom they were trying to arrest in New York because they believed their lives were in danger, a senior Immigration and Customs Enforcement official said Friday.
Marcos Charles made the comments alongside U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and other immigration officials during a news conference in Washington meant to “highlight the dangerous consequences of sanctuary city policies.”
The 28-year-old man, whom New York City police identified as Oscar Belgal, was shot in the neck Thursday as he drove his car with a 5-year-old boy inside, officials said.
ICE agents didn’t know the child was in the car, but Belgal “was aware” and chose to evade officers, Mullin said.
Belgal was shot “superficially” in the neck as ICE officers attempted to arrest him, Charles said.
ICE had issued a detainer on Belgal and that he runs with a gang known for thefts using weapons and mopeds, he said. Officers used vehicles to block him in as he attempted to drive off. Instead, Charles said, he accelerated his vehicle toward officers, smashing some of their vehicles.
Protesters and local officials decried the shooting as an example of the dangers of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
Much of Mullin’s remarks were reserved for excoriating New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his immigration policy.
“Sanctuary politicians, they create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for the American citizens to be safe,” he said.
Mullin said ICE has requested more than 14,000 detainers in the state of New York for individuals in local custody that they’re seeking to deport.
“Silence. Absolute silence is what we have gotten back,” he said. “Why would they release these individuals back onto the streets?”
“We’re enforcing our nation’s laws. We’re not picking and choosing,” Mullin continued. “Why is that controversial? We should all want law and order on our streets.”

title: Vance expresses doubts about Pentagon plan to livestream Fort Hood shooter's execution
text:
HEBRON, Ky. (AP) — Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on Friday whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December but told reporters that if it is livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.”
The Republican vice president said, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” when asked about the plans that the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday. But Vance then tried to set aside the controversy over the shocking plans for a public execution and said Hasan’s crimes should not be forgotten.
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting spree at the military base in 2009.
“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” the Republican said.
“Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it,” he said.
Earlier, President Donald Trump told a White House event that Hasan will be getting “the death penalty through firing squad. And he deserves it.”
Trump, who approved Hasan’s execution, called him “a maniac.”
Trump, who has long been a vocal supporter of capital punishment, didn’t mention the plans that the Pentagon has announced to livestream the execution so that the broader public can see it.
___
This story has been corrected to show the military base’s name is Fort Hood, not Ford Hood.
___
Associated Press writer Will Weissert in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Appeals court dismisses Maine lobster defamation lawsuit
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals overturned a federal judge’s ruling and dismissed the Maine lobster industry’s defamation lawsuit against a California aquarium on Friday.
The Maine Lobstermen’s Association, Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association and three lobster businesses sued the Monterey Bay Aquarium Foundation in 2023 after the organization’s Seafood Watch program put lobster on a “red list,” urging consumers to avoid the seafood. The foundation had claimed measures in the fishery don’t do enough to reduce entanglement or promote recovery of the critically endangered North Atlantic right whale population.
The plaintiffs argued the foundation made “false and defamatory statements” about the Maine lobster industry’s practices and misled consumers and businesses about the fishery’s “integrity.” In the lawsuit, they claimed to lose business, with some consumers specifically citing the red listing.
The foundation moved to dismiss the lawsuit, but a judge allowed the suit to advance in 2025. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals overruled that decision Friday, and ordered the lawsuit to be dismissed.
The court ruled that calls to action, including boycotting products or industries, are protected under the First Amendment, and concluded that the listing did not make any specific reference to the plaintiffs in the case.
“People’s choices have the power to shape the future of the ocean,” the aquarium said in a statement on the court’s decision. “Programs like Seafood Watch guide consumers and businesses toward environmentally sustainable choices that support a healthy, thriving ocean, benefiting food security, fisheries and coastal communities whose livelihoods depend on the ocean.”
Spokespeople for the Maine Lobstermen’s Association and the Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association did not respond to a request for comment Friday evening.
The aquarium assigned Maine lobster a yellow rating on its Seafood Watch in 2014, recommending consumers “be aware there are concerns” with how the seafood is caught and managed. It ultimately gave it a “red” rating, along with other Canadian and U.S. fisheries, in September 2022. It claims one threat to the species is entanglement in fishing gear, including buoy lines used by lobstermen.
In a report on the new red ratings in 2022, the Seafood Watch program advised consumers to avoid “American lobster caught by trap from Georges Bank and the Gulf of Maine stocks due to risks to the critically endangered North Atlantic right whale and insufficient measures for reducing these risks.”
“This decision is a victory for all environmental advocates and freedom of speech,” said Sarah Shahabi, an attorney at the Conservation Law Foundation, which filed a friend-of-the-court brief supporting Monterey Bay Aquarium. “We can’t effectively fight threats to the natural world without naming them. Speaking openly and honestly about environmental challenges is essential to protecting our planet.”

title: Firefighter killed, 2 others hurt fighting massive fire in North Carolina
text:

title: Christa Pike is walking with help and eating after failed execution attempt, her attorneys say
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Christa Pike has begun walking and eating again at a hospital a week after surviving Tennessee’s attempt to execute her with lethal drugs, her attorneys said Thursday.
Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state sought to give her a lethal injection eight days ago for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The drug didn’t kill her, and her arms were left burned and blistered, according to her lawyers. For the first few days of her hospitalization, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator.
Her first steps on Wednesday were “limited,” and she required some assistance as she walked on Thursday, her lawyers said in a statement. She is also regaining mobility in her arms, and she was able to eat for the first time.
But the lawyers warned uncertainty remains about her physical recovery and her legal standing after the attempt to carry out her death sentence.
Questions remain about Pike’s recovery and legal case
The failed execution on Sept. 30 has renewed scrutiny of how states carry out the death penalty. Texas on Wednesday carried out the first execution in the U.S. since the Tennessee attempt.
“While her physical recovery has been remarkable, significant questions remain about the long-term effects of what she endured,” her attorneys said in Thursday’s statement. “Christa is dealing with the profound psychological trauma of having survived a failed execution, including the terror, pain and uncertainty of believing she was about to die.”
Pike regained consciousness Tuesday and was able to speak after awakening, they said.
They initially described her as “confused” soon after regaining consciousness, and said Thursday that she continued to struggle with concentration and memory. Doctors say it is too early to assess the long-term impacts, the attorneys added.
It also remains unclear whether Tennessee will try to execute her again. Her attorneys have said that they will urge Republican Gov. Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life in prison without parole.
“She should never be subjected to another execution attempt,” they said in the statement.
What went wrong with the execution remains unclear
Lee has since postponed the state’s only other scheduled execution this year and ordered a review of why the execution failed. The state’s prison chief resigned after the execution attempt.
Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on whether a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue instead of entering her bloodstream.
Pike’s attorneys wrote in a court filing that “apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed.”
State officials have offered no explanation of what occurred.
As the process got underway, Pike was asked if she had a final statement and she spoke of being at peace. About five minutes later, she raised her head and said her arm hurt. Later, she appeared to lose consciousness but could be heard breathing heavily until media witnesses were escorted from the witness room nearly 90 minutes into the execution. An ambulance took her to a hospital.

title: BREAKING NEWS: At the Puddle, Incident Involving Unwanted Physical Contact
text:
At 3:30pm on Friday, Oct. 9, Bates College community members received an alert through the emergency messaging system regarding an incident near Lake Andrews, commonly known to students as the puddle.
“At approximately 2:33pm a student experienced unwanted physical contact near Lake Andrews. Please be alert and aware of a white male, with brown hair and shaved head, approximately 5′ 8′ [corrected in a later statement to The Student as 5’8″], wearing a black T-shirt with design.” The message was accompanied with the request to notify campus safety if a person matching the description was spotted.
In a statement by the college given to The Student, the incident happened while a student was “walking near Lake Andrews.” Additionally, “the individual was unknown to the student and is not believed to be part of the community.”
The college shared that “the Lewiston Police Department responded to campus and are investigating” and that “Bates staff members are working to support the impacted student.”
While the original alert message noted the unknown individual as having brown hair, the later statement from the college specified this description as “brown eyebrows.”
The alert was sent out, the college shared in their statement, in line with the Clery Act, which requires colleges to send out timely emergency notification when an incident has occurred which may pose an ongoing or serious threat.
The college further encouraged community members to “immediately report any sightings of this person to Campus Safety.” The Bates Campus Safety emergency number is 207-786-6111. The college also noted that “students with any concerns about walking alone on campus tonight can connect with Campus Safety for a safety escort.”
Bates community members seeking support may find a wide range of supports on campus, including timely support from Area Coordinators from the Residence Life team (available via the Campus Safety non-emergency number 207-786-6254) and an on-call counselor from Counseling and Psychological Services (available via 786-6200 and dial zero).

title: State warns of contractor scams as Hurricane Isaias approaches
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MONTGOMERY, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - The Alabama Home Builders Licensure Board is warning homeowners about the potential for scams, fraud and price gouging during storm cleanup, repair and rebuilding as Hurricane Isaias threatens the Gulf Coast and central Alabama.
The board is urging residents to be cautious when hiring anyone to repair storm damage or purchase needed items.
Emergency proclamation triggers felony law
Gov. Kay Ivey issued an emergency proclamation Wednesday covering dozens of counties ahead of the potential hurricane landfall, including Autauga, Baldwin, Barbour, Bibb, Bullock, Butler, Chambers, Chilton, Clarke, Choctaw, Coffee, Conecuh, Coosa, Covington, Crenshaw, Dale, Dallas, Elmore, Escambia, Geneva, Greene, Hale, Henry, Houston, Lee, Lowndes, Macon, Marengo, Mobile, Monroe, Montgomery, Perry, Pickens, Pike, Russell, Sumter, Tallapoosa, Tuscaloosa, Washington and Wilcox counties.
The proclamation triggers consumer protection laws, including the Aggravated Home Repair Fraud law, which makes unlicensed homebuilding a class C felony when services are offered after an emergency declaration.
License requirements
A state homebuilders license is required when the cost of a job exceeds $10,000. The Home Builders Licensure Board encourages consumers to seek licensed professionals even when the cost of work does not exceed that amount.
A roofer’s license is required for replacing a storm-damaged roof when the cost of the job exceeds $2,500. Performing or offering unlicensed services is normally a class A misdemeanor, but becomes a felony when someone takes advantage of homeowners after an emergency weather event.
“With the Governor’s emergency proclamation, anyone unlicensed who takes advantage of Alabamians with storm damage to their homes, the Home Builders Licensure Board will work with law enforcement and district attorneys to charge and prosecute you for the felony crime of aggravated home repair fraud,” said Seth Gowan, executive director of the Alabama Home Builders Licensure Board. “Taking advantage of fellow Alabamians who suffer damage or loss of property will not be tolerated,” Gowan said.
Steps before hiring a contractor
The Alabama Home Builders Licensure Board outlined steps consumers should take before hiring anyone to perform repairs:
- Ask if the contractor is licensed with the Alabama Home Builders Licensure Board and ask to see the license card. Consumers can also verify licensure status by calling 1-800-304-0853 or visiting www.hblb.alabama.gov.
- Ask for and check references, especially if the builder makes unsolicited contact or is from out of town.
- Make sure quotes and contracts are in writing and include the Home Builders Licensure Board license number. Licensed homebuilders must use a written contract that includes the contractor’s full name, address, telephone number, a description of the work to be performed, starting and estimated completion dates, and the total cost of the job.
Gowan encouraged residents “to be cautious and patient. Work with your insurance company, check to make sure contractors are licensed, ask a lot of questions, and if you believe a contractor is not in the area for the right reasons, call law enforcement.”
Reporting fraud
Consumers may report alleged fraud or price gouging to the Attorney General’s Office for investigation. Complaints can be filed online at www.alabamaag.gov under the “consumer complaint” link, or by calling the Consumer Interest Division toll-free at 1-800-392-5658.
For information about home repair licensing and potential fraud, contact the Home Builders Licensure Board at 445 Herron St., Montgomery, Alabama 36104, 334-242-2230 or 1-800-304-0853, or visit www.hblb.alabama.gov.

title: Troy Jackson has 4-point lead over Susan Collins in Washington Post poll
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Troy Jackson is narrowly leading U.S. Sen. Susan Collins in a new poll released Friday.
That poll, conducted by the Washington Post and the Schar School, found 50% of likely Maine voters favored the Democrat, compared with 46% for the Republican incumbent. Jackson’s lead falls within the margin of error, the Post reported.
Those results mirror other recent polls that have given Jackson single-digit leads over Collins, who has led in just one recent poll.
It underscores how competitive the race has become since Jackson became his party’s nominee after Graham Platner dropped out in July when an ex-girlfriend accused him of rape. Republicans and Democrats are spending big in Maine in a midterm election that could upend the balance of power in Washington. Vice President JD Vance has twice visited Maine this year to boost for Republicans, while President Donald Trump has mused about stumping here ahead of the election. Former President Barack Obama endorsed Jackson on Thursday.
One drag on Collins’ odds this November is Trump’s falling approval rating, with just 36% of likely voters approving of him in the Post-Schar poll. Meanwhile, 58% of voters felt Collins has been too supportive of Trump’s agenda in the U.S. Senate.
Collins has historically been carried to victory, including in 2020 over Democrat Sara Gideon, by ticket-splitting Democratic voters, but there have been signs that fewer Democrats may be willing to cross over into her column under Trump. A Bangor Daily News analysis last month found that Collins needs at least 1 in 10 voters who backed Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential election to carry her to victory.
The Post-Schar poll found that voters favored Jackson on abortion, cost of living and healthcare.
But the poll found positive signs for Collins. She had a 24-point lead over Jackson for her ability to bring federal dollars into Maine. The Pine Tree State has long been a net recipient of federal dollars, getting a $1.68 back for every $1 in taxes paid, according to one estimate. It’s a point that Collins’ campaign has leaned heavily on this season.
The poll surveyed about 800 likely voters between Sept. 30 to Oct. 5, ahead of their two recent debates.
It will be an uphill battle for Democrats to unseat Collins, who officially announced her historic bid for a sixth term in February. The Republican has handily beaten back challengers, including in 2020 when she defied polls and expectations to secure a fifth term in the Senate. But Collins, who has been ranked the country’s most bipartisan senator and relied on cross-party appeal to carry her to victory, has seen her popularity slump since Trump’s first term in the White House.
If Collins is successful in winning a sixth term, she would be Maine’s longest-serving U.S. senator.

title: Electric heater likely sparked Caribou fire in old ambulance being used as a camper
text:
An electric heater likely caused a Thursday fire involving a privately owned ambulance in which someone was living, Caribou fire officials said.
The owner had returned from errands to find the vehicle on fire, Caribou Fire and Ambulance Capt. Scott Dow said Friday.
“Someone was living in it and had turned it into a camper,” Dow said. “Neighbors had called the fire department, and when we arrived, the owner was trying to put it out with a garden hose.”
The department is not releasing the owner’s name, he said.
No one was injured.
Firefighters suspect an electric heater, which had been left running inside the out-of-service ambulance, ignited nearby contents and caused a “significant” fire, the department posted on social media.
Crews put out the blaze using about 750 gallons of water.

title: Maine residents could qualify for compensation in generic drug price-fixing settlements
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - Maine residents who purchased certain generic prescription medications between 2009 and 2019 could be eligible for compensation under settlements that were proposed involving three pharmaceutical manufacturers accused of conspiring to artificially inflate drug prices.
Attorney General Aaron M. Frey announced that Maine is joining a coalition of 45 states and territories that are seeking court approval of settlements involving Ascend Laboratories, Citron Pharma and Mayne Pharma.
Under the proposed agreements Ascend will pay $400,000 to the states, and Mayne will pay $650,000. Citron Pharma’s settlement only includes nonmonetary terms because the company no longer exists.
All three companies agreed to reforms intended to promote fair competition and compliance with antitrust laws.
According to the AG, investigators reviewed more than 20 million documents and millions of phone records as part of the multistate investigation.
The latest agreements follow previous settlements with several other pharmaceutical companies totaling approximately $496.5 million.
Maine residents who purchased certain generic prescription drugs between May 2009 and December 2019 may be eligible for compensation.
Consumers can learn more by visiting AGGenericDrugs.com, emailing info@AGGenericDrugs.com or calling 1-866-290-0182.
The settlements proposed still require court approval. The first trial is scheduled for February 2027 in Hartford, Connecticut.

title: Residents evacuate, National Guard troops deploy as Hurricane Isaias nears US Gulf Coast
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Residents boarded up windows and stacked sandbags Thursday while thousands of National Guard soldiers were deploying in anticipation of Hurricane Isaias, which packed swift winds and threatened to bring a storm surge with devastating floods to the U.S. Gulf Coast.
Isaias is the first hurricane of the Atlantic season and was expected to usher in dangerous conditions in the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi when it makes landfall late Friday. Heavy rain and flooding were possible into the weekend as far north as Tennessee and North Carolina.
The Category 2 hurricane is most likely to strike along the Alabama-Florida state line and bring life-threatening storm surge across Pensacola Bay, according to the National Weather Service in Mobile, Alabama. But there’s a small chance it could hit further west and have a major impact on Mobile, or further east and have a strong effect on the Florida cities of Pensacola and Destin.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon, which formed as a tropical storm on Wednesday off of Mexico and became a hurricane late Thursday, was forecast to strengthen into a Category 4 hurricane.
Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 kph), according to the hurricane center. It was headed north-northeast at 14 mph (22 kph) and was centered about 230 miles (370 kilometers) south of the mouth of the Mississippi River.
A hurricane warning was in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay-Gulf County line in Florida, the hurricane center said. A storm surge warning was in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi to the Suwannee River.
Preparations underway
Coastal communities moved quickly to prepare Thursday, as Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey ordered non-residents to immediately evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island. Videos on social media showed traffic at a standstill on a highway leading out of Gulf Shores, where double-red beach flags signaled water access was closed.
At least four Florida school districts canceled late-week classes, while several counties announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency for dozens of counties, with Florida’s Ron DeSantis saying about 5,000 National Guard troops were expected to mobilize by Friday.
On Dauphin Island, a 15-mile (24-kilometer) barrier island off the Alabama coast, officials encouraged voluntary evacuations, particularly on its popular western section, which is vulnerable to storm surge.
Mayor Jeff Collier said he did not anticipate substantial damage, “but at the same time, these things are very fickle and a little jog here or there, or some last-minute increase in strength — we just have to be prepared for the worst.”
Water from the storm surge and high tide could reach heights of 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2 meters) in parts of Alabama and Florida, forecasters said. Isaias also could dump up to 15 inches (38 centimeters) of rain on coastal areas and spawn tornadoes overnight Friday into Saturday from Alabama to the Florida Panhandle and southwestern Georgia. The hurricane is expected to quickly weaken after coming ashore.
The National Weather Service warned of possible “long-duration power outages.”
The hurricane formed late in the season
Isaias developed more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season and was one day short of tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane. That record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over the Atlantic. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Hurricane Simon formed. Farther north, Tropical Storm Rachel was expected to reach Baja California, Mexico, and Southern California this weekend.
Isaias is expected to strike a swath of coastline that’s familiar with major hurricanes.
One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Oil production and tourism are already affected
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.
As of Thursday, about 63% of the oil production in the region had been temporarily halted, taking nearly 1.3 million barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said 121 of the Gulf’s 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated.
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
In Loxley, a small Alabama community where county officials urged voluntary evacuations, Nichole Eubanks and her husband prepared to ride out the storm on their farm, which is home to dozens of animals, including pigs, donkeys and about 20 rescued cats.
They planned to put contact information on the hooves of their goats, donkeys and pigs in case they got loose.
“It’s definitely scary, and you never really know where these storms are going to go and how bad it’s going to be until it gets there,” said Eubanks, 35.
In the Alabama fishing village of Bayou La Batre, Tony Rice and Lance Connor installed doors on their fishing boat Thursday to protect the vessel. The boat was one of many moored there, and Rice said they planned to move it to a less-crowded spot to decrease the chances of it bumping into others.
In Pensacola, Florida, officials said the airport will close to commercial flights Friday morning. Mayor D.C. Reeves urged residents to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”
___
Rico reported from Atlanta and Collins reported from Hartford, Connecticut. Also contributing were Associated Press reporters Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama; Hallie Golden in Seattle; Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; John Raby in Charleston, West Virginia; Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas; and Julie Walker in New York.
