title: Here’s what’s on the ballot in Brunswick
text:
Voting has begun in Maine, and in Brunswick, residents will be filling four Town Council seats and three school board seats, in addition to chiming in on Maine House races and high-profile elections for governor and U.S. Senate.
In-person voting will take place at the Brunswick Recreation Center on Election Day. Before that, voters can vote early, pick up a ballot and register to vote at Town Hall through Oct. 29.
The Curtis Memorial Library will host a “meet the candidates” night from 5 to 6:30 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 16.
Here’s what’s on the local ballot in Brunswick.
TOWN COUNCIL
District 5: Jennifer Hicks
Sitting Town Councilor Jennifer Hicks is running unopposed for a second term. Hicks is a 10-year Brunswick resident and directs outreach and communication for Maine Woodland Owners.
In her responses to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Hicks said that her priorities include being responsive to residents and “countering the impacts of misguided and harmful federal actions.” She also highlighted affordability as a challenge and said deciding on the next town manager will be an opportunity for the council, once manager Julia Henze retires next year.
District 7: Steven Weems
Councilor Steven Weems is also running unopposed for reelection to his District 7 seat. Weems won council elections in 1990, 1992 and 2023. He describes himself as a semi-retired businessman and nonprofit executive and has lived in Brunswick for about 40 years.
Weems also highlighted the search for the next town manager. His top three priorities were managing growth, putting restraints on property taxes and upgrading the town’s recycling and solid waste strategy. He also said housing affordability, particularly for seniors and low-income residents, is a significant challenge in Brunswick.
At-large seat (one-year term): Jennifer Navarro, Nathaniel Shed, Paul Whitcomb
Three candidates are vying to serve the remainder of the term for the seat currently held by Katherine Wilson, who is stepping down.
They include former councilor Nathaniel Shed, who served District 6 from 2023-2025. Shed said his priorities include supporting affordable housing options, implementing Brunswick’s climate goals and supporting a vibrant downtown by adding parking. He also said building a new, environmentally sound public works facility is a priority.
Also vying for the special election seat is newcomer Jennifer Navarro. Navarro said she plans on focusing on town fiscal responsibility that protects taxpayers, responsible growth and transparency in government. She said growth and spending are “moving faster than infrastructure, process, and public trust can support” and that Brunswick should grow where it has the capacity to.
Paul Whitcomb, who has spoken in council meetings recently to oppose the Brunswick Public Works fuel station project, is the third candidate for the seat. Whitcomb did not respond to the voter guide survey.
At-large seat (full term): Sarah Brayman, Robert Moulton
Sarah Brayman, a former council chair, and Robert Moulton, a one-time council candidate, are running for a full-term at-large seat on the council.
Brayman served two terms on the council from 2012-2017 and has served on the boards of Brunswick Public Art and the Curtis Memorial Library. She’s also been the chairperson and vice chairperson of the council. In her Voter Guide survey, she said she wants to focus on affordability, good governance, transparency and a strong environment. Brayman said she’ll listen carefully on council and “carefully consider competing perspectives.”
Moulton, who ran unsuccessfully in 2022, said Brunswick must “(restore) trust in how major decisions are made” by providing balanced information and accepting public input. His priorities include ensuring fairness in property taxes and supporting business and housing growth that aligns with Brunswick’s character.
SCHOOL BOARD
Three candidates are running unopposed for Brunswick School Board seats. They are W. Benjamin Walsh in District 5, Sarah Singer in District 7 and William Thompson, who is running for an at-large seat. All three are seeking reelection to their current seats.
The candidates did not respond to the Voter Guide survey.
OTHER RACES
Voters in House District 99 will decide between incumbent Rep. Cheryl Golek, a Democrat, and challenger Republican Braeden Webber.
District 100’s legislative candidates are Democratic Rep. Daniel Ankeles, also seeking reelection, and Republican Brett Barrett.
Democratic Rep. Poppy Arford is up for reelection in District 101, and will face Republican Ravi Jackson.
State Senate President Mattie Daughtry, owner of Moderation Brewing in Brunswick, will also seek reelection to her seat, against Republican Bernard Porter.
Read more about Brunswick candidates’ campaign goals on the Press Herald Voter Guide.

Woman murdered by Christa Pike remembered as 'computer geek' with nurturing heart
text:
Colleen Slemmer, murdered by Christa Pike, remembered as a ‘computer geek’ with a nurturing heart
A driven and caring 19-year-old packed her belongings in Florida and traveled over 500 miles to live out her dream of studying computing in Knoxville, Tennessee.
It was there, in January 1995, that Colleen Slemmer’s life was cut short. She was murdered by her 18-year-old classmate Christa Pike.
Pike was sentenced to death in 1996, and despite her attorneys’ efforts to commute her sentence, her execution date was set for last week.
But after a botched execution attempt, Pike remains alive and speaking. Since then, Slemmer’s mother, May Martinez, feels like her daughter is being left out of the narrative.
“The criminals get so much attention. Why?” Martinez told WBIR. “She has been lost in this … she’s been forgotten.”
She loved helping children
Much of Slemmer’s life was spent in her hometown of Orange Park, Florida, where she lived with her mother, stepfather and little sister, according to WVLT. Her mother described Slemmer as kind, nurturing and passionate. As a child, she had a compassionate nature, especially with children, sparked by her upbringing, Martinez told WVLT in 2025.
“Colleen loved doing things. She babysat. She loved to do anything with kids, and I think it was part of me because I had daycare for 40 years,” Martinez said.
That caring nature extended to her community as well, which was evident in her time volunteering with the Special Olympics, according to the Associated Press. She also spent time working with children with disabilities and autism, spending her lunch break feeding and playing with them, Martinez told WBIR.
Slemmer was friendly, easygoing and loved roller skating, her mother told WBIR. Slemmer’s laugh and memories with her stepfather have stayed with Martinez for years, and are brought up often when she thinks about the life her daughter could have lived.
Teachers remembered her as mild-mannered and sweet, but family and friends also highlighted her independence, her mother told WVLT. She strived to make a career out of her love for computers and technology.
“She was a computer geek to begin with. She and my husband would build and tear apart the computers constantly,” Martinez told AP. “She trusted everybody, and that was her downfall.”
A mother searches for justice
Three months after Slemmer moved to Tennessee to start at Job Corps, a federal career building program, Pike lured her to a secluded area away from campus where she and her boyfriend tortured and killed her, according to a Tennessee Supreme Court opinion. The boyfriend was also convicted in the killing.
Slemmer and her mother spoke for the last time on the night of her murder, but because of bad reception, the call was brief. When Martinez tried to call her back, Slemmer didn’t pick up, she told AP.
Phil Keith, who was the Knoxville police chief when Pike was sentenced, told WVLT he hasn’t been able to forget the details of the crime.
“I saw quite a bit, and it’s imprinted in my brain, my memory,” he said. “I’ll never forget it.”
Michelle Nowell, a Tennessee resident, said the state has “paid enough for” Pike.
“We have paid for Christa Pike, and now we’re paying for attorneys, and now we’re paying for hospital bills, and now they’re talking about lawsuits,” Nowell told CNN. “And the worst part is that Colleen has been forgotten.”
Martinez and her husband traveled from Florida to watch Pike’s execution in Nashville. She held a photo of Colleen as she stood in the gallery.
But after the curtain closed in the execution room and witnesses were asked to leave, Martinez was informed Pike had been taken to the hospital. Something had gone wrong with the execution. She would later find out Pike was still alive.
Martinez told WTLV she feels like the state failed her family. “I think the state owes me a big apology,” she said, regarding the botched execution.
Martinez is focused on one thing: Justice for her daughter.
“Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst,” Martinez told AP.
Slemmer’s family marked her birthday just last month. She would have been 51.

title: Why is there a piece of the Berlin Wall in Portland’s Old Port?
text:
In our series AskME, we explore your questions about Maine's history, culture and customs. What have you been wondering? We’ll work to find an answer. Explore the questions, or submit your own, at pressherald.com/ask-me.
On a dock in the Old Port lies a collection of remnants of the Cold War.
Three pieces of the Berlin Wall, which once divided East and West Berlin, stand on a pier just east of Portland Lobster Company. One has faded portraits of the American and Soviet Flags, and reads “A Time For Peace,” with the word “peace” in both English and Russian. Another depicts what appears to be a burning hammer and sickle.
It is the middle section, with text written after the fall of the wall in 1989, that is the most striking, with text reading, “Forget not the tyranny of this wall horrid place. Nor the love of freedom that made it fall — LAID WASTE.”
What is this relic of history doing in Maine?
According to an article from WBLM, the Portland segments of the wall were among several donated by the German government to cities across the United States. The segments were bought by the DiMillo family, owners of DiMillo’s On the Water, a floating restaurant in the Old Port, and installed nearby in 1996.
Steve DiMillo Jr. said the wall was purchased by his grandfather, Tony DiMillo. DiMillo also explained the story behind another interesting landmark near his family’s restaurant: a piece of fence covered with locks, located adjacent to the wall. DiMillo said the locks were previously part of a fence marking the boundary of the DiMillo family’s property, decorated with “locks of love.” However, the locks eventually ended up weighing down the fence, which was dismantled by the city, with the DiMillo family allowed to keep a piece of it.
“It’s one of those kind of cool things, people bring it up now and then,” said DiMillo of the Berlin Wall segment.
The remnants of the Berlin Wall in the Old Port are not Maine’s only Cold War connection. Running through South Portland is the Samantha Smith Highway, named for Maine’s young peace activist.

text:
DEAR SUN SPOTS: The residents at The Chapman House, 41 Pleasant St. in Auburn, are upgrading their community library and are asking for donations of large-print hardcover books. If you have any books to spare, we would love to give them a new home here. Thank you so much for your kindness and support! — Sheryll, Auburn
ANSWER: The Chapman House provides care to senior women who need assistance with tasks of daily living. As I was reading the newsletter, I also saw that the organization will hold its annual Holiday Craft Fair on Saturday, Nov. 14, from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. If you or someone you know would like to rent a space, please contact Sheryll at 783-0961 to RSVP. DEAR SUN SPOTS: I had something scary and stressful happen to me last week and I want to alert fellow readers to yet another scam.
I received a batch of fast and furious text messages from multiple places. They were all different and I received 217 of them in 20 minutes. I didn’t understand what was going on!
Luckily, my grandson helped me look up what was happening. While we were reading information about what to do, I received a fraud alert from my credit card company. They blocked my card immediately because all these messages were a scam — a smoke screen to distract me and try to bury the fraud alert from my bank indicating that someone else was attempting to charge $500 to my card.
I just want others to know if this happens to them to call their financial institution immediately and lock down your accounts. Do not click on or answer any of these! — Lorina, no town
ANSWER: That’s extremely stressful but it sounds like you handled it all like a champ with help from your grandson. You were experiencing a “text bomb” (also known as an SMS flood or bombing), which scammers use as a distraction technique to hide unauthorized account activity or fraudulent purchases.
When they triggered the avalanche of texts to your phone, their goal was to bury legitimate fraud alerts from your bank or credit card company so you wouldn’t notice them trying to use your credit card.
If this happens to you, dear readers, here are the immediate steps to take: freeze or lock your credit card immediately. You can open your banking app and look for a “Freeze,” “Lock,” or “Control” card option. This blocks all new transactions instantly.
Call your bank’s fraud department using the number on the back of your credit card (do not trust numbers in the text messages saying they are from your bank). Report that your card has been compromised and that you are under an active SMS bombing attack. They’ll cancel the card and issue a new one.
Check your other accounts. Scammers often use SMS bombing when they have compromised other accounts like your Amazon, PayPal, or email).
There is more you can do to clear things up. Stay tuned and I’ll continue this thread at a later time.

title: The midterms stakes are high for these 2028 presidential prospects
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — As most of the political world focuses on next month’s midterm elections, the shadow primary for the 2028 presidential contest is quietly playing out in public view.
Democratic and Republican presidential prospects have been crisscrossing the country, raising money and tapping their political connections to help boost their parties’ candidates — and their own White House ambitions.
Here’s a closer look at some of the leading prospects and how their political futures may be influenced by what happens Nov. 3.
Newsom has a Southern strategy
Gavin Newsom leaves the California governor’s office at the end of the year, and he’s been among the most active Democrats throughout the midterms.
He’s paid particular attention to the South, where he’s campaigned with candidates up and down the ballot in states like Alabama, Mississippi, North Carolina and, not surprisingly, South Carolina, which hosts the party’s first presidential primary contest in 2028.
The Southern focus aligns with the mission of Newsom’s Campaign for Democracy political action committee, which was established in 2023 to help his party compete in red states. But it could also help endear him to African American voters, who make up the heart of the Democratic base.
Newsom’s star power — and his extensive email list — has strengthened his relationships with key Democratic officials in states like Nevada and New Hampshire, where he’s sent out fundraising emails that have generated a surge of donations in recent months.
Perhaps Newsom’s biggest midterm contribution was backing Proposition 50, California’s response to the Texas Republican mid-decade gerrymander. The proposition, approved by California voters last year, created a new congressional map that may allow Democrats to pick up as many as five additional U.S. House seats in California this fall.
As a presidential candidate, the California governor could argue that he was on the front lines of the redistricting battle. But if Democrats do not win all five seats in his state, Newsom’s message could be muffled.
Vance’s fate is tied to Trump
No potential candidate’s fate is as closely tied to President Donald Trump and Republicans’ performance as Vice President JD Vance.
The 42-year-old has embarked on an aggressive midterm campaign schedule — from the Midwest, to the South, to Alaska — and focused on the administration’s efforts to root out fraud.
A key state will be Ohio, which Vance briefly represented in the Senate. Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vance’s seat in 2025, is facing an aggressive challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown. And in the governor’s race, Democrat Amy Acton is in a close contest with Republican Vivek Ramaswamy.
The effectiveness of the conservative group Turning Point Action will also be scrutinized. Erika Kirk, the widow of Turning Point co-founder Charlie Kirk and the organization’s new leader, has already endorsed Vance’s potential presidential bid and leaders have said they intend to use the group to support his campaign.
Vance has said he is not focused on running for president, but “trying to help elect Republicans.”
Shapiro is all about Pennsylvania
Among the Democrats leading the 2028 conversation, none have done less beyond their home state than Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro. He hasn’t visited any early primary states or campaigned with any midterm candidates beyond his state.
That’s by design for a 53-year-old Democrat whose selling point as a presidential candidate might be his clout in Pennsylvania, which has emerged as perhaps the most important swing state in the nation.
Shapiro is expected to cruise to reelection over his Republican challenger, state Treasurer Stacy Garrity, which has allowed him to spend his political capital elsewhere.
Shapiro has gone all in to ensure Democrats win both chambers of the state legislature in November, and he’s devoted significant time and resources to flipping four congressional seats.
If Shapiro can demonstrate strength in swing counties like Beaver, Luzerne or Erie, it could help him make a credible claim to winning back some of the working-class voters that Democrats have lost in the Trump era.
Beshear faces risk and reward
As chairman of the Democratic Governors Association, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear may have done more than any other potential candidate to boost his national profile during the midterms. He’ll headline a get-out-the-vote tour through key states, beginning with Nevada on Oct. 22.
He also spent some of the campaign on a national book tour, allowing him to cozy up to influential Democrats in early states.
Still, Beshear’s spending decisions as chief of the governors association in 2026 may present the highest risk and reward for him heading into 2028.
He’s been active in supporting Democratic candidates in traditional swing states like Wisconsin, Michigan and Arizona while pushing into Republican-leaning states like Ohio and Iowa, places he argues could be critical in the next White House campaign.
But Democrats in other states are clamoring for more resources and warning Beshear of blowback if he doesn’t deliver. Under pressure, the governors association sent $1 million this week to help the candidate for Texas governor, Gina Hinojosa.
Cruz hits the road
Texas Sen. Ted Cruz has long been one of his party’s most active campaigners and fundraisers, continuing those efforts this year as he openly weighs another presidential bid.
His Truth and Courage PAC has spent more than $2.4 million this year on ads supporting midterm candidates, according to AdImpact, mostly to help Senate candidate Ken Paxton in his home state.
Cruz has traveled three times to Iowa, the first state on Republicans’ nominating calendar and where he won the caucuses during the 2016 primary. He’ll be in Alaska next week, and is also planning trips to South Carolina, North Carolina and most likely Michigan.
Pritzker’s money plays
Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker is seeking his third term in November, but the Democrat has focused more on helping midterm candidates in other states.
Pritzker’s team says the billionaire Democrat has already donated $38 million to the party’s midterm efforts, including personal donations and roughly $20 million through his Ready for the Fight PAC, which is focused on taking down MAGA candidates, even in long shot districts.
More than other 2028 prospects, Pritzker has been focused on the Texas governor’s race, where he donated $1 million this week, on top of $200,000 he gave earlier. He’s also been active on the speaker circuit, having participated in more than 75 events across the country, including in Nevada and New Hampshire. He’s expected to visit South Carolina before Election Day as well.
AOC’s progressive politics face a test
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York has been increasingly open about a potential presidential run, where she would be a major player in the Democratic Party’s progressive lane.
But first, she’s trying to prove that her brand of politics can succeed in a presidential swing state like Michigan, where she has thrown her weight behind Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. They appeared together this week at a New York City fundraiser, and she cast his campaign as a broader test for the progressive movement.
“If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere,” Ocasio-Cortez told the audience.
Ocasio-Cortez and other Democrats have acknowledged that she’ll face questions about whether she can appeal to voters across the country. Ocasio-Cortez argues an El-Sayed victory in Michigan, which is one of the early states in the next Democratic presidential primary, could challenge some of those assumptions.
Buttigieg keeps a busy schedule
Since leaving his job as transportation secretary under President Joe Biden, Pete Buttigieg has had the luxury of free time. He has used it to aggressively travel across the country, raising money and campaigning for Democrats on the ballot this year.
Buttigieg has endorsed nearly 100 candidates this cycle, from state legislative contests to U.S. Senate races, and has appeared on the campaign trail with roughly half of them, according to his team. He has visited 37 states since leaving office.
The range of those appearances also offers a glimpse at Buttigieg’s appeal within the party.
Democrats have welcomed him even in deeply Republican territory, including Nancy Lacore, a U.S. House candidate in South Carolina who campaigned with Buttigieg in August. He also helped bring Democratic candidates together for a Michigan unity event in August after hotly contested primaries.

title: Andrew Oliver releases crime novel ‘Means and Motive’ set in western Maine
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Andrew Oliver has released his first novel, “Means and Motive,” set in the western Maine.
Book summary
“In the middle of a fierce snowstorm, a police chief in Franklin County has just stumbled upon a dead man. The body is warm, and the suspect is still nearby.
“A murder in the western Maine foothills sends police chief Jack Durant searching high and low for the perpetrator. Can he solve the case with the state Major Crimes Unit breathing down his neck? Will the fearsome weather block the investigation before it reaches fruition? And will any of this distract the chief from his broken heart?
“Means and Motive will take you on a fast-paced journey through western Maine at its most dangerous time of year, the dead of winter. Ride along with Jack Durant as he follows clues, suspects, and his heart on a pulse-pounding, non-stop race to find the truth.”
Author grew up in western Maine
Oliver lives in California, but grew up in western Maine. “Means and Motive,” is shaped by a frigid Maine winter, and features numerous western Maine locales.
“Growing up in western Maine, I experienced its unique blend of natural beauty and small-town life. Especially now, having spent some time away from Maine, I think the mountains, lakes, and endless greenery are even more inspiring. When I thought about where to place my first novel, there was no second thought in my mind, it had to be Franklin County,” Oliver said. “As far as the genre, I’ve been inspired by Maine crime and thriller novels from Paul Doiron and Stephen King, and numerous police shows and movies like Southland and The Rookie. Mixing elements of a murder mystery with the challenge and drama of the Maine winter landscape seemed like an intriguing combination.”

title: Death Notice: Ronald “Ron-Ronnie” E. Pelletier
Isaias could create higher fuel prices. Here’s why
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News) - Hurricane Isaias is forecast to miss the oil industry’s biggest hubs along the Gulf Coast but could still nudge fuel prices higher if it triggers power outages that shut down refineries for processing crude, according to industry experts.
An extended shutdown of refineries would put a crimp in fuel supplies that already have taken a hit from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Chevron’s facility in Pascagoula, Mississippi, and Vertex Energy’s refinery in Mobile, Alabama, which constitute 2.4% of the nation’s refining capacity, are at risk of flooding and power outages, said Andrew Lipow, a Houston-based oil analyst. Any problems could take the facilities offline at a time when diesel supplies are already low.
Isaias strengthened into a major hurricane Friday as it barreled toward the Gulf Coast, where final preparations were underway for potentially life-threatening storm surges and high winds.
If the storm moves through quickly and its impacts are minimal, refineries would continue to run at reduced capacity and prices for gasoline and diesel could rise just a few cents, said Carl Larry with the energy analysis firm Enverus. But if refineries such as Chevron’s shut down completely, it could take them weeks to recover and that could cause fuel prices to jump more significantly, Larry said.
“Major issues, like a power shutdown, and the prices will spike immediately. It’s possible a dollar,” he said. “Those diesel prices that already are above $6 could start approaching $7.”
Other experts said even if the refineries take a hit, the gas price impacts should be minimal.
“We’re talking about potentially under a million barrels a day, probably somewhere in the ballpark of 500,000 barrels a day, of refining capacity,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “That may have a small impact on gas prices, primarily in the Gulf Coast, but I don’t think it rises to a criteria that would impact gas prices nationally.”
Hurricane Isaias already has caused widespread shutdowns in offshore oil production across the region that provides about 15% of U.S. crude.
Personnel from 121 production platforms — about a third of the facilities in the Gulf — were evacuated, according to the federal Marine Minerals Administration.
Almost two-thirds of oil production was shut down, equal to almost 1.3 million barrels (54 million gallons) a day, the agency said. Chevron, BP and Shell were among companies that reported evacuating personnel and shutting platforms.
The storm’s impact on oil and gas prices so far is dwarfed by the effect of the conflict in the Middle East. And once the storm passes, workers will be able to return to platforms in the Gulf and quickly resume operations, barring significant damage.
“I would expect that the shut-in oil production will probably return pretty quickly within just a couple of days,” De Haan said.
Prices for Brent crude, the international standard, were above $104 a barrel Friday. That price has varied between $96 and nearly $110 over the last month driven by uncertainty over the war with Iran.

title: Norridgewock board orders noise study for burnout pit
text:
NORRIDGEWOCK — The Planning Board on Thursday heard competing accounts of a tire burnout pit that the town shut down in August for lack of a proper permit.
Some neighbors say this summer’s events, during which drivers spin their tires while keeping their vehicles largely stationary, created unbearable noise and produced obnoxious smoke.
Supporters, including some other neighbors, say those concerns are unfounded. The pit provides a safe place for auto enthusiasts to participate in a rapidly growing motorsport, they say, and keep them from tearing up public roads.
It’s now up to the planning board to retroactively approve or deny the site plan application; the asphalt pad within a family compound off Ward Hill Road, known as Jeffrey’s Automotive Battleground, has already been built.
But applicant Jeffrey Daniels, who built the burnout pit on his grandmother’s property at 23 Family Circle Drive, and those on both sides of the issue walked away Thursday evening from a well-attended, hourlong public hearing and board deliberations without a final decision.
Instead, the board’s five elected members unanimously voted to proceed with a professional noise study to help them figure out whose side to believe.
“There is a controversy about whether or not there is a noise problem,” Chair Jean Lancaster said.
In a 4-1 vote, the board also required Daniels to post $1,000 to be held in escrow for hiring the consultant, which is allowed under Norridgewock’s Site Plan Review Ordinance.
Daniels, 23, said he has already bought a decibel meter and collected his own data showing the noise cannot be the major nuisance his neighbors describe. The board agreed he could hire his own consultant to do the study, provided the person is qualified.
“At this point, I feel like I’m really wasting my time with all this, honestly,” Daniels said. “I feel like I’m just being dragged along and being told ‘no’ at the end of the day.”
The study is not expected to be conducted during a burnout event, Town Manager Richard LaBelle said.
A licensed professional will be tasked to “determine the average decibel level generated by a vehicle under average conditions,” LaBelle said, “and then take a look at topography and any other potential sound barriers to determine what the decibel level would be at the property line or any other given location.”
Thursday’s meeting drew more than 100 people — more than typically attend the annual town meeting — who filled nearly every folding chair in the Mill Stream Elementary School gymnasium.
Some were there to comment on a separate project, a proposed gun shop and shooting range on Skowhegan Road. In that case, the Planning Board also ordered a noise study, while requesting additional information and setting a November public hearing.
Hovering in the background of both applications is a proposed 180-day moratorium on certain noise-intensive nonresidential developments. The pause is aimed at giving town officials time to develop proposed noise regulations before the annual town meeting in March.
Residents will vote on the moratorium at a special town meeting Oct. 21.
The planning board’s 18 review criteria for site plan applications include a provision that “the proposed activity will not have a significant detrimental effect on adjacent land uses or other properties, which might be affected by waste, noise, glare, fumes, smoke, dust, odors or their effects.”
That’s the biggest outstanding item for Daniels’ application that the planning board has yet to decide. It has already determined his application has met the other criteria and imposed some conditions, including requirements that Daniels water down the asphalt to limit smoke, hire a sheriff’s deputy for traffic detail during events and get a contractor in place for proper waste disposal.
Other compromises discussed include requiring participants use mufflers on their vehicles, increasing the tree buffer and limiting operating hours.
Daniels’ application, submitted Aug. 5, states the pit was paved in June in an existing sandpit in the woods. It includes a 60-foot diameter asphalt pad and a 10-foot wide, 30-foot long access road, which cost about $30,000.
The pit, on the farthest part of the property from the road, is surrounded by tree-lined embankments. Jeffrey Daniels’ grandmother, 78-year-old Josephine Daniels, owns the property and several family members live there.
Code Enforcement Officer Matt Everett issued a stop work order in August. Everett, also chairman of the Norridgewock Select Board, denied that had anything to do with his June purchase of two parcels off Ward Hill Road about a half mile downhill from the Daniels compound.
The town received complaints about the pit earlier in the summer, and, at some point, asked the Danielses to stop hosting events, LaBelle said previously. Officials then saw on social media in August that Jeffrey Daniels was planning another large event, which led to the stop work order that effectively shut it down, he said.
Events were generally on Sundays and averaged about 150 attendees, Daniels’ application says. Some fairs in Maine have put on similar meets, and Daniels said people travel hours to participate.
The events Daniels hosted were family-friendly, and some were fundraisers, he said. No drugs are allowed. Participants must sign waivers. Portable toilets are brought in. Vehicle radiators must be filled with water, to prevent hazardous radiator fluid from going into the ground.
“I thought the noise people were talking about is greatly exaggerated,” Daniels said Thursday. “I realize they probably do hear it, but, if anything, I’m saying it’s probably a slight annoyance versus this extreme nuisance that they’re talking about.”
Kevin Paluch, who lives in Madison just over the town line from the Daniels property, likened the noise to “water torture.”
“This has made me a nervous wreck,” Leslie Korhonen, whose home is also just over the town line, said of the noise.
Joy Caswell, also a neighbor in Madison, said she did not appreciate being called a liar for her complaints. She said it forces her inside, and every so often, tire smoke makes it way on to her property.
“I understand what they are trying to do for the area … however, what they’re also doing to the area is not kind,” Caswell said.
Those in support of the burnout pit said it has provided them or their children with a safe place to do the activity, and Daniels enforces his rules. It is also an economic boost, they said, bringing attendees to gas stations and convenience stores in town on event days. Two who live on Ward Hill Road said the noise does not bother them at their homes.
Cody Cyr, part of the burnout pit crew, said there is far worse environmental pollution from the Waste Management landfill, paper mills in the region and a local quarry. He called the noise and pollution complaints “a load of crap.”
“There’s needles and dopeheads and crackheads and drunks all over the town of Norridgewock,” he told the board. “A burnout pit is the least of everyone’s concerns.”

title: ICE officers shot New York man because they believed they were in danger, official says
text:
ICE officers shot New York man because they believed they were in danger, official says
Federal immigration officers opened fire on a Dominican man whom they were trying to arrest in New York because they believed their lives were in danger, a senior Immigration and Customs Enforcement official said Friday.
Marcos Charles made the comments alongside U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and other immigration officials during a news conference in Washington meant to “highlight the dangerous consequences of sanctuary city policies.”
The 28-year-old man, whom New York City police identified as Oscar Belgal, was shot in the neck Thursday as he drove his car with a 5-year-old boy inside, officials said.
ICE agents didn't know the child was in the car, but Belgal “was aware” and chose to evade officers, Mullin said.
Belgal was shot “superficially” in the neck as ICE officers attempted to arrest him, Charles said.
ICE had issued a detainer on Belgal and that he runs with a gang known for thefts using weapons and mopeds, he said. Officers used vehicles to block him in as he attempted to drive off. Instead, Charles said, he accelerated his vehicle toward officers, smashing some of their vehicles.
Protesters and local officials decried the shooting as an example of the dangers of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
Video below: "No explanation": New York Mayor Mamdani addresses reporters after ICE shooting
Much of Mullin’s remarks were reserved for excoriating New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his immigration policy.
“Sanctuary politicians, they create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for the American citizens to be safe,” he said.
Mullin said ICE has requested more than 14,000 detainers in the state of New York for individuals in local custody that they’re seeking to deport.
“Silence. Absolute silence is what we have gotten back,” he said. “Why would they release these individuals back onto the streets?”
“We’re enforcing our nation’s laws. We’re not picking and choosing,” Mullin continued. “Why is that controversial? We should all want law and order on our streets.”

title: UMaine TPUSA hosts “Pick Up the Mic” debate, students react
text:
The University of Maine’s Turning Point USA (TPUSA) chapter held a debate on the Mall on Thursday, Oct. 8 as part of their “Pick Up the Mic” initiative. The event featured Savannah Craven as speaker and encouraged students to ask questions and participate in a discussion. The event drew a large crowd and officers from the University of Maine Police Department (UMPD) were on standby throughout the debate.
Molly Curtis, a third year nursing student and president of UMaine’s TPUSA chapter, expanded on the purpose and results of the event.
“I think the point of a ‘prove me wrong’ [TPUSA’s slogan] is more to bridge the gap [between ideas],” said Curtis. “I think it went exactly like we wanted it to go. You know, a lot of people asking questions, and the discussion was very rich.”
Curtis said that topics of discussion ranged from abortion to immigration.
Payton Warren, a third year finance and management student and president of UMaine College Republicans, stated that abortion was the primary topic of conversation because of a viral clip of Craven being hit by another woman during a street interview on the topic. Curtis added that the discussion mostly remained civil with the exception of a few minor incidents.
“Some people did a little drive-by, flip off or cuss word, but other than that, nobody came up and was obscene,” said Curtis.
“There was a few people yelling,” said Warren. “People just walked by and yelled and then left.”
Other students interviewed by the Maine Campus commented on the event’s reception. Jessica Murphy, a first year biology student, and Matthew Cooper, a fourth year wildlife ecology and marine science student, stated that they were unable to hear the speaker at times due to obscene language being shouted at her.
“There were people behind me calling the speaker slurs,” said Murphy. “You can disagree with someone but still not want to harm them.”
“I was next to people who were holding signs and making comments and jeering, and not overall saying very nice things,” said Cooper. “I did hear people saying slurs about her [Craven] and saying things like, ‘how can you as an xyz say these things?’ They’re using identity politics. I don’t think that’s okay.”
Murphy stated that she had intended to talk to Craven during the debate, but wound up being in line behind the last person allowed to participate.
“I was gonna ask if a ten year old got raped and needed an abortion, what would you do in that situation, because it seems cruel to have them deliver the baby,” said Murphy. “I knew she was gonna say that she would make them deliver the baby, but what would she do to support the ten year old? Because that just seems like an extremely traumatic experience.”
Menelik Mekonen, a graduate student studying math, explained that the audience may have had a difficult time hearing Craven because the microphone was turned off part way through the event.
“The speakers were originally on earlier on, but I think students in nearby classrooms were complaining about the noise so they had to turn off the speakers, and so most people weren’t even sure what was being discussed,” said Mekonen.
Warren confirmed Mekonen’s explanation about why the speakers were turned off.
Mekonen stated that he had been able to participate in the debate, but had been cut off abruptly. He was also concerned about the level of transparency TPUSA would convey in their video footage.
“The footage isn’t going to be fully publicly available, it’s gonna be clipped up and chopped into bits,” said Mekonen. He added that much of what Craven said seemed to be designed for social media content rather than discussion at the debate itself. “I’m interested to see how the final product is going to come out.”
Craven declined to comment.

title: Inflatable pumpkin tumbles into traffic, forces driver to swerve
text:
DUBUQUE, Iowa (KCRG/Gray News) — A giant inflatable pumpkin got loose and tumbled through downtown Dubuque on Tuesday afternoon, bumping into parked cars and forcing an SUV to swerve out of the way on Main Street.
“This is not AI-generated. This actually truly happened, and I was the car involved in this,” Pam McCarron said. “I think I was pretty calm, but you don’t see that every day.”
Driver describes the moment
McCarron said she did not expect the inflatable pumpkin to come flying toward her in the wind on her way to a work meeting on Tuesday.
“Is it gonna hit me? Is it gonna hit my car? Is it gonna like go over my car?” McCarron said. “It’s big enough that I couldn’t see around it to know if there was anything on the other side, when [the inflatable] was on the other side of the street. I was like, I don’t know if there’s a car coming.”
Police react to traffic camera video
Dubuque Police Lt. Luke Bock first saw the traffic camera video on Facebook on Thursday morning.
“Immediately I was like, hey, that looks like one of our traffic cameras,” Bock said. “Then I was like, boy, that’s a big pumpkin, so obviously the police officer side of me was like, we don’t really need those things bouncing down the roadway.”
Bock said he can laugh at the video because there was no oncoming traffic at the time.
“It’s entertaining. Like it’s funny to watch it, but you just, I guess, a lot of times you think about what could have happened, what if?” Bock said.
Bock said incidents like this can happen when decorations are not properly grounded.
“We would just ask that you follow the manufacturer’s instructions,” said Bock. “Secure them down to your yard, so that something like this doesn’t happen and we don’t see somebody swerve and potentially get in a crash or obstruct our highways, or hit somebody that’s walking down the roadway.”
A Dubuque homeowner’s experience
Jennifer Edwards said large inflatables can be difficult to stake down.
She is hosting her eighth year of month-long trick-or-treating on Fridays and Saturdays from 5 to 9 p.m. at her home, 3750 Mount Alpine Street, barring bad weather. Her decorations do not include inflatables, despite using them in previous years.
“Safety is a big, big, big concern. Inflatables are really hard to keep staked. They’re really hard to get them to level out and balance them, so we took it out,” Edwards said.
McCarron said the flying pumpkin should serve as a reminder to make sure decorations are stable. She said she now has one question.
“What’s going to pop up today? Like, you know, what’s it going to be, like, you know, Frankenstein or something?” McCarron said.

title: State gives Harrison more time to decide on withdrawal from school district
text:
The Maine Department of Education has awarded the town of Harrison an extension on its petition to withdraw from Maine School Administrative District 17, based in Paris.
Harrison began considering withdrawal two years ago after learning that building an elementary school in the Oxford Hills school district would mean schools in Harrison, Norway and Waterford would close and consolidate into one facility, most likely in Norway.
In January 2025, the town seated a committee of residents, led by Selectperson Deb Kane, to determine education options that would: allow its youngest students to continue attending Harrison Elementary School; potentially join other area districts; or maintain school independence with its middle and high school students going to other districts on a tuition basis.
In June, a majority of Harrison residents voted to create a formal withdrawal committee to conduct a 22-step research process to withdraw from MSAD 17.
The process does not mean the town will withdraw; officials may decide at any time to abandon the committee’s work and stay in the district.
Harrison has reached step seven of the process: convening a committee appointed by town officials, with one school board liaison.
Kane is the committee chair, Amy Gerry is vice chair and Andrea Lavery is secretary. All served on the town’s education options committee. Mark Curran, vice chair of the MSAD 17 board of directors, is the liaison.
The next step, which is to negotiate a withdrawal agreement, cannot begin until a number of contingencies within the district are determined.
Harrison is watching the progress of the district’s elementary school construction committee, which is between steps six and seven of a separate 21-step process mandated by DOE for state-funded construction projects. That step, which is selecting the site of a new school, is being repeated after real estate negotiations on the district’s first choice broke down and were abandoned.
The board of directors authorized interim Superintendent Jonathon Ross to enter into negotiations with the owner of a second location at its Oct. 8 business meeting.
One contingency affecting Harrison is the new elementary school’s location. If the site requires children as young as 4 or 5 to ride a bus 45 minutes or more twice a day, the withdrawal committee is likely to move forward. Long transportation routes are among the biggest objections Harrison residents have to a new school in Norway.
But location choices are limited. A new school needs to have a certain acreage per number of students and have access to three-phase electricity and public utility services, among other requirements.
Town officials are also highly concerned with maintaining a community-based elementary school, which they see as a draw for young families moving to Harrison. If a majority of voters from the eight district towns vote to approve the new school, it could tip the scales toward withdrawal for Harrison.
During the Oct. 1 meeting, Curran confirmed to the committee that MSAD 17 owns Harrison Elementary School and would be under no obligation to transfer it to the town, as it did with Agnes Gray Elementary School to West Paris and is likely to do with Waterford Memorial School in that town.
West Paris and Waterford owned their elementary schools before joining the district. Harrison Elementary, however, was built by the district.
Besides Harrison, Waterford, Norway and West Paris, the other district towns are Hebron Otisfield, Oxford and Paris.
Leaving the district would also result in Harrison losing all state funding for its special education, expenses that would have to be paid from local taxpayer shares in the future. It would also require Harrison to hire teachers, support staff and administrators, including a part-time superintendent.
In September, the Maine Department of Education granted an extension to Harrison, giving it time to see how school construction plans progress over the next several months. Kane told the committee that the state will allow the town to request multiple extensions if necessary.
If the school construction project advances to a districtwide referendum, the issue will likely be on the ballot in June 2027.
Harrison’s committee would then determine whether to continue the process to withdraw from the district.
The committee meets again Nov. 5 at the Harrison Town Office, 20 Front St.

title: Key money lessons parents should teach teens before college
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — For a young adult stepping into college or a first job, financial decisions can feel overwhelming. Teresa Murray, a consumer watchdog with US PIRG, said that makes financial planning for teens and young adults especially important.
“We’re kind of assuming here that once somebody’s in high school or going off to college, that their parents have already taught them a little bit about needs versus wants and being able to budget your spending, not blowing your allowance every week,” Murray said. “But it’s always important for young adults, high schoolers going off to college, to be able to figure out needs versus wants and avoid the impulse spending.”
One key lesson, Murray said, is helping young adults understand how credit works and how long it follows them.
“You need to explain to them, like, hey, your credit history lives with you for a while,” Murray said. “If you have a lousy credit score, once you graduate from college, you’re going to have difficulty renting an apartment no matter how good of a job you have, without having a co-signer.”
Murray said another overlooked lesson is the connection between sharing too much personal information online and financial risk.
“They have open accounts, open profiles with Facebook or Instagram or whatever, and they’re spraying it all over the place,” Murray said. “It’s about protecting your personal information, which could end up hurting you financially, but it’s also about protecting your safety and the safety of those around you.”
Murray said simply keeping track of spending, even informally, helps young adults understand how quickly costs add up.
“Even if they’re using cash, they should just jot it down,” Murray said. “Just have a note on your phone that you keep track of your expenses. Round them off — you don’t have to have it exactly to the penny. And then you look back and you’re like, ‘Oh, dang, I had this and I had this.’ It adds up quickly.”
Budgeting, credit, privacy and tracking spending are small habits that can pay off for years to come, according to Murray.
The FDIC also offers tips for parents on its website, including information on youth banking programs — partnerships between schools and banks that allow students to open a real savings account and begin building good money habits while still in the classroom.

title: Friday’s high school football: Edward Little falls to Windham
text:
Windham quarterback Patrick Davenport finished with three rushing touchdowns and another on the ground, leading Windham to a 34-9 win over Edward Little in a Class A North football game Friday in Auburn.
Landon Wyman scored two touchdowns — one rushing, one receiving.
Windham (3-3) led 7-0 after one quarter, thanks to a 12-yard scamper by Davenport.
Alexander Gagnon kicked a 23-yard field goal for Edward Little (2-3) at the beginning of the second quarter, but Wyman scored on a 15-yard reverse late in the quarter for a 14-3 halftime lead.
Davenport extended the margin in the third quarter with TD runs of 11 and 71 yards.
Evan Madigan scored EL’s only touchdown from 3 yards early in the fourth quarter. Wyman capped the scoring by catching a 60-yard pass from Davenport.
LEAVITT 48, GARDINER 7: Darren Flagg scored five touchdowns and intercepted two passes as the unbeaten Hornets (6-0) cruised to another dominating victory, beating the Tigers (3-3) in Gardiner.
Leavitt, ranked seventh in the Varsity Maine poll, has outscored its last four opponents 177-7.
Flagg scored on runs of 4 and 47 yards, caught 12- and 27-yard touchdown passes from Landon Marquis, and returned an interception 35 yards for a score.
Brody Poland (5-yard run) and Jeremiah McKenzie (15-yard run) also scored for the Hornets.
Flagg intercepted a pass late in the first half. His pick-6, which was first tipped by linebacker Jamison L’Italien, was one of three interceptions by Leavitt in the third quarter. Trey Hinkley had the other two, which both set up touchdowns.
L’Italien recovered a fumble forced by Jackson Brooks late in the first half and returned it to the Gardiner 26. Marquis and Flagg connected for a TD on the next play. Owen Thompson added a fourth-quarter interception.
Gardiner scored in the first quarter on a 24-yard halfback pass from Justin Doody to Isaac Marquis.

title: Woman suing funeral home says wrong body was placed in mother’s casket
text:
HORRY COUNTY, S.C. (WMBF/Gray News) — A South Carolina woman has filed a lawsuit alleging a funeral home put the wrong body in her mother’s casket.
Iris Gordon of Horry County filed the lawsuit Tuesday against Ocean View Funeral Home and Cremation Services, located on Carver Street near Graham Avenue.
Funeral arrangements made after mother’s death
Gordon’s mother, 87-year-old Iris Evans, died Jan. 14. After her mother’s death, Gordon contacted Ocean View and met with Atu Williams, one of the owners, to make funeral arrangements, according to the lawsuit.
Gordon had a contract with Ocean View and paid $13,820.55 for funeral services. She gave Williams her mother’s black and gold African attire, scarf, hat, wig and undergarments, the lawsuit said.
The viewing was held at Ocean View Funeral Home Conway Chapel on Grainer Road in Conway on Jan. 30. The funeral was held at True Worship United Pentecostal Church on Main Street in Conway on Jan. 31, according to the lawsuit.
Wrong body found in casket
At around 3 p.m. at Ocean View, Gordon and other family members arrived and saw that the body in the casket was not Evans, but an unknown person wearing her provided attire, the lawsuit said.
Gordon told Ocean View staff members, and Williams was contacted. In a phone call, Williams admitted Ocean View had made a mistake, according to the lawsuit.
The viewing was rescheduled for 5 p.m. that afternoon, and Evans was in the casket at that time, the lawsuit said.
Damages sought
Gordon claimed she suffered emotional distress, mental anguish, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, depression and loss of the ability to sleep soundly because of the incident.
Gordon requested $13,820.55, the cost of the funeral, along with other damages.
Ocean View has not responded.

title: Two powerful earthquakes and multiple aftershocks rock Panama
text:
PANAMA CITY (AP) — Two powerful 7.7 and 6.6 magnitude earthquakes and a series of aftershocks struck Panama Friday afternoon, collapsing buildings near the epicenter and prompting evacuations across the country, the U.S. Geological Survey said.
The earlier quake, felt as far away as neighboring Colombia, was centered about 10 kilometers (6 miles) southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, in the central province of Herrera, the USGS said. It struck at a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles).
The USGS initially reported the first quake as magnitude 8, then revised it to 7.6 and later to 7.7.
Visibly shaken residents of Panama City gathered outside as they waited for news of the quake’s impact on Friday.
“We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we’re okay, though we’re very scared,” Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared.”
Multiple aftershocks continued to rattle Panama, including several measuring magnitude 5.8, 5.5 and 5.2. Seismologists at the University of Panama recorded more than 45 aftershocks, though many were too weak to be felt.
Calls for calm and reports of collapsed buildings
Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino called for calm on Friday, writing on X: “What happened should not be used to cause alarm or disorder.”
Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service said on the Telemetro Reporta news channel that damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos. He said there were no reports of damage in the capital, which is known for its hundreds of skyscrapers.
Smith said several injuries have been reported, including one person struck by debris from a partially collapsed structure in the city of Penonomé, around 93 miles (150 km) from the capital. He confirmed a partial collapse and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage in the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel. No casualties were immediately reported.
Local news outlets also reported that the Church of San Atanasio, a colonial-style Catholic church in Panama’s Los Santos province, had collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938. Elsewhere, including in Veraguas province, large fissures ran along roadways.
Tocumen International Airport in Panama City, one of the region’s busiest airports with more than 20 million travelers in 2025, said it would temporarily suspend operations and activated evacuation plans. It said operations would resume once security conditions have been checked.
The Panama Canal Authority said operations were continuing normally along the key global trade route. It said its priority was the safety of employees, vessels and crews and that specialized technical teams were inspecting facilities for possible damage.
Tsunami warnings as far as Chile’s Easter Island
The last major earthquake to cause widespread damage in Panama struck in 1991. A magnitude 7.4 quake, centered in nearby Costa Rica killed 23 people, injured 559, and left thousands of people homeless in the border Bocas de Toro region.
Earthquakes are common, especially along Panama’s border with Costa Rica and its Pacific coast, because of the interaction of several tectonic plates, including Cocos, Nazca, and Caribbean plates.
Panama lies along the “Ring of Fire,” a 40,000-kilometer (25,000-mile) arc of volcanoes and fault lines around the Pacific Basin, where most of the world’s earthquakes occur.
The National Weather Service issued a tsunami warning Friday for the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua and Guatemala. It warned that waves ranging from 3 to 9 feet (1 to 3 meters) above tide may occur in some coastal areas of Panama.
Alerts were also issued in El Salvador and as far as Chile’s Easter Island, about 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles) off Chile’s mainland coast. Chile’s government placed the island under a precautionary advisory.
Nearby countries sent messages of support Friday afternoon. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, whose country was recently hit by earthquakes, expressed his solidarity with the Panamanian people and their government during what he called “difficult times.”
“Panama is not alone! You can count on Colombia’s support and our full willingness to provide whatever assistance is needed,” he wrote on X.
The U.S. Embassy in Panama said it was “closely monitoring” the aftermath of the quake and accounting for the welfare of its citizens in Panama, a well-known retirement destination for Americans.
___
Janetsky reported from Mexico City, and Solís reported from Panama City. Gabriela Molina in Quito, Ecuador, Clara Preve in Buenos Aires, Argentina, Eléonore Hughes in Rio de Janeiro, María Verza in Mexico City and Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, contributed.

title: Firefighter killed, 2 others hurt fighting massive fire in North Carolina
text:
DURHAM, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A firefighter was killed and two others were injured while battling a fire in central North Carolina, officials said.
The North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation confirmed the Durham firefighter’s death and the injuries in an Oct. 8 social media post.
A picture in the agency’s post showed large flames coming from the roof of a building. Investigators later said the blaze was on Marly Drive in Durham, near Highway 70.
Officials said part of the building’s roof collapsed, causing the second floor to collapse. Several firefighters were trapped on the first floor during the collapse.
Officials have not said what caused the fire.
Marly Drive is about 10 minutes southeast of downtown Durham, between Raleigh and Durham.
After the firefighter’s death was announced, fire departments across the state expressed support, including departments in the Charlotte area.
“This heartbreaking loss serves as a stark reminder of the dangers firefighters face every time they answer the call,” Matthews Fire and EMS said on social media. “Behind every uniform is a family, friends, and loved ones who pray for their safe return home. Please join us in keeping the fallen firefighter’s family, friends, and fellow firefighters in your thoughts and prayers.”
