title: President Trump's memorial arch faces new lawsuit from Arlington County, Virginia
text:
Trump's Triumphal Arch faces first government lawsuit as Arlington County, Virginia, challenges project
The Arlington County Board in Virginia filed a lawsuit Thursday opposing the construction of the Triumphal Arch, becoming the first governmental body to take legal action against President Donald Trump's planned monument.
The lawsuit, filed in the Eastern District of Virginia, criticized the speed at which the project slated for Memorial Circle has moved without going through the full review process.
"The National Park Service, the agency responsible for projects on national park land such as Memorial Circle, is proceeding full-speed toward ground-disturbing construction," the lawsuit said. "Although the agency has claimed that a final decision to construct the Arch has not yet been made and purports to be engaged in a routine decisional process, that rushed process appears to be a pretext designed to shore up justifications for building the Arch in accordance with the President's repeated marching orders."
The lawsuit asks that "the agency's feverish pace toward construction of the arch" be halted to ensure that the requirements of the National Environmental Policy Act be followed and proper analysis and testing be done.
"The Arlington County Board has filed this lawsuit because our community has the most to lose from this egregious and unlawful proposed project," Arlington County Board Chair Matt de Ferranti said in a statement. He added that the county has acted in good faith in the review process, pointing out the "severe, unique, and wide-ranging negative impacts" the project will have on the county and its residents, only to see them ignored.
The county is being represented in the lawsuit by legal advocacy group Democracy Forward.
The White House and Interior Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The lawsuit comes just a day after Association of Flight Attendants-CWA President Sara Nelson expressed concerns that the 250-foot (76-meter) arch compounds multiple safety issues that she said have gone unaddressed since a deadly January 2025 crash over the Potomac River that killed 67 people. Nelson also criticized Trump's plan to turn the arch into "a top grade military complex" able to host drones and snipers while storing ammunition.
Though the arch has received early approval from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts, whose members were all tapped by Trump, a group of three veterans and an architectural historian sued in federal court in Washington, D.C., saying the project needs to be approved by Congress.
The arch is one of several projects around Washington that Trump has undertaken as he remakes the city, from renovating one of its storied public golf courses to threatening to demolish the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

title: How candidates for governor would change Maine healthcare policy
text:
Policy experts have warned that Mainers are facing a cliff in affordable, accessible healthcare. About 31,000 Maine residents could lose MaineCare coverage as the result of federal cuts to Medicaid, while some 78,000 could be subject to new work requirements. Residents of Maine’s most rural counties could be hit hardest by these cuts.
Parts of the state are already facing diminishing services: Maine has the second-highest rate of maternity unit closures since 2020 in the country. The scheduled closure this December of MaineHealth Lincoln Hospital’s labor and delivery unit in Damariscotta will mark the 12th such closure since 2015.
The Maine Medical Association, which represents doctors, has called for significant reforms to the U.S. healthcare system, saying that it fails patients and physicians in multiple ways: Healthcare is too expensive; inequities in access fall largely on marginalized groups; and doctors are overburdened with paperwork that takes away from patient care. The association supports federally backed universal health insurance coverage but, acknowledging that it is unlikely in the near term, called on Maine officials to work toward statewide universal health insurance coverage.
Ahead of next month’s election, The Maine Monitor reviewed the three gubernatorial candidates’ healthcare policy proposals. All three — independent Rick Bennett, Republican Bobby Charles and Democrat Hannah Pingree — called for increased Medicaid reimbursements for providers, intensifying efforts to recruit new providers to the state and incentivizing established providers to remain. Bennett and Pingree aligned on several points, including working toward universal health insurance coverage, while Charles has opposed Medicaid expansion and was an outlier on issues such as abortion, addiction response and alleged Medicaid fraud.
Here’s a look at what the candidates have said about how they would tackle the most pressing issues in healthcare.
Rick Bennett
Maine should have an “affordable, accessible and stable” healthcare system, according to Bennett’s four-point healthcare policy proposal. He believes Maine can stop hemorrhaging rural healthcare services in part by increasing MaineCare reimbursements, investing in primary and preventative care, and through medical debt relief and universal healthcare.
“It’s very grim what’s happening in rural Maine in particular, but across the whole healthcare system,” Bennett told The Monitor in a September interview. “We’re losing scores of providers.”
Bennett claimed that public trust in MaineCare, the state’s Medicaid program, has diminished due to what he sees as mismanagement and a lack of transparency and accountability. MaineCare reimbursements for covered services do not adequately cover facilities’ costs to provide those services, nor does the state provide reimbursements in a timely manner, he said, which has led several providers to close.
“The very first thing I’ll do is pay our providers fairly and on time,” he said.
The independent, who until last year was a registered Republican, said that Maine operates on an “upside-down system” that spends more money on emergency and crisis services than on primary and preventative care.
He suggested that Maine could do more to build and retain its healthcare workforce through programs such as making Doctors for Maine’s Future, a scholarship program for students enrolled in eligible Maine-based medical school programs, a permanent allocation in the state budget.
Bennett said as governor he would launch a medical debt relief program, starting with an initial $2 million investment and a partnership with a national nonprofit organization that specializes in medical debt relief. He also said Maine’s abortion laws are working well, and he supports “the right of every woman to choose the kind of healthcare and reproductive care that she wishes.”
Among those who have endorsed Bennett are Rep. Lydia Crafts, a Democrat who formerly served on the Maine Recovery Council; Augusta city councilor and Maine Recovery Access Project Executive Director Courtney Gary-Allen; and the Brett M. Staples Brain Disorder Awareness Coalition.
Bobby Charles
Charles, the Republican nominee for governor, has focused primarily on what he claims is rampant fraud and mismanagement within the Maine Department of Health and Human Services, which accounts for nearly half of the state’s budget and oversees child welfare, disease prevention, public assistance and more.
Unlike the other two candidates for governor, Charles has not published a detailed healthcare policy plan. But at the top of his 20-point plan to “restore transparency and protect Maine taxpayers,” Charles said as governor he would fire all Department of Health and Human Services leaders, mid-level program managers deemed “ideological” and others involved in “corrupt contracting.”
He would also plan to slash the Department of Health and Human Services’ budget in half.
“The government has really, fundamentally, in my view, mismanaged healthcare in this state,” Charles told The Monitor. “The bills have not been paid on time. The reimbursement levels are not where they belong in order to keep a hospital moving forward.”
Charles said Maine needs to do a better job getting healthcare professionals to come to Maine by making it an attractive and affordable place to live, particularly for families. Reducing housing costs and taxes, improving schools and increasing medical residency opportunities are among the ways to do this, Charles told The Monitor.
Charles also has strong views about how the state can address substance use. He believes the state needs to do more to crack down on the illicit drug supply and end harm reduction programs in the state. Rather than focus on the distribution of sterile syringes, he said the state should ensure every person who has an overdose reversed by naloxone is immediately sent to a seven-day detoxification program, followed by a 60- to 90-day residential treatment program.
Charles often points to his time leading the U.S. State Department’s Bureau of International Narcotics and Law Enforcement Affairs under President George W. Bush as part of his crime-fighting resume. Federal auditors found the bureau under Charles’ leadership was mired in poor management.
Charles told NEWS CENTER Maine earlier this year that abortion is “abhorrent.” In an interview with the Christian Civic League in June, he said he could convince any pregnant woman to not have an abortion.
Vice President JD Vance campaigned with Charles in Brewer in September. Former House speaker Newt Gingrich and the National Rifle Association have both endorsed Charles.
Hannah Pingree
Pingree, the Democratic nominee, has a three-pronged healthcare plan that focuses on establishing a public health insurance option, expanding and maintaining healthcare access particularly in rural areas, and strengthening the “basic needs that form the foundation of healthy lives,” such as housing and food security.
Pingree said her work as director of the Governor’s Office for Policy Innovation and the Future and the eight years she spent in the state Legislature make her well-suited to tackle these issues.
The office, which was established during Gov. Janet Mills’ first term, serves as the policy hub for the administration’s initiatives on opioid response, aging, housing development and more. Pingree served as director for six years, leaving last year before launching her gubernatorial campaign. In the Legislature, she was chair of the health and human services committee and served as speaker of the House for two years.
Maine needs a public health insurance option in which the state would negotiate with insurance providers for better rates, Pingree said. This option would not replace Medicaid or private or employer-provided insurance. Maine is facing a healthcare crisis, she told The Monitor, as the result of federal cuts to Medicare and Medicaid. Meanwhile, healthcare services in rural areas are diminishing, particularly when it comes to maternity and primary care.
Pingree spoke out against the closure of the maternity unit at Lincoln Hospital earlier this year. She also said that reproductive rights, including abortion access, should be enshrined in the state Constitution.
Maine needs to “incentivize primary care,” she said, which it can do by increasing Medicaid reimbursement rates and recruiting more primary care providers to the state.
It’s also about making Maine a place where people want to settle down and raise their families, she said.
“We’re the oldest state in the country. We desperately need families,” she said. “Whether it’s ensuring that you can have a baby in certain counties in Maine or ensuring that you can access child care, we need a greater focus on ensuring that families feel comfortable and safe making a life here in the state of Maine.”
Pingree has received endorsements from a number of healthcare and public safety organizations, including Planned Parenthood, Giffords PAC, Maine Gun Safety Coalition and Reproductive Freedom For All. She has also received endorsements from Mills, U.S. Sen. Angus King, the current and two former Maine Department of Health and Human Services commissioners, and the director of the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention.
Reporter Matt Junker contributed reporting by interviewing the candidates.
This story was originally published by The Maine Monitor, a nonprofit and nonpartisan news organization. To get regular coverage from The Monitor, sign up for a free Monitor newsletter here.

title: State support is critical step in PCHC turnaround work
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Lori Dwyer is president and CEO of Penobscot Community Health Care.
We are in receipt of incredible news from Gov. Janet Mills and her leadership team. They have identified an additional $2.8 million investment in Penobscot Community Health Care through the Rural Health Transformation Program. These funds will help ensure the future of PCHC and our critical work for the people of Maine. Specifically, they will increase the support for our transition earlier this year to a new electronic medical records system and to alternative payment models.
With this investment, PCHC is no longer pursuing an imminent Chapter 11 filing. That is a significant step forward. But the next 12 months will be critical, and we have a great deal of work ahead to put PCHC on solid financial ground.
On behalf of everyone at Penobscot Community Health Care, I want to thank Gov. Mills for her leadership and her commitment to the patients we serve. The governor, her team, and the Department of Health and Human Services worked tirelessly to find a path forward. They were able to help us efficiently and in a targeted manner while requiring accountability on our part.
We know these are public dollars, and we take that very seriously. We look forward to working closely with DHHS, providing regular updates and being fully accountable for how these funds are used.
Our work is not finished. In fact, we have asked the following trusted and very experienced Mainers and community health center experts to serve on a Turnaround Advisory Council to help us recover and reinvent how we approach financial strategy so that we can best meet our mission. Among them are Dr. Guy Hudson, CEO of Northern Light Health; Troy Trejo, CEO of Encompass Health Rehabilitation Hospital of Bangor; and Dr. Margaret Flinter, senior vice president and clinical director at Community Health Center Inc.
As we look ahead, I must take a moment to acknowledge PCHC’S incredible staff. Through all of this, their work has not stopped. Every day, they deliver extraordinary care to roughly 50,000 Mainers, many of whom have nowhere else to turn. They should be incredibly proud of themselves for keeping their eye on their mission. I know I am.
I also want to thank the legislators from across Maine who signed on in support of PCHC and our patients. They stood with us when it mattered. We look forward to continuing that work with the Legislature and the next governor beginning in 2027 to secure PCHC’s long-term future. Our patients deserve nothing less.

title: Shifting school start times could address teen sleep loss, research says
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) — School in many districts across the country begins before sunrise, a schedule doctors say runs counter to how teenage brains are wired to sleep.
School did not always start this early. During the 1950s and 1960s, U.S. schools started between 8:30 and 9 a.m. because most children could walk or bike to a neighborhood school.
By the 1970s and 1980s, as suburbs spread out and commutes got longer, districts shifted to earlier hours and riding the school bus became the norm for many students. According to the urban planning website Planetizen, “as driving became the norm, so did early start times.”
In the 1960s, 42% of kids usually walked or biked to school. In recent years, that number has dropped to as low as 11%, according to the BikePGH Guide: The Decline of Walking and Bicycling.
With more research linking early start times to teen sleep loss, some communities are trying to move the clock forward.
A father’s perspective
Dr. Hanley Chiang is the father of a sixth grader in St. Louis Public Schools. Chiang said his son’s day starts at 5:50 a.m. to catch a 6:30 bus to get to school by the 7:15 start time.
“It’s always a process to get him out of bed,” Chiang said. “He is drowsy in the morning but he tends to perk up within half an hour.”
Chiang said perking up is not a reality for all kids. Chiang is also a social scientist who has studied teen sleep patterns for years.
According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, the average teenager has difficulty falling asleep before 11 p.m. Chiang advocates for middle and high school students to start school later.
“Many students in the district and around the nation are really struggling in their first period class,” Chiang said.
Some students say they see the struggle in the classroom. Elijah Morrow is a student at Huron High School in Ann Arbor, Michigan.
“First period is usually the worst,” he said. “You can see around the room a lot of kids have their head down and are sleeping.”
Experts cite recommended start times
The American Academy of Pediatrics and American Academy of Sleep Medicine both recommend middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. to give teens a better chance at the sleep their brains and bodies need.
More districts are revisiting the question as schools try to improve attendance, learning and student well-being following the pandemic.
Ann Gallagher is president of the board of directors for the advocacy group Start School Later.
“The 8:30 benchmark was determined through research,” Gallagher said. “If schools start at a particular time, overall the health indicators for that population of students increase, injury rates go down.”
Pediatricians recommend teens ages 13 to 18 get eight to 10 hours of sleep a night to support cognitive development, emotional regulation and physical growth.
Pulmonologist Dr. Humam Farah said sleep deprivation can take a toll on teens.
“Sleep deprivation contributes to poor academic performance, low concentration, increased risk of accidents on the road and depression and anxiety,” Farah said.
Farah said part of the problem is biology.
He said preadolescents become teenagers when their circadian rhythms, which help living things respond to changes in their environment, shift later. This biological change causes teens to feel sleepy later at night and want to wake up later in the morning.
Morrow said sleep does not come easy.
“You can do everything right. Put your screens away, read, relax, and sometimes you just can’t fall asleep,” Morrow said.
Morrow said there is only one way to make up the difference.
“So the question of what will kids do with the extra time? Sleep,” Morrow said.
Logistics complicate the shift
Moving the bell is not simple.
The National Education Association supports later start times, but an article published in NEA Today said, “A shift of 30 minutes or even an hour later means that students will finish their day later than 3 p.m. That triggers a domino effect for everything from after-school activities and programs, parents’ work schedules, childcare arrangements, and after-school jobs.”
The same article cited issues with bus schedules and existing driver shortages. According to the Economic Policy Institute, there were more than 21,000 fewer bus drivers employed in August 2025 compared to six years earlier.
Gallagher said those concerns are real, but districts that plan with the community have found ways to make it work.
“When school districts take those apparent obstacles into consideration they become non-obstacles,” Gallagher said. “Communities find ways to have before and after care that matches the needs of the community and after-school practices align with students’ awake time.”
Districts already making changes
In Clark County, Nevada, the nation’s fifth-largest school district, leaders approved a new schedule that pushes the high school day 30 minutes later.
Superintendent Jhone Ebert said the adjustment is intended to boost academic performance, improve attendance and support mental health.
“Improvement in mental health, which we care deeply about. Increased sleep reduces rates of depression, anxiety, and behavior problems. By moving the high school start time to a later time, we aren’t just giving our high school students a break. We’re giving them a fighting chance to succeed,” Ebert said.
In St. Louis, district leaders are weighing a move to later start times for middle and high schools, possibly as early as the 2027-2028 school year, to give them time to work out funding and other logistics.
“I sense that the district leadership and the board are very interested in finding a solution to this issue,” Chiang said.
As more communities weigh the tradeoffs, supporters say the question is whether districts can balance logistics with what doctors say teens need most: sleep.
“We cannot educate them if they are not safe and healthy,” Gallagher said.
Doctors recommend sleep habits at home
American Academy of Sleep Medicine board member Dr. Emerson Wickwire suggests keeping bedtime and wake time about the same, even on weekends.
“For adults the minimum recommended duration of sleep is 7-8 hours children depending on their ages, require significantly more sleep,” Wickwire said.
According to Johns Hopkins Medicine, starting the day in sunshine, such as having breakfast outside or by a sunny window, helps regulate the body’s clock.
Doctors also recommend banning tech from the bedroom. Using tech at night cuts into a teen’s sleep time and exposes them to a type of light that suppresses melatonin, a sleep-inducing hormone.
Doctors say a short nap of around 20 to 30 minutes can help if a teen is exhausted, but it should be early enough that it does not delay bedtime.

title: Maine Sunday Telegram, Portland Press Herald and reporters receive top New England newspaper awards
text:
The Maine Sunday Telegram, Portland Press Herald and two reporters have been honored with top awards at the New England Newspaper & Press Association’s annual fall conference.
The 2026 New England Newspaper Awards were announced Friday at a summit in Sturbridge, Massachusetts, hosted by the New England Newspaper & Press Association. The organization is the professional trade organization for newspapers in Connecticut, Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont.
The Portland Press Herald won first place for New England Newspaper of the Year for large circulation weekday publications, and the Maine Sunday Telegram won first place for New England Newspaper of the Year for large circulation Sunday publications.
“The newspaper of the year awards are a testament to the hard work of our entire newsroom staff,” said Scott Monroe, managing editor of the Maine Trust for Local News, which owns the papers. “We’ve invested in quality community and state coverage, and these awards help demonstrate that commitment is paying off for our audience.”
The runners-up in the weekday category were The Providence Journal of Rhode Island and the Bangor Daily News. The runners-up in the Sunday category were The Sunday Republican of Springfield, Massachusetts, and The Berkshire Eagle of Pittsfield, Massachusetts.
The Telegram also won the Sunday Newspaper of the Year category last year.
In other awards announced at Friday’s summit, Press Herald education reporter Riley Board’s coverage of an abuse lawsuit against Bath’s Hyde School won a Publick Occurrences award that recognizes the best work that New England newspapers produce each year. Board’s coverage examined allegations of forced labor and emotional abuse at the nearly 60-year-old private boarding school in Bath.
Emily Duggan, an education reporter for the Sun Journal and Kennebec Journal/Morning Sentinel, was also selected to receive one of the association’s A-Mark Prizes for her parents’ rights groups reporting, which investigated how Maine school boards have been confronted with organized — and sometimes disruptive — efforts to remake local education policies. The A-Mark prizes honor outstanding investigative journalism that reveals hidden truths, holds power to account, or drives public awareness or reform.
“We’re thrilled that the enterprising coverage from Riley and Emily won such distinguished recognition among the best journalism in New England,” Monroe said.
Runners-up in Maine also receiving A-Mark prizes were Sawyer Loftus from the Bangor Daily News/ProPublica, for coverage of U.S. Department of Agriculture foreclosures, and Callie Ferguson and Josh Keefe from the Bangor Daily News/The Maine Monitor for coverage of a Limerick man’s violent arrest at the hands of Maine State Police.
Ferguson, deputy investigations editor for the Bangor Daily News, was also recognized with the New England Journalist of the Year award for her reporting on the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement surge in Maine in January.

title: Residents evacuate, National Guard troops deploy as Hurricane Isaias nears US Gulf Coast
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MIAMI (AP) — Residents boarded up windows and stacked sandbags Thursday while thousands of National Guard soldiers were deploying in anticipation of Hurricane Isaias, which packed swift winds and threatened to bring a storm surge with devastating floods to the U.S. Gulf Coast.
Isaias is the first hurricane of the Atlantic season and was expected to usher in dangerous conditions in the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi when it makes landfall late Friday. Heavy rain and flooding were possible into the weekend as far north as Tennessee and North Carolina.
The Category 2 hurricane is most likely to strike along the Alabama-Florida state line and bring life-threatening storm surge across Pensacola Bay, according to the National Weather Service in Mobile, Alabama. But there’s a small chance it could hit further west and have a major impact on Mobile, or further east and have a strong effect on the Florida cities of Pensacola and Destin.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon, which formed as a tropical storm on Wednesday off of Mexico and became a hurricane late Thursday, was forecast to strengthen into a Category 4 hurricane.
Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (165 kph), according to the hurricane center. It was headed north-northeast at 14 mph (22 kph) and was centered about 230 miles (370 kilometers) south of the mouth of the Mississippi River.
A hurricane warning was in effect from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the Bay-Gulf County line in Florida, the hurricane center said. A storm surge warning was in effect from the mouth of the Mississippi to the Suwannee River.
Preparations underway
Coastal communities moved quickly to prepare Thursday, as Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey ordered non-residents to immediately evacuate Gulf Shores, Orange Beach and Dauphin Island. Videos on social media showed traffic at a standstill on a highway leading out of Gulf Shores, where double-red beach flags signaled water access was closed.
At least four Florida school districts canceled late-week classes, while several counties announced mandatory evacuations for some coastal areas. The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency for dozens of counties, with Florida’s Ron DeSantis saying about 5,000 National Guard troops were expected to mobilize by Friday.
On Dauphin Island, a 15-mile (24-kilometer) barrier island off the Alabama coast, officials encouraged voluntary evacuations, particularly on its popular western section, which is vulnerable to storm surge.
Mayor Jeff Collier said he did not anticipate substantial damage, “but at the same time, these things are very fickle and a little jog here or there, or some last-minute increase in strength — we just have to be prepared for the worst.”
Water from the storm surge and high tide could reach heights of 5 to 7 feet (1.5 to 2 meters) in parts of Alabama and Florida, forecasters said. Isaias also could dump up to 15 inches (38 centimeters) of rain on coastal areas and spawn tornadoes overnight Friday into Saturday from Alabama to the Florida Panhandle and southwestern Georgia. The hurricane is expected to quickly weaken after coming ashore.
The National Weather Service warned of possible “long-duration power outages.”
The hurricane formed late in the season
Isaias developed more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season and was one day short of tying a 121-year-old record for the area’s latest-forming hurricane. That record dates to 1905, when the year’s first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.
The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over the Atlantic. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Hurricane Simon formed. Farther north, Tropical Storm Rachel was expected to reach Baja California, Mexico, and Southern California this weekend.
Isaias is expected to strike a swath of coastline that’s familiar with major hurricanes.
One of the 20th century’s worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.
Oil production and tourism are already affected
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.
As of Thursday, about 63% of the oil production in the region had been temporarily halted, taking nearly 1.3 million barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said 121 of the Gulf’s 371 manned oil platforms had been evacuated.
With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.
As it moves inland, Isaias might also disrupt Saturday’s college football showdown between rivals Georgia and Alabama, a game President Donald Trump planned to attend.
In Loxley, a small Alabama community where county officials urged voluntary evacuations, Nichole Eubanks and her husband prepared to ride out the storm on their farm, which is home to dozens of animals, including pigs, donkeys and about 20 rescued cats.
They planned to put contact information on the hooves of their goats, donkeys and pigs in case they got loose.
“It’s definitely scary, and you never really know where these storms are going to go and how bad it’s going to be until it gets there,” said Eubanks, 35.
In the Alabama fishing village of Bayou La Batre, Tony Rice and Lance Connor installed doors on their fishing boat Thursday to protect the vessel. The boat was one of many moored there, and Rice said they planned to move it to a less-crowded spot to decrease the chances of it bumping into others.
In Pensacola, Florida, officials said the airport will close to commercial flights Friday morning. Mayor D.C. Reeves urged residents to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.
“Obviously no need to panic at this point,” Reeves told a news conference. “This is really about preparation.”
___
Rico reported from Atlanta and Collins reported from Hartford, Connecticut. Also contributing were Associated Press reporters Kim Chandler in Montgomery, Alabama; Hallie Golden in Seattle; Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire; John Raby in Charleston, West Virginia; Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas; and Julie Walker in New York.

title: Trump says US to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Trump says US to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices before midterms
President Donald Trump said that he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver another 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.
Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy economy, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.
Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."
The law he signed last month is aimed at sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt
It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.
Gas prices around the world have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.23 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.

title: ICE officers shot New York man because they believed they were in danger, official says
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal immigration officers opened fire on a Dominican man whom they were trying to arrest in New York because they believed their lives were in danger, a senior Immigration and Customs Enforcement official said Friday.
Marcos Charles made the comments alongside U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and other immigration officials during a news conference in Washington meant to “highlight the dangerous consequences of sanctuary city policies.”
The 28-year-old man, whom New York City police identified as Oscar Belgal, was shot in the neck Thursday as he drove his car with a 5-year-old boy inside, officials said.
ICE agents didn’t know the child was in the car, but Belgal “was aware” and chose to evade officers, Mullin said.
Belgal was shot “superficially” in the neck as ICE officers attempted to arrest him, Charles said.
ICE had issued a detainer on Belgal and that he runs with a gang known for thefts using weapons and mopeds, he said. Officers used vehicles to block him in as he attempted to drive off. Instead, Charles said, he accelerated his vehicle toward officers, smashing some of their vehicles.
Protesters and local officials decried the shooting as an example of the dangers of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
Much of Mullin’s remarks were reserved for excoriating New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and his immigration policy.
“Sanctuary politicians, they create an environment for criminal activity to thrive, not for the American citizens to be safe,” he said.
Mullin said ICE has requested more than 14,000 detainers in the state of New York for individuals in local custody that they’re seeking to deport.
“Silence. Absolute silence is what we have gotten back,” he said. “Why would they release these individuals back onto the streets?”
“We’re enforcing our nation’s laws. We’re not picking and choosing,” Mullin continued. “Why is that controversial? We should all want law and order on our streets.”

title: Memorial bench displaced during 2024 hurricane washes ashore 1,000 miles away
text:
DUNEDIN, Fla. (Bay News 9) — A memorial bench swept away from a Dunedin, Florida, causeway during Hurricane Helene two years ago has been found more than 1,000 miles away on the coast of Bermuda, according to the family of the man it honors.
The bench was placed along the causeway in 2018 by the aunt of Amanda Sadiku to honor her father, Medhat “Mike” Sadiku, who died in 2012. Amanda Sadiku was in seventh grade at the time of his death.
“My dad always said, ‘It’ll be alright.’ So we thought that would be perfect to put on the bench. It’ll be alright. My dad said that for absolutely everything,” Amanda Sadiku said.
Amanda Sadiku is the oldest of three daughters and remembers her father as a human calculator and the smartest man she has known.
Bench ripped away in 2024
The bench remained on the causeway until 2024, when Hurricane Helene tore it from the concrete slab where it had been fixed.
“There was a few benches that were out here in the water, but every time they pulled out benches, none of them were his. So his bench was marked missing,” Amanda Sadiku said.
The bench stayed missing until Sept. 18 of this year, when a woman in Bermuda contacted the family saying she had found it along the coast there.
“You know, at first we didn’t believe it. We were like, hold on. So we asked her for some pictures and everything else, and it was true, and we all were laughing and crying and everything else, and we were like, ‘So our dad just wanted to go to Bermuda,’” Amanda Sadiku said.
Meteorologist explains possible path
Spectrum Bay News 9 meteorologist Kyle Hanson said the bench’s path likely began with two storms in sequence. He said Hurricane Milton may have come soon enough after Helene to push the bench into the Gulf, where it could have been picked up by the loop current and carried along the Gulf Stream before washing ashore in Bermuda two years later.
“I’d say very lucky, very miraculous. The chance of this happening is lower than 1 in 100, I would say,” Hanson said.
Bench remains in Bermuda
The bench is still in Bermuda.
Amanda Sadiku said her son, Serene, Mike’s first grandson, still enjoys the spot where the bench used to sit.
“They say that babies, they meet their loved ones before they get sent down. So I feel like my son, he knows he has that feeling,” Amanda Sadiku said.
Amanda Sadiku said she is still deciding whether she will travel to see the bench or have it shipped back.

title: Wabanaki leaders endorse Hannah Pingree for Maine governor
text:
INDIAN ISLAND, Maine (WABI) - A group of Wabanaki leaders endorsed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree at a press conference on Indian Island Friday, citing her positions on tribal sovereignty, climate, health care, and the economy.
Tribal chiefs and other organizers said Pingree had their full trust and support. Some cited her work on the Climate Council and said her values align with theirs.
Pingree has pledged to support tribal sovereignty and work with tribal leaders to pass legislation within her first 100 days in office, a break from the Mills administration.
“In my many years of working on tribal sovereignty, I cannot recall a gubernatorial candidate making such a specific, public commitment to introduce legislation developed in partnership with the Wabanaki nations recognizing our sovereignty and to seek its passage within the first 100 days of taking office,” said Donna Loring, a Penobscot Nation elder.
“When the Wabanaki Nations thrive, Maine is stronger,” Pingree said. “I know that promises have been made before. And that trust has been broken before. I understand that. So I’m not asking you to take my word for it. I’m asking you to hold me to it.”
Penobscot Nation Chief Kirk Francis also cited Pingree’s health care and economic plans as reasons for his endorsement. The event came ahead of Indigenous Peoples’ Day weekend in Maine.

title: ‘Battery breakthrough’: Researchers use new material to make lithium-ion batteries safer
text:
EAST LANSING, Mich. (InvestigateTV) - Michigan State University researchers have discovered a way to make lithium-ion batteries safer using an unlikely material: wood waste.
The breakthrough comes as fire officials call rechargeable lithium-ion batteries “ticking time bombs.” These batteries power nearly every device in American homes, from electric vehicles to children’s toys.
“Every home in America has them, whether it’s an electric vehicle, e-bikes, e-scooters, children’s toys, electronic devices, cordless power tools,” said John Newman, East Lansing interim fire chief. “We all have lithium-ion batteries and we charge and use those devices without any consideration.”
Scott Swanson and his family learned about battery dangers the hard way. Last summer, they survived two lithium-ion battery fires in two weeks that destroyed their car and damaged their Meridian Township home.
PREVIOUS COVERAGE:
The culprits were a pair of children’s headphones in the car and a backup battery charger in the home office.
“It just feels like a really random thing that just happens sometimes and I’m not sure there’s a whole lot you can do about it,” Swanson said.
His wife, Rose Tantrophol, said the experience left her shaken.
“After these two fires, I was, it took me a while to feel good using these devices,” Tantrophol said. “But I really don’t have a choice. I mean, all the work that I do is really powered by, you know, devices that have lithium-ion batteries.”
When lithium-ion batteries are damaged, overcharged or exposed to heat, they can start to overheat. That heat feeds on itself in a dangerous chain reaction called “thermal runaway,” which can cause the battery to release flammable gas, catch fire or explode.
Newman said East Lansing has seen at least two lithium-ion battery fires in the past year. One involved an electric scooter. Another destroyed half a house when a cordless power tool battery that was stored on a shelf in a utility room caught fire.
“It can reach temperatures of a thousand degrees in less than a minute and cause an entire room to go into flashover, which is when everything in the room reaches a high enough temperature to burn,” Newman said.
The fires cannot be extinguished with traditional fire extinguishers because the chemical reaction and heat are generated within the battery itself.
A “battery breakthrough”
Dr. Chengcheng Fang, an assistant professor at MSU’s College of Engineering, is leading research to make batteries safer using lignin, a wood product that acts like glue to hold wood together and make it strong.
“We are trying to enable, use different materials, more sustainable materials, from the wood, which is naturally abundant, to make the separator much robust,” Fang said.
Lignin is a waste product in the paper and biofuel industry. It’s cheap and doesn’t need any treatment to function in batteries.
“It has very unique chemical and thermal properties, but it’s underutilized,” Fang said.
Current rechargeable batteries contain plastic films to separate the electrodes, but the material can shrink and melt, causing the battery to short-circuit and explode. The wood waste is more pliable and withstands heat three times better than plastic.
Research shows promising results.
The research, published in the journal Advanced Materials, shows lignin-based batteries last 60% longer than traditional batteries.
“They are enhancing some of the stability of the battery materials to facilitate a lithium-ion transport. So we actually get the demonstration of improvement in the cycle life by 60%,” Fang said.
The technology is patent-pending through the MSU Innovation Center.
Safety recommendations
Fang recommends charging batteries to around 88% rather than 100% to maintain better battery performance longer. She also advises never leaving devices charging overnight, especially on beds or couches.
Lithium-ion batteries should not be thrown in the trash. Stores like Staples and Home Depot have free collection boxes for safe recycling.

title: Maine's Jessica Meir Is Back on Earth After Eight Months in Space
text:
Maine’s Jessica Meir Is Back on Earth After Eight Months in Space
After eight months in space, one of Maine’s own is back on Earth with another mission under her belt.
👇 KEEP READING: 23 Famous People You Probably Didn't Know Were Born In Maine 👇
NASA astronaut Jessica Meir and her Crew-12 crewmates returned to Earth on Oct. 8 after nearly eight months aboard the International Space Station.
Meir, Jack Hathaway, Sophie Adenot, and Andrey Fedyaev splashed down aboard SpaceX’s Dragon Freedom spacecraft in the Pacific Ocean off Los Angeles at 11:34 a.m. EDT.
The Crew-12 astronauts spent hundreds of hours conducting scientific research aboard the International Space Station, including studies on stem cells, nutrition, and how spaceflight affects blood flow.
They also tested ways to produce IV fluids in space, supporting research aimed at improving health on Earth and preparing astronauts for future missions to the Moon and Mars.
Meir is a NASA astronaut and marine biologist who was born and raised in Caribou and graduated from Caribou High School.
Selected for astronaut training in 2013, she helped conduct the first all-female spacewalk in 2019 and later commanded NASA’s SpaceX Crew-12 mission to the International Space Station.
And there you have it! Meir has completed another major spaceflight mission, adding nearly eight more months aboard the International Space Station to her career.

Scaffolding removed from Portland's historic Trelawney Building after three years
Residents and business owners in downtown Portland are praising the removal of the scaffolding that covered the historic Trelawney Building at 655 Congress St. for three years.

title: ‘Waves are really big’: Beachgoers make last trip to Florida’s Gulf Coast before Hurricane Isaias
text:
PENSACOLA BEACH, Fla. (WALA/Gray News) - Hurricane Isaias will soon impact the Gulf Coast, and many people in Florida wanted to make one last trip to see Pensacola Beach up close before the weather takes a turn.
Stephanie Dzugan, a visitor, said she was explaining the situation to her son.
“I was explaining to my son that this is kind of the calm before the storm, sun shining. It’s beautiful, enjoy it, then follow directions and take heed and let mother nature do what she does,” Stephanie Dzugan said.
Paul Dzugan, a visitor, described the conditions at the beach.
“It’s really cool. It’s pretty beautiful and the waves are really big. I wouldn’t recommend going boogie boarding or scuba diving, and it’s really good for sea shelling,” Paul Dzugan said.
Lifeguards warn of rip current danger
While many found the waves exciting, they’re also dangerous. Lifeguards have already moved their stands off the beach and made the switch to double red flags Thursday morning to urge people to stay out of the water as the storm moves closer.
Dave Greenwood, chief of water safety, said rip currents pose the greatest risk.
“Rip currents are deadly. That’s the biggest weather phenomenon related death is by rip currents so we keep them out of the water. We’re doing preventative actions and even after the storm passes, there’s still going to be wave energy moving on shore, so be aware of that,” Greenwood said.
Visitors weigh travel plans
Several beachgoers were in town on vacation. Trey Hermann said he plans to leave for Atlanta before Pensacola International Airport closes at 10 a.m. Friday.
“Since it’s tonight, I feel like I should be alright. If I was flying out tomorrow, I’d be more concerned for sure. I think I’ve had enough time and I’d rather be going out tonight than being stuck without a ride,” Hermann said.
Others said they plan to move farther away from the coast and ride the storm out.
“We just got down here a day or two ago, and in Knoxville, we didn’t know there was a hurricane coming. We’re going to pray, we’re going to be smart and we’re going to ride it out,” Stephanie Dzugan said.
Larry Toomey, a resident, said he isn’t concerned.
“I have no fear. I don’t board up. I don’t do anything. I’ve lived here all my life basically,” Toomey said.
Beachgoers urge taking storm seriously
While there isn’t much fear over the storm, beachgoers say it’s important to have a plan and take it seriously.
“There was someone last night at a restaurant and he was asking me, ‘Should I change my flight?’ And I said, ‘If the locals are taking it serious, then I would take it serious.’ So that’s my advice. If you see the locals getting gas, taking the boats up, putting them in dry storage, I would probably get out of dodge,” Hermann said.

title: Justice Department won't enforce registration rules on silencers and certain guns after court ruling
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department moved Friday to allow more people to purchase firearm suppressors — known as silencers — short-barreled rifles and certain other guns without registering them with the federal government following a court ruling that struck down provisions of a key law.
The Trump administration announced the broad enforcement policy changes after a Texas judge in August ruled the permitting process was unconstitutional. The judge’s ruling was limited to the parties involved in that case, but the Justice Department said Friday it would no longer enforce the registration requirements more broadly.
“The direction from the President, Congress, and the courts is clear,” Rob Cekada, director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives said in an emailed statement. “ATF is now following suit with our enforcement posture while continuing to ensure we remain focused where we are needed the most: combating violent crime in American communities.”
It’s the latest move by the Trump administration to ease restrictions on firearms opposed by gun rights groups. Gun rights activists have long complained that the registration requirements — which meant filling out a form, being fingerprinted, and waiting for government approval — were overly burdensome
At issue in the Texas case were regulations in a 1930s-era law, the National Firearms Act, which was passed in response to concerns about mafia violence.
U.S. District Judge James Hendrix in Texas said the rules for purchasing a silencer, short-barreled rifle, short-barreled shotgun and other certain other firearms must fall after the Republican-controlled Congress and President Donald Trump eliminated a $200 permit tax on the devices. The Justice Department opted not to appeal the judge’s decision.
Groups that support gun restrictions decried the judge’s ruling and the Justice Department’s decision to let it stand as reckless and argued that the regulations are important for public safety.
In an interview with The Associated Press on Friday, Cekada said that after the judge’s ruling, federal law enforcement was inundated with questions from the public and members of Congress about how they were going to handle enforcement nationwide. The Trump administration believed that the “best and fairest thing to do” was to address the rules nationwide to avoid a confusing patchwork of regulations across the country, Cekada said.
Under the new guidance, ATF will no longer require registration unless the buyer lives in one of about 15 states that have state laws requiring that people go through the federal permitting process. The registration process will still apply for machine guns and what are considered “destructive devices” under federal law, the Justice Department said.
And in all cases, people will still have to fill out the standard firearms purchasing form, which includes questions about things that would disqualify someone from legal gun ownership, and they also have to pass a background check, officials said.

title: 4 Maine food products win Golden Fork Awards
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Four Maine-based products won Golden Fork Awards Thursday as part of the biennial Maine Food Producer Showcase.
Haymay Creamery of Farmington won Best in Show, Savory, for Pudge, a washed-rind cheese made with milk from local farms. Portland’s Molässa won Best in Show, Sweet, for their Hot Molasses, a light, sweet molasses with caramel notes.
Mark Foods/Bristol Seafood of Portland won Best in Show, Seafood, for Wilder Miso Sablefish; and Portland’s Three of Strong Spirits won Best in Show, Beverage, for Valley Cove Rum, a blend of three of the distillery’s oldest barrels.
The event, held at Portland’s Holiday Inn by the Bay, featured more than 70 of the state’s food, beverage and seafood producers. The gathering attracted hundreds of buyers, distributors, retailers, chefs, foodservice professionals and industry partners, and was presented by University of Maine System Graduate & Professional Center (Maine Center).
“The Maine Food Producer Showcase creates meaningful connections between producers and the buyers, distributors and industry partners who can help them grow,” said Naomi Neville, program director of the Maine Center’s Food Accelerators, in a media statement. “Each year we see new relationships formed, new products discovered and new opportunities created for Maine businesses and our broader food economy.”

title: Boothbay Region Student Aid Fund welcomes five new trustees
text:
The Boothbay Region Student Aid Fund (BRSAF) is pleased to announce the election of five new trustees to its Board of Directors. The new trustees bring experience in education, college admissions, military service, public service, and community leadership, further strengthening BRSAF's mission of helping Boothbay Region students pursue education and training beyond high school.
"We are delighted to welcome these outstanding individuals to the Board," said Board President Louise Cowan. "Each brings valuable experience, a strong commitment to our community, and a shared passion for helping local students achieve their educational goals."
Among those joining the board is Lesley Blethen, a Boothbay Region High School graduate, member of the school's 1984 girls state championship basketball team, U.S. Army veteran, and former postmaster of the Boothbay Harbor Post Office. Her lifelong connection to the Boothbay region and decades of public service reflect BRSAF's commitment to community leadership.
Also joining the board is Jane Hahn, founder of My College Advocate, who brings decades of experience in college admissions and counseling, helping students identify the educational opportunities that best fit their goals and successfully navigate the college planning process. Her expertise will help strengthen BRSAF's understanding of the evolving landscape of post-secondary education.
Peggy Splaine has dedicated her career and community service to supporting young people through education, youth athletics, and service on local and state school boards. Her experience working with children with developmental disabilities and her longstanding commitment to Boothbay Region students bring a thoughtful and compassionate perspective to the BRSAF Board.
Lisa Clarke is a Boothbay Region High School graduate and retired teacher and school administrator whose family has personally benefited from BRSAF's mission. Lisa’s career in education brings a firsthand appreciation for BRSAF's impact and a valuable perspective to the board.
Lenore Imhof, a lifelong educator and former fourth-grade teacher at Boothbay Region Elementary School, coaches swimming at the Boothbay Region YMCA. She brings decades of educational experience and a deep commitment to helping young people succeed.
For more than 60 years, BRSAF has provided need-based grants to qualifying Boothbay Region High School graduates pursuing education and training beyond high school. Through the generosity of its donors and the leadership of its volunteer Board of Directors, BRSAF has helped generations of local students pursue their educational goals.
For more information about BRSAF and its mission, visit www.brsaf.org.

title: Fort Fairfield Police Chief Named MCOPA President
text:
FORT FAIRFIELD, Maine (WAGM) - An Aroostook County police chief has been sworn in as the President of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association.
Fort Fairfield’s Police Chief Matthew Cummings was officially sworn in as the 2026-2027 President of the Maine Chiefs of Police Association on October 1st. The ceremony took place in Bangor at the Cross Insurance Center during the association’s 2026 Fall Conference. Chief Cummings has served as a law enforcement officer in the county for 23 years and has served as Chief of the Fort Fairfield Police Department since July of 2021.
In a social media post, Town Manager Aaron Huotari praised the Chief’s appointment, stating, “Chief Cummings works tirelessly every day to keep our community safe, supported, and moving forward. We know he will bring that same steady leadership and dedication to advancing professional law enforcement across the State of Maine.”

title: Shifting school start times could address teen sleep loss, research says
text:
ST. LOUIS, Mo. (InvestigateTV) — School in many districts across the country begins before sunrise, a schedule doctors say runs counter to how teenage brains are wired to sleep.
School did not always start this early. During the 1950s and 1960s, U.S. schools started between 8:30 and 9 a.m. because most children could walk or bike to a neighborhood school.
By the 1970s and 1980s, as suburbs spread out and commutes got longer, districts shifted to earlier hours and riding the school bus became the norm for many students. According to the urban planning website Planetizen, “as driving became the norm, so did early start times.”
In the 1960s, 42% of kids usually walked or biked to school. In recent years, that number has dropped to as low as 11%, according to the BikePGH Guide: The Decline of Walking and Bicycling.
With more research linking early start times to teen sleep loss, some communities are trying to move the clock forward.
A father’s perspective
Dr. Hanley Chiang is the father of a sixth grader in St. Louis Public Schools. Chiang said his son’s day starts at 5:50 a.m. to catch a 6:30 bus to get to school by the 7:15 start time.
“It’s always a process to get him out of bed,” Chiang said. “He is drowsy in the morning but he tends to perk up within half an hour.”
Chiang said perking up is not a reality for all kids. Chiang is also a social scientist who has studied teen sleep patterns for years.
According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, the average teenager has difficulty falling asleep before 11 p.m. Chiang advocates for middle and high school students to start school later.
“Many students in the district and around the nation are really struggling in their first period class,” Chiang said.
Some students say they see the struggle in the classroom. Elijah Morrow is a student at Huron High School in Ann Arbor, Michigan.
“First period is usually the worst,” he said. “You can see around the room a lot of kids have their head down and are sleeping.”
Experts cite recommended start times
The American Academy of Pediatrics and American Academy of Sleep Medicine both recommend middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. to give teens a better chance at the sleep their brains and bodies need.
More districts are revisiting the question as schools try to improve attendance, learning and student well-being following the pandemic.
Ann Gallagher is president of the board of directors for the advocacy group Start School Later.
“The 8:30 benchmark was determined through research,” Gallagher said. “If schools start at a particular time, overall the health indicators for that population of students increase, injury rates go down.”
Pediatricians recommend teens ages 13 to 18 get eight to 10 hours of sleep a night to support cognitive development, emotional regulation and physical growth.
Pulmonologist Dr. Humam Farah said sleep deprivation can take a toll on teens.
“Sleep deprivation contributes to poor academic performance, low concentration, increased risk of accidents on the road and depression and anxiety,” Farah said.
Farah said part of the problem is biology.
He said preadolescents become teenagers when their circadian rhythms, which help living things respond to changes in their environment, shift later. This biological change causes teens to feel sleepy later at night and want to wake up later in the morning.
Morrow said sleep does not come easy.
“You can do everything right. Put your screens away, read, relax, and sometimes you just can’t fall asleep,” Morrow said.
Morrow said there is only one way to make up the difference.
“So the question of what will kids do with the extra time? Sleep,” Morrow said.
Logistics complicate the shift
Moving the bell is not simple.
The National Education Association supports later start times, but an article published in NEA Today said, “A shift of 30 minutes or even an hour later means that students will finish their day later than 3 p.m. That triggers a domino effect for everything from after-school activities and programs, parents’ work schedules, childcare arrangements, and after-school jobs.”
The same article cited issues with bus schedules and existing driver shortages. According to the Economic Policy Institute, there were more than 21,000 fewer bus drivers employed in August 2025 compared to six years earlier.
Gallagher said those concerns are real, but districts that plan with the community have found ways to make it work.
“When school districts take those apparent obstacles into consideration they become non-obstacles,” Gallagher said. “Communities find ways to have before and after care that matches the needs of the community and after-school practices align with students’ awake time.”
Districts already making changes
In Clark County, Nevada, the nation’s fifth-largest school district, leaders approved a new schedule that pushes the high school day 30 minutes later.
Superintendent Jhone Ebert said the adjustment is intended to boost academic performance, improve attendance and support mental health.
“Improvement in mental health, which we care deeply about. Increased sleep reduces rates of depression, anxiety, and behavior problems. By moving the high school start time to a later time, we aren’t just giving our high school students a break. We’re giving them a fighting chance to succeed,” Ebert said.
In St. Louis, district leaders are weighing a move to later start times for middle and high schools, possibly as early as the 2027-2028 school year, to give them time to work out funding and other logistics.
“I sense that the district leadership and the board are very interested in finding a solution to this issue,” Chiang said.
As more communities weigh the tradeoffs, supporters say the question is whether districts can balance logistics with what doctors say teens need most: sleep.
“We cannot educate them if they are not safe and healthy,” Gallagher said.
Doctors recommend sleep habits at home
American Academy of Sleep Medicine board member Dr. Emerson Wickwire suggests keeping bedtime and wake time about the same, even on weekends.
“For adults the minimum recommended duration of sleep is 7-8 hours children depending on their ages, require significantly more sleep,” Wickwire said.
According to Johns Hopkins Medicine, starting the day in sunshine, such as having breakfast outside or by a sunny window, helps regulate the body’s clock.
Doctors also recommend banning tech from the bedroom. Using tech at night cuts into a teen’s sleep time and exposes them to a type of light that suppresses melatonin, a sleep-inducing hormone.
Doctors say a short nap of around 20 to 30 minutes can help if a teen is exhausted, but it should be early enough that it does not delay bedtime.

title: Cheverus golf repeats as Class A champion
text:
VASSALBORO — With its possession of the Class A state championship at stake, the Cheverus golf team dusted off a familiar gameplan — and even a familiar speech.
Sam Sirois shot even-par 72 for medalist honors, and Keane McGrath and Joe Stratman were among eight players who tied for second with 76s as the Stags successfully defended their state title Friday, shooting 304 to hold off Falmouth (314), Messalonskee (324), Thornton Academy (328), South Portland and Gorham (340 each) at Natanis Golf Course.
Falmouth’s Dante Iannetta, Gorham’s Charlie Sands, Messalonskee’s Greyson Dooley, Bangor’s Jacoby Harvey, Mt. Ararat’s Caleb Greenleaf and Oxford Hills’ Sawyer Poland joined Stratman and McGrath at 4 over.
Lila Dailey of Camden Hills and Jacquelin Sirois of Cheverus shot 97 to share the title in the girls division.
“It feels great, again,” said Sirois, who tied for second individually last year. “Going into this, we didn’t really think we had a shot, so I’m really glad we got it done.”
Such doubt was reasonable after Falmouth rolled to the SMAA championship at the same Tomahawk course on Monday, shooting 304 to beat the Stags by nine shots while getting scores under 80 from five players.
Cheverus coach Billy Goodman told his players there was no way to beat the Navigators if they were that hot, a similar angle he used when addressing the girls basketball team in February before the Stags turned a 19-point deficit into a 63-61 overtime victory against Hampden Academy in the Class A final.
“I told my team going back to Portland, it was kind of like the halftime speech for my basketball team,” he said. “‘If they shoot like that again, they’re going to win.’ But we just had a really good week of practice. A lot of kids focused and did better than Monday.”
The Stags’ roadmap to victory looked like last year’s, when it had the medalist in Mick Madden and a second-place finisher in Sirois. This time, Sirois jumped to the top spot, hitting 11 greens in regulation and carding four birdies, one coming when he rolled in a 20-foot putt on the fourth hole.
“Teamwise, I knew we all had to play well,” Sirois said. “I didn’t want to let my teammates down.”
The rest of the scores fell in line. McGrath, who was third at the SMAAs with a 74, was excellent again, notching 13 pars and an eagle on the par-5 third. Stratman, who had an 81 on Monday, improved by five shots. Ray, who shot 87 on Monday, improved by seven strokes. Garrett Thees went from a 90 to an 84.
“I guess it was Cheverus’ day today. We did really well, everyone kind of came together,” McGrath said. “Everyone was very focused this morning, it was a different mood than the SMAA.”
Stratman didn’t play in the state championship last year. He was front and center this time.
“I fed off the pressure, it’s one of the greatest things to do,” said Stratman, who carded four birdies. “I shot 106 in the qualifiers last year. It really pushed me to work harder.”
Iannetta tied for second for the second straight year. He was joined by Alex Novick (78), Griffin Jacobsen (78) and Anthony Graceffa (82) among the Falmouth scorers.
“I hit the ball pretty solid all day, it’s just putts didn’t fall,” Iannetta said. “Golf’s a game that happens on one day. When a tournament’s only one day long, anything can happen. It’s tough. … I believe we could have gone lower than 304, but it just wasn’t today. It’s unfortunate.”
Messalonskee’s Dooley, the first-place finisher at the KVAC qualifier, notched four birdies, one of which stabilized his round. It came two holes after a triple bogey on the par 3 10th.
“It was basically putting today that saved me,” he said. “It was mostly just a mental game out there, and having to just stay through it the rest of the round.”

title: InvestigateTV+: Wealthy ranchers profit from public lands
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — As family farms struggle to stay afloat, InvestigateTV+ found the benefits of a taxpayer-funded federal land program go to billionaires and big businesses.
Plus, we explore a rise in lithium-ion battery fires, and the unlikely material scientists are using to prevent them.
Then, we share the story of a couple with a cosmic coincidence.
Ranchers profit from public lands
The public lands grazing program, formalized in the 1930s to contain the rampant overgrazing that contributed to the Dust Bowl, has grown to serve operations including billionaire hobby ranchers, mining companies, utilities and large corporate outfits, providing benefits unimagined by its founding law.
President Donald Trump’s administration plans to make the program even more generous — pushing to open even more of the 240 million acres of Bureau of Land Management and Forest Service grazing land to livestock while reducing oversight of the environmental damage.
This, members of the administration contend, will further its goal of using public lands to fuel the economy and eliminate the national debt.
Battery breakthrough
Michigan State University researchers have discovered a way to make lithium-ion batteries safer using an unlikely material: wood waste.
The breakthrough comes as fire officials call rechargeable lithium-ion batteries “ticking time bombs.” These batteries power nearly every device in American homes, from electric vehicles to children’s toys.
The Butterfly Whisperer
The monarch butterfly, known for its vibrant orange and deep black hues, is dangerously close to disappearing forever.
A 2026 report from the Center for Biological Diversity found the migratory eastern monarch remains vulnerable to extinction.
In South Carolina, Diedre Richardson has turned her backyard into a sanctuary for butterflies, earning her the nickname “Butterfly Whisperer.”
Born on the same day, now getting married
It’s not out of the ordinary for high school sweethearts to get married. It’s also not too unusual that both of their moms also graduated from the same school.
So, what is so unusual about this love story?
“I was born on July 7th, 2006,” Lorene said.
“[I was born on] July 7th, 2006,” Brayden said.

title: Driver fell asleep before deadly crash killing Amish woman, horse, troopers say
text:

Michigan State Police troopers were called to the crash on Peck Road near Maple Valley Road in Flynn Township. The crash happened around 4:43 p.m.
Investigators believe a 55-year-old North Branch man fell asleep at the wheel and hit the woman’s buggy.
The woman and the horse were killed at the scene.

title: Visit 1778 at Pownalborough Court House
text:
On Saturday, Sept. 19, visitors to Pownalborough Court House in Dresden will have the opportunity to interact with life in 1778, when the American Revolution was still being fought and the new nation was taking shape.
Historical theater reenactors portraying real people who lived and worked in the region will be incorporated into the Court House's regular museum tours throughout the day. Meet Samuel and Elizabeth Goodwin, who lived at the Court House and operated its tavern; Doctor Colman, a local physician; Martha McGill, a local resident; and militia members Corporal Jacob Lowel and Christopher Erskin. Their stories offer perspectives on community life, medicine, family, and military service in this region during the Revolutionary War.
At 1 p.m., Anette Ruppel Rodrigues, portraying the mother of a Hessian soldier, will present The British King's German Allies in the American War of Independence: A Mother's Perspective, exploring the experiences of German soldiers who served with the British Crown and the families who accompanied them.
Regular tours begin on the hour from 10 a.m. through 3 p.m., with the historical interpreters incorporated into the tour experience. The special presentation will take place separately from tours at 1 p.m. in the courtroom.
All are welcome. Admission is $15 for adults, and free for children, active-duty military personnel, and LCHA members.
Lincoln County Historical Association is a non-profit organization that provides stewardship for the 1754 Chapman-Hall House in Damariscotta, the 1761 Pownalborough Court House in Dresden, and the 1811 Old Jail and Museum in Wiscasset. For more information, please visit www.lincolncountyhistory.org or Facebook at Lincoln County Historical Association (Maine).

title: Officials release names in fatal Lovell crash Thursday
text:
Authorities Friday released the names of the two people involved in a head-on crash in Lovell Thursday that killed a young Lovell woman and sent an Andover man to the hospital.
Police said Ivy Thomson, 25, died when her 2015 Ford Flex collided head-on with a 2003 Chevrolet Silverado driven by Mark Farrington, 66, in the 600 block of Main Street shortly before noon.
According to authorities, Thomson died at the scene. Farrington was taken to Maine Medical Center in Portland with life-threatening injuries. No information on his condition was offered Friday.
There were no passengers.
The crash was being investigated by the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office, which was assisted by Fryeburg police, Fryeburg rescue, and crews from the Lovell Fire Department.
The investigation is ongoing, authorities said Friday, and may take time to complete. They are asking anyone with information on the crash to contact the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office at (207) 743-9554.

title: Who is Katie Zacharia, Trump's new White House press secretary?
text:
Who is Katie Zacharia, Trump's new White House press secretary?
President Donald Trump announced Friday that Katie Zacharia will succeed Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary.
In the social media announcement, Trump described her as "a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning."
Who is Katie Zacharia?
Zacharia is currently a communications adviser for Trump Media & Technology Group, which operates Trump's social media website Truth Social.
Zacharia previously served as a spokesperson for former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem at the Department of Homeland Security and has also worked as a commentator for Fox News and Newsmax.
Her LinkedIn profile also states that she is general counsel for the conservative nonprofit Fix California and that she was a White House intern in 2006, during President George W. Bush’s second term.
Zacharia received a Bachelor's degree in political science and government from Pepperdine University and a law degree from Pepperdine Caruso School of Law.
She is married to Tyler Zacharia, a film producer whose recent films include "Young Washington" and "David," both productions of Angel Studios, a faith-based film company. Tyler Zacharia also worked on "The Irishman," a 2019 movie starring Robert De Niro and Al Pacino.
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Dr. Oz defends rural health care spending amid Medicaid cut questions
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Cost of health care is a major issue for voters ahead of the midterms, and the Trump administration is trying to get ahead of the messaging. Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, sat down with Gray Media Washington News Bureau reporter Molly Martinez, and the conversation grew heated.
Dr. Oz’s authority over spending is limited by Congress. The Trump administration is touting a record $50 billion in spending for rural health care approved in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The actual numbers tell a different story.
“The Big Beautiful Bill cut $137 billion in rural health care spending. That’s there was money there. So this seems to be a solution to a problem that the administration may have created,” Martinez asked Oz.
“You’re repeating talking points that are not only wrong but deliberately duplicitous. What is wrong? That number is incorrect,” Oz responded.
The $137 billion cut figure is a direct analysis from the non-partisan KFF group. The non-partisan Congressional Budget Office estimates 10 billion Americans will lose health care as a result of the Big Beautiful Bill in the next decade.
Oz was pressed on why reform was necessary.
“Some states like New York and California take advantage of the system and those states take money from the federal coffers of other states, because why should Kentucky and Mississippi and New Mexico be paying higher federal taxes so that California and New York can put more money into programs?” Oz said.
Leslie Dach, an Obama alumnus and chair of Protect Our Care, responded.
“It is not true that the big blue states are the ones who benefit because there’s equal access in 49 states. So you know, he’s just using kind of a stereotype to make believe that certain people probably in red states or rural states are getting ripped off,” Dach said.
The administration maintains that pulling nearly a trillion dollars in health care spending is in the name of fraud prevention and financial solvency. Dach said there is a human cost.
“He acts as if all these actions they’ve taken were making health care better. That is the biggest boldfaced lie everywhere. Go ask people who are shutting down their hospitals has to last, can’t find a maternity ward, have a heart attack and has to drive the people who can’t afford their health insurance anymore,” Dach said.
The Trump administration has vowed to expand spending, including $17 million for new mental health clinics in North Carolina.
