title: Selectmen approve ballot question for Nov. 3 election regarding ordinance changes
Debate made it clear why Matt Dunlap is the best choice in 2nd District
text:
Amy Fried is professor emerita of political science at the University of Maine. She lives in Bangor. These views are her own and do not reflect those of the University of Maine.
In 2014, then running for reelection, Gov. Paul LePage debated his opponents: Democrat U.S. Rep. Mike Michaud and independent candidate Eliot Cutler. With Cutler and LePage joining forces to attack him, Michaud struggled to put in a strong performance, while LePage employed details in defending his record.
A dozen years later, the LePage of earlier times is a faded memory. When Paul LePage met Matt Dunlap on the debate stage on Oct. 1, the contrast between the two times and current candidates could not have been starker.
LePage looked like he had lost several steps. His breathing seemed labored and his voice raspier than ever. Rather than speaking directly to questioners and the audience, LePage frequently looked down, reading directly from notes. In contrast, Dunlap looked crisp, nimble, and focused. He answered questions cleanly, offered quick factual corrections, and clearly explained policy and constitutional matters.
When LePage praised federal healthcare cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill and touted a rural hospital fund, Dunlap quickly noted that Maine’s overall healthcare cut is far more than additional money from that fund. To make matters worse, LePage seemed to laugh, as if rural hospitals losing crucial funding and people losing coverage were just a joke.
Mainers across the 2nd District are hurting economically. Dunlap humanized that struggle with something he saw at an auto shop in Old Town, where a woman learned she had to buy expensive new tires while also facing a huge annual increase in heating oil costs.
Dunlap sympathized but went further, pointing to the underlying federal policies making life harder: tariffs, foreign conflict in Iran, and runaway healthcare costs.
LePage, on the other hand, seemed disconnected from daily life in the district. Perhaps that’s not surprising, given how much time he’s spent living in Florida, where he doesn’t have a Maine heating oil tank to fill anymore.
When asked about their top priorities, both candidates turned to healthcare. LePage mentioned expanding dental coverage for veterans. That’s a worthy goal, but one that targets a narrow slice of the population. Dunlap aimed broader, focusing on restoring Affordable Care Act subsidies. That would help tens of thousands of Mainers, particularly low-income elderly and rural residents, keep their health insurance.
As governor, LePage repeatedly blocked Medicaid expansion, vetoing legislation six times and defying a state court order after 59% of Maine voters backed a referendum to expand MaineCare. On stage last week, he defended that record, falsely claiming that hospitals are better off receiving zero reimbursement for uncompensated care rather than slightly lower Medicaid rates. In fact, data shows that expanding MaineCare measurably reduced uncompensated care costs for rural emergency rooms. Getting covered also removes a reason sick people don’t seek care.
When the discussion turned to the Iran war, LePage’s positions were wildly contradictory. He said he opposed the war but then endorsed military action in Iran to stop a nuclear bomb (which experts say the country wasn’t close to getting), and then declared he rejects ceasefires and wants Donald Trump to “go in and finish it.”
In contrast, Dunlap was clear, opposing the war and reminding viewers that Congress has the constitutional responsibility to declare war and conduct executive oversight.
Unlike LePage, Dunlap, in addition to having served as secretary of state and state auditor, has been a legislator and student of history. So perhaps that’s why Dunlap demonstrated a firm grasp of the House of Representative’s oversight, lawmaking, budgetary, and war powers. Still, it was striking that at times LePage seemed oddly confused about the job he’s seeking. For example, LePage suggested that he might personally negotiate trade agreements with Canada because he speaks French, and wrongly claimed war-making is a purely presidential power.
I think LePage lacked the energy, sharpness, and constructive ideas that Dunlap brought from start to finish. Voters in Maine’s 2nd District will soon decide who represents them in Washington, and the debate made the choice crystal clear.

title: OpenAI fires 3 safety researchers in dispute over AI risks
text:
OpenAI fires 3 safety researchers in dispute over AI risks
OpenAI said on Friday that it fired three safety researchers for a “breach of trust," defending the dismissals after the trio accused the company of putting its corporate interests before safety as the reason for removing them.
The ChatGPT maker said in a post on X that it “parted ways” with the researchers after an investigation found “they violated clear policies on handling sensitive information.”
The statement comes after the three researchers, Tomek Korbak, Jasmine Wang and Mikita Balesni, posted a letter to OpenAI's various safety oversight groups detailing the circumstances around their firings and their concerns about AI.
The researchers said they feared that the “internal and external communications” about their dismissals have chilled the company's culture that encouraged speaking freely and disagreeing openly about safety concerns. They urged OpenAI to stick to its promise to allow third-party safety monitors inside the company and preserve the ability to monitor rapidly advancing frontier AI models that could pose unknown risks.
The firings, which were first reported by The Wall Street Journal, are the latest sign of turmoil inside leading AI companies over the safety of the technology, highlighted by a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents.
The issue erupted in July when OpenAI revealed that a swarm of its AI agents escaped from a testing ground and used stolen credentials to break into the servers of Hugging Face, an AI development hub and marketplace, to obtain information needed for a task.
OpenAI disputed the researchers' version of events, saying the firings “were not about safety concerns or speaking out."
It was not more specific about why they were fired, but said: “We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust.”
Korbak said in a post on X that he was told he was being fired because of the way he communicated with METR, an independent nonprofit AI evaluation firm that OpenAI brought in to investigate the Hugging Face incident.
METR released a detailed report about the Hugging Face incident in late August. Korbak said that “talking to METR” was his job, but he wasn't given any more details.
Balesni was doing “cross-company work” on OpenAI's commitments to preserve the ability to monitor AI, and had taken care “to remove sensitive details from materials before sharing them,” the letter said. He wrote on X that he believes the three were “fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation.”

title: 'A hot mess': Delta flight diversion leaves local passengers stranded
text:
Delta flight diverted to Bermuda leaves Boston travelers stranded for hours
What started as a routine domestic flight turned into a travel nightmare for many people returning to Massachusetts on Tuesday.
A Delta Air Lines flight from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Boston was diverted to Bermuda due to a medical emergency.
The unusual situation made a four-hour flight last about 30 hours.
“We got stuck on an airplane for basically almost three hours and finally just got out,” said Damaris Montanez of Springfield.
A Delta Air Lines spokesperson said the crew timed out, so passengers were put in hotels overnight.
Travelers described the experience as disorganized.
Video below: Second man released from immigration custody after flight diverted out of U.S.
“By the time we got to the hotel in Bermuda, it was like 3, 3:30 in the morning,” Montanez said.
“I didn’t get into a hotel until 3 in the morning, and then at 6:40 they’re knocking on the door, and we had to get back on the shuttle bus to get back to the airport,” said Luz Rodriguez of Lowell.
After staying in the hotel on Monday, passengers were brought back to the Bermuda airport early Tuesday, but still faced delays.
The flight made its way back to Boston, but travelers couldn't deboard the plane for hours due to a customs issue.
“People are hungry, babies are crying, no diapers, elderly people who needed medical attention,” Rodriguez said.
The diversion to Bermuda on what started as a domestic flight caused major problems because most people on board didn't have their passports. Yet they still had to wait hours to clear customs in Boston.
“When we came back into the States, they should’ve already had that set plan for how they were going to do it. No, they waited for us to get here to set up a plan,” Montanez said.
“They verified, reverified, and triple verified that I was a citizen, so they let me go,” said Amanda Cintron, who was on the flight.
Passengers said they were glad the flight landed to help the man in need but felt the rest of the situation was poorly handled.
“It was just a hot mess. It was tempers high, it wasn’t a lot of communication, and it was frustrating at the end of the day,” Rodriguez said.
Delta released a statement saying, “The safety of our customers and crew comes before all else, and we thank our customers for their patience and understanding.”

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Sunny Weekend Ahead, Rain Chances Increase Early Next Week
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Friday. After a cooler end to the work week, high pressure will take control of our weather heading into the weekend. Saturday starts off chilly and remains cool through the afternoon, but plenty of sunshine is expected across northern Maine. A noticeable warm-up then arrives Sunday as winds turn southwesterly, pushing temperatures well into the 60s. Our attention then turns toward early next week, when moisture associated with the remnants of Hurricane Isaias and another approaching system could bring our next opportunity for more widespread rainfall.
Saturday will be a cool but otherwise great-looking day across northern Maine. High temperatures look to reach around 50 degrees across much of northern Aroostook County, including Caribou, Fort Kent and areas farther west. Presque Isle and Houlton should climb into the lower 50s.
Plenty of sunshine is expected throughout the day, although northwest winds will remain rather noticeable. Winds around 15 to 20 mph could gust to around 25 to 30 mph at times, adding an extra chill to the already cool temperatures.
Saturday night turns cold once again as high pressure settles directly over the region. Clear skies and lighter winds will allow temperatures to fall into the upper 20s for much of Aroostook County, with widespread frost expected into Sunday morning.
Temperatures rebound quickly Sunday as winds turn out of the south and southwest. Highs look to climb into the lower to mid 60s across most of northern Maine, including around 64 degrees in Presque Isle and Caribou. Some locations farther north and west could even reach the mid 60s.
That puts Sunday several degrees above average for this time of year, with Caribou’s average high now around 56 degrees. Southwest winds will become breezy as well, with gusts potentially reaching around 25 mph during the afternoon.
Sunday should remain mainly dry, making it another good day to spend some time outdoors before our weather pattern becomes more unsettled heading into the new work week.
Monday begins the transition toward our next period of unsettled weather. Clouds will increase through the day, with rain chances beginning to rise during the afternoon and becoming more likely Monday night into Tuesday.
One piece of this forecast involves the remnants of Hurricane Isaias, which will move north through the Ohio Valley over the weekend after making landfall along the Florida Panhandle. Some of its tropical moisture may eventually be drawn northeastward toward New England. At this point, however, the bulk of that moisture may remain south of northern Maine.
There is still quite a bit of uncertainty surrounding exactly how the early-week setup evolves. The remnants of Isaias are expected to move toward the East Coast while another area of low pressure develops near the Great Lakes Monday night. How those two systems interact will determine where the heaviest rainfall ultimately sets up.
For northern Maine, rain chances become increasingly likely Monday night into Tuesday, with additional rain possible into the middle of the week. The latest Weather Prediction Center outlook shows a more meaningful opportunity for rainfall across the region over the next seven days, something that will be important to watch considering the worsening drought conditions.
While this looks more promising than several of our recent rain events, it remains too early to pin down exact totals. A shift in the track of the tropical moisture farther south could reduce rainfall amounts locally, while the separate system approaching from the Great Lakes could still provide northern Maine with another period of rain regardless.
It is also worth noting that conditions could turn cold enough across far northern Maine Monday night for some snow to mix in after midnight, particularly across northwestern Aroostook County. At this point, any wintry precipitation looks limited and would occur as colder air begins working into the region.
Hurricane Isaias itself remains a Category 3 hurricane this evening with maximum sustained winds of 115 mph as it approaches the western Florida Panhandle. The storm is expected to weaken rapidly after moving inland, and we are not expecting hurricane conditions in Maine. Our concern locally is strictly with how its leftover moisture may eventually interact with the larger weather pattern early next week.
For more details on the sunny weekend ahead and our developing rain chances for the new work week, make sure to check out this evening’s First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great weekend!

title: Maine's 2nd gubernatorial debate is over. Here are some takeaways.
text:
The three candidates running to become Maine’s next governor delved into a range of weighty policy issues during a debate held at the Gracie Theater in Bangor on Thursday.
Health care costs, the state budget, housing affordability, electricity costs and immigration enforcement animated the hourlong debate, the second of four between Democrat Hannah Pingree, Republican Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett.
Each of the candidates used the forum to further narratives that have become central to their campaigns as they seek to replace Democratic Gov. Janet Mills next year.
Here’s what stood out:
Charles’ Trump pivot
In the spring, Charles steamrolled the Republican primary field by closely aligning himself with President Donald Trump and backing his controversial mass deportation campaign, including the ICE surge in Maine that drew a public backlash.
That was a winning strategy in the GOP primary, but Charles has moved sharply away from it as he seeks to win the general election. He’s softened his rhetoric and emphasized disagreements he has with the president on policy, including tariffs on Canada — Maine’s leading trade partner — and efforts to rollback powerplant emission standards.
He did that again on Thursday after he was asked by Maine Public’s Kevin Miller “which Bobby Charles” voters should expect if he wins the November election.
“There is only one Bobby Charles and he is perfectly consistent,” he said before listing off his disagreements with the president.
On immigration enforcement, Charles blamed ICE’s violent conduct on American streets, including in Maine, on a new law barring cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE agents.
“State and local and federal law enforcement should always be talking to each other. That increases public safety,” he said.
Charles also continued to pursue his attacks against Pingree, painting her as the status quo candidate because she was a key policy official in the Mills’ administration. When the debate turned to health care and managing the rising costs of Maine’s Medicaid program, MaineCare, he blamed the Democrat for allowing fraud and cost overruns to plague the program.
“I think it’s almost comical up here that we’re debating and hearing Hannah coming up with all these solutions to problems that she created,” he said.
Pingree attacks Trump — and Charles
Pingree, the former Maine House speaker, largely ignored Charles’ attacks on policies she advanced alongside Gov. Mills.
Instead, she sought to remind viewers of Charles’ statements and rhetoric during the primary, using them to suggest he would enable and comply with Trump’s agenda if he’s elected in November.
“He has wanted to open an Alligator Alcatraz to detain people here in our state,” she said. “He’s even invited ICE to come to our polls and harass Maine people as they go to vote, which is against federal law.”
Pingree has made opposing Trump a centerpiece of her campaign, a tack that follows polling showing that the president is deeply unpopular with Democrats and independents in Maine. Those same surveys show that voters want politicians who will be a check on the president’s turbulent policy agenda. Her attacks on Charles played into that theme.
Pingree also appears wary of being too closely associated with Mills, or more specifically, being labeled as a continuation of the departing administration. At several points she sought to highlight differences she’s had with the governor, including tribal sovereignty. Those differences did not appear to extend to fiscal or energy policies despite Charles’ critiques.
Bennett and partisan ‘jerseys’
Bennett, a longtime Republican and former chairman of the Maine Republican Party, pursued the well-worn path of independent candidates: labeling the two major political parties as destructive forces that exist to keep voters in constant conflict with one another.
He described the dynamic as the “political industrial complex.”
At one point, he dismissed Charles and Pingree as partisans beholden to their respective parties and incapable of collaboration and cooperation.
“Hannah Pingree has a D on her jersey. Bobby Charles has an R on his jersey. My jersey says Maine,” he said.
He was asked by Portland Press Herald reporter Billy Kobin why he left the Republican party last year.
“My party in particular has gone down a bad path where it’s become a cult of personality rather than a place of meaningful participation,” he said.
During the debate, Bennett and Pingree agreed on several topics, including the law that banned cooperation between local law enforcement and ICE. When Charles suggested the law led to more dangerous conditions in the streets, Bennett said ICE’s lawless conduct left policymakers no choice.
“ICE has not earned the benefit of the doubt in the way that they’ve acted in Maine and hurting Maine people and Maine communities,” he said.
Bennett’s sharpest critiques of the Mills administration came during the discussion of the state’s health care system and state finances. The state senator has been a frequent critic of the legislature’s opaque budgeting process, which he says has allowed wasteful spending to continue without scrutiny. While he said Maine should continue to support the MaineCare expansion approved by voters in 2017, he also said the state was shortchanging the hospital system with delayed reimbursement payments.
“The state government has made lots of promises and it’s not paying its bills,” he said.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: NFL urges the Supreme Court to rule on regulation of prediction markets
text:
NFL urges the Supreme Court to rule on regulation of prediction markets
The NFL is urging the Supreme Court to rule on the regulation of prediction markets, arguing in an amicus brief filed Thursday that states — which already regulate legal sports books — are better positioned to oversee sports-related contracts "given the current landscape."
The NFL is supporting New Jersey's request for the Supreme Court to rule on the governing authority for prediction markets, which provide an opportunity to trade — or wager — on the result of future events. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission has maintained it has exclusive federal jurisdiction, while states have argued that the array of typically yes-or-no questions is akin to gambling and falls under their purview.
"Absent the clarity that only this Court can provide, (prediction market) operators will continue exploiting the gap between state and federal regulation, endangering consumers and the integrity of sports events across the country," lawyers for the NFL wrote.
According to the NFL's brief, on the first Sunday of this season, more than half of the trading volume on prediction markets — $1.8 billion out of $3.3 billion total — was related to the league.
"Any delay from the Court will result in increasing consumer harm and risk to game integrity," the NFL wrote in its brief.
Kalshi spokeswoman Elisabeth Diana said its top priority is market integrity, and she pointed to its partnerships with the NHL, Major League Baseball and other sports organizations as evidence.
"Contrary to the NFL's statements, the CFTC is actively policing sports-related markets, which are now listed on nearly every U.S. commodities exchange," Diana said. "The CFTC's ongoing rulemaking addresses many of the NFL's supposed concerns. And those rules sit atop the same comprehensive system of federal enforcement that protects trillions of dollars of transactions in U.S. markets."
A Polymarket spokesperson said the operator "shares the NFL's commitment to preserving the integrity of the game," and it is working on "a harmonized federal framework that delivers a stronger, more consistent form of integrity compared to a patchwork of disconnected state laws built for a bygone era."
Ohio filed a brief on Wednesday urging the high court to side with New Jersey and preserve the power of all states to regulate prediction markets, as they do casino gambling and sports betting. The filing was backed by 38 states, including Republican and Democratic attorneys general from states including Arkansas, California, Illinois, Missouri, New York, South Carolina and Pennsylvania.
Roughly 20 states are involved in litigation over prediction markets, and a split has formed between appeals courts, making it more likely that the Supreme Court will take up the issue. The 6th and 9th U.S. Circuit Courts of Appeals have ruled in favor of states seeking to regulate prediction markets, while the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals agreed with Kalshi in a ruling earlier this year.
"As between the two approaches, the NFL believes the Sixth and Ninth Circuits got it right, given the current landscape," lawyers for the league wrote in their brief.
The NFL also is questioning the CFTC's enforcement capabilities. In its filing, the league writes that the commission has 543 employees and their responsibilities include a range of derivatives beyond event contracts.
"Without adequate staff engaged in oversight and enforcement, even the best regulations cannot meaningfully ensure game integrity and consumer protection," lawyers wrote in the NFL brief.
A message was left by the AP seeking comment from the CFTC.
The NFL has urged the CFTC and prediction markets to adopt a list of prohibited wagers that it feels pose the greatest threats to game integrity, according to the brief, but they have declined thus far. It also has asked the commission to adopt an age limit of 21 for trading on prediction markets, up from the current 18.
Diana said Kalshi has tried to collaborate with the NFL on market integrity, but it has received no response.
___
Associated Press writer Marc Levy contributed.
___

title: Maine patriots honored for their participation in the Boston Tea Party
text:
Maine patriots honored for their participation in the Boston Tea Party with commemorative markers
Members of the Boston Tea Party Ships and Museum have been traveling around Maine to honor patriots from the Pine Tree State who took part in the iconic 1773 political protest.
People gathered at the Western Cemetery in Portland on Thursday to place a commemorative marker at the gravestone of Richard Hunnewell Jr., who attended the Boston Tea Party with his father and brother when he was just a teenager.
"He was only 16 years old," said Evan O'Brien, creative director of the Boston Tea Party Ships and Museum. "More than likely, he got his feet wet that night. What I mean by that is it was a King's low tide, almost no water in Boston Harbor that evening. It was mud. The chests of tea piled up as high as the sides of the ships, so they sent the teenagers over the side of the vessels to smash the tea down into the muck, and Richard Hunnewell was likely one of those individuals that did that."
According to the Boston Tea Party Ships and Museum website, Hunnewell enlisted in the Continental Army in February 1777. He served in the Rhode Island campaign during the Revolutionary War and rose to the rank of lieutenant.
Land records show Hunnewell moved to Penobscot, Maine, as a merchant by 1788, and the land on which he lived became the town of Castine eight years later. Hunnewell and his family moved to Portland in 1800, and he was later appointed sheriff of Cumberland County. He also served in the War of 1812.
Hunnewell died in Portland at the age of 66 on May 14, 1823. According to the Stewards of the Western Cemetery, Hunnewell is the only identified Boston Tea Party participant who is buried in Portland.
In all, there have been 10 Mainers who have received Boston Tea Party gravestone markers, and more research is being done to identify others who participated in the Boston Tea Party.

title: Community rallies after donation box for 4-year-old’s medical treatments is stolen
text:
WAUSAU, Wis. (WSAW/Gray News) — The Wausau, Wisconsin, community is showing support after a donation box for a 4-year-old with cerebral palsy was stolen.
The former owner of Townline Market has raised money for his grandson for years.
“Someone saw the opportunity to go take a little extra cash for themselves, not caring that it’s for a sick little guy,” said David Jagler, the former owner of Townline Market.
A temporary jar is now at the counter, where donations have been coming in quickly. Jagler also raises money for Cashton Krause with golf ball and chocolate bar sales.
Cashton often travels out of state and out of the country for cerebral palsy treatments. They’re expensive and usually aren’t covered by insurance.
“We keep striving to give him every opportunity that we possibly can,” said Jennifer Imhoff, Cashton’s mother.
The family is also living in a rental home that isn’t accessible to people with disabilities. They lost their home in the Ringle tornado.
“It’s a lot. We already had our plates very full with Cashton and things that come along with having a child with a brain injury, and it just kind of added another level of stress that we didn’t really need on our plates,” Imhoff said.
Donations continue
“This has kind of been like a blessing in disguise because we’ve taken in so much more than that little box would have otherwise, and it’s going to all go to a good cause,” Jagler said.
The theft has prompted calls and donations from people looking to help. Some have dropped off $100 bills or mailed money.

title: ‘The Social Reckoning’ Review: [Clicks Angry Face Emoji]
text:
‘The Social Reckoning’ Review: [Clicks Angry Face Emoji Button]
To paraphrase one of the best lines in The Social Network: If Aaron Sorkin had created The Social Network, he would have created The Social Network.
Instead, he created The Social Reckoning. Sure, Sorkin wrote the screenplay for the 2010 film about Mark Zuckerberg and the origins of Facebook. He even won an Oscar for his script. But The Social Reckoning makes it clear that as good as Sorkin’s Social Network screenplay was, it was David Fincher’s direction that made that story sing. Serving as his own director in The Social Reckoning, Sorkin hasn’t made a good movie, but he did produce one hell of a commercial for David Fincher’s talents.
READ MORE: Every David Fincher Movie, Ranked From Worst to Best
Fincher, for example, would never have made a film about a bunch of journalists and their sources sitting in nondescript conference rooms and hotel rooms talking about algorithms and charts for two hours. He would not have structured a movie to build to a “shocking” climax where the heroes are thunderstruck at the discovery of ... a fact about Facebook that was painfully obvious to most viewers long before one of its employees named Frances Haugen exposed some of the company’s shady practices.
As The Social Reckoning begins, Frances (Anora Oscar winner Mikey Madison) is a model Facebook employee. Or at least, she would be a model employee at a responsible company that actually cared about how its products impacted their users. Frances loves Facebook, and believes in the work she does as part of the company’s Civic Integrity Team, which roots out abuse and misinformation on the platform.
Civic Integrity Team members like Frances took an oath to put the public ahead of Facebook — a noble but not necessarily profitable tact for a company that, at least in Sorkin’s script, puts money above everything else. Frances tries to voice her concerns about Facebook’s direction at town halls; instead of more accountability, her bosses shut down the Civic Integrity Team.
Eventually her attempts to improve the situation through official corporate channels get stymied one too many times. When a Wall Street Journal reporter named Jeff Horwitz (The Bear Emmy winner Jeremy Allen White) reaches out to Frances on LinkedIn, she decides to speak to him off the record about her team and a recent change to the website’s all-important algorithm.
Sorkin cuts back and forth between their investigation, which mostly takes place in 2019 and 2020, and one day in 2021 where Facebook chairman Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong, taking over for The Social Network’s Jesse Eisenberg) prepares to testify before Congress. With his stiff posture, placid face, and stilted speech patterns, Strong’s Zuckerberg doesn’t bear a strong emotional resemblance to Eisenberg’s interpretation of the tech mogul. That sort of suits The Social Reckoning; it’s as if years under the thrall of the almighty algorithm have gradually leached whatever emotions this man once had and left behind this unfeeling robot. (It’s left to his crisis PR team, including Wunmi Mosaku and Bill Burr, to coach Zuck about how to appear human on the witness stand.)
But there’s nothing much more to learn about Zuckerberg or Facebook in The Social Reckoning beyond that already apparent observation. Sorkin tries to gussy up his staid, talky script with lots of the back-and-forth banter that’s defined his career since the days of Sports Night. Whatever his other flaws as a filmmaker, he’s still got too good of an ear for this sort of repartee for The Social Reckoning not to possess a couple of fun moments as Frances and Jeff rake Facebook’s muck, and Zuckerberg’s team frantically try to contain the damage.
But that’s the only trick Sorkin’s got. Unlike Fincher’s bold camera moves and angles, Sorkin and cinematographer Jeff Cronenweth (who also shot The Social Network) rely on repetitive close-ups in the film’s ceaseless dialogue scenes. There isn’t a single visual moment that stands out; The Social Reckoning could easily be staged as a play, and sometimes feels like it was written to be one. (Let’s not even get started on what a sonic downgrade this film from The Social Network, with a turgid score by Alexandre Desplat in lieu of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross’ award-winning music.)
There are zero sparks between the pained Madison and the deadpan White, although it’s hard to fault their lack of chemistry when so many of their scenes involve Frances explaining complex concepts of computer science while Jeff (a Luddite who doesn’t have a Facebook account and can’t use his car’s GPS) acts confused — with occasional digressions for outrageously dated pop-culture references. (Did this young Wall Street Journal reporter really try to convince her not to abandon their quest to expose her employer by lecturing her about obscure Frank Capra movies?)
What The Social Reckoning makes clear, if only in retrospect, is that The Social Network wasn’t really about Facebook. The company’s origins were a backdrop for a compelling character study of a megalomaniac, and a gripping story about ambition, class, greed, power, and the dog-eat-dog world of venture capitalism. The Social Reckoning is about Facebook, full stop. It’s about people talking about Facebook, yelling about Facebook, and looking forlorn at computer screens while contemplating the deleterious effect of Facebook on our society. Even Zuckerberg, the most interesting figure in both films, is reduced to a relatively small supporting role. (And when he shows up, it’s so he can ... talk more about Facebook.)
You won’t get an argument from me about any of their findings. What I take issue with are those findings’ presentation, which make The Social Reckoning play less like a Social Network sequel than a very special episode of Aaron Sorkin’s The Newsroom. Most of the film is literally old news, and its anguished, scolding ending made me more angry at the filmmakers than its intended target.
RATING: 4/10

title: Officials release names in fatal Lovell crash Thursday
text:
Authorities Friday released the names of the two people involved in a head-on crash in Lovell Thursday that killed a young Lovell woman and sent an Andover man to the hospital.
Police said Ivy Thomson, 25, died when her 2015 Ford Flex collided head-on with a 2003 Chevrolet Silverado driven by Mark Farrington, 66, in the 600 block of Main Street shortly before noon.
According to authorities, Thomson died at the scene. Farrington was taken to Maine Medical Center in Portland with life-threatening injuries. No information on his condition was offered Friday.
There were no passengers.
The crash was being investigated by the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office, which was assisted by Fryeburg police, Fryeburg rescue, and crews from the Lovell Fire Department.
The investigation is ongoing, authorities said Friday, and may take time to complete. They are asking anyone with information on the crash to contact the Oxford County Sheriff’s Office at (207) 743-9554.

title: Hayden Panettiere's ex gets legal status to protect their daughter's inheritance
text:
Hayden Panettiere's ex Wladimir Klitschko gets legal status to protect their daughter's inheritance
Actor Hayden Panettiere's ex-fiancé, former boxer Wladimir Klitschko, was granted legal authority by a California court Thursday to protect Panettiere's property for their 11-year-old daughter after the television star's accidental overdose death left the girl as her sole heir.
Klitschko had filed the urgent petition last week, saying that pieces of Panettiere's property were being taken by federal law enforcement agents investigating her death and by an unnamed nonfamily member looking to sell them, with no one in a position to try to recover them for her daughter.
Klitschko, a Ukrainian former world champion boxer, has had full custody of the girl, Kaya, for most of her life, and she has lived with him in Ukraine. The father and daughter appeared in Los Angeles County court remotely via videoconference. They spoke only to introduce themselves at the brief hearing with only Kaya visible on camera, sitting at a table in front of curtains.
Judge Stephanie Santoro granted Klitschko the status of temporary guardian of Kaya's estate until a long-term administrator can be appointed.
Video below: Police detain late actress Hayden Panettiere’s boyfriend, arrest brother after South Carolina restaurant assault
Santoro asked Klitschko's lawyer, Diane Park, why the matter was urgent. Park said they believed a person described only as a nonrelative had taken items after Panettiere's death and had tried to sell some of her jewelry at a pawn shop. And she said assets were in danger of going unaccounted for during the death investigation. Court documents said authority was needed to deal with both the pawnshop owner and police agencies. Panettiere’s taxes also need to be filed this month, the lawyer said. Santoro, satisfied with the explanation, approved the move.
Panettiere, the former star of the TV series “Heroes” and “Nashville,” was pronounced dead in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, on Aug. 16 at age 36 after paramedics found her unresponsive. A coroner’s report obtained by The Associated Press said her death was from an accidental overdose of several drugs, including fentanyl. She had been in rehab just weeks before. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the home.
Park told Santoro that the property, the pawnshop and the nonfamily member were in Los Angeles County, where the judge's ruling held authority. Park declined to comment outside the courtroom.
Klitschko's Sept. 24 petition emphasized that his intention is solely to protect his daughter’s future assets until a permanent administrator can be put in place.
“There is a high probability that property belonging to Hayden’s Estate may be lost, damaged or dissipated," the document said.
The filing said that before her death, Panettiere and Klitschko hired security to protect her home because an unnamed person had gained unauthorized access, and it's expected the same person would continue to try to “misappropriate” her property.
Panettiere's mother, Lesley Vogel, filed a document saying she consented to Klitschko being appointed.
Klitschko, 50, an Olympic gold medalist, held several heavyweight titles between 2000 and 2015. He and Panettiere began dating in 2009 and got engaged in 2013.
His older brother Vitali, also a former champion boxer, is mayor of Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital. The two brothers, sons of a Soviet major general, have been prominent public figures in Ukraine during its war with Russia.
In her memoir released earlier this year, Panettiere acknowledged being addicted to alcohol and having postpartum depression after her daughter's birth in 2014. Kaya went to live with Klitschko full-time when she was 2. Panettiere's father told investigators that when she died she had plans to visit her daughter in Ukraine days later.

title: 2 charged in theft by deception at Wiscasset business
text:
Wiscasset Police Department posted the following press release on its Facebook page Sept. 10:
On Aug. 10, Officer Jonathan Barnes responded to Ingram Fine Arts, located at 85 Main St., for a report of a theft. During the investigation, it was learned that on Aug. 9, a male and female entered the business and inquired about gold pieces. The couple selected a piece of gold artwork valued at $8,000. A lower price was negotiated and the pair counted out the cash that consisted of $100 bills. When the store owner's attention was diverted, the two suspects substituted the currency with a stack consisting primarily of $1 bills concealed under a $100 bill.
Surveillance footage was obtained, and photographs of the suspects were distributed to law enforcement agencies across the country. With assistance from Lincoln County Sheriff's Office, Kennebunk Police Department, Fairfax County (Virginia) Police Department, and Melbourne (Florida) Police Department, the suspects were identified as Mircea Lucaci and Maria Rostas. Both individuals were found to have outstanding arrest warrants in multiple states for similar theft-related offenses. The investigation indicated that the two may allegedly be associated with a Romanian theft ring targeting gold.
As a result of the investigation, arrest warrants were prepared and issued.
Mircea Lucaci, 35, of Woodside, New York was charged with Theft by Deception, Class C.
Maria Rostas, 49, of Flushing, New York is charged with Theft by Deception, Class C.
The investigation is ongoing ... All parties are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law. Anyone with information is asked to contact Wiscasset Police Department at 207-882-8202.

title: Press Herald Toy Fund prepares for 77th year helping Maine families with holiday presents
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND — The Press Herald Toy Fund is preparing for its 77th holiday season providing gifts to Maine families — and volunteers are again expecting an increase in requests for assistance.
“People are struggling,” said the nonprofit’s operations manager, Jeff Ham. “Every year that I’ve done this, we expect a big increase, and the increase is more than we expect.”
Since 1949, the Toy Fund has provided gifts — three age-appropriate gifts and a book each — to thousands of children up to age 16 in York, Cumberland, Sagadahoc, Lincoln, Androscoggin and Knox counties who otherwise might not receive any at the holidays.
The children who receive the gifts typically never know about the Toy Fund — or the strangers who donated their money or time to brighten their December.
Last season, the Toy Fund planned to provide gifts for 4,000 children. By season’s end, it had served more than 4,400 — about 700 more than in 2024. Ham doesn’t have a firm estimate for this year, but he’s confident it will be even higher.
“The more people we can help, the better,” Ham said.
The Toy Fund offers assistance for both groups and individuals. Applications are open now at pressherald.com/toy-fund. Applications for groups close on Nov. 1, while applications for individuals close on Dec. 1.
Last year, many applicants said they were struggling to keep up with the rising cost of rent and groceries; other parents were struggling with homelessness or high medical bills.
“I pay for rent, utilities, groceries and all of the children’s needs by myself,” wrote a single mother from Cumberland County. “Everything is so expensive, and the prices just keep rising. I work full time with two part-time jobs and still live paycheck to paycheck. I would greatly appreciate the help, as I know my children would too.”
Donations from readers pay for the presents. Last year, the Toy Fund raised roughly $235,000, up from $190,000 the year before. The Portland Press Herald and the Sun Journal in Lewiston will publish lists of donations along with stories about the Toy Fund from Thanksgiving through December.
“Through the pandemic and post, it’s been very high demand, and we’ve been budgeting for that,” said Toy Fund board President Karen Beaudoin.
In recent years, the Toy Fund has also reached out to corporate sponsors such as L.L.Bean, which for the second year in a row will offer up its Bootmobiles for gift deliveries to families in the Midcoast.
“When people see two boots traveling up the highway, they’ll be delivering toys again this year,” Beaudoin said.
Nearly 40 volunteers help the Toy Fund in their efforts, which include moving inventory, packing gift bags, and handing bags out to the families and groups that will show up to the Press Herald’s South Portland office in December for pickup.
“There’s a lot of energy in the room throughout the year,” said Ham. “This is the early season, but in December, when we have days when people come to pick up their gifts, there will be a line of cars sometimes all the way out the driveway, all the way out onto Gannett Drive, and we have half a dozen or more volunteers hustling bags of toys out to them. So that’s pretty fun.”
Volunteer Priscilla O’Neil remembers reading “heartwarming” stories about the Toy Fund in the paper while growing up — memories that inspired her to volunteer as an adult. Her favorite part is when the families come to pick up the gifts.
“You actually get to see the smiles on the parents’ faces, and the relief at being able to give the kids the Christmas they want to give them,” O’Neil said.
Volunteer Carol Semple, who worked at the Press Herald for 32 years, believes the Toy Fund is important because it continues to foster a community connection.
“Newspapers need to be connected to their communities, and this is a good way to do it,” she said. “It’s just part of the fabric of Portland.”

title: ‘It sounds so realistic’ — Woman loses $45,000 in jury-duty scam
text:
(Aging Untold) — Missing jury duty can come with real consequences, including fines and jail time.
Scammers have taken advantage of that real fear, often posing as law enforcement to scare victims into handing over personal information, money or both.
In Arizona, one woman hopes that sharing her experience will help warn others after she lost $45,000.
How the scam works
Kristine received a phone call in the early afternoon on July 7 from a man impersonating a police officer. He said that she missed jury duty.
“It sounds so realistic,” said Kristine, who is being identified only by her first name.
“According to them, if I paid the citations which they were trying to give me — failure to appear in court and contempt of court — if I paid those, then the judge would dismiss my case,” she said.
Kristine said she was instructed to go meet with a bond agent and pay up to $16,000 in citations, or she would go to jail.
They told her she also had to pay bond to stay out of jail until she could meet with the judge.
“I said, ‘This is insane, you told me this is what I owe,’ and they said, ‘It’s not a big deal, you’ll get it back. Just go to the bank,’” Kristine said.
Kristine was directed to stop at four different banks to collect $35,000 to pay the so-called bond. At that point, she said she knew something was wrong.
“They followed my car. They tracked all the mileage. I had to keep telling them where I was and how much I’d gone,” she said.
Arizona ranks high for impostor scams
Kristine is not the only person this has happened to.
According to the Federal Trade Commission, Arizona is ranked as the fourth-worst state for so-called impostor scams, losing an estimated $766 million to fraudulent phone calls and payment apps.
Kristine hopes her story can help prevent others from falling victim to these scams and losing thousands of dollars.
“Just follow your gut. Because if I would have done that, it would’ve ended way sooner,” she said.

title: Decoding Medicare Advantage, from cost to coverage options
text:
(Aging Untold) — Choosing between Medicare Advantage, also known as Medicare Part C, and traditional Medicare can feel overwhelming, especially when health needs and budgets don’t always point to the same answer.
The Aging Untold experts are walking you through what families should weigh first — from monthly costs to doctor networks to a one-time enrollment rule many people don’t know about.
Start with your budget and your health history
“I think the first thing I would look at is your budget. What can you afford?” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “Typically, the Medicare Advantage plans are less expensive. Traditional Medicare, you have a supplemental plan that’s got a higher cost.”
O’Rourke said family health history matters just as much as the monthly premium.
“The other thing I look at is your family history of chronic diseases. Like do you have Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, then it’s going to be very expensive to manage,” O’Rourke said.
Check your doctors and your state’s network first
O’Rourke said patients should confirm whether their own doctors accept the plan — and that those doctors have stayed in the plan’s network.
“Do your doctors take a Medicare Advantage plan that you’re looking at? And have they switched in and out of the plans, because you don’t want to have them in one plan and then have to switch to another, and then you’ve lost your doctor,” O’Rourke said.
She said network size can vary significantly by state.
“In some of the states, the Advantage plan has such a big network that it is almost as if you have traditional Medicare, because everybody participates in that Advantage plan,” O’Rourke said. “So I think it’s important to look at your state and how big that network is to know that might be the best option for you and be affordable.”
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck added that some Advantage plans include day programs with meals, occupational therapy visits and support that allows family caregivers to keep working.
“There are some that offer day programs with meals, and it helps the family members out so they can go to work and their loved ones are here being cared for and watched. They’re getting PT (physical therapy) and OT (occupational therapy) and visits right there,” Cradduck said.
Still, she cautioned the plans aren’t one-size-fits-all.
“If you’re chronically ill, probably the Advantage plan may not be the best choice,” Cradduck said.
O’Rourke agreed, noting the decision circles back to affordability.
“It might not. And then you have to go all the way back to your money. And can you afford the supplemental plan?” O’Rourke said.
The one-time enrollment window to know about
O’Rourke said there is a single opportunity to enroll in Medicare without being screened for preexisting conditions.
“What I want also people to remember is that you get one time signing up with no medical preexisting conditions. Once you sign up for Medicare, whether it’s the private through Medicare Advantage plan or traditional Medicare, that’s the one time you get to go in with preexisting conditions,” O’Rourke said.
She said that window closes after 12 months.
“After that, 12 months after that, you are subjected to medical underwriting, which means if you have a preexisting condition, they can deny you. So if you go back to traditional Medicare, you’ll get traditional Medicare, but you might not get the supplemental insurance,” O’Rourke said.
Comparing the perks of each plan type
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, asked whether traditional Medicare offers more perks for people managing chronic conditions.
“Would you say that they get more perks with the traditional Medicare if you have a lot of chronic diseases,” Rogers asked.
O’Rourke said the value of “perks” looks different depending on the plan.
“When you say perks, I think dental, transportation — that’s what I think of in terms of perks, that traditional Medicare with a supplemental plan, although it’s more expensive, you don’t have the complication of doctors not taking the insurance,” O’Rourke said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose mentioned that some plans might offer gym memberships or devices like a watch.
“And when I think of perks, I think about on Medicare Advantage, they might be offered a gym program like Silver Sneakers. They might be offering a watch. They might be offered some things, and so it can look very attractive because you can look more affordable, and you get some free stuff with it,” Ambrose said.
Cradduck said quality varies plan to plan.
“What I know is there are programs that are absolutely wonderful. It doesn’t mean that all of them are. So it’s not a one-size fits all,” she said.
Build a team — and ask who they’d choose for their own family
Ambrose recommended building relationships with professionals ahead of time, rather than deciding alone.
“I think it’s really good to start building kind of your aging team — have professionals in different fields that you already know, have relationships with, and ask professionals who they would recommend. Like, who would you go to for your mama?” Ambrose said.
She said working with a licensed specialist who revisits the plan annually matters, since plans change even when a person’s medications don’t.
“I think it’s really helpful to be with a licensed professional that this is their specialty, and they’re helping guide you each year to make sure that, as plans change — you might not change, your meds might not change, but your plan might change,” Ambrose said. “And so you got to figure out which is the right plan. And the right plan isn’t what everybody thinks is the best plan.”
Ambrose added that the right plan is personal — even within the same household.
“It’s what is the best plan for you,” she said. “And so even a husband and wife usually don’t have the same plans.”
O’Rourke pointed to two main resources for help: a licensed Medicare insurance broker or a volunteer counseling network.
“You can use a licensed Medicare insurance broker. There’s also fabulous volunteer networks,” O’Rourke said.
In California, Cradduck said that volunteer network is called HICAP.
“We have a program called HICAP, and it is a volunteer organization, but it usually takes somebody that’s been in the field that has worked in either medical offices and they’re oftentimes retirees. They’re not just grabbing somebody that’s totally uninformed off the street,” Cradduck said. “And those folks are amazing at guiding them through this process.”
Ambrose said the key follow-up question is whether that help continues beyond initial enrollment.
“What I would want to know is they might help a lot in getting the initial plan for the year, but will they be there to help you throughout the year when you have questions or challenges? So you want to ask those questions,” Ambrose said.
Learn more
Key takeaways
- Start with budget. Medicare Advantage plans typically cost less upfront than traditional Medicare with a supplement.
- Consider family health history. Chronic conditions are costly to manage.
- Confirm your doctors are in-network — and staying there. O’Rourke said patients should check whether their doctors accept the plan and haven’t recently switched networks.
- Network size varies by state. In some states, Medicare Advantage plan networks are broad enough to function much like traditional Medicare, O’Rourke said.
- You get one shot at guaranteed enrollment. O’Rourke said there’s a single window to enroll without medical underwriting; after 12 months, preexisting conditions can affect eligibility for supplemental coverage.

title: Maine man found guilty in 1984 murder of Linda Maxwell
text:
Maine man Raymond Brown found guilty in 1984 murder of Linda Maxwell
A Maine man has been found guilty in the 1984 murder of 18-year-old Linda Maxwell, a cold case that was cracked just last year.
The jury returned the guilty verdict against Raymond Brown, 67, of Bangor, after deliberating for about an hour Thursday afternoon.
Police said Maxwell was last seen in the Calais area on Aug. 23, 1984, after spending the evening with friends. Two days later, Maxwell's naked body was recovered along the shoreline of the St. Croix River in Robbinston.
Brown, formerly of Pembroke, was arrested in May 2025 after he was indicted by a Washington County grand jury.
Before handing down their verdict, the jurors heard testimony Thursday morning. A cold-case investigator outlined the renewed investigation and witnesses gave differing accounts about evidence and Maxwell’s class ring.
Maine State Police Sgt. Chad Lindsey testified that investigators began revisiting the case in 2021, paused while the agency addressed nine homicides in Washington County, and resumed work in March 2024. The team consulted agencies involved in the original investigation, conducted 35 interviews and exhumed Maxwell’s body for a second examination in May 2024, Lindsey said.
Jurors also heard a recording of Lindsey’s July 2024 interview with Brown. In the interview, Brown recalled drinking and driving with Maxwell and friends, but said he could not remember many details. He denied sexual contact, disputed accounts about wet boots and his return time, and accused a former detective of targeting his family, according to the testimony.
Lindsey testified that earlier interviews placed Brown dropping off two friends at about 12:15 a.m. He also said in the interview that three witnesses reported hearing screams from the river. Lindsey testified he did not consider a bra and undergarment found in 1984 credibly connected to Maxwell and did not seek additional testing. He also discussed changes to evidence-handling procedures.
Witnesses offer differing accounts of class ring
Defense witnesses gave differing accounts about Maxwell’s high school class ring. A friend testified that Maxwell had been in his car with friends and left her ring there. He said he later retrieved it from the car and an officer took it from him, though he could not recall how it first ended up in the vehicle.
A former Maine State Police detective who helped with interviews and canvassing testified that he saw the ring but did not take it. Earlier, another witness testified she had told police she knew a different man had the ring, but said that was not based on her own observation.
Testimony revisits 1984 investigation
A former Maine State Police detective previously testified that Brown said he took Maxwell to Milltown and returned to Calais. The defense questioned why police did not search a burn barrel on Brown’s property and challenged the thoroughness of the original investigation.
A Maine game warden testified that, based on the river conditions he reviewed, it would have been essentially impossible for a body to travel 14 miles down the St. Croix River.
Earlier testimony included a cousin’s account that Brown said his pants were wet after Maxwell’s body was found, that he burned clothing and was frustrated with the investigation. A jailhouse witness also testified that Brown described trying to have sex with Maxwell, holding her underwater after an argument, leaving her body at a boat landing and later burning clothing. The defense challenged that witness’ credibility, citing a recorded call in which he said he might lie if his bail request was denied.
Prosecution and defense reflect on trial
Defense attorney Steven Smith said after the trial that he does not believe there was enough evidence to convict Brown, and that his legal team plans to appeal the verdict.
“After 42 years, we don’t think Ray deserved this. We absolutely intend to appeal. There was absolutely no physical evidence, and nobody can tell what happened to Linda in the 36 hours between the time she left the party and the time she was found,” Smith said.
“Testing the statements against the evidence and once you looked at the physical geography of the scene, once you looked at what he was saying and where he was saying it, it was incredible,” Assistant Attorney General Leanne Robbin told WMTW media partner WABI. “Did not pass the straight face test, and it was that analysis that brought us here today.”
Robbin said it is sad Maxwell’s parents were not alive to see justice served, but she hopes this gives the family a sense of closure.
Brown will be sentenced at a later date and is being held without bail.

title: Maine Hospital Association, others sue the federal government over changes to drug discount program
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Hospital Association, Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor and others filed a lawsuit in federal court in Portland on Friday contesting changes to a discount drug program that saves money for hospitals.
Also listed as plaintiffs are the American Hospital Association and hospitals in New York, Arkansas and North Dakota.
The federal 340B program requires drug companies to sell certain outpatient medications at discounted rates. The savings are reinvested into hospital charity care and other services, such as behavioral health.
The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Portland, contends that changes by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services would expand use of a rebate model that is projected to cost hospitals $1 billion annually. The federal government estimates the cost to hospitals would be $537 million, according to a news release from the plaintiffs on Friday.
“Maine hospitals cannot afford this,” Jeff Austin, president of the Maine Hospital Association, said in a statement in the news release. “They already operate with an average of less than two weeks cash-on-hand, so these significant new costs will jeopardize their ability to care for the most vulnerable patients in their communities and affect the affordability and accessibility of care across Maine.”
HHS officials said in a statement on Thursday, before the lawsuit was filed, that the program needs to change because it has “expanded beyond its original intent to help safety-net providers care for their underserved populations, resulting in large growth in participation and costs associated with the program.”
HHS did not respond to questions from the Portland Press Herald on Friday about the lawsuit.
The federal agency attempted similar revisions to the program in 2025, but federal courts halted the changes because HHS failed to account for the cost to hospitals, according to the plaintiffs’ news release.
“Shortly thereafter, HHS moved forward with a revised version” that was “even more expensive,” according to the news release.
Steve Walsh, president and CEO of the American Hospital Association, said in a statement on Friday that the rebate program would “impose massive new costs and divert resources that support care for millions of patients. We also proposed viable alternatives that would address concerns about transparency and program integrity.”
Molly Jenkins, a spokesperson for the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America trade group, said in a statement on Friday that the HHS changes will stop duplicate discounts and improve accountability. The trade group is not a party in the lawsuit.
“Big, tax-exempt hospitals have long exploited 340B to line their pockets, and now they are fighting commonsense steps to prevent duplicate discounts in the program,” Jenkins said.

title: ICE officer shoots a man while making an arrest in New York, officials say
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A federal immigration officer shot a Dominican man in the neck as he drove in a car with a 5-year-old boy Thursday afternoon, officials said. The Department of Homeland Security said it was seeking to arrest the man in a “targeted enforcement operation,” but protesters and local officials decried it as an example of the dangers of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.
The 28-year-old man, whom city police identified as Oscar Belgal, survived and was treated at a hospital.
DHS did not describe exactly what led to the shooting, saying only that “during the incident, an ICE officer discharged his weapon” and that the man was injured.
But city Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Belgal was pulling into a parking space when a federal officer in plainclothes approached with gun drawn, followed by another federal officer who also wasn’t in uniform. Belgal started to pull the car forward, and then at least one of the officers fired seven rounds, hitting the man below his left ear, Tisch said at a news conference near the shooting site late Thursday.
The child was unharmed and with a relative, said Tisch, who noted that city police weren’t involved in the operation but heard the shots and responded.
DHS said in a statement that it was seeking to arrest a “criminal illegal alien” with a grand larceny conviction and a history of other arrests. But an irate Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the shooting an outrage.
“There is no justification for what we have seen today,” Mamdani said. He said the federal officers who surrounded the vehicle wore construction vests and masks, making it difficult to identify them as immigration officers.
The mayor, a Democrat, said he had spent two hours Thursday night pressing Republican President Donald Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin to release the wounded man, to no avail, and urging them to stop immigration enforcement operations in the city. He said that late Thursday night, federal authorities removed the man from the hospital and took him away.
Gov. Kathy Hochul, also a Democrat, said in a statement that she had delivered a similar message to Trump and Mullin by phone.
Videos show aftermath of the shooting
The gunfire erupted around 4 p.m. in Marble Hill, a small part of Manhattan that is attached to the Bronx.
Tisch said that an NYPD security camera had recorded some of the events leading up to the gunfire, but not the shooting itself.
Pedro Almaraz, an employee at a nearby restaurant, said he heard several gunshots and saw a man on the ground surrounded by several officers wearing face masks and vests with Department of Homeland Security branding. Witnesses, he said, were screaming.
Bystander videos and photos posted by on social media showed a man sitting on the ground with his hands behind his back, in the immediate aftermath of the shooting. Another video shows New York City police officers picking up Belgal and carrying him into a police vehicle.
Nearby, a damaged car sat blocking the roadway with small holes in two of its windows. Tisch said the shooting left the car with a bullet entry point on its front windshield and an exit point in one of its rear windows.
Heated protest and press conference
At a heated press conference at the shooting scene Thursday night, several local politicians condemned the shooting.
“We are heartbroken and enraged,” City Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, a Democrat who emigrated from the Dominican Republic and now represents areas including Marble Hill. Some other elected officials cursed ICE and Trump, a Republican.
Demonstrators at the scene chanted, “ICE off our streets now!” and then marched to the hospital where the injured man was being treated. A sizable crowd blocked an intersection at the hospital entry, and as police began to set barricades so that ambulances and other vehicles could pass, some protesters shoved at the barriers and hurled water bottles at officers.
More clashes at the barricades followed, and police made some arrests.
Homeland Security blames “sanctuary policies”
DHS complained that its officers “are forced to make arrests at large in the community in unpredictable and dangerous environments” when “dangerous illegal aliens” get released. The agency blamed “reckless sanctuary policies” in Democrat-led areas. There is no clear definition of sanctuary jurisdictions, but the term is generally applied to state and local governments that limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
Belgal had been arrested on a robbery charge in 2023, later pleaded guilty to grand larceny and was sentenced to probation, Tisch said, adding that he later was arrested on a drug-sale charge that hasn’t yet been resolved. Electronic court records show that Belgal has pleaded not guilty in the drug case.
ICE agents have fired their guns during more than a dozen vehicle stops since last year, killing at least four people and wounding others. In late September, ICE ordered its officers not to engage in high-speed car chases and to make vehicle stops only if they have completed specific training.
Marble Hill resident Alfred Silva, 38, called for federal officers to more clearly identify themselves, saying one was wearing a construction safety vest.
“We need to have better transparency to understand who we’re dealing with, because anybody in the street can just put on a vest and pull out a gun and claim to be ICE,” he said.
“I feel like regardless if you’re left or right, we should understand that this shouldn’t be happening.”
___
Associated Press writer Michael R. Sisak contributed.

title: Federal government auditing Maine’s Medicaid program
text:
The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services has launched a program integrity audit of Maine’s Medicaid program, federal officials confirmed.
The agency said in a statement Friday that the audit will examine MaineCare’s “oversight operations and processes in high-risk areas.”
“The audit will assess the state’s safeguards against fraud, waste, and abuse, including how it identifies risks, refers suspected fraud, and addresses improper payments,” according to the agency’s statement.
CMS oversees the Medicaid program, which is operated by the states with federal oversight. Medicaid programs, which include insurance and healthcare services for lower-income people, are funded with a blend of federal and state dollars.
The statement offered that no further details, including what specific programs the agency is auditing, will be available while the audit is ongoing.
Maine was in the crosshairs of federal regulators earlier this year, when a U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General audit found the state had made at least $45.6 million in improper payments. The audit, which examined support services for autistic children in 2023, said Maine failed to document services correctly and did not complete “post-payment reviews.”
At the time, Maine officials responded by noting that the Office of Inspector General’s audit did not include accusations of fraud.
In response to CMS announcing that the agency is conducting an audit, Lindsay Hammes, a Maine Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson, said in a statement on Friday that “protecting MaineCare from fraud and abuse is essential to making sure that health care remains available for the people and families who rely on it and that taxpayer dollars are invested responsibly.”
Hammes said the state DHHS has its own program integrity unit to monitor MaineCare programs for fraud. When needed, the Office of the Maine Attorney General will investigate potential crimes, she said.
In late 2025, Maine DHHS suspended payments to Portland-based Gateway Community Services and continues to investigate the provider for accusations of falsifying billing records. Gateway provides Medicaid services for people with disabilities. Gateway officials have denied the allegations.

text:
The Maine Hospital Association, Northern Light Eastern Maine Medical Center in Bangor and others filed a lawsuit in federal court in Portland on Friday contesting changes to a discount drug program that saves money for hospitals.
Also listed as plaintiffs are the American Hospital Association and hospitals in New York, Arkansas and North Dakota.
The federal 340B program requires drug companies to sell certain outpatient medications at discounted rates. The savings are reinvested into hospital charity care and other services, such as behavioral health.
The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Portland, contends that changes by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services would expand use of a rebate model that is projected to cost hospitals $1 billion annually. The federal government estimates the cost to hospitals would be $537 million, according to a news release from the plaintiffs on Friday.
“Maine hospitals cannot afford this,” Jeff Austin, president of the Maine Hospital Association, said in a statement in the news release. “They already operate with an average of less than two weeks cash-on-hand, so these significant new costs will jeopardize their ability to care for the most vulnerable patients in their communities and affect the affordability and accessibility of care across Maine.”
HHS officials said in a statement on Thursday, before the lawsuit was filed, that the program needs to change because it has “expanded beyond its original intent to help safety-net providers care for their underserved populations, resulting in large growth in participation and costs associated with the program.”
HHS did not respond to questions from the Portland Press Herald on Friday about the lawsuit.
The federal agency attempted similar revisions to the program in 2025, but federal courts halted the changes because HHS failed to account for the cost to hospitals, according to the plaintiffs’ news release.
“Shortly thereafter, HHS moved forward with a revised version” that was “even more expensive,” according to the news release.
Steve Walsh, president and CEO of the American Hospital Association, said in a statement on Friday that the rebate program would “impose massive new costs and divert resources that support care for millions of patients. We also proposed viable alternatives that would address concerns about transparency and program integrity.”
Molly Jenkins, a spokesperson for the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America trade group, said in a statement on Friday that the HHS changes will stop duplicate discounts and improve accountability. The trade group is not a party in the lawsuit.
“Big, tax-exempt hospitals have long exploited 340B to line their pockets, and now they are fighting commonsense steps to prevent duplicate discounts in the program,” Jenkins said.

title: Hand, head or voice tremors: Essential tremor vs. other conditions
text:
(Aging Untold) — A new tremor in your hands, head, voice or legs can be unsettling, especially for older adults who immediately worry about Parkinson’s disease.
But there’s an important difference between essential tremor and the tremors associated with Parkinson’s, according to Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician. And the distinction often comes down to a physical exam and a careful look at medical history.
An essential tremor is a movement disorder that causes parts of your body to shake, according to the Cleveland Clinic.
What sets essential tremor apart
“Essential tremors, you’ll tend to see those without neurological things accompanying, like paralysis or weakness or some kind of a neurological change in mental status,” Rogers said. “You really need to go to the doctor because there’s other reasons behind that, that you want to rule out before you say it’s just an essential tremor.”
Rogers said some causes behind a new tremor can be treated and reversed.
“There are things that can be correctable, such like thyroid disease, low blood sugars. It can be an indication that something else is going on,” Rogers said. “Or, if you have a lot of anxiety or stress, that can bring that on — and medication. So you want to review your medication list.”
She recommends sitting down with a physician to rule out underlying causes before assuming a tremor is benign.
“Review all the different things that can be ruled out and treat it before you just assume that it’s just an essential tremor,” Rogers said.
Rest versus activity is a key clue
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said the timing of a tremor offers an important clue for diagnosis.
“I think it’s important to note that an essential tremor happens on activity. Usually you’re writing, you’re doing something,” Cradduck said. “A Parkinson’s tremor will happen at rest.”
Cradduck added that any new tremor still deserves medical attention, regardless of when it happens.
“Doesn’t mean that you don’t check out a new tremor,” she said. “Anything new, you’re always going to go find out what’s going on.”
Cradduck shared that her youngest son lives with an essential tremor that affects his handwriting and artwork.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said that her father went through a full medical workup before his essential tremor was confirmed. Staff at a nursing facility initially labeled it “Parkinsonism,” she said.
Rogers noted that essential tremor can run in families.
“It may be genetic. So again, it may have a genetic component to it as well,” Rogers said.
O’Rourke said her father recalled that his father had the same thing.
Other symptoms point to the real cause
Rogers said looking at accompanying symptoms helps doctors trace a tremor back to its source.
“If you look for the other clues and other symptoms that accompany, then that’s how you can tell what system that’s coming from,” Rogers said. “If you’re really anxious and your heart rate’s going up, then that might be the anxiety. If it’s your thyroid, you’ll see other clues there. If it’s your blood sugar — you can get other symptoms accompanying that give you the clue as to where it’s coming from.”
Living — and adapting — with essential tremor
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose described watching her friend and longtime hairstylist’s essential tremor progress over more than two decades, first appearing in her voice and later in her hands.
“Over time, it’s steadily gotten worse. But she still does my hair. We still have great conversations,” Ambrose said.
She said her friend can no longer raise a glass in a toast.
“Over time, things may have to be adjusted,” Ambrose said.
Cradduck said there are tools available to help people manage daily tasks affected by hand tremors.
“There are dual handled cups and devices and weighted utensils,” Cradduck said. “So there are things that you can get to help with essential tremors that are happening in your hands that are problematic when you’re eating.”
Key takeaways
- Tremors are a clue, not a diagnosis. Doctors look for other medical issues before confirming essential tremor.
- Timing matters. Parkinson’s-related shaking typically starts at rest, while essential tremor occurs during active movement.
- Watch for warning signs. Sudden shaking on one side of the body or tremors paired with memory issues call for immediate evaluation.

title: Woman suing funeral home says wrong body was placed in mother’s casket
text:
HORRY COUNTY, S.C. (WMBF/Gray News) — A South Carolina woman has filed a lawsuit alleging a funeral home put the wrong body in her mother’s casket.
Iris Gordon of Horry County filed the lawsuit Tuesday against Ocean View Funeral Home and Cremation Services, located on Carver Street near Graham Avenue.
Funeral arrangements made after mother’s death
Gordon’s mother, 87-year-old Iris Evans, died Jan. 14. After her mother’s death, Gordon contacted Ocean View and met with Atu Williams, one of the owners, to make funeral arrangements, according to the lawsuit.
Gordon had a contract with Ocean View and paid $13,820.55 for funeral services. She gave Williams her mother’s black and gold African attire, scarf, hat, wig and undergarments, the lawsuit said.
The viewing was held at Ocean View Funeral Home Conway Chapel on Grainer Road in Conway on Jan. 30. The funeral was held at True Worship United Pentecostal Church on Main Street in Conway on Jan. 31, according to the lawsuit.
Wrong body found in casket
At around 3 p.m. at Ocean View, Gordon and other family members arrived and saw that the body in the casket was not Evans, but an unknown person wearing her provided attire, the lawsuit said.
Gordon told Ocean View staff members, and Williams was contacted. In a phone call, Williams admitted Ocean View had made a mistake, according to the lawsuit.
The viewing was rescheduled for 5 p.m. that afternoon, and Evans was in the casket at that time, the lawsuit said.
Damages sought
Gordon claimed she suffered emotional distress, mental anguish, post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety, depression and loss of the ability to sleep soundly because of the incident.
Gordon requested $13,820.55, the cost of the funeral, along with other damages.
Ocean View has not responded.
