title: More than 100 service members meet newborns for first time as USS Abraham Lincoln docks
text:
SAN DIEGO (CNN) — The USS Abraham Lincoln docked in Southern California Thursday, marking the end of the second-longest Navy aircraft carrier deployment since the Vietnam War.
About 5,000 sailors and Marines returned home Thursday.
Among them were 122 new fathers, including one who was greeted with, “Hello, daddy’s home.”
“I can’t explain it. This is incredible,” one returning service member said.
Record time at sea
The Lincoln left San Diego in late November 2025. The deployment lasted 322 days, with most of that time spent aboard the vessel. The ship set a record for the most consecutive days at sea without a port call.
“Two-hundred-sixty-five continuous days,” Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said.
During a speech Wednesday, Hegseth announced that sailors aboard the Lincoln and other ships in its strike group would receive the Presidential Unit Citation, the U.S. military’s highest honor for a unit in battle.
The carrier played a leading role in support of Operation Epic Fury, the joint U.S. and Israeli military campaign against Iran.
Morale concerns during deployment
Reports of worsening morale and mental health among crew members brought the unit into the spotlight during the deployment.
“It’s been trying, but one thing, sailors and marines are a lot tougher than many people think, but we’re ready to get home,” said Lt. James Holliday, chaplain.
In September, a letter from the Navy’s acting secretary revealed “a total of eight suicide attempts across the strike group.”
In August, a sailor went overboard but was rescued.
The Lincoln was relieved in the Middle East by the USS George Washington.

title: 86-year-old volunteer repairs electronics for a good cause
text:
HANOVER, Va. (Aging Untold) — An 86-year-old volunteer in Virginia is helping Habitat for Humanity by taking apart donated electronics and appliances for recycling.
Marshall Johnson helps keep the recycling program running at the Hanover and King William Habitat for Humanity store. The program relies on donations of gently used electronics and appliances.
Johnson has worked as a handyman for most of his life.
“Well, I always enjoy seeing how things are made because all my life I’ve been in our factories and seen all the pieces, parts that go into power tools and appliances,” Johnson said.
From product design to recycling
Johnson previously worked as a product designer for appliance companies, including Black & Decker and Home Depot. His designs are on display at the Hagley Museum and Library in Wilmington, Delaware.
“I’m just innately curious about, how do people make things?” Johnson said.
Johnson, 86, is blind in one eye and uses a cane. He volunteers on Tuesdays, Thursdays and Saturdays.
“There’s so many wonderful people and products, and that’s the fun I get here is seeing what comes in,” Johnson said.
Johnson sorts through metals and electronics and takes them apart to be sold. The recycling program raises money for Habitat for Humanity and reduces waste at local landfills.
“Don’t take this stuff to the dump, just bring it in here and people like Marshall will be more than happy to spend their time taking it apart,” Mark Adams, a volunteer at the store, said. “Separating a different metals and getting it to the metal recycling places so we can make a few dollars for Habitat.”
Volunteer also delivers food to pantry
Adams said Johnson also delivers food to a church for its food pantry.
“I mean, he gets up in the morning and he’s going, whether he’s volunteering here, delivering or taking food from Feed More to a church in Highland Springs for their food pantry program,” Adams said.

title: Weak NECEC conservation plan deserves the pushback
text:
Sen. Stacy Brenner, D-Cumberland, lives in Scarborough and serves on the Environment and Natural Resources Committee. Sen. Henry Ingwersen, D-Cumberland, lives in Arundel and serves on the Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Committee.
We commend the Board of Environmental Protection for standing up for mature forest
conservation when it recently told state regulators that more work needs to be done to ensure that Central Maine Power (CMP) mitigates the environmental damage caused by the New England Clean Energy Connect (NECEC) transmission corridor.
At a mid-September meeting, the board voted unanimously to direct the Department of Environmental Protection to address its concerns with the NECEC conservation plan — particularly regarding protection of large blocks of mature forest, as required by the NECEC permit.
As Board Chair Bob Duchesne succinctly stated, “I’m not convinced there’s any mitigation whatsoever [provided by the NECEC plan].”
Last year, CMP provided the department with a mitigation plan involving a conservation easement on 50,000 acres of heavily cutover timberlands in Somerset County. The easement allows logging everywhere except in small riparian buffer areas and uses a “shifting mosaic” harvesting strategy that allows the very “mature forest” stands that NECEC is supposed to protect to be cut once they reach a height of 50 feet or taller. For most of the acreage, the trees won’t grow that tall until at least 2065.
Several of Maine’s leading environmental organizations appealed the department’s approval of the plan. They argued that it fails to meet the permit’s required conservation goals by allowing forest stands to be harvested before they reach full ecological maturity, by delaying mitigation for 40 or more years and by using a flawed definition of “mature forest” that could set a bad precedent for future conservation efforts.
As participants in this proceeding, we are following the board’s actions and share the strong concerns that Maine people and organizations have raised about CMP’s plan. Along with other lawmakers, we filed comments on the draft plan last June and strongly oppose the current version.
The NECEC is the largest fragmenting structure ever permitted in Maine’s North Woods, cutting a 53-mile corridor through western Maine forestlands. Electricity has been flowing since January, and habitat disruption started when construction began in 2021 and will persist for the life of the project.
CMP’s plan requires Maine’s people and wildlife to wait decades before a so-called “mature forest” emerges. Even then, forest stands could be harvested once they reach a certain height, and no protection is provided for most of the older trees that still exist in the area.
We wish CMP had proposed a plan that met both the spirit and the letter of the permit. We wish CMP had used the conservation plan as an opportunity to build increased trust and confidence in their company.
That’s not what happened. Every environmental group that commented on the plan said it failed to meet the requirements; state agency experts voiced concerns that a bad precedent would be set by the “mature forest” definition; and now the board has voiced similar concerns.
During the September meeting, board member Steven Pelletier said, “There’s nothing in this plan that I felt comfortable with.” He also said, “I saw a number of things that were not just yellow flags, but red flags for me.”
Red flags mean stop, go back and try again.
Although the board roundly rejected CMP’s plan, it still needs to make a final decision about how to fix it. As a guiding principle, it should require that CMP’s plan ensures that significant blocks of forestland are allowed to become the type of ecologically mature stands preferred by many Maine species, and that such stands are connected to facilitate wildlife movement.
The board seemed receptive to this idea. Board member Robert Marvinney observed that areas of older forest under CMP’s current plan may exist for only “a very brief period of time.”
Likewise, a good guiding principle for the board would be to ensure that the plan sets a precedent that Maine can be proud of — a precedent that holds CMP accountable for meeting the permit requirements to which it agreed.

title: Matt Dunlap understands how we in Maine feel
text:
I recently attended a town hall meeting in Auburn to listen to Matt Dunlap, candidate for Congress. I didn’t know Dunlap. I know Paul LePage, his opponent.
When Dunlap said “government feels more vengeful,” I nodded and noticed others around me doing the same. Government does feel vengeful, right now, especially to hardworking families.
If elected, I believe LePage would reinforce the GOP call to prolong the war and permit the Medicare cuts proposed in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. A LePage victory would result in an echo chamber for MAGA policies. LePage has described himself as “a big fan” of data centers. The values shared by most Americans suggest strong opposition to the war in Iran, tariffs and the development of data centers.
Before becoming Maine’s state auditor, Matt Dunlap served as secretary of state. His values align more closely with working people I know. His experience in both offices demonstrates a balanced approach to public service.
Dunlap’s message to Mainers reflects my priorities, including greater affordability for childcare, lower taxes for working families and reduced tariffs. Mainers also face rising energy costs at the pump and for home heating. As energy demand grows, we will need solutions that reduce our reliance on fossil fuels. I am voting for Matt Dunlap. I hope you will join me in electing new lawmakers who recognize what real Mainers want.
Marianne O’Connor
Lisbon Falls

title: Man shot after allegedly threatening and attacking DoorDash driver
text:
MARTINEZ, Ga. (WRDW/Gray News) - A man was shot Thursday after allegedly threatening to take a DoorDash driver’s vehicle and firearm before lunging at him, deputies said.
Columbia County deputies went to 3830 Washington Road near Davis Road at around 5:41 p.m. to investigate a reported shooting.
When deputies arrived, a DoorDash driver identified himself as the shooter, the sheriff’s office said. Deputies also found a man who had been shot multiple times in the torso.
A surveillance camera captured the incident on video, deputies said.
Investigators said that moments after the DoorDash driver got out of his vehicle, the man approached the driver and yelled at him, saying, “buy me a 20 piece.”
The man shoved the driver after he refused, witnesses said. The man also appeared to be behaving erratically and was significantly larger than the driver, witnesses said.
Deputies also said that the man approached people entering the Asian Market, yelling aggressively and offering them $20, though it was unclear what he wanted in return.
After the DoorDash driver returned to his vehicle, the man again demanded that the driver buy him a “20 piece,” the sheriff’s office said.
When the DoorDash driver refused, the man allegedly said he was going to take the vehicle and opened the front passenger-side door.
The DoorDash driver, who was in the driver’s seat, took out a firearm and told the man he did not want any more trouble, deputies said.
The man said he would take the firearm, went around the vehicle and lunged through the open driver’s-side door, investigators said.
The DoorDash driver fired three shots, striking the man each time, according to the sheriff’s office.
The man was taken to a hospital, where he underwent surgery, deputies said.
The evidence collected so far indicates the DoorDash driver acted in self-defense, the sheriff’s office said. No charges will be filed against the driver at this time, pending the conclusion of the investigation, authorities said.

title: Bonny Eagle rolls to 6-0 with impressive win against Oxford Hills
text:
STANDISH — Bonny Eagle’s football team excelled in all facets Friday night and continued to be led by the brilliance of senior quarterback Lucas Klehn.
Klehn ran for 170 yards and four scores and threw a 67-yard touchdown pass as the unbeaten Scots rolled up 497 yards in a convincing 45-6 Class A win against previously unbeaten Oxford Hills.
“There are a lot of good players in the state of Maine, but I find it hard to believe that any of them are playing better than Lucas Klehn. He’s been unbelievable for us,” said Bonny Eagle coach Kevin Cooper.
Oxford Hills (4-1) had allowed only 27 points in its four wins. The Vikings will look to bounce back next Friday at home against Portland — the other top team in Class A North.
“It’s good for these guys to have some adversity,” said Oxford Hills coach Nate Danforth. “The first time this year we’ve had any adversity, really. We just have to get home, figure things out, and get back to work Monday.”
Bonny Eagle, ranked second in the Varsity Maine poll, is 6-0 thanks to Klehn and strong play in all three phases. The Scots play at home next week against Exeter, New Hampshire, then face arch-rival and also unbeaten Thornton Academy in Saco on Oct. 24.
OFFENSE
Klehn set the tone when he tore through the middle of the Oxford Hills defense, making people miss and running through tackles for a 61-yard touchdown. On Bonny Eagle’s next possession, Ben Noe got things rolling with a 30-yard burst, and the Scots unveiled for the first time this season an extremely fast-paced tempo. The seven-play, 81-yard drive took less than two minutes without any clock stoppages. Klehn finished it with a 20-yard run.
“It adds a whole new facet to our offense,” Klehn said. “We looked at their five guys up front and thought our five guys up front were more conditioned. And that turned out to be true and we wore them down real fast.”
Bonny Eagle made it 21-0 in one play, when Klehn threw deep to Drew Gervais. The New England 100-meter track champion in the spring, Gervais saw the ball descending and appeared to give his legs just a bit of extra gas, collecting the ball in stride and easily running to the end zone for a 67-yard score.
The Scots used the supercharged attack once more in the second quarter, going 56 yards in eight plays that took just over two minutes, with Klehn scoring his third TD on a 5-yard run.
Klehn’s fourth touchdown was from 11 yards and capped the scoring.
DEFENSE
Oxford Hills had averaged nearly 35 points in its four wins. The Vikings were without top back Keegan Ridley (nursing an injury), but his brother, Mason, and quarterback Toby Oufiero did combine for 160 rushing yards and the offensive line got a good push quite often. But Oufiero’s 11-yard run in the second quarter that cut the lead to 21-6 was the only touchdown for the Vikings.
“Overall, there’s a lot of good things we can take from our defense today. They have a lot of good offensive players,” Cooper said.
In the second half, Oxford Hills had drives that reached the Scots 9 and 20. Both were stymied by pass breakups from defensive backs Marcus Katane, Noe and Wes Pinkham.
“It’s all about trust. Trust your teammates and then go and get the job done,” Noe said.
SPECIAL TEAMS
Bonny Eagle’s Ben Havu was 6 for 6 on point-after kicks and made the team’s first field goal of the season, a 21-yarder for a 24-6 lead.
His biggest play was as a punter. On fourth-and-17 from his own 15, Havu rolled a bit to his right in the rugby-style approach and then took off. He made a nice move behind blocking to get the first down, ran along his team’s sideline for another 15 or so yards, then avoided a defender and sprinted the rest of the way for an 85-yard score.
STATISTICS
Oxford Hills: Toby Oufiero (7 of 17 passing, 59 yards; 17 carries, 100 yards, 1 TD), Mason Ridley (15 carries, 60 yards), Kamden Record (3 catches, 23 yards)
Bonny Eagle: Lucas Klehn (10 carries, 170 yards, 4 TDs; 4 of 5 passing, 91 yards, 1 TD), Ben Noe (12 carries, 137 yards), Ben Havu (5 carries, 97 yards)

title: Senior discounts: Where to find them and why you should ask
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — Senior discounts show up almost everywhere, from museums to hardware stores to prescription drugs, but many older adults hesitate to ask for them.
The Aging Untold experts are breaking down where these discounts hide, how to think about accepting them and why asking should become second nature.
Assume a discount exists everywhere you go
“I think the baseline should be the assumption that everybody’s going to give a discount,” Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “So no matter where you go, I’m going to get a discount. And I’d be brave enough to ask it.”
O’Rourke said the list of places offering senior discounts is long. “Museums, transportation, Amtrak, drug discounts, cell phone plans, property taxes, homeowner’s insurance, the list goes on and on,” she said.
She added one tip for anyone heading out to ask: “Bring your ID.”
Don’t be ashamed to ask
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said some seniors feel uncomfortable requesting a discount, but she compared it to how a veteran might react to being thanked for their service. “You don’t see a veteran at a checkout line when they say, ‘Oh, thank you for your service, here’s your veteran’s discount code’ go, ‘Oh, no, no, no, I don’t want that.’ ... So be accepting of it. You earned it,” she said.
She framed the discounts as a form of respect.
“This is respect and dignity in its best form, to be able to say, hey, you’ve lived enough, you’ve given us enough, we’re going to give you a discount,” Cradduck said. “This isn’t about your income. It’s not about anything else. It’s about you being who you’ve been for us.”
It’s also marketing — and that’s OK
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said seniors shouldn’t assume discounts are only about charity — it could just be about marketing and enticing seniors to spend.
“So remember that this could be marketing. Senior day is maybe a slow Tuesday lunch day, so they want seniors to come in. It is marketing,” Ambrose.
She said many older adults hold tightly to their savings because they worry about outliving their money, and discounts can help ease that hesitation to spend.
“They get a reward for buying at the hardware store,” she said. “Just assume there’s probably one and ask for it.”
For some, the savings are essential
Cradduck said that while some discounts are simply a bonus, for others they make a real financial difference.
“Let’s be honest, there’s a huge percentage that are really living on that fixed income that really do need, really do deserve,” she said.
She pointed to specific examples. “When you think about prescription drugs, utility assistance, property taxes — this could keep me in my home,” Cradduck said. “This could be the difference between whether or not I have to leave my home and move in with my children prematurely, or something else, or whether or not I can stay here.”
Reframe the discount as a raise
O’Rourke described turning 65 and receiving what she called a “pay raise” because of the discounts that became available to her.
“I take pride when I turned 65, I got a pay raise because of all the discounts, and I was very happy,” she said.
She said older adults play an active role in supporting local businesses and organizations.
“I’m proud that our generation supports the culture in the country, that we keep the movie theaters going in the middle of the afternoon,” O’Rourke said. “I think we’re a support structure for a lot of organizations that if we weren’t around, how would they keep their doors open?”
Ambrose also pointed to a shifting population.
“Soon people 65 years of age and older are going to outnumber our people that are 18 and younger,” Ambrose said. “So it’s really important to keep the money changing hands.”
Where to look
Cradduck said there isn’t one master list of every senior discount available, so the best approach is to ask directly.
“There’s not a comprehensive list,” she said. “So assume that everybody is going to offer [a discount], and ask.”
She suggested checking before booking travel or making larger purchases.
“If you want to go see your grandkids ... does the airline offer a senior discount? You want to go on a cruise ship? They may offer it to you,” Cradduck said.
Ambrose said property taxes are a particularly important discount to pursue, since rising taxes can price older residents out of homes they’ve lived in for years.
“Our elders put a lot into these communities,” Ambrose said. “They’ve been paying the taxes, they’ve been building the schools, they’ve been doing all the things so that we have these communities to enjoy.”
Resources
More places where you might be able to get a senior discount:
- Cell phone plans
- Homeowner’s insurance
- Museums
- Transportation
- Prescription drugs
- Property taxes
- Transportation/travel
- Utility assistance
Key takeaways
- Assume a senior discount is available everywhere you go, and ask for it directly.
- Bring identification, since some discounts require proof of age.
- Discounts on prescriptions, utilities and property taxes can make a difference.
- There is no single comprehensive list of senior discounts, so check with individual businesses, airlines, hotels and membership organizations.

title: US government asks judge to dismiss lawsuit over Army's handling of Lewiston mass shooter
text:
A federal judge in Maine heard arguments Thursday on a motion to dismiss a lawsuit against the U.S. government brought by more than 100 survivors and family members of those killed in the Lewiston mass shooting in October of 2023.
U.S. Army Reservist Robert Card killed 18 people and injured 13 others in shootings at two businesses: a bowling alley and a bar. Card was later found dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.
The lawsuit alleges the U.S. Army knew Card suffered from deteriorating mental health and had threatened a mass shooting, but failed to provide adequate treatment and monitoring and take away his firearms.
In court Thursday, U.S. Attorney Brandon Capece argued that the Army’s decisions about Card were judgment calls and therefore the federal government can’t be held liable.
“There’s no mandatory policy language that has been identified that specifically controls how Card’s chain of command should have acted,” Capece said.
But Jamal Alsaffar, an attorney for survivors and victims’ families, disputed that argument. He said the Department of Defense’s inspector general concluded that the Army failed to follow mandatory policies in response to Card’s threats.
“The DOD IG also said that the failure — the failure to follow these mandatory obligations increased the risk of violent incidences like the one on October 25th, 2023,” Alsaffar said.
Alsaffar said families and survivors deserve to know to what extent the Army was negligent in its handling of Card.

title: She turned her backyard into a butterfly sanctuary
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, SC (InvestigateTV) - The monarch butterfly, known for its vibrant orange and deep black hues, is dangerously close to disappearing forever.
A 2026 report from the Center for Biological Diversity found the migratory eastern monarch remains vulnerable to extinction.
This butterfly is particularly remarkable because it has one of the longest migration patterns of any insect. At the end of summer, they can travel up to 3,000 miles from Canada and the northern U.S. all the way to central Mexico.
In South Carolina, Diedre Richardson has turned her backyard into a sanctuary for butterflies, earning her the nickname “Butterfly Whisperer.”
“They’re fascinating,” Richardson said. “They’re all different from each other. From when they’re butterflies to when they’re caterpillars, their host plants. Everything.”
In her backyard, Richardson likens her sanctuary “like a conveyor belt” where she’ll spend hours tending to insects.
She started caring for the delicate winged insects in 2014, raising them from caterpillars to beautiful butterflies.
“It’s fun. It’s like, oh, this one is coming out now, this one is coming out now,” said Richards.
She dotes on monarchs, black swallowtails, and fritillaries, but monarchs are her favorite. She got her latest army in January.
“Some ladies contacted me on Facebook because they had come across some starving caterpillars on a milkweed plant they brought in the garage,” she said.
Richardson grows the scarce plant so they can feast, and she can capture every eager bite.
“They start running around, and they’re not sure where to start first because they’re so excited about it,” she said.
The caterpillars then curl into a shimmering chrysalis. Richardson said the transformation takes about 10 to 14 days, depending on the heat and humidity, before their fragile and wet pair of wings emerges.
“A lot of times they’ll just hang out on your hand for a while, and you just get to look at how beautiful they are and just watch them experience for the first time the sun on them and the wind,” she said. “I feel like I’m their mom. I know that’s silly.”
That’s why Richardson is working hard to protect the monarchs that fly the Carolinas year-round and the Coastal wetlands, which studies show are their breeding ground.
“Not only do the wetlands protect us from flooding, but now we realize that they’re home to monarchs,” she said. “They’re not endangered yet, but they’re on a severe decline. So if this is one way to protect them, I’m all for it.”
Richardson has launched social media pages to share knowledge and tips, hoping to inspire others to care for the delicate wings that brighten our world.
You can find Richardson on her Facebook page, Raising Butterflies in Myrtle Beach, or Monarch Butterfly Whisperer on Instagram.

title: Press Herald Toy Fund prepares for 77th year helping Maine families with holiday presents
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
SOUTH PORTLAND — The Press Herald Toy Fund is preparing for its 77th holiday season providing gifts to Maine families — and volunteers are again expecting an increase in requests for assistance.
“People are struggling,” said the nonprofit’s operations manager, Jeff Ham. “Every year that I’ve done this, we expect a big increase, and the increase is more than we expect.”
Since 1949, the Toy Fund has provided gifts — three age-appropriate gifts and a book each — to thousands of children up to age 16 in York, Cumberland, Sagadahoc, Lincoln, Androscoggin and Knox counties who otherwise might not receive any at the holidays.
The children who receive the gifts typically never know about the Toy Fund — or the strangers who donated their money or time to brighten their December.
Last season, the Toy Fund planned to provide gifts for 4,000 children. By season’s end, it had served more than 4,400 — about 700 more than in 2024. Ham doesn’t have a firm estimate for this year, but he’s confident it will be even higher.
“The more people we can help, the better,” Ham said.
The Toy Fund offers assistance for both groups and individuals. Applications are open now at pressherald.com/toy-fund. Applications for groups close on Nov. 1, while applications for individuals close on Dec. 1.
Last year, many applicants said they were struggling to keep up with the rising cost of rent and groceries; other parents were struggling with homelessness or high medical bills.
“I pay for rent, utilities, groceries and all of the children’s needs by myself,” wrote a single mother from Cumberland County. “Everything is so expensive, and the prices just keep rising. I work full time with two part-time jobs and still live paycheck to paycheck. I would greatly appreciate the help, as I know my children would too.”
Donations from readers pay for the presents. Last year, the Toy Fund raised roughly $235,000, up from $190,000 the year before. The Portland Press Herald and the Sun Journal in Lewiston will publish lists of donations along with stories about the Toy Fund from Thanksgiving through December.
“Through the pandemic and post, it’s been very high demand, and we’ve been budgeting for that,” said Toy Fund board President Karen Beaudoin.
In recent years, the Toy Fund has also reached out to corporate sponsors such as L.L.Bean, which for the second year in a row will offer up its Bootmobiles for gift deliveries to families in the Midcoast.
“When people see two boots traveling up the highway, they’ll be delivering toys again this year,” Beaudoin said.
Nearly 40 volunteers help the Toy Fund in their efforts, which include moving inventory, packing gift bags, and handing bags out to the families and groups that will show up to the Press Herald’s South Portland office in December for pickup.
“There’s a lot of energy in the room throughout the year,” said Ham. “This is the early season, but in December, when we have days when people come to pick up their gifts, there will be a line of cars sometimes all the way out the driveway, all the way out onto Gannett Drive, and we have half a dozen or more volunteers hustling bags of toys out to them. So that’s pretty fun.”
Volunteer Priscilla O’Neil remembers reading “heartwarming” stories about the Toy Fund in the paper while growing up — memories that inspired her to volunteer as an adult. Her favorite part is when the families come to pick up the gifts.
“You actually get to see the smiles on the parents’ faces, and the relief at being able to give the kids the Christmas they want to give them,” O’Neil said.
Volunteer Carol Semple, who worked at the Press Herald for 32 years, believes the Toy Fund is important because it continues to foster a community connection.
“Newspapers need to be connected to their communities, and this is a good way to do it,” she said. “It’s just part of the fabric of Portland.”

title: Legal path seems narrow to challenge livestream of Fort Hood shooter's execution, experts say
text:
Any effort to challenge the Trump administration’s plan to livestream the firing-squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan might rest solely with the man sentenced to death for killing 13 people at the Texas military base in 2009, experts say.
Broadcasting the event worldwide isn’t mentioned in the Army rules governing how rare military executions are carried out. But that doesn’t mean there is a viable legal path to oppose it by anyone besides Hasan. And he hasn’t signaled whether he will even try to stop anything related to his Dec. 3 death sentence.
Officials at the Pentagon said Thursday that Hasan’s execution by a firing squad would be livestreamed and that more details would follow. A day earlier, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said, “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public.”
“Other than Hasan, I’m not sure anyone could” have legal standing to stop a livestream, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova University’s law school and an expert in military justice.
Could US parents try to halt livestream?
Fissell, however, tossed up a novel possibility: parents who don’t want their children to see a person blasted with bullets on the internet, either in real time or viewed later. Army regulations say, “No person under the age of 18 shall witness” a military execution.
“That’s explicit,” Fissell said. “It’s a question of whether a livestream counts as a presence. … I think it violates the spirit of the regulation.”
The regulations, he added, weren’t written to contemplate witnesses outside the actual site of an execution — and certainly not a livestream.
“This actually has not been explored enough,” Fissell said.
Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specializing in military law, said he doesn’t see a lot of legal options to challenge most of the unfolding details of Hasan’s execution, though he agrees that Hasan would have standing to object with a petition, known as habeas corpus, in U.S. District Court.
“Arguing the Army can’t livestream it because some parent wouldn’t be able to stop their kid from watching it on the computer strikes me as a very unlikely piece of litigation,” Fidell said. “Better legal minds than me maybe can come up with a way to make that argument, but I don’t see it.”
Last firing squad was in WWII
Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building on Nov. 5, 2009, where soldiers at Fort Hood were waiting to receive medical clearance for deployment. He shouted “Allahu akbar” — Arabic for “God is great!” — and opened fire and also shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.
Hasan said it was an effort to stop them from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims. He is paralyzed from the waist down after being shot in the back by law enforcement, and he now uses a wheelchair.
Clergy, including U.S. Catholic bishops, and some officials criticized the livestreaming announcement. Vice President JD Vance, meanwhile, told reporters that he wouldn’t watch it and expressed some doubt whether a livestream would happen.
President Donald Trump signed off on Hasan’s execution, which would be the first by a firing squad since World War II. The last military execution happened on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was killed by hanging.
A 2023 update to the Army regulation on executions gave the Secretary of the Army discretion on choosing a method, in part to ease hurdles to conducting executions at Guantanamo Bay, Fidell said.
A firing squad is “clearly a legal method of execution in the military,” Fissell said.

title: Isaias may weaken before landfall, but storm surge and flooding remain threats
text:
(AP) - A supersized El Niño’s decapitating winds and the Gulf of Mexico’s toasty, storm-fueling waters are battling over the future strength of Hurricane Isaias. And the storm’s tilt and eye show who’s winning.
For now, it’s the waters charged by climate change.
All Atlantic hurricane season there has been “this battle between shear and just the overall conducive conditions,” said Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach.
El Niño — the natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps weather worldwide — dominated. Its wind patterns smothered almost any wisp of a storm from strengthening in the Atlantic, while boosting what will soon be record high levels in the Pacific, Klotzbach said.
Wind shear versus warm waters
It’s called wind shear and it pushes the tops and middle of storms around, making them lopsided and keeping them from making a complete circular eyewall, which is when storms can really power up, Klotzbach and University at Albany’s Kristen Corbosiero said.
The other ingredients for a storm to turbocharge a storm are pushing back. There is plenty of fuel in warm water and moisture. The Gulf of Mexico is about 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit (1.5 degrees Celsius) warmer than normal. The 86 degree waters (30 degrees Celsius) are 100 to 500 times more likely to be that extra hot because of climate change from the burning of coal, oil and gas, said climate scientist Kristina Dahl, vice president of the nonprofit Climate Central, which calculates the boost global warming causes to extreme weather.
“But there’s a certain point where it’s like, I don’t care how hot the waters are and how much moisture you have, if shear gets to a certain point, the shear is gonna win,” Klotzbach said.
The thunderstorm seeds of something bigger earlier in the week grew from circular winds over Central America but often were lopsided and couldn’t quite form a crucial eyewall, all because of El Niño’s high-level strong winds that pushed a would-be storm’s top sideways, experts said.
Then a window of moderation opened for just a couple of days, but it was enough, Corbosiero said. It makes sense it was in the Gulf of Mexico and in October, because El Niño has less of an effect in the Gulf than it does in the main Atlantic, she said. And storms often pop up in that region in October because of more northerly storm systems that help foster the right conditions.
Wind shear wasn’t exactly low, but it was a moderate level, when other factors like unusually warm waters and heavy moisture can kick in. Isaias rapidly intensified from 40 mph to 80 mph (64 kph to 129 kph) in a day and by late Wednesday, Isaias became the latest-in-the-season first Atlantic hurricane to form since 1914, Klotzbach said.
“The warm waters and high moisture won,” Klotzbach said. Isaias Friday was not tilting and had a strong eye, the hurricane center said.
By Friday morning, Isaias blew past the threshold for becoming a major hurricane with winds of 111 mph (178 kph), strengthening to 120 mph winds (195 kph). The National Hurricane Center forecasts it to weaken to a strong Category 2 storm before landfall.
What to expect before landfall
Before Isaias comes ashore — forecast for probably somewhere from the Mississippi and Alabama coast to the Florida Panhandle late Friday night or early Saturday — the wind shear will strengthen from moderate levels of around 20 mph (32 kph) to 52 mph (84 kph) and then Isaias will start to struggle, which is good news for coastal residents, Klotzbach said.
But as of Friday morning, hurricane center forecasters said the coast is in “a tenuous spot” because it would only take a six-hour delay in the onset of that more intense wind shear for Isaias to bring a stronger-than-expected landfall. Regardless of what will happen with wind shear, it will still be a dangerous hurricane when it hits land, forecasters said.
“Once it gets to the coast, we know that the storm surge is going to be deeper and farther reaching because of sea level rise caused by climate change,” Dahl said. “So in this part of the world, there’s been about six and a half inches of sea level rise over the past 100 years or so that’s attributable directly to climate change.”
The National Hurricane Center is calling the surge “life-threatening.”
A warmer atmosphere means storms hold and then dump more rain, worsening flooding, Dahl said. The hurricane center is warning about urban, river and flash flooding in the Southeast this weekend.
“There’s a little bit of a battle here going on, but I think the really important thing to remember is that climate change is like this long-term big kahuna warming everywhere, and El Niño’s like a little icing on the cake,” Dahl said.

title: The Waffle House index: Have any locations closed ahead of Isaias?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News/AP) – When hurricanes tear through Southeastern towns, the hot meals and bold yellow signs of the local Waffle House provide another kind of comfort.
If a Waffle House stays open in town, even in a limited capacity, neighbors are reassured that the coming storm is unlikely to cause devastation.
A closed location of the dependable diner chain has come to indicate impending disaster. The metric is known as the Waffle House Index.
What might sound like silly logic has become one of the most reliable ways for Southerners — and even federal officials — to gauge a storm’s severity and identify communities most in need of immediate aid.
The restaurant chain’s reputation for remaining open when people desperately needed a place to warm up, charge devices and grab a hot meal became a fairly reliable — albeit amusing — resource to help track recovery efforts. The company even operates its own storm center.
State Rep. Michelle Salzman, a Republican who represents the Escambia County area, posted on X saying, “When @WaffleHouse closes… You know it’s time to hunker down.”
The post showed a sign on the front door of Waffle House showing the restaurant closed at 9:30 a.m.
“Waffle House confirmed to the News Journal that all Escambia and Santa Rosa County locations will close today at 10 a.m. and remain closed until conditions are safe following Hurricane Isaias,” the Pensacola News Journal reported.
How does the index work?
Waffle House’s social media shares color-coded maps of its restaurant locations in certain regions that will soon be hit or are recovering from storm damage. The Federal Emergency Management Agency also offers some live tracking.
Green means the location is serving a full menu, indicating minimal damage in the surrounding area. The lights are on and the syrup is flowing.
Yellow means the restaurant is serving a limited menu, a signal that it’s pulling power from a generator and might have a low food supply. The area might not have running water or electricity, but there’s enough gas to fry up bacon for hungry customers.
Red means the location is closed, a sign of unsafe operating conditions and severe destruction to the restaurant or nearby communities.
How did the index start?
Former FEMA Administrator Craig Fugate has said he thought up the Waffle House Index while leading Florida’s emergency management efforts in 2004. He had been searching for something to eat while surveying the devastation left by Hurricane Charley and was only able to find a Waffle House serving a limited menu.
His team began to notice other open Waffle Houses in communities without power or running water. The restaurants eventually became a key feature on a color-coded map that his team provided to help the public and local officials identify where storm damage was most severe.
Fugate continued to use his color-coded map when he joined FEMA under President Barack Obama. He was the agency’s administrator in 2011 when a deadly tornado tore through the town of Joplin, Missouri. Both of the town’s Waffle Houses reportedly stayed open.
The restaurant chain’s disaster readiness is no coincidence. Seven locations were destroyed and 100 more shut down in 2005 during Hurricane Katrina, but company executives saw business skyrocket at restaurants that reopened quickly.
They soon embraced a business strategy centered around keeping their restaurants operable during and after a disaster, according to the company’s website. The chain said it has invested in portable generators, bought a mobile command center and trained employees on what they can still serve if they lose electricity.

title: President Trump no longer attending Alabama-Georgia game amid Hurricane Isaias threat
text:
TUSCALOOSA, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - President Trump will not be attending the Alabama-Georgia game Saturday as originally planned.
According to the White House, the president canceled his visit to Saturday’s highly anticipated college football game in Tuscaloosa as Hurricane Isaias continued its path to the Gulf Coast on Friday.
Trump also confirmed his decision to not attend the game in a Truth Social post, stating that it was important to have first responders staying focued on storm response.
“Based on the fact that a huge hurricane/storm is coming, it is important to have our wonderful first responders, law enforcement, and others focused on that storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the president,” his message read.
Earlier in the week, the president announced his plans to visit Bryant-Denny Stadium when Alabama hosts Georgia in a Top 10 matchup following an afternoon rally in Tennessee.
“Well, hurricane and football? I love Alabama. I gotta go to the game. It’d be awfully hard,” Trump said in a Wednesday interview when asked whether Hurricane Isaias might alter his plans.
Trump continued to say that day that he would not want to take the focus of first responders and law enforcement away from their response to the storm, adding he wanted people to be safe.
College football officials are continuing to discuss how Hurricane Isaias might affect the game. As of now, the game is scheduled to kick off at 6:30 p.m. Alabama time.
According to the National Hurricane Center, Hurricane Isaias had grown into a Category 3 storm on Friday and was expected to make landfall Friday night.

title: Some Medicare beneficiaries in Maine to receive $90 rebate

text:
BREWER, Maine (WABI) - Some Medicare Part B beneficiaries in Maine will receive a one-time $90 payment from the Medicare Improvement Fund. Medicare Advantage enrollees, as well as low-income older adults and people with disabilities who receive premium assistance, are not eligible.
Ann Shea, Medicare supervisor at Eastern Area Agency on Aging, said eligible beneficiaries who receive Social Security retirement or disability benefits will get a direct deposit. Others will receive a paper check in the mail. Payments could begin as soon as today.
“$90 is $90,” Shea said. “People are really struggling with the cost of everything these days.” She said the payment is a one-time benefit, not long-term assistance.
Eastern Area Agency on Aging’s SHIP program offers free assistance to Medicare-eligible Mainers, family members and caregivers. Learn more at https://eaaa.org/health-insurance-counseling/. To check eligibility for the rebate, call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).

title: Bucksport joins list of municipalities to pass temporary data center ban
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BUCKSPORT, Maine (WABI) - The Town of Bucksport has approved a six-month moratorium on data center development, joining other Maine communities that have enacted temporary bans.
Councilors approved the moratorium Wednesday night after advancing the measure last week.
The town says a few companies have already eyed the former Verso paper mill as a potential site, though no formal proposals have been submitted.
One councilor who opposed the moratorium said its language was too broad and should have focused on large-scale data centers.
A councilor who voted in favor said the moratorium would give the town time to study potential impacts and develop regulations before a proposal is submitted.
The measure passed five to two.
The City of Old Town approved its own six-month moratorium on Monday.

title: ‘Get the heck out’: Officials make desperate plea to residents as Hurricane Isaias approaches
text:
(Gray News) - Officials issued a desperate plea as Hurricane Isaias approaches the Gulf Coast with possible “devastating” winds.
Florida Sen. Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible and warned in a social media post: “This is your LAST CHANCE to get prepared. Listen to local officials. If they say evacuate, then GET THE HECK OUT.”
Isaias has grown into a Category 3 storm, the first of an unusually quiet Atlantic season. The storm is expected to make landfall Friday night.
Forecasters warned of a significant storm surge, damaging winds, flooding and possibly even tornadoes before the storm loses steam as it moves inland and delivers strong winds and rain well north into Atlanta.
Isaias is expected to come ashore between Mobile Bay on the Alabama coast and the city of Destin in the Florida Panhandle — a low-lying coastal stretch known for powdery white sand beaches dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks.
One of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could be as high as 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters), according to the National Hurricane Center. Places most at risk include Florida’s Pensacola Beach and the Gulf Islands National Seashore.
Scott said he had spoken to President Donald Trump the day before and the president told him the Federal Emergency Management Agency would be there to respond following the storm.
