title: The Latest: Hurricane Isaias strengthens to a Category 3 ahead of expected landfall
text:
Isaias strengthened into a major hurricane Friday as it headed toward the U.S. Gulf Coast, where final preparations were underway for potentially life-threatening storm surges and high winds.
Meanwhile, Hurricane Simon was headed toward Mexico’s Pacific coast and forecast to strengthen significantly. U.S. forecasters issued a hurricane warning for parts of the central and southwest coast, where hurricane-force winds were expected within 36 hours.
Tropical storm activity has been above average this season in the Pacific because of a strong El Niño, a natural, temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps weather worldwide. In the Atlantic, El Niño’s decapitating winds and the Gulf of Mexico’s toasty, storm-fueling waters are battling over Isaias’s future strength.
Here’s the latest:
DeSantis requests an emergency declaration
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Thursday requested an emergency declaration which, if approved by President Donald Trump, would authorize federal support for the state’s emergency protective measures.
Atlantic hurricanes starting with ‘I’ typically bring death and destruction. Isaias is up next
Be wary of hurricanes that start with the letter “I.”
The ninth letter of the alphabet leads all others in the number of named Atlantic storms that have been retired over the decades due to their destruction or high death tolls. The names may be out of circulation, but storms including Ian, Ida, Igor, Ike, Inez, Ingrid, Iota, Irene, Irma, Isabel and Ivan left lasting legacies.
Next up is Isaias, which became the first hurricane of the Atlantic season Wednesday night. Whether it lives up to the misery of others whose first letter it shares remains to be seen. The latest forecast suggested Isaias could be less dramatic, but still “extremely dangerous.”
“It’s the ‘I’ storm, which usually we have a lot earlier in the year,” said Kristen Corbosiero, a professor of atmospheric and environmental sciences at the University at Albany. “It’s always the ‘I’ storms that seem to cause problems.”
FEMA says its staff is ‘fully engaged’
The Federal Emergency Management Agency urged Gulf Coast residents on Thursday to prepare for the hurricane and said that its offices were “fully engaged.”
FEMA staff were embedded in state emergency operations centers and incident management teams deployed to Alabama and Florida. The agency prepositioned emergency supplies at Maxwell Air Force Base in Montgomery, Alabama, and has activated multiple national urban search and rescue teams “for potential movement if needed.”
Disaster response is led by local and state jurisdictions, with FEMA in a supporting role to coordinate federal support as needed and requested.
El Niño’s storm-killer winds and climate’s warming waters are in a fight over Isaias’ future
A supersized El Niño’s decapitating winds and the Gulf of Mexico’s toasty, storm-fueling waters are battling over the future strength of Hurricane Isaias. And the storm’s tilt and eye show who’s winning.
For now, it’s the waters charged by climate change.
All Atlantic hurricane season, there has been “this battle between shear and just the overall conducive conditions,” said Colorado State University hurricane researcher Phil Klotzbach.
El Niño — the natural temporary warming of parts of the Pacific that warps weather worldwide — dominated. Its wind patterns smothered almost any wisp of a storm from strengthening in the Atlantic, while boosting what will soon be record-high levels in the Pacific, Klotzbach said.
Gov. DeSantis warns of significant storm surge and wind damage
At a Friday morning news conference, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned of significant storm surge and likely wind damage.
“But the surge is really what puts a lot of people’s lives in jeopardy if they haven’t heeded evacuation orders, and does the most significant damage from these storms,” he said. “Everywhere from Pensacola all the way into the Big Bend section of north Florida, you could see storm surge. So please take caution of that.”
He added, “And we always say you hide from the wind, but you run from the water. When the water’s rising and things are happening, it’s a very, very difficult conundrum — and you do not want to be caught in that.”
Shelters are opening for residents along the US Gulf Coast ahead of Isaias
Some areas, including several counties in the Florida Panhandle, are under mandatory evacuation orders. Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey has told tourists and visitors in the state’s coastal areas to leave immediately.
There are three shelters opening Friday morning at schools in Mobile County, Alabama. At least four churches in Dothan, Alabama, are being offered as shelters Friday, and they’re even providing snacks and drinks. The Red Cross has opened overnight shelters in the Florida panhandle, including one at Northwest Florida State College’s arena.
Isaias is forecast to make landfall late Friday.
Isaias strengthens into a dangerous Category 3 hurricane on track toward the US Gulf Coast
Isaias strengthened Friday into a major hurricane as it headed toward the U.S. Gulf Coast, where final preparations were being made for potentially life-threatening storm surges and high winds.
The hurricane is forecast to make landfall late Friday somewhere along the Alabama-Florida line and create dangerous conditions in the Florida Panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, the National Hurricane Center said. Rain began falling along the coast Friday morning, and tropical storm conditions were expected to begin early in the afternoon.
The Category 3 storm was packing 120 mph (193 kph) winds and was expected to continue strengthening. Category 3 storms, considered major hurricanes, are capable of causing devastating damage, the center said.
Isaias was expected to weaken quickly as it hits shore and be downgraded to a tropical storm by Saturday afternoon as it moves north and inland along the Alabama-Mississippi line, the center said.

title: Mike Ditka, the quintessential Chicago Bear and a Pro Football Hall of Famer, dies at 86
text:
CHICAGO (AP) — Mike Ditka, who personified the toughness and grit of Chicago in a Hall of Fame career as a player and coach of the Bears and the leader of arguably the most dominant team in NFL history, has died. He was 86.
Ditka’s family announced his death on Friday in a statement.
“It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka,” the family said. “While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears’ Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever.”
Nicknamed “Iron Mike” as a player, Ditka helped revolutionize the tight end position and in 1988 was the first to play at the spot to be inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. He then moved to the sidelines and later took over as Chicago’s coach. His 1985 team featured one of the game’s most dominant defenses ever. It also had enough outsized personalities to record a rap video, “The Super Bowl Shuffle,” and back up their boasting in the championship game three months later.
He was arguably the NFL’s most recognizable — and imitated — personality during his time as Chicago’s coach with his thick but neatly groomed mustache and sweater vest with “BEARS” emblazoned across the chest. The iconic look is still mimicked by fans at Bears games decades later. That along with his fiery, red-faced sideline tantrums inspired the popular “Da Bears” skit on “Saturday Night Live” during the 1980s.
After retiring as a coach, Ditka became a restaurateur, pitchman and TV personality, as well as a forceful advocate for improved medical and retirement benefits for former players.
Ditka was tough and gruff, the quintessential Chicago Bear. He did everything from order off the menu to knock defensive backs on their butts with a growl. His adopted hometown reveled in every minute.
Revered as “Da Coach,” Ditka was the ringmaster of the 1985 Bears, one of the most dominant and perhaps the zaniest Super Bowl-winning team in league history.
“When I got to Chicago in the summer of 1985, Mike Ditka and the Chicago Bears were king,” former President Barack Obama wrote on X. “Coach Ditka set the tone for a team that was punishing, dominant, and fun — and the city loved him for it. I’m thinking of the Ditka family and Bears fans everywhere on the passing of a legend.”
Ditka was enshrined in the College and Pro Football Halls of Fame and the Bears said during a ceremony in 2013 that his “No. 89” jersey will be the last one retired by the team.
“Player. Coach. Legend,” the Bears wrote in a tribute on social media. “Mike Ditka embodied the spirit of Chicago and will be deeply missed.”
Ditka was the first person enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio, who had won Super Bowls as a player, assistant coach and head coach. Tom Flores, inducted in 2021, is the only other person to accomplish the feat.
NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said Ditka “epitomized football over so many years” during his career.
“He brought intensity, authenticity and an unmistakable personality to everything he did,” Goodell said in a statement. “As a Hall of Fame player, Super Bowl-winning coach with his beloved and iconic Bears, and as a broadcaster, Mike served as an ambassador for the game and inspired generations of fans. Through his work with the Gridiron Greats Assistance Fund, Mike was a champion for taking care of those who helped build our game. We extend our deepest condolences to Diana and the Ditka family.”
Ditka got his “Iron Mike” nickname during his western Pennsylvania upbringing
He was born in Carnegie, Pennsylvania, the son of a welder who changed the family name from Dyczko. He grew up in nearby Aliquippa — which also later produced fellow Pro Football Hall of Famers Ty Law and Darrelle Revis — close to the coal-mining and steel-manufacturing plants that dotted the western part of the state, a big, talented, three-sport athlete and All-American at Pitt whose bruising style made his first nickname, “Iron Mike,” a good fit.
“When our players see Mike Ditka’s name, I want them to understand how he competed,” current Pitt football coach Pat Narduzzi said in a statement. “He gave everything he had and expected the same from the guys beside him. That’s Pitt. He showed us that tough people find a way through tough times and taught us to fight for the names on the front and back of our jerseys.”
Selected fifth overall by flinty Chicago owner George Halas in the 1961 draft, Ditka went on to Rookie of the Year honors, multiple Pro Bowl trips and the 1963 NFL Championship. He and Baltimore’s John Mackey changed the tight end position and offensive schemes forever. He was a battering ram of a blocker, but Ditka was just as likely to catch a short pass and pinball through an entire secondary or outrace a lone safety on a deep touchdown throw.
He left Chicago in 1966, playing briefly for Philadelphia and Dallas.
Soon after his playing days, Ditka became “Da Coach” of the Bears
Ditka moved to the sideline in 1973 as an assistant to the revered Tom Landry and stayed with the Cowboys for eight years, including winning the Super Bowl during the 1977 season, before returning to a hero’s welcome in Chicago as head coach in 1982.
Ditka’s return to the Bears lasted 10 tumultuous years, including five straight NFC Central titles, the Super Bowl win, a DUI conviction, a heart attack, a long-running feud with defensive coordinator Buddy Ryan and, finally, a new nickname — “Da Coach.”
To Hall of Fame linebacker Mike Singletary, the seeds of what was to come were planted in Ditka’s first meeting with the team. He laid out his vision, saying Chicago would be in the Super Bowl in three years — and many of the players in the room would not be around for it.
“When I first heard him when he walked in the room, to me Coach Ditka had the opportunity to be the greatest coach of all time because he had the fire,” Singletary said at the Bears’ 100th anniversary celebration in June 2019. “I don’t know how George Halas coached. But I can imagine that the fire and intensity and passion that Coach Ditka exuded that first day set the tone for exactly what he said: ‘Three years from now, we’re going to be in the Super Bowl.’ And that was 1982. In ’85, we were there and it was because of that vision.”
The Bears were a colorful bunch, with Ditka leading the way
The public beefs with Ryan mirrored the behind-the-scenes battles that Ditka waged trying to contain a team bristling with outsized personalities.
“It was more than a team,” Ditka once said. “It was a team of characters that had character that played for a crazy man, who let him be crazy and had fun doing it and don’t apologize for it ever. I wouldn’t want to be one of these suits walking around on the sideline today.
“I have no desire to be that. I was what I was and they were what they were and, damn, it was fun.”
It wasn’t until two dozen players recorded “The Super Bowl Shuffle” — an audacious rap-styled video released three months ahead of the 1986 title game — that the rest of the football world wondered whether Ditka was losing his grip.
His players never did.
“We call him ‘Sybil’ after that girl in the movie,” quarterback Jim McMahon once explained. “You know, the one that had all those personalities. Mike will be calm one minute, then throw a clipboard the next. People don’t understand that, but we do.”
The Bears demolished the New England Patriots 46-10 in the Super Bowl, but Ditka often said he regretted having McMahon and defensive tackle William “The Refrigerator” Perry run for touchdowns instead of Walter Payton, Chicago’s loyal and long-suffering running back.
Ryan departed for a head coaching job in Philadelphia soon after. While the Bears continued to be a contender for most of the next five years, a 5-11 season prompted Ditka’s departure in 1992.
Ditka’s last coaching tenure in New Orleans was highlighted by a stunning trade
After a five-year absence, he returned to coaching with the New Orleans Saints, but failed to revive the franchise. His tenure with the team might be best remembered for the trade before the 1999 NFL draft when he dealt a package of eight draft picks — including each one the Saints had that year and two of its first three selections in 2000 — to Washington to move up from 12th overall to No. 5 so New Orleans could select running back Ricky Williams.
After a miserable 1999 season ended with a 3-13 record — Ditka’s worst as either a player or coach — he left the sidelines for good.
“We proudly honor his chapters as a head coach in New Orleans,” the Saints said in a statement. “While his time leading our franchise on the field was brief in longevity, his presence left an indelible mark on our organization. Mike approached his tenure with the Saints with the same bold authenticity and relentless drive that defined his entire career.”
Ditka’s post-football career featured TV appearances and advocating for former players
Ditka’s face and demeanor were so familiar by then that a second act became an easy segue. He began building a stable of restaurants and appeared as himself in TV sitcoms from “Cheers” to “Third Rock from the Sun,” as well as shows such as “L.A. Law.”
He also stayed close to the game as an NFL analyst and game-day show personality — first at NBC after his Bears tenure, and then at CBS and ESPN after his time with the Saints.
“Mike Ditka was larger than life, an iconic football figure whose presence commanded attention the moment he walked into a room,” ESPN VP and executive producer Seth Markman said in a statement. “He was fearless and candid on the air, bringing the same authenticity and conviction that defined his football career.
“For those of us who worked with him at ESPN, we were able to experience another side of Mike: a kind, generous and genuinely caring colleague who treated everyone with warmth and respect, whether he knew you or not.”
Ditka’s high-profile status also made him an effective advocate to secure improved health and retirement benefits for former players.
His name also circulated for years in Illinois political circles. Though he never ran for office, Ditka described himself as a staunch conservative and was mentioned several times as a possible Republican candidate, including a congressional race against then state representative Obama for the U.S. Senate.
“Mike Ditka,” ESPN NFL host Chris Berman said in a statement, “was a national treasure.”
Story by Jim Litke, AP Sports Writer. AP Pro Football Writer Dennis Waszak Jr. and AP Sports Writers Jay Cohen and Joe Reedy contributed to this report.

title: 3D-Printed Meat Now Arriving in Maine Grocery Stores
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
3D-Printed Meat Now Arriving in Maine Grocery Stores
There is little debate that people in America love to eat meat. Over the last couple of years, meat consumption in the U.S. has increased despite prices going up.
Because of that rising demand as well as the spike in prices, both customers and suppliers have been looking at ways to satisfy demand while keeping prices stable.
And the best way to reach that goal seems to be in the form of 3D-printed meat.
Perfecta Plant-Based Meat Begins to Roll Out in Stores Across Maine
Across a handful of grocery stores in Maine, you'll begin to see a new option showing up in the meat department.
The brand is called Perfecta. It is a plant-based meat that offers a different style than other plant-based meat offerings. Perfecta uses 3D-printing technology to better mimic traditional cuts of beef, poultry and fish.
Currently, Perfecta is slowly phasing in some of their products at independent grocery stores and co-ops throughout Maine.
While you won't find Perfecta at larger stores like Hannaford, Market Basket or Shaw's yet, Perfecta hopes that will change by the end of this year.
Perfecta is Bringing Three Different Meat Options to Stores Currently
While Perfecta plans to offer additional items like salmon, tuna and filet mignon in the future, their current focus is rolling out three specific 3d-printed meat options this year.
Those three initial options are plant-based marbled steak, plant-based chicken breast and plant-based whitefish patties.
The question remains on whether consumers in the northeast will actually buy-in. According to ScienceDirect, there still remains a rather large stigma about plant-based meats and specifically plant-based meats that are 3D-printed for effect.

title: Wabanaki Alliance to host Indigenous Peoples’ Day celebration
text:
AUGUSTA — The Wabanaki Alliance will host an Indigenous Peoples’ Day celebration on Monday, Oct. 12 in Capitol Park at 33 Union St. in Augusta.
The opening ceremony begins at 10 a.m. and will be led by Maulian Bryant, executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance. The event will feature drumming, dancing and screenings of the films “We are the Warriors” and “Bounty”, followed by guided reflection and discussion. The event will close at 2 p.m. with a round dance.
“Rooted in our homelands now called Maine, the strength of our community reaches far and wide,” Bryant said. “As a new dawn rises, we gather to honor our enduring presence as Wabanaki people – standing side by side with our friends, partners and allies in celebration.”
Event schedule:
10 a.m. – Opening ceremony & prayer: Traditional invocation and introductory greetings by Maulian Bryant, establishing the cultural and historical framework for the day
10:15 a.m. – Cultural Grounds & Demonstration Tents open: Live drumming and dancing cycles begin on the main grounds; the basketmaking, beading and policy info tables open to the public
11 a.m. – Morning Film Screening: Attendees gather in the main pavilion for a showing of “We Are the Warriors”
1:30 p.m. – Afternoon feature event: A screening of “Bounty”
2 p.m. – Closing ceremony and Round Dance
For more information, contact monica@wabanakialliance.com or 207-240-2581.

title: Trump purchased up to $5 million of SpaceX bonds days before major space order
text:
Trump purchased up to $5 million of SpaceX bonds days before major space order
Just two days before launching an effort to slash red tape for commercial space transportation, President Donald Trump last month purchased up to $5 million of bonds issued by SpaceX, a major federal contractor run by Elon Musk, according to ethics filings made public on Thursday.
The SpaceX bond buy was among 517 trades Trump made in August, transactions that spotlight conflict of interest concerns that have hovered over his presidency.
Beyond SpaceX debt, Trump purchased up to $25 million of Meta shares, up to $6 million of Microsoft stock and a smaller amount of Oracle shares, filings show.
Those trades occurred weeks before Trump convened Musk, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and other AI leaders for a White House summit. Notably, Trump forcefully pushed back on calls for a regulatory crackdown to address safety fears, opting for a lighter touch instead.
“There is a conflict of interest. I’m not saying he’s doing anything illegal, but this really gives the appearance of corruption,” Richard Painter, the top ethics lawyer under President George W. Bush, told CNN on Thursday.
Painter, now a professor at the University of Minnesota Law School, noted that the president, vice president and members of Congress are not subject to federal conflict of interest laws.
The White House insists Trump was not personally involved in the latest flurry of trades.
“President Trump’s stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions,” Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement to CNN. “All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000.”
Ingle added that neither Trump nor “any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold.”
“All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers. There are no conflicts of interest,” the White House spokesperson said.
However, the timing of the large-scale purchases of Meta and SpaceX securities are noteworthy.
The filings indicate that on Aug. 18, Trump purchased between $1,000,001 and $5 million of senior unsecured SpaceX bonds due July 2031 paying a 5.35% interest rate.
Two days later, the White House announced Trump signed a national security presidential memorandum aimed at accelerating the “golden age” of America’s space transportation.
SpaceX stands to gain from the new policy, which aims to enable more than 1,000 launches and reentries on American soil annually by 2030 in part by expediting permitting and environmental review.
Asked how he would have advised Bush about making a similar purchase of securities in a federal contractor, Painter said: “No effing way. Don’t buy the bonds. Don’t do that.”
Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren told CNN in a statement: “Rather than bringing down the cost of gas and groceries, President Trump is using his office to enrich himself. That’s corruption, plain and simple.”
“It’s long past time for Congress to act and ban stock ownership and trading by members of Congress and the president,” Warren said.

title: Fact-checking Senate debate between Collins and Jackson
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Fact-checking Maine Senate debate between Susan Collins and Troy Jackson on Roe v. Wade, electric rates, Iran
Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, faced off in a Maine Senate debate, repeating a host of familiar attacks in the contest that polls show as a close race.
In the hour-long debate hosted by PolitiFact partner WMTW-TV, Collins and Jackson sparred over abortion, tariffs, the Iran war and how consistently her voting has aligned with President Donald Trump’s agenda.
At times, the debate became testy. Referring to a ProPublica article about her dealings with a defense contractor who later pleaded guilty to crimes related to political contributions, Collins called the allegations by the investigative journalism outlet “absolutely false.”
At another point, Jackson accused Collins of profiting from the Iran war, an allegation she called “outrageous” and said he should apologize for.
The candidates demonstrated one moment of unity, however, when Collins agreed with Jackson that higher earners should pay more Social Security taxes — even though a pro-Collins political action committee has aired ads saying that very position means Jackson supports “raising taxes on your Social Security.”
PolitiFact senior correspondent Amy Sherman joined Maine's Total Coverage just hours after the debate to discuss claims made by the candidates. You can watch the interview with Sherman in the video embedded below.
The morning after the debate, PolitiFact chief correspondent Louis Jacobson joined Maine's Total Coverage to discuss different claims. You can watch the interview with Jacobson in the video embedded below.
Below are fact-checks of several key claims during the debate.
Abortion
Jackson: Collins “put people like Brett Kavanaugh on the Supreme Court that took away Roe v. Wade.”
Collins voted for Trump’s Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh but it’s misleading to draw a direct line between Collins and Roe v. Wade’s end.
Collins also voted to confirm justices who ruled in the minority to uphold Roe, including Elena Kagan and Sonia Sotomayor, both of whom were nominated by President Barack Obama.
When the Senate was deadlocked in 2018 over whether to confirm Kavanaugh, Collins gave a 43-minute floor speech about her decision to vote yes. Collins said that she wanted to protect abortion rights and Kavanaugh told her that Roe v. Wade’s precedent is rooted in the Constitution. Courts had ruled in favor of abortion for decades.
Collins’ vote was a tie-breaker, but even if she had voted against Kavanaugh, then-Vice President Mike Pence was poised to break a tie in favor of Trump’s nominee.
In 2022, the Supreme Court ruled 5-4 with Kavanaugh agreeing with the majority to uphold a Mississippi law that banned abortion after 15 weeks, with the majority opinion saying, “the Constitution makes no express reference to a right to obtain an abortion.” The decision reversed Roe v. Wade, ending nearly 50 years of federally protected access to abortion and returned power to states to set their own laws.
Collins said she was disappointed in the Supreme Court’s abortion ruling but stood by her vote for Kavanaugh.
Collins: Jackson, “from the year 2000 until he ran for the House seat in 2013-2014, was very anti-choice” on abortion policy.
This is accurate.
Jackson has changed his view on abortion rights. In 2003 and 2010, he received perfect voting scores from the anti-abortion Maine Right to Life and, in 2011, he voted for a bill to create criminal penalties for actions against an “unborn” child.
Over the past decade, however, Jackson has aligned himself with the Democratic Party’s position in favor of abortion rights. In recent years he received 100% ratings on his legislative record from a Planned Parenthood group and, in 2023, voted to ensure state abortion access following the Supreme Court ruling to reverse Roe v. Wade.
Jackson told The New York Times in July that, growing up Catholic, he had “a hard time getting to a place I felt comfortable.”
Electric rates
Collins: “It’s under Troy’s leadership that electric rates in Maine became the fourth highest in the nation.”
That’s exaggerated.
Jackson served as Maine’s Senate president from 2018 to 2024. In 2018, Maine ranked eighth nationally for electric rates, behind Hawaii, Alaska, Connecticut, New Hampshire, California, Vermont and New York.
By 2024, Maine was still in eighth, tied with New York. The seven states with higher electricity rates were Hawaii, California, Connecticut, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Alaska and New Hampshire.
That said, although Maine’s national ranking remained steady, prices in the state did surge during that period, from 13.44 cents per kilowatt-hour to 19.66 cents per kilowatt-hour. That’s a 46% increase over a six-year period.
Jackson’s actions don’t explain most of that gain, however.
Collins’ campaign said Jackson voted in 2023 against a bill called LD 1347, which aimed to curb the growing cost of Maine’s Net Energy Billing renewable energy promotion program. Jackson’s campaign said he subsequently voted for a different bill, LD 1986, that overhauled the program; it was signed into law.
In any case, the state’s public advocate said in an October report that a typical Central Maine Power customer’s monthly household bill rose from about $91 in October 2020 to about $157 in October 2026, an increase of 72%.
The office said that “no single cause explains it” and cited rising New England natural gas prices as the largest reason, followed by higher distribution costs that largely came from storm damage infrastructure repair expenses.
The program to promote renewables “added about $9” to customers’ bills, the state’s public advocate wrote. “Focusing on that issue alone misses about $57 of the $66 increase.”
Iran war
Jackson: “Sen. Collins and her husband are making money off of this war.”
Collins’ husband, Thomas Daffron, owns some defense and energy stocks, but it is a small fraction of the couple’s overall assets. Collins’ net worth is between $4 million and $10 million, the Maine Morning Star reported.
Daffron owns stock in two U.S. military defense contractors, Boeing and RTX. According to the couple’s 2025 financial disclosure, filed in May 2026, Daffron held between $15,001 and $50,000 in stock in each company.
The financial disclosure also shows that he owns between $15,001 and $50,000 in ConocoPhillips stock.
A Collins spokesperson told the Maine Independent that her husband’s investments are managed by a third-party adviser and that no individual stocks had been bought or sold from his account in more than three years.
Collins' voting record
Jackson: “Sen. Collins is voting with Donald Trump 96% of the time.”
This is close.
A CQ Roll Call analysis of her votes between the start of Trump’s second term and the beginning of October found that Collins voted with Trump’s position 92% of the time. During Trump’s first term, she sided with Trump on about 90% of votes.
The analyzed votes are a fraction of all votes that Congress takes.
Only two GOP senators had lower percentages: Rand Paul of Kentucky at 85% and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska at 90%.
The 96% figure comes from a Bangor Daily News article that cited CQ Roll Call data but is now more than a year out of date.
Collins has voted contrary to Trump’s position 76 times during his two terms, ranking second to Paul with 103. Among these were some high-profile measures. In 2026, Collins sided with Democrats to block a nearly $1.8 billion weaponization fund for Trump allies and voted in favor of a resolution directing the removal of U.S. armed forces from hostilities against Iran.
In Trump’s first term, Collins voted in favor of keeping the Affordable Care Act, which Trump was trying to scuttle.
Collins replied to Jackson’s statement, saying, “If you look at all of the votes that were cast, I have voted with the administration about 72% of the time.”
Senate voting data can be calculated in different ways and Collins’ campaign said she was citing a different and broader way of calculating than the CQ Roll Call analysis.
One Big Beautiful Bill Act
Collins, when asked why she voted to advance Trump’s domestic policy bill when she objected to its cuts to Medicaid and rural hospitals: “I created the $50 billion rural healthcare fund.”
Health policy experts have said those dollars will not erase the cut from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Collins introduced the Rural Health Transformation Program to provide $50 billion over five years for states to invest in rural health care. Maine in late July announced it would release $30 million through the federal program for rural hospitals across the state.
KFF, a national health care policy think tank, estimated that the $50 billion could mitigate but will not fully offset $137 billion in Medicaid cuts states, combined, will see over 10 years.
Maine projected in July 2025 that 31,000 MaineCare expansion members are at risk of losing coverage because of new work requirements.
Nine Maine hospitals or maternity wards had announced closures in the past decade as of 2025, the Maine Beacon reported, reflecting a national trend. Hospital administrators say the closures are due to the difficulty in hiring, declining births and reimbursement rates that don’t cover the cost of services.
Jackson: Collins “advanced the Big, Beautiful Bill out of committee.”
That’s wrong.
Collins chaired the Senate Appropriations Committee, but the legislation did not go through that committee for a vote. It was part of the budget reconciliation process, which allows legislation to pass with a simple majority in the Senate.
When the Senate took up the bill, Collins voted on a motion to proceed and said if the legislation didn’t change to her liking, she would reject it. Jackson’s campaign later clarified that the motion to proceed is what he meant to reference, not a committee vote. She voted against the bill at final passage, citing its cuts to Medicaid as the reason she objected.
PolitiFact Staff Writers Samantha Putterman and Cami Henry-Seymore, PolitiFact New York reporter Conor Amendola and News Researcher Caryn Baird contributed to this report.

title: 4 Wabanaki chiefs back Hannah Pingree in Maine governor’s race
text:
Tribal leaders from four Wabanaki communities in Maine endorsed Democrat Hannah Pingree in the race for governor, she announced at a news conference Friday on the Penobscot reservation, Indian Island.
Chiefs Clarissa Sabattis, of the Houlton Band of Maliseet Indians; Kirk Francis, of the Penobscot Nation; and Sheila McCormack, of the Mi’kmaq Nation were all present to make the announcement, alongside Maulian Bryant, Penobscot Nation Tribal Councilor, and Donna Loring, a Penobscot elder, former tribal representative and adviser to two governors.
“Sovereignty is not a favor from the state. It is overdue,” Pingree said. “Restoring it means Tribal Nations will have the same rights and autonomy as every other federally recognized Tribe. It is an issue of fairness.”
Chief William “Billy” Nicholas Sr. of the Passamaquoddy Tribe at Motahkomikuk was not present but also endorsed Pingree. His counterpart on the other Passamaquoddy reservation at Sipayik, Amkuwiposohehs “Pos” Bassett, did not make an endorsement in the race.
Pingree, a Democrat, has pledged to sign in the first 100 days legislation that would recognize full tribal sovereignty.
Such legislation would alter the terms of the 1980 settlement act to recognize the unrestrained authority of tribes over tribal lands, and could make federal Indian law applicable in Maine.
“In my many years of working on Tribal sovereignty, I cannot recall a gubernatorial candidate making such a specific public commitment,” Loring said, according to a copy of her remarks.
Pingree has made a point in her campaign to highlight that this is one of the issues where she does not align with Gov. Janet Mills, who has long opposed the sweeping reforms to Maine’s approach to tribal relations.
On stage in the second gubernatorial debate Thursday night, Pingree distanced herself from Mills on the issue.
Independent Rick Bennett, a state senator from Oxford County and former Republican, highlighted his own bona fides on the topic Thursday, noting that he has sponsored the kind of legislation sought by tribal leaders in the past and was named a tribal champion by the Wabanaki Alliance.
The endorsement can be read as a tactical choice by tribal leaders, who are banking on the hope that the next governor will be more friendly to their cause. Although both Bennett and Pingree are aligned with tribal interests, Bennett has lagged in polls and fundraising to both Pingree, the clear front-runner, and Republican Bobby Charles.
And more importantly, Pingree has made a point to visit tribal communities, including Motahkomikuk. Bennett would likely have been a contender for an endorsement from leaders at that reservation, Chief Nicholas said in an interview, if he had made an effort at outreach.
“He hasn’t paid a visit here, and Hannah has, and she’s been in contact with our community, and she’s came and visited,” Nicholas said.
Charles, a Leeds lawyer and former assistant U.S. secretary of state, has not said that he supports tribal sovereignty.
“My attitude on this is, ‘Come to me as governor. Sit down and put it before me,'” he said during the debate. “We’ve talked details with them, and as a lawyer, I understand the complexity.”
Nicholas said neither he nor anybody in his office had been contacted by Charles.
Reuben M. Schafir is a Report for America corps member who writes about Indigenous and rural communities for the Portland Press Herald.

title: President Trump no longer attending Alabama-Georgia game amid Hurricane Isaias threat
text:
TUSCALOOSA, Ala. (WBRC/Gray News) - President Trump will not be attending the Alabama-Georgia game Saturday as originally planned.
According to the White House, the president canceled his visit to Saturday’s highly anticipated college football game in Tuscaloosa as Hurricane Isaias continued its path to the Gulf Coast on Friday.
Trump also confirmed his decision to not attend the game in a Truth Social post, stating that it was important to have first responders staying focued on storm response.
“Based on the fact that a huge hurricane/storm is coming, it is important to have our wonderful first responders, law enforcement, and others focused on that storm, and in no way be thinking about the safety, or presence, of the president,” his message read.
Earlier in the week, the president announced his plans to visit Bryant-Denny Stadium when Alabama hosts Georgia in a Top 10 matchup following an afternoon rally in Tennessee.
“Well, hurricane and football? I love Alabama. I gotta go to the game. It’d be awfully hard,” Trump said in a Wednesday interview when asked whether Hurricane Isaias might alter his plans.
Trump continued to say that day that he would not want to take the focus of first responders and law enforcement away from their response to the storm, adding he wanted people to be safe.
College football officials are continuing to discuss how Hurricane Isaias might affect the game. As of now, the game is scheduled to kick off at 6:30 p.m. Alabama time.
According to the National Hurricane Center, Hurricane Isaias had grown into a Category 3 storm on Friday and was expected to make landfall Friday night.

title: Understanding the difference between psychosis and schizophrenia
text:
Understanding the difference between psychosis and schizophrenia with help of Sweetser's PRTF medical director
The word psychosis can carry a lot of fear and misunderstanding, but experiencing symptoms like hearing voices does not necessarily mean someone has schizophrenia.
Dr. Abhilasha Khurana, Sweetser's psychiatric residential treatment facility medical director, joined Maine's Total Coverage on Friday to explain the difference between psychosis and schizophrenia.
Khurana said psychosis is a collection of symptoms that involves loss of contact with reality, which leads to difficulty distinguishing between what is real and what is not. Individuals can experience changes in their thoughts, perceptions or behavior, and psychosis can occur with several different psychiatric or medical conditions.
Schizophrenia, on the other hand, is a specific mental health disorder. Khurana said psychosis is part of schizophrenia, but experiencing psychosis does not automatically mean someone has schizophrenia. The distinction is important because when someone is experiencing symptoms of psychosis, there should be careful clinical assessment.
Are there warning signs that families, friends, or professionals should pay attention to?
Khurana said there are warning signs, though one sign alone does not necessarily mean a person has psychosis. The following are signs to look out for:
- Growing suspiciousness or paranoia;
- Strongly held beliefs that are not held by people in the person's culture or community;
- Hearing or seeing things which are not there;
- Not spending as much time with friends or family;
- A noticeable drop in school, work or everyday functioning;
- Trouble thinking clearly or communicating; and
- Changes in sleep, self-care or personal hygiene.
Khurana said that in order for a person to have psychosis, they typically would have more than one sign or symptom. She also noted that simply hearing a voice does not mean someone has psychosis.
What can treatment look like for someone experiencing psychosis?
Khurana said treatment is individualized because no two people experience psychosis in exactly the same way. Depending on the underlying cause and the person's needs, treatment may include medication, individual therapy, family education and support, case management, and help staying connected to school, work and other important parts of life.
According to Khurana, early evaluation matters because research shows people experiencing psychosis tend to have better outcomes when effective treatment begins sooner.
Khurana said there are a lot of reasons for hope because psychosis, though a serious condition, is treatable. With appropriate care, people can manage symptoms and return to the things that are important to them. Khurana said holistic treatment allows people who have had psychosis to lead fulfilling lives.
Upcoming workshop on psychosis and what people can expect to learn
Khurana is leading a workshop called "Demystifying Psychosis," and the goal is to help make clinicians feel more comfortable assessing psychosis symptoms rather than being intimidated by them.
The workshop will look at diagnostic criteria for psychotic disorders and feature discussion about the symptoms practitioners may encounter, as well as symptoms that can occur in other conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder, depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Khurana said the workshop will also review treatment options and practical next steps, so clinicians leave feeling better prepared when someone presents with these symptoms.
People can learn more and register for Sweetser’s Training Institute workshop at Sweetser.org/Training.

title: Lewiston man sentenced to 8 years in jail for 4-year-old stepson’s shooting death
text:
AUBURN — A Lewiston man was sentenced Friday in Androscoggin County Superior Court to 17 years in prison, with all but eight suspended, for the death of his 4-year-old stepson, Jasper Smith, who fatally shot himself with an unsecured handgun on May 17, 2025.
Robert McCoy, 37, will serve eight years followed by six years of probation. He had faced up to 30 years on the manslaughter charge.
McCoy pleaded guilty to the charges on Aug. 3.
In addition, Justice Jennifer Archer sentenced him to 364 days on a child endangerment charge and two years on a violation of probation charge to be served at the same time as the manslaughter sentence.
While serving probation, McCoy cannot have contact with children under age 6, cannot possess firearms or ammunition, and can undergo random searches.
The child found his stepfather’s loaded 9 mm Luger handgun in a zipped cross-body bag near a basinet at the family’s apartment on Pierce Street in Lewiston. He brought it to his bedroom he shared with an 8-year-old brother and took the gun out and shot himself, Archer said.
The child shot himself in the forehead in his bed, Deputy Attorney General Lisa Bogue told the court.
McCoy went to his stepson and picked him up and carried him to his wife, who he asked to call 911, and then returned him to his bed, Archer said.
His older brother, who was in the bathroom with bloodshot eyes, said he “was sorry” that he had been sleeping and not protecting his brother, according witness statements discussed briefly by Archer during the sentencing.
Prosecutors said the person who did have a duty to protect his children — his parent — violated that duty.
The handgun was kept in a gun safe many times, but had been left within the children’s reach several times, witnesses told police. The older brother told police he had access to the cross-body bag and had touched the gun before, according to testimony. There are four children in the family, the other two were 2 years old and 6 months old.
This was “reckless criminal negligence,” Bogue said.
Law enforcement officers, including members of the Lewiston Police Department and Maine State Police, were in the courtroom during the hearing. Many of those involved in the difficult case are still dealing with the effects, Bogue said.
Jasper’s mother, Mikayla Smith, read a prewritten statement through her tears.
She said she had loved McCoy before the fatal shooting and trusted him to take care of the children. Smith repeated her son’s name, “Jasper Smith,” who she said she will carry through the rest of her life.
“I loved you,” she told McCoy, “but I loved my child more.”
Jasper’s biological father, Andrew Northam, told the court he had been trying to get back into his child’s life.
“I lost my son before I ever got a chance to know him” he said on Zoom into the courtroom.
Jasper’s uncle Anthony Smith wrote in a statement that the death should have and could have been prevented. He referred to Jasper as an “innocent angel” and a fun-loving child.
Jasper’s aunt Laura Smith said the family has suffered tremendously over the past 17 months. Her nephew would have been 6 now. “Until we meet again, I will love you,” she said.
McCoy’s attorney, Justin Leary, told the court that his client acknowledged he was criminally negligent and that he did practice gun safety many days. McCoy doesn’t have a prior criminal history.
“He did love and care for his children,” Leary said, and he is “crushed and haunted” by the death of Jasper.
McCoy, wearing a gray jail uniform, stood up to speak to the court through his tears, which made it difficult to understand.
He was the one who got the children up for school and made sure they were dressed, he said. After school, he took the children to the park to play.
He has nightmares and anxiety attacks and will live with this for the rest of his life, McCoy said.
“He was a child,” he said. “I am sorry. … I failed you all. I deeply loved my son. I love you Jasper as I do my own children.”
Family members previously said Maine Department of Health and Human Services had a total of 17 calls from various people in Jasper’s life. Seven investigations followed with no findings, a family member had said.
The aggravating and mitigating factors Archer said she considered in her sentence included that some supporters had written McCoy was a hardworking man who loved his children, McCoy’s “genuine sadness” about the death, and his cavalier attitude toward gun safety that caused him to leave a loaded handgun accessible to his children.
McCoy was arrested in June 2025. Maine strengthened its child endangerment laws in 2021, which made it illegal to leave unsecured firearms accessible to children.

title: The Waffle House index: Have any locations closed ahead of Isaias?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Gray News/AP) – When hurricanes tear through Southeastern towns, the hot meals and bold yellow signs of the local Waffle House provide another kind of comfort.
If a Waffle House stays open in town, even in a limited capacity, neighbors are reassured that the coming storm is unlikely to cause devastation.
A closed location of the dependable diner chain has come to indicate impending disaster. The metric is known as the Waffle House Index.
What might sound like silly logic has become one of the most reliable ways for Southerners — and even federal officials — to gauge a storm’s severity and identify communities most in need of immediate aid.
The restaurant chain’s reputation for remaining open when people desperately needed a place to warm up, charge devices and grab a hot meal became a fairly reliable — albeit amusing — resource to help track recovery efforts. The company even operates its own storm center.
State Rep. Michelle Salzman, a Republican who represents the Escambia County area, posted on X saying, “When @WaffleHouse closes… You know it’s time to hunker down.”
The post showed a sign on the front door of Waffle House showing the restaurant closed at 9:30 a.m.
“Waffle House confirmed to the News Journal that all Escambia and Santa Rosa County locations will close today at 10 a.m. and remain closed until conditions are safe following Hurricane Isaias,” the Pensacola News Journal reported.
How does the index work?
Waffle House’s social media shares color-coded maps of its restaurant locations in certain regions that will soon be hit or are recovering from storm damage. The Federal Emergency Management Agency also offers some live tracking.
Green means the location is serving a full menu, indicating minimal damage in the surrounding area. The lights are on and the syrup is flowing.
Yellow means the restaurant is serving a limited menu, a signal that it’s pulling power from a generator and might have a low food supply. The area might not have running water or electricity, but there’s enough gas to fry up bacon for hungry customers.
Red means the location is closed, a sign of unsafe operating conditions and severe destruction to the restaurant or nearby communities.
How did the index start?
Former FEMA Administrator Craig Fugate has said he thought up the Waffle House Index while leading Florida’s emergency management efforts in 2004. He had been searching for something to eat while surveying the devastation left by Hurricane Charley and was only able to find a Waffle House serving a limited menu.
His team began to notice other open Waffle Houses in communities without power or running water. The restaurants eventually became a key feature on a color-coded map that his team provided to help the public and local officials identify where storm damage was most severe.
Fugate continued to use his color-coded map when he joined FEMA under President Barack Obama. He was the agency’s administrator in 2011 when a deadly tornado tore through the town of Joplin, Missouri. Both of the town’s Waffle Houses reportedly stayed open.
The restaurant chain’s disaster readiness is no coincidence. Seven locations were destroyed and 100 more shut down in 2005 during Hurricane Katrina, but company executives saw business skyrocket at restaurants that reopened quickly.
They soon embraced a business strategy centered around keeping their restaurants operable during and after a disaster, according to the company’s website. The chain said it has invested in portable generators, bought a mobile command center and trained employees on what they can still serve if they lose electricity.

title: Subtle Change Coming to Target Stores in Maine This November
text:
Subtle Change Coming to Target Stores in Maine This November
Earlier this year, Target announced that some sweeping changes were coming to their stores across the United States.
Some of those changes would be more obvious than others. That included Target ending their partnership with Ulta and launching their own beauty studio within stores.
Another promised change from Target was expanding their grocery department at all Target stores that offer them. But shoppers across Maine will notice another subtle change on top of new items.
Target Will Have Dedicated Grocery Employees at Stores Across Maine
As Target works towards expanding their popular Good & Gather brand, some feedback from regular Target shoppers has inspired another change.
According to Supermarket News, one of the top complaints of Target shoppers who consistently shop for groceries at their stores was the lack of dedicated employees in the grocery section.
That will change at stores in Maine and across the country in November as Target will roll out dedicated grocery employees. You'll be able to spot those employees as they will adorn hats and aprons versus the typical Target employee outfit.
Target Has Been Quietly Changing Other Sections of Their Stores Across Maine
Beyond the introduction of the Target Beauty Studio, there have been some other subtle changes happening inside Target stores.
Target has been merging some of their departments including electronics, books and toys. Target will trim some of their electronics offerings where sales have slowed and increase stock of plushies, Legos and more unique toys and games that customers are more likely to be after.
Shoppers will also changes in the home goods and clothing sections.
From bedding to decorative items and more, Target plans to redo about 75% of their home goods department by the end of the year.
Target also plans to collaborate with more designers and feature unique items that customers can only find through Target. There will also be an advanced partnership with Levi's Jeans, which will be more widely available at Target stores nationwide.

title: Don’t feel like yourself? It could be a vitamin deficiency
text:
(Aging Untold) — As we get older, our bodies can have a harder time absorbing key vitamins and minerals — and the warning signs are easy to miss.
The Aging Untold hosts are breaking down which vitamin deficiencies are most common in older adults, what to watch for and what to ask your doctor.
‘I just don’t feel like myself’
When someone describes that vague, hard-to-pin-down feeling, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said a handful of nutrient deficiencies are often behind it.
“Vitamins and trace minerals are very key for every cell in the body to function,” Rogers said. “So the other organs, they can’t function alone.”
She points to two deficiencies in particular — vitamin B12 and vitamin D.
“When I look at things like vitamin B12 deficiency, a lot of people will have those, and they will have some mood issues and sensory issues, nerve issues and things like that,” Rogers said. “And a big one is vitamin D — when there’s no sunlight out, people really get kind of depressed and all that in the wintertime.”
Low vitamin D can also show up in less obvious ways, she said.
“Atrial fibrillation could be manifest in someone with a vitamin D deficiency, and irritable bowel syndrome,” Rogers said. “I say that the vitamins — they can steal your vitality. So they are thieves.”
Why a basic blood test isn’t enough
Rogers said checking blood levels is a good first step, but it has limits.
“The blood levels fluctuate daily. They don’t test whether your receptors are working. They don’t test whether you can transport [nutrients]. And they don’t test what your tissue is expressing,” Rogers said. “If you can go to the next level and get a personalized test called genomics, it looks at how you’re metabolizing so you can be guided specifically on what you need.”
She said that kind of testing should happen with guidance from a doctor who can determine potential interactions with medications the patient is taking.
“This really needs to be physician-driven, not just grabbing things off the shelf,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
Rogers stressed that as well.
“I think people identify with, ‘Oh man, I’m so tired,’ and the commercial comes on and, ‘Oh, I want to get some of that,” Rogers responded.
Start with food, not supplements
Before reaching for a bottle, diet should come first, aging expert Amy O’Rourke said.
“I’m going to put out a vote for a really balanced diet — low processed foods. Start there and eat well,” O’Rourke said. “And then if you feel like you’re having some symptoms, go to a doctor and say, this is what I’m eating. Make sure it’s healthy, and you can do it in an affordable way.”
She said that conversation should include a direct question for your doctor.
“And then ask your doctor, ‘This is what I’m eating. How am I doing, and what should I be taking, if anything?’” O’Rourke said. “I’m a believer that if you eat well, you might not need all the supplements.”
Ambrose added that the goal is giving the body what it needs to function at full capacity.
“If we want to increase our capacity, we want to make sure that we’re optimizing our nutrients,” Ambrose said. “We sometimes get criticized as a country as being a nation of overfed and undernourished.”
If you do take supplements, check the label
Rogers said not all supplements on store shelves are created equal.
“Look at your source — look at the source of your vitamins and nutrients, even in the stores and all that. Look on the bottle to see if it’s third-party tested,” Rogers said. “Look for third-party testing. Look at the ingredients. If you have a lot of fillers in there, you know that’s not a good thing.”
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said shortcuts aren’t worth it.
“You don’t want to take a capsule full of sand just because somebody’s selling it to you as the next quick fix to make you feel better, think better and keep your brain clear,” Cradduck said.
The most common deficiencies in older adults
Rogers said that B vitamins and vitamin D top the list for older adults.
“There’s a B complex — B1, B2, B3, B6, biotin is B7, and then you have your B12,” Rogers said. “But absolutely, vitamin B complex is huge in pretty much all chemical reactions in the body, as is D, as is magnesium. Magnesium is huge.”
Ambrose said the bigger-picture message is about how health care itself is changing.
“The big untold truth here is that health care today is shifting more to personalized, customized health care versus one size fits all,” she said.
Key takeaways
- They mimic aging. Low levels of B12 or vitamin D can cause fatigue, memory loss and muscle weakness — symptoms that are easily mistaken for simply growing older.
- Don’t guess, assess. Personalized lab tests can target what your body actually needs instead of relying on guesswork.
- Loop in your doctor. Supplement decisions should be physician-driven to avoid harmful interactions with medications you’re already taking.

title: County treasurers submit resignations
text:
Washington County government's provisional treasurer and deputy treasurer both submitted their resignations on September 28, effective on October 9, in part because of the work environment at the county offices.
Provisional Treasurer Grace Falzarano of Columbia Falls states in her resignation letter, "The specific project I was brought in to complete for the county is now finalized. In light of current hostile working conditions, I feel it is the right time to step down." She is also resigning from all county committees that she serves on.
Sondra Small of Jonesport resigned as deputy treasurer so that she would not be automatically appointed to assume the treasurer's duties, as required under Maine law. She will continue as the county's finance manager. She notes in her letter that her resignation "will allow me to narrow my daily focus down to fewer overall responsibilities and dedicate my attention to the many other daily tasks on my plate."
As for the working conditions in county government offices, at a special meeting on September 2 the county commissioners had hired Bangor attorney Jonathan Pottle to help with reorganizing county government and manage mounting internal tensions. Those tensions came to a head on July 2, when two of the county commissioners voted to fire County Manager Renee Gray. Gray then sued the county and two of its commissioners, David Burns and Billy Howard, alleging numerous violations, including firing her illegally and subjecting her to sexually discriminatory and derogatory language. A settlement among the parties, adding legal protections to her contract, was then reached, which was signed on September 10 by Gray and the commissioners. The settlement also included payment of $2,500 to Gray, along with her attorney fees of $7,000.
When the lawsuit was filed, Falzarano says she was told, indirectly, that the county's attorneys directed all staff not to speak to anyone outside of the county government offices.
Falzarano was appointed as the provisional treasurer by the commissioners in September 2025, following the resignation of Jill Holmes after the county's severe budget crisis was discovered. Holmes had served as treasurer for 25 years. Falzarano was named provisional treasurer to compile the financial information needed for the county audits for 2022 and 2023, with the 2023 audit completed this past August.
Other members of the county's finance department include the finance director, Jenny Windsor, who began work on June 1 after being hired as the county's first finance director. Machias Savings Bank had required the appointment of a finance director as a condition for approving a tax-anticipation note for the county. The department also includes a payroll clerk, Megan Huffman.
The county commissioners were expected to consider the resignations following an executive session during their October 8 meeting.
Ballot question on treasurer
The county's fiscal crisis and the debate over how it was caused have led some to advocate for having the county commissioners appoint the county treasurer to ensure that the position is held by a professional. State law says an appointed treasurer must be qualified in the matters of business administration and finance.
County voters will weigh in on the issue during the November 3 election, when they will be asked it they want to abolish the elected treasurer position and replace it with a treasurer appointed by the commissioners.

title: What’s on the ballot in Westbrook?
text:
Although Westbrook doesn’t have any local seats up for election in November, residents will be asked to vote on county, state and national races.
Here’s what residents can expect to see on their ballots Nov. 3:
STATE RACES
Westbrook is divided into two state Senate districts — 26 and 27 — and three state Representative districts — 126, 127 and 128.
In state Senate District 26, Republican Kenneth Cianchette faces Democrat Tim Nangle. In District 27, Democrat Jill Duson is the only candidate on the ballot.
Andrew Gattine and Ethan Mongue are the Democratic and Republican candidates for the Maine House of Representatives District 126 seat, respectively. Democrat Morgan Rielly is the only candidate for the District 127 seat. In District 128, Democrat Suzanne Salisbury is facing Lawrence McWilliams, who is unenrolled.
Voters will also choose between Democratic nominee Hannah Pingree, Republican nominee Bobby Charles and independent Rick Bennett for governor.
OTHER RACES
Westbrook residents will vote in the U.S. Senate race between Democrat Troy Jackson and Republican incumbent Susan Collins.
In Maine’s 1st Congressional District, Democratic Rep. Chellie Pingree will face Republican Ronald Russell.
The Board of Cumberland County Commissioners oversees the financial operations of the county and manages county property. Westbrook is represented by the District 4 commissioner, and Patricia Smith is the only candidate for that position.
Cumberland County Sheriff Kevin Joyce is the only candidate in the sheriff’s race. Paul Aranson is the only candidate for judge of probate.
Stephanie Anderson, who is independent, and Jacqueline Sartoris, a Democrat, are running for Cumberland County district attorney. The Cumberland County district attorney serves 4 years and prosecutes all criminal cases, except homicides, which are handled by the attorney general.
HOW TO VOTE
Residents can vote at the Westbrook Community Center at 426 Bridge St. from 6 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Election Day.
Oct. 13 is the last day to accept mailed in or online voter registration before Election Day; afterward it must be in person. Oct. 29 is the last day to request an absentee ballot without a special circumstance. In-person absentee voting takes place at City Hall from Oct. 5 to 29, and City Hall business hours are 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday through Friday.

title: Glenburn Elementary's Halloween Trail Opens Nightly Through October 31st, Free Admission And Family-friendly Scares
text:
Glenburn’s Getting Spooky With A Haunted Trail And A ‘Boos & Bumpers’ Event This Month
Six years ago, as folks were looking for fun ways to celebrate the Halloween season amidst a pandemic, the Glenburn Parks and Rec Department created a spooky, family-friendly trail behind the Glenburn Elementary School at 991 Hudson Road that gave small groups an excuse to get outside and enjoy a little holiday fun.
Since then, it's grown to become a much-loved tradition in this small Penobscot County town.
Read More: Is Bangor Opera House Haunted? Take a Halloween Tour & Find Out
The trail is decorated with a different theme each year. There's never anything too jumpy or gory, so it's ok for kids of all ages.
The roots and stumps are well marked in white paint, so you don't trip and there are cameras monitoring the trail as well, for safety.
Some tips for you, if you've never been: wear comfy shoes, bring a flashlight and stay on the path.
There's a bit of a walk from the end of the trail to the parking lot, but they do sometimes have hayrides that you can hop onto to hitch a ride back.

title: Here's What You Need to Know About the Min Wage Increase in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
We have some good news for people working minimum wage hourly jobs and jobs where a significant portion of your pay is based on tips and gratuities.
The Increase to Maine's Minimum Wage
According to an article on the WABI website, Maine law requires the Maine Department of Labor to review and adjust the state’s minimum wage each year based on changes in the cost of living in the Northeast. This requirement was approved by Maine voters in 2016.
Because of this, the state's minimum wage will increase from $15.10 to $15.70 on January 1st, 2027
Maine's Tip Wage Is Increasing
If you work a job where a significant amount of your pay comes from tips, we've got some good news.
Maine’s minimum cash wage for tipped workers will increase from $7.55 to $7.85 per hour, and their combined wages and tips must equal at least $15.70 per hour. Workers must also earn at least $199 per month in tips to qualify as service employees.
The Overtime Exemption Level Is Increasing
If you work a salaried position, there is a good chance that you are "exempt". Basically, that means that you are required to perform your duties no matter how many hours it takes. This means you may end up working 35 hours or 55 hours. The benefit is that you will always make the same amount of money. The downside is that you may work way more than 40 hours in a week and get stuck with the same pay.
For years, there has been an exemption level. Basically, a certain minimum salary to make it lawful for you to be exempt from overtime. If you were paid over that, you could not get overtime. If you were paid less, you could claim overtime if you worked more than 40 hours a week.
That amount is now increasing.
As of January 1st, it will go from $45,300 to about $47,100.
A Brief History of Minimum Wage Laws in the United States
According to the Economic Policy Institute, the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) was created during the Great Depression in the 1930s, when millions of Americans struggled to find work and support their families.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the law on June 25, 1938. It established a federal minimum wage, limited the number of hours employees could work before earning overtime pay, and placed restrictions on child labor. The first minimum wage was $0.25 per hour.
Supporters believed the law would protect workers from unfair treatment and improve working conditions. Although some businesses argued that higher wages would cost jobs, the FLSA became an important step toward protecting American workers.

title: Lewiston man sentenced to 8 years in jail for 4-year-old stepson’s shooting death
text:
AUBURN — A Lewiston man was sentenced Friday in Androscoggin County Superior Court to 17 years in prison, with all but eight suspended, for the death of his 4-year-old stepson, Jasper Smith, who fatally shot himself with an unsecured handgun on May 17, 2025.
Robert McCoy, 37, will serve eight years followed by six years of probation. He had faced up to 30 years on the manslaughter charge.
McCoy pleaded guilty to the charges on Aug. 3.
In addition, Justice Jennifer Archer sentenced him to 364 days on a child endangerment charge and two years on a violation of probation charge to be served at the same time as the manslaughter sentence.
While serving probation, McCoy cannot have contact with children under age 6, cannot possess firearms or ammunition, and can undergo random searches.
The child found his stepfather’s loaded 9 mm Luger handgun in a zipped cross-body bag near a basinet at the family’s apartment on Pierce Street in Lewiston. He brought it to his bedroom he shared with an 8-year-old brother and took the gun out and shot himself, Archer said.
The child shot himself in the forehead in his bed, Deputy Attorney General Lisa Bogue told the court.
McCoy went to his stepson and picked him up and carried him to his wife, who he asked to call 911, and then returned him to his bed, Archer said.
His older brother, who was in the bathroom with bloodshot eyes, said he “was sorry” that he had been sleeping and not protecting his brother, according witness statements discussed briefly by Archer during the sentencing.
Prosecutors said the person who did have a duty to protect his children — his parent — violated that duty.
The handgun was kept in a gun safe many times, but had been left within the children’s reach several times, witnesses told police. The older brother told police he had access to the cross-body bag and had touched the gun before, according to testimony. There are four children in the family, the other two were 2 years old and 6 months old.
This was “reckless criminal negligence,” Bogue said.
Law enforcement officers, including members of the Lewiston Police Department and Maine State Police, were in the courtroom during the hearing. Many of those involved in the difficult case are still dealing with the effects, Bogue said.
Jasper’s mother, Mikayla Smith, read a prewritten statement through her tears.
She said she had loved McCoy before the fatal shooting and trusted him to take care of the children. Smith repeated her son’s name, “Jasper Smith,” who she said she will carry through the rest of her life.
“I loved you,” she told McCoy, “but I loved my child more.”
Jasper’s biological father, Andrew Northam, told the court he had been trying to get back into his child’s life.
“I lost my son before I ever got a chance to know him” he said on Zoom into the courtroom.
Jasper’s uncle Anthony Smith wrote in a statement that the death should have and could have been prevented. He referred to Jasper as an “innocent angel” and a fun-loving child.
Jasper’s aunt Laura Smith said the family has suffered tremendously over the past 17 months. Her nephew would have been 6 now. “Until we meet again, I will love you,” she said.
McCoy’s attorney, Justin Leary, told the court that his client acknowledged he was criminally negligent and that he did practice gun safety many days. McCoy doesn’t have a prior criminal history.
“He did love and care for his children,” Leary said, and he is “crushed and haunted” by the death of Jasper.
McCoy, wearing a gray jail uniform, stood up to speak to the court through his tears, which made it difficult to understand.
He was the one who got the children up for school and made sure they were dressed, he said. After school, he took the children to the park to play.
He has nightmares and anxiety attacks and will live with this for the rest of his life, McCoy said.
“He was a child,” he said. “I am sorry. … I failed you all. I deeply loved my son. I love you Jasper as I do my own children.”
Family members previously said Maine Department of Health and Human Services had a total of 17 calls from various people in Jasper’s life. Seven investigations followed with no findings, a family member had said.
The aggravating and mitigating factors Archer said she considered in her sentence included that some supporters had written McCoy was a hardworking man who loved his children, McCoy’s “genuine sadness” about the death, and his cavalier attitude toward gun safety that caused him to leave a loaded handgun accessible to his children.
McCoy was arrested in June 2025. Maine strengthened its child endangerment laws in 2021, which made it illegal to leave unsecured firearms accessible to children.

title: Yarmouth breaks ground on 18 affordable housing units behind town hall
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Construction began this week to raise 18 units of affordable housing in Yarmouth. The development on Cleaves Street, in Yarmouth Village behind Town Hall , is the first affordable housing project built in the town since 2018.
The development follows the Town Council turning its attention to the need for affordable housing over the past six years, with both a local affordable housing committee and nonprofit arising from the effort to assess and increase affordable housing stock.
The 18 one-bedroom apartments, split between two buildings, will have a projected monthly rent of $1,800 including utilities, according to the developer, 36 Cleaves Street, LLC. MaineHousing helped fund the bulk of the development with a $3.1 million subsidy from the Rural Affordable Rental Housing Program and a $2.9 million interest-free loan, said a MaineHousing spokesperson. The total cost of the development is $6.3 million.
“We’re laying the foundation for a more inclusive, welcoming, and resilient community,” said Council Chair David Craig at the groundbreaking ceremony Thursday.
“We’re leading by example by authorizing this project to be built right here in the heart of the village, literally in the Town’s Hall’s backyard.”
Affordable housing developments are few and far between in Yarmouth, with a new build about every 20 years over the past half-century. The most recent project was Bartlett Woods, which was approved in 2015 and completed in 2018, bringing 28 units of senior housing through a collaboration between the nonprofits Avesta Housing and Yarmouth Senior Housing.
To address the lack of affordable housing in Yarmouth, in 2020 the Town Council established the Yarmouth Affordable Housing Committee. In 2024, based on the committee’s recommendation, the Town Council adopted the goal of producing 431 units of affordable housing in Yarmouth over the next decade.
Approved by the Planning Board in January 2025, the Cleaves Street units are the first 18 steps forward toward meeting that goal.
As the Yarmouth Affordable Housing Committee serves to advise the town, three years ago residents formed the nonprofit Yarmouth Housing Collaborative to actively spur affordable housing projects such as 36 Cleaves Street.
“We’re not developers, but we’re the spark,” said Margaret Downing, executive director and board chair of the Yarmouth Housing Collaborative.
Construction on Cleaves Street is expected to last one year, with the buildings set to be enclosed by January. Apartment applications will open in 2027. To qualify, applicants must make less than $77,920 for a single-person household or $89,040 for a two-person household, which is 80% of the area median income, according to the developer.
The impacts of the construction on Cleaves Street are expected to be limited, said town staff. During construction, parking at Town Hall is being temporarily reconfigured and will be permanently adjusted after the project is complete. The ballot drop box, currently in the rear parking lot behind Town Hall, will be moved to the horseshoe parking lot between the front of Town Hall and Memorial Green soon, said the town.
