title: Failed executions troubled other states before Christa Pike. Here’s what happened
text:
(AP) - Tennessee’s bungled attempt to execute Christa Pike was not the first time a state has failed to carry out a lethal injection over problems in the death chamber.
Pike, 50, has regained consciousness and is speaking a week after Tennessee gave her two lethal doses of pentobarbital. Outgoing Republican Gov. Bill Lee has ordered a review into what went wrong and the state has not said whether they will again try executing her, which experts say could wade into uncharted legal waters.
Pike, who was sentenced to die for torturing and killing 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer in 1995, is one of at least eight condemned inmates in the U.S. who left their state’s execution chamber still alive because of problems carrying out the punishment, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Pike is the only one who was actually administered lethal drugs before the process was halted, according to the organization.
Not all have faced execution a second time. Three of the inmates would die years later in prison, two remain alive and two were executed after another attempt.
Lethal injection failures in Ohio
Ohio unsuccessfully tried to put Romell Broom to death by lethal injection in September 2009. The execution was called off after two hours when technicians could not find a suitable vein, and Broom cried in pain while receiving 18 needle sticks.
Broom died in December 2020 of possible complications of COVID-19 while on Ohio’s death row.
Ohio also failed to execute another inmate, Alva Campbell, in November 2017 by lethal injection. The execution was halted after executioners couldn’t find a usable vein.
Campbell was found unresponsive in his death row cell in March 2018. It was determined that he died from natural causes.
Alabama executed inmates a second time after failed attempts
Alabama called off the execution of Doyle Lee Hamm in February 2018 because of problems getting the intravenous line connected. A doctor hired by Hamm’s legal team later wrote in a report, filed in court, that Hamm had to be carried back to his cell by correctional officers after the execution was called off because he was in so much pain.
Hamm died of natural causes on death row in November 2021.
In September 2022, Alabama unsuccessfully executed Alan Eugene Miller by lethal injection when executioners spent more than an hour trying and failing to properly insert the catheter, repeatedly puncturing Miller with needles trying to find a vein. At one point, they left him hanging vertically on a gurney before state officials made the decision to call off the execution, according to news coverage at the time.
Miller had originally asked for nitrogen gas, but the Alabama Department of Corrections told a federal district court that they could not complete the execution that way.
The state successfully executed him two years later in September 2024 with nitrogen gas.
Almost two months after failing to execute Miller, Alabama had a second failed execution, when executioners did not have enough time to get a second IV line in before the death warrant expired at midnight for Kenneth Eugene Smith.
Smith was the first person to die by nitrogen gas as an execution method in January 2024.
Idaho prisoner remains alive
Idaho halted the execution of Thomas Eugene Creech in February 2024 after medical team members repeatedly failed to find a vein to carry out the lethal injection. In some cases, they couldn’t access the vein, and in others they could but had concerns about vein quality. They attempted sites in his arms, legs, hands and feet. At one point, a medical team member left to gather more supplies.
After eight attempts, the prison warden told them to give up. Creech remains alive and on death row.
Pike was the 2nd failed execution in Tennessee this year
Four months before Pike’s execution went awry, Tennessee officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers in May after his executioners tried and failed for over an hour to establish an intravenous line.
Lee announced soon afterward that the state would not try to execute Carruthers again for at least a year. Tennessee prison officials have said medical personnel had quickly established a primary IV line but were unable to find a suitable vein for a backup line as required by the state’s execution protocol. Efforts to insert a central line also failed.
Carruthers remains alive and on death row.

title: Obituary: Ronald “Ron-Ronnie” E. Pelletier
text:
ORR’S ISLAND – Ronald “Ron-Ronnie” E. Pelletier, 88, passed away peacefully at his home Sept. 20, 2026. He had lived on Orr’s Island with his beloved wife, Irene, his high school sweetheart, for the past six years.
Ron was born in Topsham on April 16, 1938, to Emile and Leona Burbee Pelletier. He graduated from Edward Little High School in Auburn in 1957.
Ron served in the U.S. Army at Fort Belvoir, Virginia, from 1959 to 1965. His love of cars and trucks began at an early age and remained a lifelong passion, leading him to a career owning and operating transmission shops in Virginia, Florida, and Arkansas.
Ron was a deeply religious man of faith. His belief in the Lord was evident in the way he lived, and his generosity and willingness to help others touched the lives of many who knew him. Ron enjoyed buying peanuts from Virginia and making his famous peanut brittle, which he loved sharing with family, friends, and anyone who crossed his path.
Ron’s love for his family was unwavering and unconditional. He devoted his time, knowledge, and heart to those he held most dear.
He was predeceased by his parents; and siblings, Barbara, Gene, and Sherman Pelletier.
Ron is survived by his wife M. Irene David Thibault Pelletier; his children, Anne-Marie Pelletier, Jeffrey Pelletier, Lisa Brasch, and Mary Ann Moser; stepchildren, Lisa and husband Roger Aube, Paula Malin, D. Jayson and wife Hollie Crowell Thibault; brother, Maurice Pelletier of Kentucky; many grandchildren; and great-grandchildren. He also shared a special bond with his loving niece, Anna Pelletier Sliger, and his loving nephew, Maurice Pelletier Jr.
Visiting hours will be held Sunday, Oct. 18, from 12 p.m. to 2 p.m. at Daigle Funeral Home, 819 High St., Bath. Burial with military honors will follow at Orr’s Island Cemetery, followed by a gathering at the Bailey Island Library Hall, Bailey Island.

title: Maine GOP holds press conference to criticize gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree

AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Maine House Republican Assistant Leader Katrina Smith criticized Pingree’s record in the Mills administration, citing low childhood literacy rates in 2024. Smith also cited what she described as a lack of child-welfare oversight on the Children’s Cabinet while four children died in 2021 under Department of Health and Human Services supervision.
Maine mother Jennifer Navarro joined Smith and said there is a lack of services and providers for children with autism and other disabilities.
Smith and Navarro questioned Pingree’s role in the issues they raised.

“So now, when Hannah Pingree asks the Maine people to make her governor, I believe it is entirely fair to ask about the results of the government that she helped to lead. Where was Hannah,” Smith said.
Smith said Pingree should answer for the outcomes during her time in the Mills administration. Smith said Maine needs accountability and change.

title: ‘Felt like God told me’: 18-year-old goes viral for giving older stranger the shoes off his feet
text:
MARICOPA, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A young man in Arizona is being recognized for his kindness and caring good deed that was caught on camera, unbeknownst to him.
Jordan Hope, 18, didn’t know anyone was watching when he pulled over to help a stranger outside a Maricopa storefront. But by the next day, a lot of people were.
Yareli Madrid captured the moment on video over the weekend that showed Hope stopping to help an older man he spotted walking in a Walgreens parking lot with his shoes barely hanging onto his feet.
“Watching this young man take the shoes off his own feet and give them to an older man who needed them truly touched my heart,” Madrid said in the post. “What makes it even more special is that he did it without anyone watching, without cameras, without expecting recognition or praise. He simply saw someone in need and helped from the goodness of his heart.”
Madrid added a message to Hope’s parents: “If this is your son, you did something right. Please know he is amazing.”
The post quickly drew hundreds of comments, including from someone who said they recognized Hope as a former student, leading the post back to the young man.
“I had no idea,” Hope said of the moment he learned he’d been filmed. “I saw a truck facing me, and I did not know what they were doing. And then the next day, after I found out that it was on Facebook, I was like, whoa.”
‘I just felt like God told me to go over’
Hope said he was on his way to the bank to deposit some money when he passed the Walgreens and noticed the man’s worn-out shoes.
“I looked at his feet, and his shoes were like maybe a fourth on his foot,” Hope said. “I just felt like God told me to go over there, turn around, and just give him some new slides. So I took off my own shoes. I gave them to him, and I just felt like I brought maybe a peace in his life.”
After driving away, something told him to turn back.
Hope found the man inside the Walgreens trying to buy candy and bought it for him. That’s when he learned the man’s wife had died just two weeks earlier.
“That honestly broke my heart,” Hope said. “I just think he needed a friend. It’s hard asking for help sometimes. And I’m just glad that God brought me there in that moment to just show my light on other people.”
Hope offered to take the man to lunch at Culver’s, but a medical condition that causes severe leg swelling made it hard for him to get into Hope’s car. So Hope called him a rideshare, met him at the restaurant, picked up the food, followed him home — and stayed a while just to talk.
“So he didn’t feel that loneliness, you know?” Hope said.
‘We’re hungrier, and we just want to help’
Hope has stayed in touch, checking in on the man by phone every day.
A GoFundMe started on the man’s behalf has already raised more than $2,000 within a couple of days, money Hope said will go toward groceries and other expenses.
Asked why he stopped when so many others might have just walked by, Hope credited his parents, his youth pastor and his faith.
“It wasn’t something out of my comfort zone,” he said. “I knew a tug pulled on my heart, and it was definitely from God... He interrupted my plans for that day to carry on his plans.”
The recent high school graduate, who runs his own computer-building business in Maricopa and Casa Grande, pushed back on the idea that young people don’t care about others.
“People say that this newer generation is just like they don’t care, you know? But I don’t believe that,” Hope said. “I believe that we’re hungrier and we just want to help as much as we can, and we need to be that light.”
As for what’s next, Hope said he hopes to keep building his business while staying active as a leader at his church.
“I’m just a man trying to spread positivity in the Lord’s work,” he said.

title: A botched execution and plans for one in public show the US is conflicted about capital punishment
text:
Americans have long been divided over the death penalty, with nearly half of states banning capital punishment outright and just a handful of others carrying out most of the nation’s executions each year.
The longstanding but uneasy relationship with executing the nation’s worst criminals has been on clear display in recent weeks, first following a botched lethal injection in Tennessee and later after the military announced plans to livestream a death by firing squad. Both have prompted fresh calls for abolition from death penalty opponents and led supporters to publicly grapple with how to humanely carry out government executions.
When Christa Pike was sentenced to die in 1996 after being convicted of murdering a classmate, Tennessee was among 37 states that had capital punishment, and the number of annual executions in the U.S. was on the rise. Since then, 10 states have abolished capital punishment, and executions haven’t approached their late 1990s peak.
Still, it is unlikely the U.S. is headed for complete abolition. Thirty inmates have been executed this year, and another eight executions have been scheduled, most of them in Texas and Florida. The military’s planned firing-squad execution for Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan is scheduled for Dec. 3.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s announcement Thursday that the military would livestream Hasan’s execution shocked even some capital punishment supporters. Vice President JD Vance on Friday questioned whether it would happen and said he wouldn’t watch. Retiring North Carolina Republican U.S. Sen. Thom Tillis called a livestream “beyond disgusting.”
American attitudes on the death penalty are complicated
While about two-thirds of U.S. adults see the death penalty as morally justified for people who have committed murder, according to a Pew Research Center poll conducted in July, about 6 in 10 say the death penalty does not deter crime. About 7 in 10 say there is some risk an innocent person would be put to death. Gallup’s trend suggests that support for capital punishment has fallen considerably since the 1990s.
Victims’ families are often among the most vocal advocates on either side of the debate. The family of Colleen Slemmer, whom Pike was convicted of killing, has supported Pike’s execution.
On the opposite side is Rachel Sutphin, a Presbyterian pastor whose father was killed in the line of duty as a sheriff’s deputy. The man convicted of killing him was the last person Virginia executed, in 2017. Sutphin was part of a coalition that successfully argued for abolishing the death penalty in the state in 2021. She said the Pentagon’s announcement was so shocking it might push her back into advocacy work.
“This place where (in) the name of revenge, taking an eye for an eye, has become socially acceptable and has almost become a form of entertainment — that very much concerns me,” she said.
In Tennessee, Republican legislators weren’t backing off their support for the death penalty after Pike survived her attempted execution Oct. 1. Instead, they contemplated returning to the electric chair or allowing firing squads. Idaho recently made the firing squad the state’s primary execution method, viewing it as more humane because the death is quicker and the chances of botching it are remote.
Idaho state Republican Rep. Bruce Skaug, a retired attorney who introduced that legislation, said he believes the death penalty should be rare but that once the court issues such a punishment, it’s the government’s duty to “carry it out properly.”
But Skaug was surprised by the Pentagon’s announcement and still pondering it Friday.
“That’s a difficult one for me to swallow.”
Public executions used to be common in the U.S.
From the Revolution and into the 20th century, American executions were often public and sometimes treated like mass entertainment. But no public executions have taken place since the late 1930s.
Brenner Fissell, vice president of the National Institute of Military Justice, said public executions “are seen by most civilized societies as grotesque and barbaric.” Almost every European nation has abolished capital punishment.
But, Fissell added, he did not know of any legal obstacles that would prohibit the administration from livestreaming Hasan’s execution.
“You don’t have a right to a secret death,” he said.
But Robert Blecker, a professor emeritus at New York Law School, said there are arguments in favor of making executions public. He said it forces the government to take responsibility for executing someone.
“Shouldn’t the people have access to what’s being done in their name?” he said. “If we can’t stomach and can’t tolerate it, then abolish it.”
Religious institutions highlight conflicting attitudes on death penalty
American culture is replete with portrayals of clergy being around execution, either advising and comforting the condemned or even occasionally giving a moral lecture from the gallows before a hanging. They have been a major part of the ongoing debate over capital punishment.
Blecker, who agrees with some criticism of how capital punishment is administered but believes it is morally appropriate in a few cases involving the worst criminals, said that idea came from the ancient Hebrews and Greeks. They reasoned that failing to adequately punish criminals polluted the population as a whole.
Hegseth’s church and denomination were co-founded by archconservative pastor Doug Wilson, who supports capital punishment.
Christian denominations such as the Southern Baptist Convention and the Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod support the death penalty, citing Biblical passages that mandate retributive justice under an authority granted by God to punish grave crimes. Supporters in these faith traditions view the death penalty as necessary to uphold the moral order and as a just response to the taking of innocent life.
But major religious denominations including the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops and several mainline Protestant denominations have taken official stances opposing the death penalty. Those positions are anchored in their theology of redemption and value for the “sanctity of life.”
Many clergy members, chaplains and volunteers from faith groups provide spiritual counseling, prayer and human connection to death row inmates and their families. Faith-based groups routinely organize prayer vigils and letter-writing campaigns while lobbying legislators to commute sentences or abolish capital punishment.
Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, on Friday issued a statement sharply condemning the military’s plans to livestream Hasan’s execution.
“This decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” he said.
__ Hanna reported from Topeka, Kansas; Rankin, from Richmond, Virginia, and Bharath from Los Angeles. Also contributing reporting were Associated Press writers Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, South Carolina, Gene Johnson in Seattle, and Tiffany Stanley in Washington.

title: Affordability crunch takes us back to 1974
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
An unpopular president; surging oil prices causing significant inflation; and an upcoming midterm election.
No, I’m not talking about 2026, but 1974. President Gerald Ford had just pardoned Richard Nixon in September, a decision unpopular with much of the American public who had Watergate still fresh in their minds. Oil prices surged in October 1973 after the OPEC oil embargo, which led to inflation running above 10%. The 1974 midterm elections brought a Democratic landslide victory, with the party winning 49 seats in the House and four in the Senate. Will 2026 be, quoting Yogi Berra, “like déjà vu all over again”?
Current indications suggest it may well be. Many Republican held seats in Congress appear to be up for grabs, even those in some “deep red” districts. Why? An unpopular president, Donald Trump, whose action and inaction is felt to have led to the highest inflation in years.
The question for Democrats, should they prevail Nov. 3, is: How will they govern? The temptation for many Democrats will be to hold endless congressional investigations into President Trump and his appointees for possible corrupt dealings. While I agree that there are valid concerns, is this what voters really want Congress to focus on? From everything I read, I think not.
One word comes up again and again: affordability. Democrats’ failure to address this concern may well lead to problems in the 2028 election. An out-of-touch party is soon an out-of-office party.
Samuel Rosenthal
Portland

title: Another poll shows Troy Jackson leading a tight Maine Senate race
text:
A new poll released Friday by the Washington Post shows Democrat Troy Jackson maintaining a narrow lead over Republican Susan Collins in Maine’s U.S. Senate race, despite a bombshell report linking Collins’ circle with a convicted fraudster.
Jackson held a four-point lead, 50% to 46%, over the five-term incumbent in the poll — roughly the same as the survey’s margin of error of 3.6 percentage points. Three percent of those polled did not select a choice, while 1% said they’d vote for someone else.
“Another poll shows that Troy is connecting with voters on the issues that matter the most to Mainers,” senior campaign adviser David Farmer said in an emailed statement. “He’s working class and understands the issues that Mainers are facing.”
The survey is further evidence that the closely watched race will likely be a barn burner — one that may hinge on a small pool of undecided voters.
Jackson, a fifth-generation logger and former state Senate president, holds a two-point lead over Collins, according to a polling averages compiled by FiftyPlusOne. But some surveys, including a New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll released two weeks ago, showed Collins with a narrow lead, albeit within the margin of error.
The Post survey, done in partnership with the George Washington University Schar School of Policy and Government, was conducted from Sept. 30 to Oct. 5.
It entered the field a week after ProPublica published a story about how the FBI had years ago begun a sweeping investigation into whether Collins engaged in an illegal pay-to-play scheme by steering government contracts to a donor. (Collins has denied any wrongdoing, saying she was cleared by the Biden administration. ProPublica has reported investigators were looking into Collins’ orbit until President Donald Trump took power in early 2025.)
The Washington Post poll showed the volatile waters that Collins, 73, is trying to navigate to win a sixth term. Fifty-two percent of voters said her 30 years in the Senate was a bad thing. That’s despite respondents giving her a 24 percentage point edge on bringing federal money back to Maine and giving her better marks for bipartisanship.
And President Donald Trump continues to loom large over the race. Sixty-three percent of respondents disapproved of the president’s job performance. And 58% said that Collins sides with Trump too often, compared to 33% who said she’s handled her relationship with the president “about right.”
A majority — 55% — said they wanted Democrats to win the Senate, compared to 42% for Republicans. That metric shows Collins is having at least some success pushing against the national political headwinds.
The top issues for voters were the cost of living (41%), immigration (13%), healthcare (12%) and taxes (6%).
Jackson, meanwhile, had a +1 net approval rating, but 13% of respondents had no opinion or skipped the question. That leaves a small opening for Republicans, who have a significant funding advantage, to introduce the Democrat to voters on their own terms through paid ads.
The 58-year-old Jackson held a 13-point lead among independents, 53% to 40%. His crossover appeal was also higher than Collins, pulling 9% support from Republicans compared to the incumbent’s 6% from Democrats, the poll found.
The survey also asked about Maine’s three-way race for governor. Again, Democrat Hannah Pingree held a double-digit lead over Republican Bobby Charles, 49%-36%. Independent Rick Bennett drew 11% support — his best showing in polling to date.

title: Don’t feel like yourself? It could be a vitamin deficiency
text:
(Aging Untold) — As we get older, our bodies can have a harder time absorbing key vitamins and minerals — and the warning signs are easy to miss.
The Aging Untold hosts are breaking down which vitamin deficiencies are most common in older adults, what to watch for and what to ask your doctor.
‘I just don’t feel like myself’
When someone describes that vague, hard-to-pin-down feeling, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said a handful of nutrient deficiencies are often behind it.
“Vitamins and trace minerals are very key for every cell in the body to function,” Rogers said. “So the other organs, they can’t function alone.”
She points to two deficiencies in particular — vitamin B12 and vitamin D.
“When I look at things like vitamin B12 deficiency, a lot of people will have those, and they will have some mood issues and sensory issues, nerve issues and things like that,” Rogers said. “And a big one is vitamin D — when there’s no sunlight out, people really get kind of depressed and all that in the wintertime.”
Low vitamin D can also show up in less obvious ways, she said.
“Atrial fibrillation could be manifest in someone with a vitamin D deficiency, and irritable bowel syndrome,” Rogers said. “I say that the vitamins — they can steal your vitality. So they are thieves.”
Why a basic blood test isn’t enough
Rogers said checking blood levels is a good first step, but it has limits.
“The blood levels fluctuate daily. They don’t test whether your receptors are working. They don’t test whether you can transport [nutrients]. And they don’t test what your tissue is expressing,” Rogers said. “If you can go to the next level and get a personalized test called genomics, it looks at how you’re metabolizing so you can be guided specifically on what you need.”
She said that kind of testing should happen with guidance from a doctor who can determine potential interactions with medications the patient is taking.
“This really needs to be physician-driven, not just grabbing things off the shelf,” aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said.
Rogers stressed that as well.
“I think people identify with, ‘Oh man, I’m so tired,’ and the commercial comes on and, ‘Oh, I want to get some of that,” Rogers responded.
Start with food, not supplements
Before reaching for a bottle, diet should come first, aging expert Amy O’Rourke said.
“I’m going to put out a vote for a really balanced diet — low processed foods. Start there and eat well,” O’Rourke said. “And then if you feel like you’re having some symptoms, go to a doctor and say, this is what I’m eating. Make sure it’s healthy, and you can do it in an affordable way.”
She said that conversation should include a direct question for your doctor.
“And then ask your doctor, ‘This is what I’m eating. How am I doing, and what should I be taking, if anything?’” O’Rourke said. “I’m a believer that if you eat well, you might not need all the supplements.”
Ambrose added that the goal is giving the body what it needs to function at full capacity.
“If we want to increase our capacity, we want to make sure that we’re optimizing our nutrients,” Ambrose said. “We sometimes get criticized as a country as being a nation of overfed and undernourished.”
If you do take supplements, check the label
Rogers said not all supplements on store shelves are created equal.
“Look at your source — look at the source of your vitamins and nutrients, even in the stores and all that. Look on the bottle to see if it’s third-party tested,” Rogers said. “Look for third-party testing. Look at the ingredients. If you have a lot of fillers in there, you know that’s not a good thing.”
Gerontologist Sam Cradduck said shortcuts aren’t worth it.
“You don’t want to take a capsule full of sand just because somebody’s selling it to you as the next quick fix to make you feel better, think better and keep your brain clear,” Cradduck said.
The most common deficiencies in older adults
Rogers said that B vitamins and vitamin D top the list for older adults.
“There’s a B complex — B1, B2, B3, B6, biotin is B7, and then you have your B12,” Rogers said. “But absolutely, vitamin B complex is huge in pretty much all chemical reactions in the body, as is D, as is magnesium. Magnesium is huge.”
Ambrose said the bigger-picture message is about how health care itself is changing.
“The big untold truth here is that health care today is shifting more to personalized, customized health care versus one size fits all,” she said.
Key takeaways
- They mimic aging. Low levels of B12 or vitamin D can cause fatigue, memory loss and muscle weakness — symptoms that are easily mistaken for simply growing older.
- Don’t guess, assess. Personalized lab tests can target what your body actually needs instead of relying on guesswork.
- Loop in your doctor. Supplement decisions should be physician-driven to avoid harmful interactions with medications you’re already taking.

title: Americans 75 and older are wealthiest age group, Fed survey finds
text:
Americans 75 and older are wealthiest age group, Fed survey finds
Bolstered by steady gains in the stock market, families headed by someone aged 75 or older are now America's wealthiest, while the youngest families saw their wealth decline in the past three years, a government report released Friday said.
The finding from the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances underscores how robust stock market gains have made wealthier American families even richer since the survey, conducted every three years, was last completed in 2022. The median net worth of the richest one-tenth of American families soared 31% to $3.6 million from 2022 to 2025, the survey found. The median is the midpoint between the richest and poorest families.
For the oldest families aged 75 and over, median net worth jumped to nearly $505,000, up from just over $367,000 in 2022. Three years ago, families aged 65 to 74 were the richest. All the figures are adjusted for inflation.
Average wealth for the oldest age group rose 10% to $1.96 million. The higher average, compared with the median, reflects the fact that wealthier Americans pulled up the average relative to the median.
Those aged 35 and below reported median net worth of $33,000, a drop of 23% from 2022.
Overall, the survey found broad gains in income, even after adjusting for inflation, which slightly reduced income inequality compared with three years earlier. Higher-income families actually saw their incomes drop, likely because of declines in business income, which the Fed said can be volatile.
Median family incomes rose about 7% from 2021 to 2024, the Fed said, to about $82,000. The survey measures incomes in the year prior to the periods covered by the report. The middle one-fifth of families saw the biggest income gain, while the top fifth reported lower incomes.
Even so, the proportion of Americans struggling with high debt payments and falling behind on their payments jumped, a sign of the toll that sharply higher inflation and higher interest rates have taken on lower-income Americans.
In 2025, nearly 20% of U.S. families said they had been late on a loan payment in the previous year, up sharply from 12.2% in 2022. And the proportion of families dedicating 40% or more of their incomes to debt payments jumped to 8.6%, the highest in at least 12 years, the report showed.

title: Maine military moms celebrate new chapter of Blue Star Mothers of America
text:
When Maine mothers of military personnel saw in March that war in Iran was escalating, they bonded together to organize a statewide support network for active duty service members, military mothers, families and veterans.
Rosie Vanadestine of Skowhegan and Jane Thorndike of Avon, who both have sons who are gunnery sergeants in the U.S. Marines, along with 10 other military mothers, worked to establish a Maine chapter of the Blue Star Mothers of America.
“It has been a long road getting over the finish line that is for sure,” Vanadestine, president of the chapter, wrote in an email Wednesday. “This group of women are amazing. We have become so important to each other and have become the first outreach when any of us are struggling. The more I learn and the more organizations we are connecting to, the more excited I am about what (Blue Star Mothers of America) ME3 will accomplish in service of our active military, our veterans and all the military families here in Maine.”
The formation of the Maine chapter was inspired by Vanadestine when her child entered military service. After discovering there was no active chapter in the state, she started outreach, which quickly gained momentum.
With the official installation ceremony completed at the national level, a local celebratory event is planned for Oct. 25 in Augusta.
Thorndike is happy the chapter is finally established. “Blue Star Mothers is a way for us ‘moms’/stepmoms/grandmothers or even other family members to support one another and to give back to our veterans and service members. ‘Once a mom, always a mom,’” Thorndike wrote in a message.
Her son, Gunnery Sgt. Barry Thorndike II, who was deployed on the USS Abraham Lincoln for over seven months in the Middle East, got off the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier when it arrived in San Diego on Thursday. He will be stationed there for the next two years.
“Both my boys will stand on USA soil again. I thank God and that hardworking USS Abraham Lincoln crew for getting him back to us,” Thorndike wrote Thursday.
Thorndike’s husband and sister-in-law were on the way to see him Wednesday. Thorndike stayed behind because of work and other obligations.
“Military families should never have to walk this journey alone. Our mission is to support troops, veterans, military families, and the families of fallen heroes while supporting one another through every stage of military life,” Vanadestine wrote.
Blue Star Mothers of America is a national nonprofit organization founded in 1942 and chartered by Congress in 1960. With more than 6,000 members across 200 chapters nationwide, the organization provides support, service, and advocacy for military communities across the country.
Leaders of the Maine chapter plan to provide peer support for military families, send care packages to deployed service members, assist veterans, support Gold Star families, participate in community service projects, and partner with organizations serving Maine’s military and veteran communities.
Full membership is open to mothers, stepmothers, grandmothers, foster mothers, and female legal guardians of active-duty service members, National Guard members, Reservists, veterans, and fallen service members. Associate membership is available for all other family members and individuals seeking opportunities to support the organization’s mission through volunteer service and community involvement.
Anyone wanting more information can contact Vanadestine by email at [email protected] or by phone at 207-576-2960.
The celebratory event for the new Maine chapter is planned for 2 p.m. Oct. 25 at VFW Post 886 at 509 Leighton Road in Augusta. It is intended to bring together military families, veteran organizations, elected officials, community leaders and members of the public to celebrate the milestone and formally launch the new Maine chapter.
The distinguished guest speaker is Maj. Gen. Diane L. Dunn, who serves as the 41st adjutant general of the Maine National Guard and commissioner of the Department of Defense, Veterans and Emergency Management. Light refreshments will follow.
Anyone interested in learning more about the Blue Star Mothers organization is invited to attend.

title: Partners for Peace holds walk and vigil in Lincoln for Domestic Violence Awareness Month
text:
LINCOLN, Maine (WABI) -October is Domestic Violence Awareness Month.
For over 50 years, local nonprofit Partners for Peace has been dedicated to serving and supporting survivors in Penobscot and Piscataquis counties.
Thursday night, the organization held a walk and vigil at the Lincoln gazebo.
Their theme to mark the month is “Every Story Matters.”
Their goal is to create a space to allow those affected by domestic abuse and violence to share their stories.
“It’s so wonderful to be here in Lincoln. We love being here every year to have this close-knit community come together and hear the stories of survivors and walk together, remember together, and just be here in community. This was an annual event that we held for many, many years before the pandemic. Last year was the first year that we brought it back. And then this being the second year, we have such a great turnout and we anticipate that that will happen every single year,” said Casey Faulkingham-Bixby, Partners for Peace director of development and engagement.
There are plenty of ways you can get involved, too.
You can host a fundraiser or donation drive, make a donation to Partners for Peace, or simply share their social posts and promote events.
To see a full list of events, visit PartnersForPeaceME.org.
And, if you or someone you know has been impacted by domestic abuse, help is just one call away.
The Partners for Peace helpline is 1-800-863-9909.

title: Peak color, hidden trails: Fall hiking in western Maine
text:
Fall hiking can be especially rewarding during peak foliage, but it also requires extra preparation.
The Maine Warden Service advises hikers to choose trails carefully, check local conditions, tell someone where they are going and when they plan to return, dress in layers and carry a flashlight separate from the one on a phone. Hikers should also be prepared for little or no cell service and know their route without relying on a phone.
The Appalachian Mountain Club recommends carrying its 10 Essentials, including water, extra food, navigation tools, emergency shelter, extra layers, illumination, a fire starter, first-aid supplies, a repair kit and sun protection. AMC also recommends carrying a map and compass and not relying solely on smartphones, GPS watches or other electronic navigation devices.
As more leaves come down across western Maine, trails can become harder to follow and rocks, roots and trail markers may disappear beneath a thick layer of foliage. The Warden Service recommends sturdy hiking boots with good tread, high-protein snacks, water, enough personal medication for two days and a fire starter, along with a backup plan if trail or road conditions change.
Fall hikers should also account for shorter daylight, rapidly changing temperatures, slick leaves and the possibility of ice or snow at higher elevations.
For places to hike, the Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands directs visitors to Maine Trail Finder, a searchable database of trails throughout the state.

title: Maine attorney files ethics complaint against Sen. Susan Collins
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WMTW) - A Maine attorney has filed a complaint with the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Ethics against Sen. Susan Collins, hoping the committee will investigate allegations reported by ProPublica that Collins accepted campaign donations in exchange for government contracts.
The bipartisan committee, which is composed of three Democrats and three Republicans, provides ethical guidance and investigates complaints against senators and Senate staff members.
“I believe that it’s important to demand the best of our elected officials,” said Valerie Adams, who filed the complaint. “I believe that these are issues that we as voters should pay attention to, and I hope that the committee will act on it and open an investigation.”
Anyone can file a complaint. The committee receives dozens of allegations each year, but according to annual reports reviewed by 8 Investigates, most are dismissed, either because of a lack of evidence or because the alleged conduct does not violate Senate rules.
Over the last five years, 91% of complaints were dismissed without an investigation.
“I believe the issue needs media attention in order to put pressure on the committee to open an investigation,” Adams said.
Complaints that are not dismissed proceed to an initial inquiry. Over the past five years, 63% of complaints that reached this stage were ultimately dismissed.
For minor violations, the committee can issue a public or private letter telling a senator they violated Senate ethics rules. It issued three letters over the past five years.
If the committee finds serious ethical concerns, it may open a formal review, which could result in disciplinary action. The committee opened one review over the past five years. The review was closed after its subject, New Jersey Sen. Robert Menendez (D), resigned.
The committee has not issued any formal sanctions in recent history.
“I don’t think we should ever lose hope that what we’re doing will matter, and whether or not an investigation is opened, I think it’s important that the issue is getting attention, and I think it’s important to request that an investigation be opened,” Adams said.
In response to the complaint, a Collins campaign spokesperson wrote: “This is getting to be pathetic. For the third consecutive week, a recently failed Democratic candidate has parroted false charges that they know nothing about, against Susan Collins.”
Adams previously worked as an assistant district attorney for Cumberland County. This spring, she lost her primary race against incumbent District Attorney Jacqueline Sartoris.
Because of confidentiality requirements, much of the committee’s work takes place behind closed doors.

title: Appeals court dismisses Maine lobster defamation lawsuit
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals overturned a federal judge’s ruling and dismissed the Maine lobster industry’s defamation lawsuit against a California aquarium on Friday.
The Maine Lobstermen’s Association, Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association and three lobster businesses sued the Monterey Bay Aquarium Foundation in 2023 after the organization’s Seafood Watch program put lobster on a “red list,” urging consumers to avoid the seafood. The foundation had claimed measures in the fishery don’t do enough to reduce entanglement or promote recovery of the critically endangered North Atlantic right whale population.
The plaintiffs argued the foundation made “false and defamatory statements” about the Maine lobster industry’s practices and misled consumers and businesses about the fishery’s “integrity.” In the lawsuit, they claimed to lose business, with some consumers specifically citing the red listing.
The foundation moved to dismiss the lawsuit, but a judge allowed the suit to advance in 2025. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals overruled that decision Friday, and ordered the lawsuit to be dismissed.
The court ruled that calls to action, including boycotting products or industries, are protected under the First Amendment, and concluded that the listing did not make any specific reference to the plaintiffs in the case.
“People’s choices have the power to shape the future of the ocean,” the aquarium said in a statement on the court’s decision. “Programs like Seafood Watch guide consumers and businesses toward environmentally sustainable choices that support a healthy, thriving ocean, benefiting food security, fisheries and coastal communities whose livelihoods depend on the ocean.”
Spokespeople for the Maine Lobstermen’s Association and the Maine Coast Fishermen’s Association did not respond to a request for comment Friday evening.
The aquarium assigned Maine lobster a yellow rating on its Seafood Watch in 2014, recommending consumers “be aware there are concerns” with how the seafood is caught and managed. It ultimately gave it a “red” rating, along with other Canadian and U.S. fisheries, in September 2022. It claims one threat to the species is entanglement in fishing gear, including buoy lines used by lobstermen.
In a report on the new red ratings in 2022, the Seafood Watch program advised consumers to avoid “American lobster caught by trap from Georges Bank and the Gulf of Maine stocks due to risks to the critically endangered North Atlantic right whale and insufficient measures for reducing these risks.”
“This decision is a victory for all environmental advocates and freedom of speech,” said Sarah Shahabi, an attorney at the Conservation Law Foundation, which filed a friend-of-the-court brief supporting Monterey Bay Aquarium. “We can’t effectively fight threats to the natural world without naming them. Speaking openly and honestly about environmental challenges is essential to protecting our planet.”

title: Why kidney stones hurt so much — and how to prevent them
text:
(Aging Untold) — A kidney stone may be tiny, but anyone who’s had one knows the pain can feel anything but small. Hydration, diet and certain medical conditions can all affect your risk.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, breaks down what causes kidney stones, why they hurt so much and what you can do to lower your risk.
What exactly is a kidney stone?
“They’re hard, mineral and salt deposits that form from the kidneys,” Rogers said. “They’re really small, but just think of anything that’s blocking something. So you’re actually providing a blockage in a small tube in your body. And that’s very, very painful, excruciating pain.”
Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said she has had four kidney stones and nothing she has experienced has been as painful.
“This is like putting a jagged stone through a straw,” Cradduck said. “This took me to my knees.”
What causes them
Several factors contribute to kidney stone formation, Rogers said.
“What forms these kidney stones are a lot of times our genetics, family history, dehydration — diet plays a huge role too. And certain medications,” she said.
She explained that a natural compound in urine called citrate normally helps protect against stones. A reduction in it also reduces the protective factor.
“There actually is a natural compound in your urine that’s actually protective. It’s called citrate,” Rogers said. “And so anything that reduces that citrate reduces the ability of your urine to be able to form around those calcium stones and diminish those.”
She said high sodium intake can reduce citrate levels, while foods high in oxalate — such as spinach and beets — can raise uric acid levels and contribute to stone formation for some people.
“So you can eat a low oxalate diet if you’ve been having consistent stones,” Rogers said.
Infections can also contribute to forming stones.
“There’s some infections that will cause you to get a stone also with the bacteria,” Rogers added.
How to lower your risk
Rogers said boosting citrate levels naturally can help protect against stones.
“Anything that increases that citrate in your urine will be protective, like lime and lemon in your water. That helps,” she said. “Decrease the sodium. Animal fat, protein diets — those tend to be higher in uric acid. So you can try to minimize that.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke mentioned resources for people managing recurring stones.
“I was reading about the National Kidney Foundation being of help — the stonecollab.org can be of help,” she said. “So get some resources.”
(Find more resources below.)
O’Rourke added that climate matters too.
“Warmer climates — you’re dehydrated more, so drink more,” she said.
Doctors can also analyze a passed stone to determine its cause.
“What’s really important for people is when you do pass a stone, a lot of times we’ll take that stone to see what it really is made out of,” Rogers said. “That will help you to see why you got it in the first place.”
Resources/Links to learn more
Key takeaways
- Dehydration is a leading risk factor. Warmer climates and low fluid intake directly contribute to painful mineral deposits forming in the kidneys.
- Kidney stones are mineral and salt deposits that block small tubes in the body, causing severe pain.
- Genetics, family history, diet and certain medications all play a role in whether stones form.
- Citrate naturally protects against stones, and drinking water with lime or lemon can help boost it.
- High sodium, animal protein and high-oxalate foods like spinach and beets can increase risk for some people.
- Stress has also been linked to kidney stone development, alongside genetic factors.

title: She turned her backyard into a butterfly sanctuary
text:
MYRTLE BEACH, SC (InvestigateTV) - The monarch butterfly, known for its vibrant orange and deep black hues, is dangerously close to disappearing forever.
A 2026 report from the Center for Biological Diversity found the migratory eastern monarch remains vulnerable to extinction.
This butterfly is particularly remarkable because it has one of the longest migration patterns of any insect. At the end of summer, they can travel up to 3,000 miles from Canada and the northern U.S. all the way to central Mexico.
In South Carolina, Diedre Richardson has turned her backyard into a sanctuary for butterflies, earning her the nickname “Butterfly Whisperer.”
“They’re fascinating,” Richardson said. “They’re all different from each other. From when they’re butterflies to when they’re caterpillars, their host plants. Everything.”
In her backyard, Richardson likens her sanctuary “like a conveyor belt” where she’ll spend hours tending to insects.
She started caring for the delicate winged insects in 2014, raising them from caterpillars to beautiful butterflies.
“It’s fun. It’s like, oh, this one is coming out now, this one is coming out now,” said Richards.
She dotes on monarchs, black swallowtails, and fritillaries, but monarchs are her favorite. She got her latest army in January.
“Some ladies contacted me on Facebook because they had come across some starving caterpillars on a milkweed plant they brought in the garage,” she said.
Richardson grows the scarce plant so they can feast, and she can capture every eager bite.
“They start running around, and they’re not sure where to start first because they’re so excited about it,” she said.
The caterpillars then curl into a shimmering chrysalis. Richardson said the transformation takes about 10 to 14 days, depending on the heat and humidity, before their fragile and wet pair of wings emerges.
“A lot of times they’ll just hang out on your hand for a while, and you just get to look at how beautiful they are and just watch them experience for the first time the sun on them and the wind,” she said. “I feel like I’m their mom. I know that’s silly.”
That’s why Richardson is working hard to protect the monarchs that fly the Carolinas year-round and the Coastal wetlands, which studies show are their breeding ground.
“Not only do the wetlands protect us from flooding, but now we realize that they’re home to monarchs,” she said. “They’re not endangered yet, but they’re on a severe decline. So if this is one way to protect them, I’m all for it.”
Richardson has launched social media pages to share knowledge and tips, hoping to inspire others to care for the delicate wings that brighten our world.
You can find Richardson on her Facebook page, Raising Butterflies in Myrtle Beach, or Monarch Butterfly Whisperer on Instagram.

title: Turn down the heat on Maine’s annual furnace debate
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
It’s strange when a war halfway across the globe could have you fumbling to operate a TV remote in winter gloves, but that’s where we are — or are about to be.
With temperatures in Maine dipping into the 30s overnight and heating oil prices hovering around a record-high $6 a gallon, the annual debate about when to turn on the heat is already underway.
For many Mainers, this is not a First-World problem but an unbearable expense on top of already strained finances. (If you’re in that position, see our guide for where to find heating and other assistance.) Here, however, I’m focusing on households where this is primarily a source of relationship strife — a battle between the budget watchers and those who want to be cozy.
Even for these relatively fortunate people, though, it’s not always as simple as it seems.
“This is exactly the kind of disagreement that can sound trivial from the outside but actually taps into a lot of the things couples argue about,” said Andrea Medaris, director of Psychology Specialists of Maine’s Center for Relationships in Brunswick.
To help sort it out, we turned to Maine experts for their advice about staying warm this winter without going broke (or breaking up).
If it’s about cost
The chillier half of the household has an uphill battle this year. Former TV meteorologist Keith Carson has a solution: math.
Many frugal Mainers live by the rule “no heat until trick or treat,” if not “turkey meat.” In a video for Maine Conservation Voters, the spokesman (and occasional Press Herald weather writer) shows how crunching some numbers can help your case for cranking up the heat when the temperature drops, rather than holding out for a certain date.
Turning the thermostat down by one degree for three hours on a 20-degree day in February will cover the cost of heating up the average Maine house on a 40-degree fall morning, he explains.
In theory, by agreeing to do that later, you should get your way now. But you’ll have to brush up on your algebra.
If it’s about comfort
Now, for a science lesson.
A lot of these arguments stem from biological differences that determine how well we can tolerate the cold. We know smaller people, with a higher ratio of skin surface area to body mass, lose heat more easily, while more muscular people retain it better.
For advice on how to keep your core temperature up, we turned to Tim Smith, founder of the Jack Mountain Bushcraft School in Masardis, who provided the list of tips he gives guests of his guided snowshoe trips in Aroostook County.
Some were practical: wear a hat, then another one, then a hoodie over that. Others were on the silly side, like keeping a picture of Timothee Chalamet in your chest pocket. (He had Patrick Swayze on there, until some younger associates informed him they didn’t know who that was.)
Another — to drink warm liquids, “especially ones that are bad for you” — is only half true. Although alcohol will make you feel flushed, Smith said, it actually lowers your body temperature.
But there was one unconventional method for keeping warm that seemed like it could work for warring couples: Putting cayenne pepper in your socks will irritate the skin and drive circulation, he said. If your shivering partner happens to like a foot rub, you can keep the argument at bay by offering one, extra spicy.
If it’s about something else
Medaris, the psychologist, said the meanings that get attached to conflicts like these — that one person is constantly critical or the other always gets their way — is what couples need to step away from when the heat debate starts escalating.
“One person is cold, the other is thinking about the heating bill, and pretty quickly it can turn into ‘you’re unreasonable’ or ‘you don’t care that I’m uncomfortable,’” she said.
Her advice is to “get on the same side against the problem,” recognizing each person’s needs and working together on a solution, whether that’s agreeing on a thermostat range or putting a space heater in a certain room.
Efficiency Maine has all sorts of tips for keeping in the heat — with caulk, window treatments, reflectors and weather stripping — perfect for a joint DIY project that could help with both comfort and cost.
If that doesn’t go well, research the rates for seeing a couples therapist. That might prompt the stingy spouse to give up a few degrees on the thermostat.

title: Maine’s tallest mountain is greening faster than others in New England
text:
High above the tree line on Katahdin, where biting winds and sub-zero winters hold the rocky landscape in a frozen grip for much of the year, the mountaintop is turning noticeably greener.
Four decades worth of satellite observations reveal that alpine tundra across the Northeast are undergoing widespread vegetation expansion, not just at the advancing tree line but well above it, too. The new growth is transforming rare, high-elevation ecosystems once thought buffered from rapid change.
And Katahdin, Maine’s highest peak at 5,268 feet, is greening faster than any other New England summit. Vegetation has increased there by 7.9% from 1984 to 2024, according to a recent study in the journal Ecosphere by scientists at Dartmouth College and the Appalachian Mountain Club.
“Greening isn’t necessarily good or bad, but it’s happening,” said Dartmouth College geographer Jonathan Chipman. “The reason may be a concern. It might mean rare plants are being crowded out by aggressive interlopers that can now live in areas when they couldn’t survive in the past.”
The study used thousands of NASA images to track greening on 35 alpine summits from New York to Quebec. Co-author Jordon Tourville provided field perspective as an alpine ecologist with the Appalachian Mountain Club to explore the potential reasons for the greening.
As a geographer, Chipman said he is often asked to work with other researchers to analyze or map data in their fields of study. As an avid climber, he has long wanted to use his skills to research what is happening at the tops of New England’s summits.
“I grew up in New England,” Chipman said. “I climbed Katahdin when I was a kid. I climbed Mount Washington too many times to count. A lot of people, including me, are very concerned about the future of these precious little sky islands.”
For Mainers who hike Baxter State Park or look up at the Longfellow Mountains, the findings suggest that environmental pressures are actively reshaping the summits of New England that are so isolated that naturalists call them “sky islands.”
These summits support fragile plant communities, such as cushion plants and arctic sedges, that survived the last ice age and thrive in conditions too harsh for trees. Some animals are found only in these areas, such as the Katahdin Arctic butterfly, or breed only here, like the American Pipit.
There are only about 50 square miles of alpine ecosystem in the Northeast, Tourville said.
“That makes it the rarest ecosystem type in the region,” Tourville said. “We suspect that because they’re so small, and because the plants there are already existing really at the edge of what plants can withstand, that any amount of change will destroy this system.”
Across Maine’s six studied alpine summits — Katahdin and North Brother in Baxter State Park and Sugarloaf, Bigelow, Saddleback and Mount Abraham in the Longfellow Range — greenness expanded over the four-decade study period, but not at the same pace.
While Katahdin clocked a 7.9% greening trend, the average greening rate of all the peaks studied was 5.2%. Records show a 5.8% increase at North Brother at Baxter, a 5% increase at Sugarloaf, a 4.8% increase at Saddleback and a 4.7% increase at mounts Bigelow and Abraham.
Ground mapping on Katahdin shows that greening is hitting alpine sedge meadows particularly hard. The windswept lawns of Carex bigelowii appear to be undergoing invasion by the woody dwarf heath shrubs that thrive in warmer temperatures and higher nutrient levels.
Baxter State Park officials acknowledged that the shift is a serious concern. They have been collaborating with other researchers to map Katahdin’s alpine plant boundaries, monitor trail corridors and track shrub encroachment into sedge meadows, according to park manager Kevin Adam and natural resources director Nava Tabak.
Strict “stay-on-trail” policies, supported by visitor quotas, summit stewards, signage and string fencing are the park’s most vital tools to help the fragile root systems withstand atmospheric stresses, Adam and Tabak said.
But researchers suspect warming temperatures are hardly the only environmental force at play.
The greening trend accelerated through the 1980s and 1990s before flattening around 2005 to 2009, a trajectory that aligns with ecological recovery following federal Clean Air Act regulations that curbed acid rain and sulfur pollution across New England peaks.
“A lot of people focus on temperature, but I think we missed the nitrogen signal,” Tourville said. “The soils in the alpine zone are extremely nitrogen poor. For decades, we essentially dumped nitrogen fertilizer up there. That probably had a pretty profound impact.”
Topography and severe weather also shape the landscape. Sheltered east- and north-facing slopes across the region’s peaks showed rapid greening, but exposed ridges seem to have resisted plant expansion.
For park stewards, the 40-year satellite record provides a crucial baseline to guide future conservation. But it also highlights a fundamental disagreement over how to manage wilderness in an era of global climate change.
Tourville argued that traditional, hands-off wilderness management may no longer be enough.
“My message to them was, it might be time in the near future to rethink that stance in terms of hands-off, no management up in the park, especially in the alpine zone, because climate change does not respect park boundaries,” Tourville said. “And climate change is not hands-off.”
Baxter State Park leadership firmly defended the park’s “Forever Wild” mandate, arguing direct human intervention is not the answer.
“Our response to stressors from climate extremes, as illustrated by this research, is to continue to minimize human impacts so that the natural communities and species have the best chance to adapt,” Adam and Tabak said in an emailed statement. “Though our approach to stewardship of the Park’s alpine areas is unique, these areas may over time serve as an experimental control that can be compared with other northeastern alpine areas that are more directly managed.”
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Oct. 9 to include comments from Baxter State Park officials.

title: ‘We couldn’t believe it’: Couple reeling after losing life savings in $14 million Ponzi scheme
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
TOMAHAWK, Wis. (WSAW/Gray News) - A Wisconsin couple says they are having to adjust their life after losing hundreds of thousands of dollars to someone they considered a close friend.
Brian and Jeanine Tesch said they have been left with barely any money in their accounts thanks to Stanley Pophal, who, federal prosecutors say, defrauded 190 investors of $14.25 million over six years in a multimillion-dollar Ponzi scheme.
The couple said the investment began with a $165,000 check before Pophal came for their life savings.
“We wanted to have a beautiful future when we retired, help our kids out and our grandchildren. But that was taken away from us,” Jeanine Tesch said. “He talked us into selling our home and our land and everything.”
Pophal promised their investments would double in five years and that he would have their backs if they didn’t. He sent them several checks, including some for $6,000 and one for $35,000.
Jeanine said he was dangling a carrot in front of them, taking advantage of their decadeslong friendship.
“He was like a brother to me,” Brian Tesch said. “Right up until the end, actually. Right up until the last week.”
Pophal was trying to get their 401(k). But before he got access to it, the Teschs said they saw his mug shot.
“Our hearts just sank. We started bawling and just trembling. And we couldn’t believe it,” said Jeanine Tesch.
They later learned he had spent investors’ money on snowmobiles, bikes, cars and other items.
The Teschs said the paperwork they signed appeared legitimate, and they did not expect Pophal to be unable to repay them.
IRS Criminal Investigation Acting Special Agent in Charge Robert Kuszynski said Pophal was very good at convincing people.
“The victims of the Pophal investigation were charmed by an individual. Uh, and he made promises and provided information that was false that any investor could have, uh, seen and believed to be true,” Kuszynski said.
Pophal was ordered to pay $14.25 million in restitution. However, the Teschs have not received anything yet.
They had planned to retire in Florida. Instead, they now split their time between a trailer in Tomahawk and a rental in Mexico, where Jeanine Tesch said the lower cost of living helps them make ends meet.
“The life savings that we had, the hopes and the dreams for a bright future. And now we just struggle to find joy in living. And not the future that we hoped for or we dreamt of that he took away from us. And from so many other families. It’s devastating right in your own hometown,” Jeanine Tesch said.
They also can’t afford to be in Wisconsin for the birth of their newest grandchild.
“The devastation that Stan has done to us and our families and our friends and all the other victims won’t define us,” said Jeanine Tesch. “There will be judgment day for Stan Pophal. He didn’t get justice here, but I believe someday he will.”
The Teschs said Pophal would often capitalize on people’s faith, saying he was working in God’s name. The couple said it’s their faith that is keeping them going after everything.

title: JD Vance expresses doubt about livestreaming Fort Hood shooter execution, says he wouldn't watch
text:
'I'm not gonna be watching it': JD Vance expresses doubt about livestreaming Fort Hood shooter execution
Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on Friday whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December but told reporters that if it is livestreamed, "I'm not going to be watching it."
The Republican vice president said, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen," when asked about the plans that the Pentagon confirmed on Thursday. But Vance then tried to set aside the controversy over the shocking plans for a public execution and said Hasan's crimes should not be forgotten.
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting spree at the military base in 2009.
"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said.
"Now, that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it," he added.
Vance is a convert to the Catholic Church, which has long opposed capital punishment.
Earlier Friday morning, the head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the U.S. government's decision to livestream Hasan's execution.
"It is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War's decision to publicly livestream the execution of Nidal Hassan. Our God is the God of life. In no way can Hassan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," said Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the Conference, in a statement.
Earlier, President Donald Trump told a White House event that Hasan will be getting "the death penalty through firing squad. And he deserves it."
Trump, who approved Hasan's execution, called him "a maniac."
The president approved the method of execution by firing squad days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection late last month pushed Tennessee's governor to halt further executions in that state this year.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military hasn't executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
Trump, who has long been a vocal supporter of capital punishment, didn't mention the plans that the Pentagon has announced to livestream the execution so that the broader public can see it.
___
Associated Press writers Will Weissert in Washington and Holly Meyer in Nashville, Tennessee contributed to this report.

title: Verizon offers storm-related service relief as Isaias approaches Gulf Coast
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA/Gray News) - Verizon is offering affected customers in parts of Alabama, Florida and Mississippi unlimited domestic calling, texting and data from Oct. 9 through Oct. 15 as Hurricane Isaias approaches the Gulf Coast.
The offer applies automatically to active postpaid and small-business customers with billing addresses in the affected counties. Verizon Value customers—including those using Verizon Prepaid, Straight Talk, Total Wireless, Tracfone, Simple Mobile, Walmart Family Mobile, Page Plus, Net10 and SafeLink—will have their service end dates extended through Oct. 15. Customers do not need to take action, and eligible overage charges will be credited automatically.
In Alabama, the offer covers Baldwin, Clarke, Coffee, Conecuh, Covington, Escambia, Geneva, Mobile, Monroe and Washington counties. In Florida, it includes Bay, Escambia, Holmes, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Walton and Washington counties. In Mississippi, it covers Forrest, George, Greene, Harrison, Jackson, Perry and Stone counties.
Verizon says its response teams are on standby with mobile and satellite assets, portable generators and other equipment. The company says all of its regional macro cell sites have backup battery power, nearly all have generator power, and more than 1,000 mobile generators are available for deployment.
Verizon’s Frontline Crisis Response Team is also available around the clock to provide communications support to public safety agencies at no cost. Customers can check Verizon’s Emergency Resource Center for storm-response updates and store hours.

title: Affordability crunch takes us back to 1974
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
An unpopular president; surging oil prices causing significant inflation; and an upcoming midterm election.
No, I’m not talking about 2026, but 1974. President Gerald Ford had just pardoned Richard Nixon in September, a decision unpopular with much of the American public who had Watergate still fresh in their minds. Oil prices surged in October 1973 after the OPEC oil embargo, which led to inflation running above 10%. The 1974 midterm elections brought a Democratic landslide victory, with the party winning 49 seats in the House and four in the Senate. Will 2026 be, quoting Yogi Berra, “like déjà vu all over again”?
Current indications suggest it may well be. Many Republican held seats in Congress appear to be up for grabs, even those in some “deep red” districts. Why? An unpopular president, Donald Trump, whose action and inaction is felt to have led to the highest inflation in years.
The question for Democrats, should they prevail Nov. 3, is: How will they govern? The temptation for many Democrats will be to hold endless congressional investigations into President Trump and his appointees for possible corrupt dealings. While I agree that there are valid concerns, is this what voters really want Congress to focus on? From everything I read, I think not.
One word comes up again and again: affordability. Democrats’ failure to address this concern may well lead to problems in the 2028 election. An out-of-touch party is soon an out-of-office party.
Samuel Rosenthal
Portland

title: AT&T data breach settlement gets final approval. See how much customers could receive
text:
(Gray News) - A federal judge has granted final approval to AT&T’s $177 million settlement involving breaches that exposed customers’ personal information.
Last year, AT&T reached a combined $177 million settlement over two data breaches that were disclosed in 2024 and established a claim form for affected customers to submit.
The reported data involved in the breaches belonged to millions of current and former AT&T customers and dated as far back as 2019.
Now, with the judge’s final approval, those who submitted a claim could receive their payments soon.
According to the settlement, consumers impacted by the first breach may be eligible for up to $5,000, and those affected by the second breach may be eligible for up to $2,500.
Final payment amounts were expected to vary depending on the losses documented by each claimant and the total number of settlement claims received.
Those with knowledge of the settlement said most eligible customers were expected to qualify for payments ranging from $6.50 to $40.
Payments are said to be going out after the appeals period has expired, with the settlement calling for payments to be distributed within 60 days of the effective date.

title: Gov. Mills agrees to fund Penobscot Community Health Care
text:
Gov. Janet Mills agrees to fund Penobscot Community Health Care
Governor plans to make $2.8 million available from Rural Health Transformation Funds
Gov. Janet Mills agrees to fund Penobscot Community Health Care
Governor plans to make $2.8 million available from Rural Health Transformation Funds
Gov. Janet Mills announced Thursday that she would make $2.8 million available from Rural Health Transformation Funds for Penobscot Community Health Care (PCHC).
This follows PCHC's announcement that it would close its Adult Wellness Center on Union St. in Bangor and transition patient care services to its other locations.
PCHC said the majority of services provided at the Adult Wellness Center will transition to the Penobscot Community Health Center at 1012 Union St., while some specialty services will transition to other locations within the organization.
"I remain deeply concerned about the extent to which the organization finds itself overextended and underfunded due to a lack of appropriate planning and management," Mills said in a letter. "This situation is particularly troubling given the significant investments the State has made in federally qualified health care centers (FQHCs), including PCHC, over the last several years. MaineCare's total spending on FQHC services has increased by nearly 50 percent over the last three years, totaling over $100 million in calendar year 2025. Regarding PCHC in particular, in those same three years, PCHC's MaineCare encounter rate has reached $283.89 — an increase of 45 percent."
In a letter, PCHC wrote that "The governor, her team, and the Department of Health and Human Services worked tirelessly to find a path forward. They were able to help us efficiently and in a targeted manner while requiring accountability on our part. We know these are public dollars, and we take that very seriously. We look forward to working closely with DHHS, providing regular updates, and being fully accountable for how these funds are used."
PCHC adds that it is looking forward to working with the Maine Legislature more in 2027.

title: Unity creator’s word game gains online following
text:
UNITY, Maine (WABI) -A new online word game is gaining a following, and it now has a special WABI twist.
Gardiner Bryant of Unity has made a living online for nearly 14 years as a YouTuber, programmer and media producer. He created his publication The Bryant Review in 2024 after growing frustrated with platforms that decide what people see and which creators get rewarded.
“In general, the things that I produce on the internet, I just want to respect people’s attention, their time, their autonomy,” Bryant said.
How the game works
The website is also home to Bryant’s newest game, Uppercase, which is gaining momentum.
“It works kind of like Wordle crossed with Hangman,” Bryant said. “It’s a simple word game where there’s a keyboard on the screen. You click the keys to guess a letter that you think might be in the puzzle. If it’s in the puzzle, it gets revealed. If it’s not, you earn a strike.”
For Bryant, the game is about more than entertainment. It is designed to give people a quiet place to focus.
“What can I do to help people and to make, you know, prolong attention spans rather than detract from them?” Bryant said. “Attention is a muscle just like anything else. So for me, it’s like, how can I help people just focus for a minute?”
Thousands of players
Bryant said Uppercase is now attracting thousands of players. In its first month, the game brought in nearly 4,000 unique players and about 8,000 plays.

title: Legendary coach, Hall of Fame tight end Mike Ditka dies at age 86
text:
Legendary coach, Hall of Fame tight end Mike Ditka dies at age 86
Legendary coach and Pro Football Hall of Famer Mike Ditka has died. He was 86.
Ditka, nicknamed "Iron Mike" for his toughness, rose from a standout athlete in Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, to become a legendary NFL player and coach.
He stayed close to home for college, attending the University of Pittsburgh, where he also played three sports: football, baseball, and basketball. On the football field, Ditka played on both sides of the ball as a tight end and defensive lineman, earning All-American honors.
He once said, "I was probably a better defensive player," and thought he might be drafted as a linebacker.
Instead, the Chicago Bears selected him as a tight end with the fifth overall pick in the 1961 NFL Draft. His pass-catching ability was immediately showcased, helping to revolutionize the tight end position.
Ditka won championships as a player with the Bears and Cowboys and later led the Bears to a Super Bowl victory as head coach, becoming an enduring icon in Chicago. His influence extended into pop culture, inspiring look-alike costumes and becoming a recurring subject of the "Superfan" skit on "Saturday Night Live."
In 1988, Ditka became the first tight end inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
After retiring as a coach, Ditka became a restaurateur, pitchman and TV personality, as well as a forceful advocate for improved medical and retirement benefits for former players.
Ditka’s family announced news of his death on Friday. "It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka," his family said in a statement to ESPN.
A cause of death has not been released.
Ditka suffered a pair of heart attacks, including one in 1988 while he was Bears coach, as well as a minor stroke in 2012.
