title: Long-term benzene levels in parts of South Portland were double state's guideline, report says
text:
Long-term benzene levels in parts of South Portland were double Maine's guideline, report says
A report from the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention (Maine CDC) indicates that an area of South Portland is experiencing long-term levels of benzene, a known carcinogen, that are higher than the state's guideline.
According to the report, the elevated long-term benzene levels are due to emissions from petroleum tank terminals.
One of the terminals at 102 Mechanic St., which is operated by Citgo, had long-term benzene levels from November 2019 to November 2025 that were double Maine's acceptable risk level.
The information featured in the Maine CDC's report comes from a six-year study conducted by the Maine Department of Environmental Protection (DEP). The study was started in 2019 in response to community concerns about the petroleum tank terminals.
Representatives from the Maine CDC and the DEP will present the results of the study to the Portland City Council on Oct. 27.
Our previous reporting
Maine's Total Coverage chief investigative reporter Norah Hogan found that approximately 12,693 people live within 1 mile of the Citgo petroleum tank terminal.
South Portland is home to six petroleum storage facilities, many located near densely populated residential neighborhoods. The DEP has been monitoring air quality around the sites, tracking several harmful chemicals, including benzene.
The state uses two benchmarks to measure emissions: one for acute risk, which reflects immediate health concerns, and another benchmark known as the ambient air guidelines for long-term exposure. While all facilities tested below the acute threshold, two sites — Citgo and South Portland Terminal — exceeded the long-term guideline.
Long-term exposure to benzene has been linked to dizziness, headaches, blood disorders and cancer.
Previously, oil companies were allowed to self-monitor their emissions and were subject to stricter regulations only if they reported elevated toxin levels.

title: Learn the Secrets Behind the Grossest Horror Movie Effects Ever
text:
The 10 Grossest Horror Movie Practical Effects, and How They Did It
Horror movies live and die on the images they conjure: Images of suspense, images of terror, images of disgust. One easy way to get a reaction out of your audience is to make your images as gross as possible — nothing sticks in the mind as well as something that makes someone go “Ewww!” Plenty of gooey, goopy, messy, bloody effects have been conjured with digital effects, but for the really yucky stuff, it’s always best to keep things practical.
There’s an art to making a truly disgusting practical effect. You have to know what makes an audience squirm, and you have to know how to achieve it in reality. Practical gore effects are best when they’re as close to life as they can be. Yes, that really is a limb getting twisted and stretched into pieces, even if it’s a fake one. Yes, that really is an actor drenched in liters of blood, even if it is made of syrup and food coloring. We know it’s not really happening, but it sure looks legit.
Whether it’s layers of prosthetic makeup or gallons of fake organs and goop, many of the best practical horror movie effects are achieved with tricks that might surprise you. For every monster built with hydraulic animatronics, there’s a tub of blood and guts made with common household items like apples and mayonnaise. To honor all the hard work that makes us cringe in our seats, we’ve chosen the ten best horror movies with the grossest practical effects of all time. Knowing how they were made won’t make them any less disgusting, but it’ll definitely give you a better appreciation for how it was done.

title: Obituary: Ellen Linda (Curtis) Gaddis
text:
WISCASSET – Ellen Linda (Curtis) Gaddis of Wiscasset passed away at home on Sept. 28, 2026.
She was born Sept. 14, 1949 in Machias, the daughter of Richard S. Curtis, Sr. and Barbara (Gatcomb) Curtis. She lived her life in Edmunds and graduated in 1967 as Salutatorian at Washington Academy in East Machias. She attended Beal Business College.
Ellen married Christopher E. Gaddis in 1969. They moved to the Wiscasset area while Christopher completed an apprenticeship program at Bath Iron Works. They had two daughters, Laurie and Barbara. She worked from 1971 to 1974 in the QA Department at Bath Iron Works, leaving for the birth of her daughter, Barbara. She returned in 1977, working in the purchasing department for the next 45 years. There, she met Joan Pratt, who became a treasured friend.
She joined the Bible Baptist Church in Wiscasset in 1984 and served as Sunday school secretary and assistant treasurer for many years.
She is survived by her daughters Laurie Gaddis Barrett of Glocester, R.I. and Barbara Coulter and her husband, Lee of Marietta, Ga.; a sister, Carol Robinson and her husband, Albert of Wiscasset, a brother, Richard Curtis, Jr. and his wife, Jennifer, of Edmunds; Rosemary Harmon (formerly Curtis) of Pembroke, a member of Ellen’s family for many years; and two grandchildren, Ethan Coulter and Margaret “Maggie” Barrett.
Ellen was predeceased by her father, Richard S. Curtis, Sr., her mother, Barbara (Gatcomb) Curtis; and her children’s father, Christopher E. Gaddis.
Services will be observed privately. Interment will be in Dennysville Cemetery, Dennysville, Maine. Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.

title: Letter to the Editor: Proud to support Trevor Doiron
Mamdani's Oct. 7 commemoration outrages supporters and critics of Israel
text:
Mamdani's Oct. 7 commemoration outrages supporters and critics of Israel
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani tried to thread a needle on the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 attacks by condemning Hamas' "horrific war crimes" and denouncing Israel's "genocide" in Gaza. It did not go well.
Instead, his comments further angered some Jewish critics who consider his strong opposition to Israel antisemitic, and pro-Palestinian protesters interrupted a Wednesday night vigil for victims of Hamas' attack to confront the mayor and cast him as a traitor to their cause.
Mamdani, a Democrat and the city's first Muslim mayor, has long been a fierce defender of Palestinian human rights and is one of the country's most prominent political critics of Israel's military actions in Gaza. His stance has drawn scrutiny in a city with the largest Jewish population outside Israel, while at times some on the far-left have bashed him for not doing enough to hold Israel to account.
On Thursday, Mamdani appeared to take the protest in stride, telling reporters: "I am the mayor of New York City and this is what I signed up for."
A parsed statement
The maelstrom began when Mamdani commemorated the victims of Hamas' surprise attack on Israel with a statement that began with a solemn recognition of the "unthinkable loss" suffered by Israelis but then focused on castigating Israel's military response.
"The suffering did not begin nor end that day," the statement read. "It instead continued through the Israeli government's devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children."
The statement reignited criticism that Mamdani harbors antisemitic views — a claim he has vehemently denied — and was blaming Israel for the attack.
"This is a reprehensible statement on the anniversary of the horrific terrorist attack by a Palestinian terrorist organization against innocent Israelis," U.S. Rep. Dan Goldman, a Jewish Democrat in New York, wrote on X. "In the guise of 'grieving' with those mourning that day, Mayor Mamdani asserts as fact hotly disputed allegations that he knows full well will offend and further upset those same people he pretends to grieve with."
Ofir Akunis, consul general of Israel in New York, called the mayor's statement a "disgrace, shame, and insult to the memory of those who were murdered on October 7."
Asked Thursday whether he would change his statement if given the chance, Mamdani said: "It is critically important to be able to mourn for all of those who were killed and have been killed since, especially given that we know this is ongoing, as opposed to something simply that was three years ago."
Rabbi Rick Jacobs, president of the Union for Reform Judaism, who met with the mayor earlier this year over his rhetoric, said Mamdani had "doubled down" by signaling he would not temper his language around Israel.
"It seems like there's an opportunity for him to, you know, make an adjustment. I don't think anybody asked him to stop being who he is," Jacobs said in an interview. "But he has failed to see how his deeply held beliefs endanger New Yorkers."
Simmering tensions
Mamdani, who took office in January, has moved to assuage concerns that his criticism of Israel's government is antisemitic, courting high-profile Jewish political allies and late last month debuting a sweeping plan to address antisemitism and hate crimes in the city.
At the same time, he has continued to employ, and defend, heated rhetoric toward Israel, which includes calling for the arrest of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he calls a "war criminal" and "the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people."
Netanyahu, in an address at the United Nations General Assembly last month, called Mamdani "the antisemitic mayor of New York" and charged that "many Jews no longer feel safe in New York."
Mamdani also marked the anniversary by attending a candlelight vigil at Union Square in Manhattan organized by Israelis For Peace, which describes itself as a group of Israeli anti-occupation activists. The vigil was disrupted by protesters who waved Palestinian flags and chanted.
Mamdani, who did not speak at the vigil, appeared somber while protesters booed and yelled: "Zohran, your hands are red!"
At one point, Brad Lander, a Jewish politician who struck up an alliance with Mamdani when they were both running for mayor last year, denounced the violence overseas, saying "no matter what country or nationality or religion, every mother, every mother gives birth to her children and wants the best for them, wants life for them." Protesters jeered.
"We refused to compromise on anyone's humanity. No amount of shouting stopped us," Lander, the Democratic nominee for a House seat in Manhattan and Brooklyn, later wrote on X with a photo taken at the vigil. "May their memory be for a blessing."
